THE
PARLIAMENTARY DEBATES
(OFFICIAL REPORT)
IN THE
FIRST SESSION OF THE THIRD PARLIAMENT OF NORTHERN IRELAND
APPOINTED TO MEET THE TWENTY-NINTH DAY OF MAY, IN THE
TWENTIETH YEAR OF THE REIGN OF
HIS MAJESTY
KING GEORGE V.
VOLUME XI.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

---

Wednesday, 29th May, 1929.
The Parliament begun and held at the
City of Belfast, on Wednesday, the
Twenty-ninth day of May, in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of Our Sovereign
Lord George, by the Grace of God, of the
United Kingdom of Great Britain and
Northern Ireland and of the British
Dominions beyond the Seas, King,
Defender of the Faith, and in the year
of our Lord, 1929.
On which day, at Ten Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, being the first day
of the meeting of this Parliament, pursuant to a Proclamation, Arthur O'Neill
Chichester, Esq., M.C., Clerk of the
Parliaments of Northern Ireland, and
Major George Thomson, D.S.O., Clerk
Assistant of the House of Commons,
attending in the House, Andrew Newton
Anderson, Esq., Clerk of the Crown,
delivered to the said Arthur O'Neill
Chichester a Book containing a List of the
Names of the Members returned to serve
in this Parliament.
Several of the Members repaired to
their seats.
A Message was delivered by Major T.
Dalby Hackett, D.S.O., Gentleman Usher
of the Black Rod, as followeth :-
Members of the House of Commons,
his Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
Accordingly the House proceeded to
attend his Grace in the Senate.
The Clerk of the Senate was commanded
by his Grace to read the Dissolution
Proclamation.
His Grace then said:
SENATORS AND MEMBERS OF THE
HOUSE OF COMMONS OF
NORTHERN IRELAND,
causes
In the name of and on behalf of
his Majesty I have to let you know
that, as soon as the Members of both
Houses shall have been sworn, the
of his Majesty's calling this
Parliament of Northern Ireland will
be declared to you; and it being necessary that a Speaker of the House of
Commons of Northern Ireland should be
first chosen, I declare his Majesty's
pleasure that you, Members of the House
of Commons, do proceed to the choice of
a Speaker, and that you present such
person whom you shall so choose here for
his Majesty's Royal Approbation.
The House having returned,
Mr. CRAWFORD (addressing himself
to the Clerk of the House, who, standing
up, pointed at him and then sat down):
A
Election of Speaker
Election of Speaker
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Crawford]
Mr. Chichester, in compliance with the
gracious wish of his Majesty, conveyed to
us through his Grace the Governor that
we should forthwith proceed to elect a
Speaker, I have very great pleasure in
proposing "That the Hon. Harry Mulholland do take the Chair of this House
as Speaker." (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). As I have been a Member of the
House since its formation, an occasion such
as this opens the floodgates of memory,
and although eight years have passed and
two Parliaments have spent their force
there flashes before me the time when the
late Mr. Coote, in language of lasting
beauty, proposed the election of the first
Speaker of the Parliament of Northern
Ireland. The eyes of all turned then towards one of the Members for County
Antrim, and in the person of Major the
Hon. Hugh O'Neill it was believed were
centred all the qualities necessary for a
successful Speaker. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). With absolute unanimity he
was called to the Chair, and subsequent
events proved the wisdom of the choice.
During the life of the first Parliament he
presided with dignity and marvellous.
efficiency, and when the second was formed
it was the desire of every Member that he
should continue in the office. During all
these years his ruling was never questioned,
no scenes of disturbance or confusion occurred, and when it became known that
his services would be no longer available,
the generous words of praise that emanated
from both sides of the House showed the
esteem in which he was held, and his
kindly but firm control, his tact and action
generally have left behind him the most
fragrant of memories. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
And now it is our duty to seek a successor, one who will in our name lay claim
for us to all the ancient privileges of the
Commons, who will be the president and
spokesman of the House, with authority
to keep order vested in him by our desire,
a man who will be the guardian of our
liberties, the protector of minorities, the
friend and adviser of all. To fill this
position we need a man of judicial mind,
a knowledge of Parliamentary procedure,
a sense of dignity, an extraordinary store
of patience, and, using the words of Mr.
Kyle, who was Leader of the Opposition
in the last Parliament when seconding the
election of the Speaker, that charity which
St. Paul spoke of "that suffereth long and
is kind." These virtues, seasoned with a
sense of humour, if found in the man of
our choice, will make him a worthy successor to Sir Hugh O'Neill. The position
is no sinecure and the excellence with
which the duties have been discharged
makes it even more difficult, but it is because I believe these and other virtues will
be found in him that with confident anticipation of his proving himself a worthy
Speaker I now move
"That the Hon. Harry Mulholland do
take the Chair of this House as Speaker."
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Mr. P. O'NEILL: Mr. Chichester, it is
certainly with a very full sense of responsibility that I rise to second the Motion
moved by the hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. Crawford). The proposition is that
the Hon. Harry Mulholland should occupy
the chair of this House and become its
Speaker. With that proposition I am in
full agreement. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I believe that in Mr. Mulholland
we will have a very desirable and very acceptable Member as Speaker. I am sure
that he will carry out his duties as his
precedessor did with absolute fairness and
impartiality. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I think I can assure him on behalf of the Members on this side of the
House that he will have their sympathy
and support in the duties which pertain
to his position. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). No doubt he may occasionally
find, as far as this side of the House and
even the other side of the House are concerned, that his patience may be nearly
exhausted, but I have faith that in the
wisdom and discretion of the hon. Member Mr. Mulholland will give satisfaction
to all. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I have, therefore, pleasure in seconding
the Motion which has been proposed by the
hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford).
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Mr. BEATTIE: I am sorry at this
period of our sitting that anything of a
discordant nature should manifest itself
in the selection of my hon. Friend (Mr.
Mulholland) as Speaker. I do not intend to do that, because I think we could
not do better than elect the person
whom the House is asked to select to fill
the position-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear) but speaking as the representative
of a working-class area where starvation
and hunger are rampant, I think before
proceeding to incur such a heavy liability
as this office carries with it, it is my
bounden duty to ask the Government and
Election of Speaker

29 MAY 1929
Election of Speaker
this House that they should give a
guarantee that the cost of this office will
be reduced by at least fifty per cent. I
would like to draw the attention of the
House to Canada, Ontario. Quebec and other
States, and I am sure the Government will
realise that the people of Northern Ireland do not desire a perfect and matured
model of the Imperial House of Commons.
We are a Six-County Parliament; we have
a population of 1 millions, and yet we
are asked to pay towards this position
£4,500 all told. I say that is ridiculous,
exorbitant and outrageous and out of
all common decency to the working
classes of Northern Ireland. First there
is £2,000, then there is £1,500 to the Deputy-Speaker, which is part and parcel
of the job, and the total cost of the building will be about £1,000 a year. When
we work it out we find that the House sits
about sixty afternoons in the year and the
cost to the taxpayers is £75 per sitting.
That cost is out of all reason.
I
As I said at the beginning, I think we
are going to have a perfect model as
Speaker in the person the House is asked
to select (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-but I feel, coming from a constituency
where distress exists, that the money received from the Consolidated Fund towards this office could be used for the
purpose of alleviating that distress.
think a sacrifice can be made as far as
this position is concerned. I think that
sacrifice should be made now before any
selection is made and the person who is
appointed should be given to understand.
that we, in our capacity as public representatives, have found that the Province
is not capable of maintaining the standard

I want a definite assurance from the

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I also

with ancient usage and custom I humbly

Election of Speaker
Election of Speaker
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Mulholland]
When I realised that I would have to
make a speech in submitting myself to the
House I saw there were two courses I
could take. The first course was that I
could make up a regular little set speech
and read it out, and the second point of
view was that I could make a speech just
as the words came into my brain and from
the bottom of my heart. When I considered the matter carefully and when I
realised and I think I may claim thisthe friends I have made in the House
during the past eight years (hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-and even the
friends I number amongst the new Members as well, I thought that perhaps the
best speech might be that made in rather
more homely manner than is customary in
other Parliaments throughout the world.
In the first place I would like to thank
very much the proposer of this Motion,
the hon. Member for Mid-Antrim (Mr.
Crawford). During my work in the past.
four or five years I have come in contact
with the hon. Member on more than one
occasion; he has always been willing and
obliging, and has tried to carry out what
I wanted him to do. That he should make
such an eloquent speech on my behalf is
only what I would have expected from
him and it really touches me to the depths
of my heart. When I refer to my old
friend, the hon. Member for the Mourne
Division of County Down (Mr. Patrick
O'Neill), I remember that we are both
County Down men. Perhaps it would be
unnecessary to say very much more than
that, but in any case I want to express to
him also my heartiest thanks for the very
kind words he said on my behalf.
When we consider the high standard of
excellence which our last Speaker reached
in the Chair here, the dignity with which
he adorned the House, and the fairmindedness with which he treated all hon. Members, in whatever quarter of the House
they sat, the House will agree that it will
be very, very difficult for me to attain to
that same high standard. Even if I can
only come within reasonable reach of the
standard set by the late Speaker, and
secure one tithe of the affection which this
House had for him then I will be satisfied
at the end of my term of office.
The Speaker's duties are to preserve the
rights, privileges, and traditions of the
House. As far as those are concerned, if
I am appointed by the House to this responsible position I will carry on to the
very best of my ability the traditions set
by the right hon. Gentleman, Sir Hugh
O'Neill. The even-handed justice which
he meted out reminds me of my cricket
days, when an umpire had to be appointed.
at a cricket match and, regardless of what
side he favoured, he had to mete out absolutely even-handed justice to both sides.
That even-handed justice will, if I am
selected, be meted out by me to every
individual Member of the House, in whatever quarter he may sit or from whatever
quarter he may have been elected. With
the help and support of my old friendsand I hope I may say of my new friendsin the House when the time comes for me
to relinquish this office my hope and determination will be to hand over unsullied
and untarnished the position to which I
have been called, and I pray God to give
me strength to fulfil that ambition.
(Cheers).
The House then having again unanimously called Mr. Henry George Hill
Mulholland to the Chair, he was taken
out of his place and conducted to the
Chair by Mr. Crawford and Mr. Patrick
O'Neill.
Mr. SPEAKER-ELECT (standing on
the upper step): Before taking the Chair
of this House I wish to express to the
House my deep sense of the high honour
it has conferred upon me by electing me
as its Speaker.
Mr. SPEAKER-ELECT sat down in
the Chair.
Then the Mace (which before lay under
the Table) was placed upon the Table by the
Serjeant-at-Arms (Brigadier-General H
G. Young, C.I.E., D.S.O.).
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): Mr. Speaker-Elect, I need
hardly assure the House that it gives me
more pleasure than I can say to be the
first to congratulate you and the assembly
itself upon the choice which has unani
mously fallen upon you to-day.
When
we look back upon the last eight years we
have nothing but the greatest satisfaction
to express with regard to the occupant of
the Chair, and I feel confident that you
will be able to carry on the high traditions that have already been set. We,
ourselves, as Members, are all most jealous.
of the rights and privileges of this House
of Commons and it will be our duty and
our pleasure to support you in every way
possible in the onerous duties that will
fall upon you.

As a County Down man myself I must
join with the others, including the hon.
Member for the Mourne Division (Mr.
Patrick O'Neill) opposite in saying that
it is another credit to our county to have
you as Speaker of this House; and when
I add to that the fact that our new
Speaker comes of a very distinguished
family bearing an honoured name in
all parts of the Empire it increases
greatly the pleasure it gives me to be the
first to pay this small tribute to you upon
the choice that has fallen upon you.
I
can only express the hope-and I am sure
I may say it is in the hearts of all Members of the House-that, whatever our
proceedings in the future years may hold
for us, we may count upon you to exercise that power of justice and of the protection of minorities because I can assure
hon. Members opposite also that the Government are most jealous also of the full
privileges that rest upon minorities-and
that you will mete out to them that special
protection which is one of the most important duties of any Speaker in any
House of Commons. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
The House could not have made a better choice. I am quite confident that
you will fully justify the highest expectations that I and all hon. Members hold
with regard to your future career. I
can promise you support and growing
affection from all sides, and I am perfectly certain that you, yourself, will
look back upon the position which you
now hold of Speaker of the third Administration of the Parliament of Northern
Ireland as one of the happiest and most
distinguished in your life. I congratulate you, Sir. (Cheers).

the House that in the Senate His Grace
the Governor, on behalf of His Majesty
the King, has been pleased to approve of

name, and on your behalf, laid claim by

of Northern Ireland by the Government
of Ireland Act, 1920, and that the most
favourable construction may be placed on
all your proceedings. All these His
Grace, on behalf of His Majesty, has

Chair of this House.
I must now call upon the Members of

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
elections for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debatę; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such Bribery or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime or
misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant-at-
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND
RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings,
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
that he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no person but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges be appointed.

Election of Speaker
Election of Deputy-Speaker
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. BEATTIE: Are we to understand
that at the opening of this House in the
year 1929 the maladministration of public
money is going to continue in regard to
offices such as that of Chairman of Ways
and Means? If it is the intention of the
Government to pursue this wildly extravagant course while industry is declining and
while the lives and well-being of the people
are being sacrificed then I cannot understand the mentality of the electorate that
returned the noble Lord with a larger
majority than he had in the previous
Parliament.
I think the time has now come for this
House to set up a Committee with a view
to the reduction of all the salaries as set
out by the Committee appointed in the first
House of this Parliament. At that time
a special Committee was formed when the
cost of living was high and when there
were high falutin ideas in the minds of
politicians that their compensation for
their loyalty to Northern Ireland should
be based upon the standard adopted by
greater nations than we can expect to be.
That Committee deliberated, and reported,
and by agreement with the Cabinet they
came forward to this House and set out
salaries for the Chairman of Ways and
Means, for Cabinet Ministers, and for
Members of the Senate.
Now that Committee was subject to the
approval of the Cabinet. If they had not
had the Cabinet's approval the Committee's recommendations would not have been
accepted by this House. Therefore, they
set out those salaries deliberately and-
I make the charge against the Cabinetmaliciously for themselves. Proof of that
lies in Hansard where it is recorded that
seven Members of the Cabinet deliberately
came into this House and voted in favour
of the high salaries they are now receiving.
I speak as a representative of the people,
who are suffering to-day as a result of the
squandermania of the Northern Government directing their finances to the wrong
objects. Instead of directing their attention to the assistance of industry, the uplifting of the people, the improvement of
trade, the assisting of the destitute and
down-and-out, who owe their positions to the
Government, instead of doing that they
are still directing their attention to basing
their loyalty on the £.s.d. standard.
I could not allow my voice to be silent
in this House or my vote not to be placed
on record against £1,500 being allocated
to this office. What is the actual position?
That of Chairman of Ways and Means.
He takes the Chair in Committee, and on
the average of sixty afternoons per annum,
between the salary of the Speaker and the
Deputy Speaker, it works out at £75 per
afternoon. But take the basis of a salary
of £1,500, take fifty per cent. of the total
sittings, and we get an average of about
£30 per sitting.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister
does he fully realise that the whole British
Isles are looking upon this little country
as a country of squandermaniacs, maniacs
gone to the very extreme as far as the
public purse is concerned. I do not think
he does. I think he is still living in a
fools' paradise. The sooner the people of
Ulster refuse at election times to listen to
the false promises and the wild-cat cries of
their loyalists the sooner they will come
down to bed-rock, study the economic
position they occupy in this Province, and
then measure the loyalty of the people who
go on the basis of the £.s.d. they take away
from Ulster.
Loyalty is conditional as far as the
Government are concerned. Their loyalty
no longer remains when the purse is closed
against them. On this particular occasion,
before we make any selection, I ask the
Prime Minister to again reduce the amount
of the salary attached to this office by fifty
per cent., or, in the alternative, to appoint
a Select Committee of this House representing all parties in the House to go into
the question of what is a reasonable wage
for the work done. The Government always claim that the workers are entitled
to give a fair day's work for a fair day's
pay. I do not object to giving a fair day's
pay for a fair day's work. I stand for the
highest standard which it is possible to
give in the Province, but I do not stand
for the profiteering, the plunder, the exploitation that is now taking place under
the loyalty stunt that is carried out at
election times by the Government.
re-
I want now to prove to the electors in
my division, and to the electorate in the
divisions that returned the most
actionary party in the world—I want to
put this test to Members on the Government side: Are you now prepared to
prove your loyalty in practical manner
by voting with me for the reduction of
the present cost of our Government by
fifty per cent.? The late Mr. Coote, who,
I presume, was as great a loyalist as any
Member on the benches opposite, stood
in this House alone and defended the
statement I am now making.
He put

forward an amendment that the cost of
Cabinet Ministers and other offices was
too high for the financial standing of the
Six Counties. I put it to you now one
and all, if you are agreed with the late
Mr. Coote, if you are agreed after eight

by him were correct, then you will be
compelled on this occasion to walk into
the Lobby into which I shall have the
pleasure of going on this occasion.
I fearlessly and openly challenge any
Member of the Government to point out to
me one country in Europe, or throughout
the world, with an equal population, with
an equal acreage to govern, where the
Speaker gets £2,000 a year plus a free
house, or where the Chairman of Ways
and Means, who is the Speaker's deputy,
gets £1,500. As I say, I am open to be
challenged by any hon. Member on that
side of the House, or on this side, and
if I am I will defend that challenge and
will be successful. Not in any other
country in the world would such a financial position be allowed to continue only
under the Craigavon administration, who
care little for the poor but everything
for the rich. The sooner that position is
altered the better. The sooner we, as
representatives of the public, realise that
we are not fit to carry this on the better,
just as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) has discovered to his own satisfaction that he took upon himself an
uneconomic proposition.
This matter is not going to stop here.
It is going to go further than here. You
say you are loyal to Britain, but the
Prime Minister says that he is only loyal
so long as he can drag out of Britain
financial arrangements suitable to the
rich being given sinecure jobs and idle.
drones being placed in positions where
no positions actually exist. I do not
stand for that. I believe in equality of
treatment all right. Britain is as good
to me to-day as she is to the Prime Minister, but Britain is not making her
workers sacrifice in the same way as the
workers of Northern Ireland to-day.
She is legislating on sympathetic lines in
connection with unemployment insurance,
but the Craigavon Government are not
walking step by step as far as that is
concerned. They are not walking step.
by step in regard to old-age pensioners,
or in regard to widows and orphans, in
regard to which many anomalies exist today in Northern Ireland that do not exist
in Great Britain. But I have been told
repeatedly that the Government believe
in the step-by-step policy. If you do,
then pay your Ministers according to the
population you govern. Then, if Stanley
Baldwin gets £5,000 a year for being
Prime Minister over 46,000,000 people,
let you yourself and your respective Ministers be paid on a percentage basis from
that. Similarly, the Chairman of Ways
and Means should be paid on a percentage basis and every officer of this House
should be paid on that basis according
to the work required of him.
I have made my voice heard so far as
your own position, Mr. Speaker, and this
position are concerned. I am fully determined during my life in this Parlia
ment to see equality of treatment meted
out to all classes of the community, irrespective of to what class they belong, but I
am not going to sit idly by and see the
rich classes receive all the benefits and
perquisites while the poor are left suffering and starving, and then cast on the
scrap heap by the Prime Minister, who
poses as their defender. I oppose this
appointment until an assurance is given
that consideration will be given to the
salary allotted to the office.
Mr. COLLINS: I rise to support some

agriculture and other trades are in a very

of all other salaries that are paid on too
elaborate a scale altogether.

The PRIME MINISTER: May I
peal to hon. Members opposite not to
force a division in the House on this
occasion! The real question before the
House is who shall occupy the position of
Chairman of Ways and Means, and that
only. The question of salary will arise
in the course of a very few days on the
Estimates, and then if a discussion takes
place upon that particular Estimate my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) will be
able to explain to the House, what the
House probably has forgotten, that if we
were to deduct certain amounts from the
salaries of the right hon. Gentleman and
of others in the House the amount of the
deduction would merely swell our contribution to Great Britain, and would
not, as a matter of fact, devolve to any
other Service over which we have control.
Those salaries have all been agreed
upon as being fair by those in authority
on the other side. When we were setting
up this Parliament, the Committee, of
which my hon. Friend behind me (Mr.
Grant) was a Member, before reporting
to this House took the opinion of people
on the other side. I think they went
into the matter most meticulously in
order that no question should be raised
aftewards. There was no Member of the
Government on that Committee; it was
a Committee of the House. In any event
I would like this appointment to be
carried unanimously to-day, and then in
a very short time the question of salaries
can be debated on the Estimates. A full
opportunity for debate will be given on
the Estimates, and the question can be
settled, if necessary, by a division of the
House. One must bear in mind the responsibility devolving upon the Chairinan of Committees. One must remember that when our Parliament was first
established we had no other person with
the technical knowledge that the right
hon. Gentleman possesses, and that the
duties of the Chairman of Ways and
Means do not by any means cease when
he leaves this Chair or leaves this House,
but that he has to deal with all the intricacies in connection with Private Bill
legislation-intricacies that very often call
for consultations with learned counsel,
not only on this side of the water, but on
the other side as well.
If that is done, one sees that the
position is one of the most responsible
in the House. The whole of the Private
Bills promoted by persons and public companies depend to a very large extent
upon the guidance, upon the wisdom,
and upon the fair-mindedness of the
Chairman of Ways and Means. With
this explanation, I hope the House will
take into consideration the fact that we
are merely paying a tribute to the right
hon. Gentleman by placing him in the
position which he has adorned for so
many years. Anyone who looks back
upon the legislation for public companies
and private individuals that has been
carried through this House will realize
that that side of our work has been admirably done, thanks to the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Moles). If we can get
him into the Chair without a division, I
think the wishes of the whole House will
be met, and, as I say, when the salaries
come to be discussed, my hon. Friends
opposite can force a Division.

Mr. O'NEILL: Before we enter upon
the Debate upon the Address, I would
like to know if the House is going to sit
to-morrow. As hon. Members are aware
the British parliamentary elections take
place to-morrow. I understand that if a
Motion is not made now this House would
automatically sit to-morrow, which I think
would be an unreasonable course to follow.
I suggest that the Prime Minister, before
the business of to-day is taken up, should
introduce a Motion to enable us to adjourn
to some later day instead of sitting tomorrow. As a matter of courtesy I think
this request should be granted.

House, at its rising this day, do adjourn
until Friday next." Would that meet
with general approval?

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report to
the House that the House has this day
attended in the Senate to hear His Grace's
Speech on behalf of the Crown, to both
Houses of Parliament; of which I have
for greater accuracy obtained a copy.
The Speech is as follows:-
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
I feel confident that the new Parliament now inaugurated will conduct
with wisdom and moderation the important matters entrusted to its control.
My Government, recognising as it
does the great extent to which the
material prosperity of so many of our
people is dependent upon the revival
and development of our staple industries, will continue to foster the demand for Northern Ireland products
in British markets by a continuance of
King's Speech
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
the policy of active participation in the
various displays organised by the Empire Marketing Board throughout
Great Britain, by encouragement of
the efforts made to stimulate a demand
within Northern Ireland for the goods
produced by Home manufacturers and
by the constant study and the dissemination, in close collaboration with the
overseas officers and the relative Departments of His Britannic Majesty's
Government, of information respecting
trade conditions and trade openings
in Dominion, Colonial and Foreign
Markets.
Although I regret that many industrial workers are unfortunately still
unemployed, I observe with gratification that there has been a gradual
and steady improvement in the employment position since last summer.
My
Government will strive by every practical method to encourage Agriculture
and to foster the progress and the
expansion of Industry, and will continue to render financial assistance to
public bodies to enable them to promote
works of permanent benefit to the
community, which are designed to
afford additional employment.
It is my earnest hope that harmonious relations between employers
and employed should remain undisturbed and that a general spirit of
goodwill in Industry should prevail so
that nothing may be lacking which
would tend towards the fostering of
prosperity in our midst.
Proposals will be laid before you for
according relief of rates to Agriculture
and to Industry and for making appropriate financial provision for recouping
to Local Authorities sums in lieu of the
amounts from which Industry and
Agriculture will be exempted.
I am
glad that it has been found possible to
make arrangements, so far as agricultural land is concerned, that this concession shall operate retrospectively as
from the 1st April last.
You will be invited to pass a Bill
embodying proposals for the relief of
flooding in the area of Lough Neagh
and the River Bann.
It was found impracticable last
Session to consider proposals relative to
the amendment of the Law in connection with the control of Licensing of
Public Service Vehicles, empowering
the Royal Ulster Constabulary to
exercise the powers of inspection under
Part 1 of the Weeds and Agricultural
Seeds Act, 1999, and the amendment of
the Law relating to Bankruptcy. Bills
dealing with these matters will be submitted in due course for your consideration.
Other measures will be laid before
you dealing with Street Trading and
Dairying.
Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public Services
will be laid before you in due course.
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
I am glad to observe that the importance of Electrical Development is
fully realised and that every encouragement is being afforded to schemes
designed for the purpose of linking up
the industrial centres of Northern Ireland by main transmission lines.
The Harbours around our shores
constitute such a valuable asset for
affording facilities for profitable employment that I am greatly pleased to
learn that the necessary work of dredging, rock removal and other improvements is to be vigorously proceeded
with by efficient up-to-date plant now
available for the purpose.
My Government will continue to
direct its efforts to the maintenance of
that atmosphere of law and order and
of contentment amongst the people in
which alone the establishment of new
industries may be encouraged and
the prosperity of existing industries
fostered.
I pray that the blessing of Almighty
God may rest upon your deliberations.

I would desire at the outset to express
my appreciation of the honour which has
been conferred upon me to-day in asking
me to move the Address. I fully realize
that it is not a personal honour but that
it is a compliment to the city which I
have the honour to represent.

Members: Hear, hear). May I be allowed
to say that it is an additional privilege
to move the Address to one so intimately
associated with the City of Derry as his
Grace the Governor. The gracious Speech
to which we have listened emphasizes the
determination of the Government to
stimulate the demand for the products
of the industry and agriculture of Northern Ireland in the markets of Great
Britain as well as throughout the Empire
and in foreign countries. The success
that has been already attained in securing
orders for the two great shipyards in this
city, despite the keen competition which
exists, is an outstanding example of the
results which have been already achieved
by the policy of the Government, while,
thanks to the efforts of the Ministry of
Agriculture, the demand for the agricultural produce of Northern Ireland is.
increasing steadily with the steady improvement in the quality of this produce.

he hoped that the efforts which are being
made to restore prosperity to the Linen
Industry may before long be attended by
an equal measure of success.
When speaking of the steps which are
being taken to improve the demand for
the produce of Northern Ireland I should
like to emphasize the special importance
which attaches to every improvement in
the transport facilities between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, so that our
factories may be enabled to place their
manufactured goods on the markets of
Great Britain with the least possible
delay, a consideration of great importance
to manufacturers and farmers generally
and of special consequence to the shirt
factories in the City of Derry. These
factories, as hon. Members I am sure
know, have to face very keen competition
in England, and owing to the geographical position of the City of Derry are
dependent to a very large degree upon

The improvement in the demand for
the produce of our factories and our farms
is the only means of effecting a real and
permanent cure for the serious problem

The introduction of a Bill dealing with

also indicated in the Gracious Speech to

prehension seems
to the
principles on which legislation on this subject should be based. In view of the increasing number of fatal and non-fatal

motor traffic, the necessity for control
over public service vehicles cannot be disputed, but in some quarters it does not
appear to be recognized that such control
is necessary, not merely to secure the safety
of the passengers who use them, and of
all others who use our roads, but also to
secure the adequacy and convenience of
the bus services, and the maintenence of
the bus fare at a reasonable level. So
far from creating a monopoly, the
rational control of public service vehicles
is the only safeguard against the consequences of a monopoly, and I am confident that wise legislation providing for
the control of public service vehicles will,
when understood, command general support.
The Gracious Speech concludes with a
reference to the determination of the
Government to maintain an atmosphere
of law, and order, and contentment. The
restoration of law and order in Northern
Ireland, thanks to the firm action of the
Government, supported by the efforts of
the Special Constabulary and R.U.C.,
has long since been an accomplished fact,
and all sections of the population, however widely they may differ on questions
of politics, recognize that the prosperity
of Northern Ireland as a whole, and the
interests of each individual are bound up
with the maintenance of the present
state of peace and quiet. The orderliness
and good humour which prevailed
throughout the constituencies during the
general election was remarkable,
and
while members on this side of the House
are naturally delighted by the signal expression of confidence in the Prime Minister and his Cabinet which this election
has afforded, I think the Members on
both sides of the House can agree in this,
that the good temper generally displayed
reflects credit on all parties and is a happy
augury for the future peace of Northern
Ireland, and the contentment which, we
trust, will prevail more and more widely
as prosperity increases. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
Major BLAKISTON-HOUSTON (in

them. I consider that this compliment

as a real compliment to the ex-Servicemen

I feel sure that all right hon. and hon.

return to Windsor. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). It is the heartfelt desire

Counties to hear that the rapid progress
which his Majesty is making towards
complete recovery may be maintained.
The Gracious Speech from the Throne
expresses an earnest desire for peace and
prosperity, and I am sure that the Government will do all that lies in their
power to encourage industry and promote
work for our people. There is an improvement in the shipbuilding industry, and
with the prospect of a new dock unemployment should be reduced in the city.
When the Derating Bill comes into full
operation it should give great encouragement to the agricultural community in
the Six Counties. I am glad to learn
that there has been included in the Parliamentary programme the Bill in connection with the Lough Neagh and River
Bann flooded area-a measure which
should improve the rural districts.

With regard to the Speech itself, it is
remarkable for what is omitted from it

The Derating Bill, of course, is a copy of
the Bill that has been introduced in the
British House, and, although it is not
yet passed there, I am sure it will be
passed in a short time. I do not know
that it will give to the farmers the relief
to which they are fully entitled. I am
afraid it will not. While, unquestionably, it will be of assistance to them, I
do not think it will be sufficient to relieve
them of the distress in which they are
presently fixed.
The farming industry, as has been said
by the mover of the Address, is in a
parlous condition. Whether the Derating
Bill will revive it or not is a question on
which I, at any rate, have some doubts.
If the Government were able to secure
something like a fixed price for the produce of the farmers it would be much
more satisfactory for them and for those
engaged in the industry than any relief
they may give by way of subsidies.
At
the present time many farmers have large
stocks of potatoes which they have grown
this year. In some instances they are
prevented even from marketing those
potatoes, and in other instances where
they have an open market there are no
buyers. That is a serious condition of
affairs for the farmers and one that, in my
opinion, could be remedied if the Government were earnest about it. I do not see
why the Government could not arrange for
a fixed price for this particular articlepotatoes. I do not know whether they
might adopt the co-operative system or
not, but I believe it is feasible. I believe
it is within the power of the Government
to secure a fixed and stable price for potatoes. Certainly you will admit that it is
an immense hardship on those engaged in
the farming industry after the worry,
trouble, and expense connected with raising this article to find that, at the end of
it all, they cannot get a buyer for their
potatoes and that in some instances, due to
restrictions, they are not even allowed to
market them. That is a state of affairs
that I think any Government should be
able to remedy, but I see nothing in the
King's Speech further than the statements
regarding Empire marketing that will give
relief to the farmers in this particular
direction. The Government should have
stated that some measure would be introduced in order to put the farming industry
-the principal industry in the Six Counties on a basis whereby they would get
some semblance of a living. They do not
get that now.
Another matter not mentioned in the

Another matter that I thought-indeed I

I understood, and I think my memory

the different managers of schools, the different people who take an interest in the

It is not the first time that I have

what I had read in connection with the

There are only two matters of much
importance mentioned in the Speech.
One, as I have said, is the relief of rates
on agricultural land, and the other is the
question of the flooding in the area round
Lough Neagh. As the House knows this
matter is overdue for a very long time,
just as long as I can remember. I do not
blame the Government for those early
days, but since they came into power eight
years ago some effort might have been
made to solve this difficult problem.
However, it is better late than never, and
I hope that the cause of the complaints
that have been continually made with regard to the flooding of the area along the
River Bann and Lough Neagh will now
be removed.
Before I sit down I should like to refer
to the election itself. I think that the
Mover of the Address made some remarkable statements regarding the election,
particularly on the question of unemployment. He said that the result of the election went to prove that the unemployed
were satisfied with the efforts which the
Government had made. I think that if
we make a close examination of the
figures it will be found that the confidence
in the Government is not there to the extent of the numbers by which the Government were returned. I think an examination of the figures will go to prove that
the Government's action in abolishing
Proportional Representation has resulted
in their being supported in this House by
numbers out of proportion to the electors
who voted for them at the polls. We have
only to examine the figures, particularly
in connection with the Belfast elections,
in which there were more than a dozen
contests, to find that the Government have
many more Members than-at least twice
as many as-Proportional Representation
would have given them. I am speaking of
the constituencies in which none of the
Members of my party was engaged. The
statement which the hon. Member for the
City of Derry (Mr. Murphy) has made,
that the voters in the Six Counties are
satisfied with the Government, is not
justified by the figures of the election.
There is one other matter that I wish
to mention; it is one on which I had an
Amendment to the Address just twelve
months ago. I thought, in face of what
has happened since, that some mention
would have been made of it in the King's
Speech-that is, in regard to leaseholders
This is a matter that has been debated
in this House very often, and I understand that a Report has been published
from the Committee that was set up to
inquire into the matter. Apparently the
Government do not intend to introduce
legislation in connection with it, and I
think, if that is so, we are entitled to
know the reason why. Later on in the
Debate on the Address I hope to move
an Amendment on this question of leaseholders, and another one on the subject
of education. I shall, therefore, defer

29 MAY 1929
The PRIME MINISTER: Almost at
this date four years ago, I remember our
late friend and colleague, Dr. Morrison,
moved the Address in this House, and I
take this opportunity, the first I have
had, of expressing on behalf of all
quarters of the House our deep regret at
his recent passing away. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Dr. Morrison was an
esteemed citizen of the County of Derry,
and during the time that he represented
the University here he gained the respect
and affection of all Members of the House.
Also, four years ago, the present Member
for South Tyrone (Mr. Elliott) said:-
I hope that when the present Parliament comes to be dissolved we may all
be able to look back on our record of
work done with satisfaction, and that
we will have the gratification of knowing we have at least done something to
make Northern Ireland one of the
brightest spots in the King's Dominions.
I think hon. Members who served on all
sides of the House in the last Parliament
may take credit for having laboured
earnestly to do something to make Northern Ireland a brighter and happier spot.
To-day we enter upon a new Parliament, and a further Session has been inaugurated by my hon. and learned Friend,
the Member for the City of Derry (Mr.
Murphy), whose rapier-like oratory will
be a great asset to those of my friends on
this side of the House who will have to
meet the attacks of hon. Members opposite later on in the Session, but no more
useful than the broadsword of my innocent Friend in the Dock (Major Blakiston-
Houston), who will, I feel sure, as time
goes on enjoy the sort of harmonious
scrapping that takes place between the
two parties in Parliament. I congratulate
them both very much upon their first
appearance in this House. There is no
necessity to dwell on any effort on the part
of such a learned Gentleman as the hon.
Member for Derry City, because his name
is known throughout the whole of Ireland,
and it has been well earned by his practice
in the Courts. With regard to my old
Friend behind me (Major Blakiston-
Houston) I can only say personally how
delighted I am to find him here in the
midst of a good, loyal, Unionist team.
The hon. and learned Member for Derry
City referred to the great advantage it
would be for the Maiden City if greater
facilities could possibly be provided for
transport from Great Britain to that parmay
ticular port. I can only say that any sugthrow
gestions that he or his friends
out with regard to assisting more than is
done at the present moment will not fall
upon deaf ears. But I was hopeful that
the steps already taken by my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, at the
conclusion of the last Parliament, to ease
the burden of rates upon the carriage both
by land and sea of the goods that are
manufactured in Derry, and of the raw
material that they require in Derry, would
have materially eased the situation, and
that as time goes on that, together with
the de-rating of the industries in Derry
itself, would perhaps meet the requirements which he has voiced to-day in his
maiden speech in this House.
Then I come to the hon. Member for
Mourne (Mr. Patrick O'Neill) and I must
say that it is a great gratification to me
at any rate to know that after eight years
in the saddle the hardest thing that can
be said regarding the misdeeds and deeds
of the Government has been said by the
hon. Member opposite. I think on the
whole we cannot have produced an altogether barren result when we hear the best
of the thunder of the hon. Member. He
did mention one or two points that I will
be glad to meet. He said he would like
the Government to begin now to improvise
some scheme for fixing the price for the
produce of the agricultural community.
Of course, he and his friends in the Mourne
district know that when he talks like that,
with a twinkle in his eye, he is asking for
something that is absolutely impossible.
Mr. O'NEILL: Not at all.
The PRIME MINISTER: Imagine the
Government fixing the price of potatoes,
fixing the price of flax, or fixing the price
of
any other commodities?
Mr. O'NEILL: Why not?
The PRIME MINISTER: I am going
to tell the hon. Member why not.
Mr. LEEKE: It will be very interesting to hear it.
The PRIME MINISTER: It will be
very interesting. Suppose we fix the
price, and there is nobody found to pay
the price? How would the hon. Member
get over that difficulty?
Mr. O'NEILL: Find a market for
them; they have to find it.

The PRIME MINISTER: I think the
hon. Member must be referring to some
war measure. Of course the war is over for
a long time, and we have got back to
ordinary economic conditions. I think the
whole country would rise up if one was to
suggest bringing in anything in the nature.
of D.O.R.A.
The unfortunate position with regard to
potatoes is fully realized by my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Agriculture, and
as I explained in Downpatrick a few days
ago, he has made most valiant efforts in
order to meet the peculiar position that has
arisen, and he is the most vigilant and
most earnest of Ministers in looking after
the interests of his Department. However, the hon. Member for Mourne need
have no fear but that anything that can
be done will be done to assist those who
are engaged not only in the cultivation of
potatoes but of any other agricultural
produce.
Then he spoke about unemployment.
Unemployment, in my opinion, at the
present moment is better than it
has been since we took up the reins
of office. One of our great difficulties
is this, that prior to the introduction of unemployment insurance there
were no reliable statistics on which we
could base the unemployed population.
either of this country or of Great Britain.
Therefore nobody to-day knows what the
actual conditions were prior to the war.
All we can do is to go on as we have been
doing in the past, endeavouring to provide
work for the people, and I think everybody
admits that our efforts in that direction
have been attended with the greatest possible success. I do not wish to be unduly
optimistic, but I am hopeful at any rate
that good news will reach one of our shipbuilding yards within the next few days
of an order that I hope will give employment to a large number of those who are
at present not employed.
We are doing all we can. My right hon.
Friend (Mr. Pollock) through his Loans
Guarantee Act has done more to provide
work for the unemployed in the City of
Belfast than any action that has been taken
before in the Ulster area. That, of course,
is still going on; it is not done yet, and we
hope to be able to do still more in the
future.
The hon. Member for Mourne said that
there had been no mention of Education
in the King's Speech. I should explain
to the House that when the deputation
first met my right hon. Friend, the noble
Lord the Minister of Education, and myself, I explained that the ground to be
covered was so large and the time was so
short that it would be impossible for us to
tackle the Bill dealing with those intricate
matters in this Session of Parliament. I
also pointed out that in a matter of such
importance it was customary to have it
mentioned in the King's Speech, but there
was no time to embody it in the King's
Speech, which at that time had received
his Grace's approval. Therefore, it is a
matter which will have to lie over till
another Session.
The hon. Member (Mr. O'Neill) mentioned the subject of the Landlord and
Tenant Inquiry, the report of which, I
think, has only just been published. This
is a matter which will require very careful
study by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Home Affairs. It will then
be submitted to the Cabinet for very careful consideration, and later on if any question is put down as to what our future
action is to be we will be very glad indeed
to give a reply. I think those are the only
points that the hon. Member referred to.
I have dealt with them quite shortly, it is
true, but I hope sufficiently fully to meet
the situation.
Now, I would like to say-and I intend
to be very brief-that I think Members
on all sides of the House should consider
themselves exceedingly lucky to be returned as Members of this particular
Parliament, the third administration we
have had in Northern Ireland, because we
meet, without doubt, with a more rosy outlook in front of us than at any other time
I can recollect since we took on the duties
of Government. If one just thinks of the
anxieties of all of us at one time with
regard to the burden of unemployment

nsurance, what a satisfaction it is for

Then, hon. Members are also sitting in

whole of land purchase in Northern Ireland is actually behind us instead of, as

to the minds of all of us who are sincere
in our desire to see land purchase cleared
up. I am sure one and all agree that we
are relieved in our hearts to know that the

Then, as has been mentioned by the
mover and seconder of the Address, we
will be in the position of seeing the fruition
of the long-delayed drainage of the River
Bann. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
All through my parliamentary career at
Westminister it was the most burning and
pressing question, and if it falls to my lot
to see success attending that scheme of
that success I am assured or I would not
have put my hand to it-it will be one

Hon. Members will also be here to help

always tries to throw rather a wet blanket
over this derating scheme, but I think that
his political instinct is running away with

line he did this afternoon. Who can deny

benefit to the farming community, and

the old rents and the new annual instalments.
Surely that would be a matter for
us all to rejoice about.
We will all of us, I hope, be able to see

Courts of Justice which will be a credit to

us to know that we were here when the

Then I cannot forget the fact that we
Parliament
all hope to sit in the new
House during the course of this Parliament, and when that new Parliament
House and the administrative buildings

brought in a Fishery Bill, and I am

If the Minister had consulted those interests which are cognisant of the working of the Fishery Laws in Ulster he

especially to the fishing community round
the coast. Instead of that, he only consulted the English combines which today hold in their grasp the fishery laws
and fisheries of Northern Ireland. He

remote parts of the country and seen
what could be done in the way of advancing capital to the small fishermen
who to-day are fighting an uphill fight
against adverse circumstances in the

Then there is the question of town
tenants. The Prime Minister says he
had not time to study this question properly in order to bring in a Bill. That
is right enough. I am broadminded
enough to recognize that. There are
people in places like Maghera and Dungiven who are suffering a great deal
through harsh laws, and they are
depending on the success of the agricultural community. I hope that the
great wave of prosperity foreshadowed
by the Prime Minister will come this
time. Anything which would give these
people security of tenure in their homes.
and an opportunity to develop their

As to education, the Prime Minister

Bill. That is all they ask-only a fair

I am sorry no reference has been made

traffic. I thought the Government would
have taken some steps in that direction.
I was talking to one of the biggest hotel
proprietors in Northern Ireland, and he
said one of the things they were suffering
from was the difficulty of getting trained
servants. They have to send across to
France and Belgium for chefs and servants
of that character. I have always held it
to be nonsense that these professions should
be the monopoly of any country. Some of
these chefs get from £500 to £1,000 a year.
If the Government established a training
school, worked in connection with the
system of technical education, you could
train Irish servants for hotels who would
be as good as those coming from
the Continent. After all, the great
attraction is efficiency of service in hotels.
Why should you bring across foreigners
to carry out these duties in hotels? It
shows that the Government is lacking in
appreciation of what a good servant is.
The next thing is the Motor Licensing
Bill which is foreshadowed. I am a bit
suspicious of this. I suspect there is some
insidious move behind it to crush out the
motor buses and further the interests of
the big railway companies. I have noticed
a tendency on the part of the Government
recently to help the big railway companies
against the motor buses. You must remember that these buses have been godsends to the more remote towns and agricultural areas, and any attempt on the
part of the Government to restrict or curtail those services in the interests of big
railway monopolists will be looked upon
with indignation by the people. I should
like an assurance from the Government
that in bringing in this Bill they intend

Both hon. Members are new. We welcome them to the House. They have

The hon. Member also said he would
like to see the Government do something
to develop the tourist traffic.
It may
be news for the hon. Member if I tell
him that I was in the town of Antrim
a short time ago. I even ventured into
a hotel, and I was glad to find that the
owner of that hotel was adding some
twenty bedrooms to deal with the increasing tourist traffic. The gentleman's
name is Fawcett, and he told me that in
Antrim town they had had to quadruple
their bedroom accommodation in order to
deal with the increased tourist traffic in
Northern Ireland. That speaks for itself,
and I for one am delighted that people
are coming to Northern Ireland in increased numbers. I believe the Government will do anything they can to encourage and to develop the tourist
traffic. It is one of the best traffics we
can support and does a great deal to
bring more money into our area.
With reference to the Redistribution

at the passing of Proportional Represention. The abolition of that system gave
us an opportunity of getting into personal
contact with our electors, and I congratulate the Government once again on removing from the Statute Book an Act which
never should have been placed there.
Coming to what really concerns us most
this afternoon, namely, the King's Speech,
I would like to say that I gladly welcome
the proposals outlined in that Gracious
Speech from the Throne.

I quite recognize that it is necessary to

Northern Ireland in a monopoly, I am

have in our rural districts at the present

Sittings of the House
Debate on Address
31 MAY 1929
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Friday, 31st May, 1929.
The House met at Three of the clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Sittings of the House.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That notwithstanding anything contained in Standing Order No. 1 (Sittings
of the House), business be not interrupted
at half-past Six o'clock this day."-(The
Prime Minister.)
Mr. BEATTIE: Before you put that
Motion I want to ask for your ruling.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
cannot debate it.
Mr. BEATTIE: No, I only want your
ruling. This is a Parliamentary day,
different to any other Parliamentary day
of the week, and I claim that precedent
rules the custom of this House. The law
in the Imperial House of Commons is that
the House meets at Eleven o'clock on
Fridays, and without any suspension of
the Standing Orders it adjourns at three
o'clock. I understand the British custom
is that unless there is something of grave
public importance to be raised, the suspension of the Standing Orders is never
moved. I ask you to give a ruling on
that point, seeing that we are carrying on
on parallel lines with Great Britain.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
will allow me to point out that there is
nothing to stop the Government putting
down a Motion of this kind.
Mr. BEATTIE: No, but I ask for your
ruling.
Mr. SPEAKER: This question cannot
be debated, and no Amendment to it can
be discussed in any shape or form. I am
bound to put the Question.
Mr. BEATTIE: I have to ask you for
a ruling. I want you to give a ruling as
to whether we are in order in violating
the British custom? Surely I am in order
in asking that.
Mr. SPEAKER: I can only reply that
this Motion is perfectly in order, and that
is my ruling. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Question put and agreed to.

BILL,
"to enable certain local authorities to

Bates), supported by the Parliamentary

(Mr. Hanna); to be read a Second time on

NOXIOUS WEEDS BILL,
"to amend the Weeds and Agricultural
Seeds (Ireland) Act, 1909, in its application to noxious weeds," presented by the
Minister of Agriculture (Sir Edward Archdale), supported by Sir Dawson Bates; to
be read a Second time on Tuesday, and

"That an Humble Address be presented
to His Grace the Governor of Northern

Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern
Ireland, in Parliament assembled, beg
leave to offer our humble thanks to your
Grace for the Speech which your Grace
has addressed to both Houses of Parliament." (Mr. Murphy).
Mr. BEATTIE: I regret that a
precedent of the British House of Commons
has been violated at this day's sitting of
the House. I can find no record of any
suspension of the Standing Orders being
put into operation on a Friday by the
Imperial Government. I lodge my indig-

Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
nant protest against this violation of the
custom and precedent of the Imperial
House of Commons. Before proceeding to
deal with the King's Speech perhaps I
might be allowed to congratulate the hon.
Member for Derry (Mr. Murphy) and the
hon. Member for Dock (Major Blakiston-
Houston) on their maiden speeches in this
House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
As to the King's Speech, we have heard
of "Document No. 1" and "Document
No. 2," but I think I would christen the
King's Speech a document full of
emptiness as far as the people are concerned. I would have thought that
shortly after the election some consideration would have been given to questions
which affect the well-being of the industrial
classes of Northern Ireland. Unfortunately, that has not taken place.
We had the King's Speech in March
and an Amendment on unemployment
was moved and debated. I thought after
the enlightenment the Government then
got on the question of unemployment
that they would have given this matter
consideration, but what hopes are held
out for the people in the King's Speech?
None. There is no hope for the unemployed. Unemployment is to be a
permanent fixture in our midst. It is a
fixture that is necessary and essential for
the protection of those exploiters and
profiteers who care more for money than
they do for human life. I have been
chided here by a Member on the opposite Benches as being a great Socialist.
That word does not apply to me. I
stand on this floor, as I stood all my life,
as a Labour Member. I thought the
Government would have really learned
some lessons as regards the bringing in
of documents of this kind to a House of
this description. We have been put out
of this House by the gerrymandering of
constituencies. Labour representation
has been reduced from three Members to
one. That is a matter that will have our
fuller consideration. The conditions at
present point towards that position being
given satisfactory consideration when the
British electorate have finished counting
the votes. I claim on behalf of Labour
and on behalf of the largest electorate represented by one Member that this document presented to the House is a shame
and a disgrace to the party responsible
for drawing it up.
The Prime Minister has declared that
if the salaries of himself and the Cabinet
and others holding sinecure positions of
no useful service to the State were reduced the amount saved by that
reduction would go to the Imperial contribution. Britain would have the benefit of that reduction which the Cabinet
are now enjoying at the expense of the
taxpayers. I have stood for the retention of the Imperial contribution, providing, as it does, for the widows and
orphans who are now suffering under the
law you placed on the Statute Book. You
made it class legislation, confining the
scheme to about 266,000 workers, although there are double that number of
workers depending on wages for an existence. I also asked the Prime Minister
would it not be better to put that money,
which averages about threepence per head
of the population, into the pockets of the
down-and-outs and let the Unemployment Fund meet this liability of
£100,000 a year, and by that you will
also be doing a service. But the Prime
Minister has a deaf ear for requests of this
kind. The only ear the Prime Minister
has is for the landed gentry or the aristocratic class in Northern Ireland. When
they cry out for assistance he makes provision in the Estimates for their financial
assistance. But when the working class
cry out the reply is that the regulations
in regard to unemployment insurance
must be adhered to. The grinding of
the wheel still continues week after week.
Every week in Northern Ireland hundreds of people are thrown off unemployment benefit by the regulations. Hundreds of people are being driven to the
workhouse and placed upon the rates. I
claim, on behalf of the workers, that this
is not giving them a fair crack of the
whip. I claim the Government should
take over responsibility for the unemployed because the City of Belfast is an
industrial area. The City of Belfast
rates for the upkeep of persons unemployed outside the two years constitute a
very heavy burden. We have in our city
a Relief Committee, but the representatives of the rates are the representatives
of the Tory party, and they will only
grant a very meagre allowance to sustain
these people, who have no alternative but
to go
to the Poor Law Guardians. I
claim it is the duty of the Government to
take over the full responsibility.
I made that claim when I was a member
of the Board of Guardians, and when I
appeared before the Minister of Home
Affairs I advocated that system. There
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
31 MAY 1929
is only one way of solving the problem,
and that is by placing it on the shoulders
of the many and taking it off the shoulders
of the few. The unemployment question
should be a national question, and not a
local question as it is to-day.
If the
King's Speech did not contain a solution.
for unemployment I would have thought
that it would have dealt with the fact
that industry in Northern Ireland to-day
is not able to absorb the number of hands
it is necessary should be absorbed in order
to do away with unemployment. I would
have thought the Government would have
directed their attention to reducing the
pensionable age to 60, to increasing pensions to £1 a week, and that they would
have given those pensions to the industrial
classes, because to-day the pension of 10:
a week is not sufficient to maintain old age
outside industry. Old age must go back
to industry to augment that 10s a week in
order to live in decency and comfort.
Further, I would have thought the
Government would have directed their
attention to removing from industry the
young children between the ages of fourteen and sixteen years. Industry could
be relieved of thousands of these young
people. You could make provision by
giving an allowance to these young people.
to enable them to be educated and
thoroughly equipped for the battle of life.
They should not be allowed to go into
industry until they were at least fifteen
years of age. But, no, there is no hope
for the child. The child has still got to
be the victim of the grinding system which
this Government is supporting at the
present time.
The regulation of hours should have
been one of the things contained in the
King's Speech. There is no mention in
it of a 48-hour week, or any agreement
made under the Washington Convention.
British representatives appeared
there, and gave their word of honour,
but the Tory Government dishonoured
the representatives' mandate. To-day,
in some industries, we are working up to
70 hours a week. I say a 48-hour week
should have been given consideration in
the King's Speech. I hope that if a
solution of the unemployment problem is
not brought about by this present Government it will be brought about by the other
alternative left to the workers, and that
the question of a further reduction in
working hours and an increase in wages
will be taken up by the whole trade union
movement in Northern Ireland. We
cannot afford to allow our craftsmen and
other citizens to be running about for
years losing their skill and their vitality.
This is one of the greatest evils that could
exist in any community, and the Government has made no effort towards meeting
it.
The next thing I would like to draw
the attention of the Government to is that
no mention has been made of fixed prices
for agricultural commodities. In the last
Parliament the agricultural community
were ably represented on this side of the
House, and the farmers will now miss the
presence of the hon. Member (Mr. George
Henderson). Perhaps the reason of this
omission in the Speech is that the middle
man is a friend of the Government. The
difference between what the farmer gets
and what the consumer pays, as the hon.
Member for South Tyrone (Mr. Elliott)
says, is a wonderful revelation. I myself
have been a victim. I was on a farm and
received complaints about the prices received by the farmer, and I found that an
increase of anything from 300 per cent.
to 400 per cent. was paid by me to the
retailer. I am quite satisfied the retailer
is not the villain of the piece. There is a
certain circle that comes between the producer and the consumer, and the sooner
fixed prices for farmers with control at the
marketing centres are introduced the
better it will be for the farmers of
Northern Ireland.
A most vicious Act
was passed last
Session, and in view of the results of the
Imperial elections which I see in to-day's
Press I hope it will be rescinded. I hope
to be in this House to take part in the
rescinding of that Act, that is the Trades
Disputes Act.
Mr. GRANT: Never.
Mr. BEATTIE: You will find out, my
dear fellow, before you are long in this
House whether it will be rescinded or not.
The liberties of half a century were filched
away from the working class in three
weeks. That Act should never be on the
Statute Book, and this Government should
take the lead in wiping it off. At the
present moment it is a disgrace to the
Statute Book upon which it rests. The
British electorate to-day are performing
one of the most wonderful acts ever performed in the British Isles. On the 29th
May word was sent to the electors of Pottinger Division from the British electorsit was addressed to Jack Beattie, M.P.-
that is what I am known as outside-say-

are spending, The results to-day prove

fund, in his great haste to get the service,

the workers' purchasing power is well below what it was in 1914. (Hon. Members: No.) The result of that decreased

under consumption is more unemployment
in the manufacturing end and other ends
of production.
I want to tell the proposer of the
Address (Mr. Murphy) that shipbuilding, while it may be prosperous,
is by no means going to maintain the
standard of continuity of employment in
1929 and 1930 it maintained in 1912 and
1914 or previous to that date. The
average yearly earning of a worker in the
shipbuilding trade is 30 weeks' wages.
Thirty weeks' wages is the average purchasing power of the worker, and 30
weeks' wages, averaging £3, is £90 per
annum. Forty weeks' wages pre-war,
say at £2, was £80. If you take away the
war-time increase and the percentage of
rent to wages now you will find that the
purchasing power is greatly reduced from
what it was pre-war, and the continuity
of employment is lessened by ten weeks.
Therefore I say the shipbuilding industry
may be prosperous-and nobody desires
that more than I do. I have ten of a
family, father, brothers and others-but
prosperity can be brought about in only
one way and not by the way it has been
conducted since 1922. Reducing wages
of workers will not bring prosperity.

I sat on a reduction conference, and I
was told by the employing class that we
must have a reduction of labour cost, and
the reason was it would bring orders to
the Queen's Island. But every reduction
of wages that took place from 1920 onwards
meant an increase in unemployment.
only one period in 1924 was there any improvement made so far as employment is
concerned. A reduction of wages only
causes unemployment. Pay a good wage
and give good purchasing power and you
will create consuming power, and good
consuming power will give you a good
market for production. Creating a market
will make the wheels of industry go round
and you will get prosperity in that way
and not by the starvation you have to-day.

the Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie)
appears to me that he thinks he is the
only representative of Labour in this
House. The constituency I represent is
fairly industrial in character, and I am
here purely and solely on the Government's record during the past eight years.
Their record, I believe, is something that
one should be proud of. The Member for
Pottinger said that nothing had been
done to solve the problem of unemployment, but if his policy was
as constructive as it is destructive
it would have more beneficial results.
The hon. Member referred to the Civil
Authorities (Special Powers) Act. Does
he want that Act removed from the
Statuto Book? Is he not a law-abiding
citizen?
Mr. BEATTIE: I say it is unnecessary
that it should be on the Statute Book.
Mr. MINFORD: With regard to the
derating scheme, I believe I am in a
position to tell the hon. Member that you
cannot ask the farmers to produce goods
and sell them at a cheaper rate than they
are doing at the present time. Potatoes
are being sold at 9d per cwt., and if the
hon. Member would only take the opportunity of going amongst his class to find
out the cost of farm produce he would do
much more good than he is doing by talking what, in my opinion, is a lot of balderdash. With regard to the question of
unemployment, I think the Government
have made splendid strides in trying to
solve that problem. I should have liked to
have seen the Member for Pottinger put
forward his policy for solving that problem,
because he seems to think that he is the
only man who can do and has done anything to cure unemployment. I might
say that in one industrial part of my constituency I was able to secure 99 per cent.
of the votes, which goes to show that
Labour in that part of the Province has
implicit trust in the Government.
In our efforts to try to reduce unemployment I think we have done as well as
any other part of the Empire, and the
people whom I represent are quite prepared to place themselves in the hands of
the Government so far as this or any other
question is concerned. The hon. Member
said that lower wages always bring
about unemployment, but if he considers
what has been accomplished by the
Government through the medium of the
Loans Guarantee Act he will surely admit
that the Government has done something
to increase employment. I was surprised
to hear the hon. Member say the land
drainage scheme would do nothing to
create employment, because I thought it
would provide a good deal of work for

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Minford]
the unemployed.
I would like to hear
from the hon. Member what he thinks is
the best way to solve this problem of unemployment.
With regard to housing, which was not
mentioned in the King's Speech, I was
delighted to hear the Prime Minister
refer to that question. In the area I represent we have a shortage of houses, but
Rome was not built in a day, and I have
every confidence that in a short time the
people will have houses that they will be
proud to live in. The Member for
Pottinger also, fortunately or unfortunately, talked about the "B" Specials.
I do not know what kind of constituency
the hon. Member represents, but the
people who sent me here welcomed the
"B" Specials at a time when it was a
godsend to have them. I am sure the
hon. Member will agree with me that law
and order is one of the most essential
things in a community, and the past record of the Government in maintaining
law and order was responsible for their
return to this House. The record of the
Government is one of which the people of
the County of Antrim are justly proud,
and they are quite prepared to allow
their destinies to remain in the hands of
that Government rather than in the
hands of the so-called Opposition.
But I do not think we are here to talk
about the results of past work. We are
here to do our utmost for all classes of the
community. If the farmer only pays his.
rent and gets 2 per cent. against capital
investments he cannot produce food any
cheaper than it is to-day. I do not wish
to take up the time of the House, and if
I have made any remarks which are not
in order I hope that as a new Member I
shall be forgiven. To revert to unemployment, we must all admit that there
are periods when unemployment is worse
than it is at other times, and in regard
to the linen industry I would suggest
that if all sections were brought together
and tried to make Northern Ireland a

it would, perhaps, provide a means of restoring that industry to its former
prosperity.

agriculturist, and as representing an
gricultural constituency, I very much
welcome the derating scheme which has

needed.
I can assure the hon. Member
