Mr. CONNELLAN: On behalf of my
constituents in a rural community who
have tasted none of the benefits we have
heard so much about since the opening of
this debate, I wish to say that I am here
in a two-fold capacity. In the first place
I am here to protest on their behalf
against the partition of Ireland, which
we strongly believe and are convinced is
the cause of practically all the industrial
depression and all the agricultural backwardness, and all the gloom that hangs
over the Six Counties at the present time.
In saying that I may add that I have no
more admiration for that branch of partition which is represented by the partition
Parliament of the Twenty-Six Counties
than I have for that represented by the
partition Parliament of the Six Counties
here. The King's Speech, about which
we have heard so much, is bristling with
nothing more than pious sentiments and
pious platitudes, and its omissions are
more significant than anything it
contains.
It really has been a feat on the part of
those who have spoken to the Address
that they have been able to say so much
about the Speech. It reminds me of Dr.
Johnson and the dancing dog. He was
not surprised that the dog danced badly,
but he was surprised it was able to dance
at all. That is practically the feat
which those who have spoken on the
Government's behalf have performed in
this case. Every speech we have heard
from the Government side of the House
has been one of self-satisfaction and selflaudation. Everything that has been
claimed on behalf of the Government and
its policy in the past has been of a purely
negative character. Practically nothing
has been mentioned except what
fortuitous circumstances have brought
about. Nothing has been mentioned
that is due to the initiative of the Government apart from those fortuitous
circumstances. Nobody outside this
House will be foolish enough to swallow
the many claims that have been made
on behalf of the Government during this
debate.
Much has been said about the Government's work in building up a state of
peace
and contentment
the Six
in

Counties, and one speaker a few days ago
even claimed credit for the good weather
we are having at the present time. That
s very far-fetched indeed, and I do not
think that in any part of the Six
Counties you will find anybody foolish
enough to believe that the Government
is responsible for the good weather that
is prevailing, and that as a result the
farmers of the Six Counties will find
themselves in a regular El Dorado in the
course of a few months. We come here
one
representing the greatest individual
party in the Six Counties, and
might think that after having been,
treated. as we were treated, in
the past, and having been invited and
practically implored to take part in the
affairs of this House, the Government
would have been a little gracious to our
people, that they would have said we
had supped sufficiently of the cup of
suffering, and that the time had come
when an effort should be made to bring
about a reconciliation and an appeasement between the different parties.
But instead of that the Government
resort to a plan to cut our numbers down
still further. They adopted their system
of gerrymandering. Gerrymandering,
by the way, is infinitely too polite a word
with which to describe the machine
created by the Government for the
reduction of our numbers, and for the
reduction of our people to a state bordering almost on complete powerlessness.
When the Government had invented this
machine, pressed the button, and set it
into working order, and when the very
effect it was intended to produce was produced, they came into this Chamber, and
in a spirit of exultation, in a spirit of
self-satisfaction, said, "Look at the grand
achievement to our credit; look at what
we have been able to accomplish at the
polls," as if this were some miracle from
heaven, and all this had not been foreseen.
Before the entry of our party to this
Parliament, the Government party were
imploring us practically to come in as an
Opposition. The Government party were
practically dying of ennui, dotting each
others i's and crossing each others t's,
and no sooner had we entered this Parliament than every effort was made to render our efforts for our people abortive,
and to create a condition of affairs which
not only has proved useless so far as the
bringing about of any amelioration of our
people's circumstances is concerned, but
which has been practically holding us up
to ridicule as a party. If it was the
Government's intention to behave, as it
has behaved, during the term of our
appearance in this House, it would have
been infinitely more gracious if it had
told us practically at that time it did not
want us at all, and that it would be better
for us to keep out of this House.
We have repeatedly put up pleas here
on behalf of our people's views on the
question of education. All those pleas
have been ignored, and the state of our
schools to-day is as bad as if we never
had put in any attendance at this House
at all. Now the introduction of an
Amendment to the Education Act is
promised, but I am afraid that, judging
by our bitter experience of the past, we
can expect very little to help us in satisfying the claims and aspirations of our
people in the matter of education. A
few days ago somebody on the Government side referred to the magnificent reform which had been created by this Government in the realm of education, particularly in regard to school buildings,
and referred in a special manner to the
sanitation of schools, that is, the
material sanitation: But there is something higher even than the material
sanitation of schools, and that is the
spiritual sanitation, which has been
completely ignored, and every voice
raised by us might as well have been
raised in the desert of Sahara as raised
here for the purpose of creating any
improvement in the conditions under
which our schools exist at the present
time.
But the Government's policy in this respect is quite in accord with its policy all
round. We fail to obtain in any branch
of the Government's policy anything
bordering on a democratic outlook, and if
democracy should rule anywhere, surely it
is in this small corner of Ireland where we
are not dealing with a rich and powerful
people, but where we are dealing with the
farmer's mind in the country places, and.
the labourer's mind in the towns, where
the rich and powerful count for very little
in numbers. So anti-democratic has
the Government been in its policy, so regardless has it been with regard to the
real needs of education, that it has done
what no other country that I know of has
done-it has held the schoolmaster and
the schoolmistress up to the scorn and the
opprobrium of practically the smallest
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Connellan]
child attending every public elementary
school in the Six Counties.
No schoolmaster, no schoolmistress, can
take any interest whatever in political
affairs. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
They may teach the children this, that,
and the other branches of knowledge, but
so far as exercising the rights of citizens
with regard to ventilating their own
grievances in a public way, or championing the cause of others as their mind
directs, they are absolutely debarred from
taking any part in public affairs. Why
is not the Government remorselessly logical and consistent ? If it is a crime for a
schoolmaster or a schoolmistress to take
any part in public affairs, it is equally
criminal on their part to read the newspaper regarding political matters, to form
any opinion regarding the respective
merits of political parties, or to go to the
ballot box and record their votes. And
to be consistent the Government should debar all teachers from casting their votes,
for that is a political act based upon the
study of political circumstances. I do
not know that in any other country in the
world there exists any such anti-democratic policy with regard to the teaching profession, and I merely mention it as
showing the Government's shortsightedness with regard to the importance of
education generally.
As I have said, the Speech is packed
with inanities and platitudes, and that is
fully in accord with the policy of a
government of negation, as this Government is. Everything of vital importance
to the people is excluded from mention
in this Speech. Everything regarding say
a guaranteed price for flax and other commodities is ignored. We have talk of
electrical development, and surely it is
farcical at this stage, when all the rest of
the country outside the Six Counties is
availing of one of the most magnificent
electrical schemes in the world, that we
here should be so divorced from the life
of the country as to be unable to avail at
a cheap rate of the services of the
Shannon, which is as much our river as it
the river of the people of any other part
of Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear,
ar.) Still for the purpose of pursuing
this feeble policy of cutting off our noses
to spite our faces, we adhere to the superstition that it is absolutely wrong and sinful to have any contact with the rest of
the country.
If there is industrial depression here at
the present time, that depression springs
perhaps more from the fact that partition
has cut us off from our nearest customers
in the Twenty-Six Counties, from three
millions of a population, than from any
other cause. All the hopes of the future
are based merely, as far as I can see, on the
promises of the Prime Minister. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) One of those
promises is to complete the erection of the
Government Buildings and the Law
Courts. How far that will relieve industrial depression, how far it will give
further employment, is a very moot
question, but there is one sure thing, that
if ever there was an instance of the gilded
halo hovering around decay it is in the
erection of those palatial buildings and
the squandering of so much money in this
way, when you have poverty and distress
all around, when you have the spectre of
hunger standing at the door of practically
every workingman's house.
There is one thing sure, if the Government is solicitous to bring additional
lustre to these Six Counties, if it is
solicitous of doing something that will
redound to the credit of the Six Counties,
it should certainly see in future that
those who are highly placed in this part
of the country uphold the traditions of
their office, and that they shall at least
appear before the public of the world as
educated men. Talking of these Law
Courts, I may say that it is just a few
months since an important case
heard in the Law Courts here in Belfast.
A political leader from the South was
arrested for entering the Six Counties in
spite of a warrant or order operating
against him, and when he was charged in
the Law Courts in Belfast he made use
of a few words in Irish in answer to a
question addressed to him, and what did
the chief functionary at that Court say—

withdraw. If that is so, then the position

Correct me if I am wrong, because I do

What is the position with regard to
the green card? This is it exactly. If

told to get a green card. When he goes

said. The next thing he is brought before a court of referees, and sometimes

seeking work. I can get you thousands of
men and women, too, who are out every

the old boots they wear off their feet, and

are not genuinely seeking work" when he
is looking for work all the time, then you
are adding insult to injury.
You are actually calling him a loafer.

what I said. I believe the Government
are going to grant Strannix a free pardon,
and I want them to do it quickly. That
boy is in a starving condition. Most of
his family are unemployed. If you leave
any person in a starving condition in the
City of Belfast you immediately drive him
into crime. That is all I wish to say at
the present time about that case. It is
terrible case, and I could say a lot more
about it if I wished.
Just one more word and I shall have
finished. A lot of the Members on both
sides of the House seem to applaud what
the electors have done in regard to the
elections in Northern Ireland.
I am
well satisfied. Whatever the electors do
always pleases me. They always get
what they want to get. I am not saying
it is bad, and I am not saying it is good.
I thank you, Sir.
Mr. STEWART: I can find nothing in
the King's Speech that will really benefit
the community in Northern Ireland outside the Derating Bill. I may say, at the
outset, that I heartily welcome that Bill
if it is to be a benefit to the farming
community in the Six Counties. The
Prime Minister, I am sorry to see, is not
here, but on Wednesday he gave us a
very rosy picture of the condition of
affairs in the Six Counties. In Cookstown, the premier town of the constituency which I represent, for the last
number of years the wheels of the
inachinery which at one time made it a
prosperous township have not been going.
Unemployment is rife. The people there
are in a state of despair. They are practically in starvation for want of work,
and a few ladies and gentlemen in the
town within the last couple of years have
organised soup kitchens for the children
attending school.
In the district of Cookstown, and
especially in the urban area, when you
meet men and women-it is a horrible
thing to relate-you see starvation
pictured in the faces of those who have
been out of employment. That is a bit
of a contrast to the rosy picture painted
here for us by the Prime Minister of
Northern Ireland. The Prime Minister
probably has not had time to visit Cookstown-he has probably been too busy in
other parts of the Six Counties-but I
hope he will find it convenient at some
future date to come and see for himself
the condition of affairs in the Cookstown
area.
In regard to houses for the workers,
the Government have introduced a
scheme, but what is wrong with the
houses that have been erected, especially
those under the urban authorities, is that
the rents are entirely too high. Poor
people, and especially men earning wages
of from 30s to 35s a week, cannot possibly
afford to pay the rents charged for the
houses under the control of the urban
authorities.
The Prime Minister stated very fairly
in his speech on Wednesday that he
would welcome suggestions from this side
of the House. This is my first appearance in a parliamentary institution, and
I must say I accepted in good faith what
he said, although some of my colleagues,
who have been here for a number of years,
say, "It is piffle, don't believe him, he
does not mean it." I accept in good
faith what he said, and I am going to
give him a couple of suggestions. The
first is in regard to the position of
farmers in the Six Counties. Although
I am not a farmer I am actively
associated with the farmers of the district, and especially those of the district
which my hon. Friend (Mr. Elliott)
represents in South Tyrone.
I have held close contact with the farming community for a number of years,
and I know that for the past three or
four years the farmers of the entire
country have been passing through a most
difficult time. As a matter of fact, in
some instances farmers have not been
living at all, they have scarcely been existing. Owing to bad crops and bad
prices for their produce, with every other
thing militating against them, they have
suffered a tremendous lot, and I would
suggest to the Government that in
addition to this Derating Bill, which I
hope will be of great benefit, that they
take into consideration the possibility-
I am not sure that this is within the
province of this Parliament, which I
understand is a subordinate Parliamentof cutting the annuities payable to the
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
31 MAY 1929
Land Commission by half, and, if possible, spreading payment over a term of
years in order to tide the farmers over
a most trying and difficult time, possibly
the most difficult time they have had for
years.
I understand a Bill is to be introduced
in connection with motor buses. I may
also suggest to the Government that when
they introduce this Bill they should take
into consideration the very difficult position that the owners of motor buses, and
the drivers and conductors are in. I my.
self, as a magistrate for the county, sit
occasionally at Quarter Sessions in Dungannon. The police force is an excellent
force, and it is their duty to do what is
the will of the legislature here. From
time to time they bring before the court
bus owners, bus drivers, and bus conductors for paltry offences, such as for having
two or three extra passengers on their
buses. Possibly the gentlemen who
framed this Bill do not have to ride in
buses. These bus men have done a considerable service to the rural areas in
running buses all over the country, especially on fair and market days. On a wet
day there may be an old man or an old
woman waiting in the rain for a bus,
and although it is full the conductor,
having a kind heart, may take the extra
passenger. Then when the bus reaches
the town it is stopped by a policeman in
the course of his duty, and the conductor
is brought before the court.
Mr. ELLIOTT: And you would dismiss him.
Mr. STEWART: I would if I could.
The worst feature of the whole thing is
that the fines in these cases are mandatory.
As I have stated at the Sessions at Dungannon, the magistrates are only registering machines for the will of the
Gentlemen sitting opposite. As to emigration, it is near time the Government
stopped this business of training people
for other countries. There is absolutely
no reason, if the Government were active
in providing employment for the youth
of the country, why they should not be
kept here. On the contrary, the Government have gone out of their way to encourage and assist the youth, the blood
and sinew of this land, to leave it.
my mind this is a mistake and the Government will live to regret it.

Mr. McALEER: Though some very
necessary Measures were mentioned in
the King's Speech, it is to be regretted
that matters of very serious consequence
and of paramount importance were omitted. During the debate it was frequently
emphasized that farming is the staple industry of these Six Counties, and except
the special references to derating (which
was made to look like a panacea for all
our troubles), the unfortunate plight of
our struggling farmers was practically
overlooked by the Government side of the
House, except the very sympathetic and
sensible remarks made by the Member for
South Tyrone, and also the hon. Member
for Antrim. The farmers are
on the
verge of bankruptcy, and when unfavourable seasons come their way, and when
only very poor and indifferent prices are
obtained for their cattle and farm produce, trade is crippled, and all branches
of the community suffer. The Rev. T.
M. Johnstone stated: "It is the considered opinion of nearly every business
man that unless some great economic step
is straightway decided on, nothing can
really save the trade and commerce of the
Six Counties."
Captain DIXON: Do you agree with
Rev. T. M. Johnstone?
Mr. McALEER: Well, he would not
sit on these benches if he was here. A
serious and an earnest move should be
made urging the Imperial Parliament to
give a full and complete and comprehensive Measure of land purchase to meet
all classes of holdings, no matter how
held, or how situated. The past two
seasons very seriously affected the farming interest, and even agriculturists
working under the best conditions could
not make ends meet.
I come from the centre of Tyrone, and
I have failed to see where there is prosperity among the farming class. The
derating scheme comes in very useful as a
temporary relief, but as this has been deducted from the transferred account it
may not be a permanent boon to those
engaged in farming pursuits.
It is undesirable to have to get doles
from the British Parliament when in
financial difficulties, and this kind of
assistance is tantamount to out-door
relief. We should try to make our
Government self-supporting. I am entirely in favour of getting all the money
possible from the Imperial Government,
as it will take the predominant partner a
long time to pay back even a tithe of what
was fleeced from Ireland in the way of
excessive taxation, as was proved and
adopted by the Childers Commission.
I would request our Government to
give generous and sufficient grants and
subsidies to increase and improve the
housing accommodation in our towns and
villages, as small, dark, leaky, and unsanitary hovels are absolutely unsuitable
for the proper upbringing of families,
both from physical and moral viewpoints. (Hon. Members. Hear, hear).
I hope the Government will make still
greater efforts to assist in having better
and healthier houses for the workers and
town dwellers, and by so doing they will.
be applying a remedy to this long-standing menace to our moral and physical
welfare. Town tenants and those inhabiting cottages under the Labourers'
Acts should get an opportunity of buying
out these houses and plots, if they so desire. on terms similar to those given to
the farmers under the Land Purchase
Acts. I would appeal to the Prime
Minister to see and get the Imperial
Government to deal liberally with us on
the completion of land purchase, also the
transfer of houses and plots to those
wishing to purchase them on easy terms.
I would earnestly request the Government to assist Secondary Schools in every

possible way. Secondary Teachers should

cannot congratulate the Prime
Minister on the alleged prosperity of the
Six Counties. The number idle and

Mr. McNEILL: I have very little to

Speech I should like to express the

heard the Address proposed by my
learned Friend, the Member for Derry
City (Mr. Murphy). It is a pleasure to
me to see him sit here in this assembly.
I think I can assure the House that he
would adorn any assembly in the land.
It was also a pleasure to hear the seconder
of the Address.
Now, there are only one or two points
to which I should like to draw attention.
I see that no reference was made in the
Speech to the Education Act, or to those
proposals which have now been set on foot
for the purpose of modifying that Act in
some degree. On behalf of a very large
educational interests in
section of
Northern Ireland I would suggest that
all those proposals which have been put
on foot for the purpose of modifying the
Act may be very carefully examined, and
very carefully scrutinized, because if they
have the effect of bringing back the
system which prevailed before the passing
of that Act in 1923-the system of
denominationalism and the denominational spirit in education, then I say
that this Measure, or these suggestions
to modify the Act are very pernicious
indeed. I regard the Act of 1923, which
is founded on a wide democratic basis,
as the best justification for the existence
of this Parliament. Had we still
remained as we were, and sent representatives to the Imperial Parliament at
Westminster, and had no Parliament of
our own, I do not think there would have
been the slightest chance of that magnificent Measure ever seeing the light of the
Statute Book. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
That Measure must be carefully
guarded. I have a letter in my pocket
to-day from an important education
authority in County Derry congratulating me on a recent victory, and he says
that, in his opinion, if that Act is left.
alone and untampered with the result
will be that in five years Northern Ireland will have the best primary education
system of any State in the world, and I
assure the House that I verily believe it.
I am sorry-education is what I am
primarily interested in-there is no
mention of secondary teachers' pensions.
I do not know whether it ought to have
been mentioned in the King's Speech. I
am not sufficiently competent in Parliamentary practice. But I can assure the
House, and all sections to-day, that this
is a most vital question, and that personally I would regard my Parliamentary
career, no matter how brief it may be,
as a complete failure unless something
is done to put secondary teachers, with
regard to their pensions, on a basis corresponding to the basis which prevails in
England. Otherwise the result is that
education in Northern Ireland, which
has advanced immeasurably on the primary side, will recede on the secondary
side. We will not get teachers who will
be willing to accept the small emoluments
which we offer here when they can get
very much larger emoluments across the
water. They will fly our country, and
education will suffer, because if we have
not got competent teachers, men of

we are going to maintain that

it is done indirectly, and if it is going to

extreme, indeed, that they would not enter

obtain from certain of our friends and
supporters a great deal of opprobrium for
entering it. It is, however, a fact that
the redistribution scheme has not given
us the representation to which we are
entitled in the Six Counties. On a proportional representation basis, we are
entitled to seventeen Members; at least
we are entitled to sixteen. I remember
a former Member of this House, Sir
Robert Anderson, telling me that we
were at least entitled to sixteen Members,
and I certainly venture to suggest that
with the increase in the franchise, our
numbers should have been increased.
I think it is a wholly unfortunate thing
that these constituencies have been
divided in the way that they have been.
No doubt, the Prime Minister has

achieved his object, which is to have an

in the community. If you can imagine

One other remark that was made here,

think that remark was made by the Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie).
Mr. BEATTIE: I said he had a multitude of followers.
Mr. McCARROLL: Will anyone take
the figures at the contested elections and
try to tell me where the multitude comes
in? Take the Belfast constituencies. We
find in the Belfast constituencies that the
official Members of the Government party
obtained 69,608 votes. The Members
opposed to the Government party-certainly I do not say that many of them
have my ideas, but at any rate they were
opposed to the Government party-got
81,381. The 69,608 votes for the Government obtained eight seats; the 81,381 votes
obtained five seats, thanks, of course, to
gerrymandering; thanks to the abolition
of P.R., and thanks to the redistribution
of seats, done, of course, to give fair play
to us.
Take the county constituencies that were
contested. The Government party obtained 77,491 votes, and got 10 seats.
Those who were opposed to the official
candidates nominated in the county constituencies got 61,867 votes, and only got
three seats. And yet the Government
party say here that they represent the
great mass of the people. According to
one of the Members who spoke on the opening day, the result of this election
indicates a wonderful wave of loyalty
and enthusiasm for the Government, yet
the results of the voting show that they
have got their enormous strength in this
House on a minority. I merely wish to
make those observations with a view to
correcting, as far as I can at any rate, the
statements that were made here on the
I would venture to go
opening day.
somewhat further, and to say that the
fact that this Government party to-day
has its enormous majority leaves us not
a bit despondent-
The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
Mr. McCARROLL and not a bit
dismayed. We have entered this House,
and as I say, some of us will have earned

Members: Hear, hear.) I have made

I come from a constituency and from a
city where gerrymandering has been
carried out to the most extraordinary
extent in the world, that is, to such an
extent that the majority of the community is in the minority on the municipal council. For over twenty-five years
we have seen the effects of gerrymandering. Coming from that city, I feel bound
to say, on the first occasion on which I
have the opportunity of speaking here,
that we do not regard as final the settlement that has been set up here, which
divides this country into two parts-(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)—and which has
set up this Parliament here and a Parliament in Dublin. Notwithstanding all
that was said by the Prime Minister on
the opening day in relation to the
permanence that is going to be attached in
the next four years to the institutions in
this area, that is, the erection of Royal
Courts of Justice and the completion of
the Parliament House-notwithstanding
all that, we yet have the hope that partition, the dismemberment of this little
island, is not the destiny of it, but that
there is something better for it, and, if
there is not, heaven help it. It is not
going to thrive and prosper under the
present arrangement.
The hon. and learned Member for
Derry (Mr. Murphy) in moving the
Address in reply to the Speech, spoke of
peace and goodwill, and of the fact that
these things were essential for the development of prosperity in the community. We
-I, at least absolutely agree with those

I do not want to say a word further that

justice and fair play.
us here will have anything to gain by our

We say that unless we get them it is

the services. I have mentioned education

The yard
has been dismantled. Is there any hope

The yard
is in his constituency, but I think I am

any hope that the Loans Guarantee Act

Again, I noticed in the Press the other

question.
Might I, in this connection,

I mean Watt's Distillery. I suggest that

desirable in every way. I suggest that

Another matter referred to in the

of legislation in regard to motor vehicles.
Would it be possible in the legislation.
that is to be introduced to revise the

I understand there is a certain grievance
in Northern Ireland in relation to the
commercial
licence duty payable on
motors. What I am told is that a commercial motor weighing 25 cwt. is licensed
at £16. If that motor is 26 cwt. the
licence duty jumps to £30. I do not
know whether that is correct or not, but
it has been so represented to me, and I
wonder if it would be possible in the legislation that is promised to insert a Clause
or a provision that would satisfy the demands of those using commercial motors
in this area.
Another point is housing. I would
like to know why there has been a comparative cessation of house-building in
Derry city, and why, in the schemes that
have been carried out, the houses have been

I understand that an inquiry was held

areas, but should utilise the open spaces
and give the people more healthy surroundings than they have had in the past.
In regard to the unemployment question, while I do not personally represent
the labour point of view, my sympathy is

desire to conclude and to thank the House

Commander CHICHESTER-CLARK:
I wish to join with other hon. Members in
congratulating the mover and seconder of

the Address. I am distinctly glad that
the mover of the Address proved such an
eloquent speaker, and that, at any rate, in
County Derry we have somebody who can
make a speech. The thing that struck
me most as a new Member was the fact
that any of the original Government of
Northern Ireland should be here at all,
or that any of their followers should be
sitting behind them. It would seem to
me that if the Government had had their
deserts, or if they had had committed one
quarter, or one hundredth part of the
crimes that I have heard hurled against
them, they ought to be put in the lethal
chamber and put out of pain as quickly as
possible. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Instead of which, wonderful to relate,
some of us are here, and some of us are
representing the working-classes. There
are other workers besides town workers.
There are, I may say, working-class people
in my constituency, and yet they returned
me unopposed. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
There are two things mentioned in the
Gracious Speech from the Throne that
affect the agricultural community, especially the constituency I have the honour
to represent. One, of course, is the Bill
for the drainage of the Bann. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I welcome that
Bill from the bottom of my heart. Living
in the area which will be drained,
the huge catchment area of over 2,000
square miles, I can assure any hon.
Members who are not cognisant of the
situation there, that when that Bill is
passed and the drainage completed a
wonderful effect will come upon the
dwellers there. We have a pestilent
swamp in the middle of our Six Counties,
and that swamp is increasing year by
year as the drainage in the catchment
area improves. The water is being shot
down more and more quickly, and the
plight of the dwellers in the flooded area
is rapidly becoming worse and worse. I
feel that this measure will benefit everybody. It will certainly benefit constituencies that are represented by a great
many hon. Members opposite.
The next thing that naturally affects
a representative of a farming constituency is the Derating Bill. Speaking as
a new Member, I must say that I heard
a most remarkable statement fall from the
lips of the hon. Member for Pottinger
(Mr. Beattie). He said, or I understood
him to say, that the benefit that the poor
farmers were to receive through derating
was to be passed on to the consumers of
their agricultural produce. I suppose he
means the people who eat their meat and
buy their potatoes. Really, if I may say
so with due modesty, such a statement
just shows to the farming man how little
is understood of his profession and trade.
After all, what is agricultural land? To
the farmer it is the raw material of his
trade. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
It is the tool with which he earns his
money. Would the hon. Member (Mr.
Beattie) opposite, if I may say so, in his
trade-take the blacksmith's trade-rate
that man's anvil or his sledgehammer?
Mr. BEATTIE: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. and gallant Gentleman,
but I did not make the statement he has
attributed to me. I asked were the Government prepared to give any guarantee
to the consumer that the consumer will
get cheaper produce, and the farmer a
better price. I was referring to the
difference between the price paid by the
farmer and charged to the consumer, of
which I have had personal experience.
That was the point I was on.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: The hon.
Member (Mr. Beattie) is a very experienced parliamentarian, and dealing
with a young Member making his maiden
speech I am sure he will extend to him
the courtesy that is always given on such
occasions.
Commander CHICHESTER-CLARK:
If I have said anything to offend the hon.
Member (Mr. Beattie) I beg to withdraw
it. That was only the way I understood
him, and I think from what other hon.
Members have said it is the way they took
it up, too. However, if what he meant
was to have a slap at the middleman I am
entirely on his side. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I do hope that, at any rate,
as far as the derating of agricultural land
and buildings is concerned, we will have
a very unanimous feeling, and that the
Bill will be expedited with all despatch.
One more word-I am afraid I cannot
help referring to the remarks of the hon.

who said he wanted to go into the Free
State. The best statistics in the world as
to the cost of living are those of one's

Another hon. Member referred to the

am inclined to agree with him that there

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I feel

that the Nationalist party, at any rate

Hear, hear.) As far as County Derry is

Mr. MARK: I do not intend to keep
the House for any great length of time.
I would not have spoken at all except for
some remarks made by the hon. Member
for Foyle (Mr. McCarroll). He seeurs
dissatisfied with the manner in which the
county and city of Derry were carved out.
I agree with all the remarks made by the
hon. Member for South Derry (Commander Chichester-Clark).
I represent
a constituency in that county which has
18,401 voters, and over 15,000 are
Unionist voters. The intention of the
Government was to frame a Bill that
would give fair play all round. I think
the cutting up of the city and county of
Derry could not have been done more
fairly to the Opposition than it has been
done.
We have heard very many cures for
the various ills from which the people
of the Six Counties are suffering to-day.
The hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.
Beattie) wants fixed prices. We were
told that fixed prices in Ulster during the
war were a success I would point out
that the fixed prices in those days were
prices on the down grade. If we were
to have fixed prices now they would have
to be on the up grade. The Prime
Minister was right in his reply when he
asked how could we compel the Italian
Government to pay £3 a ton for potatoes
when they buy them from Russia for £1
a ton. Would the Labour Party in
Great Britain agree to fixed prices so far
as potatoes are concerned? Would they
make it compulsory for any Government
to buy potatoes at £3 a ton when they
can be bought in France, Belgium, Germany, or Holland for £2? I do not see
how any Government can enter into the
question of fixing prices unless in war
time.
I am well aware that farmers are
receiving very low prices to-day in the
potato market. We know that farmers
can have a paying crop when they have
five tons to the acre, and a losing crop
when they have seven tons to the acre.
This year the average was well over seven
tons per acre, and that left something
like 12,000 tons of a surplus, which
affected the prices in the market.

With regard to the many Bills
mentioned in the King's Speech, I am
well satisfied. I welcome the Derating
Bill. All land will be derated, and I
hope the Minister of Finance will make
sure that all the lands held in connection
with labourers' cottages under the
Labourers Acts will be derated in the
same way as lands occupied by farmers.
I think that would be only fair to the
agricultural labourers. As to the derating of railways and the benefits which
will accrue therefrom to agriculture, I
know that an experimental scheme has
been in operation for some time. I have
been going over the matter in my own
mind, and I am convinced that derating
should go upon crops produced in
Northern Ireland alone. I mention this
matter so that the Minister of Finance
may give it some thought and see if it
would be better to derate our
produce.
own
In regard to adequate transport facilities I think we are badly off for a change.
If we could get the cross-Channel freights
back to anything like pre-war level the
farmers could compete with their English
brethren on the same terms as in pre-war
days. To-day it takes a great deal more
per ton to put his produce on the market,
especially if you have to go to Sheffield or
Birmingham. Besides, it is a matter of
common knowledge in Belfast that during
last summer lambs sold in Belfast were
short-shipped every Monday night from
June until the month of September.
I
do not blame the Government for this, but
I know that the Ministers of Agriculture
and Commerce will make themselves busy
In order to see what can be done with the
shipping companies about getting better
services for the farmers.
I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture if he could not during the coming
Session or in the next Session introduce
legislation on the lines of the Maxwell Report, which was framed some years ago.
This report contained many recommendations in regard to the growing of flax. If
we had legislation on the basis of that report with its recommendations, flax-growing would get a great fillip in Northern
Ireland.
As regards the Fishery Act that was
assed, I cannot say that that Measure
has given satisfaction in all quarters.
Within the last week I had a complaint
from some gentlemen on the Bann, who
had been in the habit of going out on Sun-

days in a little boat and fishing with a
line and worms. They take objection to
the fact that they have been noticed by
the fishery authorities to abstain from
doing so in the future. In Derry City
last week some gentlemen from the constituency of the hon. Member (Mr.
Murphy) were stopped fishing by the
fishery authorities. I do not say that it
was the recent Act that gave them the
authority, but they are usurping an
authority, and they should be curbed. I
had a letter some time ago from a gentleman in regard to the question of fishing
rights. He states:
Some years ago when fishing on the
River Roe I had forgotten my licence
and was challenged by the water bailiff.
No explanation was of any avail. I was
summoned and brought before the
Limavady bench, and despite the fact
I had shown the licence twice that
same year, and held them for 12 years
previous, I was fined £2. Now sir, is
this the way to encourage tourists to our
shores?
I think that these gentlemen who take
over our rivers for the sake of profit, and
who are really not North of Ireland men
at all, should be kept under control. I
know that many poor fishermen who were
in the habit of fishing in the rivers have
ceased doing so since the increase in the
licence duty was put on. I know that the
whole system of fishery rights in Northern
Ireland is in a complicated state, and I
would like if the Minister of Commerce
could see his way to grant an inquiry into
the working of these Acts. I believe the
outcome of such an inquiry would prove
satisfactory to all parties. Complaints
have been made in regard to the
Education Acts. I should point out that
those who object are in no worse position
than they were previously, and possibly
they are in a much better position.
Mr. BYRNE: I intend to be very
brief in my statement,
as you have
listened to so many speeches. I regret
that we have not more prospects with
regard to the relief of unemployment.
As one representing a working-class constituency I am very much disappointed.
I have read speeches made in this Parliament on unemployment, and complaints
were made from these benches that the
Government had not taken the matter
up seriously. There are hundreds of
people to-day signing on at the Labour
Exchanges for work and can get no work.
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Byrne]
That is an awful state of affairs to exist
in a city like this. Men are calling on
me from day to day saying that they
have signed on at the Labour Exchange
two, three, and up to four years, and
that their time has not come for getting
employment. I am quite aware that the
Government has done a good deal in
giving grants for street construction and
other works, but I think an effort should
be made to give further grants for reconditioning the streets and roads.
We have a road leading from Belfast
to Bangor. There is great motor traffic
on that road. It is agreed by all parties
that motor traffic is coming to stay. I
think it would be a good thing if the
Government widened that road and made
it safe for motor traffic. I think in that
way they would absorb a great many of
the people who are signing on at the
Labour Exchanges. I know many of
these poor people would far rather be
working than looking for what is known
as the dole. There are still a number
of cobble-paved streets in the city of Belfast which could be concreted, and this
would give employment to many people.
It would also, in the end, save a great
deal of money as far as the upkeep of the
streets is concerned.
I sincerely welcome what the Prime
Minister promised in his speech the other
day. He said he would welcome any
suggestions from this side of the House.
I hope and trust that all sections will be
brought together, and that something will
be done to relieve the state of unemployment that exists in this city at the present
time. With regard to agriculture, I
welcome very much this scheme. I know
a great deal about the state of agriculture
in the country. I know that farmers
for the last four or five years have been
losing money. I was sorry to hear some
of our friends on the opposite side saying
that there could be no such thing as fixed
prices. I would agree to an extent with
regard to potatoes, but I think as regards
oats, wheat, and flax, we could have fixed
prices. The Member for Clifton (Major
Hall-Thompson) said that we are not able
to grow the flax in this country that is
required for the linen produced. I
understood that some of the best flax can
be grown here. I know the farmers are
refusing to grow flax because it is not remunerative. I was speaking the other
day to a farmer who every year grew a
quantity of flax, and he says that this
year he will cease to grow it because he
cannot get prices to pay him. If something could be done with regard to wheat,
oats, and flax, it would be a great
encouragement to the farmers of the Six
Counties to cultivate more land.
I know districts where thousands of
acres to-day are under grass, and within
my own memory all that land was cultivated, and hundreds of people were
employed in ploughing, harrowing, shearing, and all that sort of thing. But today there is no employment. I would
much rather see young men trained for
employment in their own country than
being sent away to other countries to look
for work, which to a certain extent is very
uncertain. I sincerely hope something
will be done for the farmer. If we can
have a prosperous farming community it.
will be a great asset to the Six Counties.
With regard to safeguarding, this is one
of the most important matters touching
not only this city but the whole of the Six
Counties. We know that there are many
mills and factories in Belfast, Lurgan,
Portadown, in fact in every district of the
Six Counties, and we know the linen industry has been in a very depressed state
for a long time. If something is not done.
for it the consequence will be very serious.
I do hope that something will be done,
that safeguarding will be applied, and
that this very important industry will be
returned to its former prosperity. Many
thousands of people are dependent on it.
The shipyards are very good, and many
people are employed there, but the
number is nothing when you take the
whole of the Six Counties in comparison
with the number employed in the linen
business. I sincerely hope and trust that
something will be done to relieve the state
of affairs that exists.
I quite agree the Government has done
a good deal with regard to housing, but as
member of the Housing Committee of
the Belfast Corporation I find there are
many people to-day who want houses but
cannot afford to pay the rent charged for
them. I think it would be possible for a
register to be made. These poor people,
who are living in rooms and unhealthy
houses, could be asked to register at a
certain place-I do not care whether it is
at Corporation or Government offices-and
say how they are living and what rent they
could pay.
Then it could be seen if
houses could not be erected which could
be let at rents they could afford to pay.
It has been suggested-it was mentioned

in some of the election speeches-that the
slums should be cleared away. I would
like to see the people living in comfortable, healthy homes. I know plenty of
houses have been erected in healthy districts, but the poor people are not able to
ay the rent of those houses, and until
times get more prosperous and trade improves something should be done with the
dilapidated property in the city in which,
unfortunately, many of the people are
forced to live. I hope the Government

Then education has been referred to. I

upon the Prime Minister, at which Sir

great encouragement in regard to an
Amending Bill being brought in. I say
hey are quite right to get an Amending

suffering. It must be admitted we are
suffering very severely. We have to pay
the tax for the working of the schools, and
we are not able to take the advantage. As
my hon. Friend (Mr. McCarroll) said, we
never will, and never can, take advantage
of those schools.
I was sorry to hear the hon. and
learned Member for the University (Mr.
McNeill) saying he was of the opinion the
Act should be left alone. The Grand
Master of the Orangemen says it should not
be left alone, and I quite agree that it
should not be left alone. We want religion,
and we want our children taught their own
religion. The Prime Minister, in the
course of his speech, explained very fully
that he had not time to include the
Amending Bill in the present Parliamentary programme. I had great hope
that it would be introduced, and that
all parties of every religious denomination would be satisfied with the Amendments made, and that we would all get a
fair share of the rates to which we contribute.
So long as this is denied to us it will be
seen there will be a great deal of dissatisfaction. We are the poor members of
the community, but we did a great deal
for our schools before the Education Act
was passed. We built our schools, and it
is very difficult now for the poor section
of the community to have to contribute to
the rate for schools and derive no benefit.
No wonder there has been delay, as has
been stated by the hon. and gallant Member for Clifton (Major-Hall Thompson),
and that we have not taken advantage of
the Act. It has been stated many times
in this House, and we state it here
again, that we cannot take advantage of
it. Why not give us the privilege which
we claim? It is admitted on all sides
that this is unfair to the Catholic community. We want our children brought
up and taught the religion their forefathers held. We claim equal rights
with others. I sincerely hope this
Amending Bill will be brought in, and
that it will include all classes of the
community no matter at what altar they
worship.
I do not think there is anything more
that I can say. I could only repeat what
some other Members on this side of the
House have said. As a new Member of
of this Parliament, as has been stated by
some of my friends here, I say that we
only claim and ask what is reasonable,
and I appeal to the Government to give
us justice and fair play. Let it be sent
across the country to Irishmen, no matter
where they live, that we in this Province
are getting justice and fair play. It will
add to the trade and prosperity of this
State, and will be of immense benefit to
the people generally.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Street Trading (Regulation) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time"
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The object of this
measure is to confer on local authorities
the power of control over street traders.
Hon. Members are aware that for many
years past it has been the custom for
itinerant traders to attend at provincial
towns on market days and erect stalls
from which they sell their goods. Hon.
Members will appreciate that, with the
advent of the motor car and the cheaper
facilities afforded, this practice has increased enormously within recent years.
At present, the local authorities have absolutely no control whatever over these
traders, and they can, without regard
to the convenience of the public, or the
rights of the local traders, set up their
stalls when and where they like. The
result has been serious obstruction in
many cases, resulting in inconvenience to
the public using the markets and the
streets.
For some time past representations
have been made to the Government by
the various local authorities, either individually, or through their representative body, the General Council of Municipal Authorities of Northern Ireland,
asking that power should be conferred
on the local authorities to regulate this
form of trading. One of the argumentsapart from those I have already referred
to-has been the great expense which is
caused to the local rates by reason of
the litter and refuse that was left behind
by those traders which have to be removed at the expense of the local ratepayers. The Government have come to
the conclusion that the request made by
the local authorities is both desirable and
reasonable. I may point out that the
Bill in no way interferes with the general
principle that an itinerant trader has a
right to trade where he likes, subject to
his conforming to the reasonable regulations laid down by the local authority,
and here I would like to emphasise that
these traders will be protected against
captious or unreasonable restrictions being
made by reason of the fact that before
the regulations are made, they will have
to come before the Ministry of Home
Affairs for confirmation or amendment as
the case may be.
Before dealing with the Clauses I should
also point out that these Regulations do
not apply to the trader who moves about
the country calling upon his customers and
stopping from time to time on the road to
sell his wares, such as the ice cream merchant or the travelling butcher.
Let me now come to the Clauses of the
Bill. The effect of Clause 1 is, that after
the 1st January next, no trader will be
allowed to sell goods from a stationary stall
in urban district or town governed by
any
town commissioners unless he has first obtained a licence from the local authority.
While the Bill applies only to urban
districts and towns governed by town commissioners, at the same time, hon. Members
will realise that in certain rural areas there
are most important market towns which
have not commissioners, and in these circumstances we propose that it shall be open
to any rural district council to have the Act
made applicable to any town under its
jurisdiction. This provision will be found
in Clause 11.
as
As regards county boroughs, such
Belfast and Derry, we propose to give them
power, if they so desire, to apply to the
Ministry to put into operation the Clauses
of this Bill.
Street Trading Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
I
With regard to Clause 2, this Clause sets
out the procedure for obtaining a licence,
and it also sets out the circumstances under
which a local authority can either refuse to
grant or refuse to revoke a licence.
think hon. Members will see that these
conditions are only reasonable and proper.
I would draw the special attention of the
House to the safeguards which are inserted
in the Bill with a view of protecting any
street trader against unfair or capricious
administration of the Bill by any local
authority. For example, before a local
authority can refuse to grant a licence
they must allow the applicant to appear before the authority, and thus enable him to
state his reasons why the application should
be granted. It will be found by reference
to Clause 5 that if a local authority, having
heard the applicant, still refuses to grant
a licence, the applicant can then go before
a court of summary jurisdiction, consisting
of a resident magistrate, where his case will
be dealt with.
In Clauses 3 and 4 it will be found here
that the licence fee is merely a nominal one
of 5s, and will last for one year unless
revoked by misconduct of the holder. It,
therefore, cannot be suggested that the
local authorities are endeavouring to make
a profit out of the administration of this
Bill.
Clause 6 gives a power to the local
authorities to make by-laws regulating the
conditions under which street trading shall
be carried out in the future. For example,
they may prescribe the days and the times
in which trading under these licences may
be carried out, and they can allocate the
general arrangement of the stalls and their
number. They can also prescribe for the
conditions under which articles of food are
to be exposed with a view to ensuring that
they will not be kept under unsanitary
conditions. Before the by-laws come into
operation the usual notices will have to be
given by the local authorities of their intention to make such an application in
order to give ample opportunity to the
various interested parties to lodge any objections with the Ministry, when an
inquiry will be held as to whether or not
the by-laws should be passed in their entirety or in an amended form.
Clause 7 gives power to the local authorities to recover from any of these traders
any expense that they may be put to in removing litter or rubbish left behind by the
trader.
Clause 8 sets out the penalties for
breach of the Act.
a

ditions, that local authorities should have
sole control of all markets.

TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): It is very gratifying to know the approval that has been
expressed from all sides of the House as
to the policy of this Bill. It is generally
and universally recognised that street
trading ought to be reasonably and properly
controlled and that the proper authorities
to exercise that control are the local authorities in the different parts of our area.
While the Bill, in the first instance, simply
gives power to urban districts and those
towns where there are town commissioners,
if hon. Members will refer to Clause 11 of
the Bill they will find that rural district
councils may, on application, if they think
fit, apply the Bill in their areas, so that
the hon. Member's (Mr. O'Neill) constituency, which he indicated in his reference
to Kilkeel and Castlewellan, would come
within the provisions of the Bill at the
option of the rural district council. That
is a matter we have anticipated.
In reference to the difficulty the hon.
Member (Mr. O'Neill) raised about squares
and diamonds in the middle of many of our
market towns, some of those squares are
owned by private individuals and are not
vested in the town at all. Very often no
authority is exercised over those squares by
the local authority, but it may be of
interest to the House, and particularly to
hon. Members on either side who have mentioned the matter, to know that there are
powers under this Bill as drafted and as it
appears before the House that will enable
local authorities to acquire, compulsorily if
need be, the interests of those who have
been receiving tolls or money in respect of
the markets which have been used in their
towns. There are quite a number of those,
and the machinery that is provided under
the Bill is tried machinery so far as the
compulsory acquisition of land or property
is concerned. It is simplified and modified
to a considerable extent by allowing agreement to be reached if possible, and failing
agreement an arbitration will be held and
fair compensation paid.
With respect to the charge that is being
made for the acquisition of the licence, the
House will understand that there are a
great number of people engaged in this
street trading simply because, by reason of
the industrial upheaval, they have not been
able to find work. Many of them, too, are
disabled ex-Servicemen who are trying to
earn an honest livelihood by selling wares
in the market places and streets of our
towns. I am sure hon. Members, when

Noxious Weeds Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Question: "That the Bill be now read a
Second time," put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.
Noxious Weeds Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The main object
of this Measure is to transfer to the police
the duty of securing the destruction of
noxious weeds at the proper
Heretime.
tofore this duty has been discharged by
about fourteen temporary inspectors appointed each summer by the Ministry of
Agriculture. It is, however, physically
impossible for any reasonable number of
inspectors to go round the farms in
Northern Ireland and see that the weeds
are destroyed. For example, in 1927 the
inspectors could visit only 7,715 farms,
whereas there are 104,000 agricultural
holdings in Northern Ireland. Similarly,
in 1928, 10,648 farms, or only 10 per cent.
of the holdings, could be inspected.
It is obvious, therefore, that the police.
force could carry out a much more comprehensive inspection and secure a more
through compliance with the provisions of
the Act than is possible under the existing
arrangements. It should be mentioned
that the weeds concerned are ragwort,
thistle, dock and ox-eye daisy, which require no expert knowledge to identify, so
that no question of technical qualifications
arises.
The present Act is unsatisfactory in
another respect in that the weeds to be
destroyed in the different counties are not
always the same. For example, in the
County of Londonderry ragwort is not considered a noxious weed. This has created
an anomalous position, because farmers in
the adjoining counties of Antrim and
Tyrone are compelled to cut ragwort while
their neighbours in County Londonderry
are free to let the weed multiply. The
seeds can be wafted all over the place and
give unpleasant Christmas boxes and
birthday presents to neighbouring counties.
It will be obvious that weeds legislation
in a comparatively small area such as
Northern Ireland should be uniform, and
it is, therefore, proposed to have this done
in the present Bill.
With regard to fines, the 1909 Act provided a penalty not exceeding five pounds
for the first offence and not exceeding ten
pounds for a second or subsequent offence.
In actual practice, however, the fines inflicted have been so small that in many
cases it would be cheaper to pay the fine
than incur the cost of cutting the weeds.
For instance, last season the fines imposed
ranged from 6d to 10s. Quite clearly
penalties of this description are calculated
to bring the legislation into disrepute. It
is accordingly proposed in this Bill to provide that the penalty shall be £1, or any
greater sum not exceeding £3 for the first
offence, and £2, or any greater sum not
exceeding £5 for the second or subsequent
offence.
Clause 3 (2) of the Bill gives the Ministry
the necessary powers to enter lands and
destroy weeds where such destruction cannot be otherwise secured. Obviously,
however, these powers would only be exercised in exceptional cases where there was
no other remedy. Finally, Clause 4 provides that no prosecution can be instituted without the consent of the Ministry
of Agriculture. This Clause ensures that
no farmer will be brought into Court until
his case has been fully reviewed by the
Ministry. The Bill has been approved by
the Ministry's Consultative Committee
representing County Committees of Agriculture and by the Farmers' Union.
beg to move.

JOINERS' STRIKE AT QUEEN'S
ISLAND.
Mr. GRANT (by Private Notice) asked
the Minister of Labour whether he will
make a statement as regards the position
affecting the joiners' strike, which has now
been proceeding for a considerable time.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have been in close touch,
since the strike began, with both the employers and the workers' representatives,
and I regret to say that so far no way has
been found to end a dispute which I am
very disappointed should have occurred
here.
I do not think that it is in the public
interest that I should say more at the
moment than to express the hope that
the strike may be brought to an end at an
early date, and I have reason to fear
greatly that serious damage will be done
to the shipbuilding industry in Belfast if
the strike is prolonged.

The CHAIRMAN: Before entering on
Committee of Supply it may be helpful to
new Members of the House if I indicate
to them for their convenience, what the
procedure is. When we take up the
first of the Estimates belonging to any
particular Ministry is the time to
discuss the general policy of that Ministry.
The reason for that is that the Minister's
salary figures in that first Estimate, and
his salary is supposed to cover all the
activities of the Ministry. It affords an
opportunity for criticism of the Ministry
as a whole. When we take the subsequent Estimates of that Ministry, discussion must be confined to the details of the
particular Estimate under review. I
hope that may be of some use to new Members who desire to embark on a discussion
of the policy in relation to the Ministry
whose Vote we are about to examine.

on
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): Northern Ireland is a country of small holdings depending primarily on agriculture and
producing mainly for an export market.
During the year the Ministry has completed and published a survey on the
agricultural output of Northern Ireland,
a work which has received high praise
from the English and Scottish Press.
Arising out of this survey of production,
I would like to draw attention to one or
two important facts which must be borne
in mind when considering agricultural
policy and the development of the
industry.
was
The total value of the produce sold off
Northern Ireland farms in 1925
£15,000,000, and is greater than any
other single industry. Of this amount
£12,000,000, or 78 per cent., represents
the value of live stock produce. Each of
the principal groups of animal produce,
namely, live stock, eggs and poultry, and
milk and butter, exceeds the total value
of the output of farm crops. These facts
explain why, since the inception of the
Ministry, we have continued by means of
education, experiments and demonstrations and by legislative means to lay
emphasis on the development and improvement of our live stock and live stock
products.
The survey of our agricultural output
also reveals that farms of 50 acres and
under carry 68 per cent. of the milch cows,
per cent. of the calves, 62 per cent. of
the pigs, and 76 per cent. of the poultry.
These figures afford ample justification for
the Ministry's policy of concentrating on
the small farmers, particularly in the hilly
and more backward districts. Our policy
has been to pay special attention to early
maturity and quality in the production of
heef, mutton, and pork, higher yields of
milk and butter fat in the case of dairy
cows, and in the case of poultry, to larger
egg records and an improved size of egg.
I should like to take this opportunity
of giving you a brief review of the substantial progress which has been made.
Improved milk and beef yields depend in
the first place upon improving the type of
cattle. The most effective means of
attaining this end is by using better sires.
The Live Stock Breeding Act and the
premium or subsidy bull schemes are the
means towards this end. There have been
criticisms as to the severity of the Bull
Licensing Act, mainly from persons whose
bulls have been rejected. All that need
be said in reply to such criticism is that
far more complaints are made about the
leniency of the Ministry's standard than
its severity. I am perfectly satisfied that
the bull licensing work is, and will continue to be, productive of much lasting
good. Praise from our competitors is a
sure indication that we are succeeding.
During the past two years the British and
Agricultural Press has paid tribute after
tribute to the improvement in quality
and in early maturity of our cattle, this
continued improvement they attribute
entirely to our premium and licensing
schemes.
Now as to the subsidised bulls which
through the medium of the county agricultural committees, the Ministry is
responsible under its various schemes for
placing throughout Northern Ireland.
It will suffice, I think, to ask your consideration of the following figures. There
is one subsidised bull for every 2,168 cows
in England and Wales, for every 604 in
Irish Free State, for every 491 in Scotland, and for every 434 in Northern
Ireland.
These figures afford ample testimony to
the fact that we are forging ahead at a
more rapid rate than any other Agricultural Department in the British Isles.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Before I
leave this particular aspect of the problem may I mention that, in accordance
with the Ministry's policy of bringing its
work down to the smallest and most
struggling of our farms, 265 bulls have
been placed, through the county agricultural committees, in the mountainous or
poor districts. Provided the owners keep
the bulls in good condition during a
period of three years, the animals will
have cost them nothing by the end of that
period.
Hon. Members may ask how do we
know that this work is improving the
quality of our cattle. To anyone who
doubts I would say, ask any British salesmaster who handles our exports, and who
has had experience of our cattle during
the past ten years. The British salesmaster's estimate on a conservative basis
is that our export cattle have improved
in value by £5 per head. On this con-

You have all heard the criticism
that milk is being driven out of the
country, and of the mythical heavy
milch COWS that used to exist.
Such complaints are on
with
the statements
of how much better
life was in the "good old days, " but when
we really visualise the good old days there
are few, if any, of us who would like to
go back to those days. The stories of the
wonderful cows that once existed are like
the stories of the wonderful men and the
degeneration which has followed-when
submitted to the test they fail. It has been
established beyond question that the average man to-day could not be crushed into
the armour worn by his alleged superior
ancestors. So it is with the dairy cow;
every test that can be devised shows the
present-day cow to be superior to her
ancestors. Whenever we succeed in
establishing a Milk Recording Society in
a hitherto undeveloped district, we find
milk yields far below those of the more
progressive areas.
Progress is being made in the establishment of Milk Recording Societies, and farmers are becoming alive to the importance
of breeding only from their good yielding
cows, and also of feeding suitable rations.
In 1921 there were six Milk Recording
Assosiations, and there were 1,244 cows
recorded, and in 1928 there were 66 associations and 12,607 cows recorded. The
average yield of recorded cows in 1922
was 553 gallons, and in 1928 was 652
gallons. There will, I hope, be 70 associations this year. Considerable progress
has been made, but when we consider that
only 12,000 cows out of a total of 274,000
are being recorded it surely indicates that
farmers are not taking full advantage of
this scheme.
Hon. Members will be glad to know
that the number of registered dairy shorthorn bulls subsidised by the Ministry and
county committees of agriculture shows a
very substantial increase from 79 in 1922
to 192 in 1928.
The survey of our agricultural output
to which I referred shows that in 1927
our ploughed area was less than half what
it was in 1861. Notwithstanding the
fact that our acreage under oats and
potatoes has declined to such a great extent, our total output has been increased.
Could a greater tribute be paid to the
application of scientific knowledge and
experiments? Let me illustrate this with
the figures for potatoes:-In the ten-year
period 1857-1866 there were 260,000 acres
of potatoes, and the yield was 871,000
tons; and in the period 1917-1926 there
were only 168,000 acres, but the yield
was 1,000,000 tons. During the past two
years very gratifying progress has been
made in the development of our forestry
work. The Ministry's aim is to secure
gradually four centres each of 10,000
acres in districts where land is suitable
for forestry purposes, and to work to a
programme of clearing and planting
1,000 acres each year. When the
Ministry was established in 1922 we possessed 3,845 acres. Until 1927 no
further land was purchased owing to the
fact that the prices asked were prohibitive
for forestry purposes. The policy of
waiting has proved highly successful, as
now the Ministry is being approached
and offered suitable land at economic
prices. Since 1927 the Ministry has
procured 7,959 additional acres, and
negotiations are practically completed for
the purchase of a further 1,475 acres.
When these negotiations are completed
the Ministry will possess 13,279 acres of
forestry land.
At the moment we have actual possession of 11,804 acres, of which 4,700 have
been planted or are under trees. Last
year we planted 800 acres, and we expect
that from now onwards we will continue
to plant at our maximum rate of approximately 1,000 acres per annum. Up to
the end of March, 1929, we have planted
approximately 6,000,000 trees. During
the past two years 101 persons have
availed themselves of the Ministry's
scheme whereby farmers who wish to
plant on a small scale are supplied with
suitable trees at a reduced price.
this purpose 127,000 trees have been
supplied to farmers.
For
I have already indicated that education
is the only sound basis upon which to
build agricultural development, and I
should like to give Members some particulars of the progress made. The
foundation for the higher agricultural
education is the winter agricultural
classes. Each county instructor conducts
annually at two centres within his area
classes for farmers' sons and daughters,
as the case may be, in agriculture, horticulture, dairying and poultry keeping.
Ministry of Agriculture.
Estimates-

4 JUNE 1929
In 1921 there were 46 classes with 619
students, and in 1928 there were 66
classes with 1,043 students. Satisfactory
though this progress may be, it still falls
far short of what it might be. The
Ministry may provide the classes, but it
cannot force farmers to send their sons
and daughters.
At present when the need for keeping
abreast of modern developments is becoming more and more pressing, I would
appeal to farmers, and particularly to
their wives, to be more generous to those
of their sons and daughters who are to
remain on the land, and, in particular,
to avail themselves of the opportunities
which these winter classes provide. They
are timed for a period of the year when
their sons and daughters can best be
spared from farm work, and it is shortsighted policy-and I would go as far as
to say suicidal policy-to prevent these
young folk from obtaining the benefit of
the education which is provided for them.
We have in Northern Ireland three
farm schools or colleges-the Greenmount
Agricultural College for boys, and the
Ulster Dairy School and the North-West
Agricultural School both reserved for
girls.
of
Prior to the Ministry's taking over control, the majority of girls attending the
Ulster Dairy School at Cookstown were
drawn from outside the area constituting
Northern Ireland. For a number
sessions past, however, all the students in
training at the school have been Northern Ireland girls. There is accommodation for 50 students, and there are 49
students at the current session. There is
a waiting list of 45 Northern Ireland
applicants.
Of those who have been at the school 50
per cent. returned to their homes-I may
say we want as many as possible to return
to their homes-30 per cent. obtained
posts as instructors, teachers, poultry or
dairy maids, etc. 16 per cent took up
non-agricultural employment, and 4 per
cent. emigrated. Perhaps some of those
who took up non-agricultural employment
are getting married, because a great
number of the ladies from the school get
married. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Before the Ministry assumed control of
the North-West Agricultural School,
Strabane, a considerable proportion of the
places were filled by girls residing outside
Northern Ireland. Since 1925, however,
all the students have been Northern Ireland girls. The school accommodates 24
students, and there are 23 in attendance
at the current session. The school serves
as a feeder to the Ulster Dairy School.
Of those who have been at the school
85 per cent. returned to their homes, 9
per cent. obtained agricultural posts, 4
per cent. took up non-agricultural employment, and 2 per cent. emigrated.
At Greenmount Agricultural and Horticultural College in 1922 we had only
accommodation for 25 students, and had
only 6 in residence. The Ministry enlarged the building and provided accommodation for 50 students, and there are
39 students at the current session, all of
whom are holders of scholarships from
County Committees of Agriculture. The
college is managed by the Antrim County
Committee, and the purpose of the college
is to train boys who intend to return to
their farms.
Of those who have passed through the
college 75 per cent. returned to farms,
17 per cent. obtained agricultural posts,
6 per cent emigrated, and 2 per cent. took
up non-agricultural employment. Therefore the cry that we do not train boys for
work on the farms is not correct so far as
Greenmount Agricultural College is concerned.
The Faculty of Agriculture at the
University, the entire cost of which is
borne by this Ministry, continues to make
excellent progress. This session there are
29 students pursuing the four years'
course for a degree in agriculture. Up to
June, 1928, ten students completed their
course and secured their degree. All of
these students, with one exception, have
received appointments. Five received
appointments under our own Ministry, 1
from the Colonial Office-he received a
very good travelling position-1 from
Imperial Chemicals, 1 from Leeds University, and one student is managing a farm
in Northern Ireland. No one can say we
are not doing our best to educate pupils
to work on the farms and to become good
and useful citizens of Northern Ireland.
We have had to bring on a few extra
people on account of the forestry increase.
We have had to put on some more foresters
and also some more men as potato inspectors because of the grading, which we have
found most useful. The addition to the
staff in the forestry department is one

Just before the end of the last Parliament the House made provision for relieving unemployment by the improvement of
roads and drainage. That seems to have
