Mr. HEALY: I beg to propose the reduction of this estimate by £100. The
Minister of Agriculture (Sir Edward
Archdale) has given us a very interesting
statistical account of the work of his Department for the past year, and I am sure
that on both sides of the Committee we
shall read the report in Hansard with a
great deal of interest. If statistics could
prove that farming is in a prosperous condition I have not the least doubt that
the officials of the Ministry of Agriculture
could make an excellent case. But, unfortunately, we who live in the country and
are close to actualities know that, however
rosy a picture the Minister may paint by
means of statistics, the fact is that agriculture is not in a thriving condition. I
think it will be admitted by hon. Members on both sides of the Committee that
the farming community have not had a
worse period for many years than that
which closed in 1927, and the last year,
notwithstanding a slight improvement,
has not been at all of a satisfactory
character.
The Ministry of Agriculture is one of
the Departments in which one would like
to find something to praise, because there
are more people depending upon agriculture in Northern Ireland-and indeed in
all parts of Ireland-than in all other industries combined. But I find that the
Ministry of Agriculture estimate is at the
back of the book, figuratively and in
reality. It is taken behind the Prisons
Vote, behind the Police Vote, and behind
every other service in Northern Ireland.
If you take into account the fact that
more people are employed on the land in
the Six Counties than there are in all the
combined industries you will see how very
essential it is that the Government should
de ote all their energies to the encourageinent and helping of agriculture in every
possible way.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: Hear,
hear.
Mr. HEALY: But if you contrast
the amount of financial aid that has been
given, say, to shipbuilding in Belfast with
the monetary help that has been given to
agriculture in the Six Counties, you will
find that it bears practically no proportion
or an infinitesimally small proportion. I
find that the Government have guaranteed
loans to shipbuilding in Belfast to the extent of £12,000,000. That is, the whole
of Northern Ireland, including the land,
has been put in pawn to relieve the shipbuilding industry. I do not complain, if
that be necessary, but I say that if it be
necessary to extend a helping hand to
shipbuildng to that extent then the farming industry ought to have been treated
in a much more generous way than is evident from this estimate.
Linen may be, and is, a very important
industry, but again it bears no proportion
to the importance of agriculture. You
have given to the linen publicity
campaign a sum of £17,500, and an
additional amount of £2,000 for linen research. Again, if you compare that with
the meagre sum you have given for cattle
replacement within the last few years you
will find that it is in the proportion of
about £100 to 1s. Therefore, I do not
think the Government are devoting the
attention to agriculture that that important industry ought to receive. The item
for replacement of livestock in the present
estimate is only a small sum of £9,873.
We know that a great many farmers have
suffered losses in the past few years, and
this is a wholly inadequate sum for the
purpose it is intended to cover. The
figures that the Minister of Agriculture
has given you this afternoon deal too
much with cattle. You cannot restore
prosperity to agriculture merely by driving the people off the land and replacing
them by cattle, even cattle of a superior
breed. The interests of human beings
come before cattle or any other interest.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: Hear,
hear.

It is a very different matter making an
experiment for the benefit of the farmers,
testing out different things, whether seeds,
manures, different processes, and everything that modern science can suggest for
the benefit of agriculture-testing them
in a scientific way and trying to put these
results before the farmers for their own
benefit and then let practical men adopt
them. I do not know what benefit it
would be to farmers if this whole Ministry
were wiped out. I believe it would be a
great detriment to them. It is not every
experiment that proves successful.
great many things must be tried and may
prove failures. The Ministry of Agricul
ture enables farmers to avoid the result
of these failures. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). If farmers had to undertake these
experiments themselves they might have
their whole crop wasted by an experiment
proving a failure. They avoid all that by
having these things tested as far as they
can be tested by the Department. It is
then put to the service of farmers and
tested out in practice. The farmers,
whether they know it or not, all over the
country get the benefit of the Ministry of
Agriculture experiments.
There is one aspect that occurs to me
and is very serious for the farmers. I
remember years ago when one of our most
profitable sources of litigation at the
sessions was our civil bills brought by
farmers for breach of warranty of
seeds. Farmers bought seeds and
sowed them and no crop would appear.
Then an action would be brought
against the vender of the seeds by
the farmer, who nearly always failed,
because the seed vendors could nearly all
bring up men to whom they had sold
seed from the same bag, which produced
a great crop. Now, we never hear of that
class of case, because of the care with
which the Ministry of Agriculture looks
after the vendor of seeds. Such a thing

We pay in the present year £216,000
here in these Ministry of Agriculture
estimates for the benefit of farmers-not
loans but money paid out of our resources
for the benefit of the farmer, and this
House votes that money with the object
of spending it for the benefit of farmers
in Northern Ireland. There may be different ideas as to how the money should
be spent and as to the results of it, but
there is no doubt about the anxiety
of Members of this House to spend

farming industry and that it should
be spent in the best way possible.
is easy to criticise the way the money

It is easy to say that the interests of the
people should be above those of cattle,
but we are not trying to establish large
grazing ranches in Northern Ireland for
the purpose of driving out the people.
One has only to look at the country to
see that it is quite unsuitable for grazing
ranches. We know that cattle will be
raised here. We know there are mixed
farms on which cattle will be raised, and
we are doing what we can to help to improve the breed of cattle, and to help
our people to make more money out of
cattle than they are doing.
I do agree that everything that we can
do should be done to see that the farmers
get a proper return for their work-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-and to see that
there is not such a difference between
the price paid to the farmer, say for potatoes when they are sold on his farm, and
the price paid by the consumer in the
large towns. The more attention we can
pay to that the better; everybody is

subject some time ago, and witnesses were

difficult thing to interfere with farmers.
No doubt, there is a great depression in

a Government cannot interfere with that
we do what we can to see that the loss
is as little as possible between the time

hands of the consumer.
There is considerable activity to get more for the
farmer, and to minimise the loss as far
as it can be humanly minimised.

MINISTRY OF COMMERCE.

Mr. O'NEILL: Before the Minister
commences his speech I should like to ask
if the same procedure is to be adopted on
this and the following Estimate as was
adopted yesterday; that is, may we discuss both Estimates when dealing with
the question of policy.
The CHAIRMAN: When the first Estimate of any Ministry is introduced, provided that the main Estimate includes the
Minister's salary, which is supposed co
cover all the activities of the Ministry, it
affords an opportunity of surveying the
entire field of policy.
Mr. O'NEILL: Would it not be possible to allow discussion of the items in
the second Estimate, when dealing with
the question of policy on the first Estimate?
The CHAIRMAN: What I desire to
do, as I am sure the Committee realises,
is to be helpful as far as I can. It will
be observed that I wish policy and detail
to be kept separate, the reason being the
obvious one that you cannot mix policy
and detail, and go from policy to detail
and back to policy without causing confusion. I can quite perceive the hon.
Member's difficulty, and I will be as indulgent as I can if the Committee will be
content to be guided by me.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): In introducing the Estimates for the Ministry of Commerce on
this occasion, I hope the older Members
will bear with me if, for the benefit of
those who have not hitherto sat on this
Committee, I explain in some detail the
organisation and functions of the Ministry, even if in doing so I may go over
ground already covered on similar occasions in the past.
At the outset I should, perhaps, explain that the Ministry of Commerce has
no exact prototype in Great Britain. In
Great Britain functions spread over a
number of departments have, in our case,
been grouped under the control of a single
Ministry. The necessity for compression
in this way is, of course, obvious in the
case of the smaller area, but, as I should
like to impress upon the Committee,
compression, while it ensures economy of
administration, does not render the problems arising more easily soluble than
would be the case if the whole of the
Ministry's activities were devoted to the
administration
of only one or two
Services.
5 JUNE 1929
Supply-

Committee
all that in point of fullness and expedition
the commercial intelligence service now
enjoyed by our traders is of substantial
benefit to them, and is at least equal to
that in any country in the world.
In the Ministry of Commerce is combined a great part of the functions discharged by the Board of Trade, the
Department of Overseas Trade, the
Ministry of Transport and the Fisheries
Department of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries in Great Britain.
Such a combination of functions has,
perhaps, made it difficult for the average
member of the public to form a full conception of the Ministry's work. Even
at present, instances often arise in which
inquirers express surprise in finding that
some matter in which they are interested,
falls within the field of the Ministry's
activities. With these prefatory remarks, I shall now pass to the work of
the two branches of the Ministry in some
detail.
The Commerce, Economic, and Fisheries
Branch discharges the functions of the
Board of Trade in so far as they are
directly related to industry and commerce
and of the Department of Overseas Trade.
It has also inherited the duties previously
devolving upon the Department of Agriculture and Technical Instruction for Ireand in respect of Northern Ireland
Fisheries. There are various ways in
which a Government Department can
*rve trade and commerce; one method is
to supplement by financial assistance the
fforts made by industries themselves to
follow certain lines of development which,
without assistance, they might be unable
to attack. This method, as I shall
presently show, has not been neglected by
the Ministry, although it is one to which
recourse can only be made in exceptional
circumstances. Another method which
can be and, I think, is being made equally
effective, is by helping our traders to procure business where, with their more
limited channels of information, they
might not be able to procure it themselves.
The means which we have employed to
this end are, first, the establishment of the
closest possible liaison with the Department of Overseas Trade, and through it
with officers of His Majesty's Consular,
Commercial, Diplomatic, and Trade Commissioner services throughout the world.
This enables us promptly to bring to the
notice of Ulster firms interested in export
trade every matter, be it a trade opening,
something of moment in regard to the
market conditions, a change in the tariff
or tariff regulations, or, in fact, anything
directly bearing on trade with a particular country. There can be no doubt at
ex-
Another way in which the Ministry has
been able to render assistance is by placing our exporters in touch with efficient
and reputable representatives in overseas
markets and vice versa. To discharge
these functions properly the Ministry has
compiled what is called a trade index of
Northern Ireland manufacturers,
porters, and agents, classifying these
under the heads of their various interests,
not only as regards the commodities in
which they trade, but also as regards the
particular countries in which they are or
might be interested. With this index as
a basis the Ministry is able to disseminate
the information it procures in an effectively
systematic manner. The Committee will
not assume, however, that the initiative
in all these matters can invariably come
from the Ministry. I may say that while
endeavouring to satisfy the collective requirements of the industries of the Province the Ministry is always ready to
assist, where possible, the individual
trader in securing any specific information
he may desire.
The Committee will naturally expect me
to say something in regard to the Ministry's policy towards the linen industry.
The problems with which our linen manufacturers are faced are serious and not
likely to be easily overcome. There is
the shortage of raw material, a decreased
use of linen goods and the increasingly
intensive foreign competition in our principal markets, in which the situation has
been further complicated by changes in
fashion and the advent of a competitive
fabric in artificial silk. In the matter of
raw material, prior to the war almost unlimited quantities of Russian flax were
procurable at prices which enabled our
manufacturers to place the finished fabric
on the market at a price relatively cheap
as compared with cotton and other competitive fabrics. The industry now is
compelled to cast around for alternative
sources of supply, which, however, can
with difficulty ever become as satisfactory
in the matter of price as was the case with
Russia.
A solution is being sought along the
lines of evolving and bulking a series of
strains of pedigree flax suitable to the
varying conditions of those parts of the
Empire offering the possibility of flax cul-
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
tivation on a commercial scale. Work
towards this end, as most of the Committee will know, began several years ago
in the evolution and bulking by the Linen
Industry Research Association, at Lambeg, of the J.W.S. strain of pedigree flax.
Even at that early stage the Ministry's
assistance was extended in the form of
annual grants to the association. When
a sufficient quantity of J.W.S. seed had
been bulked by the association, efforts
were directed towards securing the financial co-operation of the Imperial Government in establishing a body adequately
equipped in the district in England best
adapted to the successful conduct of such
operations to carry on bulking on a commercial scale. These resulted in a body
known as the Flax Industry Development
Society, being constituted in 1925 for this
purpose.
Increasingly large parcels of pedigree
seed have been distributed each year to
those parts of the Empire where conditions offered the greatest prospect of introducing flax cultivation. Amongst the
countries to which seed has been distributed by the society are Canada, New
Zealand, and South Africa. It became
evident at an early stage that something
more was required, namely, the provision
of means whereby the flax-straw itself
could be turned into the marketable commodity, fibre, or, in other words, the
evolution of the best method of pulling,
retting, and scutching under the conditions obtaining overseas. An attempt to
solve these later difficulties is now foreshadowed by the scheme formulated by
the Linen Industry Research Association,
towards which financial assistance from
the Empire Marketing Board is being
sought. The scheme at the moment is
awaiting the consideration of the Empire
Marketing Board, with whom the Northern Government has indicated its willingness to co-operate financially.
the
The second part of the problem to which
I have referred, namely, the problem of
finding and developing a market for linen
outside our own shores, is also one towards
which the Ministry has contributed substantial financial assistance. As
Committee will be aware, the United
States is by far our most important overseas customer for linen goods. Prior to
the war Ulster linen might almost be considered supreme in that market. Following the post-war boom, however, the sale
of such goods in the United States showed
a marked decline, and while this was n
part attributable to a change in fashion
and the advent of competitive fabrics, it
was also partly due to the challenge to
our ascendancy from foreign competitors,
such as Belgium, Czecho-Slovakia, and
France. The economic conditions obtaining in these competing countries enabled
their manufacturers to place their
products on the market at a price often
considerably less than was possible to
home manufacturers, and coupled with
this they displayed commendable initiative
in the evolution of new designs, colour
schemes, and finishing methods. Our
Ulster manufacturers are dealing energetically with these new features and the
Ulster product, in addition to its longstanding superiority in the matter of
quality, can now be said to rank in the
matter of design with the products of
even our most progressive competitors.
This digression on the matter of design
has, perhaps, led me away from what I had
intended to say in regard to the efforts
that are being made to push the sale of
Ulster linen goods in every important
centre throughout the United States and
the Empire. To assist a publicity campaign organised along modern lines the
Ministry has already contributed a sum
approximately to £35,000 which, coupled
with the contributions from the trade
itself and other sources, brings the total
amount spent under this head during the
last three years to some £93,000.
the first two years the campaign was confined to the United States, but last year
the field was extended to cover not only
the States, but also the home and
Dominion markets.

the stores, but in the schools and colleges,
and in art and domestic science classes at
numerous centres.
The opportunities offered by wireless.
broadcasting, as well as by women's clubs,
have also been turned to the best account.
As regards work in the newly-added
fields, I am as yet only able to indicate
in mere outline the special steps contemplated. With a view to eliciting new and
novel ideas as to the most effective
methods of marketing linen goods at
home a competition carrying substantial
prize money was recently inaugurated
throughout Great Britain and Northern
Ireland. The suggestions which have
thus been procured include many which
will, no doubt, find expression not only
in the publicity schemes itself but in
subsequent publicity work undertaken by
individual firms.
When I come to Vote 2 of the Ministry, I propose to explain how we are cooperating with the Empire Marketing
Board in the displays organised by that
Board at various centres throughout
Great Britain. One of the slogans of the
Empire Marketing Board, namely, "Empire Buying Begins at Home," is forming,
at the present time, the subject of discussion between my Ministry and local
manufacturers of goods other than linen.
We have in our midst a number of minor
industries which cater for the home and
domestic market. Local manufacturers,
under existing conditions, are adopting
various methods of propaganda in impressing upon the public the desirability
of purchasing the locally made goods.
My Ministry is, therefore, exploring, with
a representative group of such manufacturers, the feasibility of co-operative
action towards this end. The campaign
is largely educational, and is not in any
way directed towards placing any embargo on other Empire goods, but is, as
I have indicated, designed primarily
towards an intensive application of the
slogan, "Empire Buying Begins at
Home."
The activities of the section of the
Ministry which deals with fishery matters.
are, to some extent, determined by the
code of Irish Fishery Law, which has been
built up through almost a hundred years
of legislation. We have in Northern
Ireland valuable salmon fisheries. We
have also, in Lough Neagh, the finest
natural eel fishery in Europe. The fact
that this Lough is at present producing
but a fraction of its potential capacity is
a matter of serious concern and, within
the limits of its statutory powers, the
Ministry is endeavouring to improve the
situation. Then, apart from these commercial fisheries, we have in Ulster a
valuable asset in our trout fishing, the
possibilities of which, from the point of
view of attracting tourists, are, as yet,
far from being fully exploited. Finally,
but not least, we have around the coasts
of Ulster a body of men who devote their
lives to sea fishing, and who look to the
Government for assistance in the provision of harbour accommodation, fishing
equipment, and assistance in marketing
their catches.
With regard to inland fisheries, there
are three methods by which productivity
can be increased. The first of these
is by the provision of adequate protection for the fish against the
activities, not only of poachers, but
also of those who might be tempted to
sacrifice the future development of the
fisheries for the sake of immediate gain.
The Ministry does not itself provide such
protection since, in a very large proportion of cases, protection is obviously a
matter for those deriving profit from the
fisheries. The fishery code, however,
provides for such protection through
Boards of Conservators, who employ the
necessary watchers, and derive their revenue from the licence duties payable on
the various classes of fishing instruments
employed. Unfortunately, the revenue
thus obtained has proved insufficient to
provide adequate protection of the
fisheries, and for this purpose the Ministry has been obliged to make contributions each year to the funds of Boards of
Conservators.
The second method by which fish stocks
can be improved is by supplementing
natural by artificial propagation in
hatcheries. This again is primarily a
matter for the owners of fisheries, but the
Ministry has endeavoured to encourage
artificial propagation by way of annual
grants based on the number of salmon ova
hatched from native fish. The third
method of improving the fish stocks is
primarily the concern of the Ministry in
its capacity as the central fishery
authority. Within the last two years
the Ministry has held three public
inquiries into matters affecting both the
inland and sea fisheries and, in conjunc-
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
tion with the Ministry of Agriculture, has
conducted a series of experiments touching
the problem of flax water poisoning.
Many of the Committee will recollect that
last year, as the outcome of these inquiries, an amending Fisheries Bill was
passed, in addition to by-laws controlling
the movement of ova and fry, with the
object of protecting Northern Ireland
against infection with salmon disease.
further by-law relating to eel fishing is at
present before the Privy Council. I have
no doubt that with the increasing experience which the Ministry is gaining in
the administration of this service means
will be found to protect and develop the
fishery asset of the Province to a degree
not hitherto attained.
A
The interests of the sea fishing industry
have, at the same time, not been overlooked. The Committee may recollect
that the subject of fishery harbour
accommodation was thoroughly examined
and reported upon by a Departmental
Committee. I propose, however, to defer
my remarks in regard to the action which
has been taken on the Departmental Committee's recommendations until I come to
speak of harbours generally. At this
point I shall confine myself to stating that
the effectiveness of our sea fishing fleet
has been promoted as a result of the loans
which have been granted to fishermen since
the fishery services were transferred to the
Northern Government.
The Committee, I am sure, will approve
of the Ministry's action in extending the
scheme under which loans for the purchase
of nets had formerly been granted to the
purchase of boats, engines, and other
equipment. Loans granted under the
Ministry's scheme are repayable over
periods varying between three and five
years, and I am happy to be able to inform the Committee that, with very few
exceptions, indeed, the fishermen are meeting their obligations in the matter of repayments in a very satisfactory manner.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The total
amount of the loans so far granted under
the Ministry's scheme is £4,000.
Another way in which the Ministry is
helping the sea-fishing industry is by the
branding of herrings with a special mark
where the quality conforms to a certain
standard. The standard of quality which
the Ministry has set is extremely high,
so that little surprise will be felt when
I state that Government-branded Northern Irish herrings command the very
highest prices on the Continental markets,
and are always a marketable commodity,
even when business is sluggish.
The Ministry's interest in the herrings
landed in Northern Ireland does not cease
with the application of the brand, but
extends right up to the point of sale.
Last year the fishery officer of the Ministry paid a visit to the principal markets
for Northern Irish-cured herrings, and
examined numerous consignments of our
native cure which were being held in
store. In this way it has been possible
to ensure proper warehousing and also to
satisfy ourselves that the methods employed in curing were such as prevented
deterioration. The visit also served the
useful purpose of bringing to the notice
of the importers and others interested
the actual significance of the brand, and
of ascertaining, with an exactitude that
would not otherwise have been possible,
the special requirements of the various
markets.
I now pass to the power, transport and
companies' branch of my Department. In
addition to its statutory functions, with
which the Committee is familiar, this
branch is responsible for dealing with
questions of harbour development and
electricity.
I have been criticised in certain
quarters for not embarking upon large
schemes of fishery harbour development, which would impose substantial
burdens upon the taxpayers of Northern Ireland, and I think it important,
accordingly, to direct the attention of the
Committee for a few moments to the true
proportions of the sea-fisheries problem.
Of the population of our Province, less
than 700 men are wholly dependent upon
sea fishing for a livelihood. They live in
scattered communities in the small fishing
ports, or hamlets, around our coasts, and
they ply their trade for the most part in
small craft. I am advised that, if a
central fishing port could be provided in
Northern Ireland, it would be difficult, if
not impossible, to induce these fishermen
to leave their present homes and migrate
to it. If we exclude the herring catch
which is landed at the port of Ardglass,
mainly from Scottish drifters, we find that
the total value of the fish landed by our
own community in all ports is only some
£24,000 per annum.
Clearly under these circumstances it is
difficult to establish a case for the expenditure of a large sum of public money
Supply-
Committee
5 JUNE 1929
upon the development of a new fishing
centre. Members of the Committee will
nave observed from the Report of the
Departmental Advisory Committee, which
I set up in 1927 to consider the question
of the development of fishery harbours in
Northern Ireland, that there is little
prospect of developing a white fishing industry in Northern Ireland because of
the eclectic nature of the local demand,
which deprives our fishermen of a local
market for the coarser varieties of white
fish caught. Moreover, irregularity in
the landings of white fish around our
coasts makes it difficult for local dealers
to secure steady supplies, and they have,
accordingly, been forced to import their
requirements from those large centres
across the Channel, from which supplies
can be obtained. It must also be borne
in mind that for the white fishing industry, as distinct from the herring industry, ample accommodation already
exists at the ports of Belfast and Londonderry, and, to a lesser extent, at Larne.
I have, accordingly, thought it best to
pursue the policy of consolidating our
present position, and of carrying on deveopments along normal and business-like
lines, rather than to commit the Province
to large expenditure which, in my belief,
would prove to be barely remunerative
from the point of view of the Province,
even if we were to succeed in attracting
to our coasts a larger proportion of the
Scotch herring fleet than we do at the
present time.
In pursuance of this policy we have
recently acquired dredging and rockbreaking craft, specially adapted to conditions on our coasts, and we shall use
this craft for the purpose of improving
the accommodation in our small ports
from Portstewart to Kilkeel, thus making
it easier for our scattered fishing commmunities to trade upon a more regular and
a more remunerative basis. At the same
time, the Ministry is in negotiation with
the County Councils of Antrim and Down
for overtaking certain arrears of maintenance in the small fishing ports, so that
not only will these harbours be rendered
easier of access by dredging and rockbreaking, but also their quays will be put
into a proper state of repair as well.
this means we hope to consolidate and to
improve the position of an industry which
has for some time past been struggling
bravely against adverse physical conditions.
By
So far as the herring fishery is concerned, we are making every effort to
consolidate the position which we hold in
the port of Ardglass, and to increase our
proportion of the landings of the Irish
Sea herring catch. By far the greater
part of the herrings are landed by Scottish
steam drifters and are handled by Scottish fisher-girls, who are brought in by
the large cross-channel herring-curing
firms.. I am glad to be able to tell the
Committee, however, that the activity of
Northern Irish curers is increasing, and
that Northern Ireland workers are now
beginning to be trained for this work at
Ardglass.
It will be appreciated that the influx
of a large number of herring drifters into
Ardglass, and of herring girls seeking
accommodation during the season, represents the expenditure of considerable
sums of money in our area, but I would
ask the Committee, in considering suggestions made from time to time, that
very large capital expenditure should be
made to create an alternative port at
Killough, to remember that the profits
which we derive are largely of an indirect
nature, and that the present accommodation at the port of Ardglass is ample,
except in the height of a good season.
We are now preparing to improve this
accommodation by the provision of a
water supply, and by increasing the
depth of water at the existing quays.
Turning now to electricity, I am glad
to be able to inform the Committee that
the development of electricity services in
the Six Counties is making steady progress. In this sphere also we must have
regard, in framing policy, to our special
local conditions. The Committee are
well aware that the distribution of population over our area is very uneven, and
that it tends to concentration in the district around Belfast and the city of
Londonderry. I am advised, in factand this will surprise the Committeethat at the present time more than onethird of our population has a public
supply of electricity available at its
doors.
It is our policy, nevertheless, to spread,
as widely as is consistent with economic
considerations, the network of power
lines over our Province, and we hope that
within a few years time the majority of
the factories which stud our countryside
may be able to obtain cheap power from
high tension transmission lines in their
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
vicinity. Such a transmission line runs
to-day, as some hon. Members are aware,
between Belfast and Lisburn, but it is
only the first link in the chain. Before
the end of the year another line will run
from Holywood to Bangor, and will, we
hope, shortly be extended to Newtownards. We look forward, in the near
future, to extension down the Lagan
Valley, and to the linking up of the
principal towns in County Antrim.
Pending the construction of high
tension transmission lines, provincial
urban centres have not been discouraged
from establishing electricity undertakings
with local generating plant. Care has,
however, been taken to ensure a standardised frequency and uniform systems of
distribution, so that such undertakings
will readily be able to link up with a main
transmission system, when such is available.
It is, perhaps, unnecessary for me to
explain in detail the work of the Ministry
in regard to such matters as the registration of companies, friendly societies, etc.
Reports on these branches of the Ministry's activities are submitted annually to
the House. I should, however, refer
briefly to the subject of industrial assurance. The Industrial Assurance Act
(Northern Ireland), 1924, affords protection to holders of small policies, and provides machinery for the settlement of disputes between Assurance Companies and
policy holders, whose limited
means
might otherwise render redress a matter
of difficulty. The duties of the Industrial Assurance Commissioner are carried
out by the Permanent Secretary of the
Ministry, and these duties include the
exercise of judicial powers in dealing with
disputes referred to him.
The large increase in the number of
cases referred to the Commissioner is sufficient evidence of the real benefit which
this Act has conferred upon the class of
policy-holders affected. In 1925-the
first year of the operation of the Actthe number of cases dealt with was 155,
whereas during 1928 the number had increased to 737.
Turning now to the various sub-heads of
the Vote we have first of all Sub-head A.
This sub-head makes provision for the
salaries and wages of the staff of the
Ministry. As compared with the previous year, the provision made shows an
increase of £1,059. This increase is
accounted for under three heads, firstly,
provision of a sum of £300 as fees to a
consultant appointed in connection with
fisheries; secondly, provision of a similar
amount payable as fees to a legal assistant
to the Industrial Assurance Commissioner; and then the award of ordinary
annual increments to the staff of the
Ministry.
The amount provided in respect of
fisheries is to cover the services, as and
when required, of an officer of the Fishery
Board for Scotland in connection with
questions affecting fisheries that may be
expected to arise during the progress of
the work on the River Bann scheme.
The second item is, as I have already
indicated, in respect of fees payable to a
legal assistant to the Industrial Assurance Commissioner. The large increase
in the number of cases referred to the
Commissioner has necessitated the employment of a legal assistant competent
to hear and determine cases which frequently involve intricate questions of
law.
Sub-head B makes provision for travelling and subsistence expenses connected
with the work of the Ministry, and shows
a reduction of £50 as compared with the
amount voted for the previous year.
Sub-head C is a service which has been
transferred from the Vote for Fisheries,
Harbours, Railways and Commercial Services (Class VII, No. 2). The provision
made represents the cost of collection of
traffic and fishery statistics and is similar
in amount to the provision made by the
Committee in the previous financial year.
Sub-heads D1, D2, and D3 are in
respect of the ordinary establishment and
maintenance charges. The total amount
required shows a reduction of £56 as
compared with last year.
Sub-heads E1, E2, and E3 are required
to defray the cost of these services, and
the total amount shows and increase of
£135 over last year's estimate. This is
due to the fact that Sub-head E3 makes
provision for the cost of printing the final
report of the Northern Ireland Census of
Production.
Hon. Members will be aware that the
cost of taking this census, which was
carried out by the Board of Trade on
Supply-
Committee
5 JUNE 1929
behalf of my Ministry under an agency
agreement has hitherto been borne on the
Ministry's No. 2 Vote. It has, however,
been decided to have the printing of the
inal report carried out locally, and provision for this purpose has accordingly
been made under this Sub-head.
None of the other items in the Estimate
seems to call for special explanation at
this stage, but I will endeavour to deal
with any points upon which hon.
Members may desire further information.
I beg to move.
The CHAIRMAN: Before proceeding
with the discussion I would like to turn
for a moment to the point mentioned
earlier by the hon. Member for the
Mourne Division (Mr. O'Neill).
It will
be observed that on his first estimate
there is no sum set down for the Ministry's salary. That might be supposed to
restrict fatally the discussion upon
general questions of policy. That would
be too literal an interpretation of the
rule, in my judgment, and I do not propose to follow it. I propose to interpret
the rule in the spirit of it. It will also
have been observed that nearly the entire of the right hon. Gentleman's speech
related to the second Vote and not to the
first, the reason being that the whole
questions of policy were connected with
the second Vote. The first Vote relates
mainly to salaries, travelling expenses.
printing, stationery, postage, and incidentals. What I suggest to the Committee.
therefore, is that on this first Vote we
should take merely such discussion as may
be necessary for the purpose of dealing
with these items and keep open for the
second Vote, which will follow immediately thereafter, the entire questions of
policy as well as the details of that, estimate. I think that will be for the convenience of the Committee generally, and
if there be general concurrence, I propose
to follow that course. Therefore, what
will happen in the meantime is that only
this first estimate will be open for discussion, as far as the details are concerned, and I will reserve the whole
question of policy as well in relation to
this estimate--if there be any policy in
it as to the second estimate itself. That
is to say, that the entire question of
policy will be kept open and the rights
of hon. Members preserved.
Question put, and agreed to.

work of maintaining the harbour has

As regards Newry, the Committee is
aware that a sum of £3,500 has already
been granted towards the cost of repair
of a damaged culvert, in the Canal. The
Canal has been closed for the past six
months and the repairs to the culvert
have not yet been completed.
As regards the improvement of the
Canal generally, in respect of which provision is now sought, I should explain
that representations have been made by
the Urban District Council of Newry, the
Newry Port and Harbour Trust, and
others to convince the Government that
the efficiency of the port of Newry is a
matter of vital importance to the counties
of Armagh and Down, in particular, and
to the Province in general.
The question of providing a tidal river
approach to the town of Newry has been
under consideration for many years, and
as recently as two years ago a Joint Committee of the Urban District, Council and
the Harbour Trust was appointed to consider the question. Plans were prepared
to carry out this scheme, and the cost
of carrying out the scheme was estimated at £110,000. Mainly owing to
financial considerations the work was not
proceeded with, and it is now intended
to carry out a modified scheme for the
improvement of the Canal.
This new scheme, in connection with
which engineers have already been appointed, provides for:—
(1) The lengthening of the existing
lock chamber at the entrance, and the provision of a pair of new gates.
(2) A certain amount of repairs to the
existing masonry and culverts, etc., here.
and probably some dredging at the lower
entrance to improve the approach from
the sea; and
(3) The removal of all the stones at
present lying in the bottom of the channel, and the deepening of the whole
channel from the locks to the Albert
Basin to give a minimum depth of 16 feet
(the present maximum depth is 13 feet),
and with necessary pitching for the slopes.
The cost of this work is estimated
roughly at £60,000.
Having regard to the importance of the
Canal, the Government proposes, firstly,
to defray 50 per cent. of the total expenditure incurred, exclusive of engineer's
fees, subject to a maximum contribution
from Government funds of £30,000;
secondly, to defray the cost of the services
of the engineer; and, thirdly, to make
available, where practicable, the services
of the Government dredging and rockbreaking plant free of charge.
It will be impossible to complete this
work during the current financial year,
and the provision now sought represents
the amount likely to be required in
1929/30 in respect of the grant-in-aid
and the cost of the services of the engineer during the year.

With regard to Exhibitions, I agree

Britain, are not nearly as representative

that they are really not up to what we
would expect them to be. I hope my
right hon. Friend will take a note of that

There was another subject which the
hon. Member has not touched, but which
probably some Member opposite will deal
with more fully, that is the amount of
money to be paid for the Newry canal.
This happens to be a subject I know
something about, and I have no hesitation
in saying that, in my humble judgment,
you are going to throw this money away.
The idea, which, I believe, emanated in
the days of the Irish Parliament-the
Parliament for all Ireland-of making a
canal alongside a tidal river struck me as
being particularly foolish, and now we
have a chance of carrying out a scheme
which has been adumbrated for years, the
deepening of the tidal river right up to
Newry, and of discontinuing the canal,
which can never be any great benefit, and
will cost far more to maintain than it is
worth. I think it would be a great advantage to have the original scheme,
which has been under consideration in
Newry for thirty years, taken up by the
Government. If this were done I believe
the benefit not only to Newry but to a
great part of Northern Ireland would
be enormous. I hope it is not too late.

There is no question of Russian flax being
shut out of Northern Ireland, and never
As a matter of fact, the fact that
the British Government has not an ambassador in the Soviet capital has, curiously enough, never interfered with the
flax trade between Russia and Northern
Ireland. The sole reason for the high
price of Russian flax and its scarcity today in the Belfast market is the policy
of the Soviet Government which has
carried Socialism to the height of absurdity. They give the Russian peasant
no encouragement at all to grow flax.
The Russian Government commandeers
the flax from the Russian peasant at an
absurdly low price, and then the control
of the export of flax is in their own hands.

the high price and the scarcity of Russian
flax in Northern Ireland. If it were not
for the fact that some of the Baltic republics, such as Esthonia and Lithuania,
are, thank goodness, free of the Government of Soviet Russia, the scarcity of
Russian flax would be greater than ever.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): There are only two items in this
Estimate which appear to me to call for
ny comment, all the other features, if I
ay say so, being automatic and selfexplanatory. The item to which I wish
› call special attention at the moment is
the sub-head providing for the salaries,
wages, and allowances of the officers of the
Houses of Parliament. Mr. Dasent, who
was Clerk of the Parliament up to quite
recently, has resigned, and so the opportunity presented itself of rearranging the
remuneration attached to the position,
with the result that the salary has now
been reduced to the scale of £1,000 to
£1,150. Therefore, hon. Members must
discard the amount which appears in the
Estimate. In addition to that the house
allowance of £300 automatically disappears, so that you will find that in this
respect there is a saving.
The other point to which I wish to
draw the attention of the Members of the
Committee concerns the provision of
£1,000, under Sub-head D4, for expenditure to be incurred on the planting of
trees on the Stormont Estate. I should
make it clear that the Imperial Government is providing for the planting of
ornamental trees on either side of the processional road. Therefore, although that
sum appears on the Estimate it will not
be borne by the Province.
Mr. COLLINS: Is the £1,000 borne
by it?
Mr. POLLOCK: Not altogether. It
is thought right, in view of the general
opinion on the subject of afforestation,
that those areas of land surrounding Stormont which are suitable for
afforestation should be taken advantage
of in the usual way, so that ultimately
when we are no longer here there will be
some revenue derived from that source.
Those are the only two items that call for
any comment. The others are small and
self-explanatory, and so I merely submit.
the Estimate.

The next thing to which I would like

In that sense

I refer to the messengers, attendants, and

of the attendants and messengers in the

in Great Britain.

I want to tell you another thing.
number of hours wrought by these men

working in other districts, but when the

was the average. I understand that an
increase to the messengers and attendants
and that class of servant throughout
Great Britain is under consideration at

Government, and I presume the matter

which is now in office.
Mr. POLLOCK: Of course, whatever
material information is produced in respect of changes that may be made will
have a bearing on our position and
action, but I do not think it can be contended that our scale of remuneration for
officers in these positions is lower than
that which is admitted and provided by
the British Government for officers in a
similar position. Indeed, our remuneration is better; I can say that definitely.
Take Edinburgh, Liverpool, and other
centres where the devolution of government necessitates the appointment of
officers of various kinds. The officers engaged there are paid on a lower scale
than those engaged in London, because
house rents are higher in London, and
the cost of transport is greater.
Therefore, whether these officers are
receiving sufficient in itself or not, I can
make the statement at any rate that they
are not any worse off than if they were
living in Edinburgh, Liverpool or Glasgow. It may be argued that, as this is
a subordinate institution, the officers
should be paid on a lower scale than
others. Our Friends on the opposite side
do not hesitate to talk in that way.
Then, obviously, it is not a question of
our paying the same scale as obtains elsewhere.
In respect of the general Vote, I wish
to say that when this Parliament was established, provision was deliberately
made by the British Government for the
purpose of providing, as a free gift, for
the institutions that were necessary, and,
therefore, it does not affect the taxpayer
of Northern Ireland in any form. I
quite admit that any economies we can
effect in these institutions should be
effected, as they would, perhaps, enable
us to make provision for other necessary
matters. At the same time, so far as the
taxpayers of Ulster are concerned, it
does not affect them to the extent of one
penny.
When our Parliament was established
originally, all these material facts were

other side. It was held that the figures
we have put before you in this Estimate
formed a fair basis for a subordinate Parliament, such as has been necessitated
here. There are positions of responsibility, and, after all, responsibility must
be paid for, because, if a man has a responsible position, he must be a person
with knowledge and experience in order

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. POLLOCK: Those who were
Members in our last Parliament are
familiar with this small Vote, but as
there are a number of new Members in
the House, it may not be out of place for
me to explain in some detail the way in
which the money provided in this Estimate is used. The money is paid into a
Fund from which payments are made
only on the personal authorisation of the
Minister of Finance, who first satisfies
himself that the expenditure to be met
has been incurred on objects properly
coming within the ambit of the Fund, as,
for example, the entertainment of distinguished visitors to the Province, or of
representative bodies from other countries
visiting Northern Ireland for the purpose
of exchanging views on matters relating
to education, agriculture, etc., with the
corresponding bodies in this country. As
an example of the latter, I may mention
the visits paid to Northern Ireland last
year by representatives of the World's
Dairy Congress, the Agricultural Education Association, the Agricultural Research Association, and the Empire
Farmers. I am sure the Committee will
agree with me that it is very desirable,
from every point of view, that when bodies
of such importance visit the Province the
Government should do what it can to
foster an atmosphere of friendship and
goodwill.
Most of the expenditure from the Fund
is incurred in entertainments such as
these, and, in general, the scope of the
fund is restricted to affording hospitality
on the occasion of important visits from
outside. Instances sometimes occur,
however, when it is in the public interest
that payments should be made for some
more local purposes, and in considering
such cases I am, of course, governed by
the requirement that the money must be
used in the public interest.
I would repeat the statement which I made when
moving this Estimate on the last occasion,
namely, that I am personally accountable
to Parliament for the payments which are
made, and that just as the administration
of the corresponding fund in Great
Britain is left in the hands of a Minister
of the Crown, so I hope that this Com-
Imittee will continue to extend to me the
same degree of trust as is extended to
the Imperial Minister at Westminster.
There is no secrecv about the expenditure,
and the objects by this time should be
well known.
The amount of £1,500, included in che
Estimate this year will be paid into the
Hospitality Fund, from which payments
will be paid as occasion arises; any balance
remaining in the Fund at the end of the
year is not liable to surrender, as is money
voted for other purposes. It is carried
over into the following year, which
means, of course, that if the amount of
the balance is considerable, a smaller
amount will require to be voted in the
following year. I do not anticipate that
the actual expenditure out of the Fund,
during the
year, will approach the amount
of £1,500. I think the Committee will
appreciate, however, that in a matter of
this kind, it is not possible to make any
close estimate, and it is essential that the
Fund should contain a reasonable margin
for contingencies. There are generally
certain items of expenditure which can be
foreseen when the Estimate for the year
is being prepared. The Government proposes, for example, in the present year to
repeat the very successful function held
last year in honour of those taking part
in the International Motor Race. Then
again, a certain amount of expenditure of
this kind will be incurred in connection
with the ceremony of the opening of he
Lecture Buildings at Stranmillis
Training College, which we expect to take
place in the early autumn. Other occasions which cannot be foreseen are, however, almost certain to arise, and for
these some provision must be made.
new
I think Members of the House should
have no difficulty in realising the object
of the Fund, and I feel perfectly satisfied
they will approve of it. I have no hesitation in asking the Committee to pass the
Vote, which I now beg to move.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Loans Guarantee (Money).
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the
Loans Guarantee Acts (Northern Ireland), 1922 to 1928, by increasing from
eleven million five hundred thousand
pounds to fourteen million pounds the
limit on the aggregate capital amount of
the Loans, the principal or interest of
which may be guaranteed by the Ministry
of Finance under the Loans Guarantee
Act (Northern Ireland), 1922; and by extending to the 31st day of March, 1931,
the period within which guarantees may
be given thereunder; and to charge on the
Consolidated Fund of Northern Ireland
any moneys required for fulfilling any
sich guarantees.”—(Governor's Recommendation signified)-(Mr. Barbour).
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The Resolution which appears
on the Order Paper is, of course, the
precursor of a Bill with which most hon.
Members are familiar, and which is designed to continue a scheme of unemployment relief combined with assistance
to industry which has been endorsed on
The
many occasions by Parliament.
Government has found it necessary to continue this emergency legislation from
year to year since 1922, and although,
when moving a similar Resolution last
year, and also in 1927, the hope was expressed that circumstances would make it
possible for Government to discontinue
these facilities, the success which has attended this legislation and the existence
of unemployment in our midst has moved
the Government to the view that it would
not be justified in relaxing its efforts to
assist by this means.
If we include a sum of £600,000, which
I am hopeful will have been ear-marked
within the next few days, maybe even
within hours, in connection with an important contract, the position is that guarantees will have been issued amounting to approximately £10,280,657 leaving available
a balance of approximately £1,200,000.
Despite this substantial balance, the
Government considers it advisable to increase the margin by a very large amount,
and to provide now for the extension of
the scheme to 31st March, 1931.
Government is satisfied that the state of
The
employment is such as to warrant this
further extension of time and of amount,
and I can only repeat that every effort
will be made by co-operation with our
great shipyards to maintain the improved
conditions which have, happily, been
brought about in the course of the last
eighteen months.
Once again I would take the opportunity of expressing the thanks of the
Government to the members of the Advisory Committee for the work which
they have carried out in investigating the
various applications which have come before them. This work has been carried
on by three eminent business men, and
the Government is indeed
debt of gratitude to them for what they
under a
have done, and what they are doing.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
interval which has elapsed since the
In the

and had acted as Chairman for a number
of years.
This is the first Parliamentary
opportunity which has presented itself to
pay tribute to the great work which he
performed. We have been fortunate in
prevailing upon Mr. H. L. M'Cready to

Oral Answer to Question.
PARLIAMENT AND
ADMINISTRATIVE BUILDINGS.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the
terms of contract for the building of the
Parliament House at Stormont; whether
the contract was made with the contractors by the Imperial Government and
paid for by the Imperial Government, or
whether the contract was made by the
Northern Government and paid for by
them out of the funds provided by the
Imperial Government for that purpose.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The liability for providing
buildings and equipment for the Parliament and Public Departments of Northern Ireland was imposed on the Imperial
Government by Section 34 of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920. The contract
for the erection of the new building at
Stormont was entered into by the Imperial
Government, which provides the amounts
payable to the contractors.
I am unable to specify the actual terms
of the contract, but have no doubt that
it is in the usual form of Government
building contracts.
Mr. BEATTIE: The Minister of
Finance states that the responsibility for
the erection of the Parliament Buildings
rests with the Imperial Board of Works,
and I would like to ask the Minister
whether he could state if it is legal for
the contractor for that building to be a
Member of the Imperial House of Commons.
Mr. SPEAKER: I must point out to
the hon. Member that as this is a question
for the Imperial Parliament it cannot be
discussed here at all.

:
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) The work of the Ministry of
Labour goes on week after week, patiently
and effectively performed, and then at
the end of the year the responsible
political head of the Department is expected in a speech of reasonable length to
give an account of his stewardship. I
crave your indulgence in doing so because
I feel that, in connection with labour
matters, policy and facts and figures are
so closely associated and interwoven that
it is almost impossible to separate them.
A general feeling exists, I am afraid,
amongst our community that the principal
work which the Ministry of Labour does
is to collect small contributions from
people who are not particularly anxious
to pay, and then week after week in a
somewhat indiscriminate way to pay out
benefit and pensions to those who apply
for them. I can assure you that that is
quite a wrong impression in the public
mind.
As a matter of fact, the Department
always is, and always will be, open to two
forms of attack. On the one hand we are
told that our
administration is too
lenient, on the other hand we are told
that it is not as sympathetic as it ought
to be, and it is between those two views
So
is
of public opinion that the Department
has continually to hold the balance.
far as I am concerned, neither expression of opinion worries me very much, so
long as I feel that the Department
faithfully carrying out the provisions of
our various Acts of Parliament as sympathetically as can be done within the four
walls of those Acts.
I
If I were asked in a few words to say
what the policy of the Department is,
should say that our desire is in co-operation with the other Departments of the
State, particularly the Ministry of
Finance and the Ministry of Commerce,
to find work for as many of our people as
possible through the ordinary industries
of which Ulster has always been very
proud; then, for those for whom it is not
possible to find work in that way in cooperation with our local authorities we
desire that schemes of public utility
would
which
should be undertaken
not otherwise be undertaken for two
that men
years at least, in order
may be usefully employed in that way;
and then when everything has been done
that can possibly be done to obtain work
for as many of our people as possible, the
to the
Department's duty is to come
rescue of those of our community who are
passing through a period of adversity,
whether that adversity is due to
employment, to sickness, to bereavement,
or to old age.
un-
One of the principal duties which I feel
that the Department is called upon to discharge is that associated with preserving
industrial peace in our community, and I
think I can claim that Northern Ireland
has been specially free from industrial
troubles during the last eight years. The
Ministry does not claim an undue share
of credit for that, because I am very glad
to be able to state I realise that a real
desire exists between our employers and
our workers to accommodate with each
other, and to adjust their differences along
reasonable and possible lines. But, still,
the Ministry of Labour has to keep watch
upon the industrial situation in this as
well as in other respects.
When we hear that trouble is brewing,
and we almost always hear either from
the representatives of labour or from the
employers-in fact as a rule we hear from
both-we get busy to try to have the
differences adjusted before actual trouble
takes place. This is a work which is performed to a far greater extent than is
349 Supply Committee-

10 JUNE 1929
Ministry of Labour
generally known, because it is not in the
public eye. But, no matter how faithfully the Department discharges its duty
in this respect, always bearing in mind
our policy that prevention is better than
cure, at times trouble will occur, no matter
how much care is taken, and I deeply regret that in connection with one of the
trades in our shipbuilding industry
trouble has occurred between the joiners
and their employers.
It is not for me to express an opinion
one way or the other-it is my duty to
remain absolutely neutral-but I do take
advantage of this opportunity earnestly to
express the hope that before long peace
will again be restored, because, if not, I
am absolutely satisfied that many in other
trades in connection with our great shipbuilding industry will suffer, as well as
their wives and families, and irreparable.
damage may be done to the industry itself
if this strike is unduly prolonged.
the
In addition to dealing with industrial
relations, the responsibility rests with the
Department of administering our Trade
Board Acts. That has not only been a
difficult but a delicate task. When the
Department took over these powers in
1922 we found that a great deal of dissatisfaction existed as regards trade board
legislation and administration. One of
the first Acts which the Department
undertook to get passed through
House was a new Bill dealing with trade
boards, and I am glad to think that that
Act has worked, on the whole, remarkably satisfactorily-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and that owing to careful administration-reasonableness always being an
outstanding factor in connection with the
Department's policy in this matteremployers and workers in Northern
Ireland associated with these particular
trades have come to realise that they are
not, as they feared they always would be,
a nuisance; but, on the contrary, that
the trade board is one of the best ways
of settling wages' matters along reasonable
lines. In Northern Ireland we have 18
trade boards, and, comparatively recently,
five district committees have been set up
with the view that statutory rates should
be fixed in our country districts at such
a level as to allow our country concerns
to compete with those larger firms often
more favourably situated in this city and
other large towns throughout Northern
Ireland.
Factory legislation is another part of
the Department's duty which requires
a
careful dealing with, and I am glad to
be able to say that our mills and factories
in Northern Ireland are now in
healthier and more sanitary condition
than they were at any other time. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Objectionable
gases and dust are removed as far as possible immediately they are created, or
else provision is made to prevent them
being created at all. In that way the
general health of our industrial classes
has, in my opinion, enormously improved,
and the returns furnished by those best
capable of judging show that as regards
chest troubles, in particular, there has
been a very considerable reduction.
Workmen's Compensation Acts are Acts
which do not give us very great trouble
to administer, because I find that eminsurers
ployers and
are invariably
anxious when workers do suffer accidents
in the course of their employment, that
they should be compensated in the way
that the law provides for.
I have referred to the fact that it was
the policy of the Department when all our
people could not be employed in connection with our established industries to get
work for them in connection with relief
schemes promoted jointly by our local
authorities and the Government.
I am
sure it will interest hon. Members on both
sides of the Committee to know that great
improvements have been and are being
carried out to our harbours, hospitals,
railways, roads, and in the direction
of electrical development throughout
Northern Ireland, to which grants
have been given, or have been promised by my Department to the
extent of one million pounds. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) In addition
to that, in connection with other
schemes, such as drainage schemes, sewerage schemes, and schemes of a somewhat
similar nature affecting our smaller
towns, the Department has either given
or promised grants to the extent of
£620,000. There are, at the present
time, 78 schemes in operation, providing
useful employment for 1,196 men. I am
glad to be able to tell the Committee that
a considerable number of other schemes
are under consideration, so that the continuity of employment in this direction is
likely to be maintained throughout the
year everywhere.
I feel it to be my duty to refer to what
is known as the Richhill Training Scheme,
because it is very closely associated with
Supply Committee-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
the Department's policy.
At Richhill
we take young men from this city and
other towns throughout Northern Ireland,
who have got into a blind alley. Many
of them have served an apprenticeship in
connection with some of our handicrafts,
but from the time the apprenticeship
was completed they have never been able
to be employed as tradesmen. Year after
year they have since remained unemployed. The Department is not forcing
anyone to leave Northern Ireland who
wishes to stay in Northern Ireland. All
that the Department is doing is to bring
within the reach of those who desire to
go, not to a foreign land, but to another
part of the same Empire, the same opportunities and the same facilities for gratifying their own desire that their brothers
across the Channel possess.
From Richhill there have already gone
to Canada 430 men, and to Australia 154
men. I am glad to say, from reports
which I receive, that they are all mostly
doing well. I have had many very gratifying letters from those who have gone,
and who have already been established in
those far-flung parts of the British Empire, thanking the Government for the
opportunity which they obtained to seek
employment in those lands, and to assist
in the
the development of those great
Dominions, instead of hanging about in
our cities and towns here doing nothing
at all. There are 95 men in training at
Richhill at the present time, and there is
another group anxiously waiting to get
there. I do think that it is a very strong
course for any hon. Member to take to
speak in any derogatory sense of this
effort on the Government's part.
After all, there is another side to this
question, and an important one, too,
These young men of ours go out to the
Dominions and help to keep the flag flying there. In addition to that-and this
is very important from our standpoint.
here they form potential customers for
the commodities which we produce at
home and which they in those lands require. Those who have studied the
export trade figures as to the Kingdom
will realise how great a factor the
Dominions now are in the industrial prosperity of these islands of ours.
Again, we as a Department do everything possible to help our disabled ex-
Service men who have our special
sympathy, no matter on which side of the
Committee we sit. I am glad to be able
to tell hon. Members that there is a
larger number of firms now enrolled than
ever before, thanks to the exertions of
those very patriotic committees who are
the advisers of the Ministry of Labour in
connection with this matter. There are 976
firms and 31 local authorities enrolled at
the present time. There are 4,835 disabled
men employed at the present time. I
regret to say that in Northern Ireland
there are 1,324 still unemployed, and of
this number 896 reside in this city. I do
not hesitate to say that I do feel that
some employers do not fully realise their
responsibility to these men. They might
do a little more than they have done up to
the present time.
In connection with our various social
service schemes, with which this principal
Vote is very largely associated, I would
just like to say that we are spending no
less a sum than £4,000,000 per annum to
help those who are passing through
periods of adversity in our midst. It
will interest hon. Members to know that
of that sum 16 per cent. is contributed by
the workers themselves. A very startling
figure was brought before my notice the
other day. There are 120,500 persons on
an average each week in Northern Ireland, not counting the dependents of unemployed, who are receiving at present
financial benefits under our four main
social service schemes, which are administered by my Department. That means
this, if we take the population of Northern
Ireland to be 14 millions one in every ten
persons in our area is receiving direct
financial assistance each week through the
medium of these four social service
schemes exactly the same fraction which
the great founder of the Salvation Army,
General Booth, referred to many years
ago as the submerged tenth who were
under his care. This one-tenth which I
regret to say exists in our midst to-day is
the care, and the very direct care, of the
Government of which I have the honour
to be a Member. But it does give food
for reflection when we come to consider
these social service schemes-how wide
they are and how many people in our
midst are largely depending on them for
their daily bread.
As regards unemployment, although
it is the most important subject that we
could consider, I do not think it is necessary that I should speak at any very great
length on it to-day, because this House
Supply Committee-
10 JUNE 1929
Ministry of Labour
during the last year or so has frequently
discussed it at great length. But I am
thankful to be able to say that the
position is gradually improving, and anyone who says it is not, in my opinion at
any rate, is not speaking in accordance
with the facts. In August last 47,240 of
our people were unemployed. In
January that number had fallen to
42,543, in March to 39,361, and it is now
34,555, showing a decrease since August
last of 13,000. Last year our percentage
of unemployment was 18.1.
This year
the figures in these Estimates are
based on a percentage of unemployment of 16, and I have no hesitation in saying that I feel that that is a
conservative estimate. At the moment
the actual percentage of unemployment is
14.7.
The reason I say this is a conservative
estimate is that we all know that, apart
from the strike, to which I have already
referred, the prospect in the shipbuilding and engineering industries is much
better than it has been for a considerable
time. Then, again, I take a sanguine
view as regards our linen trade as a
whole. It is true that some of our mills
are not fully employed, and some of them
may not be fully employed for a very
considerable time. But that is only one
branch of the linen industry, and what
is of the utmost importance is that our
factories are well employed at the present
time, probably better employed than they
have been for a considerable number of
years.
I am sure hon. Members on both sides of
the Committee will rejoice to know that
there is not a single damask weaver in Northern Ireland available for work, who is
not employed at the present time-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)—and I am advised
that in Belfast there are only forty plain
weavers unemployed. I think these two
facts alone show that the trade from the
employment standpoint, as far as the
manufacturing end of it is concerned, is
in a reasonably satisfactory condition, to
put it very mildly. Those who say that
the linen trade is dying, that the linen
trade is almost dead, are, in my opinion,
doing irreparable harm, and certainly
hon. Members who sit opposite-and who
should not forget that, after all, they are
in a very responsible position as representing large constituencies ought to be
very careful that they do not overstate
the case against an industry upon which
we in Northern Ireland are so much dependent. After all, our customers read
what is said in this Committee and attach
more importance to what is said in this
Committee sometimes than they ought to
attach, and, therefore, when they come
to buy and when they read that the trade
is not in a satisfactory condition, when.
they read the exaggerated expressions
which hon. Members sometimes use, such
statements influence customers, they influence purchasers to postpone buying,
and in that way bring about unemployment in our midst for which hon. Members must be prepared to accept responsibility.
I am also glad to be able to say
that the staple trade of Derry-the shirt
and collar trade-is in a satisfactory condition, from the employment standpoint
at any rate, and I am only judging from
the standpoint of unemployment. There
are only 4.4 per cent. of those engaged in
that important industry in the Maiden.
City unemployed to-day. Our building
trade in Northern Ireland is in a reasonably satisfactory condition, and very few
of those associated with that industry,
apart from labourers, are unemployed at
the present time. Of course, I know that
that is largely due to the large number
of houses that are being built for our
working people through our subsidy
arrangements, and also to the fact that
there are a large number of Government
buildings being erected throughout the
whole country in the form of schools,
police barracks, etcetera, as well as the
large building at Stormont, which is to
house us, I hope, and also the Law Courts
here in the City of Belfast.
I need not refer to our other industries
because they are more or less subsidiary,
but they are practically all in a better
condition than they were some little time
ago.
But in dealing with the question
of unemployment there are two facts that
we should not altogether forget. We
should remember that the birth rate in
Northern Ireland exceeds the death rate
by about 8,000 a year on the average.
That means that those 8,000 have either
to be absorbed into increasing industries
in Northern Ireland, or else they have to
migrate to another part of the Empire,
or become unemployed. There is no way
out of the difficulty except through relief
schemes, which, of course, can be carried
on to any extent for which money can
be found to carry them on. But

But there is another aspect of this case

unemployment, and are inclined to

had an opportunity recently of studying the last Census figures in this

people signified the fact that they were

and 506,500 stated that they were

34,555 which we have to regard as still
unemployed. I think that is a rather
hopeful way of looking at the situation,
and, although I do not want to take too

referring now to the objectionable term
"not genuinely seeking work." This is
a matter that affects many of my constituents, and also many constituents of other
divisions in Belfast. I feel very strong
on this point. I am very glad that the
hon. Member (Mr. Nixon) who sits-I do
not know just where-agrees with me.
I would appeal to the Minister to change.
the term, which is insulting to a straight
working man or woman.
I speak of what I know, and the hon.
Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) will
bear me out in regard to the chairmen
of the Referees' Courts and the Appeal
Courts. I have appreciated the attitude of many of those people who came
before me in an indignant way, because
they were charged, as it were, with not
genuinely seeking work. There is a
sting in the phrase. The persons who go
before the Courts of Referees are of two
kinds. There is the man or the woman
who comes looking for work, but hoping
that work will not be found, so long as
the unemployment benefit continues to be
paid. Then there is the good straight
man or woman who is not only looking for
work, but hoping it will turn up, so that he
or she may discontinue the drawing of
unemployment benefit. Those are the
people I am referring to now. They are
genuinely seeking work, perhaps in an indirect way, perhaps in a blind alley.
Let me give you an instance. Take a
man who has been employed as a carter,
driving a horse. As we all know, horses
are going out, and motor vehicles are
coming in, but that man has been so long
at his occupation that he cannot adopt the
idea of driving a motor lorry, and he says,
"I am trying Wordie's; I am trying
different places." You say to him, "there
is no chance of your getting work there,"
but he does not know any better, yet he
is genuinely seeking work. Take a
woman who is a damask worker. The
damask weaving industry is in a bad way,
and she cannot turn her hand to weaving plain linens, but she is willing and
anxious to work, and it takes that woman
some time before she makes up her mind
to take charing or similar work.
I ask the Minister to change this phrase
in some way that will take the accusation
out of it. The number of stamps to a
man's credit does not always show that
he is genuinely seeking work. A person
comes before the Court with the requisite
number of stamps, which is the basis of
all benefit, but that does not necessarily determine that he is genuinely seeking work.
It is for the Court to determine that, and
the Court does so in the best way possible
by means of the information available.
I do not know that the Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) is altogether an expert in regard to the Courts.
He has appeared before my Courts. I may bring
to his mind an occasion on which he appeared before my Court with a man who
had been a soldier. He claimed that this
man had sufficient stamps. How many
stamps did he have?

With regard to the question of genuinely
seeking work, it is very difficult to know
on what lines the Department come to a
decision at all. If a man brings his case
cleverly he is likely to secure benefit, but
if he tells the plain truth of the story he

say a man in the motor trade is unemployed in a provincial town where there
are only one or two openings in the place.
He may walk round each of these from

seen, whether in the motor industry or in

referee on the ground that he is not
genuinely seeking work.

Beattie) put a splendid suggestion before
