Sir ROBERT LYNN: I am sure the
Committee agrees that there is no more
difficult problem than this question of unemployment, and yet I notice that when
we come to debate it we always seem to
deal with nearly everything else but the
question of how to find a solution for it.
The hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.
Beattie) has now disappointed me twice.
Three or four years ago he assured the
House that he had a ready-made cure for
it, but I have been waiting ever since to
hear what it was. To-day, he started his
speech by declaring that he was going to
make a suggestion that would cure unemployment. I have listened with the
greatest care to his speech, and to the
following speeches, and I do not think.
there has been anything at all said yet
that is going to help the Minister of
Labour. As a Member of this Committee
who has been probably brought more.
into contact with the Ministry of Labour
than with any other Department of the
State, I would like, with other hon. Members, to pay my tribute not only to the
capable but to the very sympathetic way
in which the Ministry have administered
the Unemployment Acts. I have discovered that where the Minister of Labour
can stretch a point at all on the side of the
unemployed he is always ready to do it,
and the members of his Department have
all been doing their work under difficult
conditions as well as any Department
could possibly do it. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
The hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.
Beattie) raised a number of points which
have been emphasised by the hon. Member for South Fermanagh (Mr. Healy),
who has just sat down. He raised the
question of emigration, for example. So
far as emigration is concerned, I am sure
there is not a single Member of this Committee, no matter on which side he sits,
who wants to see a single boy or girl going
out of the country if work can be had for
them at home. We are all anxious that
the population should be kept at home,
and that it should grow strong.
But
surely no Member would suggest that
people should be compelled to remain at
home in idleness if there is a prospect for
them to blaze the trail and to make their
fortune abroad. There is no other
country in the world whose people have
done so well abroad as the Irish people,
both North and South. They have done
splendidly, not only in our own Dominions,
but in the United States. I take it that
what the Minister of Labour is principally aiming at is that those Ulster boys
who go out from here to Canada,
Australia, New Zealand, or South Africa
should go out equipped for the fight in
which they have to take part. Surely
that is a work that is worthy of encouragement rather than disparagement every
time it is mentioned.
Then, with regard to industrial peace,
does any Member of this Committee suggest that anyone could do better than the
Minister of Labour with regard to creating good feeling between capital and
labour. I know no one who is better
qualified than he is to smooth down the
little difficulties that may arise, or who
has done more than he has done to relieve
difficulties that often might have landed
us in very serious industrial strife. I am
sure that in the present trouble, that is
in the minds of some of us, so far as he
is concerned, nothing that can be done
to help will be left undone.
The hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.
Beattie) talked glibly about increased
pensions. I suppose everyone would like
not only increased pensions, but increased
salaries, but I ask myself the question,
where is the money to come from.

There were two or three points which

I would be

I would just like to say I am sure I

wish to pay a tribute to the way in which

in the world, under the great British

udon. A lot of work could be done in

On the 28th November, 1923, the Prime

reliable, but there are a great many unemployed, who are so disgusted and

The increase is the sum of £1,000. Now
it has become necessary for us here in
Northern Ireland to have a separate
index made of the Statutes applicable to
Northern Ireland. Formerly there was

It has become necessary, therefore, to
prepare a separate index to deal with
Northern Ireland, so that the courts and
those who have to deal with statutes can
find easily the branch of law dealing with
each particular subject. It is quite impossible for anvone connected with the
law to work through all the statutes and
search through the different years. Any
lawyer, magistrate, judge or whoever is
concerned with the administration of justice and the investigation of statute law
Supply Committee--

would tell you that such an index is absolutely necessary. Therefore, it has become necessary to have such' provided for
Northern Ireland, and the entire increase
here is the first part of the preparation of
a chronological index to the statutes,
£500, and the printing of the index £323.
It is a very difficult matter to prepare this
index. It needs a tremendous amount of
labour and a tremendous amount of expert knowledge of statute law to be able
to prepare it. It is not a matter of going
into an office and asking a clerk to
prepare the index. It requires a knowledge of statute law, and a knowledge of
the powers of the two Governments, and
what statutes are applicable to Northern
Ireland and what are not. These have to
be picked out and a separate index prepared, a very slow, laborious, and difficult job. And so far as I can form an
estimate of the time and labour for the
preparation, the fee of £500 would be
rather under than over the mark compared with the amount of work required.
I know nothing about what the cost
of the printing would be, but I am sure
£323 would not be excessive. That is
an item of expenditure which will not
occur every year. Once it is prepared it
will be merely a matter of bringing it up
to date, and the expense in future will
be very small.

nd it will be found on page 49 of the

ike to take the opportunity of drawing

has made many interesting and valuable

the coming year. The quest for records
relating to Ulster in repositories in Great
Britain is continuing to produce valuable

historical discoveries, and the documents

in Canada, for it clearly proves that an

On the Ancient Monuments side, most
expenditure has been, and for some time,

Castles of Carrickfergus and Dunluce. In

examined, and steps are being taken by
the removal of modern plaster and internal walling, to restore its ancient appearance so far as possible. In the process old doors, windows, and stairways
have been disclosed. At Dunluce the
debris, which covered the ground to a
depth in some places of several feet, has
been removed, and ancient-flagged and
tiled paving brought to light; also a
paved approach leading down to the
castle. A souterrain or underground
chamber has also been found, and is
undergoing examination.

CLASS II. No. 3.
PUBLIC WORKS AND BUILDINGS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That a sum not exceeding £203,497 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during the
year ending the 31st March, 1929, in
respect of Public Works and Buildings,
Including expenses of Dredger and
Auxiliary Craft."-(Note.-£90,000 has
been voted on account.)
Mr. BARBOUR: The total of the
three sections which make up the Estimate for Public Works and Buildings
exceeds, by about £48,000, the corresronding figure for last year, this increase
being accounted for to the extent of
£29,000 by an increase in the Section I
Expenditure which, as hon. Members are
aware, is the liability of the Imperial
Government, and which for the reasons
stated in the footnote must be voted, in
the first instance, by the Parliament of
Northern Ireland.
I propose to deal with the three sections of the Estimate in turn, and I would
refer hon. Members to pages 28 and 29
of the Estimates, which contain what I
may call the Imperial part of the Estimate. For the benefit of those hon.
Members who have not previously taken
part in the consideration of this Estimate,
I would explain that under the Government of Ireland Act, the expenditure on
the provision of the new Parliament House
and the Northern Ireland Departmental
Buildings must be voted by this House
in the first instance, although the Imperial Government are under the necessity of putting our Exchequer in funds to
a corresponding extent.
The principal item in this section is, of
course, the sum of £166,265 for the continuation of the work of erection of the
new Parliament Buildings at Stormont.
The increase of £34,000, as compared with
last year, is an indication that the building works are proceeding at accelerated
pace.
I am informed by His Majesty's
Office of Works that the main superstructure-the contract for which was
begun in February of last year-is making
steady progress, as is also the contract for
the heating installation which is proceeding concurrently. It is anticipated that
the building will be ready for occupation
in three years' time.
Turning now to the Belfast Custom
House reconstruction and the new Law
Court Building, these items would not in
the ordinary course of events find a place
in our Estimates, as the Custom House is
primarily intended for the use of the
Customs and Excise and other reserved
and Imperial Departments, with the result that the main expenditure has to be
provided on Imperial Estimates.
The expenditure on the new Law Courts
building is in the same category, having
to be met directly from the Votes of the
Imperial Government under the provisions
of Section 24 of the Government of Ireland
Act, 1920. It happens, however, that a
part of each of these buildings is to be
utilised for the city offices of certain
Departments of the Northern Government, that is to sav, for financial purposes
the expenditure on such parts falls into
the same category as expenditure on the
Stormont buildings, and, though equally
the ultimate liability of the Imperial
Government, must be voted in this Section
as falling under Section 34 of the Government of Ireland Act.
Hon. Members will, I am sure, be interested to learn that the work of erecting
Supply Committee

of the Estimate is a re-vote of the amount

for a contribution to be made from Northern Ireland funds towards the cost of

Government was responsible.
In regard to the token Vote of £100
for completing the purchase of the

the dredger is now employed in improving

A further sum is required for the work
of drainage investigation now taking place
at the Lough and River Erne. Members will realize that before a drainage
scheme can be formulated, it is necessary
that accurate information should be available as to levels, strata, and other technical aspects of the problem.
The sum of £125 for the purchase of
property adjoining Carrickfergus Castle,
now in our custody as an ancient monument, is a re-vote of last year's provision
-some delay having taken place in the
completion of the legal formalities.
The item of £425 for improving the
main entrance drive at Government
House is provided, so that the roadway
may be given special treatment to ensure a suitable surface in all conditions of
weather, and to reduce maintenance
costs for the future.
The last item in the list is the most
of
important, namely, the provision
£40,000 for the Bann drainage. I need
not point out to hon. Members that the
scheme of drainage is that recommended
in the Report of the Drainage Advisory
Committee, dated 9th November, 1928.
A Bill to secure the necessary statutory
powers will require to be introduced in
this House. As far as can be foreseen,
the contract for the work should be placed
towards the close of the current calendar
year. The provision of a sum of £40,000
is in the nature of a token vote in this
connection. The various items of maintenance and other recurring expenditure
in Sub-heads F, G, and H require no
special comment, from me.
I now come to Section III, which summarises the works expenditure incurred
on behalf of the various Northern Ireland Departments, and which is recovered
from the Departmental Votes being
brought to account in this vote as an appropriation-in-aid. The various new

proposed are set out under separate headings in the tabular statement to be found

My first reference is to the adaptation
work which has for some time past been
undertaken with the object of utilising a
portion of the Belfast Prison as a convict
prison. These works are now well advanced, and it is anticipated that they will
be practically completed before the end of
this financial year. Londonderry Prison
is now to be adapted in order that part of

and so enable the Northern Ireland
criminal lunatics, who are at the present
time looked after in the Central Lunatic
Asylum at Dundrum, County Dublin, to
be transferred to a Northern Ireland institution. A token sum only was included
for this work in last year's Estimates, and
the amount now included represents the
whole cost of the work, as it is anticipated
that the alterations will be completed before the end of December next.

Against the Malone Training School

The Lecture Block contract at Stranmillis has not proceeded quite so rapidly
as was anticipated, but I am able to say
that the building will probably be ready
for occupation in the early autumn. The
adaptation of Hampton House for use as
a men's hostel has been completed, and
the sum included in this estimate is merely
for the settlement of outstanding accounts.
A token provision was included in last
vear's Estimates for the proposed women's
hostel, and it is expected that a start will
be made on this work before the end of
the present year. Owing to site difficulties we are, unfortunately, not yet in a

Practising School, and the sum included is

A reference has been made since the
opening of this Parliament to the scheme.
of forestry development which is now.
being proceeded with, and it has been

The requirements of the Ministry of
Labour necessitate the inclusion of two
substantial sums, the first for an Employment Exchange at Lisburn-the rented
premises now occupied by the Lisburn
Employment Exchange having proved

The second provision is that for
the Training Centres for Unemployed
Juveniles, which I have no doubt will be
of special interest to hon. Members, inasmuch as it denotes the inauguration
of a scheme for dealing with the unemployment problem as it affects the youth
of the country. These centres have been
established in Great Britain, and have
proved most useful in guiding boys and
girls into permanent avocations, and so
keeping them out of "blind alley" employments. Central premises have been
acquired in Belfast, and the sum now
provided is the estimate of the cost of
these premises. A further sum will be
required to meet the cost of the necessary adaptation, and this will form the
subject of a Supplementary Estimate at
a later date.

this. It is expected that a public supply will be provided for the town in the
near future, and it is hoped that the ex
tension of this supply to the harbour now

Mr. ELLIOTT: I intervene in this debate just for a moment. I should like to
reply to one or two criticisms that have
been made by hon. Members opposite with
regard to this Estimate. First of all,
something has been said against the
Minister of Labour providing Employment Exchanges throughout the Six
Counties. I hold that in doing so the
Minister of Labour is doing a great deal
to relieve the unemployment situation,
Public Works and Buildings 456
Supply Committee-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Elliott]
because he is giving an opportunity to
people in rural districts to go to the Exchanges which are being established
throughout the length and breadth of the
area, and there to get into touch with
those who want men for work.
I hold that these Exchanges-call
them Unemployment or Employment Exchanges are very necessary throughout
the Six Counties, and I welcome the opening of new Exchanges in places where they
can be utilised, both by the unemployed
and by those in search of labour. I think
hon. Members will admit that we are frequently approached by old-age pensioners
and by people who are looking for health
insurance and other benefits from the
social services. We are frequently able
to assist them in getting what they think
are their legitimate rights, and it is a
great convenience, I think, that we can
go into these Employment Exchanges or
Labour Exchanges, here and there, and
put the case of our constituents before the
managers. I find that in that way we
are able to get something done for those
people in a much quicker way than perhaps we could do if we had always to
come to the central Exchange here in
Belfast. I welcome, therefore, the development of these exchanges throughout
the length and breadth of our area.
Something has also been said about
police barracks. The hon. Member for
Mid-Tyrone (Mr. McAleer) and the hon.
Member for South Fermanagh (Mr.
Healy) have said that there is no necessity
for any improvements or additions to

hold that the Government are pursuing

comfortable police barracks to house the
Royal Ulster Constabulary. A great
many of the police barracks, we all know,

force. I could take the hon. Members to
police barracks in my own constituency,

fair-minded man would admit are
not suitable for our police force. I welcome the great improvement that has
taken place in the construction and reconstruction of our police barracks, and
I support this Vote whole-heartedly. In
my own constituency, I am glad to say
that several new police barracks are being
erected, because I think our police force
are doing a good work. They are mainhaining law and order in Northern Ireland.
I hold they should be well and comfortably housed, and that any house that we
can erect for them is not one bit too good
for our Royal Ulster Constabulary.

for 1929-30 amounts to £29,255, and

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
House of Commons, and the decreased
cost of supplying stationery, books, and
office supplies for the use of the Government Departments. During the past two
years, as a result of a scrutiny of the demands for stationery and printing supplies, it has been apparent that the
various Government Departments, having
now approached normal working conditions, were exercising close scrutiny over
their requirements in this connection.
Moreover, the completion of the Census
has removed the necessity for a provision
in respect of printing which, in the year
1928-29, amounted to some £1,500.
It must be remembered that in the
early years it was a matter of great difficulty to forecast the precise requirements
of the public departments-including the
library of this House-in the matter of
printing, stationery, books and other
similar supplies; and my Ministry was
not inclined to sanction expenditure,
although a good prima facie case could be
shown, until the experience of some years
working had proved the necessity. The
Departments, accordingly, in some cases,
did not complete their essential equipment
in the matter of stationery, etc., supplies
at the outset, but only as and when experience proved the necessity. Accordingly, the annual provision now required
can be confined to normal requirements
with the exception, of course, of special
provision for any special services which
may be required in future years. This
gratifying result is due, in no small
measure, to the co-operation of the
Departments, in themselves exercising
close scrutiny over stationery and printing
demands. I beg to move.

Financial Statement, 1929-30.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That this House approves the proposals
of the Government for meeting the financial requirements of the year."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): When I presented my seventh
Financial Statement a year ago in this
House, I expressed the hope that as the
first seven years of our federal life as a
Province had been marked by an unprecedented, and indeed uninterrupted spell
of depressing trade conditions, that—
relying on tradition-possibly the beginnings of a fresh septennate would bring
with it an era of greater prosperity and
Contentment.
While, as a people, we have much to
be thankful for during the year which
has recently ended on the 31st March,
it cannot be said that my early expectations have been fully realised. The best
that can be said of 1928-29 is that trade
conditions have shewn a partial recuperation. Prices of agricultural produce
have not been remunerative; the world
demand for the product of our mills and
factories has not by any means fully responded to our hopes; and of our great
basic industries, shipbuilding is the only
trade of which it can be said that it has
enjoyed a fair measure of prosperity.
But from many indices, which I need
not enter into, there are indications of
a more hopeful feeling in commerce and
industry-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-and with world conditions improving
there cannot be any doubt that we shall
share in the result. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
Hon. Members have had supplied to
them a preliminary Financial Statement,
in which the estimated revenue and expenditure for the current year are left
blank. It gives, however, a complete
picture of the actual outcome of our
finances for the year which closed on the
31st March last, and the blanks to which
I have just referred relate to the estimated
revenue and expenditure for the present
financial year.
I will give the figures in
the course of my statement, and those
Members who are sufficiently interested
will be able, if they so wish, to fill in
the blanks as I go along. In any case, a
complete statement will be issued during
the course of the afternoon.
This
For the moment, I propose to confine
myself to the results of last year.

In view of this, it is not so necessary for

The estimated expenditure, as shown

In the form of our Accounts, I should
point out the distinction which is shown
between Consolidated Fund Services and
Supply Services.
Expenditure under the head of Consolidated Fund Services is authorised
definitely by Statute, and is a first charge
upon the Consolidated Fund. On the
other hand, provision for Supply Services
is made in the form of Estimates, and the
details are fully discussed each year in
the Committee of Supply, as we know
from our experience of the last week or
two.
So far as last year's Consolidated Fund
Services are concerned, the only item I
need mention concerns the operations on
the Residuary Share Suspense Account,
which are shown to the amount of
£159,000 in respect of adjustments for
past years. This is, of course, an item
that cannot be estimated. The Suspense
Account was, in fact, created under an
Act of this Parliament passed in 1927,
to provide a suitable medium for the many
adjustments consequential upon the intricate character of our financial relations with Great Britain. The Imperial
contribution is not finally determined for
any one year, until one, or perhaps two
years later, and other adjustments in respect of the Reserved Taxes are similarly
delayed until final figures are available.
Consequently, this Suspense Account
serves the purpose of preventing the distortion of the accounts for any one year
by reason of adjustments relating to previous years, and enables us to present the
accounts in their proper perspective.
Supply Services have run their normal
course, and, compared with earlier years,
the Estimates were very close.

fact that Postal revenues so nearly approximate to the cost of the Service is
an excellent example of the value of the

little appreciate. Our Post Office, being

Before concluding my review of last
year's operations, I wish to take this
opportunity of referring to a few of the
more important features of the Parliamentary and Administrative work that
was carried out, and of their effect on our
financial position.
In the forefront, I place the arrangements with the British Government-now
The Budget-
Finance Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
happily on a permanent Statutory basisfor the future of our Unemployment Insurance Fund. This subject was dealt
with exhaustively by my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Labour, at the
time, and I will not weary the Committee
with a recapitulation of all its details. It
is right, however, to emphasise especially
the facts, firstly, that the taxpayers of
this Province are providing no less than
£300,000 this year to keep the Fund on
a parity with the British Fund, while
Great Britain, on its part, is contributing
£470,000; and, secondly, that we have
already written off £424,000 of the old
Unemployment Insurance Debt, and have
undertaken to continue to do so by
£100,000 per annum.
We have just been careful to safeguard
the interests of our industrial workers.
We have been no less concerned with the
position of our farmers, and the arrangements embodied in the Land Act recently
passed into law at Westminster will, we
have every reason to believe, be the final
instalment of the series of settlements of
the many burning questions associated
with land purchase schemes. The determination of the 27th of last month as a
common appointed day will place an
additional burden of about £42,000 on
our Exchequer, but I count the money
well spent if it means timely relief to
fifteen or twenty thousand of our smaller
farmers.
We have naturally followed with interest the introduction of a separate currency in the Free State, more especially
since, in consequence, we became directly
concerned with various questions affecting the circulation and issue of bank
notes by the different banks operating
in our area.
In order to encourage banking in Ireland, the Imperial Government in 1845
allowed Irish banks the privilege of a fiduciary issue of bank notes-that is to say,
the banks were permitted to issue their
own notes up to certain limits without
holding cash as cover against the issue.
There is no doubt that this policy brought
about the results it was intended to
achieve; it enabled the banks to open
branches in small towns and villages
where the volume of business alone would
would not have enabled a bank to be
carried on, and so banking facilities were
made available even in the poorest and
most scattered districts in the land.
But as the note issues of banks in the
Free State are now regulated by its own
Currency Commission, it is evident that
the fiduciary issues fixed for the whole of
Ireland could not equitably be applied to
the restricted area of the Six Counties,
and an apportionment became necessary.
This matter, though apparently
academic in character, has an important
bearing on the ordinary trade and industry of the Province, and we are all,
therefore, under an obligation to the
Treasury for the very helpful attitude
they displayed which greatly facilitated
the settlement of the question. The new
arrangements received the force of law
by an Act of the Imperial Parliament
passed last year.
I should, perhaps, mention to the
House that a somewhat difficult situation
arose in regard to the assessment of composition stamp duty on the expiring
issues of all-Ireland bank notes during
the transitional period between the issue
of the new Northern Ireland notes and
the withdrawal of the old note issue.
I am glad to say, however, that the
powers conferred on my Ministry by the
Finance Act of last autumn, coupled
with discussions and co-operation with the
Free State Currency Commission,
abled these difficulties to be satisfactorily
overcome.

The total under these headings of Consolidated Fund Services, Supply Services, and Reserved Services is thus
£10,094,000, and I will now deal with
the last item chargeable against revenue,
namely, the Imperial Contribution for
1929-30.
Our responsibility for the payment of
a contribution towards the cost of
Imperial Services has for some years past
aroused a certain amount of discussion in
this House. It is well-known that
originally the contribution was fixed at
no less than £7,920,000 per annum. The
White Papers which were issued to explain the financial provisions of the Government of Ireland Act, purported to
show that Northern Ireland would, after
paying that contribution, and after meeting the cost of all services, still have
available substantial margins for development generally
This promised well, but before six
months had passed, it was too clear that
these rosy anticipations would not be
realised, and following a long series of
discussions, the Colwyn Committee was
appointed to report on the matter.
The Colwyn Report has often been referred to here, and its basic principles.
should be, perhaps, more clearly understood. It set up standards of revenue
and expenditure, and recommended that
in determining the contribution for future
years, regard should be had to variations
from these standards as regards both
British revenue collection and British expenditure on social services. That is to
say, the contribution reflects variations in
taxation, and changes up or down in the
expenditure on local services.
Since 1920, when the financial basis of
the Government of Ireland Act was determined, there have been many changes in
Reserved Taxation-that is to say,
changes made by the Imperial Government itself.

It
As regards taxation, income tax has
fallen from 6s to 4s, and the rates of relief
in respect of earned income and children
have been substantially increased.
must also be remembered that relief of
this character means a relatively much
greater loss in revenue here than in Great
Britain, since the proportion of smaller
incomes here is much higher. Corporation
Profits Tax and Excess Profits Duty have
disappeared, although a few arrears continue to be collected.
Important changes have been made in
Customs and Excise. Articles that were
on the tariff list in 1920 have disappeared;
others have been put on; and in other
cases the rates of duty have been altered.
Postage rates have come down, as have
also telephone and telegraph charges.
The Government of Ireland Act finance
was based on a reserved revenue of over
fourteen millions. Last year just over
seven and a half millions were collected,
so that circumstances altogether outside
our control have resulted in the fact that
the Estimates of 1920 exceed the actual
results of last year by no less than six
and a half millions.
On the expenditure side, the last eight
years have witnessed the introduction of
new social services, the extension of existing ones, the assumption by the State of
heavy burdens in respect of rates, and
many other forms of increased activity in
what are termed local services.

TRANSFERRED REVENUE, 1929-30.
I estimate the total of our transferred

Death Duties are expected to produce
£600,000. The yield of this form of

big estates, and I think it is safer to rely
on this figure, although last year we
received £666,000. Looking at the last
few years, I find that in each year a
quarter of this revenue has been derived
from one or two estates, which clearly
shows how uncertain is the yield of these
taxes.
The Stamp Duties provide a fairly
steady source of income, and I expect
them to yield £280,000 this year. While
on this subject, I would like to
take this opportunity of referring
to the Stamp Duties payable on

Transferred Excise Duties are estimated to yield £130,000.
Lastly, I anticipate a small increase in
the yield of Motor Vehicles Duties, and I
am budgeting for £440,000. This is
balanced by payment of a like sum into
the Road Fund.
The grading of Commercial Motor
Vehicles for purposes of taxation has been
occupying my mind for some time past,
and I have appointed a Departmental
Committee to examine the question in detail, and to advise as to what changes
may be required.
But I must make my position perfectly
plain. Whatever may be done in regard
to Motor taxation, the Road Fund must
be self-supporting. In this I have the
entire support of my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Home Affairs, who is immediately responsible for the administration of that Fund. I will not be a party
to any adjustments in taxation, which
throw even a remote liability on the Exchequer so far as the upkeep and construction of roads are concerned.
I could make comparisons with Great
Britain, which would clearly prove that
our motor users are not less favourably
treated than those in Great Britain, but
such comparisons are beside the point.
The only thing that matters is that the
Road Fund must be self-supporting, and
my only concern is to secure the equitable
apportionment of this burden.
RESERVED REVENUE, 1929-30.
Estimates for the yield of reserved taxes
are provided for us by the Departments
concerned, and my comments cannot,
therefore, be of a very exhaustive nature.
Customs and Excise Duties on commodities retained for consumption in Northern
Ireland are estimated at £3,861,000.
This figure allows for the loss resulting
from the repeal of the duty on tea, which
is calculated to cost us £143,000. I will
not weary the Committee with a lengthy
recital of details, but I would point out
that, on the whole, the revenue under
these heads is increasing, pointing to improvement both in general conditions and
in the standard of living.
Income Tax and Super Tax are put at
£2,870,000--a figure which does not differ
materially from last year's results-and
the now defunct Corporation Profits Tax
and Excess Profits Duty will produce
another £10,000.
The total from reserved taxes is thus
put at £6,741,000, bringing the total estimated tax revenue up to £8,186,000.
I now come to the last head of Revenue,
namely, Non-tax Revenue, which forms a
very important part of our total receipts.
The biggest item is the Post Office,
which is expected to bring in this year
£870,000. The gradual increase in Post
Office receipts is indicative of a steady
and well-sustained improvement in general
trade conditions, and although the Post
Office is not yet on a self-supporting basis
-the Estimates show that we expect a
loss of £37,000 this year-yet I am hopeful that the day is not far distant when,
instead of showing a deficit, the Post
Office with improved facilities will actually
contribute to the general Services of the
State.
Land Purchase Annuities are estimated
to amount in all to £665,000, and, I
think, that having dealt with this subject
so extensively in the earlier part of my
statement, I need not dwell further on
the matter now.
Receipts from Church Temporary Rentcharges, etc., will produce £17,000.
Miscellaneous Receipts of £257,000 are
budgeted for in connection with mainly
interest on investments and interest payable by the Unemployment Insurance
Fund in respect of advances to it. This
is necessarily considerably below the
actual receipts of last year, since special
items, to which I referred earlier, will
not recur.
The total receipts under the head of
Non-Tax Revenue amount to £1,809,000.
Under Section 34 (1) of the Government of Ireland Act, the cost of providing
buildings and initial equipment for
Public Departments in Northern Ireland
forms a charge on the Consolidated Fund
of the United Kingdom. £244,000 is expected to be received this year in connection mainly with the building works
now in progress at Stormont. This is.
of course, offset by a corresponding expenditure on the other side of the Account.
Finally, under the Unemployment Insurance Agreement, it is expected that

I was amazed at the Member for

Where I come from this question of
noxious weeds never comes up at all. I
welcome this scheme for the derating of
agriculture, which will relieve agriculture
to an extent somewhere about £600.000
or £700,000 a year. This could not have
come in a more opportune time. Agriculture is going through a terrible time.
I do not think in the history of Ulster has
agriculture had a more depressing time.
This will not relieve agriculture to the
extent one would think. I would like
to have seen embraced in the Budget a

Sir DAWSON BATES: I feel it a
great privilege to be in the position of
moving in this House the Second Reading of the Derating Bill, because I realise
that the Bill is an epoch-making one,
which, in the days to come, will be regarded in something of the same light as
the Local Government Act of 1898.
which placed local government administration in the hands of the elected representatives of the people.
So much has been said about the Bill
in this Parliament already, so much has
been written and spoken about it outside,
and it has formed the subject of so many
conferences and discussions with local
authorities that I feel in a sense that it
is, perhaps, unnecessary for me to speak
at any great length on it, but the Bill,
as I have already stated, is such an important one, and its effects are so farreaching, that I feel I would not be doing
justice to it or to the House were I not
to give a brief outline of the events which
have led up to its introduction and of
its object and effect.
Hon. Members who have taken the
trouble to study the history of local government administration are, no doubt,
aware that in the early days of
local government administration the
State left the local government authorities severely to themselves, and it
was only in comparatively recent
years that Parliament accepted the
principle of according State assistance
to the local authorities in order to
relieve them, partially, of the growing
burdens which they were called upon to
assume by virtue of the improved services they were supplying to the ratepayers.
Although we have had local government for over a century, it is only a matter of 40 years ago that the first real
attempt was made to accord State assistance in relief of rates. In the year
1887 it was decided that the proceeds of
certain probate and licence duties should
be applied towards the relief of expenditure on specified local government services. After the passing of the Local
£35 Local Government Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Government Act of 1898, a considerable
number of our public health, poor law,
asylum, and road services were subsidized
from what was known as the Local Taxation Account, which was established by
the Act, and which derived its revenue
from the proceeas of certain taxes and
duties.
Gradually, however, as time went on
Parliament began to realise that this
system of paying grants to local authorities out of what may be described as "assigned revenues" was unsatisfactory, as
it deprived Parliament of the opportunity
of controlling the financial operations of
the central local government department
in respect of these grants.
Under more recent Acts passed by the
Imperial Parliament since 1898, grants
for new services were provided each year
from voted moneys. Following this
principle, arrangements were made as
soon as possible after the establishment
of the Government of Northern Ireland
to obtain parliamentary sanction to the
alteration of the old disjointed system,
and to the substitution of a new system,
under which all the grants payable to the
local authorities would be shown in the
Estimates and voted by Parliament
annually.
One of the most important of these
grants was the grant in relief of rates
on agricultural land. This grant was
first established by the Local Government Act of 1898, and was calculated
on the basis of half poor rate and county
cess payable on agricultural land in the
standard year-that standard year was
taken as 1897-and it was realised, even
at that time, that if agricultural land
had to meet the full charge of the rates
it would involve an unduly heavy burden. It was, accordingly, a stereotyped
grant, and so it remained for nearly
thirty years.
On the establishment of the Government of Northern Ireland, it was realised
by us that with the growing burden of
local taxation a grant to the farmers,
which was fixed to meet conditions as
they existed in 1898, was inadequate.
and inequitable, and, accordingly, in the
year 1924, this House was asked to double
the agricultural grant. Accordingly,
the figure of £128,644 was increased to
£257,288.
Having regard to the continued depression in agriculture and industry, the
Government have now decided to accord
a still further measure of relief to agriculture, and, at the same time, to introduce a new feature into our local government system by giving a substantial
measure of rate relief to productive industry.
This Bill gives effect to that decision,
and its main features are:-
(a) Agricultural land and farm
buildings will be relieved from all
local rates, with one or two minor exceptions, for example, rates for malicious injury decrees, drainage rates,
and certain water rates, which are
really rents.
(b) Productive industries will be
relieved of 75 per cent. of their rates.
(c) Transport undertakings (including docks and canals) will similarly be
relieved of 75 per cent. of their rates,
but on the condition that the relief is
passed on in the form of rebates to
manufacturers and farmers, in respect
of carriage of raw materials, etc.
(d) Salmon and eel fishery undertakings will benefit to the extent of 60
per cent. relief of rates on their properties.
It should not be difficult to visualise
what a distinct boon these measures will
be to industry generally. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). At present our industries and our farmers are suffering
from external competition, and, undoubtedly, the benefits of this Bill should
enable them to extend their undertakings and to improve their position in the
markets of the world.
I have, up to the present, confined my
remarks to the objects of the Bill,
namely, the relief to industry, and now
I will deal with the measures which the
Bill prescribes in connection with the recoupment to the local authorities of the
loss of revenue which will fall on them
by reason of the derating proposals. I
will take the Urban Authorities first, as
their problem is the simpler one. In the
case of the urban areas, agricultural land
forms a very small part of the hereditaments, and the derating proposals will,
therefore, apply mainly to premises used for
productive industries. The loss of rates to
the urban authorities will, accordingly,
form but a small part (approximately 12
per cent.) of the total rates to be collected by those authorities, and, accord-
Local Government Bill-
Second Reading.
13 JUNE 1929
ingly, it is our proposal to recoup in each
case to the local authorities the actual
loss of revenue sustained by them.
I now turn to the rural portions of
each of the counties, and here the problem is a much more complicated one,
by reason of the fact that in these areas
the rates on agricultural land form the
bulk (approximately 80 per cent.) of the
rates assessed by the local authorities.
Accordingly, the net result will be that,
in the future, the Ministry of Home
Affairs, acting on behalf of the Government, will become the largest ratepayer
in the counties. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
While the Ministry has been entrusted
with a certain measure of control over
the activities of the various local authorities in the counties, at a later stage, undoubtedly, it will be necessary and desirable, in view of the greater financial
responsibility which the Government is
undertaking, to accord the Ministry a
greater measure of control over the financial operations of the local government
authorities.
In the meantime, we cannot apply to
the county areas the principle which we
have agreed to apply in the case of the
urban districts-that of merely recouping
each year's loss. If we did, there would
be nothing to stop the local authorities
from spending recklessly at the expense
of the Government, and so we have devised a scheme under which the local
authorities will be paid each year standard deficiency grants, based, generally
on what would have been required during the last three years, to meet their
losses if the farmers and the proprietors
of productive industries, etc., had been
relieved during that period of rates in
the manner which the Bill now proposes,
due allowance being made for abnormalities in expenditure.
As the new educational services are still
in their infancy, we propose to base our
standard on the expenditure of education
authorities for one year only, instead of
three, namely, the last financial year.
These general deficiency grants wi'l be
calculated on the basis I have referred to
and will be stereotyped as standard
grants for a period of five years. At the
end of the five-year period they will be
revised in the light of new conditions. I
think hon. Members will agree that this
is a great improvement on the old system
of stereotyping grants for all time.
While fixing the standard grants for the
various authorities and charges for the
next five years, we realise that in the
normal course of events during that period
there may be in some cases appropriate
and normal increases of expenditure which
may not be counterbalanced by savings
in other directions. In connection with
such increases the Government realise that
in regard to them a certain and substantial measure of relief should be available
and granted, but at the same time the
State cannot in this connection undertake
unlimited liability. The Imperial
Government has adopted in this regard a
somewhat elaborate series of formulae and
adjustments to meet growing expenditure,
but on considering the matter in the light
of the conditions which exist in Northern
Ireland, and having discussed it fully with
the representatives of the local authorities,
we have decided to adopt a more simple
and appropriate system of payment of
supplemental grants to meet growing expenditure.

I have dealt with cases of increased expenditure. I will now deal with the converse case. It is possible-though highly

of course, cannot be contemplated. Το

I will now deal briefly with a few minor
points of detail in the Bill. In the first
place, while the Bill makes provision for
standard and supplemental grants to
county councils and rural district councils,
for the next five years, the necessary
calculation will take time, and so
have, at the request of the county
we
councils in Clause 14 (5) made a special
provision for this financial year under
which the local authorities will be recouped this year their actual loss. It
will be understood that the rates had
actually been struck in the counties before it was known that the derating provisions would apply as from the 1st
April.
As soon as we had made the decision
to make the Bill apply as from the 1st
April, we found it necessary to issue instructions to the county councils not to
collect rates If we had not done so,
and had allowed even portion of the rates
to be collected we would have found it a
matter of great complication and difficulty to make the necessary refunds later.
The Bill gives covering authority for
this arrangement, and also requires the
county councils to collect the rates for
the year in one instalment, instead of in
two moieties, as at present. At the same
time, we realise that a single rate collection might operate somewhat harshly
on poorer classes of tenants, and while
provision is made for one collection in
the future, arrangements are also made
whereby the rate on smaller hereditaments, that is, £8 valuation and under,
can be collected in two moieties. Hon.
Members will see that this applies only
to the counties.
It will also be realised that the introduction of the derating principle will,
to a very considerable extent, affect the
amounts to be collected by the various
rate collectors throughout the country,
and, of course, would incidentally affect
their emoluments where these emoluments are paid by way of poundage fees.
At the same time, the collectors will still
have to visit the ratepayers generally in
their districts, and to serve demand notes
on them, even for reduced amounts, so
actually the amount of labour will be
practically the same. Accordingly,
Clause 20 of the Bill safeguards the existing rights and emoluments of the
existing collectors, subject, however, in
every case to efficient and due discharge
of their duties.
I should also draw attention to the
arrangements which are provided for in
Clause 14 of the Bill. in regard to the
time and the manner of payment of both
the standard and supplemental grants.
This is a matter which has formed the
subiect of consultation with the local
authorities, and in consequence of their
representations we have agreed to pay the

standard grant in four instalments on
fixed dates in June, September, January
and March, which will meet the full requirements and needs of the local authorities.
As regards the supplemental grants, it
will be understood that they are not of a
stereotyped character, and depend on
varying circumstances. Accordingly,
they will have to be calculated on the
basis of estimate rather than on fixed
quantity. We propose, therefore, to
adopt the same principle in regard to
them as we do in the case of the road
grants, namely, to pay 90 per cent.
during the course of the year concerned,
in four instalments, leaving the balance
of 10 per cent. over for subsequent adjustment between the Ministry and the local
authority.
I would also like to refer to Clause 7,
which provides that in the future all
charges for such purely local services as
waterworks, sewerage, etcetera, will be
borne over the rural districts concerned,
and will not be confined to townlands, to
dispensary districts, or to other local areas
of charge, as in the past. The reason for
this alteration in the law is an obvious
one. Under the old system, where no
Government grants were available, it was
difficult to persuade the council of a rural
district to accept a general financial responsibility for a service such as a waterworks or a sewerage scheme which was of
purely local benefit, and it was, accordingly, a matter of great difficulty for the
central government, that is, the Local
Government Board in Dublin, and the
Ministry of Home Affairs in Belfast, to
secure the formulation and the carrying
out of such necessary schemes owing to the
conflict between the local authority and
the people of the locality as to the areas
of charge. The rural district council
naturally wanted the local village to pay
the full cost, while the people of the
village and the neighbouring locality
were unable to undertake the financial
responsibility, and felt that the rural
district as a whole should shoulder
part of the expenses. The result was,
and is at the present time in many
country districts, that the schemes have
been abandoned simply through difficulty
in getting the rural district council to
shoulder the responsibility.
Now, however, the situation will be entirely different. As I have already
pointed out, the Government is shouldering the major portion of the financial
burden in the rural areas, and, accordingly, there is no justification whatever
for any rural district council to refuse to
bear, as a district charge, the balance of
the expense of providing a much-needed
water supply scheme, or sewerage scheme,
for a particular town or village in their
midst.
We realise that if this change in policy
and principle were to be applied to existing schemes, without some counterbalancing adjustment, there would be
undoubtedly some inequity and reasonable
ground for grievance on the part of the
ratepayers in those localities where such
services have not up to the present been
provided, as they would suddenly find
themselves called upon to pay their proportionate part of the district charges for
the water, sewerage and other services
have already been provided in more fortunate areas.
In order to meet such objection, the
Government will come to the rescue of
these down-trodden ratepayers, and we
are making provision in the Bill, under
which no ratepayer will be called upon
to bear any extra charge on foot of such
existing schemes. I think that it will be
agreed that this provision will dispose of
any objection to the new principle which
we are establishing in Northern Ireland.
I think that I have outlined generally
the salient points of the Bill. It will be
observed that I have, in the main, confined myself to the local government
aspect of the Bill, and have not attempted
to deal with the complications of rebates
to transport undertakings. This matter
was explained to the House at length by
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock), in November last,
when introducing the Rating and Valuation Act, 1928, and I feel sure that he will
gladly explain any points of difficulty or
doubt in this regard.
As regards the question of relief to our
salmon and eel fisheries, I should say that
these matters come within the jurisdiction
of my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Commerce (Mr. Barbour), and while I
have no doubt that this proposal will
commend itself to the House, I should
say that he, similarly, will be prepared to
explain any matters in regard to fisheries
which may call for attention. But
dealing with the Bill as a whole, as I have
already explained, it is an epoch-making
Measure and just as important as the
great Act of 1898, which conferred upon

Derry, and it would be worth while for
some Members who are advocating a reduction in the tax on these heavy motor
lorries to travel between Magherafelt and
Toomebridge and see the condition these
roads, recently repaired, are placed in by
these heavy lorries, and if they can come
back to this House and advocate a reduction in the tax on these heavy lorries, all I
say is, I would not do it, as a representative of the farming community. Because
we must remember if these lorries are not
going to be made to pay a tax in some
measure commensurate with the damage
they are doing to the roads, it simply
means that the farming community have
got to pay to make up the condition.
And as far as the Road Fund is concerned, the Minister of Finance stated
clearly yesterday that the Road Fund must
hang by itself. The Road Fund has not
been raided for any purpose, and all the
money going into the Fund has been put
to remaking and improving the roads.
If we are going to deplete it, then it would

the farmers on the one hand, and putting

going to raid the Road Fund or reduce
the Road Fund, it would mean the agriculturists would have to pay more for the

roads.

ervices generally will follow at a not very

Bankruptcy (Amendment) Bill [S.]
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time
Mr. BARBOUR: It will be within the
knowledge of hon. Members that our
Bankruptcy Law in Ireland has grown in
the course of years into a somewhat
shapeless fabric, in which are to be found
at several points important divergencies
from the law obtaining in England, with
whose commercial community we are so
closely linked. It was accordingly
borne in upon us, soon after I assumed
the responsibility for the direction of the
Ministry of Commerce, that a change in
the law was necessary, and, in order that
the many aspects of a difficult and complex problem might be thoroughly investigated I set up in the Autumn of 1926
a small but expert committee under the
able chairmanship of my hon. Friend, the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry
of Education, who, as the House will be
aware, has made a special study of this
subject.
13 JUNE 1929
Bankruptcy Bill-

Second Reading.
With regard to the changes which we
propose to make, I should like to say, in
the first place, that it is not our intention
to make any radical change in the
machinery of administration. On this
point I may, perhaps, be permitted to
quote from the Report of the Committee
of Inquiry:-
The Committee to which I have referred produced a report containing recommendations, which are the basis of
the Bill before you. The deliberations
of the Committee covered a considerable
period, and witnesses were examined
from every interest involved, whether
legal or commercial. I am satisfied that
the recommendations which the committee have made will go far towards simplifying the existing Bankruptcy Code,
and, whilst the consolidation of bankruptcy law as a whole must necessarily
take some considerable time, in view of
the ramifications of the existing law on
the subject, the Government have thought
it right to introduce this Bill immediately, in order that certain anomalies,
the most important of which I shall endeavour to explain to the House, might
be remedied forthwith, and that in
general the important step should be
taken of bringing our existing bankruptcy law into as close conformity as
local circumstances permit with the present law on the subject in England,
which, as hon. Members will be aware, has
recently undergone substantial amendment.
Before referring in any detail to the
provisions of the Bill, I should like to
make a brief reference to the legislative
position as it exists to-day. For all
practical purposes the Law of Bankruptcy in Ireland is just over 70 years
old. The law took definite shape in the
Irish Bankrupt and Insolvent Act, 1857.
This Act was amended in some respects
by the Bankruptcy (Ireland) Amendment Act, 1872, but, apart from this,
there has been no attempt to secure a
comprehensive revision in Ireland, and
so, to-day, the Act of 1857 still stands
as the corner stone of our Bankruptcy
Code.
In this respect we are far behind
Great Britain. There the whole Law of
Insolvency, relating both to bankruptcy
and to private arrangement, was revised
and consolidated in 1913. Bankruptcy
and arrangement matters were given
separate Acts in 1914. Even the Bankruptcy Act of 1914, complete as it was,
was amended in certain important particulars in 1926, by an Act which owed
its inspirations largely to Chambers of
Commerce, bankers, and business men
generally, who desired to see the law still
further modernised to bring it more into
accord with post-war business conditions.
"All the
professional witnesses
familiar with local bankruptcy practice told us that it worked very well
and that the people had become accustomed to it. Under these circumstances, we do not recommend a change
in the existing system."
The Committee did, however, make
one suggestion for speeding up the procedure, which the Government has considered it very necessary to adopt. I refer to the provision contained in Sections
4 and 5 of the Bill for speeding up the
court machinery by abolishing the second
sitting before the court, both in
arrangements and compositions after
bankruptcy. The saving of time, not
less than a fortnight, and of expenses will
be found to be of the greatest advantage,
coming, as it does, in the earlier stages
of the proceedings.
The House will not, I am sure, expect
me to make a detailed reference to all the
Clauses of the Bill, some of which are of
a highly technical nature. There are
some, however, of great practical importance, which it is incumbent upon me
to explain to the House.
In the first place, a radical change has
been made with regard to the scope of
bankruptcy offences and the penalties provided. Honourable Members will notice
on reference to Clause 22 that the three
principal commercial irregularities, which
post-war conditions have considerably
aggravated, have been singled out for
the special penalty of penal servitude for
any term not exceeding five years, or to
imprisonment for a term not exceeding
two years, with or without hard labour.
These offences in relation to bankruptcy
are: Obtaining property by fraud; obtaining property under false pretence of
carrying on a business, and disposing of
property otherwise than in the normal
course of trade.
The last-mentioned offences-disposing
of goods otherwise than in the ordinary
course of business-is also further distinguished: The pledgee or receiver of the
goods with a knowledge of the circum-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
stances is deemed to be guilty of a misdemeanour. The next clause, No. 23,
also contains a very necessary reform,
making it a misdemeanour for an undischarged bankrupt to obtain credit to the
extent of £10 or upwards, without disclosing his bankruptcy.
Important evidence was tendered to
the Committee touching the losses sustained by Northern Ireland traders
through the weakness of our law in these
respects, and it has been felt that these
offences are such as should, in the interests
of the creditor, have a greater penalty
attached to them. I can assure the
House that the honest and unfortunate
debtor is in no way prejudiced by the
provisions I have mentioned. Our objective is the dishonest, evasive, or reckless debtor, and I feel sure that honourable Members will agree that against
such a one a creditor deserves all the protection he can get.
In
Another important provision is the
liability to keep proper books of account,
imposed by Clause 25 of the Bill.
English law, the failure of a bankrupt
to keep books has always been regarded
as a serious bankruptcy offence, justifying suspension or the refusal of a discharge, but it was not until the Act of
1914, to which I have referred, that it
was made a misdemeanour, and even
then only on the trader's second bankruptcy. Now, under Section 7 of the
Bankruptcy Amendment Act of 1926,
this distinction is swept away and a bankrupt failing to keep the usual books of
account, as defined by the section, is
liable to prosecution on his first bankruptcy.
The clause to which I am now directing the particular attention of the House
virtually adopts the legislative position
as it exists in England to-day. Honourable Members will observe that a distinction is made between a first-time
bankrupt and one who has previously
failed. The former is not to be prosecuted unless his liabilities amount to
£500 or over, but in the case of a debtor
who has previously failed prosecution
may be instituted if the liabilities amount
to £100. There is no doubt that in this
matter of
of keeping even elementary
accounts there is a great need for improvement, especially among the small
traders in our cities and country towns,
although in recent years the operation of
the Income Tax Acts has brought about
some improvement in this respect.
On the question of possible hardship,
I think it will be agreed that the limit
of liabilities to which I have referred will
prevent the clause from pressing unduly
on the very small trader whose turnover
is so negligible as to render the keeping
of accounts comparatively unimportant.
It is not the intention of the Government,
however, to introduce these particular
provisions as to the keeping of accounts
without warning, for it will be seen that
a period of two years from the passing
that
of the Act is being allowed so
traders may make the necessary arrangements during the period of grace.
We also propose to make some radical
changes in the Law of Bankruptcy as it
affects married women. These changes
are given effect to in Clauses 10 and 20
of the Bill. Some of the witnesses who
appeared before the Committee advocated
the imposition on married women of restrictions of a somewhat drastic character
in regard to trading. It has been felt,
however, that it would be inadvisable to
proceed in advance of Great Britain in
this matter. There a married woman
who carries on a trade or business is liable
to bankruptcy proceedings, irrespective of
whether her trade or business is carried
on separately from her husband or not,
and is also liable to be served with a Bankruptcy Notice on a Final Judgment or
Order as though she were personally
bound to pay the debt.
Furthermore, the husband of a bankrupt married woman is not entitled to
claim any dividend as a creditor in respect of any money, or other asset, lent
or entrusted by him to his wife for the
purposes of her trade or business, until
all claims of the other creditors of his
wife have been satisfied. Similarly, in
the bankruptcy of the husband, the
claims of the wife are postponed to those
of other creditors. In Ireland the position
of a married woman is governed by the
Married Woman's Property Act, 1882,
Section 1 (5) of which provides that
"every married woman carrying on a
trade separately from her husband shall,
in respect of her separate property, be
subject to the Bankruptcy Laws in the
same way as if she were a 'femme sole.' "
Thus as the law stands at present a
marred woman in Northern Ireland cannot be made bankrupt unless she carry on
a trade and carry it on separately from
her husband. Hon. Members will, I am
Bankruptcy Bill-
Second Reading.
13 JUNE 1929
sure, agree that for married women to continue to enjoy this privileged position constitutes an anomaly which is completely
out of accord with post-war business conditions, and one which should be removed
without delay..
Another matter to which I desire to
make a brief reference is the scope of the
various Acts of Bankruptcy as defined in
our Bankruptcy Code. Here there has
been no great widening of the net through
the years, for there is remarkable similarity between the Acts of Bankruptcy as
enumerated for England in Section 1 of
the Act of 1914, and the list for Ireland
set forth in Section 21 of the Bankruptcy
(Ireland) Amendment Act, 1872. In this
matter we propose to go a step further
than the legislative position in England
by making [in clause 1(b)] a return of
"No Goods" by the Sheriff an Act of
Bankruptcy in Northern Ireland. Apart
from the fact that this reform was advocated by nearly all the professional and
commercial interests that gave evidence
before the Committee, it is difficult to
appreciate why a debtor who has no goods
to seize should escape this penalty which
attaches to debtors who have goods subject
to seizure. In one respect, however, we
propose to bring the law into line with
England by making [in clause 1(d)]
"Fraudulent Preference" an Act of
Bankruptcy.
Other reforms to which, perhaps, a
passing reference may be made at this
stage are:-
the sweeping away of old distinctions
between traders and non-traders
which left the latter in a very
sheltered position (Clause 1),
preventing creditors from unreasonably withholding their consent to
a Deed of Assignment outside the
Court where the debtor has secured
a proper measure of support for
his proposal (Clause 2),
giving an option to a creditor of a
deceased insolvent of proceeding in
the Bankruptcy Court instead of in
the Chancery Division (Clause 21),
imposing penalties for rash speculation or gambling by bankrupts
(Clause 24).
I have now, I think, explained the
clauses of the most importance and those
to which the commercial community will
give the greatest consideration.
Before I sit down I should like to
express in a word or two the Government's appreciation of the public-spirited
and disinterested manner in which professional and business men, as members
of the Bankruptcy Committee, gave their
valuable time to the consideration of this
subject. The Bill owes much to their
ungrudging labours. I beg to move.
Mr. HEALY: I do not think that
serious objection can be taken to this
Measure on any side of the House. There
have been certain anomalies between the
law in England and the law in Ireland
for a considerable time that must have
borne harshly on creditors. For instance,
in the matter of a return of "no goods"
by the sheriff's officer-I suppose that
sheriffs' officers are not any different from
other people and sometimes it has been
alleged that returns of this kind were
made when the facts of the situation did
not justify them, with the result, as the
Minister has pointed out, that a man who
had no goods was immune from bankruptcy, whereas a man with some goods
was liable to be made a bankrupt. I am
glad that anomaly has been wiped away
and that the failure of the sheriff's officer
to do his duty or to make a correct return
will not conduce to the benefit of a dishonest person anywhere.
There is also the question of the distinction between traders and non-traders.
Hitherto, as I understand it, unless a man
was engaged in business it was difficult to
make him a bankrupt. Now, whether he
be in business or technically out of business and in private life the law is intended
to apply equally. There is one form of
fraud that is rather prevalent, probably
to a greater extent across the water than
in this country, that is what is known
as the long firm fraud, in which a man
obtains goods with the deliberate intention of disposing of them and then
clearing out.
There are three conditions under which
a person may leave himself liable to a long
term of imprisonment. The first is by
obtaining property by fraud, the second
by obtaining property by the false pretence of carrying on a business of some
kind, and the third by disposing of property otherwise than in the ordinary way
of trade. It has sometimes happened that
people who have had no place of business.
and no bona fide intention of conducting
a business have obtained credit and have
put the trustful creditors into an awkward
position. In all these matters one must
remember that if a trader be in the

School Teachers (Oath and Declaration)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
very
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): I do not propose to detain the House long in moving
the Second Reading of this
short Bill. Briefly, the Bill is designed
to remove a difficulty which has caused a
certain amount of inconvenience in the
administration of Section 5 of the Local
Government Act (N.I.), 1922, and of the
Promissory Oaths Act (N.I.), 1923, so
far as they relate to teachers. As hon.
Members are aware, Section 5 (2) of the
Local Government Act of 1922 enacts
Government Loans Bill 592
School Teachers Bill
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
that every officer holding an office of profit under a local authority (or committee
appointed by that authority) shall make
a declaration of allegiance in the prescribed form.
The Promissory Oaths Act, 1923,
enacts that any person employed in the
Civil Service, or otherwise employed by
any authority under the Government (in
which category all teachers in schools receiving grants from the Ministry of
Education are deemed to be included)
shall subscribe to an oath of allegiance
in the prescribed form, the wording of
which is almost identical to that prescribed by the Local Government Act of
1922. The declaration of allegiance is
applicable only to teachers holding
appointments under a local authority,
whereas the oath of allegiance is obligatory for all teachers.
As a result it becomes necessary that
public elementary teachers, who had
taken the oath of allegiance while in previous employment in a voluntary school
should, on transfer to employment under
a local education authority, make, in
addition, the declaration of allegiance;
and that, further, they should repeat the
declaration (but not the oath) if transferred to the service of another authority
or even on promotion to another post
under the same authority. Such instances
are frequent, as many schools, with their
staffs, have been and are being transferred from voluntary management to the
control of local education authorities in
accordance with the provisions of the
Education Act of 1923. It is estimated
that upwards of 1,000 public elementary
teachers are now serving in schools under
the new education authorities, the great
majority of whom were formerly serving
in voluntary schools.
Considerable inconvenience arises also
in the cases of certain technical teachers.
Many of these are part-time only and are
re-appointed at the beginning of each
school session, the period of employment
being that during which the school is
open, and some teachers hold such
appointments concurrently under two or
more authorities. The existing legislation would require that such a teacher
should take the oath (once) and, in
addition, should make the declaration
yearly on each occasion of reappointment,
and with each of the two or more
authorities.
Hon. Members will, I am sure, agree
that no useful purpose is served by requiring that teachers who have taken the
oath should also be obliged to make the
declaration of allegiance which is in almost
identical terms, and the present Bill is
designed to take away the necessity for
them to do so, by providing that a teacher
who has at any time taken the oath prescribed by the Act of 1923, shall be
deemed to have complied with the
Section 5 (2) of the Act of 1922 in respect
of any office or employment as a school
teacher held by him to which that Subsection applies. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.
Government Loans Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Mr. BARBOUR: This Bill is a short
Bill dealing with the replenishment of the
Government Loans Fund, which hon.
Members will remember was established in
order that local authorities might be
financed in the same way as similar bodies
are financed in Great Britain through the
Local Loans Fund. In our own case the
scope of the Government Loans Fund is
somewhat wider, inasmuch as the Act of
1925, which established it, provided for
advances being made to the Exchequer in
respect of housing expenditure and capital
expenditure on police barracks.
The provisions of this Bill are simple
in character. In order to explain the first
clause of the Bill, I should state that previous legislation placed two limits on our
Government Loans Fund advances, one a
time limit, beyond which advances could
not be made to local authorities, the other
a money limit. The time limit was provided for in our original Government
Loans Act of 1925, and the present limit,
which expired on the 31st March last, was
extended to that date under an amending
Government Loans Act of 1926.
As regards the money limit, this plays
a two-fold part. In the first place, it prevents issues being made to local authorities
and for the other purposes of the Government Loans Fund in an unlimited manner,
that is to say, it makes it necessary for the
€93 Government Loans Bill
13 JUNE 1929
€94
Supply
In
Ministry of Finance to come to this House
from time to time for fresh powers.
the second place, the money limit forms
also the limit beyond which the Ministry
cannot issue Ulster Loans Stock, which is
used for feeding the Government Loans
Fund. At the present time sums amounting, approximately, to £3,500,000 have
been issued to local authorities and for the
other purposes authorised by our Government Loans Acts out of a total authorised
maximum of £4,250,000.
It may be of interest to the House to
know how we have raised this
money. The
first issue of Ulster Loans Stock was made
in the year 1925 by means of a public
issue under-written on the London market.
The total of the first issue amounted to
£2,000,000. The proceeds of this issue
were exhausted in the year 1927, and in
that year a further issue of £1,100,000 was
made privately to such Irish banks and a
few insurance companies, and so forth, as
were willing to take up the stock at an
agreed price. By this means the cost of
under-writing and placing on the market
a limited amount of stock was avoided.
Early in the present year the proceeds of
the last issue were exhausted, and for a
short time the Fund was financed by temporary borrowings, but some months ago
fresh negotiations with the banks and with
other bodies, including the Belfast Corporation and the Representative Body of
the Church of Ireland, resulted in arrangements being made for a further issue of
£900,000 of stock. This stock will not, in
fact, have to be created until December
next, as it was arranged that only a part
instalment would be payable in the month
of June of this year, the remainder being
payable in December. I should like to
express my appreciation of the assistance
which has been given to the Ministry in
this matter by the banks and other
institutions.
Clause 1 of the Bill proposes for the
future to abolish one of the limits,
namely, the time limit, as this limit has
little or no relevance in Northern Ireland, although it exists in the British
Local Loans Acts, and we now have ample
experience of what the normal drain on
the Fund may be expected to be. On the
other hand, the money limit will remain,
but the Bill proposes to increase the
present maximum from £4,250,000 to a
total of £7,000,000. This increase will,
it is anticipated, cover the requirements
of the next two or three years.
Clause 2 empowers the Ministry of
Finance to charge and recover interest on
arrears of the principal and interest of all
loans which may be issued out of the
Government Loans Fund, and fixes the
rate of interest for this purpose at a rate
not exceeding 6 per cent. I think this
information will suffice for the House,
and I accordingly beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill read a Second time, and committed
to a Committee of the Whole House for
to-morrow.

NEW CLAUSE (Deeds of Arrangement).
(1) Where a debtor has entered into
a deed of Arrangement for the benefit of his creditors generally, to which the
Deeds of Arrangement Act, 1887, as
amended by the Deeds of Arrangement
Amendment) Act, 1890, applies, and the
following conditions have been complied
with. namely:-
(a) the debtor has secured the assent
to such deed of three-fifths in number
and value of those of his creditors to
whom he is indebted to the amount of
£10 and upwards, the assent of any
creditor being established by his executing the deed of arrangement or
sending to the debtor or the trustee appointed by the deed his assent in writing attested by a witness; and
(b) the debtor or the trustee under
the said deed within one month from
the date of the first execution by him
or any creditor of the deed of arrangement, or within such further period as
may be allowed by order of the Court,
applies to the Court and obtains an
order of the Court declaring that he
has obtained the assent mentioned in
the preceding paragraph, and that in
all the circumstances of the case, the
proposals contained in the deed of arrangement are, in the opinion of the
Court, reasonable and proper; and
(c) the application referred to in the
preceding paragaph has been made on
notice to all the creditors given and
vouched in the same manner as notices
of sittings in arrangement matters, and
for this purpose the debtor has filed in
the office of the Court a copy of the
debtor's affidavit filed by him in compliance with sub-section (1) of section
six of the Deeds of Arrangement Act,
1887, then in such case a creditor of
such debtor shall not, unless the deed
becomes void, be entitled to present a
bankruptcy petition against the debtor
founded on the execution of the deed,
or on any other act committed by the
debtor in the course or for the purposes
of the proceedings preliminary to the
execution of the deed as an act of bankruptcy, or to apply for a debtor's summons against the debtor in respect of
an amount due or claimed to be due at
the date of the execution of the deed.
(2) In case any creditor shall, prior to
the making of the application referred to
in paragraph (b) of the preceding subsection, or pending the hearing thereof,
file a petition in bankruptcy against the
debtor, the Court may, on the application
of the debtor or the trustee under the
deed of arrangement, stay further proceedings on foot of such petition, or extend the time for showing cause against
the adjudication thereunder, upon such
