ALTERATIONS AT LONDONDERRY
PRISON.
1. Mr. McCARROLL asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
why the contract for alterations now
being carried out at Londonderry Prison
was not given out to public tender in the
ordinary course; whether he can state the
names of firms invited privately to submit
prices, how they were selected, particulars
of the contract entered into; whether the
contract for furniture and fittings has
been entered into, and, if not, whether
tenders will be advertised for in the
usual way.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I should perhaps say, at the
outset, that my right hon. Friend, in
replying to an inquiry by the hon. Member, on the 11th inst., was under a
misconception in this matter.
An exception to the general rule of
public advertisement was made in the
case of the contract for the adaptation
works now being carried out at Londonderry Prison, in consequence of the necessity for getting the work commenced and
completed at the earliest possible date.
Advertisement for tenders for the work
would have necessitated, inter alia, the
preparation of bills of quantities, which,
owing to the complicated nature of the
adaptation scheme, would have involved
substantial delay, and as considerable
savings in the cost of maintaining
Northern Ireland criminal lunatics will
be effected as soon as the building in
question becomes available for occupation,
it was desirable that the work should be
carried out with all possible expedition.
A number of firms were invited to
tender and were selected, primarily, because of their proximity to the Londonderry area, and also, because, in the
opinion of my technical advisers, they
were in a position to carry out the work
promptly and satisfactorily; but it is not
the
in the public interest to discuss
particulars of the contract entered into,
or to give the names of the firms to whom
invitations to tender were issued.
As already stated, it is the general
practice of the Ministry to advertise
publicly all works, the cost of which is
estimated to exceed £100, and unless any
special circumstances warranting a departure from this practice arise, tenders in
respect of the furniture and fittings for
the new building will be publicly advertised for in due course.

DIETARY SCALE IN PRISONS.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if the
in
prisoners confined His Majesty's
Prisons in Northen Ireland receive butter
or margarine as part of their dietary, and,
if so, the amount of butter or margarine
allowed to each prisoner per week.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The dietaries
in H.M. Prisons in Northern Ireland,
which are similar to those in English
prisons, are divided into three main
classes, and are applicable to prisoners
as follows:-
-
Class 1.-Prisoners under sentence of
imprisonment for 7 days or less, and
during the first 7 days of sentences
exceeding that period, but not exceeding
4 months:
There is no issue of butter or margarine.
Class 2. All ordinary prisoners other
than those in Class 1:-
An issue of 3 ozs. of margarine
weekly.
Class 3.-Convicts, prisoners awaiting
trial, offenders of the first and second
divisions, debtors, and contempt of court
prisoners:-
An issue of 7 ozs. of margarine weekly.
In addition to the above classes there
is an Hospital Diet, which is issued under
the directions of the Medical Officer to
the Prison.
Butter is included in this diet in such
quantities as are directed by the Medical
Officer to meet the specific requirements
of each case.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of that
answer, will the right hon. Gentleman
consider the advisability of issuing butter
to untried prisoners who have not been
convicted, and who may not be guilty of
any offence.

Vote 1 provides for the salaries and
expenses of the Ministry, and is £786
more than last year. The increase is entirely due to the provision for the awards.
of the annual salary increments and to an
increase in the salary bonus, consequent

In the second Vote-for the Educational services-there is an increase over

and the main causes of the increase will
be found in the award of annual increments to existing elementary, secondary
and technical teachers, a large increase in

Fund.

This system of awarding bonuses does
not apply to students who entered training since 1922, and it is, therefore, an
expiring liability, so that it has been

I now come to by far the largest Subhead of our Vote-that for public elementary schools, including the salaries of
teachers. There is an increase of

salaries
of additional teachers, and

I am pleased to be able to report that,
on the whole, the attendance at school of
pupils between the compulsory ages of
six and fourteen is slightly better than
last year and, of course, that year's
figures were greatly in advance of a few
years ago. For 1928 the percentage attendance in Belfast of compulsory age
pupils was maintained at the eminently
satisfactory figure of 88.3, and in the
counties of Antrim, Down, Tyrone and
Armagh slight increases took place, bringing the percentages up to 84.8 in Antrim,
85.8 in Down, 84.1 in Tyrone, and
87.9 in Armagh. In Londonderry City and
County, and in Fermanagh, decreases
took place but they were very slight.
Turning to Sub-head C we find an increase of £17,520, which is almost entirely
due to increased provision for increment
and capitation grant to secondary schools.
The Committee will, I am certain, view
this increase with gratification when I explain that it has its origin in the steady
growth in the number of pupils attending
our secondary schools. On 1st December,
1925, the number of enrolled pupils in the
secondary schools was 8,460, in 1926
there were 9,012, in 1927, 9,913, and on
1st December, 1928, 10,611. While this
is in some part due to the scholarships
awarded by local education authorities,
the Ministry believes that it may be taken
as evidence of a wider recognition on the
part of the public of the value of postelementary education. And not only so,
but there is, in turn, an increase in the
number of students sitting for the
secondary school certificate examinations,
which I may here explain are now used
as the basis of entry to the training colleges recognized by the Ministry for elementary school teachers. In consequence
of the greater number of pupils taking
these examinations the cost will be approximately £1,070 more than formerly.
A further reason for the increased estimate is the institution of a refresher
course in manual instruction for a limited
number of secondary and technical
teachers; the cost of this should not exceed £150, and I am confident that the

The increase in Sub-head D1 is due to
an automatic rise in the amount required
for the award of annual increments of the

honours graduates or similarly qualified
persons who are willing to undergo a

in scientific research, and, on the other
hand, to enable young investigators of

to devote their whole time to original research. These awards are designed not
in any way to overlap existing agencies,
but to meet a long-felt want in making
some assistance available for promising
persons who, without it, would be unable

of this kind were formerly available from
the funds at the disposal of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, but since the establishment of the
Government of Northern Ireland that Department has limited its sphere of operations to Great Britain.
Under Sub-head F there is a very large
increase in the grants payable to local

following reasons: the grant for any year
is paid in five instalments, four of which

cent. of the grant paid for the previous

very little short of £160,000, which is the

Considerable progress can be reported as

Having now reviewed the Estimates in
considerable detail, I should like to take
the opportunity of referring to a question.
of outstanding importance to our future as
a race, namely, the making of adequate
provision for medical and dental inspection
and treatment of school children. While
in some quarters-notably the City of
Belfast the problem is being squarely
faced, and real and most successful efforts
are being made to deal with it as a whole.
and in an adequate manner, I regret to
find that there is not, as yet, in all quarters
such widespread recognition of its importance as we should be entitled to expect.
There is still far too much of the attitude
that medical (and, of course, I include
dental) inspection and treatment are
luxuries which are desirable, if funds permit-and we all know how seldom that is
the case. In this matter, if anywhere, a
wider outlook is essential; we must always
bear in mind that what we are asked to
face is whether the future of our children
and, in turn, of their children, is to be
marred by preventable illness and misery,
with its consequences of poverty and hardship, or whether it is to be healthy, strong
and vigorous.
It is for the people of Ulster, through.
their representatives on local education
committees, to determine if it is worth
while shouldering some small extra burden for the purpose of securing as far
as possible that the future of a great race
shall not be spoiled by sickness and disease
which a little thought, a little foresight,
and a little money could assuredly have
prevented. We pride ourselves on our
shrewdness, and, when we care to do so,
are quite able to view most problems in
Estimates--
Ministry of Education.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
their right proportion, and to appraise
them by a true scale of values and, for
this reason I believe, in order to ensure
that it will be honestly and adequately
dealt with, that it will only be necessary
to bring the matter prominently before the
people and to get them as conscientious
and well-meaning citizens to realise their
responsibility towards it. The importance of the aim being realised, we can
then consider how best it may be secured.
It must be clearly understood that
medical and dental inspection by themselves are of little use; they must be accompanied by treatment; and even this
is only part of the picture, for the purpose of the school medical service is not
confined to the remedying of defects, but
to their prevention-sickness must be
prevented where possible. In the words
of Sir George Newman, Chief Medical
Officer of the English Board of Education,
the aims of the school medical service may
be stated as follows:-
(1) To fit the child to receive the
education provided for it by the State.
(2) To detect any departures from
the normal physiological health and
growth, any impairments, aberrations,
defects, or disease (physical or mental),
and advise the remedy or amelioration
of them (at the school or otherwise) lest
worse befall.
(3) To seek the causes and conditions
of such defect and disease, and, as far
as may be, prevent them.
(4) To teach and practise personal
hygiene in every school, so that a habit
of hygiene may be contracted by the
children, and the way of physiological
life may be followed by each coming
generation.
Sir George adds-
The whole design is an opening of the
gates of physical opportunity. Medical inspection is merely an arrangement
to explore and unveil the condition of
each child in order that the rest of the
programme may be fulfilled with a correct regard to the facts of the case.
The problem of caring for the health
of our future citizens is, thus, no simple
one, but one which presents several sides,
each of which must receive attention.
Most of our local education authorities
have made arrangements for medical inspection, but arrangements for treatment
are not so satisfactory, and this is greatly
to be deplored, as unless cases are followed up and treated it is little use discovering the defects. Then, again,
medical inspection cannot be really effective in the lives of the children if they
spend their school days, as many of them
still do, in school buildings in which proper attention is not given to cleanliness
and fresh air. What is the use of urging
upon children the importance of personal
cleanliness if a sufficient supply of washing facilities is not available in the school;
or why should we preach the gospel of
sunshine and fresh air if the schools are
not flooded with both as often as, and
whenever, possible? I have not referred
to the need of sufficient and suitable playgrounds or to the importance of organised
games (such as are provided in secondary
schools), but these are all part of the
medical service problem and should receive increased attention.
It is, of course, impossible at once to
do everything that should be done, but
there is a danger of hastening so slowly
that the value even of what we accomplish
is not what it might be. The rejoinder
that "times are hard" can only be met
by the importance of the problem. The
nation's children are its most precious
possession; into their hands the future of
the race and of the country must, in the
course of time, be placed, and, this being
so, I feel that we should look on all that
relates to their well-being and happiness
in the most unselfish and far-seeing way.
Realising the magnitude as well as the
high privilege of our responsibility, I am
confident that the people will be ready
to make sacrifices, if such are necessary;
that they will make a great venture of
faith, and that they will see to it that
lack of money is the least of the obstacles
in the way of the realization of the aim
of the school medical service. As we
are always reaping our past so are we
always sowing our future; let us see to it
that it will be as bright and promising
as we can help to make it. I beg to move.
The CHAIRMAN: With reference to
these two estimates it will be observed that
the main questions of policy arise on the
second estimate, and not upon the first.
I propose, therefore, to follow the example
of a previous estimate, and leave both estimates open for discussion as far as policy
is concerned, asking the Committee to cooperate with me in keeping a clear-cut line
between policy upon the one hand, and
mere matters of detail upon the other.

balance his Budget, and, I have no doubt,

of the secondary school teachers and my

equivalent of offering 33 per cent. devaluation of past service represented an
expenditure on the part of the Government of a capital sum of £100,000, that
was an exaggeration. I do not mean to

That amount was based on certain

numbers did not exist, or at any

too much of an estimate to make in

partial concession which was given to
these teachers.
After an examination was made of all
this subject, based on the actuarial figures
and the calculation that emerged from
it, I felt that I was justified, and I
believe the Government felt justified, in
making the following proposals to them.
These proposals, which were made to a
deputation which waited on me a day or
two ago, were, I think, favourably received. They felt they had achieved, if
not the whole of their desires, at least a
considerable part of them. May I read
them? "The present recognition of onethird of past non-contributory service to
be increased to two-thirds, subject to an
increased contribution of 1 per cent., to
be payable, as from the 1st April last, by
teachers who were serving at the inception
of the Scheme, and who will, accordingly,
benefit. In the case of teachers who have
retired between 1922 and 31st March last,
the extra concession will also be granted.”
That is to say, it will be retrospective.
Those teachers who emerged from the profession during the years that have passed
will have the benefit of this arrangement
which is suggested. The gross additional
cost is £60,000, the value of extra contributions of teachers, £16,000; leaving a
net cost to the Government of £44,000.
Any necessary consequential adjustments.
will be made in the scale of minimum
pensions.
The teachers appeared pleased with this
concession that was made. Of course, it
is a very important concession. It will
greatly enlarge the pensions which have
been already in existence for those teachers
who have resigned from secondary schools.
I hope that the Committee and those hon.
Members who are interested in this matter
will feel that the Government has gone
a great way to compensate servants who
were, since 1922, in their schools. As I
have always contended, and as I have
contended to-day, the Government was
under nothing more than a moral or sentimental obligation to these teachers. That
is the position of the whole of our treatment of the secondary school teachers
to-day.

our educational system. It is outside it
altogether, and it proposes to keep outside it. The fact of having representatives on their own governing body would
not affect that position in the slightest.
The governing body of Magee would not,
as I am given to understand directly from
itself, recognise any control or any authority on the part of anybody outside itself.
In other words, it would be an autonomous institution.

is an old foundation of 250 or 300 years,

a reason for that. That was a very big

With regard to the subject of technical
education, I have the feeling that we are
not getting the results we should get for
the money that is expended on this branch
of education. I was for many years a
member of the County Derry Technical
Committee, and I must say that although
a lot of money was expended, while the
many students who passed through the
schools did learn a little, they did not
learn sufficient to properly equip them for
any particular business or profession. I
think the Ministry should SO arrange
technical education that students would
be equipped to practice some particular
profession, instead of spending money in
teaching them something that is not sufficient to enable them to take up any particular trade or profession.
So far as the equipment of schools is
concerned, I do not think there is a single
Member of this House who is not anxious
to see in Ulster the very best schools that
can be provided. Everybody is in favour
of that. I hate raising the sectarian
question in this House, but why should.
Roman Catholics have to pay for the
building and equipment of these schools,
and yet not be allowed the same grant to
build schools for themselves. The Ministry of Education condemns schools, and
yet they will not give a grant to have
them re-built, or new schools built in their
place. That is one of the reasons why
there is any difficulty in rural areas of
having the children properly taught, or
getting them to go to school at all.
Again, the curriculum or programme
for industrial centres such as Belfast
should be altogether different from that
in rural areas. There is no doubt that
more agricultural education should be
given to the children in the public elementary schools in the rural districts, because
the child sees agriculture being carried
on, and if it is taught to observe, as it
walks along the road, it will acquire a
better knowledge of agriculture than it
would by going to some particular elementary or technical school and there studying the theory of agriculture. After all,
there are a lot of useless things taught
to children in school, and these could
easily be replaced by a few useful lessons
in agriculture, by means of which these
children will in after life have to make
their livelihood. We all agree that large
schools with sunlight and healthy surroundings are essential.

the Estimates we see mention made of

Mr. CONNELLAN: I do not think I
need express any regret for sounding a
discordant note, seeing so many have been
sounded already. I have heard a casual
reference made to the fact that the only
difference between the teaching of Irish in
the Free State and the teaching of Irish
in the Six Counties is that in the one it is
compulsory, and in the other it is optional.
I controvert the latter statement. Irish
is not an optional subject in the Six
Counties as optional subjects are generally
considered. Undoubtedly, there is liberty
for the teacher to teach Irish if he can
find the time, but I find that the programme is so crowded out, and intentionally so, I think, that there is no
opportunity for the average teacher to
find time for the teaching of Irish.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. CONNELLAN: I am glad that
my remarks have met with that assent.
In the first place, up to a certain time
the teaching of Irish was possible in Six-
County schools, and a great many
teachers and a great many managers
availed themselves of the opportunities
that were offered. But about a year ago
they found on the new programme that
certain subjects had been put in, and that
they entirely monopolised about fifteen
hours of the school programme, with the
result that there was no time left for the
teaching of Irish, which is the native
language of Ulster. And I may say, in
passing, that there is no department of
Irish, or of Irish scholarship, that is as
high as the Ulster standard, a point upon
which we should all be very proud indeed.
I am not disputing the principle here.
I am merely dealing with certain details.
There are three subjects which, within
the last year or so, have been made compulsory. Those are handwork, science,
and nature study. Now the majority of
teachers are not able to teach handwork,
for the reason that they have not the
Ministry of Education. 650
Estimates-
18 JUNE 1929
necessary qualifications.
Not one per
cent. of them are able to teach handwork.
I really do not know what is meant by
handwork, but I know it is a newlyintroduced subject. On the other hand,
nearly all the teachers are qualified to
teach science, but by reason of the fact
that in the average school you have not
the necessary equipment, science is practically ruled out all round. In the
majority of cases teachers have no qualifications either for the teaching of nature
study, but, as it has been considered
necessary to develop some of these subjects for the purpose of excluding Irish,
the teaching of nature study has been
greatly concentrated upon. What nature
study really means is bringing in a number of leaves, or a number of plants, and
teaching the children to differentiate between one and the other, a very useful
subject indeed, and one upon which a
great amount of value should be placed.
But when we consider that about five hours
per week are devoted to the teaching of
nature study, and that for all the other
subjects only fifteen hours a week are
allocated, we find that it occupies a place
on the programme out of all proportion
to its importance. My contention is that
nature study has been brought in with
the real object of ousting Irish from the
school programme. I do not wish the
statement to go out that Irish is an
optional subject on the school programme,
that it may be taught here and there.
Many of the managers in my constituency
of South Armagh, and elsewhere all over
the country, have asked for permission
to teach Irish in the schools, and so also
have the teachers, but that permission has
been refused. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The Ministry has been deaf entirely to the demands of a large section
of the teachers upon this point.
I do not know really what the reason
for the hostility to Irish is. Possibly it is
because so much attention is being given
to it in the Free State, but if that is so,
I think it is an entirely wrong policy.
Irish is the native language of this part of
the country as much as it is of the Free
State. If the adjoining State were Peru
or Bolivia, instead of the Free State, the
Government, for the purpose of encouraging friendship between the two States,
would encourage on this side the learning
of the Bolivian or the Peruvian language,
whatever it was. In this case we see a
marked bias. One reason why Irish
should be taught here, apart from any
sentimental reasons-and sentimental reasons really do count for something-is
that a great many of the people here have
friends and relatives in the Twenty-six
Counties. Irish is being made compulsory there for practically all businesses,
professions, and employments, and it is
quite possible that a great many of the
people of the Six Counties may find it
necessary some time to go to the Free
State to seek employment. If you are
giving a great deal of attention to the preparing of boys in the emigration college
over in Armagh for export to Canada and
elsewhere, it is quite reasonable to expect
that the people here, who desire to stay
at home in their own country, should have
opportunities of qualifying for occupying
those positions in the Free State, for
which the Irish language is essential.

know very well, through a Ministerial

As to the disadvantages under which

Our own consciences do speak to us in

I have one instance before my mind at
the moment. In County Armagh there
is a Catholic school. For years the
manager and his parishioners have been
striving to have a proper school erected
there as a substitute for the hovel that
has been in existence for over 100 years.
That is in Upper Killeavey. The manager

authorities, with the Regional Committee, and so on, and they have been playing him between Section 15 and Section
16 all through. Section 15 prescribes a
Four-and-Two Committee, and section 16

may be approved by the Ministry. He

under Section 16 that he would act in conformity with the Ministry's wishes, but,
notwithstanding that, he has been sent
round for the last three years from Annas
to Caiaphas, from Caiaphas to Pilate, and
so on, and he occupies at the present time
as advanced a position as he did three
years ago. That is not merely the position
of one Catholic school in the Six Counties.
It is the position of practically all, and
really in justice to yourselves and to the
future of the Six Counties, and of Ireland,
you should do something to meet our
needs in this respect, and to remove from
yourselves this reproach.
Some time ago it was stated by one
prominent in the Government ranks that
there were only two parties required in
Northern Ireland-Catholics and Protestant. I totally disagree with a statement of that kind. I think it would be
most reprehensible if a doctrine of that
sort were preached generally, but if you
continue as you are at the present time,
you certainly, inside the next fifty years,
will only have two parties. One will be
the Catholic party, and the other your
supporters, the secular party which,
through your broadening out and levelling
up, and levelling down, will be attached
to no religion at all. Their denominations
will have disappeared, and you will find
that you yourselves will be the losers in
the long run.
Perhaps you may think that that is a
contingency that we should rejoice in,
that that is something that we, as Catholics, should look forward to with prideto the time when Protestantism will have
disappeared in a big wave of secularism,

and when we are the only denominational

We look forward to a situation of that

Protestantism, after all, does represent a

Somebody here mentioned to-day in a

I do not believe it is. I do not know

the feeding of school children should be

Mr. BEATTIE: I just want to say that
a point has been in my mind for
some time. I think the Parliamentary
Secretary has overlooked the serious position that has been created as far as education is concerned, by the neglect
of two points I am about to mention.
During the election which we have passed
over it came to my notice that a very
large percentage of the workers' children
were going to school improperly clothed
and not properly fed. I found on the
estimates a certain amount allocated to
the educational authorities whereby they
could provide for necessitous school
children the necessary food and sustenance
during the school days. But I have investigated further into the situation, and
I find that these educational authorities
are prohibited from using that money
towards the feeding of the necessitous
children during the holiday period of the
schools. Now that is a menace to the
proper education of the child. If the
school is closed for one month that child
is underfed. Malnutrition sets in, and is
likely to lead to the ill health of the child.
When I made representations to the
education authorities I was informed that
the Ministry did not make any provision
for the feeding of school children during
the school holidays.
I ask the Parliamentary Secretary if it
is possible within these estimates to give
power to the local education authorities
to make that provision during the period
of closing the schools, such as July and
August. Last year, I know from my own
personal experience, a very large percentage of these little children suffered very
severely by the closing of the schools
during the holiday period, owing to their
being no feeding centres.
If you can do
anything in that way I think you would
be assisting the education of the child.

are
necessary for the better education of the

That allegation of former rights is unfounded. I have stated in this House before, and I repeat it now, that the
history of building grants for elementary
schools in Ireland is this. For a time
building grants were very freely given
upon a mistaken policy of the then
Resident Commissioner, who was delighted
to go every year to Parliament, and in his
Report say there had been so many schools
built in Ireland during the past year and
that, therefore, education must have been
progressing.
The result of that system was the
springing up all over Ireland of a large
number of small schools. They were not
efficient and they could not be kept up,
with the result that education was going
to the bad. It was finally borne in upon
the Treasury in England that these free
and easy grants for schools were a mistake,
and from the year 1900 that policy was
entirely reversed and grants were very
difficult to get, although it is quite true
that for a time further grants were given.
Building was entirely stopped during the
war, and when it was resumed no grant
was given except on specific proof to the
Treasury in England that the state of the
particular building was such that a new
building was required. The whole of the
arguments on behalf of Roman Catholics
for building grants for their voluntary
schools have been based upon the allegation, first of all, that the 1923 Act
abolished a right they had before.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Local Government (Rating and Finance)
Bill [Money.]
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Postponed
Question,
Proceeding resumed on
That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session to grant complete or
partial relief from rates in the case of
the hereditaments to which the Rating
and Valuation (Apportionment) Act
(Northern Ireland), 1928, applies, to extend the application of the last-named
Act so as to enable the aforesaid relief
to be granted to certain other hereditaments, to provide certain grants from
the Exchequer of Northern Ireland in aid
of the expenses of local authorities, and
to discontinue certain other grants, and
for purposes consequential on the matters
aforesaid, it is expedient to authorise the
payment out of moneys provided by Parliament of such grants and other expenses
as are under such Act to be payable:—
(a) For the purpose of an annual contribution, in respect of the local
financial year ending on the thirtyfirst day of March, nineteen hundred
and thirty, and each subsequent local
financial year, subject to and in accordance with the provisions of such Act,
to be paid to or on behalf of local
authorities towards making good the
losses occurring by reason of the provisions of such Act;
(b) For the purpose of paying to a
county council such sum as the Ministry of Home Affairs may certify to
represent the amount of any increase
in the rate payable in respect of a
hereditament in a rural district by
reason of the provisions of any such
Act with respect to the chargeability
of certain public health expenses in
rural districts.
(c) For defraying any expenses incurred by the Ministry of Finance in
administering the Freight Rebates
Fund established under any such Act.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): This Resolution deals with
those Clauses of the Local Government
(Rating and Finance) Bill, which involve
a charge on votes and, as will be observed,
it refers to three divisions of expenditure,
the first dealing with the main Exchequer
contribution to local authorities, namely,
that towards making good the loss of revenue from rates which they will suffer
as a result of the derating scheme; the
second, with the contingent charge on the
Exchequer involved, in the proposed
spreading of certain charges for sewerage
and water supply schemes; and the third
with the expenses of the Ministry of
Finance in administering the freight rebates scheme.
As my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson
Bates) explained, in moving the Second
Reading of the Bill on Thursday last, the
Bill contemplates that, in respect of the
first year of the scheme, that is to say, the
year ending 31st March, 1930, the Government will recoup to each local authority
the actual loss of rates arising by reason
of the derating of certain hereditaments.
681 Local Government Bill-
19 JUNE 1929

Committee
in its area. The cost to the Government
in respect of the first year will amount to
approximately £850,000, made up as
follows: Agricultural land (full year's
rates), £714,000; agricultural buildings
(full year's rates), £55,000; industrial
hereditaments other than fisheries (fivesixths of the rates for half year), £60,000;
Fisheries (three-fifths of the rates for
half-year), £1,000; freight transport hereditaments, £20,000; making a total of
£850,000.
The revised Estimate which is now in
the hands of hon. Members provides for
advances being made to local authorities
up to nine-tenths of this sum in the present financial year, that is, for £765,000.
The amount of new money required for the
complete derating of agricultural land and
buildings, as distinct from the partial derating of land previously in operation is
approximately £457,000.
As
For each of the years subsequent to the
31st March, 1930, the proposal is to continue, in the case of county boroughs,
boroughs, urban districts and the Belfast
Water Commissioners, to make good to
each authority the actual loss of rates in
the same way as in the first year.
regards the counties, however, it is proposed to pay in each case an annual grant
of a fixed amount, to be ascertained quinquennially. The amount of this fixed
grant, which is called "the standard
grant," will be based in each case on the
normal net annual expenditure, in a period
of three years, of each local authority
operating in the county area, except in
the case of education authorities where
the net expenditure for the one year ending 31st March, 1929, is taken as the
basis. For the purpose of ascertaining
the amount of the standard grant to be
paid for the five-year period commencing
1st April, 1930, the three years to which
we shall look in order to ascertain the
normal net expenditure of each local
authority, other than an education authority, is the period of three years terminating on the 31st March, 1929.
In
fixing the standard grants to be paid for
subsequent quinquennia, we shall have regard to the net expenditure of each such
local authority for each of the three
financial years preceding the certification
of the grant.
The intention is, of course, that these
standard grants shall represent that proportion of the normal annual expenditure
of each local authority which would otherwise be met by the rates struck on premises which are the subject of derating
under the Bill. As the grant is to be
fixed for periods of five years we must,
obviously, in calculating the normal net
expenditure of each local authority, on
which the grant is to be based, take care
to make allowance for items of expenditure which, though not arising in the
three years under review, will definitely
occur within the period of the currency
of the fixed Government grant, as, for
example, where a rural district council is
definitely committed to, and has actually
embarked on a scheme for the improvement of sewerage, etc., in its area, but
where no loan fund charges in this respect
will fall to be met until, say, the first
year of any quinquennium. Similarly,
we must make allowance in a contrary
sense for expenditure which occurs in the
three years period under review, but
which may be coming to an end within
a year or two. These adjustments are
provided for in the definition of net expenditure in Clause 13 (2) of the Bill.
The Government realise, however, that
local authorities must be put in a position
to obtain some assistance from the Government towards necessary increases in
their expenditure during each five-year
period arising out of the development of
the services under their control. The
Bill provides, therefore, for contributions
in the form of supplemental grants
towards such increases.
I can, perhaps, best explain the way the
supplemental grant will work by an illustration. Assume a rural area's full
valuation is £60,000 and it is derated to
the extent of £50,000. The standard
grant in such a case is based on the latter
valuation, that is, 5/6ths of the total expenditure in the standard is met by the
Government, so that assuming a standard
expenditure of £24,000, a sum of £20,000
will be payable by the Government as a
Standard Grant. Now, assume the local
expenditure increases to £25,000-the
Government will contribute the same
proportion of the new expenditure, so as
to make good the loss due to derating;
that is to say five-sixths of £25,000, or
something slightly in excess of £20,800.
There must, however, obviously be some.
limit to the amount of the supplemental
grant, in so far as it is not required for
educational services, otherwise there can
be no check on local expenditure, to
which the Government will be the main
contributor. This limit is achieved by

In the case of education, however, no
such limit on the amount of the supplemental grant is proposed, as we realise
that the development of this service under
the Act of 1923 is bound to be considerable for some years to come, and for that
reason we do not think it fair to impose
any limit in the amount of the grant in
this respect.

The expenses involved in the third part

of the administration of the transitional

to have its lands and buildings derated,
and if productive industries, some of them
paying high dividends, are to be derated,
then I say there is a justifiable claim for
the workers' dwellings to be derated during a period of unemployment.
was
The Government should have no doubt
or hesitation at all in accepting my
Amendment, because in 1915 the Gov.
ernment of the day had to bring in an
Act of Parliament to protect tenants
from the profiteering of the landlords.
That had to be further backed up by
another Act of Parliament in 1916. But
every Act of Parliament that the Conservative Party, or the Liberal Party,
put upon the Statute Book imposed a
heavier burden on the working-class
people, and that heavier burden
imposed in an indirect way. It was imposed by asking the tenants to shoulder
the responsibility of rates with a reasonable advance as profit for the landlord.
If the Government felt justified in giving
a profit to the landed gentry, then they
should feel justified now in taking over
that responsibility from the tenants and
placing it on the State. The rents of the
workers-if consideration were given to
their needs and requirements-should be
restored to their pre-war figures.
If the Government are sincere, and
anxious to do for the unemployed what
they told them they were anxious and
willing to do at the last election, they will
accept this Amendment. I am rather
afraid the Government's sincerity at
election time is not just what it should
be, but this Amendment will apply the
acid test of whether they are prepared to
relieve the dwellings of the unemployed
workers, who are so hardly pressed at the
moment by the depression of trade that
was brought about through the Government's lack of interest in those industries.
This Amendment will apply the test to
find if you are in agreement with me to
relieve the burden of war-time rates and
profit from the shoulders of the unemployed. Therefore, I have great pleasure
in moving that those words be inserted in
the Bill to achieve a most deserving
object

would like him to say if it would be better to discard the old system which puts

Sir DAWSON BATES: This Clause
is a most important one, because in the
country districts one frequently finds that
villages are prevented from having sewerage or water schemes owing to the fact
that the rural district council, while they
quite admit the schemes are necessary,
feel that the entire cost should go on
limited areas. The result is, that even
during the time I have been in office,
many schemes had to be abandoned,
which, if they were carried through would
have been of enormous advantage to the
community. This Clause is to bring in
a broad area of charge, and having regard to the way in which the Government
are meeting the ratepayers in this matter
I think it is only reasonable that this
should be passed. I should assure my
hon. Friend that in regard to any past
schemes inside a rural district, the ratepavers will not have to pay any more
than they had previously. As regards
complications, while all Acts of Parliament look complicated, I do not think
there is anything in this that will prevent
the scheme working satisfactorily.
Mr.
CRAWFORD: What is the

complicated calculations? The lines read:
"being expenses which would, but for

levied shall cause the amount of such

to time in respect of that hereditament."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The practical
effect of that is that you may have a local
charge on a district that may be inside
a very large area, one larger than a rural
district. A person living inside that
bigger area, and not inside the local area
will not, as the result of the passing of
this Bill, be liable for any larger amount
than previously. When the Bill was
being drafted the point was put to the
Government that it would be unfair to
these rural district areas that the ratepayers should have to pay for the old
schemes for which the local people were
formerly paying, and this Clause is to
make perfectly clear that those people who
were formerly not liable, will not be liable
in the future. I give the case of Portballintrae, and the area round about as
an example.

Sir DAWSON BATES: As there are
several new Members in the House who,
Ministry of Home Affairs.
Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
perhaps, may not be aware of the various
functions and services entrusted to the
Ministry of Home Affairs, I think it
would be appropriate that I should in connection with this Estimate, which I now
have to move, give a general survey of
all the services falling within the purview of the Ministry. As I have on
former occasions pointed out, the Ministry
of Home Affairs in reality comprises two
main Departments-the Home Office
Department, which deals with law
and order and ancillary services, and the
Local Government Department, which
supervises the activities of local government authorities generally. I propose,
therefore, in my statement, first of all,
to deal generally with the question of the
staff of the Ministry, and then to review
the activities of the two main Departments of the Ministry.
As regards the question of staff, it will
be noted that we are asking for a net
sum for the current financial year of
£58,210, as contrasted with £58,061,
provided for in the Estimates last year,
the net result being an increase of £149.
This increase is generally attributable to
the normal increase consequent on payment of increments, as it will be observed
that there has been no increase in the
numbers of the staff, this being 150,
the same as last year. As regards Lis
number, I should point out that it is
possible that I might have been able to
have shown a slight saving in certain
grades had it not been for the fact of the
great increase in the service of supervision of motor omnibus routes. etc., but
I am glad to say that by an adjustment
of other duties in the Ministry we have
been able, without adding to the staff of
the Ministry, to provide the necessary
personnel for this particular work.
I should also mention that the new
functions which the Ministry has been
and will be called upon to carry out in
connection with the derating proposals,
and the calculation and payment of the
complicated grants to the various local
authorities have imposed a very severe
strain on the staff of the Ministry. Up
to the present, I am glad to say, we have
been able to have the preliminary work
carried out without having to ask for
increased assistance, and we will endeavour, by all means possible, to continue with our existing staff to carry out
this particular work. Apart from these
special matters there appears to me to be
no other outstanding point in this particular Estimate calling for attention.
I should, however, like to inform the
Committee that during the course of the
year the Ministry will lose the services of
two of its most valuable and efficient
officers. I refer to the Chief Crown
Solicitor, Mr. John Moorhead, and the
Chief Medical Officer, Colonel Dawson.
Mr. Moorhead has, during the past eight
years or so, given to the Ministry and the
Government, in no grudging fashion, the
full benefit of his long experience and
exceptional ability, and it would be
impossible for me to express in adequate
terms how helpful he has been to me and
to the Government, particularly during
the long and anxious time when Northern
Ireland was in a state of disorder.
Colonel Dawson has, similarly, in his
own capacity as Chief Medical Officer,
Inspector of Lunatics, and Inspector of
Prisons and Reformatory and Industrial
Schools, been of invaluable service to the
Ministry, and, indeed, to the community.
as a whole. His unrivalled experience
and knowledge of matters pertaining to
the care and treatment of those affected
mentally have been most invaluable, and
through his influence with those officers
of the local authorities and public bodies
who have charge of institutions specially
provided for such infirmities, it has been
possible even in the few years that the
Government of Northern Ireland has
been in existence to effect considerable
improvements in the methods and
arrangements in operation for the care
and treatment of these unfortunate persons.
It is much to be regretted that owing
to the exigencies of the service it will not
be possible for me, and for the Ministry
to have at our disposal the benefit of his
advice and services during the period when
-as it is hoped-we will be carrying out
the reforms of the various local government and asylum services, but I feel sure
that with his interest in Northern Ireland
affairs he will always be ready and willing
to accord us advice, if we require it, or
assistance on any of our Committees. It
would not be out of place for me to
mention that he has, in an honorary
capacity, acted as Chairman of the Joint
Midwives and Nursing Council for
Northern Ireland, and it is, I am sure,
very largely due to his wise counsel that
the midwives and nurses of Northern
Ireland occupy such a high place in the
United Kingdom, and, indeed, perhaps,
throughout the Empire.
Ministry of Home Affairs. 726
Estimates-
20 JUNE 1929
I will now turn to the activities of the
Home Office Department, which, as I have
already explained, generally deals with
all such general matters as law and order,
prisons, reformatories and industrial
schools, Borstal institutions, police, justice, petty sessions, courts, etc. The
first and most important matter in connection with my administration-a matter which affects not only the peace but
also the prosperity of the State-is the
question of law and order, and I think
that it may be claimed that the conditions
in Northern Ireland during the last year
have been, on the whole, generally
satisfactory.
Of course, we whose business it is to
watch with meticulous care every symptom of disorder have had brought to our
notice, on several occasions during the
year, sporadic attempts which have been
made by the scattered, disloyal elements
which are still in our midst to foment disorder and to create once again those
troubles which cost us so much in lives
and money a few years ago, but I am
happy to say that owing to the powers
which Parliament has vested in us, and
owing to the activities of our police force,
we have been able to quench, at the very
outset, all such attempts. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
An index of the state of any country
will be found in the addresses which the
Judges of Assize make from time to time
to the Grand Juries. These addresses,
I think, speak more convincingly than
any remarks that I could make as to the
efficiency of our police, and the methods
for detecting and dealing with crime. For
the year ended 31st December, 1928, the
number of specially reported cases of
crime was 1,329, as compared with 1,434
similar cases for the previous corresponding period, and 1,581 similar cases for the
year ended 31st December, 1926. These
figures show steady and consistent decrease
in crime which, I think hon. Members
will agree with me, is specially gratifying.
Another test of a country's freedom
from crime can be found in the prison
statistics, and here I am again happy to
say that the prison statistics, as furnished
to me, bear out the remarks which I have
referred to above which were made by the
Judges. During the year 1927 the number of persons convicted and imprisoned
was 2,661, while the corresponding number for the year 1928 was 2,339, showing
a reduction of 322, which represents a
12 per cent. reduction.
As against this I found, on the other
hand, that during the year 1927 14 boys
were committed to the Borstal Institution, while for the year 1928 the number
was 28. This. at the outset, might be
taken to mean that crime amongst
youths had become doubled, but this is
not so. The reason for this increase is
that in the year 1927 our arrangements
for dealing with youthful criminals had
not been fully appreciated, and possibly
during that year many boys or youths
were sent to prison who might more appropriately have been dealt with in a
Borstal Institution. I am glad to say
that the Courts in Northern Ireland now
fully realise the advantage to the future
state of endeavouring to give these boys
a chance to become better citizens, and
every possible step in this direction is
being taken by us in our new Borstal
Institution at Malone.
I am also happy to say that the conduct of our prisoners at Belfast, Armagh,
and Londonderry, and of the boys at the
Borstal Institution has been most satisfactory throughout the year—(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and I would like to
take this opportunity of expressing once
again my sincere indebtedness to the
Board of Visitors and Visiting Justices of
the prison, and to the Members of the
Borstal Association, and to all the other
organisations which have done and which
are doing such excellent work, not only
for the well-being of those who are confined in our prisons, etc., but, more important still, perhaps, for their future
welfare on release.
I also think that hon. Members will be
interested to hear that we have well in
hands our arrangements for the establishment of a criminal lunatic asylum in the
disused portion of Londonderry Gaol.
As most Members are aware, there are 20
Northern Ireland criminal lunatics now
being maintained on our behalf by the
Government of the Irish Free State at
Dundrum Criminal Lunatic Asylum.
This, of course, is only a temporary expedient, and I might also mention that,
for various reasons, it is a somewhat expensive arrangement for us, and we have
every hope that when our new Institution
is in full working order in Londonderry
the cost of maintenance will be considerably abated for this unfortunate class of
the community
When considering the question of
maintenance of law and order it would
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
be improper not to make a special reference to the part that is played in this
respect by our Police Force, both Regular
and Special. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I think that we can congratulate
ourselves that we have established in
Northern Ireland police forces which are
drawn from Northern Ireland sources,
which thoroughly understand Northern
Ireland conditions, and the Members of
which command the respect and esteem
of every member of the community.
(Hon. Members: Ilear, hear.) It is
largely owing to the activities and watchfulness of our police forces that crimeor at any rate the opportunities for crime
---are slowly but steadily decreasing in
our midst, and that the forces of disorder
and disruption are prevented from creating disturbance.
In every community, no matter how
civilised, how prosperous or contented on
the whole, there are always to be found
elements of a perverted type whose apparent object it is to create dissension
and disorder in the hope of acquiring
unlawful gain or interest during such
disorders. It is only necessary for us to
throw our minds back for a few years to
realise the terrible results which can be
produced by a comparatively small
number of misguided and perverted
people, and to appreciate how necessary
it is for any stable Government to maintain a proper, adequate and efficient
Police Force.
Mr. O'NEILL: This is in preparation
for the Specials.
Mr. COLLINS: Is the right hon.
Gentleman referring to the gun-running
at Larne? I would like him to distinguish
between these troublous times.
The CHAIRMAN: If the right hon.
Gentleman is left to survey these points
he will, no doubt, develop them.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am fully
responsible for anything I have done in
the past. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
It has been suggested in various quarters
that our police forces in Northern
Ireland are unduly expensive, but with
our experience in the past we cannot
afford to take any risks, and it
would be a most short-sighted policy for
this or any other Government in power
in Northern Ireland to deprive the community of the benefit of the security and
peace and happiness which our police
force ensures.
It should also be remembered that in
addition to their ordinary police duties
there have been imposed on the Force,
by the Parliament of Northern Ireland,
various services and duties which do not
properly come within the scope of the
duties of a policeman. I refer to the
many services which the police carry out
on behalf of other Ministries, as, for example, the Ministry of Agriculture, in
connection with the collection of statistics
Mr. O'NEILL:
And weeds.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am coming
to that and the administration of the
Noxious Weeds Acts, and other services.
The police act for us in the Ministry of
Home Affairs in connection with reporting on the building of houses, and the
information they are enabled to give us
is of considerable assistance in helping
us to check the dates of commencement
and completion of houses qualifying for
subsidy. They also perform important
duties in regard to motor traffic. I need
only refer to a few other of the quasi
civil functions which the members of the
police force exercise-in particular as Inspectors of Weights and Measures, and
as enumerators under the Census Acts.
I am glad to say that our programme
of reconstruction of police barracks is
proceeding satisfactorily. During the
past year a special effort has been made
to expedite the building operations.
With this object a small Departmental
Committee has been appointed to take
charge of operations, and an indication
of the work carried out under the
auspices of that Committee may be
gauged from the fact that while a year
ago we estimated that a capital expenditure of £35,000 would be required for
this service, we estimate that for the
current year we will require no less than
£200,000. Our total programme involves the building or reconstruction of
some 196 barracks. Of these fifteen have
been completed, contracts have been
placed, and work is in hands in regard
to twenty-two more, and sites have been
acquired or are being acquired in fortyfour further cases in which contracts will
be placed as soon as practicable. Hon.
Members who recall the old housing con-
Ministry of Home Affairs. 730
Estimates-
20 JUNE 1929
ditions of the Royal Irish Constabulary,
will agree how necessary it is that our
own Royal Ulster Constabulary should
be housed in a more proper and suitable
manner.
With regard to the Special Constabulary, on which my hon. Friend (Mr.
Collins) opposite seems to have his eye, I
am glad to be able to assure the House
that the members of that splendid force
still continue to show that devoted zeal
which has from the very commencement
of our operations been the outstanding
feature of the members of this force.
The record of attendances at drills has
been highly satisfactory, and the members of the force have throughout the
year displayed the greatest possible interest in the various shooting competitions and meetings which have been
arranged from time to
time. I
am also glad to be able to welcome
into this House two distinguished members of the Force. I refer to the hon.
Member for Lisnaskea (Sir Basil Brooke),
who was until quite recently County-
Commandant for that County; also the
hon. Member for Baunside (Mr. Young),
who has occupied the prominent position
of District Commandant.
Arising out of the activities of the
police forces, I think it would not be out
of place to make a reference to the question of the steady improvement which has
taken place in what I may describe as the
sobriety of the community. To a very
large extent this welcome and beneficial
feature of our social life is due to the
operation of the two Licensing Acts
which have been passed by this Parliament in recent years, and to the wise,
fair, and impartial administration of
those Acts by the police.
Since 1923 convictions for drunkenness
have fallen by no less than 27 per cent.
The cases of drunkenness on Sunday have,
as is perhaps only to be expected, been
reduced to comparatively insignificant
dimensions. In 1923 there were three
times as many cases of drunkenness on
Sunday as there are now. The number of
offences by licensed persons in that year
was four times the present number.
am also glad to be able to state that the
number of cases of drunkenness for the
first three months of the present year is
the lowest on record. (Hon. Hembers:
Hear, hear.) I have already referred to
the fact that the sale of methylated
I
spirits and ether for drinking purposes
has been stamped out.
Mr. GRANT: What about Red Biddy?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Red Biddy is
a thing of which I have never yet been
able to get an exact definition. As hon.
Members are aware, this practice was extremely prevalent in certain country districts in our Province some time ago, and
had a most demoralising effect on those
who indulged in it.
I will now turn to other activities of
this Department of the Ministry, and
the first service which occurs to me is
that of the administration of the Pharmacy Acts.
As hon. Members are aware,
the Northern Ireland Pharmaceutical
Society was established some years ago,
and I am happy to say that since its
establishment its career has been one of
continued success. The number of
licences issued during the year 1928 was
397, as against 369 for the year 1927,
but the most important feature in connection with its position is that for the
first time in the history of pharmacy in
Northern Ireland there is now complete
statutory authority for reciprocity between the Pharmaceutical Society of
Northern Ireland and the parent body in
England. This reciprocity also involves
reciprocity and recognition as between
Northern Ireland and the British
Dominions, and I need hardly explain how
important a matter it is for the Society
and for the future generations of
chemists coming from Northern Ireland
to know that there is a career open to
them not only in Great Britain, but also
in the great Dominions across the sea.
In order to effect this scheme of reciprocity, it was necessary to accord to the
British Society special legislative powers,
and I must here, on behalf of the
Society and indeed on behalf of the
Government and Parliament of Northern Ireland, express to the Committee
and officers of the British Society, and
to the Imperial Home Secretary and his
Department, our gratification for the willing and courteous way in which they
helped to overcome all the difficulties.
I now turn to the question of the administration of the Explosives Acts, under
which the Ministry is responsible for the
arrangements made for seeing that the
necessary safeguards are effected in
connection with the storage, etc., of
explosives.
Ministry of Home Affairs. 732
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
For the more technical and highlyskilled branch of this work it has been
found economical to utilise, under an
agency arrangement and at a comparatively small charge, the services of the
four inspectors of explosives of the
British Home Office, whose skill and experience is always at our disposal as advisers, and one of whom visits Northern
Ireland from time to time and inspects
the various magazines, licensed explosive
stores, and registered premises in the Six
Counties.
In addition, I have appointed 23
sergeants and constables of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary as local inspectors
to see that the provisions of this important Act are carried out. These
Royal Ulster Constabulary inspectors
perform their ordinary police duties,
in addition, and receive no additional remuneration.
I will now turn to the activities of the
Local Government Department of the
Ministry, and as hon. Members are aware
these activities include the central administration and supervision of such
services as poor-law, public health,
housing, roads, and general local government.
With regard to poor-law administration, while on the whole the reports go
to show that the incidence of poverty
throughout Northern Ireland has somewhat decreased, I regret to have to state
that it is still found necessary in Belfast
to institute special measures for dealing
with exceptional distress. The Act
passed by this Parliament last year has
been found to fulfil its purpose effectively.
The Belfast Board of Guardians have
recently, in co-operation with the Belfast
Corporation, instituted
arrangements
under which those applying for outdoor
relief under the Act of 1928 are placed in
a position of performing useful work, for
which they are paid at the standard rate
of wages.
The works carried out under
this arrangement are of a special nature
which do not require a specialised form of
labour.
As regards the public health services,
I am glad to be able to state that the
standard of efficiency has, on the whole,
been well maintained, if not improved.
I should also say that with the exception
of a slight outbreak of scarlatina in the
Lisburu arça, and a minor outbreak of
typhus in the Strabane area, the general
health of the community has been satisfactory. I may point out that, thanks
to the way in which our local authorities
insist upon vaccination, we are at the present time in Northern Ireland, and have
been for many years past, immune from
smallpox, although epidemics of that
disease have occurred from time to time
in Great Britain.
Several water supply schemes have been
undertaken during the year, and also
several sewerage schemes, but in this connection it must be admitted that there
are many areas in Northern Ireland still
lacking in adequate and proper water and
sewerage facilities. However, it is hoped
that with the aid of the Derating Bill a
great improvement will be seen in the
coming year in regard to this matter.
Hon. Members who were in the House
will remember that in the year 1927 an
Act was passed enabling the Ministry to
grant licences to milk purveyors to sell
Tuberculin Tested Milk, where the owners
of the herds undertook to comply with certain requirements laid down by the Department of Agriculture regarding the
testing of the cattle and of the milk.
I am glad to be able to state that in
the short time since the Act was put into
operation, no less than 19 persons have
applied for and obtained licences, and
there is every reason to believe that this
number will steadily grow.
As regards the welfare of the blind,
schemes have been put into operation in
Belfast and County Down. The Ministry is at present in communication with
the other local authorities with the object
of inducing them to establish schemes for
the blind persons in their respective areas.
As regards the question of Maternity
and Child Welfare, we have now in operation 43 schemes, in all of which very excellent work is being done. While I say
that I do not claim that this is sufficient,
and I am hoping that in the near future
we shall have a satisfactory scheme working in every part of our Province.
With regard to hospital accommodation,
I am glad to find that there is an increasing tendency for Boards of Guardians to
abolish their Workhouse Infirmaries and
to substitute up-to-date District Hospitals with improved accommodation,
equipment and facilities. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I may point out that
since this Government came into office,
no fewer than eleven workhouses have
been abolished, and seven of these have

While I am on the subject of
local government
reform, I should
like to point out that the proposals
which were submitted
now
to me some
time ago by the Local Government
Commission would, perhaps, have been
before this House long ere this had it
not been for the fact that a new complication arose owing to the derating proposals which had to be worked out and
considered from every angle and which,
as hon. Members are aware, are
actually before the House in the form of a
concrete Bill. These derating proposals,
as I have already explained in the House,
altered the whole complexion of local
government, and I felt, therefore, that
as the derating proposals were of greater
urgency than the recommendations of the
Local Government Commission, it would
he more desirable for me to defer the
question of local government reform until
the derating proposals had been put into
actual operation.
I have also come to the conclusion that
in regard to the legislative proposals for
local government reform, it would be
more advisable to deal with those proposals by means of separate Bills dealing
with the various codes which come under
the heading of local government law.
It is a well-known fact that the public
health code stands out by itself.
Similarly, the lunacy code is a distinct.
code, and this also applies to the poorlaw code, while there are the general
matters of local government administration which are dealt with at present
under the Local Government Acts or the
Municipal Corporations Act.
Accordingly, it is my intention and
hope at a very early date to introduce
individual Bills amending the various
codes referred to above. The result, I
think, will be that those who have to administer the Acts hereafter will find it
much more simple to apply the Amendments to the existing codes, than if they
had one Bill containing a collection of
provisions, each dealing with separate
codes of Acts.
Turning now to the question of the
administration of the Housing Acts, I
am sure that the Members of the Committee will agree that we can claim with
satisfaction considerable success in this
respect.
Mr. NIXON: Question.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Under the
Northern Ireland Housing Acts
apcomup
to the end of March last no fewer

pleted on that date, and it 18
estimated that at the present rate of progress by the end of March next we shall
have completed well over 15,000 houses.
In addition to the houses built under the
Housing Acts, I should also make a reference to the houses which have been
erected under the Labourers Acts, and
in respect of which we give such substantial grants.
As I pointed out on a previous

made since the Government of Northern
Ireland assumed control is far and away
more effective than at any other time
since the first Labourers Act was passed
in 1883. Between 1883 and 1921, the
time of the formation of this State, the
number of labourers' cottages erected was
only in the neighbourhood of some 6,000.
Since the transfer of services schemes for
the erection of no fewer than 2,205
cottages have been lodged with the Ministry, of which 1,425 have been completed,
74 are under construction, and the remainder are pending.
Coming to the question of roads and
road transport. As the Committee is
aware, we have for some years past
carried out a policy of encouraging up to
the full limit of our resources the carrying out of schemes of road improvement
by the various road authorities, and I
think that I am not overstating the case
when I say that our road systems in Northern Ireland, and particularly in the

areas adjoining the city of Belfast, can

important artery leading from Belfast to
Londonderry, through Antrim, Ballymena, Ballymoney, and Coleraine, and
while, no doubt, the process of reconstruction may produce a certain temporary inconvenience, the result will be a matter

the roads, and will tend, I am sure, to
attract to Ulster an increased number,
each year, of tourists.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sure,
also, that those motorists who have occasion to drive through South Derry will
share with me the feeling of satisfaction
at the work of reconstruction over the
bog between Toomebridge and Castledawson. This particular stretch of road
has been a continued source of anxiety
to the Roads Department of the Ministry
and, indeed, to the county council, as

would also refer to the work which is
being carried out in Armagh County of
completing the road from Portadown
to Verner's Bridge. In South County
Down we
are having the road from
Newry to Warrenpoint improved, and the
example recently set by the Lisburn and
the Armagh Urban District Council in
making concrete streets is now rapidly
being followed by other councils, and the
day is not far distant when our urban
centres in Northern Ireland can boast of
perfect streets.
Turning from road construction, I
now come to the question of road traffic.
Members of this House, who sat in the
previous Parliament, will remember that
a question arose in the House some time
ago regarding the additional measures of
control we were imposing on bus traffic.
These measures received their impetus, I
admit, from the conditions which arose
in the City of Belfast, but those critics
who ignorantly and who misguidedly
stated that the Belfast arrangement was
the cause for the new conditions are very
wide of the mark. As I have already
stated, we have felt for a long time that
it would be necessary, in the interests of
the public, to exercise more control over
routes, fares and time-tables, and the
situation in Belfast merely brought matters to a head.
As I hope to introduce legislative proposals into this House at a very early
date, dealing with the question of control of road transportation, I do not think
it would be appropriate for me to dilate
at any length on this particular aspect,
but I think that I can say, and say with
accuracy and propriety, that the measures
that we have recently taken have proved
an undoubted success. We are getting
everywhere more satisfactory services,
while at the same time we are proving to
the smaller bus owners, who at one time
were doubtful as to our intentions, that
our measures are designed with the object of according them protection where
they have been giving adequate, cheap,
and good services.
On the other hand, we are proving to
the public and the motor trade, as a
whole, that it is not the intention of the
Government to restrict the proper development of omnibus services, but
rather we want to ensure that the development will be on proper lines and, above
all, that we should have efficient services
provided in those areas where they are
required, and provided at proper times,
and at reasonable fares, and with due
regard to the safety of the public. I beg
to move.

material was put into the houses; that

prior to the scandal. One, I think,

came within the scope of those inquiries,

letters. It is a form of complaint that
is very easily made, and in many instances, I am afraid, if not in all, it is

officers of the police pay attention to

ment of the Government of Northern

It is a mistake to have patients suffering

Local Government Administration in
Northern Ireland referring to that subject in which it says:
Tuberculosis schemes under the
general code are in force in all counties
and county boroughs in Northern Ireland, save Londonderry County and
County Borough, where there are only
schemes under the National Health
Insurance Act. Tuberculosis schemes
have taken different forms in different
counties. In Tyrone, Armagh, and
Belfast County Borough the schemes
are self-contained. Each authority has
its own sanatorium and treats all
patients within its area. The remaining counties have no sanatoria, and
have made arrangements whereby
patients suitable for sanatorium treatment are cared for in private or voluntary institutions. There is however,
an arrangement in County Down whereby non-pulmonary cases are dealt with
in the Down County Infirmary.
That Committee strongly recommend
that the permissive system of sanatoria should be made compulsory, and that
the counties should have county sanatoria
for the treatment of tuberculosis cases.
Personally I am very glad to say we have
a county sanatorium in County Armagh.
But recently I have come in touch
with a good number of cases which
were being treated and have been
treated in private institutions, and where
very serious complaints have been made in
regard to the treatment. I refer particularly to cases of ex-servicemen. I would
strongly urge upon the Ministry that more
supervision should be exercised
over
private institutions that take in cases

much to be desired. I think it is very
unfortunate that people suffering from a

the cases are remarkably well looked
after, but I do think that more supervision is required in regard to private
institutions. I think the Ministry should

Commission, and that each county should

Vote in regard to two different items on
which I think he might have given the
Committee a more satisfactory reply.
One is in regard to the religious basis of
the Force, and the other is the conditions
under which the police are supplied to
Belfast.
I understood from the reply of
the Minister, just before the Vote was
taken, that some hon. Members think
Belfast should get more facilities than it
does actually get at the present time from
the Ministry.
I certainly think that Belfast is in a
very favourable position so far as the
Force is concerned. Belfast has one-third
of the population of the Six Counties,
and it has also one-third of the
valuation of the Six Counties. Therefore, it is entitled at most to onethird of the police, but instead of onethird it gets one-half, and the only
amount it pays for the additional number of police that it has is £25,000 a
year, thereby saving the ratepayers of
the city a sum of well over £100,000 a
year at the expense of the taxpayers of
the Six Counties. That is one of the
reasons why I move a reduction in this
Vote.
The other is in regard to the religious
basis of the Force. When the Force was
established a Committee was set up-I
think its finding was subsequently put
into the form of an Act of Parliamentand it laid down that the basis of the
Force should be two-thirds from the
Protestant community. and one-third
from the community to which I belong.
I know that at the time there were difficulties in getting that number to join the
force, but I think that instead of asking
Protestant members of the force to leave
it, as has been suggested, the force should
be brought up to the standard laid down
in this Report, and also in the Act
under which the Constabulary are constituted, that is, one-third and
thirds, instead of one-sixth, which is the
proportion of members of the Catholic
faith in the police force at the present
time.

I know the force is not recruited on

where men are of equal merit and fit

to the minority in Ulster, preference
might be given in the circumstances to
Catholic applicants. That is not asking.
for any special privilege. It is what we
are entitled to, and what we claim.

The PRIME MINISTER: The hon.
Member for the Falls division (Mr. Byrne)
on the Second reading was referring to
the question of labourers' cottages, and I
interrupted him to say that the matter
had already been covered by the Bill, but
in doing so I may have created a false
impression on the House which I would
like to correct. The hon. Member was
referring to land, and I took it up that
he was still referring to land when he got
on to the question of labourers' cottages.
I interrupted and said:
Perhaps the hon. Member is not
aware that labourers' cottages do come
under the Derating Scheme.-(Official
Reports, Vol. 11, 13th June, 1929, col.
574).
What I meant to convey to the House
was, that the land attached to labourers'
cottages was exempt from rates exactly
the same as in the case of other agricultural land. I am afraid I may have conveyed to the hon. Member that the
cottages themselves were to be derated.
This, of course, is not within the compass
of the Bill. I had already dealt with the
matter outside the House rather fully.
and I explained then that land attached
to labourers' cottages was already covered
by the Bill, and I merely intended to inform the hon. Member that that was so.
If I created another impression I wish to
express regret.
Mr. BYRNE: I quite understood
the Prime Minister was referring to land.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

The people seemed to think, according to

1 would do that work willingly if it were

for them. In a short time this House
