Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
As regards work on relief schemes, to
which I presume the hon. Member refers,
that work is given on a strict priority
basis. One-third of the work is given to
Roman Catholics and two-thirds to Protestants in accordance with the conditions laid down by the Imperial Government when they gave us a grant of
approximately £500,000 for starting relief works in Northern Ireland. The
Advisory Committee, which was set up
at that time to assist me in the administering of that substantial sum, advised
that that proportion as between the two
sections of our community should continue to be preserved, and I have felt it
desirable to do SO for very obvious
reasons.
no
Then, again, a preference is given to
ex-Service men, and particularly to those
with families and those who have been
the longest time out of employment. Of
course, under these arrangements I admit
that single men stand a very poor chance
of getting work on relief schemes, but,
while I am sure we are all sympathetic
with the single man who wants work and
cannot get it, our sympathies are
doubt greater for those who have wives
and families to support. But I can assure hon. Members that it is the aim of
the Department to do absolutely fairly
in connection with the matter, and that
we are only too delighted to do anything
we can to give such work to those who require it most. If the hon. Member (Mr.
Byrne) would like to discuss the matter
with me at any time, and would do me
the honour of calling at the Ministry of
Labour, I will put all the cards on the
table before him, and if he can suggest
to me any fairer way in which such work
as there is should be distributed I will be
quite willing to adopt his suggestion.
I may say, however, that in Northern
Ireland at the present time we have 78
relief schemes in operation, and there
are 1,196 men employed on these schemes.
But, as hon. Members know, the work has
to be promoted, in the first instance, by
the local authorities. After it has been
promoted, or put before my Department,
by the local authority my Department is
in a position to pay a grant to the extent
of paying the wages of three out of every
four men employed on the work, leaving
the local authority to pay the fourth man
and also to pay the cost of the material.
But the initiation of the work does not
rest with my Department. All that I can
do is to encourage the local authorities,
or sometimes to press the local authorities, to put forward as much work as
possible in order that as many men as
possible may be employed in this way.
As regards the payment of unemployment benefit, I would like hon. Members
to appreciate the huge sums which we are
paying every week to those for whom work
cannot be found. On an average at the
present time we are paying no less a sum
than £26,000 per week We are keeping
absolutely in step with Great Britain in
connection with the payment of unemployment benefit. It is absolutely necessary that we should continue to do so,
because of the reinsurance agreement.
I need not go into the details of that
agreement now, but the foundation upon
which it is based is, that we should keep
in parity with Great Britain, and in consideration of our so doing we get from the
British Exchequer somewhere in the
neighbourhood of half a million per
annum, and from our own Exchequer
several hundreds of thousands of pounds.
So that hon. Members will see that the
hands of my Department are tied to a
considerable extent in connection with
this matter. But I can assure the Committee that it is the desire of the Department to deal as sympathetically with
these problems as possible, bearing in
mind that we must keep within the four
walls of the Acts of Parliament which it
is our responsibility to administer.
Mr. McALEER: I desire to say that
my colleagues and I are exceedingly
grateful to the Minister for the kind and
sympathetic way in which he has received
our appeal. I sincerely hope that he will
bring as much pressure as possible on
local authorities all over the Six Counties
to see that they promote public works in
order to give employment to these people.
Mr. BYRNE: I would just like, as
a member of the Corporation, to add that
many schemes have been introduced by
the Corporation-not as many as
of us would like-and I must say in fairness that they have always been encouraged by the Ministry of Labour. But
I take it now that people like myself,
who are on public boards, are to use their
efforts to get these boards to introduce
schemes, and then the Government are
prepared in all cases to give a grant.
far as I am concerned, I will use all the
pressure I can.
Question put, and agreed to.

EXTERN STUDENTS AT QUEEN'S
UNIVERSITY.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education whether he is prepared to make
representations to the Senate of Queen's
University to arrange that extern students,
who are obliged to work for their living,
can study for and obtain their Arts and
other degrees in the same manner as extern students of Trinity College, Dublin.
PARLIAMENTARY
SECRE-
The
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb): My reply to the
hon. Member's question is in the negative.
Under its Charter, the Queen's University
is strictly prohibited from awarding extern
degrees.
It is generally recognised that a degree
obtained without living contact with
teachers is not satisfactory, and no university in the British Isles grants one with the
exception of Trinity College, Dublin, and
the University of London. In the case of
Trinity College, I understand that attendance at lectures is ordinarily required, but
the University authorities may exercise a
discretionary power in special cases where
attendance is difficult or impossible.
London University was established primarily for the granting of extern degrees
and is, therefore, exceptional.
I may state, however, that the authorities of Queen's University are not unmindful of the needs of those who are unable to attend the regular University
courses, and for the benefit of such persons,
have recently appointed a special lecturer
and director of extra-mural studies.
Mr. NIXON: Might I ask the Parliamentary Secretary if he has considered the
advisability of introducing legislation to
amend the charter of Queen's University
so as to enable them to grant degrees the
same as Trinity College? Of course, I am
aware from yesterday's papers that the
Government have no control over Queen's
at present.
Mr. O'NEILL: Might I ask the hon.
and learned Gentleman if he is aware of
the request for these facilities on behalf
of the teachers generally in Northern Ireland, and if he does not consider this
request fair and reasonable?

CENSUS RETURNS
STATISTICS.
DETAILED
2. Mrs. WARING asked the Minister
of Finance whether it is proposed to supplement the volumes already published
giving the results of the 1926 Census, by
the issue of any additional and more detailed statistics
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The answer to the hon. Lady's
question is, I regret to say, in the negative. I might explain that the form and
range of the published Census statistics
are designed to give as much and as detailed information as possible, having regard to the cost of the work involved.
It will be realised that the tabulating
and other machinery used in the compilation of the Census volumes could not
have been economically employed for the
extraction of details relating to each of
a large number of small areas.
If further particulars on any definite
subject are required, they can be obtained on application to the Registrar-
General, and on repayment of the cost of
the labour involved in extracting the
information in question.
Mr. O'NEILL: Might I ask the right.
hon. Gentleman if he is aware of the cost
of the additional detailed information referred to, and if he also is aware that
in order to give the particulars of the
religious denominations in a district electoral division the cost of the whole parliamentary area would amount to something like £4. Might I further ask if he
would not consider that that information
would be both useful and necessary, and
if he will consider the possibility of giving
this information before the Census Committee is abolished?
Mr. POLLOCK: Assuming the hon.
Member's figures are correct, and I believe they are not very far from accuracy,
it would appear to me that those persons
who are interested in getting the details
of the smaller areas, such as has been indicated by the hon. Member, should not
refuse to pay such a comparatively small
sum as £4 for valuable information.
The aggregate would amount to a great
deal.
Mr. O'NEILL: Does the right hon.
Gentleman not know that this information could have been given, in the first.
instance, without much additional cost?
As the right hon. Gentleman knows, it
could have been done without much
labour or expense.

SELECTION OF MEN FOR RELIEF
WORK.
6. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state what system is adopted in the Labour Exchange
for selecting men for relief work, and for
ensuring that each man is selected in
accordance with his standing on the
priority list.
Mr. ANDREWS: In submitting men
for vacancies on relief schemes, priority
is given to men whose records of attendance at the Employment Exchange
show that they have had least employment in recent years. A preference is
given to married men before single men,
and to ex-Servicemen before civilians, and
disabled ex-Servicemen receive a special
preference for all work for which they
are fitted.
Mr. NIXON: What precautions does
the Minister take to see that the regulations as stated are carried out?
Mr. ANDREWS: Every possible precaution.
Mr. NIXON: I will raise this matter
on the adjournment too.

The Bill deals
on all sides of the House.
with two matters of considerable importance to concerns carrying on business of

so that companies and societies might be

The first point which is dealt with in

of endowment policies on the lives of relations, and will enable friendly societies
and industrial assurance companies to issue
to their members endowment policies on
There is no
the lives of near relatives.
provision permitting endowment assurances to be effected on the lives of persons
within the recognised range of relationship save a rather ineffective provision in

Notwithstanding this, it has been the

and collecting societies for many years to
issue not only whole-life policies but also

an insurable
in cases where there is

desirable to rectify the omission in the law

issued, so that the stamp of illegality may

The second point similarly arises through

the law. Hon. Members will be aware

HOUSE OF COMMONS

It
that the amount which can be insured or

is common to find a funeral expenses policy
running concurrently with an endowment
policy on the life of a child, and in the
case of the latter policy there is usually a
provision for the repayment of the
premium should the death of the child take
place before the maturity of the policy.
There was obviously no serious objection
to such a practice, and the companies and
societies have regarded themselves as acting within the law in excluding from the
calculation of the maximum sum insured
on a child's life any premiums repayable on
the death of a child in respect of an endowment policy. In a recent test case,
however, it was decided that the practice
of not including the premiums on the endowment policy in the calculation of the
maximum sum insurable or payable was
contrary to law and that, in fact, on the
language of the Statute it was illegal to
return premiums if, when added to the
sum assured under a whole life policy,
they amounted to more than the limit imposed by the Statute. The effect of
Clause 2, accordingly, is to exclude from
the calculation of the sum payable for
funeral expenses, and especially from the
sum payable on the death of a child, the
amount of any premiums refunded on an
endowment policy.
Clause 3 gives an endowment policyholder, who has paid at least one year's
premiums, the right, within one year
from the payment of the last premium,
to claim the surrender value of his policy,
either in the shape of a free paid-up
policy, assuring a proportionate part of
the sum assured or payment of a surrender value equal to 90 per cent. of
the present value of the sum payable
under the free paid-up policy. Under
the 1924 Act in Northern Ireland, rights
to free policies or surrender values in
lieu of forfeited policies accrued after
payment of five years' premiums, or. in
some cases, three years' premiums. Under this Clause these rights are given to
endowment policy-holders after one year's
premiums have been paid, and the effect
is to level up backward companies and
societies to the practice of the best companies and societies.
As I stated earlier, the Bill will, doubtless, have the approval of all parties and
of all persons interested and, in view of
the fact that a great deal of the indusalso
trial assurance business in Northern Ireland is carried on by concerns
operating in Great Britain, it is desirable that the law in this matter should
be made comformable to the law in Great
Britain at as early a date as possible. I
beg to move.
Mr. HEALY: The Bill before the
House is of a rather technical character,
and hon. Members who may doubt that
can turn to the Schedule printed on page
6 to find how exceedingly difficult it
would be for even Members of this House,
not to talk of the man in the street,
to understand what a person who had an
endowment insurance policy would be entitled to after the payment of premiums
for a particular period. In this connection it strikes me as rather extraordinary
that where the law contemplates benefiting the average person, the Section
should be worded in such technical
language that nobody but a lawyer could
possibly understand what it means.
The Northern Government is, apparently,
pursuing the old policy of the Imperial
Government-making it very difficult for
the average man to understand what his
rights in this matter are at all.
Since 1924 you have had two Bills
before this House dealing with industrial
assurance, and now you have a third Bill.
In my opinion, in 1924 the whole matters
that have been dealt with in legislation
since could have been very easily set out
simply in a Measure at that time, but,
apparently, because an English official
has discovered something in the British
Act that nobody but himself, not even
the trained lawyers, has discovered in a
period of 46 years, we must needs go to
the trouble of introducing three Amending Bills, within the space of five years.
It is assumed, I think, that your own
Industrial Assurance Commissioner has
no power of judgment at all, because it
is clear here that the difficulty that arose
in England is the precise difficulty that
must have arisen in Northern Ireland.
I believe the Industrial Assurance Commissioner in Northern Ireland had no
doubt whatever in his mind as to what
the law contemplated. I think for a
period of 20 or 30 years the best legal
minds in England had no doubt about
what the Section meant, but this peculiar
official discovered a mare's nest, or
thought he had discovered a mare's nest.
and he has not only put the Imperial
legislature to all this trouble, but he put
this House to all this trouble too.
813 Industrial Assurance Bill-

25 JUNE 1929
Second Reading.
The Act of 1864 enabled people to effect
insurance on the lives of relatives, but
chiefly of the industrial classes on the
lives of their children. The policies issued
were for a considerable time what is called
whole-life policies, that is, policies payable
at death; but after a time the insurance
companies began issuing industrial endowment policies, that is policies payable at the termination of a number
of years or at death. One would think
of the two forms of assurance the
more commendable by far would be the
endowment insurance policy-that a man
should be rather commended for insuring
for the life of his child rather than for the
death of the child. But the Industrial
Assurance Commissioner in England holds
that it is legal for him to insure his child
to die, but illegal for him to insure a sum
to educate his child if the child lives. I
never heard a more preposterous proposition in my life; it shows you that the
law is not always common-sense. What
the insurance companies and what the
public of England have assumed for a
long period of years to be correct, this
man discovers to be absolutely incorrect.
There is a peculiar anomaly here, too.
The law, as it stands, places the holder of
an industrial insurance policy in a far
superior position to the holder of an
ordinary branch insurance. The holder of
an ordinary branch insurance will not be
entitled to a cash surrender value until
three years' premiums have been paid, but
according to this Bill the holder of an industrial insurance policy for a similar sum,
with more frequent collections, and on
which there is a larger measure of expense,
will be entitled to a cash surrender value
after one year's premiums have been paid.
So the pendulum has swung from east to
west once again.
I think the Minister of Commerce will
be coming to the House very soon again to
introduce another Bill dealing with holders
of ordinary branch policies. There is no
finality to this kind of legislation. Apparently the Northern Government has no
mind of its own, and it assumes that its
officials have no mind of their own either.
I do not see why the Industrial Assurance
Commissioner of Northern Ireland should
have been bound as a definite fact to follow
the decision of the English Industrial Assurance Commissioner.
Mr. POLLOCK: It is a decision of the
Court.
Mr. HEALY: There has been no actual
decision in the High Court. A case has
never been taken to the Court of Appeal;
it has never been carried any further than
some of the minor courts in England.
But whether that be so, or whether it be
not so, a case has never been carried to
the superior Court in Northern Ireland
either by the Industrial Assurance Commissioner or by anybody else, but just because a decision has been given in England
by an Industrial Assurance Commissioner
who is not himself a judge
The PRIME MINISTER: There was a

There is no means therefore of proving

they be entitled to come into Northern

premiums under this Bill? That is a
matter that is not made clear in this Bill.

Another thing that must tend to increase unemployment is what I would call
the elimination of hand labour. We know
that the progress that has been made in
the invention of electrical and other power
devices has largely done away with hand
labour in many trades and industries.
very striking instance is provided in the
riveting and plating work formerly done
in the shipyards by hand labour and now
done by automatic power. Development
in that direction is going on every day,
and I do think the trade unions would
have been doing a great service to
their members if they had made them
familiar with the progress that is being
made in automatic machinery, and had
helped them to take advantage of it.
In dealing with the working man I
have found that very often he will not
think for himself. There is no one to
make him think. Men who are out of
employment come to me every day, and I
say to them, "Where have you sought employment." They reply, "I have been
to that place over there," and it is
generally a little twopence-halfpenny
place that puts a roof on a house after a
I say, "Why do you not go to
the big places, such as the Seaview site on
the Shore Road? It is three miles away,
but no matter, go down there." I have
got dozens of men work there. It is up
to the trade unions to get these people to
think on the right lines.

Reference was made by many Members on both sides of the House to the
administration of unemployment benefit.
Surely it cannot be said that the administration is harsh, when I am able to
state in this House, that of the average
number of claims current each week,

In other words 98.2 per cent, of the cla ms
current are granted. And yet we are

Now, a great deal has been said about
the condition known as the genuinely
seeking work condition. I know it is
very hard for a man to be told he is not

that he is. But I do not try the cases.
I do not give the decision. It is the
courts which Parliament has set up which
decides. The courts investigate the
matter. the courts hear the claimant,
they give the fullest consideration to
everything the claimant says, and the
courts decide in a judicial way, and in
a sympathetic way, whether a claimant
is entitled to benefit or not. Surely
hon. Members on both sides of the
House will realise that claims must be
investigated or else some people would
get benefit when they obviously were not
entitled to it.
May I sav in passing that it was the
Socialist Government who first introduced this test in its application to
covenanted benefit? That is an undeniable fact. Every successive British
Government has recognised that a test
is necessary, and this Government has
simply done the same. Hon. Members
know in their hearts quite well that a
test is necessary, or otherwise the community would, to some extent, be demoralised. What we want is to let
those who draw benefit feel that they get
it because they are entitled to it, because they are unemploved, because it is
recognised that they are not able to obtain work, and that they get something
that is not, in my opinion, demoralising,
because remember, it is not a dole-

Adjournment-
Killough Harbour.
25 JUNE 1929
Motion for Adjournment.
KILLOUGH HARBOUR.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn.".
(Sir Basil Brooke).
Mr. O'NEILL: There is a matter I
desire to bring before the House, and I
wish to take this opportunity of doing
so. I understand the Minister of Commerce will not be here to-morrow, and
I wish to facilitate him in stating the
policy of the Government regarding these
matters. I want to refer particularly
to what the Government are doing in
relation to some of the fishery harbours
round our coasts. When the Vote for
the Ministry of Commerce was before
this House in Committee, and when the
question of these harbours was raised
the Minister, in my opinion, dealt very
lightly with some important matters in
connection with these harbours, and particularly those used for fishing purposes.
He said that out of the total population
of our Province, less than 700 were
wholly dependent on sea fishing for their
livelihood. He also said they lived in
small, scattered communities, and that,
in his judgment, the time was not ripe
for the Government to embark on
schemes of harbour improvement on a
large scale.
To justify this, he said that the total
value of fish landed in our ports. excluding the herring fishing of Ardolass,
was only £24,000 per annum. No doubt
that is a small amount to be realised
from such an important industry in Northern Ireland, but it is rather remarkable that he left out the larger amount
that is secured from this important industry, because herrings to the value of
some £60.000, or, to be absolutely accurate, £58,941, were landed at Ardglass in
the year 1926, which was the last date
for which these statistics are available.
The Minister also said that so far as
the accommodation for these fishermen
was concerned it was quite ample, considering that only 700 people were emploved in this industry, but he could also
have told us that in addition to the 700
people constantly emploved in this industry, 700 further people were
ploved part time, so that altogether some
1,400 or 1,500 men are employed in this
industry. He told us that the accommodation at Ardglass was ample, except at
emthe very height of the season. Then, he
said, the accommodation was not quite
sufficient, but the point I want to make
is this, that a suitable harbour is available convenient to Ardglass, and that is
Killough Harbour, which should be developed. It is not the first time that
Kil'ough Harbour has been mentioned.
in this House. It has been mentioned
on many occasions by Members on both
sides of the House, and I want to extract from the Government now what
they propose to do in relation to Killough
Harbour.
Some three years ago a deputation
waited on the Prime Minister in regard
to this harbour, people who are interested
in the harbour of Killough, and would
like to see it developed, as I think it
should be developed. The Prime Minister then undertook to have a Report
made on the harbour, and he engaged
an eminent engineer to inspect it. I
hope the House will permit me to read
an extract from that Report, because it
will explain the position much better
than I can do. This Report was made
by Mr. R. Gordon Nicol, the harbour
engineer of Aberdeen.
He says:
Killough Harbour is situated on the
same coast as Ardglass Harbour, about
a mile further west. It is an inner
arm of Killough Bay well retired from
the sea and protected by a formation
of headlands that must render it comparatively quiet in stormy weather.
At the mouth of this arm or basin
there is a masonry pier which projects
from the south shore and affords good
protection to the interior. This pier,
however, requires considerable repairs.
The basin is about 3,000 feet long inside the pier by about 3,000 feet wide
and has a soft bottom which largely
dries out at low water.
I have considered the accommodation
which would be required to establish
and develop a herring industry at this
place, and have prepared the accompanying plan No. 2 for this purpose,
all new work being drawn and tinted
red.
This accommodation should, in my
opinion, be situated on the west side of
the basin, and would consist of a line
of reinforced concrete wharfage for
the accommodation of fishing boats,
having a depth alongside of 11 feet at
low water of ordinary spring tides.
The quays would be 100 feet wide with
Killough Harbour.
Adjournment-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. O'Neill]
a row of curing yards 200 feet in depth.
fronting the quays.
I estimate the cost of this scheme,
with 3,500 lineal feet of wharfage, very
approximately at £145,000.
There is no doubt that the last figure
has been the cause of the Government's
failure to do anything in connection with
this harbour, but there is also no doubt
that the harbour lends itself to considerable development for even a tithe of this
amount. The fishing industry could be
fostered and nursed there and made one
of the most important industries we have
in Northern Ireland. Members of this
House know just as well as I do, and
some a good deal better, that this harbour is convenient to one of the finest
fishing beds there is in these waters.
It being Half-past Six o'clock the
Motion for the adjournment of the
House lapsed without Question put, pursuant to the Standing Order.
Motion made, and Question again proposed, "That this House do now adjourn."-(Sir Basil Brooke).
Mr. O'NEILL: The House know that
this Harbour is capable of very great
development. I think the time has come
when the Government should make some
effort to develop the harbour, considering the size of this fishing industry, considering there is not accommodation at
Ardglass for the industry, and considering
also that the accommodation there is
availed of largely by Scottish fishermen.
That being so, it is surely up to the
Government to encourage their own men,
and not send them to Richhill to emigrate. Instead of keeping the flag flying in other parts of the Dominions it
would be as wise, and probably as loyal,
to develop this industry and keep the flag
flying at home.
I want to point out that while the
Government may have had the intention
at some time of developing this harbour,
they took what was, in my opinion, a
rather mean way of shelving it. They
must have had some intention when they
employed an eminent engineer to come
and make that report on the possibilities
of the harbour. At a later stage, they
did what Governments usually do when
they want to abandon or shelvé anything, they appointed a Departmental

Mr. BARBOUR: I welcome the opportunity afforded to me by the hon.
Member for putting the House in possession of the Government's views about harbour development at Killough. The case
for the improvement of Killough has been
put forward on two grounds, firstly, that

Northern Ireland, and secondly, that it

As regards the fishery aspect of the
matter, I would ask the House to remember that the herring fishery in the Irish
Channel is limited in its scope, and is
not capable of indefinite expansion.
Herring migrations are irregular, and
do not provide the same catches in the
same regions year by year; 1926 was a
good year, 1927 not so good, 1928 very
poor both
as regards quantity and
quality. In a good season, such as 1926,
about 400 fishing boats of all kinds

It
The herring fishing industry in the
Irish Channel is, as the House is aware,
carried on mainly by cross-Channel interests. The majority of the fishing
boats are Scottish, and they fish their
own waters so long as the catches are
good, coming to the Irish Channel to fill
in the gap some 10 or 12 weeks between
the termination of the Scottish fishing
and the opening of the east coast fishing
based on Yarmouth. Not a single steam
drifter working in the Irish Channel belongs to Northern Ireland. In spite of
all the efforts which the Government have
made to develop this herring fishing, it
is always a regret that not more of our
population seem to have been attracted
to this particular industry. In spite of
all the money spent at Ardglass, the
facilities afforded there are mainly taken
advantage of by fishermen from across
the water. In order that hon. Members
may understand the nature of the people
engaged in this industry, I may tell
them that of the herring girls who are at
work in our area while the fishing season
is going on, the approximate total is 75
--what they call "crews. That is
equal to 225 girls. Of those about 50
crews, or 150 girls, are Scottish, and the
remainder come from Donegal, with the
exception of 18 or 20 girls who are recruited locally.
""

Scottish curers. On the north pier, there
are 17 plots in all; all of those were held
last year by Scottish curers, and are
likely to be so held this year.

SO
I can assure the hon. Member that the
Government have given very earnest consideration to the claims of Killough for
development, which have been so vigorously supported in many quarters.
The physical potentialities of the Killough
basin are acknowledged on all hands, but
these in themselves are insufficient to
warrant the expenditure of a very large
sum out of public funds. We should only
be justified in superseding the port of Ardglass if it could be proved that Ardglass
were quite inadequate to cope with the
traffic as it exists to-day, or unless there
were prospects of such development as to
render the construction of a new port on
a larger scale a wise step in economic
policy. Ardglass Harbour admittedly
presents difficulties during a south-easterly
gale, but these gales are fortunately of
extremely infrequent occurrence during
the fishing season, and no one, I think,
would urge that £180,000 or more should
be spent in order that accommodation
may be provided for cross-Channel drifters
on those very rare occasions when Ardglass is inaccessible.
After a very careful examination of this
problem we are satisfied that the increase
in her share of the herring trade which
Northern Ireland might expect to secure
as a result of the development of Killough
on the lines which have been suggested
would be incommensurate with the capital
cost involved, and that the claims made
in respect of improved mails and passenger
services between Northern Ireland and
Great Britain have little to recommend
them from any point of view.
I can assure the hon. Member, as he is
aware, this has been a matter of investigation by committees, and they, after taking evidence on the subject and going
carefully into the matter, do not feel
there is sufficient reason for spending
large sums of money for developing what
I feel must only be regarded as
alternative harbour to Ardglass.

which is intended to give the Ministry
of Finance the necessary authority to
issue the aggregate sum of £5,050,627.
That is the effect of the first part of the
Measure. The following Clause deals with
the powers of borrowing in order to reach
certain results and also the method by
which the borrowing can be repaid and
such like matters that are purely financial
details in carrying out the scheme.

that may be required to be sought, and
Clause 4 provides that
A person shall not receive any payment out of a grant which may be

civil or police non-effective services
until he has subscribed such declaration as may from time to time be prescribed by a warrant from the Ministry of Finance
and so on.

one. It is well known as a Measure that
is required in order to conform to our
financial arangements. I beg to move.

I have called the attention of the House

this Government, in respect of the Treasury notes that are circulating here. He
admitted to me in answer to a question

using the coinage of another country we

are getting no credit whatever. I again
call the attention of the Minister of

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I am advised that persons,
whether themselves farmers or not, who
contract to cart milk to creameries are
required to be insured under the Health
Insurance and Contributory Pensions
Acts.
Where the contract is with the
creamery, the creamery is liable to pay
the employer's portion of the contribution. Where the contract is with a group
of farmers, the farmers concerned are
liable.
If, as sometimes happens, the carter
is paid by the creamery on behalf of
the group of farmers, the creamery is
responsible for affixing the stamps in payment of the contributions at the time
that payment is being made in respect of
the services rendered under the contract,
but in such circumstances the employee's
share of the contribution is recoverable
from the carter and the employer's share
from the group of farmers.
I am advised that these provisions.
which are contained in the National
Health Insurance Act, 1928, do not
affect the position under the Workmen's
Compensation Act.

widows' pensions and other things, could
we have an assurance from the Government that if such legislation is introduced
on the other side this House will be summoned to deal with it, so that the people
here may be on exactly parallel lines with
Great Britain?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Provision has already been
made. If any untoward incident of any
kind should arise, power will be availed
of to summon Parliament.
Mr. BYRNE: We have read in the
King's Speech that a strong effort is
going to be made on the other side to
ease unemployment. If any Measure is
introduced in the English House of Commons, could we have a guarantee that
this House would meet immediately to
put the same Measure into operation?
There is a great deal of unemployment
at the present time. Since the returns
were made I have found out that a very
large number of people have ceased to
sign for work at the Labour Exchanges.
I am very much afraid that the returus
made are not correct. Practically two
out of every three men have ceased to
sign. If any Measure is introduced and
passed in the English House of Commons.
it would be a good thing if an effort were
made to put it in operation here, in
order that something may be done for
these people who are so long out of employment.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have read with
great interest Mr. Thomas's speech.
Personally, I think it is a very reasonable and proper one. I can assure the
House that should it be necessary to call
this House together to consider any proposals brought forward in the Imperial
Parliament, Mr. Speaker has power, in
consultation with the Government, to immediately call the House together, and
knowing Mr. Speaker as I do I am sure
he would not hesitate to do so.
add, however, that most of the proposals

Oral Answer to Question.
a
a
FLOODS IN NORTHERN IRELAND.
RELIEF OF DISTRESS.
Captain CHICHESTER-CLARK (by
Private Notice) asked the Minister of Finance whether the Government is aware of
the acute distress which prevails in certain
parts of the country owing to the recent
phenomenal floods, as a consequence of
which many farmers and labourers, whose
houses lay in the track of the flood, have
lost all their means of subsistence.
Will the Minister state if steps are being
taken by the Government to come to the
immediate relief of these sufferers in the
areas most severely affected-such as the
valley of the Moyola-and are they prepared to provide grants to assist in restocking farms?
And, further, are they considering
providing grants to repair breaches in the
embankments of the most seriously affected
rivers in order to protect the lands which
are at present exposed to further serious
flooding should any rise above normal
height of water take place?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The Government have given
the most careful consideration to the position which has arisen as a result of the
abnormal flooding referred to in the hon.
and gallant Member's question.
I can assure the hon. and gallant
Member that immediate steps are being
taken to meet the circumstances.
reports which have been received show
The
that while there has been no appreciable
loss of livestock the loss of crops has been
of a serious character, and assistance will
be given to those affected by means of
loans repayable over a term varying with
the nature and extent of the loss, but not
exceeding ten years. Details of the
scheme will be communicated to the House
as soon as possible.
My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Home Affairs, is in touch with the County
Councils concerned in regard to the repair
of roads and bridges, and satisfactory
arrangements are being made by means of
grants from the Road Fund.
The responsibility for the repair of river
banks rests on the County Councils by
virtue of the Drainage Act (Northern
Ireland), 1925, but the Government has
decided, in view of the special circumstances, that if the County Councils are
prepared to make contributions from
County Funds under Section 5, Subsection (4), of the Act towards the cost
of such works, the Government will contribute a like amount. In some cases,
however, individual farmers may find it
preferable to utilize for such work the
scheme administered by the Ministry of
Agriculture, under which a substantial
portion of the cost of unemployed labour
recruited directly by farmers or groups of
farmers for special improvement works on
their farms is recouped by the Ministry.
Captain CHICHESTER - CLARK:
The answer given by the right hon.
Gentleman not being quite satisfactory, I
should like to raise the question on the
Adjournment. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
Mr. DEVLIN: Do I understand the
right hon. Gentleman proposes to offer
loans instead of grants to these people
whose property has been so seriously
damaged through no fault of their own?
Mr. SPEAKER: I understand that
the right hon. Gentleman has consented
that this matter should be discussed on
the Adjournment. That being so, perhaps it would be the wish of the House

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Marketing of Dairy Produce Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): It is the policy
of the Ministry of Agriculture to do all
in its power to improve the methods of
marketing in Great Britain of every class
of agricultural produce from Northern
Ireland. In pursuance of this policy the
Ministry obtained from Parliament
authority to deal with the egg trade, and
I am glad to say that the exercise of these
powers with the active co-operation of the
great bulk of egg exporters has placed
this commodity in a very high place in
the British markets. Similar powers in
regard to potatoes were granted this year
by Parliament, and I now submit this Bill
dealing with the dairy industry. Other
articles of agricultural produce will come
up for consideration as opportunity offers.
The main purpose of this Bill is to improve the quality and methods of marketing Ulster butter consigned to Great
Britain. The Bill falls into five parts.
Part I deals with the registration of all
premises used as auxiliary creameries,
central creameries, butter factories and
wholesale depots from which butter is
shipped. The conditions relating to registration are set out in some detail in
Clause 2. They include the suitability of
premises, machinery, equipment and
utensils, safeguards against contamination
of butter, cream and milk, and the qualifications of the staff employed at central
and auxiliary creameries. An annual fee
of £1 is chargeable for registration.
Under Part II (Licences), it is proposed to prohibit the export of butter or
cream except under licence. The object
of this proposal is to ensure that the
quality, methods of packing, types of
packages and the manner of marking of
packages will be in accordance with such
standards as will be prescribed by the
Ministry.
A further condition attached to the
issue of the licence is the duty to send
samples of butter or cream to any centre
the Ministry may fix. This is in continuation of the Ministry's surprise butter
inspections, which have hitherto been
worked on a voluntary basis, and which
have been most useful as a means of collecting information as
to the general
quality of butter produced, and of rectifying faults in manufacture.
If
Part III of the Bill provides safeguards
against the presence of adulterants in
registered premises, and against their
being added to the butter or cream.
unclean, contaminated or stale milk is
offered to a creamery the person offering
it shall be guilty of an offence, as shall
also the occupier of the creamery if such
milk is accepted. The limit of moisture
allowable in butter prepared for sale at
a registered premises is fixed at 16 per
cent.
Under Part IV of the Bill officers of
the Ministry are empowered to enter registered premises (or premises which
should be registered) for the purposes of
examination and sampling. Inspection
during transit is also provided for.
Clause 10 (2) and (3) are set out the
arrangements proposed to ensure that
In
Dairy Produce Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Edward Archdale]
such inspections are carried out with the
minimum of inconvenience to the owners
of the produce. The usual provision empowering the Ministry to make Rules is
included and power to have samples of
butter, cream or milk analysed or submitted to bacteriological or other examination is proposed. The penalties
for offences follow the lines of marketing
legislation already passed by Parliament, but there is a proviso that an
offence shall not be deemed to be a
second or subsequent offence unless the
former offence or offences were under the
same part of the Bill.
Clause 15 (1) contains a valuable provision. Without full information as to
the extent and nature of the trade transacted from all the registered premises, the
Minister would
would obviously be handicapped in giving the maximum assistance
to the industry. It is proposed to conserve the designation "creamery butter"
to butter made at premises registered as
central creameries when used in connection with butter produced in and despatched from Northern Ireland. The
use of the word "creamery" in relation
to any premises is restricted to registered
creameries. The operative date is 1st
January, 1931. While this is so, the
Ministry hopes to have completed in 1930
most of the preliminary arrangements including the inspection of premises with
a view to registration.
Members of this House will appreciate
that legislation of itself will not achieve
much improvement. The good-will and
cordial co-operation of those engaged in
the industry are also essential. All the
interests have been consulted, and with
every confidence I count on the enthusiastic assistance of the farming community, more especially those associated
with the creamery movement, to beat the
Danes in butter as we have done in eggs.
I beg to move.
Mr. HEALY: I think there will not
be any serious disagreement with the
right hon. Gentleman from any side of
this House in the Measure he has introduced this afternoon. I would like,
however, to protest against the delay in
issuing Bills of this kind to Members of
the House until the very last hour. This
is a Measure that affects particularly
creameries, creamery managers and the
committees of creameries, and they have
had no opportunity whatever-this is the
Second Reading of the Bill-of discussing this matter that affects so many of
their interests. I would, therefore, like
that the Minister of Agriculture and,
indeed, all the Ministers, would take a
note of this matter. We have raised this
point again and again with regard to
other Bills. You have had a long holiday. You have not been doing anything
very constructive in the meantime as far
as one can gather, so there is the less excuse for having delayed the issue of this
Bill until the very last second.
I notice that whilst the Ministers have
not sufficient time to produce Measures of
this kind they have ample opportunities
of going about the country as the Minister

this House. That is an unhappy precedent that was started by the Minister
of Finance some time ago and has now
been repeated by the Minister of Labour.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I am

which is in the Free State and the

941 Adoption of Children Bill-

5 NOVEMBER 1929
Second Reading.
Adoption of Children Bill.
(Mr.
Order for Second Reading read.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL
Babington): I rise to move "That the
Bill be now read a Second time."
The principle involved in this Bill will
commend itself to every Member of the
House. It follows the English Measure
that was passed in 1926, with certain
adaptations and with a few amendments
which have been inserted as a
result
of the working of the corresponding
Measure in Great Britain. The actual
terms of the Bill itself will not give rise
to any difficulty if the House approves of
its object. As the House well knows,
many benevolent people, both married
and single, adopt children under the law
as it stands at present, but, unfortunately, there is no law recognising the
relationship. Adopted children under
our present law have no legal status, and
the parents by adoption have no rights
over the children for whom they make
themselves
a
responsible. The natural
parents of the child that is adopted can
terminate the adoption at any time and
demand back the custody of the child.
Sometimes that is done when the child
arrives at an age to be of service to the
natural parents, and I have, unfortunately, known cases where child
has been demanded back by its natural
parents because they were aware that ties
of affection had been formed between
those who have adopted the child and the
child itself, and that fact has been made
use of for improper purposes. The result is that damage is often done to the
child when the moral and the legal rights
to the custody of the infant are in
different persons.
This Bill is designed to put an end to
this anomalous position, and to place this
question of adoption on a true legal basis.
If hon. Members will turn to Clause 5 of
the Bill they will find the operative
power. This is the text of the Clause:
"Upon an adoption order being
made, all rights, duties, obligations
and liabilities of the parent or parents,
guardian or guardians of the adopted
child, in relation to the future custody,
maintenance and education of the
adopted child, including all rights to
appoint a guardian or to consent or give
notice of dissent to marriage shall be extinguished, and all such rights, duties,
obligations and liabilities shall vest in
and be exercisable by and enforceable
against the adopter as though the
adopted child were a child born to the
adopter in lawful wedlock, and in respect of the same matters and in respect
of the liability of a child to maintain its
parents the adopted child shall stand
to the adopter exclusively in the position of a child born to the adopter in
lawful wedlock."
If this Bill becomes law the relationship
of the adopter and the adopted child will
from this time on have a proper legal
basis.
The Bill hedges the system of adoption
round with safeguards. In Clause i the
adoption can only be carried out with
the sanction of the Court after proper inquiry. In Clause 2 various other restrictions are placed upon adoption. No
adoption shall be made where the applicant is under the age of twenty-five, or
where the applicant is less than twentyone years older than the infant in respect
of whom the application is made. There
are various other restrictions in that
Clause to which I need not refer now.
They are all designed for the purpose of
protecting infants from improper adoption orders.
Then by Clause 3 the Court must be
satisfied that the consent of every person
interested in the child that is to be
adopted has been obtained before the
order is made. In the last paragraph of
that Clause, and also in Clause 9, there
is the very necessary provision that the
court must be satisfied that the adoption
is not being made upon a monetary basis.
By Clause 11 there is to be kept by the
Registrar-General a register of adopted
children, in which all the facts of the
adoption are to be set out, with cross references between that register and the
ordinary register of births and deaths, so
that any person who wishes to find out
anything with regard to an adoption can
do so on payment of the usual small fee.
If this Bill becomes law I believe that
many persons, who are at present afraid
to contract ties of affection for the children
of others lest they be rudely broken, will
be prepared to offer comfortable homes
and happiness to children who, through
the misfortunes of their parents, would
otherwise have to depend upon charity
and would be condemned to a childhood
barren of all pleasure or opportunity.
I think the House will agree that the
943 Adoption of Children Bill-

I beg to move.

Betting (Juvenile Messengers) Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The provisions contained in this Bill require very little explanation. The Bill has for its object the
prevention of children under 16 years of
age being used for the purpose of conveying betting messages.
The Bill closely follows the Imperial
Act which bears the same title, and which
applies to Scotland only, and which was
passed in August of last year. I feel sure
that any Measure which has for its object
the welfare of the young will be received
with sympathy by every Member of this
House, no matter what his or her own view
may be with regard to the general question of betting-a very difficult, and may
I say also a thorny subject. No doubt
every Member will agree that it is most
undesirable for children of tender years to
be allowed to familiarise themselves with
the machinery of betting.
In connection with this matter, I have
received very strong representations, in
particular from a deputation from the
Belfast District Schools Committee, pressing for the introduction of this Measure.
I may say that I was greatly impressed
with the information which was given to
me, indicating that, in certain districts,
the practice of utilising young persons as
messengers for the conveying of betting
messages was prevalent to such an extent
Betting Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
that the school attendance had been materially impaired. I have also been informed that in many cases the children's
luncheon hour, instead of being devoted to
its legitimate purpose of both refreshment
and recreation, was taken up in conveying
betting messages for their parents, and,
therefore, I think hon. Members will agree
with me that such a condition of affairs
should not be allowed to continue if it is
at all possible to remedy it. I, therefore,
hope that this House will give unanimous
approval to this Measure. I beg to move.

had in certain parts of Northern Ireland.

that other parts of the Six Counties, including Limavady and Strabane, have

moderately as I can.

that this flooding was quite phenomenal,

I would be prepared to make a betalthough he would be a brave man who

There are
men who have had all their possessions

their stock and crop and their visible

out, and if something is not done for

and a large area of land on the banks of
these various rivers will go out of cultivation altogether.
I now come to the next point,
and that is that one of the most
serious items of damage is the breaches
in the embankments of these rivers.
A good many of these breaches-in fact
I may say all of them-are enormous.
They are quite beyond the means of any
farmer to repair. What is happening?
Every time all through the winter that
the river rises a few inches above its
normal height it is pouring through all
these breaches and over good farm land,
and will continue to do so until the
breaches are repaired, thereby making
that land absolutely useless for any purpose all through the winter, and, as I
said before, until these breaches have
been stopped.
At the present moment
after last night's rain, I can safely say
that a very large acreage of land is flooded,
land which, of course, would not have
been flooded if these breaches had been
repaired. They are so bad that there
is no prospect whatever of local farmers
being able to repair them. I ask that
immediate grants should be given to have
these breaches put right, not in the fardistant future but now at once, so that
this land may be brought into cultivation
and used for farming purposes in the
coming year.
I now want for a second or two to
refer to the answer which the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) gave to my
question. It is a long answer and it is
rather hard in the hurly-burly of the
House of Commons to take it all in quite
at once. First of all he spoke of the loss
of property being of a serious character.
With all respect I would say to him that
it has been of far more than a serious
character, that it has been a catastrophe.
that it has been a complete knock-out, if
it is Parliamentary language to say so.
Then he goes on to say that the responsibility for the repair of these banks
rests with the county councils by virtue
of the Drainage Act (Northern Ireland)
of 1925. I submit to him that in that
case he is in error. The Drainage Act of
1925 empowers the county councils, at the
request of dwellers in various areas, to
bring in drainage schemes, to repair
ramparts, and that sort of thing. We
know that this Act is working very
slowly, because, as we know, there is a
Drainage Bill being brought in to try to
hasten the procedure of the county
councils under this Act. If the county
councils were to undertake the repair of
these breaches it would mean that by the
time they got their plans out and had the
work carried out this land would have
been under water for perhaps four years.
I myself have been taking some part in
getting a drainage scheme put through.
We started in 1925 and even now in 1929
there is very little done.

hon, and gallant Gentleman is quite right.
These people living in the backward parts

The meeting was for the purpose of calling attention to the grievances of the
tenant farmers, and I had with me an old

came in and asked us what we were doing

"Oh! yes.
We forgot all about that
meeting, and the Mayor and the brass

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Insurance (Money).
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair).
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to authorise as
from the first day of April, 1929, the
payment out of moneys provided by Parliament of a contribution under the Unemployment Insurance Acts (Northern
Ireland), 1920 to 1929, at a rate equal
to one-half of the aggregate amount of
the contributions paid in respect of
employed persons by themselves and their
employers, or, in the case of exempt persons, paid by their employers, under the
said Acts." (Governor's recommendation
signified.-Mr. Barbour).
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): The necessity for this Resolution is to give financial authority for the
introduction of a Bill which will increase
the amount of the State contribution to
the Unemployment Fund, and will, therefore, impose an additional charge on the
Exchequer. The White Paper which has
been circulated to hon. Members to-day
explains in detail what it is proposed to
do, and it is, therefore, only necessary for
me to refer to the additional money expenditure created which will necessitate the
taking of a Supplementary Estimate in
this House.
The increase of the Exchequer contribution from about 40 per cent. to 50 per
cent. of the amount contributed by employers and employed will, it is estimated,
increase the amount provided under Subhead "A" of the Unemployment Insurance Estimate this year by £70,000.
Sub-head"B" will also be affected by
the increased State contributions now payable both in Great Britain and Northern
Ireland, and it is estimated that the charge
against the Northern Ireland Exchequer
in respect of equalisation payment
will amount to approximately £23,000.
Present indications show, however, that
the provisions already made under this
head will suffice. I beg to move.

Mr. BARBOUR: In approaching the

Members will have observed that the

House, and I am glad of this opportunity

Turning now to the first Sub-head in
the Estimates covering grants in aid of
harbour works carried out by Local
Authorities, the first item of £6,360, relates to the Newry Ship Canal, and represents the amount required to bring up to
the figure of £9,000, the total amount of
the Government Grant towards the expenditure required to repair the damage
caused by the bursting of the culvert
under the canal in circumstances with
which the Committee are already familiar.
Provision to the extent of £3,500 was
made last year towards this work, and of
this sum only £2,640 had in fact been expended up to 31st March last and,

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
I next come to an item which has, unfortunately, figured in my Ministry's
Estimates annually since the year 1925.
I refer to the grant in aid of the
Londonderry and Lough Swilly Railway
Company, Limited, towards the loss in
working during the current calendar year.
I should perhaps explain, for the information in particular of hon. Members who
are new to this Committee, that ever since
the termination of the period of Government control this company has been
unable to pay its way, and that, if
financial assistance had not been forthcoming from public funds provided not
only by this Committee, but to a corresponding extent by the Irish Free State
Government, the railway would have been
forced to close down.
So far as the first nine months of the
current year are concerned losses on
working amount to 7,209, and it is anticipated that the loss on working during
the remaining three months of the year
will be proportionately greater, as during the winter months the receipts from
passenger traffic normally decline. It is
unlikely, therefore, that the loss during
the full year will fall far short of £10,000.
Towards this loss the Government of the
Irish Free State has agreed to give a
grant of £3,750, and authority for a grant
of a similar amount from Northern Ireland funds is now sought. I have taken
frequent opportunities to impress upon
the directors of this company that grants
from Government funds cannot continue
to be made indefinitely, and I have received assurances from the directors, and
corroborative evidence from periodical
returns, that every effort is being made
to reduce the working losses.

to move.

EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): Yesterday

His complaint with regard to Dromore
Public Elementary School was that Mr.
Henley was appointed to be principal of
that school, and was not recognised
at once as principal by the Ministry.
The facts of the case are quite simple. It
has hitherto been a rule both of the Commissioners and of the Ministry that where
a teacher is not teaching for ten years he
is not eligible for re-entry into the service.
At the time Mr. Henley was appointed he
had been out of the service for more than
ten years and so was not elegible. Accordingly, recognition of him as principal in
that school could not be granted.
Mr. NIXON: On a point of Order, I,
of course, do not know, but that is denied.
They say he was teaching as a substitute
inside ten years.

must not put as a point of Order what is
a matter of opinion.
Mr. NIXON: It is to correct a mistake.
Mr. SPEAKER: It is a matter of
correction.
Mr. ROBB: The service which Mr.
Henley gave as substitute was not service
which would bring him within the rule
which excluded him. He had not been
teaching as a recognized teacher for ten
years and consequently he was ineligible.
However, whether that be true or whether
it be not true does not really matter now,
because the case of Mr. Henley was put
up to the Ministry, and it led to the reconsideration of the whole rule. The
Ministry of Education approached the
Ministry of Finance with regard to a
modification of this rule, and we have the
consent of the Ministry of Finance to enlarging the period, so that a man or
woman will in future have to be fifteen
years out of service to debar him or her
from reappointment. That cannot be
made, and is not at the moment the rule
because a new rule has to lie upon the
Table of this House for nine days before
it can be made a rule. But Papers are
being laid to change the rule to that extent, and in the meantime Mr. Henley is
teaching, is being paid, and his recognition will be retrospective.

all
was appointed on probation, as
trainees are. A trainee appointed on
probation is not recognized as a full
teacher, and does not get full recognition,
unless he gets efficient reports for two
years. He ought to get those efficient
reports within two years, but the time
may be extended from time to time by the
Ministry. Mr. Cairns taught for three
years and never got an efficient report at
all. Consequently the Ministry informed
him that he could no longer be allowed to
teach and draw a salary as he had not
qualified as a teacher. He was acting as
a principal.
It is well known to us in the Ministry
that it is more difficult for a young man
coming in at once as a principal to get his
diploma than if he starts as an assistant
where he gets help and instruction from
his superiors. Accordingly the Ministry
suggested to Mr. Cairns that if he would
seek and obtain an appointment as an
assistant they would further extend the
period within which he might qualify for
his diploma. Mr. Cairns was not prepared to pursue that course apparently.
According to the hon. Member for Woodvale (Mr. Nixon) he went to Canada.

MINIMUM PRICE FOR POTATOES.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD: With your permission and that of the House I would
like to ask the Minister of Agriculture's
consent to substitute the word "minimum" for the word "reasonable."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale) indicated assent.
Mr. CRAWFORD accordingly asked
the Minister of Agriculture whether, in
the interests of the community, he would
consider it advisable or possible to make
such arrangements as would enable
farmers to dispose of their potatoes at a
minimum price of from £3 2s. 6d. to
£3 5s. Od. per ton?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: Arrangements such as suggested by the hon.
Member would involve a subsidy to
potato growers at the expense of the
general taxpayer. The hon. Member
will realize that this is not practicable.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Arising out of that
reply may I ask the right hon. Gentleman is he aware that at the beginning of
this year farmers were not able to dispose
of their potatoes at all and could not pay
cash for their seeds and manures; and is
he aware that they cannot now dispose of
their potatoes practically at any price? I
have been making inquiries and they cannot dispose of them at any price. Is he
aware that these people are in extreme
need, and is he prepared in these circumstances to say he cannot take any steps?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I am
very sorry indeed that the potato market
is in such a bad way, but we cannot take
steps such as he suggests.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Owing to that unsatisfactory answer I propose to raise this
matter on the adjournment of the House.

SHEEP SCAB IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
3. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether, in view
of the importance of the sheep and lamb
export trade, and the necessity for maintaining a clean bill of health, he can give
the sheep population of Northern Ireland for the year 1924, and for the year
1928, and state how the sheep scab position in the latter year compares with that
in the former?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: The
sheep population of Northern Ireland in
1924 was 509,405, and in 1928 it was
624,084. The number of confirmed outbreaks of Sheep Scab in 1924 was 92,
and in 1928 the number was 87. This
indicates a considerable improvement,
particularly having regard to the increased sheep population. It is hoped
that this improvement will be continued
until Northern Ireland has, as regards
Sheep Scab, a clean bill of health.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of that answer, which does not show a
satisfactory state of things, will the right
hon. Gentleman continue to impress on all
local authorities the utmost need for
eradicating this disease?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: We are
continuing to do that.

The following are the questions and

5. Mr. BEATTIE-To ask the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether it is necessary for the
parents and guardians of school children
to go to the expense of procuring from the
Registrars of Births and Deaths birth
certificates; whether the statement of the
parent or guardian is not sufficient for
school purposes; what is the cost of these
certificates, and whether the Registrars,
who are Clerks of the Unions, issue these
certificates during office hours?
Mr. ROBB: A parent is required by
Section 7 of Statutory Rules and Orders
of Northern Ireland, 1926, No. 50, on the
occasion of the enrolment of his child in
any school, to furnish a Registrar's certificate or other satisfactory documentary
evidence of the date of the child's birth.
A statement unsupported by proper
documentary evidence would not, therefore, fulfil this requirement.
The normal cost of a Registrar's certificate is 3s 7d, but for the purposes of
elementary education certificates can be
obtained at the reduced fee of 6d.
The Ministry has no information as to
whether or not Registrars, who are Clerks
of Unions, issue birth certificates during
their office hours.
PAYMENT OF TEACHERS'
SUBSTITUTES.
6. Mr. BEATTIE-To ask the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether it is a fact that when
a teacher of a Public Elementary School,
known as a "Model School," is on sick
leave, a substitute is paid from the rates
for a period not exceeding six months;
whether when a teacher of any other
Public Elementary School is on sick leave
his or her substitute has to be paid by
the teacher concerned, and can he state
how this difference of the award of public
funds is justified?
Mr. ROBB: Under the Commissioners
of National Education a teacher absent
owing to illness was responsible for the
salary of his substitute, but the Commissioners as Managers paid the salaries of
substitutes for sick teachers in Model
Schools for a limited period-as a rule
not over three months.
When the Model Schools were transferred to Education Authorities all
teachers serving at the date of transfer,
and who had been at least six months in
the school, were entitled to a continuance
of this right, but teachers appointed since
are not so entitled.

a resolution was adopted by the North
Antrim Regional Education Committee
which agrees with the tenor of the question, but was, of course, restricted to
women teachers in provided and transferred schools within their area.
In deciding to terminate the engagements of existing women teachers on
marriage, and in requiring new women
teachers on first appointment to have a
clause to this effect inserted in their
agreements, the Committee was exercising
a discretion given to it by existing legislation and regulations.
I am unable to state whether the late
Commissioners of National Education had
any settled practice of exempting existing
teachers from new conditions of service.
Inasmuch as it was open to the former
managers to give a three months' notice
of dismissal to women teachers on marriage, the Regional Committee in deciding
to adopt this policy is not exceeding its
lawful powers, and the Ministry has not,
therefore, taken any steps to intervene.

IMPROVEMENT OF FARM

18. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state why
it is that the Government of Northern
Ireland have not yet put into operation
the Housing Rural Workers Act, 1926, as
already in operation in Great Britain, and
whether he is aware that grants are payable in Great Britain for improvements to
farm houses, and why similar grants are
denied to the rural dwellers in Northern
Ireland?
Mr. POLLOCK: I have arranged with
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Home Affairs, to reply to this question.
The hon. Member appears to be under
a misapprehension regarding the scope of
the British Housing (Rural Workers) Act,
1926, This Act provides for grants by
local authorities, towards which the Exchequer contributes, in aid of the reconstruction of the homes of agricultural
workers, not of farmers. In Northern
Ireland the needs of agricultural workers
are amply catered for by the Housing
Acts, and the Labourers' Cottages Acts,
and, accordingly, no reason is seen for
introducing legislation comparable to the
British Act of 1926.
I am not aware that any grants are
payable in Great Britain for improvements to farm houses, and, accordingly, I
cannot agree that anything is being denied
to the farming community here which
would be available to them in Great
Britain.
I may add that Government loans are
available to farmers in Northern Ireland,
under the Landed Property Improvement
Acts, for the improvement of their
dwelling houses and farm offices, and
farmers in Northern Ireland are availing
themselves of these facilities.

reasonably low, and I do not see that

HOLYWOOD AND BELFAST RAIL-
WAY BUS SERVICE.
21. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can statę if he
has heard or received any complaints regarding the railway bus service in operation between Holywood and Belfast?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No formal
complaints have been addressed to the
Ministry, but the Ministry was aware
that complaints were being made, and,
therefore, caused investigations to be
carried out.
As recently as the 17th October last,
a careful and comprehensive test of the
service was made by persons unknown to
the Company or its officials, and as a result of these investigations, I am satisfied that the Railway Company was maintaining a service adequate to meet the
traffic requirements. A ten-minute service was kept up throughout the day from
7 a.m. till 11 p.m., and this time-table
was strictly adhered to. In addition,
extra vehicles were put on at peak hours.
The scheduled time-table provides for
98 runs each way per day, and, adding
the additional runs at peak hours, there
are approximately 110 runs each way per
day.
In February last, there were four
operators on the road, and they made.
approximately 112 runs per day, but it
must be borne in mind that a considerable
proportion of these runs were made by
the competing operators at the slack
periods when there was no traffic to justify them, and when they were not required for the public convenience.
many cases, the runs took place at the
same times.

The public is, therefore, receiving a

company than they received before the
other services were taken over.

A.O.H. HALL AT ANNAHUGH,
CO. ARMAGH.
22. Mr. CONNELLAN asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether it is a fact
that the Ancient Order of Hibernians'
Hall, at Annahugh, Co. Armagh, has been
burned down twice within a comparatively
short space of time; whether he has received reports on the occurrences from the
police in the district; whether he is prepared to make public the nature of such
reports; and whether it is intended to
bring the perpetrators to justice?
Written Answers
Bills Presented.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a factas implied in the hon. Member's Question
-that the Ancient Order of Hibernians'
Hall at Annahugh, Co. Armagh, has been
burned or otherwise injured during the
course of the present year.
The hall in question was almost completely destroyed by fire on the 18th
January last a few days before the date
of its opening. Although there was at
the time no evidence of any hostility to
the building of the hall in the district,
there was reason to believe that the fre
was not accidental, and in fact on the 15th
April at the Armagh Quarter Sessions
a sum of £170 with three guineas expenses was awarded to the representatives
of the Ancient Order of Hibernians.
On the 13th October last, between
3 a.m. and 5 a.m., the hall, which was in
process of rebuilding, was destroyed by
explosives which had been placed at the
base of the walls.
Active police inquiries are being instituted, but up to the present no evidence
has been secured which would enable any
person to be made amenable.
In this connection I should say that
since the destruction of the hall in
January last, the police authorities-with
the means at their disposal-took special
precautions to prevent a recurrence of the
incident.
Two claims for compensation have been.
lodged in connection with this recent outrage and will, it is understood, be heard
in January next.
I have been kept closely informed by
the police authorities regarding the incident, and as to the steps which are being
taken, but the hon. Member must realise
that it would be improper and contrary to
established precedent to make public these
reports, particularly having regard to the
inquiries which are being pursued by the
police, and the possibility of the offenders
being brought to justice, and to the fact
that the question will, as already stated,
form the subject of legal proceedings during the course of the next couple of
months. In conclusion I can assure the
hon. Member that every possible step is
being taken to have the matter cleared up,
and if any evidence is forthcoming to connect any person or persons with these outrages my right hon. Friend, the Attorney-
General, will take the appropriate steps
to bring the offenders to justice.
BLIND PERSONS ACT.
23. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Labour whether it is the intention of the
Government to introduce legislation at an
early date extending the operations of the
Blind Persons Act, and thereby bring in
many cases of necessitous blind which do
not come under the present Act?
It does not
Sir DAWSON BATES:
appear that any general legislation of the
nature suggested by my hon. Friend is
required at present, or, indeed, until full
advantage has been taken by the local
authorities to avail themselves of their
powers under the existing Act.
Some of the local authorities, including
the Belfast Corporation, have had for
some time past schemes in operation, but
the fact that the remaining local authorities have not availed themselves of their
powers to formulate Blind Persons
Schemes is not due to any defect in the
Act, but rather to the difficulties experienced by them in estimating what provision will be necessary or desirable in
their respective counties.
I am glad now, however, to be able to
say that following the recent publication
of the Census, giving up-to-date statistics
as to the blind population in each county,
a decided and forward move has been and
is being taken by the county councils in
Northern Ireland as a whole.
I need hardly remind the hon. Member
that these steps, which have my utmost
sympathy, are being worked out in conjunction with my Ministry.
