A.O.H. HALL, ANNAHUGH,
COUNTY ARMAGH.
Mr. CONNELLAN: Hon. Members will
remember seeing on the Order Paper today Question No. 23, addressed to the
Minister of Home Affairs, regarding the
burning of a hall. The Question was not
reached, and I agreed with the Minister
to raise the matter on the Adjournment,
and he gave me his written reply to the
Question. The Question was:---
To ask the Minister of Home Affairs
whether it is a fact that the Ancient
Order of Hibernians' Hall, at Annahugh, Co. Armagh, has been burned
down twice within a comparatively short
space of time; whether he has received
reports on the occurrences from the
police in the district; whether he is prepared to make public the nature of such
reports; and whether it is intended to
bring the perpetrators to justice.
The Minister's reply was:-
It is a fact as implied in the hon.
Member's question-that the Ancient
Order of Hibernians' Hall at Annahugh, Co. Armagh, has been burned
or otherwise injured during the course
of the present year.
The hall in question was almost completely destroyed by fire on the 18th
January last a few days before the
date of its opening. Although there
was at the time no evidence of any hostility to the building of the hall in the
district, there was reason to believe that
the fire was not accidental, and in fact
on the 15th April at the Armagh
Quarter Sessions a sum of £170 with
three guineas expenses was awarded to
the representatives of the Ancient Order
of Hibernians.
On the 13th October last, between
3 a.m. and 5 a.m. the hall, which was
in process of rebuilding, was destroyed
by explosives which had been placed at
the base of the walls.
Active police inquiries are being
instituted, but up to the present no evidence has been secured which would
enable any person to be made amenable.
In this connection I should say that
since the destruction of the hall in
January last the police authoritieswith the means at their disposal-took
special precautions to prevent a recurrence of the incident.
Two claims for compensation have
been lodged in connection with this
recent outrage and will, it is understood,
be heard in January next.
I have been kept closely informed by
the police authorities regarding the incident, and as to the steps which are
being taken, but the hon. Member must
realise that it would be improper and
contrary to established precedent to
make public these reports, particularly having regard to the enquiries
which are being pursued by the
police, and the possibility of the
offenders being brought to justice.
and to the fact that the question
will, as already stated, form the subject
of legal proceedings during the course
of the next couple of months. In conclusion I can assure the hon. Member
that every possible step is being taken
to have the matter cleared up, and if
any evidence is forthcoming to connect
any person or persons with these outrages my right hon. Friend, the
Attorney-General will take the appropriate steps to bring the offenders to
justice.
The
If we are to form any opinion at all as
to the reply of the right hon. Gentleman
it is that it discloses an appalling amount
of ignorance and an appalling amount
of impotence on the part of the Government in regard to these occurrences.
area of the Six Counties is not so vast that
it might constitute a geographical difficulty in dealing with these outrages.
Every quarter of every town and every
quarter of every townland and parish is
known to the authorities. Practically
every man, woman and child occupying
this strip of territory is known. Every
house, and every keyhole, and every door,
I may say, is known, and why this thing
should be enshrouded in mystery is a mental problem not very easily elucidated.
Here is a society, peacefully pursuing
its career as peacefully as does the Protestant Orange Insurance Society, and
without giving any cause for antipathy
at all its members are made the victims
of two very serious outrages within a comparatively short space of a year. What
is most surprising is that of the many who
have participated in this last outragescores of men carrying rifles through the

suspicion. In a case of murder we know

very well what would have happened.
The Government boast that we have law
and order firmly established throughout
our area, that we have here a force capable of detecting even the most minor
crime, and that force as we know is maintained at great expense, and it is equipped
with instruments which are by no means
antiquated. In a case of murder we
should have had an arrest before now.
We would have known practically everything about the murder from the motive
to the method, but here in this particular
case, where scores of men have been concerned, we know practically nothing up to
the present.
Now, I think that we can safely conclude that nobody from Germany was there.
They were too busy pushing in oats. Nobody from England or Scotland committed this outrage.
The area of investigation is very, very narrow, and I think
it would be quite easy for the Government, and for the authorities, to have this
thing sufficiently and satisfactorily investigated before now. Why it has not been
done is a matter indeed that is engaging
very considerable attention throughout
the Six Counties and occasioning a great
deal of comment. If such a comparatively simple case of this kind could not
be satisfactorily investigated, up to the
present, where so many people have been
involved, and where the field of investigation is so greatly narrowed down and
practically all unnecessary conjectures
are eliminated, I think it speaks very
badly for the Government, and, indeed,
justifies the people of that district, and
of any other district where it occurs, in
arriving at a conclusion of their own as
to how this hall was made the victim of
these two outrages-first in the beginning
of the year it was burned down, and just
a month ago it was blown up.

not a scrap of evidence forthcoming that
these men marched in military formation,
and if he has any evidence of the truth of
his statement I hope he will justify it by
giving it to myself or to the Attorney-
General.
Mr. HEALY: The people of the
locality say they marched in military
formation.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Let them come
forward.
Mr. HEALY: They would share the
same fate as the hall if they came forward.
Sir DAWSON BATES indicated
dissent.
Mr. HEALY: You know that well,
though you jeer at it. You offered to
protect the owners of this hall, did you
not? The result was that, five minutes
after your posse of police passed, the hall
was blown to the skies. Do you think
anybody in the locality is foolish enough,
to take your assurance that if they come
forward to give evidence you are in a
better position to protect them than you
were to protect a public building? I
believe you are not honest about this
matter You are not a bit convinced that
what you say to-day reflects the facts of
the case, because if you went before a
judge and jury of impartial people they
would not accept for one moment your
conclusions on the facts that have been
made clear. There is another fact in
connection with this case that stands out
very distinctly. A certain woman was
asked to leave her home.
She was
a
Burning of A.O.H. Hall 1116
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Healy]
friend of the invaders of the district.
She was a friend of the culprits, and they
came and coolly asked her to leave her
home in order that no injury might come
to her. They did not ask any Nationalists to vacate their homes.
Mr. POLLOCK: That is too vague.
Mr. HEALY: It is not a bit vague.
The whole circumstances one by one
point to one definite conclusion, namely,
that the people who perpetrated this
action were certain of their ground. They
were certain that the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates), and his Department were not going to use superhuman
efforts to discover them. They were
pretty certain, too, that the police force
of the district would think twice before
they incriminated another police force
of the district. Most of us who live in
the Six Counties know that it is not the
Royal Ulster Constabulary who have the
power in the various districts, but that it
is your friends, the political police, the
"B" men, who have the power.
Now, when peace has been restored to
the Six Counties for many years, it is a
disgraceful thing to think that one body
of the populace can go round the country
with arms, and, if they be so disposed,
can repeat the performance of Annahugh
anywhere in any of the Six Counties, and
that they may do it with impunity, knowing, as they do know, that you are not
going to raise a single finger to see that
the administration of justice is carried
out impartially in this area.
What other body of people than the
armed police force were in a position to
place gelignite underneath the walls of
this building? Where did they find this
explosive? That is also granted under
licence. The number of people who can
put their hands on an explosive of that
kind in this district is very small, and
they are known to the authorities. Have
the authorities tested the quantity of this
explosive they had on a particular day,
and have they had a check recently? I
suggest that there you would have a trail
which, if pursued, would lead you to the
discovery of the perpetrators of this
rascally crime.
Mr. DAVISON: I deprecate the tone
of this debate and the attempt that has
been made to suggest that there is bad
feeling in County Armagh between the
members of different religious or different
political creeds. On the contrary, there
is the best of feeling in the county and it
is in a perfectly quiet state. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). There is no sympathy
in any part of the county with outrages
of this kind by whoever they be committed. I am not at all sure who committed this outrage, and the impression
left on my mind is that there may be
another explanation for it than that suggested from the other side of the House.
We have known in years past of many
Hibernian halls being burned. There was
a very good idea of who burned them,
and it certainly was not the loyal or
official part of the populace that did it.
In those cases the facts were proved in
the criminal injury claims put before the
courts. And there were certain sections
of this community that had large stores
of explosives and large quantities of arms,
and they certainly were not the official
part of the community, nor had they
friendly feelings towards the official
Government.
Mr. DEVLIN: Might I ask the hon.
and learned Member to answer me this?
How was it that two or three Protestant
families living in the locality were asked
to leave?
Mr. DAVISON: I do not know that
they were asked to leave. I have no
information about that, and the evidence
before the Minister of Home Affairs does
not suggest that he had any evidence of
that kind.
Mr. DEVLIN: I will give it to you.
Mr. DAVISON: It is quite easy to
make statements of this kind on the floor
of this House where they cannot be tested
in any way.
Hon. Members are often
too ready to receive ex-parte statements
of this kind, and to put them before the
House as being absolutely true. If it
suits their own political view they lend
credence to those statements. It is a
pity that this debate should have been
raised and such suggestions made on such
slender foundations.
Mr. DEVLIN: We should let our halls
be burned down and say nothing.
Mr. DAVISON: One hon. Member on
the opposite side of the House, referring

Oral Answers to Questions.
RELIEF FOR UNEMPLOYED
SINGLE MEN.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
provision made or being made for the
relief of single men who are now destitute through unemployment.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Every possible
effort has been and is being made by the
Government in conjunction with the local
authorities to promote Unemployment
Relief Works with the object of affording
employment for unemployed persons.
Up to the present, schemes have been
or are being carried out by local authorities with the encouragement and support
of my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Labour, involving expenditure amounting to approximately £6,800,000, of
which approximately £1,900,000 will be
provided by the Minister of Labour.
In addition, I have encouraged road
authorities to embark on necessary and
comprehensive road schemes in respect of
which I have accorded generous financial
assistance out of the Road Fund.
Several large schemes are now pending
in furtherance of that policy which will
rank for substantial contributions either
from the Road Fund or the Unemployment Relief Fund.
I would also remind my hon. Friend
that there is at present in operation in the
City of Belfast a special scheme operated
through the co-operation of the Belfast
Board of Guardians and the Belfast Corporation, with the approval of the
Ministry of Home Affairs, under which
special relief works are being made available for heads of families who, in the
normal course, would be applicants to the
Board of Guardians for outdoor relief.
The Board of Guardians, who are the
responsible authority in this matter have
for years past been giving the matter
very careful consideration, and in the
light of their experience, and having regard to their resources and to their responsibilities to the ratepayers, they have
limited this special scheme to heads of
families, although I think it only right
to say that they interpret this definition
in a generous way.
I should also state that single men are
not ineligible for ordinary unemployment
relief works, and in cases of actual
destitution are eligible for ordinary Institutional relief from the Boards of
Guardians.
Mr. NIXON : Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that single men and
men who have no dependants are not
eligible under the Guardians' relief
scheme?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have indicated that in my answer.
Mr. NIXON: It is not a point of
catching the right hon. Gentleman, or
being clever, or anything like that. I
can assure the Minister there are men
who are not eligible under the scheme.

WORK FOR UNEMPLOYED,
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state what
efforts he has made to find work for the
unemployed; and whether he is aware.
that great distress prevails amongst
people whom his Department has turned
down for not "genuinely seeking work."
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I do not consider that the
question procedure affords a satisfactory
method of dealing with these matters.
Opportunities will arise for the hon.
Member to raise the whole question of the
steps taken by the Government to deal
with the relief of unemployment and also
of the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Acts, and I shall be glad
then to deal with the matters at length.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the Minister of Labour if he is prepared
to make a statement to this House telling
what efforts he has made to find work for
the unemployed since last we met. Is he
prepared to give this House a day in which
he can make that statement on which
there can be a debate?
Mr. ANDREWS: I understand the
hon. Member for the Central Division of
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) proposes to put down
a Motion raising the whole question of unemployment and administration. The
House will agree that that Motion will
present a favourable opportunity for dealing with the matter. I hope then to be
able to deal with the matter in such a way
as will give satisfaction to hon. Members.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister aware
that the Conservative party in England
demanded from the Minister of Labour a
statement such as this without a Motion
coming from the Opposition? Is he going
to deny this House a statement of his
efforts to find work for the unemployed
without a motion?
Mr. ANDREWS: I shall welcome an
opportunity for such a statement. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
Mr. DEVLIN: Is the right hon.
Gentleman not aware that the opening
of the Session at the earliest possible
moment is the time for such a statement,
and that it is his duty to make a statement and not to wait until a provocative
Motion is put upon the Paper?
Mr. ANDREWS: I do not look upon
any Motion which the hon. Member puts
upon the Paper as provocative.

gratified to be able to add that almost all

REMUNERATION OF CHAIRMEN

7. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of

Mr. ANDREWS: Chairmen of Courts

RICHHILL TRAINING
ESTABLISHMENT.
8. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is satisfied that the
money spent on Richhill Emigration
Training Establishment is wisely spent in
view of the large number of boys trained
there who have returned.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am satisfied as to
the wisdom of the expenditure on the
Richhill Training Centre. If the Government had not established this Centre, an
opportunity would have been denied to
unemployed young men in Northern Ireland which their fellow-countrymen in the
rest of the United Kingdom possessed.
I do not regard the number of trainees
who have returned as large when compared with the number who migrated and
are making good.

MARRIAGE OF P.E. SCHOOL
TEACHERS.
11. Mr. NIXON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Education whether he can state the policy of
his Department in regard to the proposal of some education authorities to call
for the resignation of female public elementary school teachers who get married,
or to make it a condition of appointment
that on the marriage of such teachers
they should resign their position as
teachers.
Mr. ROBB: The propriety of employing married women as teachers in schools
is a question upon which expert opinion
is divided. The late Commissioners of
National Education always looked upon
the employment of married women as a
matter for the discretion of the managers
of schools, and the Ministry has followed
this course. The discretion formerly
exercised by managers is now, in the
case of provided and transferred schools,
vested in the education authorities, and
the Ministry sees no reason to change
its practice.
Mr. NIXON: Is the hon. and learned
Gentleman aware that the late Minister
of Education (Lord Londonderry) was
opposed to the principle of putting a
penalty on women teachers getting
married?
Mr. ROBB: No, I am not aware of
that.
Mr. NIXON: I heard him say it in
this House.

has

SERVICE.

that the service referred to by the hon.
Member has proved to be of considerable
convenience to the inhabitants of the
Bellaghy district. The service arose from
the necessity of diverting the Magherafelt-
Belfast service from the direct road while

the service would normally revert to its
original route on completion of the reconstruction of the road, especially in view.
of the fact that portion of the road over
which it now runs is not suitable to carry
a permanent bus service.
I am anxious, however, that the inhabitants of the district should not be deprived

experience.

Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir.

ACTION OF DUNGANNON URBAN
COUNCIL.
15. Mr. STEWART asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he has received
the minutes of the Dungannon Urban
Council of 4th November, 1929; whether
these minutes record a resolution as being
carried by a majority giving away portion.
of a public thoroughfare in the town of
Dungannon to Messrs. Stevenson & Son,
of Dungannon; whether there is any legal
authority for this action; and, if not, what
action the Minister proposes to take in
the matter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Ministry
has received the minutes of the Dungannon Urban District Council of the 4th
November last, containing a resolution
authorising Messrs. Stevenson & Son to
make an entry into their works from the
street.
The making of this entry entails the
excavation of portion of a small area of
the roadway. I understand that there is
some doubt as to whether this ground is
portion of the public highway or not.
An urban district council is not authorized to alienate any part of a public
highway, but I am not in a position to
say whether the Council have done so in
this case or not.
Difficult legal questions would have to
be determined before this point could be
decided, but, if the Council have overstepped the law in this case, the only

Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill has
for its object the continuance of the subsidy which would otherwise expire in
March of next year, and also introduces
certain modifications of the Act to prevent
the benefits of the Act being applied in
certain directions contrary to the intenons of the Acts.
The present Bill continues in its main
features the policy which was instituted
the Government in 1923, and has been
continued for the past seven years by
means of annual Acts of Parliament.
Each year when the time came for determining the policy to be adopted in regard
to Housing for the ensuing year, the
Government examined the problem in all
its aspects in the light of the experience
which they had gained with a view to
seeing how best these Acts could be improved in order to make the Housing
Policy of the Government even
effective than it had been in the past. I
say this, as I would like hon. Members to
appreciate that the Government would
more
ot hesitate for one moment to introduce
any drastic modification if they felt that
by doing so the Housing shortage would
be more effectively met.
Repeated examination of the problem,
however, has convinced the Government
that they are proceeding along the right
lines, and upon lines which are best calculated to meet the housing shortage in the
shortest possible time. Houses are not
created by the wave of a hand, but to
meet the situation we must have both
time and money.
I think the statistics which I have repeatedly given the House, and the
statistics which I propose to give to-day
go to show that the policy of the Government has thoroughly justified itself.
Without going into much detail in regard
to the past, it may be of assistance to the
House if I were shortly to refer to the main
Acts which have been passed by this
Government since 1923, when the present
policy was first put before the House.
First of all, the Act of 1923 provided
for a subsidy for houses with a maximum
of 950 superficial feet, and, under the Act
1925, the subsidy was increased by a
further sum of £20, provided the house
built and completed within three
years. That was with the object of expediting the building of these houses.
was
Under the Act of 1927 the maximum
size of the house to which subsidies would
apply was reduced to 650 superficial feet,
it the amount of the subsidy was inreased to a sum of £100, and that policy
was re-enacted in the Act passed last
year. The immediate result of the
passing of this Measure was an enormous
increase in the number of houses erected.
Without wearying the House, I would
like to refer to the figures. The first year
I will take will be the year ended March
31st, 1927. I take that because it is the
first completed year under the old system
where the larger type of house qualified
for subsidy. I find that 1,679 houses were
Housing Bill-

approved. Therefore, comparing this
year, which I have referred to, with the
year ended 31st March, 1929, which is the
first completed year under which the reduced size of house qualified, I find that
the number of houses approved of was no
less a figure than 5,596, as against the
figure 1,679 in the year 1927.
It is interesting to note that as regards
private owners 197 houses were approved
of the size under 650 superficial feet, and
1,232 over 650 superficial feet in 1927—a
fact that I propose to deal with afterwards.
I would suggest to this House, and I
think it shows more clearly than I can
express, that if we were to go back to the
old condition of affairs, and give subsidies
for the "villa" type of house, the private
builders would concentrate on that type of
house, leaving the smaller type of house
alone. Everybody knows the builder likes
to build houses he can sell.
Striking as these figures are, I think
those for the first six months of the current year to the 30th September last are
even more interesting. I find the number
of houses approved for these six months to
be 3,046. At the same rate of progression, we will find, I hope, at the end of
the year we shall exceed the figure I have
referred to for 31st March, 1929.
The House will, therefore, see that, so
far from the rate of building showing a
tendency to decline, there is strong
evidence that it is even yet being
accelerated. As Belfast is mainly an industrial city, I think the figures for the
year ended 31st March, 1929, and for the
first six months of the coming year, might
prove interesting, because they show the
number of houses approved to be no less
than 2,759, and for the last six months
1,505-more than half. There, again, it
shows that the number of houses built in
the year ended 31st March, 1929, will be
exceeded.
In the City of Belfast there are 88,687
dwelling houses. Of these there are no
less than 54,700 odd rated at £8 or under.
These are the houses occupied by the poorer
class of working man. There are only
150 vacant houses of this type. On the
other hand, of the houses over £8 valuation, numbering 33,900, there are 670
vacant at the present time. This indicates
that the demand is more acute for the
smaller house. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
I think, therefore, that while we have
every reason to congratulate ourselves on
the progress we have made, we cannot yet
claim that we are in the position to relax
our efforts.
One of the most satisfactory features is
that there is a greater tendency on the part
of private builders to erect houses for the
purpose of letting, and there is also a far
more satisfactory tendency than this, for
there is a tendency for the rents to come
down. But, while I say this, so long as
the rents remain even at their present
level, there is a clear indication that the
supply of houses does not equal the demand, and that more houses are required.
I am sorry to say that there is still a
large number of families living in rooms,
under most unhealthy and unsanitary conditions, and paying rents which they cannot afford.
I have taken some figures from the
Census returns, which go to show that in
the City of Belfast there are 2,682
families living in one room.

Hon. Members are aware that, under

by the local authorities. We realise, of

of course, I do not lose sight of the fact

I have had an opportunity of examining the results of the efforts which have

without hesitation that we are in no way

I know we have been reproached that

it is not an ideal house and not suitable
for big families, but I have found that

smaller
size, and have been erected in order to

the maximum size of the house which will

The House is aware that our object in
limiting the grant of the subsidy to the
smaller type of house was to encourage the

within the means of the poorer class of
workers. We found that when, as I have
already shown by the figures, we fixed the

on the part of private builders was to erect
houses of this type, and the result was a
house was produced far beyond the means
f the ordinary working man. It may

Since this Bill was circulated, I have
received representations from local
authorities, as well as from Members of
this House, pressing upon the Government that there should be a slight increase in the area, SO that a third
bedroom of a more commodious size than
at present could be provided. I have had
this question again examined with care by
my technical advisers, and whilst I am
not entirely free from doubt on the
subject, I am advised that an extra fifty
feet could be allowed without great risk
of appreciable increases in the cost of the
houses, or the rent at which they could be
let. Therefore the Government have
decided to submit to the House that the
maximum limit for building should be increased from 650 to 700 square feet, and,
accordingly, I propose to put down an
amendment to this effect in Committee.
At the same time, I must utter this
warning; that should we find as a matter
of experience that the result of this increase is that houses are built which are
beyond the means of the working classes,
we will not hesitate to come again to the
House and ask for the restoration of the
lower limit.

The Government have had practical
experience of the working of these Acts.
They find that once the subsidy is

They find a clamorous demand for houses
of this type.
Only the other day a
builder erected thirty-nine of these small
houses, and there were no less than 700
applications for them. I, therefore, do
suggest to this House that these figures
and the Census returns which I have

else, that the crying need of the hour is
for houses of the type I have mentioned.
I quite sympathise with those local
authorities who desire to have larger

right hon. Gentleman if he can say what

Sir DAWSON BATES: When the
Housing Bill was before the House last
year, it was stated that the subsidy house
of 650 feet contained a kitchen sittingroom, kitchenette, bathroom, and three
bedrooms. It was complained at that
time that these three bedrooms were too
small, and the Member for North Belfast
said one was really only a boxroom. I
suggest that the addition of 50 feet will
provide three good bedrooms.
Clauses 2 and 3 are rather different
from anything which has hitherto been
included in the Housing Acts, and I
must confess I have considerable regret
that it should have been necessary to include these two Clauses in the Bill, but
I am coerced by circumstances which have
arisen to do so. The Government have
of the
felt from the very inception
Housing Acts that, in building houses,
the builders should not be hampered by
any avoidable restrictions, and that, so
long as houses of the type which the
Government and this House desired to
see erected were provided, as few restrictions as possible should be placed upon
those providing them, but when we find
builders of houses using their ingenuity
to design houses which are technically
within the provisions of the Act, but
which are entirely outside the spirit of it,
we feel that it is incumbent upon us to
take such powers as will enable us to
prevent abuse. There has always been a
tendency on the part of some individuals
to design houses which, although technically complying with the requirements of
the Act, could be enlarged subsequently.
Hitherto this tendency was of small
proportions, and my Ministry was able to
keep it in check by the exercise of the very
limited powers which it at present possesses
in this respect. During the past year, however, abuses which the Ministry was
powerless to check effectively have become
evident. Houses were designed in such a
way as to comply with the requirements
of the Act and to be eligible for subsidy,
which the Ministry had no power to refuse, but at the same time the design was
such that the house could be radically
altered and enlarged at small expense
when the subsidy had been paid. It then
became a house of a type which Parliament did not intend to subsidise, and
which was not in any way within the spirit
of the Act. There have been cases, and
indeed an appreciable number of
where semi-detached houses have been
designed so as to be convertible into one
house with the minimum of expense.

In view of these facts I submit to the
House that it is essential that extended
powers should be given to the Ministry
in order that the intentions of Parliament should not be defeated. Accordingly, we propose that where the Ministry is satisfied that a house is designed
with a view to being, or is intended upon
completion to be enlarged or altered in
such a manner that it will not then conform to the requirements of the Act as
to type and dimensions, or where houses
are designed to be amalgamated so as to
form a single house, the Ministry may refuse to pay the building grant in respect
of the house, or may suspend the payment until such time as the requirements
of the Ministry have been complied with.
a
Further, if the building grant has been
paid and the house is enlarged or amalgamated with another house within
period of five years from the date of payment the grant may be recovered, and
further, the same power of recovery is
given to a local authority where they
have also paid grants. This Clause will
not injure in any way the builder who
is honestly complying with the provisions
of the Housing Acts and building houses
which it was the object of those Acts to
render eligible for subsidy, but it will
effectively put an end to the activities of
the individuals who under colour of complying with the requirements of the Act,
set out to obtain subsidies for houses
which it was never the intention of Parliament to assist. This Clause will become operative-
Mr. BEATTIE: Retrospectively.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. It will
become operative in respect of houses
where the construction of a house is commenced or a building grant is paid or
becomes payable after the date of the
introduction of this Bill to the House.
Perhaps I might give a word of explanation as to the object of Sub-Clause
(4) of this Clause. As the House is, no
doubt, aware, under the Public Health
Acts in urban areas the local authority
may require plans of any building or
alteration of buildings in their area to be
submitted to them before the work is
undertaken. There are certain grounds
on which they can refuse assent to such
plans, but they could not refuse their assent to the plan on the ground that the
proposed alteration was in contravention
of the Housing Acts. It would be invidious that in such circumstances the
local authority should be compelled to
give assent to the modifications of a subsidy
house in its capacity as a public health
authority and later be entitled to sue for
the recovery of the subsidy paid because
of such alteration. We, therefore, propose to provide that the local authority
shall have power to refuse to approve of
the plans for such alteration on the ground
that the house will, by reason of carrying
out the alteration, cease to conform to the
requirements as to type and dimensions in
force for the purpose of building grant.
sea-
The subsidy has been taken advantage
of for the purpose of building
side houses which are intended merely for
occupation for two or three months in the
summer, either by the person building the
house or by persons to whom he lets the
house at a large monthly rent. I do not
think that the Government or Parliament
could hold that the taxpayers' money
should be used for the purpose of providing
such houses, which are, to a large extent,
a luxury, and which do not appreciably
help to meet the housing shortage. We
are not justified in continuing subsidies to
this class of house. At the same time, in
any area in which a seaside resort is included there may be houses genuinely required for full-time occupation, and such
houses should not be shut out from the
benefit of the subsidy. In Clause 3 it is
proposed to enable the Ministry to schedule
certain areas, and no house erected in
those areas will be eligible for subsidy until
the Ministry is satisfied that it is necessary
having regard to the needs of the district,
and is required and intended for continuous as distinct from casual occupation.
That is a provision which I think will
commend itself at once to the House.
Clauses 4 and 5, although they are
more or less self-explanatory, are the only
remaining ones to which I need refer.
There is some difference of legal opinion
as to whether the expression "house" as
used in the Housing Acts would include
a self-contained flat. There is no demand,
and never has been any demand, for flats
for the working classes in Northern Ire-
Housing Bill—
Second Reading.
12 NOVEMBER 1929
In two cases only have plans for selfcontained flats been submitted, and both
cases were open to grave suspicion that the
buildings were not intended for ultimate
use as flats but for conversion into a single
dwelling far outside the scope of the
Housing Acts. We have, therefore,
thought it desirable to take this opportunity of putting the matter beyond doubt.
and declaring that flats are not eligible
for subsidy under the Housing Acts.
Clause 5 is designed to remove what we
cannot but regard as an anomaly. Under the law as it stands members of any
local authority are precluded from taking
advantage of any of the housing facilities
which are offered by local authorities
either under these Housing Acts or under
the Small Dwellings Acts. In urban districts the officers of local authorities are
in the same position.
These housing
facilities are open to every Member of
the public who desires to take advantage
of them. They are surrounded by safeguards. The Ministry approves of every
advance under the Small Dwellings Acts,
and inspects all houses for which application is made for the subsidy. In these
circumstances there seems to be no substantial reason why members and officials
of local authorities should be precluded
from taking advantage of the facilities
which are offered to their fellow-citizens,
and, therefore, it is proposed in this
Clause to remove the disqualifications to
which I have referred.
I think this is all I need say about the
Measure, and I commend it to the House.
I beg to move.

our housing conditions.
It was very refreshing to hear an
honoured Member of the Belfast Corporation dilate upon good houses. I must
confess that the first thing that struck
me while the hon. Member for Falls (Mr.
Byrne) was speaking was the old adage
"Physician heal thyself." I thought
that before he attempted to tell the
Government how to build good houses it

something along that line themselves. A
great deal of the want of houses in Northern Ireland, and a great deal of the
reason why housing operations were not
so popular in Northern Ireland as they
might have been was due to the housing
scandal that existed in the Belfast Corporation. So, when the hon. Member
speaks of the country districts and their

the rural districts, and that is that up to

scandal.

the area of these subsidy houses. But I
am rather surprised that they have not

from the city but from the rural districts,
for houses of 950 square feet. At the

the Government in going along the lines
they have been pursuing up to the present have been the poor man's friend.
We know that the claims that should receive first attention are those that come
from the people who cannot provide
houses for themselves, and so the Government by confining the subsidy to the
smaller houses have done something to
relieve the housing shortage, and to provide houses that can be let at a rent
which the working men can afford to pay.
I am quite prepared to admit that
there is a good deal to be said in favour
of the attitude of the right hon. Gentleman that there is no use in building
houses that cannot be let at a rent that
the workingmen can afford to pay, but
I think it is possible, particularly if the
Government subsidy is augmented by a
subsidy from the rural or urban district
council, to build comfortable houses for
workingmen, houses that can be let at an
economic rent. If the Government want
to improve housing all over, I do not see
why they should not give an opportunity
to those who wish to build bigger houses.
There is a great demand in the rural districts, particularly at the moment, for
larger houses, and I think it is only fair
that I should voice the opinions of my
constituents by asking the Government
not to stop the subsidy at houses of 700
superficial feet, but to give it in respect
of houses up to 900 superficial feet.

I deprecate very much the uncertainty

that kind should be avoided. If I may

Minister of Great Britain was settled in

1831, almost a hundred years ago, and it

the Foreign Secretary was fixed in the same
year, and that of the Postmaster-General
in 1789, and it remains unchanged, while
the remuneration of the Minister of Agriculture was fixed in 1859. I mention

undesirable that there should be any fluctuations, if I may use that word, or any

years of Parliament. I said then, and I

the desire at least as far as the Member
for the Central Division is concerned-is
to get rid of Ministers. He and I differ.
I do not want to get rid of Ministers. I
want to see this Parliament and the
affairs of this Province run more economically than they are being run.
There is this point I think ought to be
emphasised. The campaign I carried on
in 1921 and afterwards has borne fruit,
because if Members will look at the
annual financial statement they will see
that the Minister of Finance has been
making a really honest attempt to cut down
expenditure. I say again that the initial
mistake was made when we started on too
big a scale. Now, hon. Members come
along not really for the purpose of trying
to get economy, but for the purpose of
trying to secure a party, political move in
the game. If there was a real honest
attempt to cut down expenditure and to
run the affairs of this Province more
cheaply, so far as I am concerned I am still
in the position I was in in 1921. But this
is not an honest attempt for economy at
all. It is really an opportunity for cudgelling Ministers and trying to make them
as small and as ridiculous in the eyes of
the public as possible.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 13th November, 1929.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Bill Presented.
DRAINAGE BILL,
"to constitute the Ministry of Finance
as a Drainage Authority, for the purpose
of the drainage of Lough Neagh and the
River Bann, and to abolish certain drainage and navigation authorities; to empower the said Ministry to carry out and
maintain works for the said purpose; to
provide for the making of contributions
and the maintenance of certain drainage
works by the County Councils; to amend
the Drainage Act (Northern Ireland),
1925; and for other purposes connected
therewith," presented by Mr. Pollock,
supported by Sir Dawson Bates and Mr.
Barbour; to be read a Second time tomorrow, and to be printed. (Bill 19.)
Petroleum (Consolidation) Bill.
The following Report was made from the
Joint Committee on Consolidation Bills:
The Committee have examined the
Petroleum (Consolidation) Bill, and have
made the following Amendments:
Clause 20, page 22, lines 25 and 26,
leave out "at the Standards Departments
of the Board of Trade" and insert "as
provided by this sub-section."
Page 22, line 36, at end add: "A model
of the test apparatus described in Part I
of the Second Schedule to this Act and
(so long as the same is necessary for the
purposes of this sub-section) a model of
the test apparatus described in the First
Schedule to the Petroleum Act, 1878,
shall be deposited with the Ministry of
Commerce:
as
Provided that, until a model;
described in either such Schedule, is so
deposited, the apparatus for testing
petroleum which has been stamped after
comparison with a model corresponding to
such description and deposited at the
Standards Department of the Board of
Trade shall be deemed to have been
verified and stamped by the Ministry of
Commerce in accordance with the provisions of the sub-section."
Second Schedule, page 34, leave out
lines 6 and 7.
The Committee are satisfied that the
Bill, as amended, reproduces the existing
law without alteration, and recommend
the Bill to be proceeded with.
Ordered, That the Report do lie on the
Table.
Ordered, That the Bill be recommitted
to a Committee of the Whole House for
to-morrow.

the various inspectors. I want the Home

And getting £280.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): My hon. Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Home Affairs, will reply to the great
variety of matters that have been introduced into the debate, but at this moment
I am concerned to touch for a few
minutes only upon one particular phase
of the subject. That is the apparent
insistence on the part
of the local
authorities, by resolution, on
tension of the superficial area of subsidy houses to 950 feet, and the general
principle of the increase in the superficial
area of subsidy houses. That claim has
been voiced by some hon. Members in
this House, notably by the hon. Member
for South Tyrone (Mr. Elliott), and
others, regardless of some very important
features of the subject. I do not think
that people who talk in that way in regard
to the housing scheme realise all the
implications involved in such a large increase from 650 superficial feet to 950
superficial feet in an ordinary working
man's house, because it should be understood quite clearly. that from the very
start the incidence of the scheme was that
houses should be provided for working
men who could not afford to pay a large
rent relative to their wages. That is the
essence of the whole scheme.
Originally, and before we became an
autonomous State, an altruistic Government on the other side of the water talked
of providing homes fit for heroes to live in,
and they started out with grandicse ideas
of providing people with these houses on a
scale quite out of character with the necessities of the case as they ultimately developed. The old Local Government
Board, following that ambition, insisted
upon our Corporation building houses on
a certain scale. These houses, when they
were built, were found to be totally
unsuitable for any ordinary working
man, with the result that middleclass people, paying from £1 to 25s
a week, were introduced into these
houses that were presumably built for
working men. Of course, that brought the
whole subject into the open, with the result
that the Corporation, finding the position.
they were in, came to this Government,
and under the original bargain they had
with the Imperial Government claimed
from us, when we assumed authority, the
loss sustained on those houses.
I agreed, after some difficult and long
discussions, and we paid a sum of £225,000
in order that the local authority here might
be indemnified for their loss in building
houses of 950 superficial feet. The scheme
was continued, however, with a subsidy of
£80, and the maximum of 950 ft. was admitted for some time until finally the Corporation-and I am now dealing with the
Belfast Corporation, because from the experience of our local Corporation you
can make your deductions-came to the
Government-they came as a matter of
fact to me personally and the Minister of
Home Affairs-and represented that the
results were such that there was no possibility of solving the housing problem so
long as the maximum superficial area was
maintained at 950 feet.
When we asked them what their solution
was they said a kitchen house of 650 superficial feet was the only method by which
the housing problem, in Belfast at any
rate, could be solved. They spoke only for
Belfast. What has been the result? We
agreed at that time-although I am bound
to say I was doubtful about finding the
necessary money--but we agreed at that
time that if the Corporation would proceed
actively with the building of houses of 650
feet superficial area we would increase the
subsidy from £80 to £100 in order to accelerate the movement that had been so
long delayed, a delay that had caused much
suffering to many working class people in
Belfast. What has been the result? My
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Home
Affairs, in his very graphic statement yesterday, showed how, immediately that
policy was adopted, the rate of building of
these smaller subsidy houses was increased
and has since gone on to such an extent
that at this moment the number of house
plans submitted from local authorities
amount to 450 monthly, or at the rate of
over 5,000 houses per year.
I calculate that if that policy be continued for another year we will practically
have reached the point when the housing
problem for working men will be solved.
But it must be when a surplus of houses is
reached, and not when a house is provided
for every working man's family. When
such a surplus of houses is created the
ordinary and natural law of supply and
demand will force down not only the prices
but the rents of houses. What the
Government is primarily concerned about
is that the rents of houses shall be brought
down to the level the Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) has indicated. But

it will never be done by the method he

a shilling a week to the working man, and
to a man with only £2 a week that is a
very material amount.
Mr. BEATTIE: But it is not necessary.
Mr. POLLOCK: If you will work it

superficial feet, although I am not rigid
on that point, but my very strong view
is that, judging by the success which has

a measurable time you will have reached
a position when the surplus of houses will
be such that it will force the price and

He has made no calculation whatever based
upon the interest on the money invested
in that house, and that interest in thirty
years would almost double the cost of the
house. I only mention that in passing,
because the Parliamentary Secretary will
deal with these matters in detail.
I wish to let it be known that the local
authorities' demand for a house of 950
superficial feet is something that for two
reasons cannot be agreed to. The first is
that we have not got the money to do it,
unless we tax the people in some way
that I cannot visualise. The second is
that it is providing a luxury house, or
villa-using the word luxury not in its
literal sense, but to distinguish it from
the type of house we are now discussingfor middle-class people who, we can presume, will build their own house.
desire to encourage that to the greatest
extent possible, and avenues are open to

the local authorities under the Small
Dwellings Acquisition Act. The Belfast
Corporation has extended the amount of a

We
Those urban authorities who are
anxious, no doubt, to preserve the
æsthetic character or appearance of their
town must, at the same time, realise their
own responsibilities, and their responsibilities to the citizens and the citizens
themselves must have some regard to their
own liabilities in reference to their own
houses. I just wish to make it clear that
while the exact superficial area may be
open for discussion-and I will undertake
that the matter will be considered, inasmuch as some Members have pressed for
750 feet superficial area-these are matters that have to be very carefully considered as to their ultimate effect and as
to the policy of the Government in trying
to bring the rents of working men's houses
down.
In connection with this subject the word
"slums" has been used. It has been
asked, "Why do not the Government
clear away the slums." In the first
place, there is no such thing in Belfast as
a "slum" in the British sense of the word
"slum." Working people's houses in
Belfast are self-contained single houses.
The "slums" spoken of in the sense in
which the word has been applied are these
horrible tenement houses in which people
are herded in large numbers and in conditions which are indescribable. These
are the conditions which have given rise
to the word "slum." What does exist
in Belfast is that in single houses people
are herded together in larger numbers
than hygienic conditions warrant. These
houses are in a bad condition and are unsanitary, and should be removed. But
what possible object is to be gained by
clearing out these houses, pulling them
down and sweeping them away, if you
have not got proper houses for the people
to go into. It is because we want houses
for the people to go to that we want a
surplus of houses to which these people
can go when they clear out of these unhygienic houses.
That is the essence of our whole policy.
We have directed our efforts to that end.
We have increased the subsidy, and at the
instance of the local authorities themselves we have reduced the superficial
area, and we believe that in another year
or two years our object will have been
accomplished.

At Westminster they have already

necessity for the Bill is that the Unemployment Fund in Great Britain and the
Unemployment Fund here have got into
what is tantamount to a bankrupt condition. There is no course open for us but
to ask for extended borrowing powers,
which is, of course, very objectionable,
or provide ways and means by which the
income of the Fund in future will, at any
rate, be sufficient to pay the outgoings.
The annual amount which this Bill proposes to add to our Unemployment Fund
here is £70,000. I may say that the
British Fund, on the 1st April last, was
in debt to the extent of 36 million pounds.
Our parity debt here is £784,000, and
in addition to that hon. Members are
no doubt aware that we have a suspense
debt of three million pounds. It is quite
obvious that something had to be done,
as I have said, to deal with the matter
not only here but in Great Britain.
Up to the present the contribution
which the State paid to unemployment
was 40 per cent. of the combined contributions of the employers and workers.
This Bill sets out that in future the
statutory contributions will be 50 per
cent. of the combined contributions of
employers and workers. I do not think
that it is necessary for me to detain the
House longer in explaining this Measure.
It is quite clear what the intention of
these two Clauses is, and hon. Members
will agree with me that it is a very uncontroversial Measure which we can from
our hearts as well as with our heads
enthusiastically support. I beg to move.

sent

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. HENDERSON: I did not say it
was a foreign country.
Mr. ANDREWS: Excuse me; Hansard
will show that you did, for I wrote it down
at the time. Then, again, I would like to
make it quite clear that there is not a
stockbroker in charge of the farm at
Richhill. There is a gentleman who has
had very wide experience in connection
with matters of training of young people
who was at one time a stockbroker, I
admit, not in charge of the farm at Richhill, but in charge of the administrative
side of the training centre. There is one
of the most capable farmers in Northern
Ireland in charge of the farm and in
charge of the training of these young men.
In the next place, I should like to point
out that it has been suggested that these
young men are sent to Canada, and that
they are not cared for either by us here or
by the Dominion authorities. That is
quite wrong. They go out, giving an
undertaking before they go, that they
want to be engaged in farming operations
in the Dominions. The mistake that
some of them make is this, that when they
go there they think they would rather be
in the towns than in the country districts.
They are guaranteed a job on a farm, and
if, when they are placed on a farm, they
are not satisfied with the conditions, if
they are not satisfied with the wages, or if
they are not satisfied with their employer,
generally speaking, all they have to do is
to report to the Canadian authority out
there for the purpose, and they will be
placed on another farm; and they can do
the same thing over again if they so
desire.
I quite admit that a certain section of
those who have gone-a very small percentage have not made good. There are
some people, I must frankly say, who
would not make good anywhere, but one
swallow does not make a summer, and I
am prepared to state here in the House,
and I am prepared to prove, that the vast
majority of those who have gone are making good. Hon. Members have referred
to letters which they have seen from those
who have failed. Some of them have
failed because they have tried to go into
the United States of America, and have
been deported as a result. Some of them
have failed-poor fellows!-because, although they were medically examined
four times before they went out, their
health has broken down for some reason or
other. That is a very small percentage.
Others have failed because they were not
prepared to continue in farm employment,
and, drifting into the towns, were unable
to find employment. This small percentage, I admit, has failed, but because
a small percentage has failed it would not
be right of me to agree that we should
deny to the many advantages which the
Dominions offer to them.
There is a good deal more in connection
with this matter that I could say if there
was time, but I want to make it quite
clear to the House that for every one letter
that hon. Members have seen, showing
that a particular trainee has not made
good, I have received hundreds from those
who have made good, thanking the Government for the opportunity that has been
given to them, stating in the clearest
possible way what great opportunities the
Dominions present to those who are willing to work and who want to make good,
that we are perfectly justified in carrying
on this Centre in the way we are doing,
and that if we did not do it we would not
be doing what in their opinion they consider right and proper, namely, putting
within the reach of those people an opportunity to go to our Dominions, if they
desire to do so. That is the position,
shortly expressed, and I do not think 1
need say anything more now.

Thursday, 14th November, 1929.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
DONAGHADEE URBAN DISTRICT.
PUBLIC PARKS AND RECREATION
FACILITIES.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state why the
loan of £1,500 applied for by the
Donaghadee Urban Council was not
granted by him for the term of 35 years,
as recommended by the Minister of Home
Affairs, and what loans he has sanctioned
to Local Authorities since the 1st
January, 1929, for the purpose of providing Public Parks and Recreation
Facilities.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The issue of this Loan of
£1,500 from the Government Loans Fund
was not approved, for reasons already
conveyed to the Donaghadee
Urban
Council, namely, that the extensive demands for Loans from the Fund are such
as to make it necessary to restrict issues
to essential purposes, such as housing,
sewage, and the like.
No Loans for the purpose of providing
Public Parks and Recreation Facilities
have been sanctioned by me for issue from
the Government Loans Fund since 1st
January, 1929.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask
the Minister of Finance why be treated
the Donaghadee application for a loan in a
different manner from applications received from other local bodies for similar
purposes, and whether it is to be understood that in future local authorities will
not receive from the Government loans
for the provision of recreation facilities?
Mr. POLLOCK: I think that anyone
who is familiar with the conditions
of
finance at present, and for some time past,
will realize how difficult it is to borrow
on anything like reasonable terms, and
that the amount of money that we have
had to advance for necessitous purposes
to the local authorities is very large. For
instance, loans amounting to £446,000
during the past
the past nine months have
been sanctioned for such matters as
schools, hospitals, water supply, drainage, etc.-things that are essential
for the public life of the country. In
addition to that, housing subsidies have
been advanced to the extent of £405,000.
These amounts having drained the Local
Loans Fund so greatly, it is impossible
to continue loans momentarily for purposes that are not pressing. This is the
answer I give to the supplementary question of the hon. Member.
DISSOLUTION OF THE COUNCIL.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
what are the duties that the Donaghadee
Urban District Council have refused and
failed to perform, which were imposed on
the Council by-
(1) The Local Government Act (N.I.),
1898 to 1929;
(2) The Public Health (Ireland) Act,
1878 to 1918;
(3) Orders and Directions duly issued
or given in pursuance of the said
Act;
and whether he can state if the Order,
dated 31st July, 1929, dissolving the
Urban Council is contrary to the law.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): For some time
prior to its dissolution, the Donaghadee Urban District Council had discharged its duties in a very unsatisfactory manner, with the result that
the affairs of the town got into
state of confusion; in fact, some time
previously the Council itself had passed
a resolution asking that it should be
dissolved.
a
The salaries and duties of certain
officers of the Council are, by statute, subject to the approval of the Ministry, and
cannot be varied without a like approval.
In the case of their chief technical officer,
the Council transferred an important part
of his duties without sanction to a person
who was quite unqualified. They further
reduced the salary of the officer in
question without approval. The Council
formulated no charges against the officer,
nor showed in any way that their action
was justified.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
14 NOVEMBER 1929
In the circumstances, the Ministry
directed the Council to reinstate the officer
in his salary and duties, which, however,
the Council refused to do.
In view of the persistent refusal of the
Council to obey the lawful directions of
the Ministry, and the general state of
confusion into which the affairs of the
Council had fallen, the Ministry had no
ption but to dissolve it.
The Ministry has acted strictly according to law.

WATER SUPPLY-LOCAL INQUIRY
6. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
what scheme his commissioner has prepared for the provision of an additional
water supply for Donaghadee, and whether it is in accordance with the procedure
of public bodies, and has the approval of
his Ministry, that such a proposal should
not be published for the information of
the ratepayers who will have to defray the
cost, even if the scheme is a failure.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I understand
that, as a result of strong local representations the Commissioner is considering
the question of improving the water
supply for the town of Donaghadee, but
no definite scheme has yet been formulated.
Before any scheme can be proceeded
with, the usual formalities will have to
be complied with, and a public local inquiry will be held, at which any ratepayer can put forward his views.
Public notice will be given as to the
place, date and hour of the inquiry.
MATRIMONIAL LEGISLATION.
2. Rev. Professor CORKEY asked the
Minister of Finance whether it is the intention of the Government to introduce
legislation so that the law in Northern
Ireland may be in harmony with the law
in Great Britain on the following 'matters:
(1) Equal guardianship of children,
as between husband and wife;
(2) Marriages between persons either
of whom is under the age of 16;
(3) Separation and maintenance, as
provided for in the "Summary Jurisdiction (Separation and Maintenance)
Act 1925," passed by the British House
of Commons;
and, if not, whether he can state what are
the difficulties or objections to the introduction of this legislation.
The ATTORNEY GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): I have been asked to reply
to this question.
As has already been stated on previous
occasions in this House, and in another
place, the Government is satisfied after
careful consideration, that the existing
law in Northern Ireland in regard to the
guardianship of children, and separation
and maintenance is adequate, and no
evidence has been obtained which would
indicate that legislation as suggested is
either necessary or desirable.
With regard to the suggestion that the
extended limitation of age for marriage
to 16 years, which has been enacted in the

[The Attorney-General]
Age of Marriage Act, 1929, should be
applied in Northern Ireland, I may say
that this question is at present under consideration, but it appears very doubtful
if in this country the necessity for legislation in this direction exists, and
whether, in fact, such legislation might
not, in practice, be found to operate detrimentally in preventing the partial remedying of a wrong in the only cases

The Select Committee appointed by
Parliament came to the conclusion that

CLAUSE 1 (Registration of premises).
(1) All premises used as:--
(a) an auxiliary creamery, that is
to say for the purpose of extracting
cream from the milk supplies of
several cow-keepers; or
(b) a central creamery, that is to
say, for the purpose of extracting
cream from the milk supplies of
several cow-keepers or for the assembling of cream from auxiliary
creameries, for sale as cream or for
the manufacture of butter; or
(c) a butter factory, that is to say,
any premises on which by way of
trade butter is blended, reworked, or
subjected to any other treatment,
but not so as to cease to be butter; or
(d) a wholesale depot for the purpose of collecting, examining or classifying butter for despatch, without
treatment, to Great Britain, the Irish
Free State or the Isle of Man;
shall be registered by the owner or
occupier thereof with the Ministry of
Agriculture (in this Act referred to as
"the Ministry'') in such manner as the
Ministry may prescribe, and any person using or causing to be used for any
of the above-mentioned purposes any
premises not duly registered for those
purposes shall be guilty of an offence
under this Act:
Provided that, on application being
made by the owner or occupier of any
premises registered as a central
creamery, the Ministry may authorise,
subject to such conditions as the Ministry may prescribe, the said owner or
occupier to undertake the process of
cutting bulk creamery butter (whether
made on the premises or not) into rolls
without liability on the part of the
owner or occupier to have the premises
registered as a butter factory.
(2) The registration of any premises,
unless cancelled by the Ministry, shall
remain in force until the thirty-first
day of December of the year in respect
of which the registration takes place,
but shall be renewable annually; and
the same provisions shall apply to the
renewal of the registration of any premises as apply to the original registration thereof.
(3) A fee of one pound shall be paid
to the Ministry in respect of the registration or renewal of the registration
of any premises.
(4) The Butter Trade (Ireland) Act,
1812, and section one of the Butter and
Margarine Act, 1907, so far as it relates to butter factories, are hereby repealed.

minds of the farmers now that the
Ministry of Agriculture will have registered creameries that the wisest thing they
could do would be to send their milk in
bulk to the creamery.
Take the case of an ordinary farmer
having six cows. From the month of May
to August he would get 72 quarts of milk
daily-18 gallons-and the milk would
weigh roughly 185 lb. That would
produce about 6 lb. of butter fat. Would
it not be a wiser thing instead of registering the creameries to try to encourage
the farmer, in place of carrying this heavy
weight of milk, to have it separated at
home? He would then have only to send
the small quantity of butter fat to the
creamery. That would enable him to do
it by his boy on a bicycle. If not he would
have to have a man and a cart and would
have to bear the cost of that. I would
ask the Minister of Agriculture to consider
this question and not encourage the
farmers to adopt this uneconomic way of
doing things.
I am really afraid some of the legislation we are carrying out will be harmful
to the country, and I am sure the right
hon. Gentleman does not want that. Before this registration takes place a great
many creameries have gone out of existence, but when they are registered with
so many inspectors going round what will
happen? I can tell you of eight or ten
that have gone out of existence recently.
With the inspectors going round will more
creameries not go out, and will the last
state not be worse than the first?
I hope the Minister of Agriculture will
not be annoyed by the suggestions I am
making for the separating of the milk at
home and then sending the butter fat to
the creamery. By following this course
the butter will be more uniform, and the
farmers will be encouraged to change their
cows so that they will have animals that
will produce milk during the winter season.
The farmers may say they cannot do that,
but the milk suppliers in the towns can
do it. If the Minister of Agriculture
would go along those lines I believe he
would have better results for the farming
community. I am not going to vote
against Clause 1, but I do think it is capable of amendment in several ways.

"NOT GENUINELY SEEKING
WORK" CASES.
Motion made and Question proposed :
"That this House do now adjourn."-(Sir
Basil Brooke).
Mr. BEATTIE: I take this opportunity to raise a question which is a very
important one to the unemployed workers
in Northern Ireland. I regret that so few
Members of both sides thought it worth
their while to remain to assist me in such
a deserving case as the one I am going to
present to this House. My party at any
rate is in full attendance here. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). I asked the
Minister of Labour to-day a question,
which was as follows:
Whether under the Unemployment
Insurance Act a Board of Assessors to
adjudicate in the "not genuinely seeking work" cases should be set up as has
been done in Great Britain from the
ninth of September.
I also asked him the reason why he had
failed to comply with the financial agreement that he came to with the British
Government by not following step by step
with Great Britain. His answer to my
question was that this Board of Assessors
was only an experiment to see how it
would work out, and that the Morris Committee in its finding had not thought it
worth while to recommend its adoption.
I said then that was not according to fact,
and I will endeavour to tell this House
that the answer is not according to facts.
The Board of Assessors is not an experiment. It has been appointed under
Statutory Regulations. It was appointed
and came into being on the 9th September,
1929. In section 21 of the Report of the
Morris Committee, which sat and took
evidence on the conditions and administration of unemployment at that period,
the opinion of the Committee is expressed
as follows: :--
Since the 9th September, 1929, however, by Statutory Regulations, an insurance officer at an exchange may submit to a Board of Assessors appointed
to represent employers and insured persons the question whether a claimant is
genuinely seeking work, and if the
transitional provisions (b) and (c) set
out in paragraph 12 hereof apply to the
claimant whether he satisfies those
conditions.
That is from the Morris Report, and
shows that the Board of Assessors has
been appointed under Statutory Regulations, and by no means does it show that
it is an experiment. In furtherance of
my claim I will quote the Minister of
Labour (Right hon. Margaret Bondfield)
herself. What led her to take this step
was that when the Labour Party came
into office they found that the administration under the Tories was such that
grave hardship was being inflicted upon
sufferers from unemployment. The administration had come to such a crisis that
cruelty had been applied. The investigations into the circumstances of applicants
were sometimes unbearable. The mentality of applicants at these interviews.
was something bordering on chaos
disorder. Their answers to questions were
against their own interests.
and
Similar conditions prevailed in Northern Ireland. The applicant was brought
before the insurance officer and stereotyped questions were put to him in legal
phraseology. The applicant, perhaps,
simply stumbled or fell, and that stumble
Adjournment-
N.G.S.W. Cases
14 NOVEMBER 1929
or fall was put up against him when he
came before the court of referees, and on
his own evidence before the insurance
officer he was turned down. The insurance
officer submitted him to the court of referees, but he had been already condemned
and convicted, and it was only for the
purpose of having the sentence confirmed
that he was sent to the court of referees.
The Labour Party saw the damaging
effect that had on the morale of the unemployed people. They immediately
went into conference to discover if something could be brought about to relieve
that terrible state of affairs. The Minister of Labour discovered that no matter
what turn she made she was going to
violate the law. She was advised that
the only course open to her was to have
the Act amended, but that in the meantime she could under Statutory Regulations ease the situation of the unemployed.
As a result, since the 9th September
a Board of Assessors, representative of
the employers and employees, has been
in operation in each district. When insurance benefit is disallowed on the
grounds of not genuinely seeking
work the claimant can ask for the claim
to be submitted to the Board of Assessors,
and the insurance officer can ask for a
report from the representatives of the
district wherein the applicant resided.
That has been the means of relieving
thousands of cases. Under the old conditions the applicants would have been
turned down and disallowed benefit. In
Northern Ireland we are still under the
old conditions. We have not got the
right of this Court of Appeal. We
have not the right to appeal to the employers and the employees who understand the industrial conditions of the
district and who are in a position to give
advice that might likely guide the
court coming to a decision. I claim
that that is a violation of the arrangement come to with the Imperial Government in regard to Unemployment Insurance. Miss Bondfield is quite satisfied that it was in the public interest
that the Board of Assessors in England
was set up, and she is quite satisfied that
the public interest has been well served
by the Boards that have been appointed
in the different districts.
To-day, the Ministry of Labour in Northern Ireland is driving people on to the
rates on the ground that they are not
genuinely seeking work. Belfast and
every county in the Province is being
penalised by reason of the relief that
is being given under the Poor Law system to persons who should be drawing
unemployment benefit. The Poor Law
was never intended for persons who are
genuinely seeking work and unable to
get it.
Miss Bondfield says that in the
first month after the new procedure began-in April, 1928-the figures were
temporarily increased by a large number
of doubtful claims made when the Act
of 1927 came into force. There was a
continuous rise in the monthly average
number of claims disallowed from the
four weeks ending 11th June, 1928, until
the four weeks ending 11th February,
1929. Since the latter date the number
of disallowances has steadily decreased
from month to month.

reading an official statement from the Imperial Minister of Labour to a monthly

It is on account of the sympathy of

financial arrangement in regard to unemployment insurance is going to continue, and it is only if that sympathy
continues that this financial arrangement
will be carried on. If you fail to bring

I am making this protest on two

demanded to know from him in this

Oral Answers to Questions.
CASE OF PATRICK DEACON,
CRUMLIN.
1. Mr. HEALY (for Mr. Devlin) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether his
attention has been called to the arrest of
an orphan boy, Patrick Deacon, aged 14,
in Crumlin, on a charge of stealing a
bicycle lamp; whether Constable Frazer
arrested and threatened the boy on two
occasions; whether this boy bears a good
reputation in the locality; and whether
there was any justification for confining
him in the lock-up, in view of the fact
that the owner of the lamp said he never
accused the boy?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have caused inquiry
to be made into the circumstances of the
case referred to by the hon. Member, and
I am informed that the constable referred
to during the course of his investigations
into the larceny of a bicycle lamp, ascertained that the boy, Patrick Deacon, had
been observed in the vicinity of the place
where the bicycle had been left.
The constable, therefore, in the usual
course, interviewed the boy in the presence of the boy's brother, aged 22 years,
and asked the boy to accompany him to
the barrack for the purpose of being interrogated in regard to the larceny of this
bicycle lamp.
The boy consented to do so, and went
to the barrack, accompanied by his
brother.
Oral Answers

As other business was being transacted
in the dayroom of the barrack, the boy
was brought to another room, where the
necessary inquiries were made.
He was at no time confined in the lockup, and was not arrested, nor
was he
threatened on this or any other occasion.
With regard to the character of the boy,
I am not in a position to furnish information on the point beyond the mere fact
that he has never been charged with or
convicted for any offence.
As the boy was not confined in the lockup, the latter part of the question does
not arise.

In England and Wales, in 1927, there
