ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Motor Vehicles and Road Traffic Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: Three years
ago almost to a day, I stood at this Table
to lay before the House our proposals for
the control and regulation of motor
vehicles and traffic in Northern Ireland,
which are now embodied in the Motor
Traffic Act of 1926. Up to that time, no
serious effort had been made by any of
the Parliaments in the British Islands to
grapple in a comprehensive way with this
problem which had developed with extraordinary rapidity. The legislation then
existing with regard to mechanically propelled vehicles was entirely obsolete, having been formulated when motor traffic
was in its initial stages. It was, therefore, quite inefficient to deal with modern
conditions.
The proposals which I then put forward
constituted a comprehensive scheme for
the control of motor traffic in the Province, and bearing in mind the fact that
we had no precedents on which to found
our proposals, and that the scheme I put
forward had many features which were
novel and untried, I confess that I submitted them to the House with some little
diffidence. I am glad, therefore, to be
able to stand here to-day and to claim
that they have stood the test of experience.
Road Traffic Bill-
Second Reading
19 NOVEMBER 1929
Mr. NIXON: Question.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon.
Friend will get an ample opportunity later
on to show me where I am wrong. It is
with some little pride that I can point
to the fact that our legislation on this
subject is now being quoted as an example
which might, with advantage, be followed
by the Imperial Parliament.
It is a matter of gratification to us that
the Act which was passed by this Parliament in 1926, after three years' experience, has been found to require so
little amendment. I do not claim that
the last word has been said with regard
to traffic legislation. Such a claim would
be absurd with regard to a problem which
is developing from day to day. This
amending Bill divides itself naturally
into two parts. The 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 6th
Clauses relate to Amendments of Part I.
of the Act of 1926 which dealt with the
law as to the use of all motor vehicles on
public highways.
Clauses 4 and 5 of the present Bill deal
with Amendments to Part II of the Act
of 1926, which related to the regulation of
public service vehicles. Perhaps it would
be convenient if I deal with the Bill having regard to these two divisions.
Members will recollect that Part I of the Act
of 1926 abolished the statutory speed limit
for ordinary motor cars, and imposed
severe penalities for reckless, wanton, or
dangerous driving, and for drunkenness
while in charge of a motor car. It further enabled the Ministry to fix, from
time to time, a speed limit for public service vehicles, and heavy commercial goods
vehicles. It prescribed penalties for the
offence of exceeding the speed limit.
These penalties were severe, and the
severity of them increased for the second
and subsequent convictions. It was further provided that a driver so convicted
might obtain a licence free from endorsement if he had been free of conviction for
a period of three years. The severity of
these punishments was fully justified at
the time that the 1926 Act was passed,
when speed limits were treated by the
drivers of public service vehicles with utter
contempt, and when the speed at which
these vehicles were being driven was a
veritable menace to the public safety.
I am glad to be able to say that there
has been a tremendous improvement in
this respect, and in the great majority
of cases, public service vehicles are now
being driven carefully, and with due regard to the public safety. We find that
drivers are endeavouring to observe the
law. The present position is that if a
driver of a public service vehicle has been
convicted of exceeding the speed limit
twice, and is convicted a third time, even
though there may have been a long interval between the offences he must lose
his licence, and, of course, his employment. We consider that the time has
arrived when such severe punishment with
regard to this type of offence in the case of
men who are really endeavouring to observe the law cannot be justified. We,
therefore, propose that where a driver is
convicted of exceeding a speed limit, and
has had no conviction of this kind for a
period of twelve months, any previous
convictions that he may have had for exceeding speed limits are not to be taken
into account. Hon. Members will recollect that they rather suggested that course
on the passing of the 1926 Act, but
we did not feel justified at that time in
agreeing to it.
I would like to emphasise that this
Clause does not in any way touch convictions for such offences as dangerous
driving, or drunkenness in charge of a
motor car, but merely relates to the
offence of exceeding a speed limit, and I
think that, having regard to the improved
conditions, the House will agree that this
is a reasonable modification of the Act of
1926.
May I now state very shortly the effect
of Clause 2, which, perhaps, my right hon.
Friend, the Attorney-General, will deal
with more fully at a later stage in the debate. In doing so, it may be of interest
to the House to know that 50 persons have
been indicted for manslaughter in connection with fatalities caused by motor
cars during the past three years, but in
six cases only have convictions been obtained. Where a person is knocked down
and killed the driver may be sent forward
by the magistrates for trial on indictment
for manslaughter, instead of being dealt
with summarily for the lesser offence of
dangerous driving, but it may happen
that the evidence given before the jury
is such that the jury do not feel warranted
in returning a verdict of "Guilty" on the
charge of manslaughter or of causing
grievous bodily harm, though at the same
time the evidence may well disclose an
offence such as driving recklessly or wantonly, or at a speed which is dangerous
to the public.

The third matter dealt with under this
part of the Bill relates to the minimum
age of an applicant for a licence to drive
a public service vehicle having seating
capacity for not more than six persons in
addition to the driver, that is the
ordinary taxi-cab or hackney vehicle.
Under the Act of 1926, the minimum
age for the drivers of all public service
vehicles was fixed at 21 years, and, so
far as the larger public service vehicles
are concerned, the Government are firmly
convinced that no alteration should be
made.
In the case, however, of the smaller
vehicles, a good deal of hardship was undoubtedly imposed on the hackney vehicle
owner by fixing the minimum age so high
as 21 years. There is an obvious distinction between the large heavy public
service vehicle, and the ordinary motor
car, and we are satisfied that the public
would not be in any way endangered by
the reduction of the minimum age with
regard to the lighter vehicles from 21
years to 19 years. This will enable the
owner of a small hackney vehicle,
especially in the country districts, to
employ his son in many cases where he
could not otherwise find employment.

First-That provision should be made.
for the collection of statistics as to the

Second-That an inquiry should
held into every fatal accident in which

Third-That speed limits should be

raised in the case of motor cycles from 14

Fifth, that local authorities should be

Sixth, that the drivers and owners of all

against third party risks.
Now, so much for the proposals made by
the Traffic Commission. Let us see how

public service vehicle must be reported to

is examined by the Public Service Vehicle

I turn now to the second Part of the
Bill, which deals with the system of licensing public service vehicles as laid down
in our Act of 1926, and the system of control which I explained to the House
a year ago, and to which the House then
expressed a general approval. The Second
Report of the Royal Commission is of extraordinary interest in this regard. The
subject of the control of public service
vehicles was one on which there was very
considerable difference of opinion, and a
certain amount of controversy, and I cannot but feel a great deal of gratification
that the solution of a very difficult and
controversial problem, which I laid before
the House a year ago to-day, has now
been recommended for adoption in Great
Britain by a body of such recognised
authority as the Royal Commission on
Transport. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
The very foundation of the control of
public service vehicles under the Act of
1926 was the constitution of the licensing
authority. Prior to 1926 the licensing of
omnibuses was in the hands of each local
authority. This was a survival of the
days when omnibuses were horse-drawn
and operated only within the area controlled by the local authority, but since
traffic has become practically altogether
through traffic, such a system became obsolete, and a central authority co-ordinating the services throughout a considerable area has become essential. We
were able to persuade the House in 1926
that the system of numerous local authorities licensing vehicles without any coordination was not right, and that the
whole of Northern Ireland should be made
into a single area for licensing purposes.
The Royal Committee have now recommended a precisely similar system whereby
Great Britain will be divided into a num-

ber of areas with a central licensing

:-
We would point out that the principle
of the plan proposed by us is neither
unknown nor untried, it is virtually
that which is in operation in Northern
Ireland, an area not dissimilar in size
to most of the areas proposed in
Great Britain.
In November last, I explained the
system of further control which the
Ministry proposed to put in operation, in
pursuance of the powers conferred upon
it with regard to licensing by the Act of
1926. That system involved control of
the omnibus services, the regulation of
routes, time-tables, and fares, and I explained that the object aimed at was to
ensure that proper and efficient travelling
facilities on the roads were provided for
the public at reasonable fares. We are
now proposing a modification with regard
to the control of fares in view of our experience during the past year. The principles upon which we are administering
this control are precisely those which it is
proposed should govern the activities of
the area licensing authority in Great
Britain.
The Report sets out that the factors to
be considered in the granting of licences
are:-
(a) the traffic needs of the whole
area:
(b) the provision of adequate and
efficient services throughout the area;
(c) the elimination of unnecessary
services:
(d) the provision, where possible, of
services on routes which in themselves
are unremunerative;
(e) the co-ordination of all forms of
passenger transport in the area, i.e., the
provision of motor omnibus services; to
extend and feed tramway and trackless
trolley systems rather than to compete
with them; and the co-ordination of
road and rail services.
Those were the objects which I outlined
in the speech which I made to the House
on this date last year. If any hon. Member has the curiosity to compare that
speech with the Report of the Traffic
Commission, he will see that the arguments which the Commission put forward
for a system of control of this kind are
precisely similar to those which used on
that occasion. Let me quote what is said
in the Report of unregulated bus traffic:-
In many places the congestion on the
roads is increased by unnecessary
vehicles which, by running just in advance of regular services and tapping
their traffic, render them unremunerative. In order to do this, racing and
cutting-in take place to the serious
danger of the public. Further, by
skimming the cream off the best-paying
routes they prevent the regular operators from providing services on less
remunerative routes, thereby depriving
a section of the public of convenient
facilities. In circumstances such as
these it is obvious that no sort of coordination of transport is possible. In
addition, there can be no proper inspection of these public service vehicles, with
the result that there are, undoubtedly,
at the present time, an appreciable
number of vehicles on the road which
are in an undesirable condition if not
actually unfit for use. This state of
affairs must, of necessity, increase the
risk of deplorable accidents such as those
which have of late shocked the public.
Before I ask the House to amend the
existing law, I think hon. Members are
entitled to ask me what I have done with
the powers that already exist, what success
has attended the scheme upon which I embarked and how the public have benefited,
and, further, why I desire an alteration
of the powers which already exist? One
of the grounds upon which I stated to the
House that control was necessary was that
unregulated and unco-ordinated motor
omnibus traffic swelled the appalling
casualty list which resulted from motor
traffic.
When I was speaking upon this question
last year, and when I was dealing with the
effect of omnibus traffic upon the casualty
list I made use of the following words:-
"While I quote these figures, I do not
wish to place the responsibility for these
accidents upon the buses."

I claimed that my proposals would

I will give the House some figures, but
before doing so, I would like to say that
both in Great Britain and in the Irish Free
State the number of accidents not only
shows no sign of decreasing, but, on the

During the period from 1st January to
30th September, 1928, the total number
of accidents occurring in Northern Ireland
amounted to 1,115. During the period
1st January to 30th September, 1929,
there were 1,071 accidents in Northern
Ireland, a reduction of 44 over the number in the previous period, although there
was an increase of over 2,000 in the number of vehicles on the roads. I repeat
that I do not suggest that these figures
are satisfactory, but at any rate we have
at least checked the growth of accidents
and secured an appreciable reduction in
the number.
Taking the case of Belfast alone, I propose to compare three periods; first, the
period from 1st January to 30th June,
1928, i.e., the 6 months before private bus
owners started to compete for city traffic;
secondly, from 1st July, 1928, to 31st
December, 1928, the period when they
were competing for city traffic, and
thirdly, from 1st January, 1929, to 30th
June, 1929, i.e., the 6 months after they
ceased to compete for city traffic.
In the first six months referred to there
were 21 accidents in which omnibuses were
involved. In the second six months there
were 86 accidents in which omnibuses were
involved, and in the third six months there
were 28 accidents in which omnibuses were
involved. I think that the only inference
which can be drawn from these figures is
that the presence of the private competing
omnibus on the streets of Belfast was to
increase the casualty list to an appalling
degree. But that is not quite all, because I find that in the case of every other
type of vehicle, except the taxi-cab, the
figures of accidents rose substantially
during the period that the private omnibuses were on the streets, and fell again
to their previous level when they were
taken off.
I cannot refrain from quoting some

The total number of accidents for the

same system of control and inspection of

this year. That is one
aspect of
the question.
We have already dealt with the question of fitness of vehicles, and the
qualification of drivers and conductors.
We have eliminated the vehicles that were
unfit to run on the public roads owing
to mechanical defects. We have ensured

invited to travel are safe and comfortable,
and we have ensured that the drivers are
reliable men of good character, competent

I hear on all sides testimony to the

in the manner in which these vehicles are
being driven on the roads, and I think

system of control which the Ministry has
put in force. Not only have we ensured that
these vehicles should be driven by competent men of good character, but we have
taken away the temptation of racing,
cutting-in, and other kinds of dangerous

of snatching traffic. We have, by our

Where a number of operators were

This was pure waste, and not to the advantage of the public. We have got these

start at the same time for the same destination. We insist on a reasonable interval between them and this has provided
increased facilities.
Hon. Members do not always realise

this traffic. Although the Government
utilise to the full the Road Fund, there is
still the immense burden of approximately
£750,000 per annum upon the ratepayers.
I recollect that great custodian of the ratepayers' purse, the hon. Member for Mid-
Antrim (Mr. Crawford) complaining of

I do not wish to suggest that the work

of solution. There are a number of such

The principle upon which the Ministry

I asserted last year that the situation

going to and coming from such undertakings as the Queen's Island and other
big industrial concerns. I was greatly
struck by an article which appeared in

devoted to the interests of omnibuses.
The Manchester Corporation decided to
convert a certain important route which
had hitherto been worked by tramways
into a bus route. This was held by
certain people as evidence that trams
were obsolete, and would be superseded
by buses in all systems. The article I

It pointed out that trams were unsuitable
on

It is not perhaps fully appreciated what
enormous difficulties transport authorities
have to face in handling traffic in an industrial area at peak periods. Belfast is
no exception to this rule. Something like
42,000 persons have to be conveyed between 5-30 p.m. and 6-30 p.m. How is
this to be done? At present it requires
300 trams and 50 buses. If buses alone
were to handle this traffic, something like
750 buses would be required. This problem is not so acute in cases where there
are underground facilities.
Statements have appeared in the Press
from time to time, drawing attention
to the fact that in certain towns in Great
Britain the tramways have been abolished
and buses substituted, but I think it right
to point out what certain newspapers which
are advocating the abolition of trams fail
to point out, namely, that the only cases
where trams have been scrapped are in

comparable with Belfast, which were not
ever really suitable for a tramway system.
No town approaching Belfast in size has
scrapped its tramways. Liverpool has
considered the matter, and come to the

Great damage was done to the financial
position of the Belfast Tramway Undertaking by the occurrence last year for
which, may I say, the Corporation were

Last, but not least, it is giving employment to 200 extra men.

In introducing the Act of 1926-I
remember the occasion quite well-the
strong point made by the Minister of
Home Affairs was the number of accidents
occurring daily due to mechanically propelled vehicles. In practically his first
sentence he stated:
A record has been kept of accidents
which have occurred in Northern Ireland for the year ending 30th June,
1926-
And by the way, I may state here that
he failed to give that information to the
hon. Member for Woodvale until this day
week. However, it was asked for the
full year. Those figures could have been
quoted to-day--——
I find that no fewer than 1,300
accidents have occurred in which motor
vehicles were either directly or indirectly concerned. Those accidents
involved loss of life in no fewer than
59 cases.

(Official Report,

Those were the right hon. Gentleman's
strong points in introducing that Bill,
and I should have thought that the
first thing he would have done to-day
would have been to give the number of
accidents that have since occurred. We
know that 59 accidents took place in the
year 1926. The year 1927 undoubtedly
would give good reason for believing
that the Act had reduced the number of
deaths, because there were only 56 deaths
due to accidents with motor propelled
vehicles, but it is rather remarkableand I would like to have an explanation
of it—that an increase of nearly 100 per
cent. took place the following year.
During that year there were 96 deaths
in connection with mechanically propelled vehicles, and for the first nine
months of the present year some 72
deaths have occurred.
It will, therefore be seen that no
improvement has taken place so far as
accidents are concerned and the argument
may be brought forward that there are
more motor vehicles on the roads now
than formerly but I do not think that
would satisfactorily explain why there
has been no diminution in the number
of accidents. The Minister has also mentioned that the improvement in the conditions of motor transport and the
reduction in the number of accidents are
due to this Act of 1926. I have given

been any improvement it is not due to

the operation of the Act but to the

That being
so how does the Minister propose still
further to reduce the cause of these
accidents ?
The first Clause of the Bill is entitled
"Amendments as to penalities for speed
offences." That, as anyone who reads
the Bill can see, means a reduction in the
penalties for speed offences. It has been
truthfully stated here, and I think
practically every Member of the House
will agree, that most, or in any case a
large percentage, of these accidents are
due to excessive speed. Therefore, it
seems to me that the first Clause in the
Bill will not make for a reduction of speed.
The driver of a public service vehicle can
be penalised for a speed offence, and after
one year he can again pursue the same
course.
I think the Government should have
hesitated before they made any alterations with regard to speed offences.
In
fact, I believe there should be no pardon
for a man, no matter who he may be, who
while in charge of a motor car has been
guilty of the offence of unnecessarily
speeding. He has often been fortunate
that he has taken no life, and even when
he has been convicted of the offence of
speeding he may have been fortunate, but
to allow that individual to appear before
any court with a clean sheet after the
lapse of twelve months is more than any
Government should permit.
Clause 2 also has to do with speed, because where any person is charged with an
indictable offence, either murder or manslaughter due to negligence, it is generally
due to fast driving. But does it not seem
strange, if my interpretation of the
Clause is correct, that where an individual
is charged with manslaughter arising out
of a motor accident, and the jury fail to
find him guilty, at some future date he
may be allowed to drive a motor car again.
I
agree that in some cases it may not have
been the fault of the driver that there was
a fatal accident, but the magistrates will
have power to convict him of recklessly or
wantonly driving a car. If magistrates
have that power to convict I say they
should also have power to refuse to allow
that person ever to drive a car again.
Again, will Clause 3 tend to reduce the
number of accidents, because I should
have thought it would have been the desire of the Ministry to reduce the number
of accidents that occur daily and hourly.
By reducing the minimum age limit will
Clause 3 reduce the number of accidents?
I do not think so. I think the Government should hesitate before they agree
to reduce the age limit. I agree that the
present age limit may be a hardship in
some cases where men have their sons
driving their cars, but you also have to
consider the general public who are daily
dodging motor cars, and I think that any
man under 21 years of age should not be
allowed to drive a motor car, whether it is
a public service vehicle or a private car.
The only other matter I wish to refer
to is with regard to the tribunal and the
gentleman who is to constitute that tribunal, namely Sir Lynden Macassey.
This is one of the things in the Bill about
which I really cannot understand the attitude of the Government. To begin
with, I do not think there is any necessity
for this tribunal. I should like to know
how a gentleman of the eminence of Sir
Lynden Macassey came to offer his services free to the public of the Six
Counties. I am afraid that by setting up this tribunal you are only creating
trouble, and that the fact that you have
a gentleman willing to undertake these
duties without fee or reward will only lead
to the making of a job for someone at a
not very far distant date. I am not at
all in favour of setting up such a tribunal,
because I believe that this matter could
be very well handled by the Ministry of
Home Affairs.
I should like to know whether this
House will have any opportunity of reviewing the decisions of this tribunal. We
certainly shall not have the opportunity
of hearing this gentleman defending his
actions in this House, and I should like to
know whether it is intended that he should
be a real autocrat in this matter. While
I am in agreement with many things contained in this Bill, and while I think that
such a Bill is necessary, I believe that
many of its provisions are unnecessary.
If the Bill had been designed in the interests of the general public and for the
purpose of preventing accidents it would
have received my entire support. The
real object of the Bill is to get control of
the motor traffic in Northern Ireland, and
I am afraid the result will be that a very
few companies will ultimately control the
motor services in the Six Counties. Then
we will be back to the old state of affairs
under which you dare hardly ask for a
railway ticket and had more or less to go
on your knees to get it.

I claim that this Bill will be no

Mr. BARBOUR: My right hon.
Friend (Sir Dawson Bates) in moving the Second Reading of the
Housing Bill commented at some length
upon the spurt in house construction which has attended the change in the
Government's housing policy brought
about by the Act of 1927. His references
were, however, to the increase in the
numbers of houses built rather than to
the financial implications, and as the
object of the Resolution now before the
Committee is to secure authority for the
continuance of the grants for a further
year, the Committee will expect me to inform them of the total cost of these grants
up to date, and to give some indication
of the probable expenditure which will be
incurred during the year covered by the
Resolution.
My right hon. Friend drew particular
attention to the striking increase in the
numbers of houses built since the subsidies
were made applicable only to houses
within a minimum area of 650 superficial
feet. He compared the number of houses
completed in 1927-1,659-with the number completed in 1929-3,829-and he
indicated that the increased rate of building shown by the 1929 figures had been
more than maintained in the first six
months of the current financial year
during which 2,318 have been completed.
Let us see what has been the financial
effect of this spurt in building operations.
When moving the Money Resolution
arising out of last year's Housing Bill I
estimated that in the full year up to 31st
March last a total sum of no less than
£323,000 would have to be paid, whereas
the actual sum paid amounted to approximately £385,000. Again the subsidies
payable in the current Financial Year were
estimated at a figure of approximately
£400,000, whereas in the first six months
ending 30th September a sum of approximately £230,000 had been paid, and it is
estimated that the drain on the Government Loans Fund for the full year will be
not less than £450,000.
It is, of course, difficult to forecast with
any close degree of accuracy what the
scheme will cost in the year beginning
next April, which is the period covered
by the Resolution, but present indications
are that an even larger sum estimated at
not far short of half a million pounds will
be required, so that if this Estimate
should be realised, by the end of 1931 the
Government will have spent not less than
13 millions on providing "subsidy" houses
for the working classes of the community.
When it is remembered that for the
four-year period ending 31st March, 1928,
the total payments by the Government in
respect of subsidies amounted to £459,160,
and that during the two-year period ending 31st March next the amount which
will have been paid will have increased to
approximately £1,300,000, hon. Members
will appreciate what are the financial implications underlying the continuation of

FLOOD DAMAGE IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
1. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister
of Finance whether he has received over
150 statements of damage, amounting to
more than £6,000 from farmers and others
in the Mourne, Owenkillew and Glenelly Valleys, who have suffered damage
from the great flood of October 6th;
whether he is aware that these men, who
are mostly small farmers, are now beginning to feel the pinch; whether he can
state what action the Government proposes to take to alleviate this distress,
and will he expedite that action.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) I have been asked by the
Minister of Agriculture to reply to this
question.
The reply to the first part of the question is in the affirmative. The farmers
concerned have been furnished with full
particulars, including application forms,
of the Ministry's schemes for dealing with
damage or losses due to the flooding on
the 6th October. Immediately they return the prescribed forms their applications will be dealt with.
ADVANCE OF CAPITAL TO
CREAMERIES.
2. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if he is
prepared to advance the necessary capital
to creameries who may be compelled to
spend large sums in order to carry out the
terms of the Marketing of Dairy Produce
Act, as has been done in New Zealand;
and, if so, whether he will amend the
Act to that effect?
Mr. ANDREWS: I have been asked by
the Minister of Agriculture to reply to
this question also.
The Government already possess the necessary statutory powers for the granting
of loans, and the amendment of the Bill
in this respect is not, therefore, necessary.

Sir ROBERT LYNN: In rising to
address the House on this subject I feel
somewhat in the frame of mind of Brett
Harte when he wrote:
Do I sleep, do I dream,
Do I wonder and doubt;
Are things what they seem,
Or are visions about.
A fortnight ago I read in the newspaper
a full-blooded Socialist speech by a member of the Ulster Unionist Parliamentary
Party, and I thought when I came to this
House that the Minister of Home Affairs
was one of those stern and unbending
Tories, who would never deviate from the
path of private enterprise. But I discover here that so far as the Minister of
Home Affairs is concerned he has brought
in a Bill, and asked this House to pass it,
which, in my humble judgment, is the
crudest piece of Socialism I have ever
come across.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I thought the
Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) was
rather ungracious in his speech yesterday,
in dealing with the Minister of Home
Affairs, because if I had been in his place,
instead of showering, not abuse, but
criticism on the right hon. Gentleman,
I would have been inclined to welcome
him as a comrade, and as one who has
come, whether he knows it or not, into
the Socialist fold. I am rather surprised
that the hon. Member did not make the
most of the opportunity, and did not con-
Road Traffic Bill-
20 NOVEMBER 1929
Second Reading
gratulate his small party in this House
on the fact that they had received such an
acquisition in strength as the Minister of
Home Affairs, who probably in this
matter is backed up by the Government.
This Measure, as I said, is a piece of
pure Socialism. If people are not allowed
to sell their transport services without
being encumbered and hampered at
every point by the decrees of the Ministry of Home Affairs, why are the same
arrangements not made with regard to
every other phase of life? I know that
that is what the Member for Pottinger
wants, and probably he is satisfied that
he has got the Home Secretary to take
the first step in the direction of the
socialization of industry. If we are to
arrange all the details with regard to
transport surely we have got to go on and
arrange the prices of food, clothing, and
everything else that are matters of everyday commerce. Is the Government prepared to see this to its logical conclusion?
The other day some Members of this
House were urging very strongly on the
Minister of Agriculture that something
should be done for the farmers, and that
for the time being indeed, something
should be done in the way of stabilizing
the price of potatoes. The Minister of
Agriculture refused to do anything of the
sort. But these same farmers will now
find, if this Bill becomes an Act-and I
suppose it will, because anything the Government brings in is sure to be passed by
this House, no matter whether it is for
the good or the bad of the communitythese farmers will be told-or at least I
hope they will be told-that while one
Department of the Government is prepared to regulate their fare and their
route, and to decide exactly what time a
bus is to be run between A and B points,
they are to get no help with regard to
agriculture. I think that if the Government stop for a moment and look at
the thing they will see how illogical the
whole position is.
Let me glance briefly at the Bill itself.
So far as Clauses 1, 2, and 3 are concerned they are simply the sugar that is
put round the rather bitter pill. There
is no Member in this House, no matter on
which side he sits, who is not in favour of
the regulation of motor traffic to prevent
accidents taking place on the roads. The
Minister of Home Affairs rather preened
himself yesterday on the fact that since
the Government have intervened there
has been a great decrease in the number
of motor accidents. He was careful to
give the House some details with regard
to the city of Belfast. He did not tell
us how many accidents were caused by
vehicles other than motor buses. It
would be rather interesting if we had
those figures. Of course, he pointed out
in glowing terms that as a result of driving buses off the streets there had been
fewer accidents. No doubt if he drove
every vehicle off the streets there would
be fewer still. If he brought in a Bill
making it compulsory for everybody to
walk no doubt he would be able to come
here and say the accidents were few and
far between.
I think that as a matter of fact the decrease in the number of accidents in the
City of Belfast is due not so much to the
Ministry of Home Affairs, but to the fact
that the people are beginning to adapt
themselves to the new mode of locomotion
that is developing, and that will go on
developing in spite of all the attempts of
the Ministry of Home Affairs to stop it.
After all the introduction of these buses
has worked a revolution in this Province
as it has in the United Kingdom as a
whole. Does anyone think it is going to
be stopped, or that the Home Office is
going to lay down a limit and say to the
people, "You must travel in the sort of
vehicle we select." The people in this
Province are very long-suffering. They
accept a good many things that people
elsewhere would never accept, yet I think
there is a limit to what they will agree to.
I want the House to look carefully at
this Bill, omitting the first three Clauses,
which are not really controversial at all.
You will see that the Minister of Home
Affairs is taking powers to select routes
on which vehicles may not be used, to
make arrangements for the services of the
vehicles, to make time tables and also to
arrange the fares to be charged. I said
a moment ago that this is a crude piece of
Socialism. I now say that the more one
reads the Bill, the more one understands
it, the cruder does the Socialism become.
Why should the Home Secretary be
allowed to regulate the fares?
Mr. BEATTIE: He is being converted.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: If that is the
only thing to which my hon. Friend can
convert the Home Secretary, if his mind
can only be converted to the foolish
crudities of Socialism I will make my hon.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Sir Robert Lynn]
Friend a present of him at once, and hope
he will keep him. I say this service ought
to be run on rational lines of private enterprise. It was not State aid or State regulation that brought about this transport
revolution in the country. It was due
simply and solely to private enterprise. In
a way it was indirectly due to Government
interference, because the Government interfered with regard to the railways. The
result of their interference with the railways was that nobody would travel by the
railways unless they were compelled to do
so, and trade suffered enormously because
of the very high freights. The last year
of Government control of the railways resulted in a loss to the State of something
like £60,000,000. Surely, with that
example of Government interference with
the railways before us, we should be very
careful and very chary about interfering
with this smaller but no less important
service of transport throughout the
country.
Now this House is going to allow the
Government to regulate the fares, to deal
with the routes, to say when a bus shall
or shall not start. I say the thing is hopeless, and it would be better to give it up
altogether. As with all bureaucracies an
attempt is being made to fasten a stranglehold on the country. I should have
thought that the Government, even going
so far-much further than they ought to
go-in going in for a Bill of this sort and
introducing a tribunal, would have acted
in quite different fashion. And let me
say here, with regard to the gentleman
whose name has been mentioned and
who is at the head of the tribunal, that I
have known him for twenty-five years. I
know him, perhaps, better than any
Member of this House, and no man living
holds him in higher esteem than I do.
He is a man of great gifts, a publicspirited and patriotic citizen, and a son
of whom Ulster has every right to feel
proud. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
If it were only a case where one man, and
one man only, should be appointed, then
I would say that the House could get no
better man than Sir Lynden Macassey.
His services to the public have been enormous, and may I say to one or two hon.
Members, who rather hinted that there
was something behind it, that, knowing
Sir Lynden Macassey as I do, I refuse to
believe it. As far as he is concerned, I
am sure he is offering his services wholeheartedly with the object of helping his
native Province.
But it is not the man with whom we
have to deal here at all. Those of us
who know him respect him, and always
will continue to respect him. It is a
principle that is involved here the
principle of putting the whole of the
transport services in Northern Ireland
under the control of one man, and that
one man not responsible to Parliament
or responsible to the law. The thing is
outrageous, but then it is in keeping with
the policy that the Home Office has been
carrying out in regard to this matter
from the very first. This tribunal,
which is to consist of one person, may be
appointed by the Governor. When he
is appointed by the Governor it means
that he is really appointed by the Home
Office. If there is to be a tribunal at all,
why is that tribunal not composed of, let
us say, a representative of each county
council in the Six Counties, with representatives of the County Borough of Belfast and the County Borough of Londonderry? There you would have eight
men, or women as the case might be,
forming a bureau, men who would be in
close touch with the local feelings and
needs of the Province, who would know
exactly how and where the shoe was
pinching.
The Government do not want a tribunal of this sort that is representative
of the people. They are out to set up a
monopoly, and in order to set up that
monopoly they do not want any outside
interference. If they had a bureau such
as I suggest, then there would be the
danger that these people would point out
the weaknesses, that they would show
what was best for the country.
That
the Government do not want at all. And
mark you, the Bill lays it down that the
decision of the tribunal shall be final,
and not subject to any appeal to any
court. If that is not robbing the citizens of Northern Ireland of their ancient
right to lay their grievances before his
Majesty's Courts, I do not know what
it is. That is what the Bill, if it passes
in its present form-which I hope it will
not-will simply do for the country.
Then there is another point to which
I would like to draw the attention of the
House, and that is that for the purpose
of preventing anybody from putting their
grievances before the tribunal-whatever
form the tribunal may take these people
are to put down such sum of money as
the tribunal thinks will be absolute
security for costs. The plain meaning

I am to ask that you will be so good

It is an extraordinary thing that we have
reached a stage in Northern Ireland
where it is an irregularity for a bus

what way the information as to the

3s being charged instead of 3s 2d.
I have given you these quotations from

animates the Home Office in regard to
these services. If this House is going to

to do a grave injustice to those who are
least able to defend themselves-I mean
the poorer classes who have got to use the
buses. I want to know whether this
House is going to give its judgment in
favour of increasing fares. Incidentally,
may I say that since the Home Office intervened in this business the bus fares all
over Northern Ireland have been largely
increased. The Home Secretary boasted
yesterday that the tramway fares had not
been increased. Not yet.
But if the tramway fares have not been
increased, the bus fares under the control

would like to know if that is the sort of
thing that is going to be tolerated in Northern Ireland. Are people not going to
be allowed to buy their transport services
in the cheapest market? This is happen- |
ing in other departments. I say if this
House is going to insist on regulating
fares, and if it is going to insist on much
higher fares-because that is what the
monopoly is going to lead to, much higher
fares than those that exist at presentthen it is going to do a grave injustice to
this Province.
No one recognises more than I do what
the Home Secretary has done for Northern Ireland, both before and since this
Parliament has been established, and I
think I can at least lay claim that I have
done as much as any other Member to
show my appreciation of his services. But
in this case he is going to do an enormous
disadvantage not only to his own reputation, but to the Province as a whole, and
I am afraid that, if this Bill is passed,
instead of going down as a man who has
done great service to his Province it will
be said of him that he has deprived the

existence.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: The
first matter in connection with this Bill
to which I wish to refer is the amendment
of the criminal law which is contained in
Clause 2. The House will appreciate the
object of that Clause when I draw their
attention to this fact, that a person who
is brought before a judge of assize and
jury on indictment either for manslaughter
or for causing bodily harm under the
Offences Against the Person Act, 1861,
may be acquitted. If he is acquitted on
that indictment charge he then goes scotfree, though he may be guilty of the
offence of driving recklessly or wantonly
or at a speed and in a manner dangerous
to the public. And, therefore, to link up
the offence on indictment with the small
offence under the Summary Jurisdiction
code this Clause proposes to give the jury
the right if they find the defendant not
guilty of the main offence to find him
guilty of the minor offence of driving to
the danger of the public, and then if the
jury find him guilty of the minor offence
he will not escape altogether, which he
does as the law at present stands.
The Minister of Home Affairs gave
figures of the number of cases that had
been sent forward for trial in the last
three years. I think he gave the figure
at 50. These cases all passed before me
for review before the indictments were
sent to the grand jury and before the
prisoners were put upon their trial before
a petty jury. And in a case where there
has been negligence it is very difficult for
anyone to say under what circumstances
a jury will convict. No judge has yet
been able satisfactorily to define what
degree of recklessness'amounts to a criminal
offence, and juries are very slow to convict
a man of manslaughter in the case of an
accident arising out of a motor car, because they very often take the view that
although there may be some degree of
negligence at the same time there was no
real intent, which is always an ingredient
in every criminal offence. Although the
judges in their charges direct the jury that
a man is presumed to have intended the
result of his actions, at the same time the
juries are very slow to convict. And as
the House will remember from the figures
given by the Minister of Home Affairs,
out of those 50 cases sent forward by me
for trial at the various assizes or commissions there were only six convictions.
I hope that this Amendment in our
law will at any rate result in a number
of these offenders being punished if not
for the major offence of manslaughter at
any rate for the minor offence of driving
to the danger of the public, in which case
the judge of assize or the judge presiding
at the Commission will be able to give a
sentence of two years' imprisonment and
to suspend the accused's licence and disqualify him for having a licence for such
a time as he thinks the justice of the case
may require.
There have been some statements made
here in the course of this debate with reference to the cause of the number of
accidents that occur on our roads and
streets. The hon. Member for Woodvale
said that the vast majority of the accidents occurred through excessive speed.
That is not my experience. I understood the hon. Member for Woodvale to
be speaking from his experience as a
motorist. I speak from a different standpoint. All these cases to which I am
now referring come before me for review,
and in addition I appear in my professional capacity in the courts in a great
number of accidents arising out of the
negligent driving of motor cars in the
course of the year. I affirm here in this
House, that in a very small minority of
cases that get to the criminal courts or
civil courts the accident is due to excessive speed. They are nearly all due to
bad or negligent driving at points of
danger, corners and cross roads, and places
where motorists should take proper care,
coming out of side roads on to main roads,
where I am afraid our citizens do not exercise the caution they ought to. I would like
to see the Scottish system adopted of
putting the onus on the man who comes
out of the side road to see that he does
so in safety, because it is obvious that as
he has to turn into the main line of
traffic it is he who should slow down and
be most careful to see that he performs
that manoeuvre in safety not only to himself but to other users of the road. At
the same time I do think that the care

The rest of this Bill arises out of, and is
a development of, the administration of
the Motor Vehicles Act of 1926. Under
that Act certain regulations and limits
have been imposed on public service
vehicles by the Ministry of Home Affairs
as the licensing authority, and the
authority for those regulations will be
found in Section 11 of the Act of 1926.
The House is now asked to give the Ministry the further powers contained in this
Bill, and all that this Bill contains is
further machinery for the carrying out of
the policy which this House affirmed
in 1926.
Prior to the Act of 1926 local bodies
were the licensing authorities for public
service vehicles. Some have power to
make conditions for granting the licences,
and thereby in effect to control the traffic,
and some have not. Some local bodies
have a motive for limiting and controlling
traffic, and some have not. The Belfast
Corporation had an obvious motive for
limiting traffic in the city, because they
were competing with it through their
tramway system, but a local body such as
an ordinary urban council, rural district
council, or county council, as a rule has
no object in either controlling or limiting
the traffic of these public service vehicles.
There was no general power of inspection of public service vehicles which may
be as old, and dilapidated, and unsafe as
can possibly be. There were no regulations governing through routes from one
licensing authority's area to the area of

remunerative routes, nor, indeed, was

May I refer the House again to this Report of the Royal Commission on Transport which was issued in England not very
long ago? They sum up the anomalous
state of affairs that existed prior to our
Act of 1926-they are dealing, of course,
with Great Britain and not with Northern
Ireland and after hearing evidence from
all parties, railway companies, the bus associations, members of the public, and
everybody who can give them any information, they say:
Almost without exception criticism
of the existing procedure has been adverse, the general feeling being that the
development of road passenger transport services has reached a stage which
renders present methods of licensing
obsolete. This is sufficiently apparent
in connection with local omnibus services which run at more or less frequent
intervals, but the advent of long distance coach services, which have multiplied so rapidly during the last two or
three years, has obviously created a new
set of problems for the solution of
which the existing law is wholly inadequate.

That was the conclusion they came to,
having heard the evidence of everybody
interested in Great Britain, and having
come to that conclusion they recommend
in the most positive terms that the only
way of meeting the situation is to put into

think that this Act of 1926 passed by this

and is able to control all the motor

and the many letters that appeared in the

papers, by members of the public, some

When they think of how all that criticism

That is what he has done, and as I understand the criticism that is addressed to
the present Bill in this House, it is that
the regulation and limitation of traffic
are contrary to the rights of the public.
The first matter that has been objected
to is that this regulation and limitation.
create a monopoly. It is also objected
that it is contrary to the rights of the
public as free-born citizens that the fares
they pay should be regulated. I think
we may again for a moment turn to this
Report of this Commission in Great
Britain. They recommend that the imperial Government should pass an Act
making central licensing authorities and
that those central licensing authorities
should have power to make conditions
for the issuing of licences, just as the
Minister of Home Affairs in Northern
Ireland has now power to make conditions.
Here are the conditions that they propose
should be imposed by those central
authorities:
(a) The traffic needs of the whole
area.
These are the matters they are to take
into consideration in granting licences.
(b) The provision of adequate and
efficient services throughout the area.
(c) The elimination of unnecessary
services.
(d) The provision, where possible, of
services on routes which in themselves
are unremunerative.
(e) The co-ordination of all forms of
passenger transport in the area.
Then they go on to say:
The Commissioners shall cause the
time-tables of all regular services to be
submitted to them, and shall satisfy
themselves that such time-tables are so
arranged as to provide the public with
adequate facilities at convenient hours
and in such manner that the legal
maximum speed limit for the vehicles
used will not be exceeded.
Then with regard to fares they say:
The Commissioners shall satisfy themselves that the fares charged or proposed
to be charged are reasonable and, if
representations have been made to them
and if they consider it necessary in the
public interest, may, after holding a
public inquiry, fix maximum and minimum fares for any service in their area.
That is to say, the routes, the number of
vehicles, and the fares are all to be fixed
by this central authority. That is precisely what is done by the Ministry of
Home Affairs in Northern Ireland under
the Motor Traffic Act of 1926, and this
Bill now before the House is only asking
for some further machinery to make more
clear what the Ministry's powers are and
what regulations are to be imposed.

In moving this Motion perhaps I might
be allowed a sentence or two to explain,
firstly, the reasons for the setting up of this
Committee, and secondly, its personnel.
When this Parliament was instituted we
had to set up some scale of fees in relation
to Private Bills. We took as a rough
and ready working model the scale in
operation in the Imperial Parliament.
Eight years have now elapsed and I think
the House will agree that the time has
come to investigate whether or not any
change, and, if so, what change, should
be made in the present scale of fees. I
want it to be clear to the House that these
are fees payable to the House and have no
relation whatever to fees charged by practitioners or any other
persons whatsoever.
The second point is as to personnel.
This is obviously a Committee on which
we should have the services of experts,
particularly as it relates to what is a
branch of legal charges. Therefore it was
that three legal Gentlemen, whose capacity
at any rate is not open to question here
or elsewhere, were recommended to serve
on this Committee. Those appear to me
to be all the reasons I need state for this
Motion.

at the Belfast Commission, in which he
quoted the Lord Chief Justice of England
in the matter of the charge of manslaughter. He said that to convict a man of manslaughter by negligence, the prosecutor
must prove first that he owed the man
the duty to take care; secondly, that that
duty was not discharged, in other words

that such default caused the death and
that he showed such disregard of the lives
and safety of others as amounted to a

manslaughter plainly.
Manslaughter and murder are closely
akin. We have often discussed capital

capital punishment is carried out. It is
as a deterrent to the crime of murder.
Therefore, on the same principle I say

country.
The hon. Member for North Antrim

Derry. Part of my constituency is in
that district. It is a district which used
to be served for many years by two railways, one end by the Dungiven Railway
and the other end by what we called the
Derry Central. The transport services

The advent of the bus services has been
a godsend for them. It enabled those

myself as the pedestrian described by the
hon. Member for St. Anne's (Major
M'Cormick), and am perhaps more interested in avoiding motor cars than in
driving one. As a member of the public
who like other Members, I hope, keeps
his eyes open when walking the streets, I
conceive it impossible that the future
traffic on the roads can be safeguarded unless there is some body established to
control that traffic generally. I doubt if
that principle can be seriously questioned
by any Member here. If it be questioned.
what do we find the considered opinion
to be not merely in this House, not merely
in this country but in England? The
considered opinion on this subject has been
authoritatively stated in the Report on the
Licensing and Regulation of Public Service Vehicles which has been SO constantly referred to in the debate.
May I once again remind the House of
just two passages in that Report. In one
passage the following conclusions
stated, and they cannot be seriously
doubted:
are
It follows that in many places the
congestion on the roads is increased by
unnecessary vehicles which, by running
just in advance of regular services and
tapping their traffic, render them unremunerative. In order to do this, |
racing and cutting-in take place to the
serious danger of the public. Further,
by skimming the cream off the bestpaying routes they prevent the regular
operators from providing services on
less remunerative routes, thereby depriving a section of the public of convenient facilities. In circumstances
such as these it is obvious that no sort
of co-ordination of transport is possible.
That is the condition of affairs found to
exist in England. Remember, this Royal
Commission found it to exist, because no
body had been set up in England corresponding to the Ministry in this country
and because no proper co-ordination of
transport was found to be possible. That
is the conclusion of the Royal Commission.
In arriving at their recommendations at
the end of that Report this Royal Commission has not been afraid to use the
word "monopoly," a word which has been.
constantly used in connection with this
Bill, as if by the use of that word like the
blessed word Mesopotamia the Bill would
fall of its own weight. This Commission
recognised that Commissioners, as hon.
Members will remember, should be set up
That
by the Minister of Transport.
recommendation is this:
Generally, the Commissioners shall
aim at establishing an adequate passenger transport service in their area, creating what has been termed by several
witnesses "controlled monopoly," i.e.,
the provision of services by an adequate
number of efficient undertakings which,
for the safeguarding of the interests of
the public, would be subject to strict
control.
It is that form of "controlled monopoly"
which is in the interests of the travelling
public, and is, I think, best secured and
can only be secured by the system originally set up under the Act of 1926,
and continued and amplified by the Bill
now before the House.
There is only one other observation I
wish to address to the House. The hon.
Member for North Antrim (Sir Robert
Lynn) has criticised this Bill from many
aspects. As I understood, one aspect was
that the Bill was not deserving of the approval of the House, because it followed
on an agreement between the bus companies and the Corporation of Belfast,
and that that agreement had been
honoured by the Minister of Home
Affairs. The hon. Member criticised this
Bill and the Minister because he considers
that the Minister should not have in any
Road Traffic Bill
Dairy Produce Bill
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Murphy]
way intervened or in any way interested
himself in the conflict which took place
in this city last year.
It is not within my province to submit
to the House arguments in favour of
either the bus companies or the Belfast
Corporation.
The learned Attorney-
General has stated succinctly some of the
reasons that operated in the mind of the
Minister of Home Affairs. As I understand, the hon. Member for North Antrim (Sir Robert Lynn), who disagrees
with those reasons, suggested that that
matter should have been allowed to run
its course, if I may use that expression.
The hon. Member stated the whole subject as between the tramway and the
buses was the subject of the inquiry
which is within the knowledge of every
Member of the House. The hon. Member is quite right in stating that all the
facts were brought out at that inquiry.
It is within the knowledge of every Member of this House that the inquiry was
conducted by what I might describe as
an ideal tribunal. The facts on both
sides were brought out as far as they
could be, and the finding of the tribunal
is contained in the Report which has been
presented to Parliament.
Might I just refer in conclusion to
some of their findings. I think they are
a useful commentary on some of the
arguments addressed to the House by the
Member for North Antrim. They
found:-
--
That the tramways
still form an
efficient part of passenger transport in
any large city.
That the financial administration of
the Belfast City Tramways Undertaking
has been excellent.
That the services have been on the whole
efficient. but that there has been undue
overcrowding at certain hours which
might have been avoided by better
arrangement of services.
That the Tramway Committee have not
been sufficiently active and enterprising
in the exercise of their powers for making
use of omnibuses to supplement the tramway services.
That the present competition is unequal.
That the present competition greatly
increases danger of traffic in the city.
That illegitimate methods of
petition are being used by drivers
omnibuses.
comof
That if the present competition continues the tramway undertaking will
have to close down at an early date.
That the closing of the undertaking
will have very serious financial consequences.
That the closing of the undertaking
would be detrimental to the interests of
the citizens.
In view of the conclusions arrived at
by the tribunal, after full discussion,
and after considering all the evidence
advanced on both sides, it is very hard to
see how the Minister of Home Affairs, in
view of the duty he owes to the travelling public, could have failed to have given
approval to the agreement that
ultimately arrived at between the Belfast
Corporation and the owners of the buses
for the purpose of putting an end to this
warfare which was proving detrimental to
the interests, not merely of the citizens.
but of the owners of these bus undertakings.
Resolved, "That the debate be now
adjourned."-(Mr. Elliott).
Debate to be resumed to-morrow.

MENT BENEFIT.

of Labour whether he can state the number of persons signing the Unemployed
Register in Northern Ireland who are not
receiving unemployment benefit.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): On the 21st October, 1929,
the latest date for which figures are available, 6,109 persons were signing the Unemployed Register in Northern Ireland,
and were not amongst those in receipt of
Unemployment Benefit.

UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
SCHEMES.

of Labour whether he can state what
schemes he has brought forward for the
relief of the unemployed since the 11th
July, 1929, and the number of persons
taken into employment during that

Mr. ANDREWS: Since the 11th July,
1929, the period in question, I have approved of 100 relief schemes, the estimated total cost of which is £369,668,

CADET SYSTEM IN R.U.C.
17. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he still retains the
cadet system of promotion in the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, and, if so, whether
he is aware that the method in Great
Britain and all the self-governing colonies
is to make all promotions from the ranks?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The system of
promotion to the position of District
Inspector is the same in the Royal Ulster
Constabulary as prevailed in the old Royal
Irish Constabulary under which half of
the vacancies for District Inspectors were
filled by cadets on the results of public
competitive examinations, and the other
half by promotion from the ranks on the
results of examinations.
The present arrangements are working
satisfactorily, and I do not propose to
alter them.
With regard to the second part of the
question, I am not aware that it is the
universal practice to fill vacancies by promotion from the ranks, and in any event,
each Force must be governed and administered in accordance with local circumstances and requirements.

Minister's promise to adopt the step by
step policy with Great Britain would the

carrying out these promotions in line with

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Prime
Minister's references were to social
services. I am not aware that the police
service is a social service.

Socialist service?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, certainly
not.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Drainage Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second

Mr. POLLOCK: In moving the Second
Reading of the Measure which if it receives Parliamentary sanction will be
known as the Drainage Act (N.I.), 1929,
I desire to occupy a few minutes of the
time of the House in a short historical
sketch of past conditions in connection
with the subject of the River Bann as the
central feature and picture. The task
which we are setting ourselves to-day is
an attack on elemental forces which have
defied the ingenuity of man since time
began. In the early dawn of the world,
when nature was upheaving continents
and tossing them in riotous glee, she was
indeed very unkind to Ulster in creating
a central basin, without making provision
for a suitable outlet for the superabundant waters with which we are on
occasion too plentifully provided. Had
that great upheaval carved a fissure from
Lough Neagh through the dip between
Carnmoney Hill and Knockagh overlooking Belfast Lough, you and I would not
now be discussing the Bann problem, and
the history itself of this little corner of
Ireland might have taken a different
course. There have been suggestions put
forward for the creation of a tunnel by
which the waters of Lough Neagh might
be relieved, but the difficulties, both engineering and financial, were so colossal
as not to come within the range
tical settlement.
of prac-
The Bann has always been regarded
as one of the most important rivers of this
island. The fame of its salmon fisheries
dates from an early age, and salted salmon from the Bann and the Foyle was
exported to Spain in exchange for cargoes
of wines. The value of the fisheries is
not of modern growth; the export trade
was always there. I take this oppor.
tunity of referring to the fisheries, because I wish to make it clear that the
Government has recognised their full value
to the country and has determined that
the Drainage Scheme will be so handled
as to avoid any possible diminution in
this source of wealth.
From the military point of view, when
Ulster began gradually to fall under
English sway, the Bann developed a new
importance and this is interesting from
the point of view of a study
of ancient history. In much the
same way as the Rhine formed
the classic boundary under the Cæsars
against the incursions of the Northern barbarians, so the Bann was made
the natural line of defence by the Irish
Chieftains in Tyrone and Londonderry,
against the English incursions westward
from Carrickfergus, Larne and Glenarm.
In the days of Elizabeth thick woods
clothed the sides of the river and ran
down almost to its banks. No bridges
crossed it, but there were important
ferries at Toome and Coleraine, where
bridges stand to-day. These were the
only means of getting from the Antrim
side to the Derry side.
At this point I would like to emphasise
the fact that the floods in those days were
quite as severe as those of to-day. It is
recorded that in the year 1610, twentyfive people were drowned at Coleraine.
Half a century earlier we read of a flood
occurring in September, 1564, so serious
that the Chieftain O'Neill, falling back
across the river, had to fortify the Antrim side until he could get his army over
piecemeal in small coracles.
In the year 1573, the Earl of Essex,
who had been sent by Queen Elizabeth to
subdue Ulster, wrote to the Queen this
graphic description of the river:
The greatest cause why winter is not
apt for military service in these parts
is the sudden rising of the rivers, especially the Bann and the Main water,
which is the cause that cattle rest between these rivers in quiet.
The military objects of the English were
mainly the destruction of cattle, in order
to starve out the enemy. This, however,
did not meet with success, as O'Neill's
followers salted large quantities of the
Bann eels and salmon for their winter
supplies. So Essex wrote further to the
Queen :-
Of necessity, two bridges must be
made over these rivers, whereof the one
will be at no great charge. That over
Drainage Bill—
Second Reading
21 NOVEMBER 1929
the Bann will quit the cost, because the
fishing of salmon under the bridge will
yield a great rent.
We see that in the last part of the 15th or
early part of the 16th century the value
of the salmon and eel fisheries must have
been very great. Indeed, the value of
the salmon fisheries in those days was estimated at £1,000 per annum-surely an
enormous sum at that time. This wealth
remains to some extent to-day, but another
source of wealth has gone, that is, the
woods along its banks, which were used
for centuries to manufacture the barrels
in which the salmon were packed for
export.
With regard to the navigation of the
river, it is reported that in the early days.
of Irish history the hardy Norsemen rowed
their vessels up the river and built new
fleets of boats in Lough Neagh, so that
at that period at any rate there was free
admission and emission as far as navigation is concerned from the ocean to
Lough Neagh. Owing to the absence of
roads and unbridged rivers, inland navigation in those early days had an importance which continued up to the early part
of the nineteenth century. With the
advance of rail transport, the value of
the river from the point of view of navigation was materially reduced, but, notwithstanding its relative unimportance, I
am happy to say that the drainage works
proposed in the Bill which I am now presenting to the House, do not contemplate the demolition or interference with
the navigation works on the Bann. Access
from Lough Neagh to the sea will be maintained, and indeed the recent growth of
motor-boat traffic for sporting and tourist
purposes my opinion renders it unthinkable, or, at any rate, undesirable that
either of the inlets to our great Northern
lake should be allowed to fall into disuse.
in
I have dealt at some length on the early
history of the Bann. I do not propose to
enter into the disputed questions of the
several grants of James I. and Charles I.
to the Irish Society and to various noble
houses, whose names are to-day famous in
the annals of Ulster.
to make it clear, therefore, that this Measure does not purport to alter the position
of the several disputing parties, who,
happily for many years past, have found
accommodation better than legal dispute.
I come now to a description of the
problem, and the action of different
Governments in respect of its treatment.
There are probably few subjects about
which so much has been said and written,
about which so many resolutions of public
bodies and others have been passed, as
this very vexed problem of Bann Drainage, with which the Bill now before the
House is primarily concerned. Nevertheless it is a subject on which there is
still much loose talk and loose writing,
and, therefore, I think it will perhaps
be convenient if I recite for the information of hon. Members, in a very brief
manner, something of the essentials of
the problem and the previous efforts which
have been made to solve it.
The catchment area of the Upper
River Bann and Lough Neagh comprises
some 1,865 square miles. For the rainfall over this vast area there is only one
outlet to the sea, the Lower Bann river.
The fall in the river from Lough Neagh
to the upper side of Portna weir is only
about four feet in 15 miles. As might
reasonably be expected, in the event of
heavy rainfall the river has not a sufficient discharge capacity to pass the run-off
from the catchment area at the same rate
at which it flows into Lough Neagh, with
the result that the level of the Lough
quickly rises and floods the adjoining
lands. As a direct consequence of the
rise in Lough Neagh the Upper Bann is
also held back, hence the serious floodings
in the Portadown district. At the same
time, the rising level of the Lough pours
an increased amount of water into the
Lower Bann river, which speedily be.
comes gorged, thus giving rise to flooding
troubles along its banks, and along the
banks of tributary rivers flowing into it.
In the year 1844, as a result of a petition addressed to the Commissioners of
a noted
Public Works in Ireland,
The legal profession, to their great financial advantage,
no doubt, have often argued the claims to
the bed and soil of Lough Neagh and the
Bann, and to the eel fisheries and salmon
fisheries. Fresh grants and fresh leases
have been made from time to time by way
of compromise, and it is not for me to
enter into mazes where the highest judicial
authorities have lost themselves. I wish
engineer, Mr. John McMahon, surveyed
the district, and this work appears to have
occupied him for a period of twelve years.
In due course he submitted his report,
following which certain works were begun
in 1847 and completed in 1859.
The work then carried out was a combined scheme of drainage and navigation,
consisting of soft excavation and rock re-

moval for channel discharge improvement, and the construction of weirs, locks,
jetties, quays, swing bridges, canals, and
certain deepenings of the channel through
Lough Beg for navigation, and these
works were after completion handed over
to the Boards of Trustees. I should like
to ask hon. Members to listen carefully
to the description of the authorities who
in the past have had control of the whole
area we are now discussing. The Lower
Bann Navigation, which comprised the
Navigation Channel and works situate in
the counties of Antrim and Londonderry
was handed over to the Lower Bann
Navigation Trustees. Their duties were.
concerned purely with the navigation of
the river from the sea to Lough Neagh.
The Upper Bann Navigation, comprising
the Navigation Channel and works in the
counties of Armagh, Tyrone and Down,
was placed in the care of the Upper Bann
Navigation Trustees. Drainage Trustees,
known as the Lough Neagh Drainage
Trustees, were constituted to maintain the
various drains and other drainage works,
wherever situated in Lough Neagh and
the Bann. I want hon. Members to bear
clearly in mind that these three authorities for many years past have had control
of the different interests of drainage and
navigation in the areas we are now discussing.
Mr. McMahon had estimated that a
substantial profit would be derived from
the collection of tolls for the use of the
Navigation Channels which had been completed. Unfortunately,
Unfortunately, however, for
some reason or other probably, in the
main, owing to the development of railtransport in the district at that time--
those hopes proved vain, and although the
Upper Bann Navigation has from then to
now been practically self-supporting, the
Lower Bann Navigation has been from
the start a burden on the ratepayers of
the two counties concerned.
I shall now deal with the effect of the
works on drainage, and the reasons for
the dissatisfaction which has been felt regarding the benefits derived. There is
no doubt that the works did in fact have
a
marked effect in reducing floods. I
wish to stress this because it is the habit
to regard the work of this distinguished
engineer (Mr. McMahon) as a failure. It
was very far from being such. Records
show that save on the occasion of the record
flood in the winter of 1876-77 the Lough
has never since the year 1854 risen more
than 41 feet above the statutory level of
Lough Neagh, which level was nearly
always exceeded before these works were
executed. Though very substantial benefits resulted, yet nothing like those which
had been promised materialised, partly
owing to the fact that the scheme originally proposed was inadequate to produce
those benefits, but mainly because having
ascertained that the execution of the improvements originally proposed would

estimate, Mr. McMahon's successors, in

curtailed the drainage works. These are
the prime causes of failure to attain complete success. Secondary causes of continued flooding, though trifling compared.
to the main, are, first, silting in the
Lower Bann, and, secondly, improved
field drainage; a quicker run-off of rainfall from the uplands of the catchment,
due to improved field drains, must tax the
discharge capacity of the Lower Bann to

The fact remains that severe flooding
does still take place, and despite the reports of Royal Commissions and various

I come now to Part II which treats of

administration of the Act of 1925 by

that the somewhat elaborate procedure

much, the indirect benefits. The people
who argue that every penny expended
must bring in a dividend are surely wrong
in their premises. In other words, why
should we build hospitals, lunatic asylums, and homes for incurables? Why
not put them into lethal chambers? Those
institutions return no dividends. How
can you expect a scheme of this sort to
return all the time a full cash dividend?
It is a question of doing what is necessary
for civilisation. If we took the cash dividend point of view it would not be helping
the people at all. No good would come of
it. It would be a good answer for those
who build roads or bridges or who give
work which helps the people.
I am glad to see the Government are
doing the work for the public good. They
are doing it and they are not counting the
cost. I think their reward will be in years
to come. Some of us will not live long
enough to see it, but some of us may.
There will be a vast improvement in the
land, an improvement in the health of
thousands who live in this damp and
swampy area, and an improvement in the
climate which will result from the cessation of that continual evaporation and
condensation that go on in the lands at
present flooded. What I think is more
important, if not most important of all,
the Scheme will produce an increase in
the happiness and morale of a very large
number of poor people who live in this
flooded area and who never know from year
to year whether they will reap the crops.

County Antrim have been paying a rate

were all made drawbridges. The railway

Nothing larger than a small lighter could

Navigation Scheme is concerned was a
complete failure.
The right hon. Gentleman has referred

Portna there is only a fall of four feet.
That bears out what I thought many a
time that the Bann navigation scheme
instead of improving the drainage of the
Bann made it worse, because the principle
of the Bann navigation scheme was that
instead of their being a natural fall from
Lough Neagh to the sea of forty feet
there were created four sections of slow
running water, with weir walls and lock
gates. I was glad to hear the Minister's
point of view that part of the present
scheme is to put in sluices in these weir
walls. I believe that the sluices in the
walls will in times of flood be the means
of causing very much less damage. As

Bridge to Portna in 15 miles of 4 feet,
but at Portna there is a fall of 12 feet. If
the sluice gates are erected at Portna
it will make a splendid difference in the
working of the river.

Clause 9 says:

I am informed that under the Act of

and that the owner is deprived of his
right to question the award before a judge
and jury. In other words, I have been informed that the Act called the Acquisition
of Land (Assessment of Compensation)
Act, 1919, deprives the owner of land of
the opportunity of appealing against the
decision of an arbitrator to a judge and
jury, whereas the Land Clauses Act
does give him that privilege. I also understand that when the Bann Electricity
Bill was before the House of Commons it
was finally agreed with a deputation of
ratepayers from that part of the country.
that compensation was to be assessed under the Lands Clauses Acts, thus giving

right is a powerful check on the arbitrator.
Therefore I would appeal to the right hon.

the large catchment area of 2,000 square
miles will benefit not only indirectly but
