SCARCITY OF POTATOES IN
CANADA.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of Agriculture whether his attention
has been drawn to an article in "The
Farmers' Gazette" of 2nd instant, in
which it is stated that "there is a great
scarcity of potatoes in Canada, and
whether he will endeavour to have such
arrangements made as will enable Northern Ireland merchants to export
potatoes to Canada?
""
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The reply to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative. In regard to the latter part, the
Canadian authorities, by Regulations
made under their Destructive Insect and
Pest Act, have placed a complete embargo
on the importation into Canada of potatoes from any European country. My
Ministry has made repeated efforts to
secure a relaxation of that embargo in
favour of Northern Ireland potatoes, but
without success, and I am satisfied that
nothing would be gained by further efforts.
now to secure such relaxation.
Mr. O'NEILL: Could the Minister of
Agriculture tell us what countries potatoes
can be exported to, or if there is any
country that farmers can export
potatoes to?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: There
are several countries potatoes can be exported to, but they are not giving good
prices for them. As regards Canada, if
we could get potatoes into that country
the American authorities would stop their
export across the border.
Mr. O'NEILL: Is it a fact that no
country will take potatoes from what is
known as the scheduled or black scab
areas. Is it not a fact that France and
Belgium, to which potatoes are exported,
have absolutely refused to take potatoes
from the black scab area, and will the
right hon. Gentleman consider the question of relaxing the restrictions or taking
them off the black scab area altogether?
Mr. SPEAKER: I think that would
be a question for debate. In any case,
the Minister would probably require
notice of it.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Might I ask the
Minister of Agriculture whether he has
approached the High Commissioner for
Canada in reference to this matter?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: We have
approached the authorities in Canada
several times, but not the Canadian High
Commissioner.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether the
right hon. Gentleman is prepared to
approach the High Commissioner for
Canada to see if he will use his influence
with the Canadian Government?

done a great deal already to regulate
motor vehicle traffic in this area in the

brought order out of what was nothing
else than a state of chaos.
In

anticipating this Road Traffic Bill, I must

Elliott) was speaking I envied his power
of using complimentary phraseology. I
regret exceedingly I have not got
power, for I would like also to be able to
pay a tribute to the Minister of Home
Affairs. Although some of the things I
am about to say might look as if they
were directed specially against him, I
would like to assure this House that I
believe the Minister is trying to do his
level best, though he has made some
mistakes.
I would appreciate this Bill a great
deal more if it contained something in the
nature of compulsory insurance, and a
Clause enabling hospitals throughout the
area to recover the cost of the treatment
of patients who were in them as the result
of motor accidents. I would likewise
appreciate this Bill very much—it is an
Amending Bill-if it had contained a
Clause repealing Section 11, part 2, of
the principal Act which places licensing
in the hands of the Ministry of Home
Affairs. Personally, I do not mind saying, though I may stand alone, that this
House made a mistake in 1926 when it
placed the licensing in the hands of the
Ministry of Home Affairs. We should
have courage now to face this question and
make the necessary alteration.
I would also approve of the Bill more
if it gave the right of appeal to the
judges from the decisions of the inspectors of the Ministry of Home Affairs.
I think every man in this area of ours is
entitled to the protection of the law of
the land. and if a decision is given
against him he should have a right of
appeal in all cases to the judges. I am
glad to say that no one can find fault
with their decisions. I honestly believe
the Bill would have been better if it had
contained a Clause enabling a person to
appeal. I would also have liked to have
seen it restricting the power of the Ministry of Home Affairs to make regulations as in Section 23 of the principal
Act.
In
Those are a few things which are not
in the Bill which make me not very
friendly towards it, but there are a few
things in the Bill which are even worse
than those I have referred to. I do not
think there is any necessity for reducing
the penalties for speed offences.
Section 1 of the principal Act power is
given to make the line for the first offence
from £1 to £5, for a second offence from
£2 to £20, and for a third offence £5 to
£50, or, at the discretion of the court,
three months in prison, or both fine and
imprisonment. Then for second offences
under Proviso 1, Section 4. Clause 1, the
court shall suspend the licence for three
months or longer. I like this House to
use the word "shall" because "may"
leaves it optional.
It is now proposed to alter that, and
if a man is clear of an offence for twelve
months the next offence is to be counted
as if it was a first offence. That takes
away this provision making it compulsory to suspend a licence in the case of
a second offence if twelve months have
elapsed since the first. The Minister of
Home Affairs said the condition of affairs
in the country in 1926 was of such a
nature that these regulations were necessary, and he has been able to tell the
House that the administering of these
regulations has reduced things to better
order. That being so, would it not be
wise to keep the restrictions and let the
people understand that if they commit a
second or a third offence punishment will
follow later on? Those things in my
opinion should be continued instead of
being taken away.
Clause 3 changes the age to 19, and I
am not in agreement with that either.
I think 21 years of age was the better
age to keep it at, and I cannot for the
life of me see, as the hon. Member for
Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) has said, why it
is safer to trust one young fellow of
19 years of age with six passengers than
two with twelve. If you say it is because
you want to let some person employ his
sons you ought to remember that by
doing that you are keeping two men out
of employment, and so the last state
might be worse than the first.

I come now to Clause 4. I object to
control, because in my opinion it creates
a monopoly, and I do not like the word
"monopoly." It gives the Minister power
Over routes, services, and time-tables,
and fixes the fares as at 7th November,
reserving only power to the tribunal to
alter and amend. I hold it is an unreasonable thing to place the power in
the hands of any Minister of creating a
monopoly in traffic of this description. I
should think the Ministry should examine
vehicles to ensure the safety of the
people who are travelling, they should fix
speed limits and see the laws were administered firmly so that the people
would have their immemorial right of
using the King's highway.
It should not be interfered with in this
Anyone who is prepared to provide
a vehicle that will pass the necessary examination and submit to the regulations
which ensure the safety of the public,
should have a fair crack of the whip and
be allowed to pursue what he considers an
opportunity for earning his living, and
the Ministry of Home Affairs should not
be allowed to create a monopoly. Let
competition fix the fares. The law of
supply and demand will do the rest. The
people are not fools, and are not going to
continue doing work that does not pay
them. The big firm comes along and
throws out the small
one. That is
happening in the City of Belfast and all
the towns through the country every day.
Strange people are starting and putting
cthers out of business. I say the law of
supply and demand should continue.
People should be compelled to have their
vehicles in a safe state for passengers, and
should be prepared to obey certain laws
which will enable pedestrians and others
to go over the roads safely. And I say,
the law of supply and demand, therefore,
should be allowed to continue.
Clause 5 appoints a tribunal of one.
I would like to put a question to
the Parliamentary Secretary, as he is, I
see, taking notes. He generally grinds
me to pieces when he rises. The other
day he said that I put a strain on his
intelligence. Perhaps I will put a strain
on it this afternoon. I would like to ask
him is there any precedent for a tribunal
of this description? The Attorney-
General last week made a splendid speech,
and it was followed by a magnificent speech
by the hon. Member for Derry (Mr.
Murphy), but I was not convinced
by either speech. There was no anology
between the case they submitted and this
proposal. The Railway and Canal Commission was not an analogous case to this.
If the railways in the past got a monopoly
they put the money into the undertakings
and it was important that we had a tribunal over them to see that they would
not charge too high fares under the
circumstances.
The roads are a totally different thing,
and the roads in the country are different
from the roads in the city. It should not
be said that because certain powers were
given to the Railway and Canal Commission in England, consequently, it is right
to give the same to the Ministry of Home
Affairs in Northern Ireland. The Rail,
way and Canal Commission got the maximum rates submitted to them, but they
did not interfere with the minimum rates.
I think I am safe in saying that is perfectly right. They could prevent people
from charging too much, but they did not
interfere when people were charged too
little. That was an advantage to the
people. It should not be established that
there should be a tribunal which would
say, "You must not do a thing at that
price: it is not on an economical basis.
We must make you charge a certain price
because it is a scientific and economic
price." When I asked the Government
here to fix an economic price for potatoes
they would not do it. I say it is an
illogical position to take up to say there
is an anology between the Railway and
Canal Commission and this tribunal that
is to be set up here.
Since 1921 the business of the Railway
and Canal Commission has been done by
a body known as the Railway Rates Commission. There are three permanent
members and a panel of 36 people representing different interests. When a case
is to be heard two from the panel with
special knowledge of the matter in dispute are selected, making a tribunal of
five, not a tribunal of one.
Road transport is controlled by the Ministry of
Transport, and he does not grant licences.
He takes nothing to do with fares. He
inquires as to whether the decisions of
the licensing bodies-county and borough
councils are reasonable, but he cannot
interfere with fares or conditions of service. That is what is done across the
water, and it is a totally different thing
from what is attempted to be done here.
In Lancashire there is a system whereby
representatives of the different districts.

consider and make suggestions to the
licensing body as to the needs of services.
Across the water they keep in touch with
the local authorities, but here I am afraid
this Government is ignoring the local
authorities.

It is a splendid thing for him to offer to

give remuneration to some person who

think it is a mistake to do it. We have,

Then we have inspectors inspecting

able to turn down any man whether he

I know the case of a man who had a
motor vehicle with which he was trying
to earn a living. The vehicle, the man
will admit, got into a bad condition. The
inspector said it was not fit for the job
he was doing. He said "If you do certain things it will be all right." The
man had not very much money, only a
few pounds. He spent it all and borrowed some more SO as to repair the

the inspector. He then discovered that

an
I say that is an unreasonable state of
affairs and should not be allowed to continue. In addition, we have officials
from the Home Office. They are
agreeable, civil, courteous, and obliging
set of men, but I do not mind saying
that where there is a velvet glove there
is an iron hand. They have the power
to put the screw on. They may be remarkably civil, but it is done. We have
the Parliamentary Secretary over them
again, and after that we have the Minister of Home Affairs. Now on the top
we have a tribunal of one to regulate the
traffic. I do not think this is the wisest
way of doing it. I feel certain it will
cost a great deal of money.
The result
will be that more money will be taken
from the Road Fund that should be used
for the roads, and the balance will be demanded from the unfortunate people who
get no benefit from derating. The blessed
word "economy" has been used. It has
taken £40,000 already from the Road
Fund. The police take £19,000 from the
Road Fund, and administration takes
£4,000. I believe firmly that more raids
will be made on that Fund through this
tribunal. I think it is a tremendous mistake that we should do that.
My final reason for having some objection to it is that the rural and urban
councils have protested. The consensus
of opinion is that the bus agreement in
Belfast so far as it affects the country bus
services should be abandoned. That, I
believe, is the universal opinion throughout the country. It certainly is in my
constituency. Again and again before
the election that question was put to me,
and the feeling in the district that I represent and I am here to represent itis that there was a mistake made in mixing the country up with the arrangement
in the city. I do not charge the Minister
with selling the country for the benefit
of the city, but I think it was a mistake
that the thing was done in such a way.
Consideration should be given to the
stabilising of the country bus services on
a time-table system, with a strengthening
of the regulations for the safety of the
public, and that subject to such penalties
as it may be necessary to prescribe or enforce against owners or drivers who break
the regulations there should be no restriction of licences as proposed. The
Minister was kind enough to quote a statement of mine in 1926. It would be a source
of deep and lasting regret to me if any
word of mine influenced the Minister in
coming to the decision he made. I was
always in favour of the county councils
having power to prevent unreasonable
use of district roads, but that is different
from these proposals. I do sincerely hope
that the Minister of Home Affairs will
see that a great number of amendments
will be included in this Bill in Committee
stage. If not, I am not going to vote
for it.
Mr. BYRNE: Like every other Member of this House I agree that some control is necessary in connection with vehicular traffic. I would like to see a better
safeguard provided for the public. Although it is stated that the number of

accidents has decreased I think we will
all agree that there are far too many accidents occurring through motor traffic at
the present time. I quite agree that it
is very difficult to fix a speed limit, but
I say that every person who drives at a
dangerous speed in a congested district
should be prosecuted. In Belfast we
have found great difficulties in the past
in fixing a limit. I must say taking the
majority of motor drivers, they are reasonable and take care-those who have experience-but there are a number of motor
drivers who drive at an unreasonable
speed. Steps, I believe, should be taken
in order that these people may be prosecuted. Scarcely a day passes but we have
accidents occurring both in the city and
country, and this should be a warning
to those people who are driving at an unreasonable speed.
I was at the assizes the other day.
There were cases there. There was
one case where a man admitted that
in a very congested area he was driving at
30 miles an hour. Is that a reasonable
rate at which to drive a car in a congested
district? I agree that you cannot fix the
speed for driving in a congested district,
but I think where there is dangerous
driving the police should take action and
institute a prosecution. With regard to
control, I am not satisfied at all with oneman control. In my opinion there should
be on the tribunal representatives of all
classes of people who use vehicles in the
country to arrange the services and fares.
We have many working men to-day using
the buses. They should be represented on
that committee, which would arrange the
services and fares to be paid. Since control was taken over I have heard complaints from working men that they got no
notice whatever of increase in fares. They
were told that the fare this week is 5s 6d
and the following week it is 7s for a short
distance out of Belfast. I think that
notice should be given when the change is
to take place. At least one member from
each county council should be represented
on the committee. I do not
care how
eminent the man is, he does not know the
wants and requirements of the districts all
over the Six Counties. I would strongly
oppose leaving in one man's hands,
no
matter how eminent that man may be,
the control of traffic and the fixing of fares.
I heard the Member for North Antrim
(Sir Robert Lynn) and the Member for
South Tyrone (Mr. Elliott) heaping immense abuse on the Corporation, and it is
my duty here as a member of the Corporation to defend that body. I do not say
the Corporation is everything it should be,
but I do say it is not as bad as it has been
branded in this House. At this stage I do
not want to enter into details, but I question very much whether, to an extent, the
Minister of Home Affairs is not responsible
for some of the trouble we got into in connection with the bus traffic in this city.
However, that will be a matter for discussion later on. With regard to the traffic
in the city, I think that at the present
time, taking the bus and tramway traffic,
there is a wonderful improvement compared with the conditions that existed not
very long ago, and I would not like to see
the control of the city traffic taken out of
the hands of the Corporation and placed
under the control of this eminent counsel
in whose hands it is proposed to place it.
I or some other member of the Corporation will move Amendments in Committee
with the object of leaving the control of
the city traffic in the hands of the Corporation, because I think it would be unreasonable to take it out of the control of the
Corporation. The members of the Corporation are elected by the people and they
should know the wants of the people and
be able to express their needs. I think
they are more capable of controlling the
traffic than are any outside people, and
therefore I shall consider it my duty to
move Amendments in Committee to leave
the Corporation in control of city traffic.
All credit is due to the Corporation for
the great improvement that has recently
taken place in both the bus and tramway
services of the city. At the present time
the Corporation is trying to meet the requirements of the public. I am glad to
say the tramways are running at a profit
and we are also running buses to serve the
people, in some instances at a loss.
We are even going further than that.
We are running a service of trams early
in the morning which is unprofitable, but
we are doing it to meet the needs of the
public. There are certain classes of persons, such as charwomen, postmen, and so
on, who require an early service of trams,
and now that the undertaking is in a better
position and is making some money we are
spending some of it to cater for a large
number of people who were not catered for
before. Therefore I think the Minister
should agree to amend the Bill so as to
ensure that the Corporation shall continue
to exercise control over the traffic of the
streets of the city.

There is another matter that should receive some further consideration. I refer
to the proposed tribunal. We know that
railway companies are buying up bus services all over the country. They have already bought many and they will probably
buy many more. Most of us know how the

I was pleased to hear the speech of the
Member for South Tyrone (Mr. Elliott),
who said many sensible things and seemed
to understand the wants of the people in
the country. I agree with him that a person under the influence of drink should
not under any circumstances be allowed
to drive a motor car, and if a person is
found drunk in charge of a car he should
be prosecuted and severely punished.
As far as Belfast is concerned, I think
the Government would be making a mistake to take the control of traffic out of
the hands of the Corporation, especially
considering the fact that at the present
time we have got the traffic in a very satisfactory condition. I do not say we can
please everybody, but we are trying to
cater for the public, and this is a matter
that should receive consideration.
I may
Rev. Professor CORKEY:
say to begin with that I am altogether
in favour of the main principles of this
Bill, which I support. Most of the
speakers have begun that way, and they
have also referred to the fact that the
Bill aims at reducing the number of
accidents caused by motor traffic.
Figures have been given in support of
that, but one figure which has impressed
me has not yet been quoted. I observe
that in 1928 the number of fatalities due
to motor accidents in England and Wales
was no less than over 6,000, and I will
give hon. Members a comparison which
should go home to them in connection
with this matter. That number is three
times as great as the number of men who
were killed on both sides in a sanguinary
conflict that was fought on the banks of
a famous river in Ireland about 240
years ago.
There are a few details in the Bill to
which I would like to call attention.
Like many other hon. Members who have
spoken I am not very enthusiastic about
this first Clause. In moving the Second
Reading of the Bill the Minister of Home
Affairs said it was very hard if an employee lost his employment owing to the
fact that he had been convicted three
times for offences against the speed limit.
I would point out that this first Clause
goes much beyond that. It might not
be unreasonable that a jury should restrict its attention to a man's record
when considering the question of the renewal of a licence, but this Clause
prohibits the Court from taking into
account a man's record for more than
the previous twelve months when considering the question of what penalties
shall be meted out to him. There is no
other offence I know of in respect of
which a jury is prevented from taking into
account a man's whole record when
determining the nature of the penalty.
I have been in the police courts on
Monday mornings occasionally, not for
anything I have done, but in order that
I might see what other people were doing
on the previous day. Some records were
read out that were long and lurid, and
while I think it might not be unreasonable to restrict the discretion of juries in
regard to the renewal of a licence, I think
they should have a free hand when it
comes to the question of the nature of
the additional penalties which they think
a man's offence merits.
There is another defect in the Bill to
which I wish to draw attention, although
it has been mentioned by the Member
for Falls (Mr. Byrne), and the Member
for South Tyrone (Mr. Elliott). Great
as is the importance attached to the
Report of the Royal Commission on
Transport by those who have framed this
Bill, and very naturally so, there is one
very important recommendation which
this Commission has made, which, so far
as this Bill is concerned, seems to have
altogether escaped the observation of its
framers. May I read one or two
sentences from that recommendation :-
With regard to the offence of being
drunk while in charge of a car, a difficulty has arisen since juries are often
unwilling to convict drivers for this
offence owing to the uncertainty of the
meaning of the word "drunk.' We
are of opinion that a new definition is
necessary in order that this most

serious and dangerous offence may be
adequately dealt with
instead of
the expression "drunk" we think that

reference to Lord Cecil's Road
Vehicles Regulation Bill, should be
adopted as a deânition of the offence:
"Any person found when driving
or attempting to drive a mechanically propelled vehicle to be so under
the influence of drink or drugs as to
be incapable of having proper control of such vehicle shall be liable

I would urge
that recommendation
very strongly on the attention of
the Government. I know they are
aware of that recommendation, and
I would urge it upon them on
several grounds. First of all, this word
"drunk" is as vague as any other phrase
that might be more adequate. You could
not get two men in this House or anywhere else to agree as to where exactly
the difference lay between a state of
mere exaltation and a state of being
legally drunk. You all know the opinion.
expressed, after much experience-
Not drunk is he who from the floor
Can rise again and ask for more;
But drunk is he who prostrate lies
And cannot either speak or rise.
The phrase is not only vague, but it is
very disreputable. Juries, we
are told
by this Commission, are unwilling to
convict, and I can quite appreciate that.
A man would rather be convicted almost
of manslaughter than of being drunk,
and juries do not like to convict a man
of that offence. Therefore, on that
ground also I suggest there should be a
change. The present definition of the
word "drunk" gives little or no protection to the public. You will all
agree that before the roads were in such
a congested state as they are in at the
present time the social nuisance was the
man who was drunk, but at the present
time he is not the danger at all. The
man who is drunk can do little or no
harm.
The man who is the real danger to the
public, as the Member for Falls (Mr.
Byrne) suggested, is the man who is not
drunk but has had plenty, the man who
has had two or three glasses, the man who
is in the frame of mind to think he can
speed through any maze of traffic with
wisdom and wizardry, and the people who
watch him at his antics think he is out to
see how many pedestrians he can do to
the gallon. When he has passed, as someone has said, the people on the street can
be divided into the quick and the dead--
if you are not quick you are dead. This
Clause gives very good protection to the
public as it stands, because everybody
knows that a dose of alcohol, the physiological results of which would be far short
of making a man drunk, may nevertheless
incapacitate him for the difficult task of
driving a motor car through the streets
of our city to-day. I, myself, would
like an even shorter and more stringent
phrase than that which is suggested in
this Commission's Report. Here we have
this Motor Bill going through Parliament
now, we have the recommendations of this
Commission before us, and we shall not
have another Motor Bill in this Parliament for years to come. It may be said
that the Imperial Parliament should take
the first step, but we have our chance
now. No one will blame us for changing
the law in this respect; everybody will be
in agreement with us. If we make this
change, I feel that we will take a long
step to reduce the tremendous number of
accidents which are continually occurring.
This is the only important suggestion
that I have to make. Otherwise, I may
say, I am altogether in favour of the Bill.

Something ought to be done, and it appears to me that this Bill provides the

It is no new idea. We have dozens of
Acts of Parliament enabling juries, when
a man is charged with one offence, to find
him guilty of another. We have again
and again found that difficulty has arisen
when there is only one charge before a
jury. The offence before them does not
justify conviction on that charge, and the
man gets off. Dozens of Acts of Parliament, however, give power to a jury to
find a man guilty of an alternative charge.
There is no difficulty about it. The jury
are told, "You may think this man is not
guilty of manslaughter, that his negligence is not great enough to be called
criminal negligence, which amounts to
manslaughter, but you may find him
guilty of an offence against the Statute
which does not, in my opinion, necessitate
the same degree of negligence as would be
required for the crime of manslaughter."
It therefore seems to me that the right

can be done, and something has been done

In regard to the matter of the tribunal
may I read what I wanted to say as to the
importance of the tribunal, so that we may
get a clear conception of what the duties
of the tribunal will be:-
The function of the tribunal will be
to fix fares. In fixing fares two elements have got to be taken into consideration, first, the cost of running a
bus on a route; and second, the average
receipts from the traffic per mile run.
To ascertain these a great deal of data
has to be collected and examined. With
regard to ascertaining running costs it
is essential that the bus operator should
disclose and submit to examination
every item which goes to make up his
running costs. Such items as wages,
petrol, and matters of that kind, are
not of a particularly private nature,
but the items which go to make up such
a very important part of running costs
as interest on capital, depreciation,
and so forth, are of a character which
no owner would be prepared to have
disclosed in public. It would entail,
for instance, the disclosure of his private arrangements with his bankers,
and it might involve even the details
of his financial position.
Such matters no owner would be prepared to allow to be investigated in
public, nor would they be prepared to
disclose them to any tribunal, any of
whose members might have any interest
in using them. In cases of this sort the
fewer people who have to have access

to such information the better, and certainly no bus owner would be prepared

Further, it may be necessary to ascertain running costs not over the whole
fleet, but over a particular route, and
to judge whether the costs so arrived at
are unduly high as a result of inefficient management. Matters of this
kind require a certain amount of familiarity with technical matters as well
as a capacity to weigh up evidence.
To deal with the second matter
different considerations may arise in

obvious that the route must be made
to pay, otherwise the service cannot
exist. In the second case, it may be
reasonable to say to the operator that
he has got a standard fare fixed to
cover all his routes, that this fare gives
him a handsome profit on certain routes
that are easily worked and have a thick
population, while on the other hand
they do not yield a profit on certain
"thin" routes, and that in these circumstances it is reasonable that he
should take the fat with the lean so
long as he is getting a reasonable profit for the whole undertaking.

Mr. BARBOUR: The Resolution before the Committee deals with the provision of the necessary finance for the
Government's proposals in respect of
Bann Drainage. As was explained by
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock) in moving the
Second Reading of the Drainage Bill, the
county councils are being asked to bear
one-third of the cost of the scheme up to
a maximum contribution of £200,000.
The Exchequer will provide the remaining two-thirds of the cost in so far as such
cost is below £600,000, and, in addition,
will provide the total amount by which
the cost of the scheme is in excess of
£600,000. It is estimated that the total

in connection with the works.

He
The House may not know that the medical attendant for the police is appointed
by the Government authorities. When
any Member of the force is unable to do
duty the medical attendant is sent for.
In this case the constable reported ill on
21st September, 1928, and Dr. Tweedie
was sent for. Dr. Tweedie gave a certificate exempting him from duty for
three days. The doctor saw him on 24th
September, and gave him a certificate for
six days, and gave certain instructions to
which I will come later on. On 26th
September the doctor was sent for.
arrived late and ordered the constable to
Craigavon Hospital as soon as possible.
The ambulance arrived at twelve midnight. It was clearly a stretcher case,
but the doctor made no provision for a
stretcher and the constable was put into
civilian clothes, and walked down stairs,
and got into this ambulance, and was
taken to Craigavon. He was well treated
there while he lived. I am informed
they took almost a quart of water off his
lungs when in Craigavon, and anyone
knows that does not gather in a day or
two.
While he was in the barracks he occupied a room in which there were 20 other
men. You can imagine the effect of that,
and you can imagine how that diminished
his chance of living. The room must
have been large, and it must have been
draughty. There was no one to give him
a drink, and no one to see that the clothes
were properly over him, and he had to

Dear Sir,
I beg to bring under you notice the
circumstances surrounding the death of
my late brother, Isaac E. Walmsley, a
constable of the R.U.C., stationed at
Glenravel Street Barrack, Belfast, the
facts of which I obtained from him
while he was a patient in Craigavon
Hospital, where he died
October, 1928.
on
14th
He reported unfit for duty owing to
a cold on the 21/9/28, on which date
Dr. Tweedie was called and gave a certificate that he was suffering from a
feverish cold, and excused him from
duty for three days. At the end of
this period he was unable to resume.
Dr. Tweedie visited him again on the
24th and gave him an extension of six
days.
On this date my brother complained
of a pain in the left side of his back,
and the doctor told him to get a plaster
put on. This happened on the 24th
September. The doctor did not say
who was to put the plaster on or appoint any fit and proper person to do
So. The barrack servant, Mrs. Morgan, who resides at 20 Norfolk Street,
got a plaster and put it on. My
brother was allowed to remain in barracks until he became very ill on the
night of the 26th September. I fail to
see why my brother was allowed to remain in barracks at all seeing there was
no sick room provided, much less a
whole week without attention, and in a
room in which twenty men were sleeping, and pass in and out at all hours.
There was no fire provided in the room,
and it must have been draughty on account of its size, and the number of
windows it contained.
The bed, I understand, is of the
biscuit type, very narrow, and unsuited
for a sick person in a state of perspiration. Again, the fact of his having to
rise to go to the lavatory must have
been a death trap in itself.
The doctor was again called about
9-30 p.m. on 26th September, and

arived at 10-30 p.m., and ordered his

seventeen days, to the 14th October,
when the cause of death was shown to
be, firstly, pleurisy and, secondly, a clot
of blood brought about by the pleurisy.
The facts of the case briefly are that
in my opinion he should have been sent
to hospital when he first complained of

daily, as I am convinced that on the

attended to. When the barrack servant was asked how she understood the
position in which she was to put the
plaster, she said there was a pencil
mark on the skin to indicate the place.
In considering the conduct of the
doctor my
brother was placed in a very
false position, in the fact that he believed he was getting all necessary
medical attention, whereas he was not,
and if he had known same he would
have called in another doctor. On the
three occasions on which Dr. Tweedie
did visit him he had to be sent for each

no intention of returning that day, if

I understand that the doctor made

that he should have been carried on a

greatly impaired his chance of recovery.
I am, sir,
your
obedient servant,

[Mr. Nixon]
My points in my letter to the Minister have been ignored. Why, for
instance, was the doctor allowed to
prescribe treatment for a patient who
was so ill? Why was he not removed
to hospital at once? Why was a
servant allowed to interfere with a
patient, much less put on a mustard
plaster. I know it was done by her
with the very best intentions, but why
was the onus left on an unqualified person, or what sort of a medical system
is this to permit such a thing? There
was no room provided for a person when
ill, and no fire, no extra bed-clothing,
no medicine, and not even a hot water
bottle. I was pained to learn that the
barrack servant had to purchase out of
her own pocket the prescribed mustard
plaster. Could a beast of the field be
treated in a more shameful or careless
manner?
I wish to draw your attention to
the fact that although six months have
passed since the death of my brother,
nothing has been done to prevent a recurrence of this tragedy, and my
brother's case is not the only one.
Although I have another brother serving in a barrack convenient to that of
my late brother's, he was not informed
that his brother was ill, much less
seriously ill.
Unmarried policemen in this Province are compelled to live in these illequipped barracks. When they return.
from duty, wet and cold, they have no
place to lie and rest, no comforts of
any sort, nothing save old, hard forms
to sit upon. My object in citing this
case is to focus the attention of the
people on this appalling state of affairs.
Why should sick policemen be moved.
several miles to a hospital when the
city has many better equipped ones?
I wish to make a comment on those
last lines. When I was serving I know
the Commissioners left it to the man
concerned when ordered to hospital, to
select the hospital himself, because it was
the man's life that was in danger, and
when he selects his own hospital he is
responsible. I have been told, it may
not be correct and I am not giving it for
a fact, that there is a move made to compel members of the police force to go to
Craigavon Hospital, and some of them do
not want to go. 1 have no complaint
against Craigavon Hospital, but if à man
is ill he should be allowed to select the
hospital he will go to. It is natural that
police, even in hospital, should be under
some sort of control or discipline. That
is only right, but it is provided for because the sergeant in the barrack in the
district in which the hospital is has a
certain amount of supervision over the
men there.
There is another thing I wish to comment on. The Minister's letter was not
sympathetic enough. It was not the kind
of letter one would expect under the circumstances. £84 is very poor consolation, and it is no consolation to a person
who has lost a relative. No
person would
value a relative at £84. Apart from
that, it was only adding insult to injury
to offer any sum of money. I see in his
letter the constable's brother asks for no
money.
Another point arises that is perhaps
only a side issue. By what authority or
Act of Parliament was money handed over
for this purpose? There is money voted
to the police force, but if someone makes
a mistake, as I hold Dr. Tweedie did, 1
do not see why public money should be
used to cloak that mistake. I do not
know what the public auditor has to say
about that. I do not see why a sum of
£84 should be paid out of public money
because a mistake has been made.
It was
never brought before Parliament. Money
is not voted in Parliament for that purpose, and if it is voted for that purpose
it is time that was corrected.
As I said at the outset, my attack is,
first of all, mainly on Dr. Tweedie, and
secondly, on the system. In fairness to
those who control the police I must say
the system is no worse than it was, except
as regards this thing about sending men
to a particular hospital. If that is soand I am not sure that it is-it should be
corrected, and it would be in the interests
of the authorities to correct it. When
a man is ordered to hospital, let him say
to what hospital he would like to go. Let
the authorities exercise the usual control
when he is there. There could be no complaints afterwards, and nobody belonging
to him could complain. With these
remarks I close, and I hope if I have done
nothing more than draw attention to the
matter that a similar thing will not occur
again.

BILL PRESENTED.
Appropriation (No. 2) (Session 2) Bill,
"to apply a sum out of the Consolidated
Fund of Northern Ireland to the service
of the year ending on the thirty-first day
of March, nineteen hundred and thirty,
and to appropriate the further Supplies
granted in this Session of Parliament,"
presented accordingly and read a First
time; to be read a Second time to-morrow
and to be printed. (Bill 21).
Motor Vehicles and Road Traffic
[Money].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session to amend the provisions
of the Motor Vehicles (Traffic and Regulation) Act (Northern Ireland), 1926, to
make further provision for the punishment of certain offences in connection with
the driving of motor cars, to establish a
Tribunal to fix fares and rates for certain
public service vehicles, to empower the
Ministry of Home Affairs to regulate
general traffic on public highways and for
purposes connected therewith, it is expedient to charge on, and issue out of, the
Consolidated Fund of Northern Ireland,
or the growing produce thereof, and pay
to the Road Fund (Northern Ireland) in
accordance with the directions of the
Ministry of Finance, a sum equal to the
proceeds of all sums paid into the
Exchequer of Northern Ireland, and
being sums payable, in pursuance of an
Order of the said Tribunal under such
Act, by any local authority, body, or
aggrieved person as or on account of the
costs or expenses of sittings held by the
said Tribunal." (Governor's recommendation signified)-(Mr. Barbour).
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The charge on public moneys
which necessitates the passing of this Resolution is merely a formal one and arises
from the procedure already laid down by
the Roads Act, 1920, governing payments
to the Road Fund, namely, instead of
road taxation moneys going direct into the
Road Fund they are first paid into the
Exchequer and passed therefrom to the
Road Fund. This procedure gives
statutory effect to the principle embodied
in the Exchequer and Audit Act that all
revenue is to be paid to the Exchequer.
The Road Licence Duty is a revenue
tax the same as any other, although, in
practice, the proceeds of the tax
applied to road purposes. In the particular matter now before the Committee
certain payments in the nature of costs
will have been made by those aggrieved
bodies or persons who have applied to the
Tribunal proposed to be set up by the Bill,
but whose applications are held by the
Tribunal to have been of a vexatious and
unreasonable character. As the payments
in such circumstances are received by the
Exchequer in the first instance, this Resolution enables them to be transferred to
the Road Fund.
The amounts involved are likely to be
negligible as the salutary provision in
the Bill will act as a safeguard against
frivolous applications. I beg to move.

Sir DAWSON BATES: Before I formally move the Amendment, I would like
to substitute the words "6th November,
1929" for "1st of April, 1930." I think
it will be in greater harmony.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,
in page 1, line 10, at the end ("and thirtyone') to add " Provided that in the application of the said sub-section (1) to houses
completed on or after the sixth day of
November, nineteen hundred and twentynine, a maximum of seven hundred superficial feet shall be substituted therein for
a maximum of six hundred and fifty
superficial feet."
This is to ensure that every house built
prior to the introduction of this Act will
benefit to the extent of this Amendment.
Otherwise it will mean that a house built
prior to the 1st April, 1930, would not
rank for the subsidy provided it exceeded
the figure of 650 feet. I think hon.
Members will agree that this is a very
reasonable Amendment. I do not think
it really requires any words of mine. We
have gone into the matter very carefully,
and we feel that the additional 50 feet,
that is, bringing the size of the house to
700 feet, will provide a house with either
three bedrooms and two sitting-rooms or
one sitting-room and four bedrooms, or,
if the occupant wishes, one large sittingroom and three bedrooms.
The Government have very carefully
considered this matter, and have come to
the conclusion that to substitute a higher
class of house would simply mean that the
poorer man, the working man, would not
be provided with a suitable class of house
at all. I do not think it is necessary to
repeat the arguments which I put before
the House in introducing the Bill, but the
figures which I gave on that occasion show
that when we had the larger type of house
we only got one-quarter the number of
houses built that we got when we limited
the houses to 650 superficial feet.
I move this with a certain amount of
doubt. I am not sure that in the year
that lies ahead of us we will be able to
produce houses at the rate at which we are
producing them now, but I feel certain
that if we go beyond this figure of 700
feet we will defeat the object with which
the Bill was introduced. I would love to
see everybody getting decent houses if
possible, but the first people to be considered are the poorer classes. They have
no other places to which to go. The man
in the black coat and better circumstances
Housing Bill-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
can go elsewhere, but in many cases the
ordinary working men have no place else
to go except to these small houses. I do
not suggest for a moment that this is an
ideal house, but it will enable an enormous
number of people, who at the present time
are occupying two rooms in very unsanitary conditions, to have separate houses
for themselves with proper sanitary
arrangements and proper amenities of
life. Therefore, I commend this Amendment to the Committee.

NEW CLAUSE (Cesser of Rate Exemption in certain Cases).
Where an exemption from rates has

authority or county council, under

(Northern Ireland) 1925, in respect of

been granted, the house is-

manner that it ceases to conform to
the requirements as
to type and
dimensions for the time being in
force for the purpose of the building
grant, or
(b) amalgamated with any other
house or houses so that such houses
together form a single house,
then the exemption from rates in
respect of such house shall, as from the
date of its enlargement, alterations or
amalgamation as aforesaid, cease and
be deemed to have ceased to apply to
such house."

Mr. MURPHY: This New Clause,
the Second Reading of which I move on
behalf of my hon. and learned Friend,
the Member for Willowfield, requires a
certain amount of explanation. At the
present moment if the local authority is
asked to make a loan the local authority
has no power to attach conditions to the
loan. It is, therefore, thought desirable
that the local authority when making the
loan, and when a person exercises the
option of taking that loan instead of a
grant, should have the power to attach
to the loan the condition that the person
who receives the loan should execute a
mortgage as security, and should also, if
necessary, prove his title to the house.
If a person, instead of getting a free
grant, wants a loan-if he finds it more
convenient to get a loan it is desirable
that the local authority should have some
security. The object of this proposed
New Clause is that the local authority
should get those powers which at present
it does not possess.

Oral Answers to Questions.
SHORT SHIPMENT OF SHEEP.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he is aware
that on 11th and 12th November, 1929,
sheep and lambs consigned from Belfast
to Heysham were short shipped, resulting
in loss of markets and trade; and whether
he will state what action he has taken
in the matter?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I have been
asked to take this question.
I am aware that on the dates specified
sheep and lambs intended for shipment
from Belfast to Heysham were left behind owing to want of shipping accommodation. With a view to surmounting
this recurring difficulty of the shipment
of such animals from Belfast on Monday
and Tuesday nights, frequent meetings
of representatives of the Shipping Companies, the North of Ireland Cattle
Traders' Association, the Ulster Farmers'
Union, and the Ministry, have been held
within the last twelve months. I regret
that so far, these conferences have failed
to solve the problem, which is not by
any means a simple one. I hope, however, that the negotiations will be continued, and so far as I am concerned, I
shall do anything within my power to
help towards a solution.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON : Owing to
the importance of this subject, and the
nature of the Minister's reply, I give
notice that I will raise the matter on
the Adjournment.
Mr. COLLINS: Arising out of this
Question, may I ask if the Government
will take any notice of the overcrowding
of passengers on the Cross-Channel
steamers ?
THE TELEPHONE SERVICE.
2. Mr. McALEER asked the Minister
of Commerce whether County Agricultural
Committees and other public bodies in
Northern Ireland had adopted resolutions
in favour of the extension of the telephone service all over Northern Ireland
to give farmers an opportunity of being
kept in close touch with the markets; and
whether the Government will make representation to the Imperial Government for
a greater extension of the telephone
service in Northern Ireland?
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): My attention has been.
called to resolutions to the effect indicated
in the question recently passed by the
Londonderry and Tyrone Agricultural
Committees, and by the Tyrone County
Council. While I am fully alive to the
importance of securing the widest possible.
extension of the telephone service throughout Northern Ireland, I would point out
that the terms upon which the Postmaster-
General is prepared to provide telephone
facilities in any particular district in our
area are precisely the same as those
obtaining in any corresponding district in
England, Scotland or Wales. In these

SCHOOL-LEAVING AGE.
3. Mr. COLLINS (for Mr. Beattie):
asked the Minister of Finance whether he
can state if the policy declared by responsible Members of the Government on
making the school-leaving age 15 years is
the policy of the Cabinet, and, if not,
whether he can state the policy of the
Cabinet, and whether they are prepared
to follow step by step with Great Britain
in this matter?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am not aware of any definite
announcement of future policy having
been made on behalf of the Government
in regard to the question of raising the
age of compulsory attendance at public.
elementary schools.
The hon. Member will appreciate the
manifold complexities which surround a
question of such far-reaching importance,
and while I am not in a position to give
any indication of the policy which will
ultimately be decided upon, I would
assure him that the problem with all its
implications will be considered most carefully.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES.
4. Mr. McALEER asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if representations by resolutions, or otherwise, have
reached the Government as to the desire
that occupiers of labourers' cottages should
get an opportunity of buying out their
houses and plots on the same, or even more
favourable, terms than the tenant farmers
who purchased their holdings under the
Land Purchase Acts; whether the rates
will be abolished, or largely reduced, on
these cottage plots; and whether legislation embodying the above proposals will
be introduced by the Government?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
Resolutions have been received by the
Government from a few rural district
councils and other bodies in favour of
legislation permitting the occupiers of
labourers' cottages to purchase the cottages
in which they reside.
I do not, however, consider that such
a scheme is practicable or desirable, and
would refer the hon. Member to the debate
on the subject which took place on the
Committee stage of the Labourers' Bill
on the 30th October, 1923, and to replies
to questions in this House on the same
subject on the 25th October, 1927, and
18th October, 1928.
The land attached to these cottages will
be derated under the Local Government
(Rating and Finance) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1929.
It is not proposed to introduce legislation on the lines suggested in the ques
tion.
Mr. McALEER: Would it not be
possible to secure this million of money
that was earmarked for, and unclaimed in
connection with, the Labourers Act of
1883, and have it extended to Northern
Ireland, so that more labourers' cottages
could be erected, and the plots bought out
if the tenants desired to do so?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I really do not
know what my hon. Friend refers to. I
did not think there was so much money
in connection with the subject as a million.
All I can tell the hon. Member is that
the Government are doing everything
possible to provide labourers' cottages.
The Government provide something like
36 per cent. of the cost, which I am sure
the hon. Member will agree is most
generous.
Mr. O'NEILL: Will you inquire about
this million?

5. Major McCORMICK asked the Minister of Finance whether the Government
intends to introduce legislation corresponding to the Trustee Act, 1925, as
passed by the Imperial Parliament, which
is not operating in Northern Ireland,
and, if so, when it will be introduced?
Mr. POLLOCK: This question has

past, but owing to the pressure of other
legislative proposals, final consideration
has had to be deferred.
The hon. and gallant Member may
rest assured that the matter is not being
overlooked.

Petty Sessions Clerks in Northern Ireland

Sir DAWSON BATES: Except in the

OMAGH UNION FEVER HOSPITAL.
7. Mr. McALEER asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
if the night nurse in the Omagh Union
Fever Hospital was recently transferred
from her apartments to a place which is
noisy, and where she can not secure
peaceful sleep after the long vigil of a
winter's night; whether the Ministry's
Inspector has been consulted about this
matter, and, if so, whether the nurse
will have her quarters restored, or equally
suitable ones provided for her elsewhere
in the Institution?
Sir DAWSON BATES: A communication has been received by me from the
Night Nurse in Omagh Union Fever
Hospital, stating that she had been moved
from the apartments which she formerly
occupied to others which she considered
unsuitable.
I have drawn the attention of the
Omagh Board of Guardians to the matter, and I understand they are providing
her with more suitable quarters.

On 20th October, 1927, the hon.
Member for South Tyrone (Mr. Elliott)
asked the Minister of Commerce
whether the Toome Eel Fishery Company, who claim not only the eel fishing rights of Lough Neagh (an expanse
of some 150 square miles), but also the
bed soil of the lough, contribute any
revenue to the Government, or in any
way contribute towards the services to
which they claim full rights, such as
law enforcement, police, etc., and, if
not, will he consider the introduction
of legislation to provide that all property of the company shall contribute
by rates and taxes its fair quota
towards the State and local authorities
for these services.
The Minister of Commerce replied:
The poor-law valuation of the property of the Toome Eel Fishery Company is £1,280. The company is, of
course, rated in the ordinary way on
this amount by the local authorities in
the counties of Antrim and Londonderry in respect of the portions of their
property situated in those counties respectively. They are also liable for
income tax in the same way as any
other business concern. Over and
above these rates and taxes the com.
pany is under statutory obligation to
contribute annually to the Coleraine
Board of Conservators either 10 per
cent. of the total poor-law valuation of
their property or the aggregate amount
of the statutory licence duty payable
on the engines used by them, whichever of these sums shall be the greater.
It will thus be seen that on a poor-law
valuation of £1,280 the company is
obliged to contribute at least £128
every year to the Coleraine Board.
From information furnished to me I
understand that excluding income tax
the total payments made by the company amounted in all to £725 in respect
of the year 1926. The hon. Member
is, of course, aware that these payments, in part at least, are applied to
the services mentioned in the question.
Having regard to the information
which I have given the last part of the
question does not arise.-(Official
Report, 20th October, 1927, Vol. VIII,
col. 2197).
I hold in face of those figures, which I

CLAUSE 11 (Compensation for depreciation of certain properties).
If at any time the owner of any
several fishery in the river Bann or a
navigation company, claims that the
carrying out of any work under the
scheme, or the doing of any thing by
the Ministry in the exercise of its powers
under this Part of this Act, is causing
a depreciation in the value of such
fishery, or of a navigation belonging to
the said company (as the case may be),
and that compensation in respect of
such depreciation cannot be assessed and
paid under any other provision of this
Part of this Act, the Ministry shall pay
such compensation for depreciation
(whether by way of a lump sum or of
periodical payments) as may be agreed
upon between the Ministry and the said
owner or company, or in default of
agreement as may be determined by an
arbitrator to be agreed upon by the parties, or in default of such agreement,
to be appointed by the Lord Chief Justice of Northern Ireland.
An arbitrator agreed upon or appointed under this section shall have
power to award costs, and the expenses
of the arbitration shall be defrayed as
the arbitrator may direct. The award
of the arbitrator may be made a rule of
court on the application of either party
under and in accordance with the Common Law Procedure Amendment Act
(Ireland), 1856.

Captain CHICHESTER-CLARK: I
want to support the Amendment moved by
my hon. and gallant Friend, the Member
for East Down. As one of the originators
of the Report on which this Bill was based,
I have watched with considerable interest
how it has been going through, how it has
been standing the test of critical examination. So far it has gone so well that
I feel the Advisory Committee might almost say they made a mistake when they
took the figure of £1,000 as being a suitable figure for a minor scheme. This is
rather an important point that affects all
the Six Counties and not only the dwellers
in the catchment area, and I think there
is no doubt that £1,000 is much too low.
It really means that you can only deal
with schemes costing about £500, because
no county surveyor will take the risk of
estimating very accurately what a scheme
will cost. If he is limited to £1,000, it
is obvious that he will only deal with a
scheme estimated to cost about £500.
I go one step further. The real failure
-if we can use the word failure-of the
1925 Act was due to the complicated procedure which practically prevented all the
county councils from using that scheme 'n
the way they would have liked to use it.
If the Committee will bear with me I will
give an example of what generally happens when a drainage scheme is put up.
A certain section of people say they want
to adopt a scheme, and they say to the
county council, "kindly supply us with
the county surveyor. The county council turn on those people with great fury,
and they say, "Let you have the county
surveyor! Gracious, he has all the roads
of the county to look after! Of course,
you cannot have the surveyor.
You must
get an engineer of your own to work the
scheme." They form a small committee,
and get an engineer, which is a matter
of some difficulty, because there are very
few skilled hydraulic engineers in the Six
Counties capable of dealing with these
schemes.
After a year's work, taking measurements and levels, he produces a scheme,
and the committee lay it before the county
surveyor. The county surveyor says,
"This scheme is no use; take it away, and
do it in a different way. The private
hydraulic engineer takes the scheme away,
and prepares another scheme in accordance
with the wishes of the county surveyor.
That is passed, and in due course it is put
before the Drainage Advisory Committee.
It is examined by the senior inspector of
the Office of Works. He turns it down.
He says, "I do not like this scheme; it is
all wrong; you must go and do it another
way." The scheme goes back to the unfortunate hydraulic engineer engaged by
the committee, and he starts again,
another year having been wasted.
At the present moment I am trying to
get through a drainage scheme of a kind
which the Drainage Act of 1925 was
actually brought in to cover. After four
years' struggling, we have just been turned
down by Major Shepherd. I got him
down. He was very sympathetic, and I
used every sort of bribery to get him to
pass the scheme-luncheons and plenty of
drinks but he was adamant. He said the
scheme would not do; it would have to be
done another way. After four years'
work, we are back where we started.
That is all because the Bill was much too
complicated for the county councils to
work it. Here we have a Clause which
will help the county councils to get on
with the work without this long procedure.
I submit that we should go one further,
and make this figure £3,000, which means
that the county surveyor will be able to
estimate for a scheme which he thinks is
going to cost £1,500.

NEW CLAUSE (The power of county
councils to execute work).
The following section shall be substituted for section twelve of the Act of
1925:-
(1) The county council may serve a
notice in writing upon any person who
appears to be liable by prescription or
otherwise to scour out or cleanse any
watercourse on, or running through,
any agricultural lands, requiring him to
scour out and cleanse such watercourse
within the time specified in the notice.
(2) If any person on whom no notice
is served in pursuance of this section
fails or neglects to scour out and cleanse
the watercourse within the time specified
in the notice, the county council may
take all such steps and execute all such
works as are necessary for causing the
watercourse to be scoured out and
cleansed in a proper manner, and such
works may include such widening of the
watercourse as may be reasonably necessary and the deposit of spoil on the lands
of the said person. The whole or any
part of the expenses incurred by the
county council in executing such works
shall, if they so determine, be a debt
due to the county council by the said
person, and be recoverable from him in
a summary manner.
(3) Any person who deems himself
aggrieved by the service upon him of a
notice, or by anything done by a county
council under this section, may appeal
to the county court under section
twenty-six of this Act.
(4) Any expenses incurred by the
county council under this section shall
be defrayed in the first instance out of
the county fund, and shall, so far as not
recovered by the county council, be
raised by means of the poor rate either
as a county-at-large charge or district
charge, or off some area less than a
county district, according as the
Ministry of Home Affairs may deternine."

Mr. POLLOCK : The Amendment
which is on the paper in my name involves the dropping of the present
Clause 22 of the Bill in the form in which
it appears in the Bill as introduced and
the substitution of an entirely new Clause
which appears to be of a formidable
character, but in reality simplifies matters. The Clause in the Bill involves
legislation by reference and it is proposed
to replace it by a self-contained clause or
rather series of clauses, the purport of
which I will now explain.
Section 12 of the Act of 1925 enabled
the county council to serve notice on any
person who is liable, by prescription or
otherwise, to keep clean any watercourse
or drain, requiring him to scour out the
watercourse or drain, and in the event of
his non-compliance with the notice the
county council could enter on his lands and
do the work, subsequently recovering from
the person liable. Any person aggrieved
could appeal to the Ministry of Home
Affairs.
A recent case in the County Court which
went on appeal to the High Court, and
on which judgment was only given last
week establishes two weaknesses in Section 12 of the 1925 Act, which had not
emerged at the time the present Bill was
given its First Reading-these are, firstly,
that the onus of proving liability to scour
a drain rests on the county council;
secondly, that if a council in compulsorily
scouring a drain itself widens it, in order
to give a better flow-through, the cost of
widening remains an expense of the council and the occupier can only be charged
with the actual cost of cleaning. It is
obvious, therefore, that the 1925 Act is
defective in these two particulars and the
original provision if left is likely to become a dead letter.
The first of the present Amendments,
therefore, that in sub-clause 1 of the new
Clause, is designed to give the county
council power to take the appropriate
action with regard to any person who appears to be liable, thus throwing on that
person the onus of proving that he is not
liable. The second of the Amendments
will be found in sub-clause 2, which provides for any necessary widening of the
drain and the deposit of spoil on the land.

A further Amendment is involved in the
new Clause 12, namely, it takes away the
right of appeal to the Ministry of Home
Affairs.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK : The hon. Member

Mr. BEATTIE: And your own friends
behind have not.
Mr. POLLOCK: The questions involved have been found to be mainly questions of law, and it is considered that the
appeal ought, therefore, to be to a court of
law in every case, namely, the County
Court. The 1925 Act in fact provides in
Section 26 for an appeal to the County
Court either as an alternative to appeal to
the Ministry or from a decision of the
Ministry. The Ministry's intervention is
in fact unnecessary.
The Amendment of Section 26 proposed
in the new clauses is consequential on the
proposal to abolish Home Affairs jurisdiction, and the final Amendment is designed to prevent the new provisions having retrospective effect in the case of judgments already given or proceedings already begun. I beg to move.

He has the full right of appeal. He can

faced with the difficulty in the case referred to.

SHORT SHIPMENT OF SHEEP.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn."
-(Captain Dixon).
Colonel GORDON: I rise on the Adjournment to bring up the question of the
shipment of lambs from the Port of
Belfast. This question is a most important one, affecting as it does the whole
shipping industry of Northern Ireland.
It was only the other day that the Minister
of Agriculture told this House that the
sheep population of Northern Ireland last
year was 642,000.
There may be some in this House who
do not know how this trade is carried on,
and I, therefore, propose to explain it
shortly. Every Monday in the two large
stockyards in the City of Belfast and
throughout the week in the country an
average of some 2,360 sheep or lambs are
sold for shipment to the English market.
This number is the average from April to
December, and then it slackens a bit in
the early part of the year. The principal
centres these sheep go to are Manchester,
Liverpool, Blackpool, and, in fact, all the
industrial centres and holiday resorts in
the North, and West, and Midlands.
These lambs are bought in the sale yards
here and throughout the country by agents
of the master butchers and large meat
firms on the other side of the water.
These are figures which I have taken
from the Ulster Year Book. The estimated number of sheep sold off farms in
Northern Ireland last year was 205,000
and their value was £595,000, while the
number exported was 114,000. In this
case the value is not given but this trade
may be taken as being worth at least
£230,000 to the farmers. The value of
this trade to the agricultural community
can easily be realised, and this year it has
been one of the mainstays of the farmers.
The total number of sheep and lambs
shipped during the past ten months has
been 101,556; that is from the Ministry's
return.
What are the complaints that are
brought up? They are in reference to the
handling of this trade. The complaints are
that the shipments do not leave the port
of Belfast to arrive in time for sale on
the other side. The Great Northern
Railway Company have assisted by cffering and providing facilities for sheep and
lambs to be sent via Greenore to Holyhead. What does that mean? It means
extra expense, wastage, and delay,
and most important of all, loss of trade
to the port of Belfast, and loss of trade to
us here. The whole channel of supply
from the farmer to the consumer was
liable to interruption, because the shipping companies might be unable to take
the lambs. In fact, the fear is that
owing to the shipping companies being unable to take the number of
sheep and lambs sent for shipment
be
may not
able to keep this
trade. This matter has reached a climax.
I will read you a letter from a Manchester
firm, sent in consequence of a short shipment on the 11th and 12th. The letter
is from Henry Brown & Sons, who say:
we
This
We wish to draw your attention to
the fact that on Monday, 11th, 139
lambs should have been supplied to us
from Belfast. Instead of leaving on
Monday they were not shipped until
the following Wednesday night.
meant that we did not receive them until Friday, too late for the week-end
trade. Not only did this incur additional
expense, but it caused great inconvenience to ourselves and to our customers. We must point out-
This is the most important part of the
letterthat if there is a continuance of this
regrettable business, we shall be reluctantly compelled to seek another source
for our trade.
I think the House will realise that unless
this matter is put right we will lose a
trade that is one of the mainstays of the
farming industry. This short-shipping
has taken place for three weeks in succession. Last Monday not a single
lamb was shipped via Heysham, and
in one case a shipper who complained was told that if he kicked
up a fuss he would be short-shipped in
future. What is the result of all this?

Oral Answers to Questions.
HOUSING OF WORKERS IN RURAL
DISTRICTS.
1. Mr. MINFORD asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state, in
view of the statement made by Mr. Short,
Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the
Imperial Home Office, that there is still a
sum of approximately one million pounds
available for Northern Ireland under the
Labourers (Ireland) Act, 1883; what
steps, if any, he has taken to secure payment of this sum to Northern Ireland
for the purpose of providing housing
accommodation for workers in rural districts?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked to take this
question. In order to explain clearly
what the sum of one million pounds referred to by the Parliamentary Under-
Secretary of State in the Imperial House
of Commons represents, I propose to read
first exactly what was stated by him, as
reported in the British Hansard. The
explanation was given in the course of a
debate on the Expiring Laws Bill. Here
is what he said:-
"Under Section 1, Sub-section (1)
of the Labourers (Ireland) Act, 1914,
the advances made under these Acts
must not exceed £6,250,000. I am informed that the advances made so far
amount to £5,213,181, so there is still
an outstanding amount that can yet be
advanced for the purposes for which the
money was originally designed.
future financial arrangements for Northern Ireland have been
made by the Government of Northern
Ireland itself. There are a few outstanding cases under the Acts of 1906
and 1914, which remain to be disposed
of, and these Acts must therefore be
continued under this year's Expiring
Laws Continuance Bill."
The hon. Member will observe that
there is no question of a sum of money
being available in cash. Under the
Labourers' Cottages Act (I.), 1914,
authority was given to advance up to
£6,250,000 by way of loan from the Land
Purchase Fund for the construction of
these cottages, but the money so advanced
had to be repaid, and the repayments are
effected by the rural councils, who borrowed the money, with the help of a
grant-in-aid made annually by this
House. The few remaining advances still
being made by the Imperial Government
are in respect of schemes which were in
train prior to 1921. The loans for all new
schemes are made out of the Northern
Ireland Government Loans Fund, and
provision is also made for a Government
grant-in-aid of the loan charges.
RELIEF OF UNEMPLOYMENT.
4. Mr. MINFORD asked the Minister
of Labour whether, in view of the unemployment existing throughout the urban
and rural districts, he would consider the
advisability of promoting schemes for the
relief of unemployment in these districts?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
Local authorities and other public bodies,
including urban and rural district councils,
have again recently been requested to
consider the promotion of additional
schemes of work for the relief of unemployment, and I can assure the hon.
Member that the most sympathetic consideration will be given to any schemes submitted by local authorities or public bodies
in accordance with the conditions under
which financial assistance can be given.
Mr. HEALY: Will the hon. Gentleman
say what he will do in the event of the
local body being so reactionary that it will
not promote any schemes?

THE ORDNANCE SURVEY
DEPARTMENT.
5. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he is
satisfied that the work of the Ordnance
Survey Department of his Ministry is
sufficiently up to date to be of real benefit
to those who make use of this service;
whether it is a fact that for some time all
field work was suspended, and practically
all the staff brought into the office to try
and overtake the work that had got
behind; whether it is the intention of the
Ministry to augment the present staff,
seeing that only 36 are employed in this
Department at present, whereas the
annual estimates provide for a total staff
of 47 ?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The answer
to the first part of the question
is in the affirmative. It is a fact
that for some time practically all
field work has been suspended, and the
field staff brought into the office. The
reason is that the field work was greatly
ahead of the publication work, and the
bringing of the field staff into the office
was in order to enable these arrears to be
overtaken. These arrears are mainly due
to circumstances arising out of the transfer
of services. The whole question of organisation is at present under consideration,
but there is no immediate intention of
augmenting the present staff.
THE SURPLUS POTATO CROP.
6. Mr. MINFORD asked the Minister of Commerce whether, in view of the
glut of potatoes, he will consider the
advisability of erecting a factory for the
manufacture of starch and other by-products, which could be used in the
manufacture and finishing of linen?
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): If, as might be inferred,
the suggestion underlying the question is
that the Government should erect, equip,
and, presumably, operate a factory of the
kind indicated then the answer is in the
negative. I need hardly assure my hon.
Friend, of course, that the Government
are keenly desirous of encouraging the
establishment of new industries in our
area. From such inquiries as I have
been able to make, however, I greatly
fear that the provision of a factory such
as my hon. Friend has in mind would not
provide a satisfactory solution of the problem, inasmuch as the competitive price
at which it would be necessary to place
the starch on the market would make it
impossible to give the farmer a price for
his potatoes at which he would be disposed to grow them.
Mr. MINFORD: In view of the vague
answer of the Minister of Commerce I
wish to give notice that I will raise this
question on the adjournment.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): A little more than four years
ago I had the privilege, ably assisted by
the Parliamentary Secretary, of piloting
the Widows', Orphans and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act through this
House. It was a great and beneficent
Measure which brought a little brightness, a little hope, and a little comfort
into the homes of thousands of our people
where previously there was nothing but
darkness, misery and despair. I did not
at that time think or say that I considered the Measure a final one. On the
contrary, I said in the Second Reading
speech at that time that I looked upon
1691 Contributory Pensions Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Andrews]
it as a great step forward, a foundation upon which later on others would
no doubt build. That prophecy has been
fulfilled. And I happen to be the one
who has the privilege of introducing this
amending and extending Measure to-day.
Now, during the last few weeks, I admit
I have been asked by quite a number of
my friends, and a good many of my
opponents, how I was going to justify my
position in introducing a Socialist
Measure-
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS which had been
introduced at Westminster by a Socialist
Government. Well, I have no difficulty
in doing so, because, in the first place I
do not look upon this as a Socialist
Measure. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It contains no new principle. It is
simply an extension of and amendment
to the Unionist Act of 1925. But in the
second place it has always been the policy
of this Government since we first came
into existence eight years ago, to go in
parity with Great Britain in connection
with these social services. Because we
have always felt, and still feel, that because we had a Parliament of our own
for local purposes, that was no reason
why we should deprive in any way our
industrial classes of those privileges and
advantages which their fellow countrymen in other parts of the United Kingdom enjoy. I have been very much interested in reading the speeches which
have been delivered in connection with
this Measure at Westminster.
re-

think the one naturally follows from the
