This Measure, as I have already stated,
goes a good deal further in some directions than its predecessor. At this stage
I feel I should point out that the two
Measures are so closely interwoven and
interlaced that they are really inseparable.
Therefore, I think it will meet with the
approval of hon. Members on both sides
if I briefly summarise some of the leading provisions in the 1925 Act. That
Measure, as I have said, was a great
beneficent Measure. In the first place,
its chief Clause gave pensions to widows,
whose husbands were insured and died
after the 4th January, 1926, of 10s
per week for life, or until they became
entitled to the old-age pension, and it also
gave dependents' allowances to those
widows for their children until such
children became 14 years of age or if they
remained at school until they became 16
years of age. These allowances amounted,
as hon. Members are no doubt aware, to
5s for the first or only child, and 3s for
those other children under the age I have
mentioned.
This Act also provided in the pension
scheme of things for à considerable number of pre-Act widows on a non-contributory basis. This I would ask the House to
remember. Those widows whose husbands
belonged to the insured class, notwithstanding the fact that their husbands had
died prior to the appointed day, namely,
the 4th January, 1926, became entitled
to a pension in their own right of 10s a
week, the same as the other widows I have
referred to, and also allowances for the
children provided their youngest child
was under 14 years of age. In addition
to that, this great Measure provided pensions at 65, not only for insured husbands.
but also for their wives. Of course, any
scheme of this kind must of necessity leave
out a considerable number of persons, and
this Act is, to some extent, to meet the
demand which has been general, that
more widows still should receive the advantage of these widows' pensions.
I would like to tell the House at this
stage that under the Act of 1925 no
fewer than 46,000 persons have benefited
in this area which we are called upon to
govern. This new Measure, which I have
the honour of asking the House to give
a Second Reading to to-day, goes further
in several directions than its predecessor,
and it also removes some of those inequalities and injustices which in practice
have admittedly been found to exist in
the previous Measure. This Measure

That will mean that the contribution

1707 Contributory Pensions Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Grant]
Another anomaly is that the Bill increases the age of children from 14 to 16.
The mother will be able to draw a pension
until the child is 16
years of age.
At present, after she has drawn the pension till the child is 14 years she
stops drawing it. The child may now
be 15 years and nine months and she
immediately goes on and draws the
pension for three months when she
is struck off again if she is not 55 years
of age.
We all know from personal experience that to take away something a
person has had, then give it back for three
months and once more take it away will
create enormous difficulty. That widowed
mother will require considerable explanation as to why she received a pension and
then lost it.
So much for the anomalies that the
Labour party have removed. I am bound
to say there are some weak points in the
Bill. As one who has always advocated
a policy of taking all you can get and
trying to secure more I am prepared to
accept this Bill. I know it is possible
under this Measure for many widows who
need money very badly to obtain pensions.
There is another anomaly I had almost
forgotten about. Under this Amending
Bill it is possible for a woman with an
income of £10,000 a year to get this pension of 10s a week even although her
husband died twenty years ago, while it
is not possible for a woman with no income
coming in whose husband died five years
ago, and who is under 55 years, to get
the 10s a week to which she is rightly entitled. From that point of view I am inclined to agree with the Amendment that
the House of Lords passed last night.
I come now to the good parts of the Bill.
There are a few with which I entirely
agree.
There is the pensioner who goes to
the Dominions being enabled to continue
as a voluntary contributor. He thus
brings himself within the meaning of the
Act. In connection with the workmen's
compensation, as the right hon. Gentleman
mentioned, there was an anomaly in the
principal Act. It certainly is bad enough
for a woman to lose her husband by a fatal
accident and only get a paltry £200 or
£300 compensation, but it is a shame that
that should be taken into consideration
when the fixing of the widows' and
orphans' pensions arises. I think from
that point of view whatever party introduced this Bill is entitled to every credit.
Then, again, there is the question of men
detained in lunatic asylums. Under the
principal Act the relatives of these men
were prevented from getting the benefit of
the Act. Under the Amending Bill that
anomaly is being removed. It is just the
same in regard to war pensions. The
natural parents of the children were entitled to receive the part pension under
this scheme, but if there were any of the
parents step-parents they did not get it.
It is a good thing to have that anomaly
removed.

Mr. BLACK: This 18 the Clause
which I moved in Committee, and which

should have an opportunity of looking
into the matter. I have since discussed

been built by local authorities, particularly in Belfast, and with regard to those houses the local
authorities--the Belfast Corporation at
any rate are pursuing a policy of selling
the houses to the occupiers on very favourable terms Those terms incorporate the
giving to the occupier-that is the purchasing tenant-the benefit of the £100
free loan. They also include provisions
by which the price is payable by instalments, and that the £100 free loan is
repayable by instalments spread over
a twenty-five years' period. In circumstances such as that, it is necessary that
there should be some provision as to the
conditions under which houses can be
held, the privileges that the occupier has
in regard to the house, the privileges that
the local authority has if the house is not
used properly, or if the occupier falls behind in paying the instalments and so forth.
In regard to this matter, there is a code
in the Small Dwellings Acquisition Act
which applies to houses in respect of
which the local authorities have made an
advance under that Act. It would
seem that the provisions of the
Small Dwellings Acquisition Act can very
properly be applied by reason of there
being no provision in the Housing Acts
regulating the terms on which these houses
should be held. Accordingly, in the
Clause I submit I have incorporated the
provisions of the Small Dwellings Acquisition Act, which appear to be relevant
and important. I submit this Clause to
the House so as to enable proper conditions to be arranged between the local
authorities and tenant purchasers, dealing with the various matters which must
arise in regard to that relationship.

SURPLUS POTATOES.
Mr. MINFORD: I should like to inform the House that we have to-day in
the hands of Ulster farmers 14 million
tons of potatoes. According to the figures
of the Ministry of Agriculture it takes
£4,000,000 to produce that quantity.
We have grown in Northern Ireland
151,802 acres of potatoes, and that multiplied by eight brings in the quantity I
have mentioned. Our export trade to
other countries has been somewhere about
a quarter of a million tons per annum.
Last year our export trade dropped to
156,689 tons, and this year, up to the
moment, it is only somewhere in the
neighbourhood of 3,000 tons, which leaves
a large quantity to be shipped within four
months. Hon. Members know that
£4,000,000 to farmers in these depressing
times is something one must not lose sight
of. Farmers are prepared to take
£2,000,000 for the crop; that is to say
they lose £2,000,000 in order to get
£2,000,000. The Minister of Agriculture
has done good work in telling the farmers
to grow big crops, but if bigger crops are
grown they fail to get a market for them.
My question earlier in the day was as to
the establishment of a factory, or factories, where potatoes could be utilised
in the manufacture of Farino. I would
like to point out to the Minister that when
we began the housing scheme it was
suggested that the building of a lot of
houses would mean a solution of the housing problem. I suggest that the Minister
of Agriculture and the Minister of
Commerce should take some steps to
enable us to get a market for our potatoes.
About 1,000 tons of Farino and Dextine
were imported into Belfast last year. This
product costs, roughly, £10 to £15 a ton.
It takes about 5,000 tons of potatoes to
make that quantity of Farino. It may be
pointed out that this is not an economic
question, but it is a strange thing that
they have a Farino factory in the Free
State, and this will be sending flour into
the shops of the Belfast merchants. If
the Free State is able to do that with their
potatoes, we should, I think, be in a position to utilise the vast amount of surplus
potatoes we have to-day.

present imported from Amsterdam and
Brussels. I consider that the Minister of
Agriculture and Minister of Commerce
should get into touch with the Ministers
of Agriculture in Amsterdam and Brussels and find out all information about this
industry. We are on good terms with
our European neighbours. I also consider it is the duty of this Government to
endeavour to relieve the farmers of this
glut of potatoes. It is true that the farmers have been derated, have had land
purchase conferred on them, and have got
considerable reductions in rent by way of
the annuities, and although I am not
blaming the Government, these are only
drops in the bucket compared with the
loss incurred by the enormous quantity of
potatoes going to loss. Even if 10,000
tons could be utilised in the manufacture
of Farino it would relieve the pressure to
some extent.
Last year we had all round our shores
thousands thousands of tons of potaupon
toes thrown into the sea. Surely that was
a pity when we are importing so much
maize meal. We should do something with
the potatoes. I got into touch with the
Ministries and threw out a feasible suggestion, but I have been told it is an uneconomic proposition, as to turn potatoes
into Farino to-day is not practicable owing
to foreign competition. Surely the people
in Amsterdam and Brussels do not get
potatoes for nothing. To-day the prices
of potatoes in Northern Ireland are something appalling. I believe you can buy
them for 25s a ton in the Ards Peninsula.
We have in Belfast a factory for the
manufacture of desiccated soup, and we
hear Members in this House talking about
encouraging Ulster industries. Here is a
soup which is not known in Belfast, but is
known in every house in London. I think
it is up to the Ministry to take some steps
to push this industry. Surely there is no
use in pushing Ulster industries if we are
going to allow £4,000,000 worth of potatoes to develop into manure. It amounts
to that. Here we have debated the
question of voting £600,000 for the Bann
drainage. I am not against it, but I think
steps should be taken to see that the land
worth being put under cultivation should
be cultivated.
It may be true that the farmers themselves should get into touch with
another and establish a factory, but in my
one
It may be there will be a glut of potatoes, and I think it a step in the right
direction to ask the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Commerce to call
a conference of all the people concerned in
order to find out what should be done. I
understand there was a factory at Portaferry some years ago. I did not go into

some years ago, controlled, I think, by
some people in London. I can give the

When all is said and done it amounts to
this. The Government should make in
this House a final declaration as to whether
or not it is going to be of any assistance
in the marketing of potatoes or if it is
going to give any assistance for the establishment of a factory in order to help
private enterprise. The farmers all over
the Six Counties are asking what is going
to be done with the potato crop. I do not
think we need look to England at the
moment for a large trade, because they are
in as bad a state as we are. When a
factory in Athlone can be erected and the
products of that factory be put into the
hands of the Belfast merchants the
Ministry of Agriculture and the Ministry
of Commerce should surely get into touch
and see what can be done in the way of a
factory or factories here.

The question suggested a means of getting rid of the surplus potatoes by the
manufacture of starch. Well, now, that
is entering into a very difficult field, and
I would like to remind hon. Members that
owing to the nature of its origin, starch
is the most abundant substance present in
the plant kingdom composition with the
exception of cellulose. There must be
considerable competition in the world's
markets, not only in regard to starch derived from various plants, but also
amongst the different countries producing it.
And so the potato is only one
source of very many from which starch
can be derived.
The hon. Member for East Down (Col.
Gordon) particularly asked me to state as
a matter arising out of the question the
amount of starch used in the manufacture
and finishing of linen. The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Minford), in speaking of this matter, answered a great
many of the questions put forward by
himself. He reminded the House that
the annual output of potatoes in Northern
Ireland amounts to nearly a million and
a-quarter tons. In ordinary years we
would hope to export a quarter of a million tons. Now the imports of starch
into the port of Belfast-and I think the
bulk of our supplies come that wayamount to 27,000 or 28,000 hundredweights, and in order to produce this
quantity of starch, a comparatively
negligible amount in view of the amount
of the total crop, say, 5,000 to 7,000 tons
of potatoes, would be ample—that is, to
produce the entire quantity of starch imported into the port of Belfast.
Our difficulties in the present season
undoubtedly are aggravated by the fact
that England herself this year seems to
have produced from 200,000 to 300,000
tons of potatoes in excess of her own requirements. I believe these potatoes are
now being sold throughout the English
agricultural districts at the low sum of
something like 30s a ton. As to subsidising any industry which might be
started in the North of Ireland for the
production of starch the question naturally arises, is the production of starch the
most profitable or most suitable industry
in which we ought to put any money we
have to spare? I find that a factory was
actually started in the Ards district.

That they had considered Burns's

through the Bill and made amendments

Rankin's Divorce Bill.
The following Report was made from

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Drainage Bill.
As amended considered.
CLAUSE 20 (Procedure in connection
with county councils' drainage schemes).
(1) Section one of the Drainage Act
(Northern Ireland), 1925 (in this Part
of this Act referred to as "the Act of
1925'') shall have effect as if the following sub-section were substituted for
sub-section (3) thereof :—
(3) Where the county surveyor, or
other duly authorised officer of the
county council, certifies that the probable cost of the scheme for undertaking
drainage works will amount to a sum
less than one thousand pounds, and the
scheme will not involve the compulsory
acquisition of land, the scheme may be
carried out by the county council upon
being confirmed by them. A scheme to
which this sub-section applies is in this
Act referred to as a "minor scheme,"
and a minor scheme shall specify such
matters and contain such provisions as
are authorised by, or may be prescribed
under, this Act.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In regard to the amendments
to this Measure that have been suggested
and I think agreed to generally, the first
is to be found on page 19, and it is intended to leave out the word "one"
("one thousand pounds') and insert
"two." It will be recalled that during
the discussion in the Committee stage
some doubts were entertained by those representing the county authorities that
£1,000 for a minor scheme was too low.
I was myself doubtful about it, because
I had not any expert knowledge, and
suggested it should lie over to the Report
stage. It has been considered,
having received advice from those who
claim to know, and also those representing the county authorities, it has been
suggested that £2,000 might be inserted
in the Measure instead of £1,000. I
think it is generally conceded that this is
agreeable to the authorities. I beg to
move.
Amendment agreed to.

CLAUSE 1 (Amendments as to penalties for speed offences).
(1) Where a person is convicted of a
speed offence under the Motor Vehicles
(Traffic and Regulation) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1926 (in this Act referred to
as "the principal Act'), no previous
convictions of that person for a speed
offence shall be taken into account for
the purpose of determining the penalty
for the first-mentioned offence, or in
connection with the suspension of the
licence of that person for the first-mentioned offence, if a period of twelve
months or more has elapsed since his
last such previous conviction; and paragraph (i) of the proviso to sub-section.
(1) of section four, and sub-section (2)
of section six, of the principal Act shall
be subject to the provisions of this section.
(2) The right of a person, under subsection (3) of section four of the principal Act, to obtain a new licence free
from endorsement shall, in a case where
the endorsements on the endorsed
licence relate to speed offences only,
arise when no conviction for a speed
offence has been endorsed thereon during a continuous period of twelve
months.
(3) In this section the expression
"speed offence" means an offence under
sub-section (2) of section six of the principal Act consisting of the driving of a
motor car at a speed exceeding a speed
limit referred to in that sub-section.

would remind the Committee that this

co-ordination of traffic
Hon. Members are aware that in those
days it was quite a common thing on the
road to see four or five motor buses belonging to rival owners all starting together and trying to see which would be
first at their destination. They raced
each other in order to take up traffic, and,
what was far worse, the owners brought
their influence to bear on the employees
to break the law. The unfortunate
drivers at that time were placed between
the devil and the deep, blue sea, because,
on the one hand, they were faced with a
prosecution and, on the other, with the
possibility of losing their jobs.
Owing to the co-ordination of traffic
such a thing is now impossible, as the
buses must start at regular intervals.
They are not allowed to start together
and have this road racing. I know many
men who had a clean sheet for several
years, but who as the result of this racing
have been convicted, say, twice, and at
the present time if they commit what we
may call a technical offence they would.
automatically lose their licences. My
hon. Friend who moved this Amendment
desires that a man should have a clean

one year. I say one year is quite sufficient, and I have a very much higher
opinion of the ordinary bus driver than

should make it harder for the wrongdoer

Major SHILLINGTON: I beg to move
in Clause 2, page 2, line 24, to leave out
from "court" ("at the discretion of the
court") to the end of line 27, and to insert

the
I was encouraged to put this Amendment down because I rather gathered from
the Parliamentary Secretary of
Ministry of Home Affairs (Mr. Hanna)
that he thought there was something in
the point I was trying to make on this
Clause in the course of the debate on the
Second Reading of this Bill. I would like
first of all to make it perfectly clear that
I do not at all object to the alternative
offered in the first part of this Clause, although, as far as I can gather, we are
going ahead of Great Britain in this
matter. I do not see anything about an
alternative charge in the legislation which
they are going to introduce shortly over
there. But, as we are going ahead of
them, we should be very careful to see what
the effect of this provision is going to be.
The effect, I think, is that if a man is not
found guilty of manslaughter, but found
guilty of reckless driving or of driving to
the danger of the public, he is then subject
to a much heavier penalty than if he had
in the first place been charged with reckless driving or with driving to the danger
of the public.
I do not think that bears out the elements of British justice. The Minister
must realise that if a man is found not
guilty on a manslaughter charge that
charge is wiped out altogether, and the
charge is then only one of reckless driving
or of driving to the danger of the public.
We have a set of penalties under the 1925
Act for that particular offence, and I cannot see why there should be a different set
of penalties under this Bill for exactly a
similar offence simply because it is being
tried in a different court. Of course I
know I am not going to have the support
of the legal Gentlemen in the Committee
on this Amendment. They tell me that
there is a precedent for this procedure in
the case of a number of different charges
or crimes. But if that is so I do not think
we should perpetuate a state of things like
that, but should have the same set of
penalties for any offence, whether it is tried
in a court of summary jurisdiction or in
a higher court.
As the Committee may be aware the
penalties, if the case is tried in a court of
summary jurisdiction, are for a first offence
a fine up to £10, for a second offence a
fine not exceeding £20, and for a third
offence a man is liable to a fine of £50 or
a term of imprisonment not exceeding
three months. If the charge is proven and
the man found guilty, no matter what
court he may be tried in, I think the penalties provided for in the court of summary
jurisdiction are quite sufficient for that
particular charge. It seems to be another
way of trying to formulate two different
types of charge of reckless driving, and I
think it would be a mistake to sanction
anything of that sort. I hope the
Minister, having considered the matter
since the Second Reading, will now be
willing to accept the Amendment which I
beg to move.
Mr. MURPHY: I am sorry that on this
occasion I have to differ from the hon. and
gallant Member (Major Shillington). As he
has indicated, some of the legal Members of
this Committee, at least, do not agree with
him. I am afraid I am one of them because, as I have already indicated to the

Who are those persons? In the first
instance, the person who is charged with
manslaughter, who has the misfortune,
that is to say, to kill another person while
he is driving a motor car, is charged before
the magistrates. If the magistrates are of
opinion that there is no case made against
him they refuse informations. Before the
case can go forward for trial on that charge
of manslaughter the magistrates must
make up their minds that there is sufficient evidence to present to a jury, evidence on which a jury, if they think fit to
do so, would be entitled to act. Then the
matter goes before the Attorney-General,
who again considers whether or not on the
evidence before him it is a proper case in
which a charge of manslaughter should be
preferred. The matter does not end there.
Before the case goes before the petty jury,
the grand jury again considers the evidence of course not the evidence on
behalf of the prisoner, but the evidence on
behalf of the Crown or prosecution-and
the grand jury have to make up their
minds that there is a case to go before a
petty jury. Last, but not least, at the
trial, before the matter goes to the jury,
at the close of the Crown case the judge
makes up his mind on the question "Is
this or is it not a proper case to go to the
jury, or is it a case in which I should advise the jury at the close of the Crown
case that there is not sufficient evidence on
which they should convict, and in which I
should advise or direct them to enter a

to incur.

I have very little to add to what I said on

charge of a motor car on the public highway is guilty of an offence. This Amendment is simply to find a satisfactory equivalent for the word "drunk." There is

as it stands is not ideal. The Royal Commission, which is dealing with the matter
at present, has reported in favour of a

also in favour of a change, and I notice
that the Imperial Government in their
Bill, which was published on Saturday
last, have introduced a Clause very like
that which I suggest. I notice even that
such a staid and circumspect organ of

favours the changing of the law in this
respect.

Professor JOHNSTONE: I would like
to add a word with regard to this Amendment. I must say that I do like the form
of the Amendment as drafted by my hon.
Friend and colleague in the representation
of the University, particularly because he
says "driving or attempting to drive."
For a long time I have been very much
exercised in my mind over quite a number
of cases, which I have collected from public
prints and in other ways, of men who,
owing to the conviviality and hospitality
of their friends, have had rather too much
to drink, have started out to drive a motor
car, have pulled their car into the side of
the road, gone off to sleep, and have been
later found by the police, promptly arrested, and taken off to the barracks. I
do think that is not exactly in accordance
with justice or with the intention which
lies at the back of making drunkenness in
charge of a motor car a penal offence.
The idea of making drunkenness in charge
of a motor car a penal offence is to protect the public. What better thing
could a man who is too drunk to drive
his car do than to pull his car
in
to the side of the road, and,
in colloquial language, to sleep it off?
I think the police, instead of arresting a
man like that should encourage him.
Under this Amendment he would certainly
Road Traffic Bill-

Committee.
[Professor R. J. Johnstone]
escape, whereas under the Section which
the Minister of Home Affairs has suggested he would not escape, because he
would still be in charge of the car, although
he was sleeping in it. The man who has
displayed an amount of common sensein spite of the fact that he is drunkwhich he has shown by pulling his car
up, should not be penalised for that
action, which I hold is a common sense
action.
There is another point. I am not
satisfied with this Amendment because it
says "incapable of having proper control
of such machine." I think it is common
knowledge that a good many men who
have had considerably too much drink
are perfectly capable of having proper
control of their machine, but in a great
many cases they are not capable of having
a proper regard for the other users of
the road. They are able to drive and
control their machines, but not to have
a proper regard to the other users of the
road and to the safety of the public. It
is the safety of the public that we are
considering in this whole matter. I hope
that the Minister will very carefully consider this Clause, and bring in an Amendment which will cover these points.

I am moving this new Clause in the
interests of two classes of people. The

are not motor drivers. I listened to the

Road Traffic Bill-

know that a great number-I may say

Joint Committee on Local and Divorce
Bill Fees-Report.
The Committee have examined the
scale of Fees in respect of Local Bill and
Divorce Bill legislation, and recommend
to the House the amendments specified
in the appendix.
(1) As regards Divorce Bills the
Committee consider that there should
be a reasonable relation between the
Fees charged and the time of Members
and Officers of Parliament expended in
the passing of such Bills. In this respect they consider the existing scale
of Fees too high, and recommend reductions.
(2) As regards Local Bills the Committee are of opinion that the scale of
Fees is substantially correct, but recommend that there should be a reduction in the rising scale of certain Fees
payable in accordance with the money
to be raised or expended under a Bill
and in the Committee Fees

Pollock): This Money Resolution which
I am about to submit to the Committee
is the natural corollary of the Widows',
Orphans and Old Age Contributory Pensions Bill, which received a Second
Reading in this louse a few days ago.
The Money Resolution relates to the
additional charge which will be thrown
upon the public funds by reason of the
provisions of that Measure. First, 1
should say that a White Paper was prepared some time ago, and I think it has
been in the hands of Members for some
If it is convenient or in their
days.
hands it would greatly simplify the explanation which I propose to offer in connection with the Money Resolution.
The first part of the Resolution authorises the payment to the Ministry of
Finance Pensions Account of the additional State contributions required in the
years up to March 31, 1946, to enable
that account to meet its liabilities in that
period. The Bill makes no increase in
the amount of the contributions payable
by insured persons or their employers, so
that the cost of the new pensions brought
into existence by this Bill will have to be
found entirely out of public funds.
This
additional charge is represented by the
figure of £1,050,000, shown on page 6
of the White Paper, as being the estimated additional cost in the period up to
31st March, 1936, and the sum of
£1,150,000, which is estimated to be the
total additional charge in the subsequent
ten years' period ending on the 31st
March, 1946. These Estimates are based
on the best data available, but the subject
is naturally a very complex one. These
are only estimates made by the actuaries
to the best of their ability.
In addition to these amounts, however,
a further sum of about £500,000 has to
be provided in the period ending on the
31st March, 1936, to meet the deficiency
in the Ministry of Finance Pensions
Account, which would otherwise have
arisen had the annual State contribution
to the account been limited to the sum of
£140,000 per annum provided for by the
original Act. As has been explained in
the White Paper, the income from contributions has not come up to the figure
estimated when the finance of the 1925
Act was being considered, so that the
annual State payment of £140,000 provided for by that Act has fallen short of
the amount required by a sum estimated
at approximately half-a-million pounds in
the period up to 31st March, 1936.

The total amounts to be provided out
of voted moneys as contributions to the
Ministry of Finance Pensions Account
are, therefore, in the first place,
For the period ending 31st March,

and in the second place,
In the subsequent ten years' period,
ending 31st March, 1946, a total sum

I should point out, however, that the
figures which I have given are expected
to be the full maximum, and the Bill
authorises the Ministry of Finance to correct the figures in proportion to the exact
amount which the services will require
during the period.
The second part of the resolution deals
with the additional charge which will be
thrown on the Old Age Pensions (Non-
Contributory) Vote mainly by reason of
the fact that the class of widows who become entitled to Widows' Pensions under
Clause 1 of the Bill will, on reaching
70 years of age, become entitled to Old
Age Pensions, without any means test; as
the majority of these women would, however, in any case have been entitled to
old age pensions on reaching 70 even had
the means test been applied, the additional charge on this account will not be
great, and is not expected to exceed the
sum of £2,500 a year. That, I repeat,
is also a guess, but the calculation made is
as near as possible.
The third part of the Resolution authorises the payment out of voted moneys of
the additional State contribution under
the National Health Insurance Acts by
reason of the fact that Clause 20 of the
Bill enables certain additional classes of
persons to become voluntary contributors.
Under the National Health Insurance
Acts the amount of the State grant is onefifth of the benefits in case of women, and
one-seventh in the case of men. As, however, it is quite impossible to estimate the
numbers of persons who will exercise the
right to become voluntary contributors
under this Clause, the total amount of the
additional State grant in this respect cannot be estimated. It is not, however,
expected that it will be very considerable.
The final part of the Resolution authorises the payment out of voted moneys of
the remuneration of a Deputy Umpire to
be appointed for the purposes of Section
29 of the Act of 1925. The original Act
provided only for the appointment of one
Umpire, and it has been found this has
given rise to some inconvenience on occasions when the Umpire was not available.
The present Bill is intended to remedy
this defect, and, in consequence, it is
anticipated that appeals will be dealt with
more expeditiously. I think the statement I have made is sufficiently explanatory of this Money Resolution, and I beg
to move.

NEW CLAUSE (Powers of owners in
respect of Sections 4 and 5 of this Act.)
Without prejudice to the power of
the Ministry of Home Affairs under
the principal Act to attach as a condition of any control by the owners of any
tramway undertaking in connection
with the issue of licences for omnibuses
that the service afforded by such undertaking shall be adequate and satisfactory, nothing in Sections 4 and 5 of this
Act shall diminish or interfere with the
powers of such owners in connection
with the management and control of
such undertaking under the several
statutory enactments and orders affecting the same.
Brought up and read a First time.
Mr. BYRNE: I beg to move "That the
Clause be read a Second time."
When I spoke in support of the Second
Reading of this Bill I stated that I approved of its general principles and gave
my reasons for doing so, while, at the
same time, I indicated that some slight
alteration might be necessary in the Committee Stage, which, however, would not
affect the main principle of the Measure.
You will remember that in moving the
Second Reading of this Bill the Minister
of Home Affairs stated quite clearly that
the Corporation as omnibus owners were
placed in practically the same position as
other bus owners in every respect as regards fares, services, etc. Although I am

[Mr. Byrne]
a member of that body, I am bound to
admit that the control which has hitherto
been exercised by the Minister has been
beneficial to the public, and I cannot
claim that that control should be relaxed
in any degree.
The control, however, of a statutory
body in charge of a tramway undertaking
is of a rather different kind from that
exercised over private concerns running
buses for profit on the public roads. That
this is recognised by the Minister of
Home Affairs is shown by the fact that
he made the statement which I have
quoted. He went on to say that the
Corporation would only have the exclusive right to run omnibus services in the
city so long as and no longer than adequate and satisfactory services were
provided by them. Of that condition I
thoroughly approve, and I would not ask
the Minister for one moment to recede
from it in the slightest degree.
The only object of this Amendment is
to make clear what the control exercised
by the Ministry is to be. It is unnecessary to remind the House that the fares
chargeable in connection with the tramway buses are fixed by Statute, and that
the bus undertaking, along with the remainder of the tramway undertaking is
subject to a provision according to which
the fares chargeable on the undertaking
must be fixed so that the revenue will
meet the expenditure. This is a matter,
I am quite sure, in which there is no intention on the part of the Minister to
embarrass the Corporation, and I feel that
the only control contemplated by him is
one which he exercises already, namely,
the control which enables him to say
whether or not the services run by the
Corporation are adequate and satisfactory.
It further enables him, if he does not find
it adequate and satisfactory, to permit
outside buses to run and carry passengers
in the city.
I am glad to say that the tramway service at present is in a very satisfactory
condition, and we claim that it would be
unfair for the Ministry to take any further
powers of control than they already have.
We quite admit that the tramway undertaking was in a very unsatisfactory position, and there is a difference of opinion
between the Ministry and the Corporation
as to how that was brought about. I
referred to that matter yesterday. I think
that the acceptance of this New Clause
would be only fair to the Corporation. I
would like to say that the Corporation is
endeavouring in the tramway undertaking
to give every satisfaction to the public,
and I am glad to say that there is a great
improvement in the finances of the tramways. As that position improves, we
hope to add additional services, and we
already have added additional services.
We are sending out buses now from five
o'clock in the morning to meet the wants
of the bus men, charwomen, and people
of that class who had not a service at that
time of the day. We hope to meet all
the requirements of the public. I should
just like to state that I read in the
Telegraph" last night the following

following

Major BLAKISTON-HOUSTON: I
would like to ask the Minister of Home
Affairs if he could stiffen the back of
either the rural district councils or the
county councils, or whatever authorities
there are who build subsidy houses.
When a man builds a house on his own
he has a perfect right to build it where
he likes and how he likes, but once he
gets a grant from either the State or any
other authority it should be built on
ground that is absolutely dry and not ou
swampy ground. I know a great number
of subsidy houses that have been built on
ground that is only dry in the driest.
summer and that is wet in the winter
time. We should not encourage these, as
we may call them, rheumatism halls.
would like very much to ask the Minister
of Home Affairs if he could stiffen their
backs by an Order so as to prevent these
wet and unhealthy houses being erected.
It should be done in the beginning before
the plans come in. A man should not be
allowed to build before the site is passed.

from Northern Ireland, when put into

Minister take the necessary steps to ensure

facts relating to the marketing of cold
stored eggs are as stated.

and the House shall forthwith stand
adjourned.

The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND
MEANS: Perhaps a word from me would
dispel all fears and anxieties as well as
relieve all existing doubts respecting this
matter. By general Resolution at the
setting up of this Parliament we adopted
the practice in operation in the Imperial
Parliament. That meant that when any
hon. Member called the attention of Mr.
Speaker or the Chairman of Committees
to the fact that ten Members are not present the division bells are rung for two
minutes. Mr. Speaker or the Chairman
of Committees then proceeds to count the
House, and if it be found then or earlier
that ten or more Members are present,
the business proceeds. That has been the
practice, and the addition of these words
will in no degree alter or vary the
practice. All it will do will be, as is done
in the Imperial Parliament, so to clarify
the Standing Order as to conform strictly
in accordance with the practice. That is
the whole of the Gunpowder Plot.
Mr. HEALY: Will the Chairman of
Ways and Means explain to us what is the
need for this? I am very suspicious-
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND
MEANS: All that it is intended to do is
to put the Standing Order into conformity
with the immemorial practice. It is
strictly in accordance with the Resolution
passed by this House.
Mr. BEATTIE: The explanation given
by the Chairman of Ways and Means is
not sufficient to enlighten the hon. Member for South Fermanagh (Mr. Healy).
I always see clearly when looking at a
thing direct, but I must admit on this
occasion that the insertion of these words
makes the thing about as clear as
mud.

to throw

After the word "whom" in the third line
I want to add the words "the Minister
whose decision shall be final and conclusive." That is changing the principle

to the Minister. I believe there is more

have a man, who is himself finally responsible and who appears here daily before the Opposition, you are likely to get

Ministry that may be responsible for
carrying out legislation of this kind.
I want to tell the Committee that these
words have a step-by-step tinge. They
are not Socialistic words at all. They are
Conservative words. They were placed in
the Act by a Conservative Government,
and still retain their position and dignity
in the Bill before the British House of
Commons. I am only asking this Conservative Government to follow step by
step, not with the Socialist Government
but with a Government which I believe
represents their hearts' desire, and into
whose keeping they are praying Great
Britain will soon be restored. If I can
get this principle established in this one
small way, I am satisfied that I will have
it established throughout the whole Bill.
I want hon. Members on this side of the

He desires, I understand, that, instead
of the Ministry being the body responsible
for dealing with these claims, it should
be the Minister. I understand that is what
he is getting at. As the matter stands, and
as I said on the debate on the Second
Reading, in Northern Ireland the Minister and the Ministry are exactly the same
thing. The reason for the word "Ministry" being used more frequently in this
Bill than the word "Minister,'
pared with the usuage in Great Britain,
is because of our Ministries of Northern
Ireland Act, which was passed having regard to the Act under which we first
came into existence as a Parliament. I
hope the hon. Member will be satisfied
with my assurance that the two words are

Ireland person lives in Northern Ireland

but this is where the discrimination comes
in. We have a proposition to deal with
here which they have not got in Great
Britain, because it is not possible for a

and at the same time work in Great
Britain, but it is possible to live in one of

years' qualification is applied.
After this explanation I think the hon.
Member will see that this is a very easy
test to comply with. No Northern Ireland person can be deprived of the
benefits of this Bill by virtue of this
Clause provided that when in the Free
State he becomes a voluntary contributor

If we follow step by step for social purposes we should follow if it is for the good
of Ulster. The Amendment aims at providing for the unfortunate person who is
mixed up in an accident in which he is
an innocent participant in many cases. I
think it is apparent to the House how
many of these cases will happen and the
third party-he or she may be the breadwinner of the family. They may be completely knocked out, and yet they can get
no redress from the penniless driver. I
am speaking now of the irresponsible, foolhardy driver. I do not wish to say anything against the careful person. These
people are knocked out and they can get

The
It does not meet the case by any means
to say that every person knocked down by
a motor-car is entitled to compensation.
That is not the case by any means.
third party only comes in as an actuality
where there has been negligence proved on
the part of the driver or owner of the
vehicle or his agent. Now, I have been
very much interested in looking over the
report of the Select Committee of the
House of Lords, although compulsory insurance is not dealt with to any great
length. I may say with regard to third
party risk it does not hurt the careful
driver or the responsible person. They
are invariably protected by a proviso in
their own insurance, and it will be more or
less for their own protection to see that
the third party is not in any way aggrieved
so far as getting compensation. Everyone would not require to have that insurance if the Amendment is read and
understood.
"Every applicant for a licence for a
motor vehicle shall satisfy the Ministry
of Home Affairs that the licence holder
will be in a position to satisfy all lawful
claims which may be made against the
holder of the licence in respect of
damages to persons or to property
caused by the use upon public highways
of any motor or mechanically propelled
vehicle for which the licence is sought."
Therefore, I say that firms of standing
and business people or local authorities or
the Corporation would not require to have
third party insurance. But your irresponsible or reckless person or reckless
driver or owner would. From the very
fact that they are careless the last thing
in the world they would think of is taking
out a third party insurance. These are
the people that my Amendment deals
with.
The Select Committee of the House of
Lords considered this matter in connection with the Road Vehicles Regulation
Bill. And as everyone knows this
Committee met to discuss the question
of safety, and did not meet ostensibly for
the purpose of deciding ccmpulsory third
party risk.
And in the report there are
pages after pages of safety measures such
as police measures, four-wheel brakes,
lectures and propaganda on the safetyfirst principle. The only words the Committee spoke on it were in favour of compulsory third party insurance. They did
not recommend it. Nevertheless, in spite
of that, the Imperial Government introduced another Bill. There were two
Road Traffic Bill-
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major McCormick]
reasons why they did not recommend it.
One was mainly that their Bill was for
safety purposes. The other reason set
down by the Committee was more on
account of certain technical difficulties. I
will deal with the technical difficulties
later.
I do think a great many people have
placed too much importance on
this
report of the Select Committee because
throughout it all there are only about
two dozen lines dealing with compulsory
insurance. Their recommendation so far
as safety goes is that they advocate the
removal from the public highway of the
reckless driver rather than, in their own
words, "giving the impression that we
are relying on insurance by relieving
financial liability or responsibility for the
results of reckless driving." So much
for the report of the Select Committee.
The Select Committee did not pretend
to go into the merits of compulsory insurance, and yet it has been included in
the Bill.
I find also by this report that other
countries that have accepted the principle
of compulsory insurance are countries
similar to our own-small countries such
as Denmark, Norway, Finland, and the
State of Massachusetts in America.
These have adopted third party compulsory insurance. And might I mention
another country, very often quoted in
this House for comparison-I mean in
reference to taxation and populationthat is, New Zealand. New Zealand is
having compulsory insurance coming in.
It will be in operation in June next.
Now, regarding the technical difficulty
which the Select Committee spoke of I
suggest that this analogy is favourable
to our Six County area. The reason
the Select Committee thought there were
technical difficulties was because of the
greater population and greater congestion of traffic in the United Kingdom.
We have it on record that there are something between 200,000 and 300,000 accidents occurring annually and a fatality
list of over 5,000 deaths. These are
alarming figures. I submit we have a
much more compact situation than the
Select Committee had. They might well
hesitate before they recommended that
there should be compulsory third party
risk. I might say this regarding the
difficulties that have been spoken of-

(1) of Clause 5 the following new subsection be inserted: Every applicant
for
a licence for a motor vehicle
shall satisfy the Ministry of Home

respect of

for which the licence is sought."--(Major

Major McCORMICK: I have anticipated objections to my Amendment.
What is spoken of as the greatest obstacle
is the insurance companies. In that regard I may quote from Earl Russell's
speech in the House of Lords on Thursday last. You remember Earl Russell
was a Member of the Select Committee
that brought in the report. Turning to
the question of compulsory third-party insurance, Earl Russell referred to his conference with representatives of insurance
companies, and added, "They will not
raise their premiums in consequence of
the passage of this Bill."
That was one
thing said, and said very often, that insurance companies would undoubtedly
raise their rates. There is a declaration
of a Member of the Select Committee to
the effect that they will not do so. So far
as the insurance companies are concerned
I would suggest that there should be a
register of insurance companies on the
same lines as life insurance companies if
necessary, and that there should be a
tariff drawn up after consultation, on the
same lines as the House of Lords Committee when they embodied third-party
risk in their Bill. That conference came
to a satisfactory basis. I do not see any
reason why it should not be done in the
case of this Bill.
I hesitate to suggest that the Ministry
of Home Affairs should fix the premiums
or in any way control that matter, because I feel that I might be submerged in
a flood of debate as to interference
with vested interests or be accused of
advocating State control or something
I will not do so.
along Socialistic lines.
In any case I should say that I would
allow insurance companies the right to
object to any risk, and consequently it
would be the licensing authority's
obvious duty to refuse that person's
licence. I think a great thing may be
made out of that so far as safety goes,
and I ask where a licence is refused by
a licensing authority-in this case the
Ministry of Home Affairs-and where
the insurance company will not take the
particular risk, why should the third
party not only take the risk but be
possibly the victim of accident?
Here, indeed, to my mind is a good
solution of the safety problem. I refer
to getting rid of dangerous and foolhardy drivers. The insurance companies
will get together and will form a black
list, and they will have these men segregated from the responsible and careful
driver. The result will be it will be the
obvious duty of the authority to refuse
the licence.
an
I would impress on the House the
importance of this Amendment. I
think a great deal could be done as far
as safety goes. I think indeed that
there is the onus and responsibility on
the Government, and it is their duty to
look after the safety of the public, not
only under this present Act but under the
Act of 1926. A great deal could be done
along these lines, and I think it would be
a step forward towards safety. There
are those who daily discharge the responsibility of dealing with human life or
anyhow of having it in their keeping for
the time being. I am referring now to

My experience during the last year in

most difficult and complex. Our

When we come to the question of compulsory insurance, the initial difficulty
is this. First of all every insurance
policy is drafted with the object of giving

of limiting the liability of the insurance

Road Traffic Bill-
Report.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
and not the protection of either the owner

It must be clear to everyone that the
views of the insurance company and the
insured person on the one hand, and
those of the Ministry, as representing the
general public on the other hand, are as
wide apart as the poles.
We also found that if the public are to
have adequate protection it is necessary
in all cases that the insurance policies
should be materially modified with a substantial increase of risk on the part of the
insurance company. Therefore, as I
have already said, one of our difficulties
was to obtain the necessary modifications
in the form of the insurance policies.
May I take one case as an example.
Buses are insured on a basis of so much
per seat, but every insurance policy contains a Clause which provides that, in the
event of the bus being overcrowded, the
liability of the insurance company is
limited to a proportionate number of the
total number carried. The balance of the
risk is to be provided for by the owner.
Take, for example, a 32-seater bus which
is insured, It is overcrowded and carrying 44 passengers when the accident takes
place. The insurance company is only
liable for 32/44ths of the damage, and
there is, therefore, no guarantee whatever that the owner is in a position to bear
the balance of the costs, namely 12/44ths.
Here, again, as a result of negotiations
with the insurance companies, we got an
agreement from the companies that they
would bear the total cost in the first instance and trust to getting the money back
from the insured owner.
There is another difficulty. Hon. Members are aware that the basis on which
an insurance policy is founded is the
original proposal form, and it is the
settled law that if, innocently or otherwise, there is a material mis-statement
the policy is void from the very commencement. If, for example, an applicant,
bona fide, makes a mis-statement as to
the number of accidents in which he has
been involved, that policy would be void.
I would like to ask the House, and my
hon. and gallant Friend who has moved
this amendment, how is an eventuality
like this to be guarded against. It is
not practical politics to examine and
verify proposals for insurance, and I confess at the moment I see no solution.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The object
of this Bill is to establish a Central
Criminal Lunatic Asylum in Northern
Ireland. Hon. Members are no doubt
aware that at the time of the setting up
of the Government of Northern Ireland,
there was only one Criminal Lunatic
Asylum for the whole of Ireland, and
that
Co.
was situated in Dundrum,
Dublin. At the time of the transfer of
the services, there were several criminal
lunatics from the North of Ireland incarcerated there, and some of them are
still there, and since that time, the Free
State Government allowed us to keep
them there, we paying the cost of
maintenance. Unfortunately the cost
per capita for the maintenance was a very
heavy one amounting at one time to no
less a sum than £200, and the present
figure is somewhere in the neighbourhood
of £175. There are 20 Northern Ireland
lunatics in Dundrum. Following the
establishment of the Government of
Northern Ireland, the Government went
very closely into the question of providing some solution for the difficulty.
Having regard to the small numbers in
Northern Ireland, the Government
hesitated to set up a completely new
establishment, with its consequentia

Asylum. By doing so we would be able

The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND
MEANS (Mr. Moles): When the Motion
that stands in my name was before the
House yesterday, I pointed out that it
represented the unanimous recommendations of a Select Committee which had
been set up to find out what changes ought
to be made in the scale of fees in relation
to Private Bills. You, Sir, pointed out
that it was the usual practice when the
House had delegated this authority to such
a Select Committee to rely on that Committee as having explored the whole question, and in the interests of the House
had brought forward these recommendations. I ventured to support the
recommendations in a speech which U
thought was marked by such clarity, such
a wealth of information and such eloquence as is rarely heard that it would
have carried conviction. I need hardly
say I was deeply disappointed to be told
that it left the position as clear as mud.
will now attempt the responsible task of

Γ
This scale of fees represents the scale
approximately that was in operation in relation to some Bills when promoted before
the Imperial Parliament. A very large
saving was effected by reason of the fact
that, instead of having to transport a great
body of witnesses and officials to Westminster and keeping them there sometimes
for weeks and even months on end, here
the moment we took a Bill in the Committee stage that Bill was pursued day
Local and Divorce Bills-
Fees
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Moles]
after day until its completion in say three
or four days, sometimes only one day.
There was a large saving. We propose to
effect in the interests of those who desire
to promote Bills a still further and greater
saving. Experience shows us that we can
push these Bills through upon a lesser
scale of fees than at the moment obtains.
It is to be observed that the fees lodged
are the fees payable to this House and not
otherwise. It is not the policy to make
profit out of the promotion of Private
Bills. It is the policy to see that such
cost as is incidental in the working of this
House shall be discharged by the persons
promoting them. This reduction represents what we think is as far as we can
safely go in the matter of the reduction
of fees. It will almost exactly equal
the sum which would be necessary to expend in the discharge of the various functions in private Committees of the House.
That, I hope, has succeeded in throwing
light on places not sufficiently illuminated.
I turn to one other matter calling for
explanation, that is the scale of fees in
relation to Divorce Bills. I was asked
yesterday whether I would state what
would be the amount of reduction. The
old scale of fees represented about £45 or
over, for the promotion of a Divorce Bill.
The new scale of fees which we think we
may safely introduce will bring the cost
down to about £13. The Committee do
not see their way to recommend more than
that at the moment, and I am sure the
House will be content to be guided by the
Committee of experts who have thoroughly
examined the whole question.

There was one other matter, although

Some point
was raised as to whether in fact there

do not propose to enter into a large theological question of the kind. The House
must deal with the law as it stands for
the moment. The old practice, as my
legal Friends know, where incompatibility and other matters arose, was that
access was had to the courts. If the courts
were satisfied a decree a mensa et thoro
was granted. If the parties or either of
them desired to proceed further than what
was in effect a judicial separation, they
proceeded to the House of Lords at Westminster and there promoted a Private Bill.
That was a very costly proceeding, open
only to the wealthy and surrounded with
great difficulties. But it has been contended that the poor in given circumstances have as much right to relief as
the wealthy, and so in due course the
procedure at Westminster was transferred
to here. I hope I have sufficiently justified the Motion to carry the House with
me.

way. They will be filled by friends of the
right hon. Gentleman. If they are recruited from the prison service it will leave
further vacancies for some other of his
friends. The vacancies will not be filled
by competitive examination as in most
other places. You have a Bill here, therefore, bristling with difficulties from the
point of view of the taxpayers, of the
public and of the citizens of Derry. Derry
jail is located in the very midst of the city.
No doubt when the jail was originally
built the city was a much smaller affair
than it is to-day. The prison of Derry is
set down in a big congested area. There
is no space for exercises except its dark
yards; it is surrounded by very high walls
that shut out the light to a great extent
and make the place unsuitable for either
prisoners or lunatics. I hope, therefore,
that this House will reject this Criminal
Lunatics Bill.
Mr. HANNA: The hon. Member (Mr.
Healy) suggests that there has been some
irregularity in connection with this matter.
May I remind him that when the House
discussed the Estimates an appropriate i
sum of money was granted for the purpose
of making Derry prison suitable for
criminal lunatics. This Bill only asks permission now to remove the criminal
lunatics from the place where they are at
present incarcerated to the place in Derry
provided for them. There is no Member
of the Government, and I am sure no
Member of the House, who would not be
anxious to secure for each and everyone of
these unfortunate individuals the greatest
care, medical and otherwise, that it is in
our power to secure for them.
What do we do?. The Government has
been helped in this matter by all the
different boards who take charge of the
different district asylums in our area.
1973 Criminal Lunatics Bill-

Adjournment
They work in the greatest harmony with
us. Those criminal lunatics who can
properly and with safety be taken to district asylums are admitted into these institutions and are looked after most carefully there. But there is another type
of criminal lunatic who must be kept in
a cell by himself. His disease demands
it. What can be done for him except to
have a warder in constant attendance on
him?
Mr. HEALY: Leave him where he is.
It is cheaper.
Mr. HANNA: If we leave him where
he is we leave him in a place outside our
jurisdiction. It costs almost £200 a year
per head for the maintenance of criminal
lunatics. We save money in this connection. I do not think the House would
welcome me standing up here and continuing an argument on the saving of
money in connection with the performance of duties such as we are called upon
to do. It is our job as a Government to
look after those afflicted people who come
within our jurisdiction. This House has
already approved of this matter when it
granted money for the site at Derry. All
we ask the House to do now is to give
warrant to the Government to have these
people transferred from the place where
they are to Derry. Perhaps I might say
that I think we will save something in
the neighbourhood of £1,500 a year by
reason of this change. I do hope the
House will now proceed to give the Bill
a Second Reading.
I rise to sup-
Major MCCORMICK:
port this Bill. I do so because I think it
is only right and proper that criminal
lunatics should be segregated from the
ordinary and normal criminals.
I do not
understand for one moment why the hon.
Member (Mr. Healy) should oppose such
a far-reaching Bill. Why should we keep
our criminal lunatics in the Free State
when we have accommodation for them
here? Derry prison is in an almost perfect state now to accommodate the criminal
lunatics who are in the Free State at the
present time. I think it is only right
that we in Northern Ireland should take
charge of our own criminal lunatics.
I fully appreciate the remarks of the
Parliamentary Secretary as to the need
for looking after these people. They require treatment entirely separate from
that accorded to the ordinary prisoner or
normal criminal. I see by Clause 4 of
the Bill, which deals with the transfer of
criminal lunatics to district lunatic
asylums, that power is given to the
Governor the same as provided in the
Lunacy (Ireland) Act, 1901. That is a
proper provision. It is only right in
these days of progressive civilisation that
there should be a separation of these
sections of criminals. There is one
question I would like to ask. At what
age is a person considered a criminal
lunatic?
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: That does
not arise on this Bill, the question of
a criminal lunatic having been, so far as
this Bill is concerned, determined by a
court of law.
Major MCCORMICK: I am quite satisfied with the explanation. I will conclude
by saying that I support the Second Reading of this Bill.

thereby reduce very considerably the flooding in the whole Clogher Valley area.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The Government has not so far
adopted the principle of grants in aid of
drainage schemes undertaken by county
councils. In some cases where unemployed
labour may have been specially recruited.
for the works grants on the usual basis have

malicious injuries, I cannot hold out anv
hope that the Government will find itself
in a position to depart from its present
practice.

RICHHILL P.E. SCHOOLS.
2. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Finance whether it is a fact
that in July last his Ministry proposed
to transfer certain endowments in connection with three Public Elementary Schools
in County Armagh, namely, Battlehill,
Derryhale and Richhill, to the Armagh
County Council or the Education Authority for the county, and whether he can
state why this arrangement has not been
carried out.
Mr. POLLOCK : The answer to the
first part of the hon. and gallant Member's
question is in the affirmative.
As regards the second part of the question, I should explain that Richhill School
is a newly-built provided school, while
Battlehill and Derryhale Schools are old
school buildings. The endowments belonging to the two last-named schools pass
to the Education Authority with the premises themselves, in pursuance of statutory
arrangements made under the Education
Act (Northern Ireland), 1923, but so far
my Ministry has been unable to act, as it
is still awaiting a reply from the Education Authority in regard to the formality
of transferring the securities.

the old Richhill School, which has not
been transferred, though it has ceased to

but only in those cases where hardship

illustrate.
A young widow of 28 years was left in
1927 with two small children-one seven
and the other four years old. Her husband
was an insured worker from 1912 to 1924.
He paid his contributions during that
period. In 1924 slackness came about in
his employment. He was a shipyard
worker. Before he would loaf or hang
round the bureau he set himself the task
of building subsidy houses. He would
have built a house for any individual who
could put down the capital. He did that
for two and a half years, and at the end
of that time his health broke down, and he
died in 1927, only three years from 1924.
He left a widow and two children. To-day
the Minister says, "I cannot interfere in
the matter as the Ministry has decided that
the average of three years has not been
conformed with." The rules and regulations here relating to the average basis do
not meet the claim, but I am satisfied that
if we had Mr. Greenwood here as Minister
the widow would be granted her pension.

same offence. He was fined a sum equivalent to the amount he defrauded the
Ministry of, which was quite right, and
now they are going to fine him again for
the same thing. That is contrary to all
principles of British justice that I am
acquainted with. It was always a principle of British justice not to punish a
man twice for the same offence.
Now, I dare say I can say something
about courts of referees. Courts of referees are paid by the session. They get,
I think, two guineas a session, consequently, the more courts they have the
more money the Chairman gets. I am not
saying they do it, but by rejecting claims
there is the temptation that the case may
come on again, and if it is rejected again
it comes on once more, and the more
claims they reject the more claims they
have to hear and the more sessions they
get. That is a wrong principle. I am
not saying they do it. I am not saying
that it affects their judgment, but I am
saying the temptation is there. If
they reject a great many claims these.
people are likely to appeal and come back,
and there will be another session and
another two guineas.

a week unemployment insurance benefit,
and 7s for his wife, which makes 24s. On
attaining the age of 65, he makes application for the old-age pension. The Employment Exchange, assuming that he is
65, stops his unemployment insurance
benefit. Ultimately he produces sufficient evidence to show that he is 65, and
he draws the old-age pension, but probably he does not receive any back money
to which he presumed he was entitled.
Under this Bill, when a man in those circumstances makes application for the oldage pension we do not stop his unemployment insurance benefit, nor do the health
insurance authorities stop his health insurance benefit. He still receives the 24s for
himself and his wife until he vindicates
his right to the pension of 10s a week at
the age of 65. If it is discovered that he
was entitled to the pension two months
earlier, and that during those two months
he was drawing 24s a week unemployment
insurance benefit, he recoups the authorities the amount that he is overpaid. I
think that must be perfectly plain to a
man of the legal acumen of the hon. Member for South Down.
Mr. NIXON: No; he receives nothing
for the two months.
Mr. GRANT: Repeat it again.

the conditions under which a man is entitled to a pension. I have gone over almost every section of this Bill very lucidly,

Where at the date of the commencement of this Act any infant is in the
custody of, and being brought up,
maintained and educated by any person
or two spouses jointly as his, her or their
own child under any de facto adoption,
and has for a period of not less than two
years before such commencement been
in such custody, and been so brought
up, maintained and educated, the Court
may, upon the application of such person or spouses, and notwithstanding
that the applicant is a male and the

the infant to be obtained, upon being
satisfied that in all the circumstances of

the welfare of the infant that no such
consent should be required and that an
adoption order should be made.

Oral Answer to Question.
FLOODING IN DONEGALL AVENUE
AREA, BELFAST.
Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
certain houses forming a new colony in
the Donegall Avenue area, Belfast, on
which a Government subsidy is being paid,
are erected on ground that was formerly
a series of cesspools; whether flooding took
place there two years ago; and whether
on Saturday, the 7th instant, the houses
were flooded to the extent of two feet;
whether he can state who approved of the
sites, and, in view of the recent report of
the Tuberculosis Medical Officer for Belfast, whether he will exercise a stricter
supervision in this matter in future.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In reply to the first
part of the question, I have caused inquiries to be made, and am informed that
no cesspools have ever existed in this area.
With regard to the second part of the
question, it is not the case that houses
were flooded to the depth of two feet.
The water did not reach floor level, but in
some cases water was driven by the wind
under the doors. Only six houses were
affected.
The flooding was due to the overflow
of the Blackstaff River, which rose to the
height of 3 feet above the crown of the
bridge. The street is only in course of
construction at present, and the necessary
gullies to carry off surface water have not
yet been provided.
I understand that the Corporation has
under consideration a scheme for preventing flooding by the Blackstaff.
In all cases the Ministry of Home
Affairs before passing a house for subsidy
satisfies itself that the site is suitable and
insists on proper precautions being taken
for drainage.
I need hardly point out that the recent
floods were abnormal.
Mr. HEALY: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that the flooding was of a
depth of two feet and extended over an
area of an English mile from these houses
to a place called Stockman's Lane, that
it was in width half a mile, and that
photographs which I can give to the right
hon. Gentleman show the actual flooding?
Is the right hon. Gentleman also aware
that Dr. Thomson, Medical Officer of
Health, and Dr. Trimble, Tuberculosis
Medical Officer, have constantly been laying emphasis on the importance of healthy
housing conditions being provided by the
Corporation, and that the Corporation are
apparently ignoring that advice?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
can hardly deny that he is making something in the nature of a speech.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
stated that the houses were not flooded
to the depth indicated.
Mr. HEALY: Let the right hon.
Gentleman look at these photographs and
repeat his answer if he dare.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think those
bear out my contention.
Mr. HEALY: What?
Mr. SPEAKER: This photographic
discussion may take place in the Lobby
after the House has risen.
Mr. HEALY: I beg to give notice that
I will raise this matter on the Adjournment.

Stand-
What is the good of the Tuberculosis
Officer making recommendations to the
Government and the Corporation, and
what is the good of the Medical Officer of
Health making certain suggestions if both
the Corporation and the Government are
going to ignore them? Anybody knows,
apart altogether from what the Medical
Officer may say in this matter, that it is
very unhealthy to build houses in swamps,
and that there should exist in the City of
Belfast an area of this kind subject to
periodic flooding is the best condemnation
of the whole Corporation scheme, and also
of the subsidies granted by the Government. Some of these houses are erected
by the Corporation, and some of them are
being erected by private builders, but
whether they be one or other, they are
receiving the subsidy, and the Government,
therefore, have equal responsibility for
them. My information is that this is
filled ground, that before the houses were
erected on this plot, perhaps two or three
years ago, there were a number of cesspools there, and that it is absolutely and
entirely unsuited for the erection of artisans' dwellings or any sort of houses.
In the circumstances I think that the
Government have a very grave responsibility and that they ought not to waste the
public money in this way. There are
plenty of healthy sites in the vicinity of
Belfast, without selecting swamps of this
character. I make no allegation as to any
ulterior motives, either on the part of the
Corporation or private individuals, but
there must be some explanation for choosing a locality of this kind on which to

Oral Answer to Question.
WORRYING OF LAMBS BY DOGS.
Colonel GORDON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether in view of the
approaching lambing season, he will instruct the police authorities to strictly
enforce the law regarding dogs straying
by night, and thereby prevent loss of
sheep and lambs to the farming community.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The police have already received instructions upon this
point, but their particular attention will
again be directed to the matter in question.

Woodvale (Mr. Nixon). The only thing I
have to say about it is this: Hon. Members opposite know quite well that if the
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) did
introduce an Unemployment Insurance
Bill at the moment he would simply be
cutting through the agreement he has
made with the Chancellor and the representatives of the Government on the other
side, and that when their Act was passed
on the other side, if our Act was not on
parallel lines with it, it would simply
mean that we would have violated our
agreement with the British Exchequer.
The result would be that the workpeople
of Northern Ireland, whom hon. Members
opposite profess to represent, would be the
sufferers if the Minister of Labour brought
in this hasty legislation which they are
trying to force on to-day. From that
point of view, and in the real interests of
the workers I support this Motion.
Question put: "That this House, at
its rising this day, do adjourn until
Tuesday, the 18th day of February, provided that if it appears to the satisfaction
of Mr. Speaker, after consultation with
the Government, that the public interest
requires that the House should meet at
any earlier time during the adjournment,
Mr. Speaker may give notice that he is
so satisfied, and thereupon the House
shall meet at the time stated in such
notice, and shall transact its business as
if it had been duly adjourned to that
date."
The House divided: Ayes, 18; Noes, 1.
