exceptions, indeed, the fishermen are meeting their obligations in the matter of repayments in a very satisfactory manner.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The total
amount of the loans so far granted under
the Ministry's scheme is £4,000.
Another way in which the Ministry is
helping the sea-fishing industry is by the
branding of herrings with a special mark
where the quality conforms to a certain
standard. The standard of quality which
the Ministry has set is extremely high,
so that little surprise will be felt when
I state that Government-branded Northern Irish herrings command the very
highest prices on the Continental markets,
and are always a marketable commodity,
even when business is sluggish.
The Ministry's interest in the herrings
landed in Northern Ireland does not cease
'with the application of the brand, but
extends right up to the point of sale.
Last year the fishery officer of the Ministry paid a visit to the principal markets
for Northern Irish-cured herrings, and
examined numerous consignments of our
native cure which were being held in
store. In this way it has been possible
to ensure proper warehousing and also to
satisfy ourselves that the methods employed in curing were such as prevented
deterioration. The visit also served the
useful purpose of bringing to the notice
of the importers and others interested
the actual significance of the brand, and
of ascertaining, with an exactitude that
would not otherwise have been possible,
the special requirements of the various
markets.
I now pass to the power, transport and
companies' branch of my Department. In
addition to its statutory functions, with
which the Committee is familiar, this
branch is responsible for dealing with
questions of harbour development and
electricity.
I have been criticised in certain
quarters for not embarking upon large
schemes of fishery harbour development, which would impose substantial
burdens upon the taxpayers of Northern Ireland, and I think it important,
accordingly, to direct the attention of the
Committee for a few moments to the true
proportions of the sea-fisheries problem.
Of the population of our Province, less
than 700 men are wholly dependent upon
sea fishing for a livelihood. They live in
scattered communities in the small fishing
ports, or hamlets, around our coasts, and
they ply their trade for the most part in
small craft. I am advised that, if a
central fishing port could be provided in
Northern Ireland, it would be difficult, if
not impossible, to induce these fishermen
to leave their present homes and migrate
to it. If we exclude the herring catch
which is landed at the port of Ardglass,
mainly from Scottish drifters, we find that
the total value of the fish landed by our
own community in all ports is only some
£24,000 per annum.
Clearly under these circumstances it is
difficult to establish a case for the expenditure of a large sum of public money
Supply-
Committee
5 JUNE 1929
upon the development of a new fishing
centre. Members of the Committee will
have observed from the Report of the
Departmental Advisory Committee, which
I set up in 1927 to consider the question
of the development of fishery harbours in
Northern Ireland, that there is little
prospect of developing a white fishing industry in Northern Ireland because of
the eclectic nature of the local demand,
which deprives our fishermen of a local
market for the coarser varieties of white
fish caught. Moreover, irregularity in
'the landings of white fish around our
coasts makes it difficult for local dealers
to secure steady supplies, and they have,
accordingly, been forced to import their
requirements from those large centres
across the Channel, from which supplies
can be obtained. It must also be borne
in mind that for the white fishing industry, as distinct from the herring industry, ample accommodation already
exists at the ports of Belfast and Londonderry, and, to a lesser extent, at Larne.
I have, accordingly, thought it best to
pursue the policy of consolidating our
present position, and of carrying on developments along normal and business-like
lines, rather than to commit the Province
to large expenditure which, in my belief,
would prove to be barely remunerative
from the point of view of the Province,
even if we were to succeed in attracting
to our coasts a larger proportion of the
Scotch herring fleet than we do at the
present time.
So far as the herring fishery is concerned, we are making every effort to
consolidate the position which we hold in
the port of Ardglass, and to increase our
proportion of the landings of the Irish
Sea herring catch. By far the greater
part of the herrings are landed by Scottish
steam drifters and are handled by Scottish fisher-girls, who are brought in by
the large cross-channel herring-curing
firms. I am glad to be able to tell the
Committee, however, that the activity of
Northern Irish curers is increasing, and
that Northern Ireland workers are now
beginning to be trained for this work at
Ardglass.
In pursuance of this policy we have
recently acquired dredging and rockbreaking craft, specially adapted to conditions on our coasts, and we shall use
this craft for the purpose of improving
the accommodation in our small ports
from Portstewart to Kilkeel, thus making
it easier for our scattered fishing communities to trade upon a more regular and
a more remunerative basis. At the same
time, the Ministry is in negotiation with
the County Councils of Antrim and Down
for overtaking certain arrears of maintenance in the small fishing ports, so that
not only will these harbours be rendered
easier of access by dredging and rockbreaking, but also their quays will be put
into a proper state of repair as well. By
this means we hope to consolidate and to
improve the position of an industry which
has for some time past been struggling
bravely against adverse physical conditions.
It will be appreciated that the influx
of a large number of herring drifters into
Ardglass, and of herring girls seeking
accommodation during the season, represents the expenditure of considerable
sums of money in our area, but I would
ask the Committee, in considering suggestions made from time to time, that
very large capital expenditure should be.
made to create an alternative port at
Killough, to remember that the profits
which we derive are largely of an indirect
nature, and that the present accommodation at the port of Ardglass is ample,
except in the height of a good season.
We are now preparing to improve this
accommodation by the provision of a
water supply, and by increasing the
depth of water at the existing quays.
Turning now to electricity, I am glad
to be able to inform the Committee that
the development of electricity services in
the Six Counties is making steady progress. In this sphere also we must have
regard, in framing policy, to our special
local conditions. The Committee are
well aware that the distribution of population over our area is very uneven, and
that it tends to concentration in the district around Belfast and the city of
Londonderry. I am advised, in factand this will surprise the Committeethat at the present time more than onethird of our population has a public
supply of electricity available at its
doors.
It is our policy, nevertheless, to spread,
as widely as is consistent with economic
considerations, the network of power
lines over our Province, and we hope that
within a few years time the majority of
the factories which stud our countryside
may be able to obtain cheap power from
high tension transmission lines in their

It is, perhaps, unnecessary for me to
explain in detail the work of the Ministry
in regard to such matters as the registration of companies, friendly societies, etc.
Reports on these branches of the Ministry's activities are submitted annually to
the House. I should, however, refer
briefly to the subject of industrial assurance. The Industrial Assurance Act
(Northern Ireland), 1924, affords protection to holders of small policies, and provides machinery for the settlement of disputes between Assurance Companies and
policy holders, whose limited means
might otherwise render redress a matter
of difficulty. The duties of the Industrial Assurance Commissioner are carried
out by the Permanent Secretary of the
Ministry, and these duties include the
exercise of judicial powers in dealing with
disputes referred to him.
The large increase in the number of
cases referred to the Commissioner is sufficient evidence of the real benefit which
this Act has conferred upon the class of
policy-holders affected. In 1925-the
first year of the operation of the Actthe number of cases dealt with was 155,,
whereas during 1928 the number had increased to 737.

to

printing, stationery, postage, and incidentals.
What I suggest to the Committee.
therefore, is that on this first Vote we

As regards Newry, the Committee is
aware that a sum of £3,500 has already
been granted towards the cost of repair
of a damaged culvert, in the Canal. The
Canal has been closed for the past six
months and the repairs to the culvert
have not yet been completed.
The question of providing a tidal river
approach to the town of Newry has been
under consideration for many years, and
as recently as two years ago a Joint Committee of the Urban District, Council and
the Harbour Trust was appointed to consider the question. Plans were prepared
to carry out this scheme, and the cost
of carrying out the scheme was estimated at £110,000. Mainly owing to
financial considerations the work was not
proceeded with, and it is now intended
to carry out a modified scheme for the
improvement of the Canal.
As regards the improvement of the
Canal generally, in respect of which provision is now sought, I should explain
that representations have been made by
the Urban District Council of Newry, the
Newry Port and Harbour Trust, and
others to convince the Government that
the efficiency of the port of Newry is a
matter of vital importance to the counties
of Armagh and Down, in particular, and
to the Province in general.
This new scheme, in connection with
which engineers have already been appointed, provides for:-
(1) The lengthening of the existing
lock chamber at the entrance, and the provision of a pair of new gates.
(2) A certain amount of repairs to the
existing masonry and culverts, etc., here.
and probably some dredging at the lower
entrance to improve the approach from
the sea; and
(3) The removal of all the stones at
present lying in the bottom of the channel, and the deepening of the whole
channel from the locks to the Albert
Basin to give a minimum depth of 16 feet
(the present maximum depth is 13 feet),
and with necessary pitching for the slopes.
The cost of this work is estimated
roughly at £60,000.
Having regard to the importance of the
Canal, the Government proposes, firstly,
to defray 50 per cent. of the total expenditure incurred, exclusive of engineer's
fees, subject to a maximum contribution
from Government funds of £30,000;
secondly, to defray the cost of the services.
of the engineer; and, thirdly, to make
available, where practicable, the services
of the Government dredging and rockbreaking plant free of charge.
It will be impossible to complete this
work during the current financial year,
and the provision now sought represents
the amount likely to be required in
1929/30 in respect of the grant-in-aid
and the cost of the services of the engineer during the year.

Ireland.
being shut out of Northern
There is no question of Russian flax being
shut out of Northern Ireland, and never
was. As a matter of fact, the fact that
the British Government has not an ambassador in the Soviet capital has, curiously enough, never interfered with the
flax trade between Russia and Northern
Ireland. The sole reason for the high
price of Russian flax and its scarcity today in the Belfast market is the policy
of the Soviet Government which has
carried Socialism to the height of absurdity. They give the Russian peasant
no encouragement at all to grow flax.
The Russian Government commandeers
the flax from the Russian peasant at an
absurdly low price, and then the control
of the export of flax is in their own hands.
It is that alone which has brought about
the high price and the scarcity of Russian
flax in Northern Ireland. If it were not
for the fact that some of the Baltic republics, such as Esthonia and Lithuania,
are, thank goodness, free of the Government of Soviet Russia, the scarcity of
Russian flax would be greater than ever.

employees of this Parliament House. I

basis of calculation is actually lower than
that of the British House of Commons.
I refer to the messengers, attendants, and
all those embodied in the employee section

the wages of the attendants and messengers in this House are lower than those
of the attendants and messengers in the
British House of Commons. I, therefore,

brought about in the shipbuilding and engineering trades. I find that a reduction

but of every other Government Department, on the same basis of wages as is paid
in Great Britain.

Then there is the question of the Parliamentary Secretary. The Prime Minister has urged the plea, on what principle
I do not know, that the Government must
have two representatives in the Senate.
"If," he said, one is abroad, or if one
is ill, there is no one to indicate the
Government's policy;" but how is the
Government's policy indicated in the
sister Parliament in Dublin? The Minister responsible goes into the Senate, and
he tells them what the Government wish,
and what the Government's policy in the
matter is. Could not the members of the
Cabinet, or their secretaries, whom we
seldom see in the House, go into the
Senate, and indicate to the Senate what
the Government's policy on the matter is?
That argument, I suggest to you, is not
an argument that you should entertain for
a moment.
The object here-I do not mind how
plainly I put it-is to provide a salary
for his friend, Lord Massereene, who, as
the Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie)
told you, is mostly abroad. I do not stand
for that sort of thing. I have never stood
for that sort of thing in a county council,
I have never stood for it in any public
body, and I am not going to stand for it
here. You may salve your conscience in
what way you will for going into the
lobbies and voting for it, but that is
your responsibility and not mine.

Mr. POLLOCK: Those who were
Members in our last Parliament are
familiar with this small Vote, but as
there are a number of new Members in
the House, it may not be out of place for
me to explain in some detail the way in
which the money provided in this Estimate is used. The money is paid into a
Fund from which payments are made
only on the personal authorisation of the
Minister of Finance, who first satisfies
himself that the expenditure to be met
has been incurred on objects properly
coming within the ambit of the Fund, as,
for example, the entertainment of distinguished visitors to the Province, or of
representative bodies from other countries
visiting Northern Ireland for the purpose
of exchanging views on matters relating
to education, agriculture, etc., with the
corresponding bodies in this country. As
an example of the latter, I may mention
the visits paid to Northern Ireland last
year by representatives of the World's
Dairy Congress, the Agricultural Education Association, the Agricultural Research Association, and the Empire
Farmers. I am sure the Committee will
agree with me that it is very desirable,
from every point of view, that when bodies
of such importance visit the Province the
Government should do what it can to
foster an atmosphere of friendship and
goodwill.
Most of the expenditure from the Fund
is incurred in entertainments such as
these, and, in general, the scope of the
fund is restricted to affording hospitality
on the occasion of important visits from
outside. Instances sometimes occur,
however, when it is in the public interest
that payments should be made for some
more local purposes, and in considering
such cases I am, of course, governed by
the requirement that the money must be
used in the public interest. I would repeat the statement which I made when
moving this Estimate on the last occasion,
namely, that I am personally accountable
to Parliament for the payments which are
made, and that just as the administration
of the corresponding fund in Great
Britain is left in the hands of a Minister
of the Crown, so I hope that this Committee will continue to extend to me the
same degree of trust as is extended to
the Imperial Minister at Westminster.
There is no secrecy about the expenditure,
and the objects by this time should be
well known.
The amount of £1,500, included in the
Estimate this year will be paid into the
Hospitality Fund, from which payments
will be paid as occasion arises; any balance
remaining in the Fund at the end of the
year is not liable to surrender, as is money
voted for other purposes. It is carried
over into the following year, which
means, of course, that if the amount of
the balance is considerable, a smaller
amount will require to be voted in the
following year. I do not anticipate that
the actual expenditure out of the Fund,
during the year, will approach the amount
of £1,500. I think the Committee will
appreciate, however, that in a matter of
this kind, it is not possible to make any
close estimate, and it is essential that the
Fund should contain a reasonable margin
for contingencies. There are generally
certain items of expenditure which can be
foreseen when the Estimate for the year
is being prepared. The Government proposes, for example, in the present year to
repeat the very successful function held
last year in honour of those taking part
in the International Motor Race. Then
again, a certain amount of expenditure of
this kind will be incurred in connection
with the ceremony of the opening of .he
Lecture Buildings at Stranmillis
Training College, which we expect to take
place in the early autumn. Other occasions which cannot be foreseen are, however, almost certain to arise, and for
these some provision must be made.
new

have no difficulty in realising the object
of the Fund, and I feel perfectly satisfied
they will approve of it. I have no hesitation in asking the Committee to pass the
Vote, which I now beg to move.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The Resolution which appears
on the Order Paper is, of course, the
precursor of a Bill with which most hon.
Members are familiar, and which is designed to continue a scheme of unemployment relief combined with assistance
to industry which has been endorsed on
The
many occasions by Parliament.
Government has found it necessary to continue this emergency legislation from
year to year since 1922, and although,
when moving a similar Resolution last
year, and also in 1927, the hope was expressed that circumstances would make it
possible for Government to discontinue
these facilities, the success which has attended this legislation and the existence.
of unemployment in our midst has moved
the Government to the view that it would
not be justified in relaxing its efforts to
assist by this means.
If we include a sum of £600,000, which
I am hopeful will have been ear-marked
within the next few days, maybe even
within hours, in connection with an important contract, the position is that guarantees will have been issued amounting to approximately £10,280,657 leaving available
a balance of approximately £1,200,000.
Despite this substantial balance, the
Government considers it advisable to increase the margin by a very large amount,
and to provide now for the extension of
the scheme to 31st March, 1931. The
Government is satisfied that the state of
employment is such as to warrant this
further extension of time and of amount,
and I can only repeat that every effort
will be made by co-operation with our
great shipyards to maintain the improved
conditions which have, happily, been
brought about in the course of the last
eighteen months.
Once again I would take the opportunity of expressing the thanks of the
Government to the members of the Advisory Committee for the work which
they have carried out in investigating the
various applications which have come before them. This work has been carried
on by three eminent business men, and
the Government is indeed under a
debt of gratitude to them for what they
have done, and what they are doing.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). In the
interval which has elapsed since the
House was last called upon to continue
this legislation, a great loss has been sus-.
tained by the death of Mr. J. H. Stirling, who had been a member of the Committee since the inception of the scheme
and had acted as Chairman for a number
of years. This is the first Parliamentary
opportunity which has presented itself to
pay tribute to the great work which he
performed. We have been fortunate in
prevailing upon Mr. H. L. M'Cready to

The object of this amendment is to

page 4, line 4, to leave out the words
"a fee of five shillings" and insert the
words
"such sum as the local authority may
consider fair, provided that such sum
shall not exceed five shillings for every
week that such stationary stall be occupied, except in the case of amusement
stalls or erections, in respect of which
the local authorities shall have power to
make such charge as they consider
reasonable."
The latter portion of that will, of course,
go out, that is, the charges made on
amusement stalls. The main portion of
the Amendment is in regard to the fee of
5s.
The CHAIRMAN: The Amendment
will now terminate at the word "occupied."
Mr. O'NEILL: Exactly; at the word
"occupied" as you have suggested. It is
with regard to the fee charged for such
site for these stalls. In my judgment this
fee is too small. I do not really know
how it can be defended at all. The individual can have a site in the town on a
market day for 5s per year. In other
words, for the sum of 30s per year he can
have a site in each market town, and as a
rule it is not the worst site these men
select. I consider it is most unfair, and a
disadvantage to the shopkeepers who are
in competition with these street traders
and who have large premises there, and
have to pay the full rates to the local
authorities for them.
It surely is unreasonable that an individual for the sum of 5s per year can have
the same site as an individual who is payinstances
ing many pounds, in some
hundreds of pounds, in rates. I do not
think there is any justification at all for
making the fee so small. It may be said
it would be unfair to the trader, but the
trader does not belong to the locality and,
therefore, does not pay rates. Most of
these traders come from Belfast. It has
become a custom for them to come in large
numbers from Belfast in motor-cars and
various other ways. I think if these
people were charged the sum of 5s per
week, or 5s per day, it would be fairer.
As a rule it is only one day in the week,
and in some instances only one day in the
month. I think none of them would
object to pay the sum of 5s to the local
authorities for the site.
The local authorities, of course, have
responsibilities in connection with these,
and they have to be recompensed.
As
a matter of fact, the local authorities will
be placed at a disadvantage, because at
the present time some of these people
voluntarily pay more than 5s a week. I
know of instances where they pay 35s a
week for a stall. They will not do that
now if they get a licence for 5s a year.
I think the charge should be left in the
hands of the local authorities themselves.
They are really the best judges as
what should be fixed. It is for
reason I have put down the Amendment.
I think it is a fair and reasonable proposal,
and I hope the Government will see their
way to accept it.

authorities and the individual traders who
want to do business with them. All we
can or want to do under this Bill is to
secure that no unnecessary or improper
obstacle should be put in the way of
humble people who are earning their living
in this way, and, on the other hand, that
local authorities will remain, as we consider they ought to remain, masters of the
situation, to make the conditions attaching to the manner and place of sale and
the time that it is to take place. An
arrangement between the local authorities
and street traders for the right to sell
at given places over a specified period is
a matter which no Act of Parliament of
this sort should interfere with at all.
I cannot conceive by what right we
should say to all the different local authorities that they are to charge street traders

that our street trader is to have the right
to go back to the same pitch all the time.
The licence which may be granted to him
may be revoked or altered from time to
time, as the local authority may think fit.
This is not a Bill to interfere between the
trader and a local authority in reference
to any place that that street trader may
wish to take by way of lease or term,
whether for a week, a month, or a year.
We do not interfere with their contractual relationship whatever.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) The work of the Ministry of
Labour goes on week after week, patiently
and effectively performed, and then at
the end of the year the responsible
political head of the Department is expected in a speech of reasonable length to
give an account of his stewardship. I
crave your indulgence in doing so because
I feel that, in connection with labour
matters, policy and facts and figures are
so closely associated and interwoven that
it is almost impossible to separate them.
A general feeling exists, I am afraid,
amongst our community that the principal
work which the Ministry of Labour does
is to collect small contributions from
people who are not particularly anxious
to pay, and then week after week in a
somewhat indiscriminate way to pay out
benefit and pensions to those who apply
for them. I can assure you that that is
quite a wrong impression in the public.
mind.
of public opinion that the Department

walls of those Acts.
As a matter of fact, the Department

If I were asked in a few words to say
what the policy of the Department is, I
should say that our desire is in co-operation with the other Departments of the
State, particularly the Ministry of
Finance and the Ministry of Commerce,
to find work for as many of our people as
possible through the ordinary industries
of which Ulster has always been very
proud; then, for those for whom it is not
possible to find work in that way in cooperation with our local authorities we
desire that schemes of public utility
should be undertaken which would
not otherwise be undertaken for two

years
may be usefully employed in that way;
and then when everything has been done

Department's duty is to come to the
rescue of those of our community who are
passing through a period of adversity,
whether that adversity is due to unemployment, to sickness, to bereavement,
or to old age.
men
One of the principal duties which I feel
that the Department is called upon to discharge is that associated with preserving
industrial peace in our community, and I
think I can claim that Northern Ireland
has been specially free from industrial
troubles during the last eight years. The
Ministry does not claim an undue share
of credit for that, because I am very glad
to be able to state I realise that a real
desire exists between our employers and
our workers to accommodate with each
other, and to adjust their differences along
reasonable and possible lines. But, still,
the Ministry of Labour has to keep watch
upon the industrial situation in this as
well as in other respects.
When we hear that trouble is brewing,
and we almost always hear either from
the representatives of labour or from the
employers-in fact as a rule we hear from
both-we get busy to try to have the
differences adjusted before actual trouble
takes place. This is a work which is performed to a far greater extent than is
Supply Committee-
Ministry of Labour
10 JUNE 1929
generally known, because it is not in the
public eye.
But, no matter how faithfully the Department discharges its duty
in this respect, always bearing in mind
our policy that prevention is better than
cure, at times trouble will occur, no matter
how much care is taken, and I deeply regret that in connection with one of the
trades in our shipbuilding industry
trouble has occurred between the joiners
and their employers.
It is not for me to express an opinion
one way or the other-it is my duty to
remain absolutely neutral-but I do take
advantage of this opportunity earnestly to
express the hope that before long peace.
will again be restored, because, if not, I
am absolutely satisfied that many in other
trades in connection with our great shipbuilding industry will suffer, as well as
their wives and families, and irreparable
damage may be done to the industry itself
if this strike is unduly prolonged.
In addition to dealing with industrial
relations, the responsibility rests with the
Department of administering our Trade
Board Acts. That has not only been a
difficult but a delicate task. When the
Department took over these powers in
1922 we found that a great deal of dissatisfaction existed as regards trade board
legislation and administration. One of
the first Acts which the Department
undertook to get passed through the
House was a new Bill dealing with trade
boards, and I am glad to think that that
Act has worked, on the whole, remarkably satisfactorily-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and that owing to careful administration-reasonableness always being an
outstanding factor in connection with the
Department's policy in this matteremployers and workers in Northern
Ireland associated with these particular
trades have come to realise that they are
not, as they feared they always would be,
a nuisance; but, on the contrary, that
the trade board is one of the best ways
of settling wages' matters along reasonable
lines. In Northern Ireland we have 18
trade boards, and, comparatively recently,
five district committees have been set up
with the view that statutory rates should
be fixed in our country districts at such
a level as to allow our country concerns
to compete with those larger firms often
more favourably situated in this city and
other large towns throughout Northern
Ireland.

because it is very closely associated with
Supply Committee-

Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
the Department's policy. At Richhill
we take young men from this city and
other towns throughout Northern Ireland,
who have got into a blind alley. Many
of them have served an apprenticeship in
connection with some of our handicrafts,
but from the time the apprenticeship
was completed they have never been able
to be employed as tradesmen. Year after
year they have since remained unemployed. The Department is not forcing.
anyone to leave Northern Ireland who
wishes to stay in Northern Ireland. All
that the Department is doing is to bring
within the reach of those who desire to
go, not to a foreign land, but to another
part of the same Empire, the same opportunities and the same facilities for gratifying their own desire that their brothers
across the Channel possess.
From Richhill there have already gone
to Canada 430 men, and to Australia 154
men. I am glad to say, from reports
which I receive, that they are all mostly
doing well. I have had many very gratifying letters from those who have gone,
and who have already been established in
those far-flung parts of the British Empire, thanking the Government for the
opportunity which they obtained to seek
employment in those lands, and to assist
in the development of those great
Dominions, instead of hanging about in
our cities and towns here doing nothing
at all. There are 95 men in training at
Richhill at the present time, and there is
another group anxiously waiting to get
there. I do think that it is a very strong
course for any hon. Member to take to
speak in any derogatory sense of this
effort on the Government's part.
After all, there is another side to this
question, and an important one, too,
These young men of ours go out to the

export trade figures as to the Kingdom
I will realise how great a factor the

In connection with our various social

That means
this, if we take the population of Northern

persons in our area is receiving direct

schemes exactly the same fraction which
the great founder of the Salvation Army,
General Booth, referred to many years
ago as the submerged tenth who were
under his care. This one-tenth which I
regret to say exists in our midst to-day is
the care, and the very direct care, of the

of unemployment there are two facts that
we should not altogether forget. We
should remember that the birth rate in
Northern Ireland exceeds the death rate
by about 8,000 a year on the average.
That means that those 8,000 have either
to be absorbed into increasing industries
in Northern Ireland, or else they have to
migrate to another part of the Empire,
or become unemployed. There is no way
out of the difficulty except through relief
schemes, which, of course, can be carried
on to any extent for which money can
be found to carry them on. But

With regard to the question of genuinely

are only one or two openings in the place.

turned down when he goes before the

genuinely seeking work.

The hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.

who wants to see a single boy or girl going
out of the country if work can be had for
them at home. We are all anxious that

country in the world whose people have
done so well abroad as the Irish people,

what the Minister of Labour is principally aiming at is that those Ulster boys
who go out from here to Canada,
Australia, New Zealand, or South Africa
should go out equipped for the fight in
which they have to take part. Surely

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I am sure the
Committee agrees that there is no more
difficult problem than this question of unemployment, and yet I notice that when
we come to debate it we always seem to
deal with nearly everything else but the
question of how to find a solution for it.
The hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.

Three or four years ago he assured the

Labour. As a Member of this Committee
who has been probably brought more.
into contact with the Ministry of Labour

State, I would like, with other hon. Members, to pay my tribute not only to the
capable but to the very sympathetic way

the Unemployment Acts. I have discovered that where the Minister of Labour
can stretch a point at all on the side of the

Rev. Professor CORKEY:
I rise just
to say a word about one aspect of this
Ministry which, I think, has not been referred to already. I may say I have been
watching anxiously for the moment when
I should find the House empty or almost
empty to make my few remarks. I have
spoken here before, but the atmosphere
is changed somewhat. (Laughter.) I
wish to pay a tribute to the way in which
the officers of this Ministry meet the
public, when they go in to them to make
inquiries on any subject connected with
their Department. I may say that I have
gone to almost all the offices of this particular Ministry about various matters on
different occasions, and I have always been
met with the greatest patience, and the
greatest courtesy, and the greatest helpfulness, and I think I must be only one
of a great number of people who find
occasion to seek the help of the Minister
of Labour and his assistants about matters
in which they are interested. It almost
seemed to me coming out of their offices
that they had cultivated very highly that
virtue which consists in suffering fools
gladly.
I may say that, like the hon. Member
for Duncairn (Mr. Grant), I am very
gratified at the fact that we are to have
medical benefits extended to Northern
Ireland in connection with this Ministry.
I was surprised, however, that the hon.
Member for Duncairn, in making reference to it, seemed very anxious to know
when those particular benefits would be
available. It did not seem to me that
he was in any great need of urgent
medical benefits.
There is one point on which, perhaps,
the Minister will give me a little information. Reference was made, perhaps
by more than one Member, to the fact
that the Trade Boards Act in Northern
Ireland does not apply to agricultural
labourers. I have had a great deal to
do in my time with agricultural labourers.
No one will deny the fact that they live
end
very hard, weary, depressed
monotonous lives, and if the extension of
the Trade Boards Act would benefit them
in any way it seems to me that it is a
matter that ought to receive the sympathetic consideration of the Ministry.
There may be cogent reasons why the
Trade Boards Act has not been extended
to them, but, perhaps, in his reply the
Minister will make a reference to the
matter, as it is a subject which has been
in my mind on many occasions. I thank
you.

The increase is the sum of £1,000. Now
it has become necessary for us here in

concerned.
It has become necessary, therefore, to
prepare a separate index to deal with
Northern Ireland, so that the courts and
those who have to deal with statutes can
find easily the branch of law dealing with
each particular subject. It is quite impossible for anvone connected with the
law to work through all the statutes and
search through the different years. Any
lawyer, magistrate, judge or whoever is

an office and asking a clerk to

pace. I am informed by His Majesty's
Office of Works that the main superstructure-the contract for which
begun in February of last year is making
steady progress, as is also the contract for
the heating installation which is proceeding concurrently. It is anticipated that
the building will be ready for occupation
in three years' time.
was
Turning now to the Belfast Custom
House reconstruction and the new Law
Court Building, these items would not in
the ordinary course of events find a place
in our Estimates, as the Custom House is
primarily intended for the use of the
Customs and Excise and other reserved
and Imperial Departments, with the result that the main expenditure has to be
provided on Imperial Estimates.
The expenditure on the new Law Courts
building is in the same category, having
to be met directly from the Votes of the
Imperial Government under the provisions
of Section 24 of the Government of Ireland
Act, 1920. It happens, however, that a
part of each of these buildings is to be
utilised for the city offices of certain
Departments of the Northern Government, that is to say, for financial purposes
the expenditure on such parts falls into
the same category as expenditure on the
Stormont buildings, and, though equally
the ultimate liability of the Imperial
Government, must be voted in this Section
as falling under Section 34 of the Government of Ireland Act.
Hon. Members will, I am sure, be interested to learn that the work of erecting
Supply Committee

the Law Courts is well advanced; the contract for the steel frame work is, in fact,
completed; and the contract for the necessary working of the stone has recently
been entered into; tenders have been
invited for reinforced concrete work, and
it is expected that the superstructure will
be commenced about October next. As
regards the Custom House, it is anticipated that the work will be completed.
before the end of this summer.
The remaining new work in this section.
of the Estimate is a re-vote of the amount
required to provide additional accommodation and equipment at the Ordnance
Survey offices. As was pointed out on a

required for the production of Ordnance
maps.
Turning now to Section II, on pages
30, 31 and 32, this comprises that part
of our own domestic expenditure which
does not relate specifically to the administration of any particular Government
Department. Included under Sub-head
"E," on pages 30 and 31, is provision
for a contribution to be made from Northern Ireland funds towards the cost of
providing a small part of the office accommodation in the new Parliament Building at Stormont. While the British
Government bear the bulk of this expenditure, it became necessary for our Government to make a contribution of
£30,000 in order to secure office accommodation for staffs additional to the number for which, under the terms of the

some delay having taken place in the

In regard to the token Vote of £100
for completing the purchase of the
dredger equipment, I may mention that
the dredger is now employed in improving
Carrickfergus Harbour, and other dredging works at other harbours are being
arranged in conjunction with the county
councils, so that the plant will be continuously in use.
A further sum is required for the work
of drainage investigation now taking place
at the Lough and River Erne. Members will realize that before a drainage
scheme can be formulated, it is necessary
that accurate information should be available as to levels, strata, and other technical aspects of the problem.
The sum of £125 for the purchase of
property adjoining Carrickfergus Castle,
now in our custody as an ancient monument, is a re-vote of last year's provision
The item of £425 for improving the
main entrance drive at Government
House is provided, so that the roadway
may be given special treatment to ensure a suitable surface in all conditions of
weather, and to reduce maintenance
costs for the future.
The last item in the list is the most
important, namely, the provision of
£40,000 for the Bann drainage. I need
not point out to hon. Members that the
scheme of drainage is that recommended
in the Report of the Drainage Advisory
Committee, dated 9th November, 1928.
A Bill to secure the necessary statutory
powers will require to be introduced in
this House. As far as can be foreseen,
the contract for the work should be placed
towards the close of the current calendar
year. The provision of a sum of £40,000
is in the nature of a token vote in this
connection. The various items of maintenance and other recurring expenditure
in Sub-heads F, G, and H require no
special comment from me.
I now come to Section III, which summarises the works expenditure incurred
on behalf of the various Northern Ireland Departments, and which is recovered
from the Departmental Votes being
brought to account in this vote as an appropriation-in-aid. The various new
works in progress and those which are
proposed are set out under separate headings in the tabular statement to be found
on pages 33 and 34. I propose to make
references to the more important of these
items.
My first reference is to the adaptation
work which has for some time past been
undertaken with the object of utilising a
portion of the Belfast Prison as a convict
prison. These works are now well advanced, and it is anticipated that they will
be practically completed before the end of
this financial year. Londonderry Prison.
is now to be adapted in order that part of
it may serve as a criminal lunatic asylum
and so enable the Northern Ireland
criminal lunatics, who are at the present
time looked after in the Central Lunatic
Asylum at Dundrum, County Dublin, to
be transferred to a Northern Ireland institution. A token sum only was included
for this work in last year's Estimates, and
the amount now included represents the
whole cost of the work, as it is anticipated
that the alterations will be completed before the end of December next.

A reference has been made since the
opening of this Parliament to the scheme
of forestry development which is now
being proceeded with, and it has been
necessary to provide labourers' cottages
at various of these centres in view of the
difficulty which has been experienced in
securing the services of reliable men,
owing to the lack of housing accommodation in rather remote places.
The requirements of the Ministry of
Labour necessitate the inclusion of two
substantial sums, the first for an Employment Exchange at Lisburn-the rented
premises now occupied by the Lisburn
Employment Exchange having proved
inadequate for the needs. No other
suitable premises can be obtained in the
town, and it is therefore necessary to acquire a site and build a new Exchange.
The second provision is that for
the Training Centres for Unemployed
Juveniles, which I have no doubt will be
of special interest to hon. Members, in-.
asmuch as it denotes the inauguration
of a scheme for dealing with the unemployment problem as it affects the youth
of the country. These centres have been
established in Great Britain, and have
proved most useful in guiding boys and
girls into permanent avocations, and so
keeping them out of "blind alley" employments. Central premises have been
acquired in Belfast, and the sum now
provided is the estimate of the cost of
these premises. A further sum will be
required to meet the cost of the necessary adaptation, and this will form the
subject of a Supplementary Estimate at
a later date.
The desirability of providing an adequate supply of fresh water for the boilers
of steam drifters and other fishing vessels,
and for other purposes, at Ardglass Harbour, has already been before this Committee, and the item of £300 included in
the Estimate is intended to provide for
this. It is expected that a public supply will be provided for the town in the
near future, and it is hoped that the extension of this supply to the harbour now
proposed will form a satisfactory and permanent solution of this trouble.
The only other new work deserving of
special reference is the proposal for the
improvement of landing facilities at Rathlin Island. The channel between this
island and the mainland is very rough
Supply Committee-
Public Works and Buildings 436
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
and dangerous, and the existing facilities
for landing on the island, which have
never been very satisfactory, have been
steadily growing worse owing to damage
by sea to a pier which was erected by the
Department of Agriculture between the
years 1912 and 1915. The islanders are
dependent on the mainland for doctors,
nurses, and medical supplies, in addition
to various household necessities, and their
surplus agricultural produce must be conveyed to the mainland for sale. In these
exceptional circumstances, and in particular from the humanitarian point of view,
it has been decided that the Government
should undertake the responsibility of
providing, subject to a substantial contribution by the Antrim County Council,
improved landing and embarking facilities. Speaking generally, the works
proposed consist in an improvement in
the entrance channel to Church Bay, repairs to the existing pier, and the provision of a new landing place with an approach road thereto. The Antrim County
Council will undertake future normal
maintenance.

House of Commons, and the decreased

various Government Departments, having

their requirements in this connection.
Moreover, the completion of the Census
has removed the necessity for a provision
in respect of printing which, in the year

It must be remembered that in the
early years it was a matter of great difficulty to forecast the precise requirements
of the public departments-including the
library of this House-in the matter of
printing, stationery, books and other
similar supplies; and my Ministry was
not inclined to sanction expenditure,
although a good prima facie case could be
shown, until the experience of some years
working had proved the necessity. The
Departments, accordingly, in some cases,
did not complete their essential equipment
in the matter of stationery, etc., supplies
at the outset, but only as and when experience proved the necessity. Accordingly, the annual provision now required
can be confined to normal requirements
with the exception, of course, of special
provision for any special services which
may be required in future years.
gratifying result is due, in no small

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): When I presented my seventh
Financial Statement a year ago in this
House, I expressed the hope that as the
first seven years of our federal life as a
Province had been marked by an unprecedented, and indeed uninterrupted spell
While, as a people, we have much to
be thankful for during the year which
has recently ended on the 31st March,
it cannot be said that my early expectations have been fully realised. The best
that can be said of 1928-29 is that trade
conditions have shewn a partial recuperation. Prices of agricultural produce
have not been remunerative; the world
demand for the product of our mills and
factories has not by any means fully responded to our hopes; and of our great
basic industries, shipbuilding is the only
trade of which it can be said that it has
enjoyed a fair measure of prosperity.
But from many indices, which I need
not enter into, there are indications of
a more hopeful feeling in commerce and
industry (hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-and with world conditions improving
there cannot be any doubt that we shall
share in the result. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
Hon. Members have had supplied to
them a preliminary Financial Statement,
in which the estimated revenue and expenditure for the current year are left
blank. It gives, however, a complete
picture of the actual outcome of our
finances for the year which closed on the
31st March last, and the blanks to which
I have just referred relate to the estimated
revenue and expenditure for the present
financial year. I will give the figures in
the course of my statement, and those
Members who are sufficiently interested
will be able, if they so wish, to fill in
the blanks as I go along. In any case, a
complete statement will be issued during
the course of the afternoon.
For the moment, I propose to confine
myself to the results of last year. This
is to some extent ancient history now,
since the Provisional Statement issued on
the last day of the financial year gave a
general outline of our expenditure and
our receipts, and showed a surplus, subject
to adjustment, of slightly over £77,000.
In view of this, it is not so necessary for
me to go into all the details, but I hope
to be able to make clear one or two points
of importance, which, perhaps, are a little
obscure at the moment, and also to take
this opportunity of making a few general
observations on various questions relating
to our finances.

In the form of our Accounts, I should
point out the distinction which is shown
between Consolidated Fund Services and
Supply Services.
Expenditure under the head of Consolidated Fund Services is authorised
definitely by Statute, and is a first charge
upon the Consolidated Fund. On the
other hand, provision for Supply Services
is made in the form of Estimates, and the
details are fully discussed each year in
the Committee of Supply, as we know
from our experience of the last week or
two.
So far as last year's Consolidated Fund.
Services are concerned, the only item I
need mention concerns the operations on
the Residuary Share Suspense Account,
which are shown to the amount of
£159,000 in respect of adjustments for
past years. This is, of course, an item
that cannot be estimated. The Suspense
Account was, in fact, created under an
Act of this Parliament passed in 1927,
to provide a suitable medium for the many
adjustments consequential upon the intricate character of our financial relations with Great Britain. The Imperial
contribution is not finally determined for
any one year, until one, or perhaps two
years later, and other adjustments in respect of the Reserved Taxes are similarly
delayed until final figures are available.
Consequently, this Suspense Account
serves the purpose of preventing the distortion of the accounts for any one year
by reason of adjustments relating to previous years, and enables us to present the
accounts in their proper perspective.
Supply Services have run their normal
course, and, compared with earlier years,
the Estimates were very close.
I do not think that hon. Members will
expect me to enter in detail into the comparison between Estimates and outcome
of the various items of last year's expenditure. These have already been before
the House and are available in our printed
statements.
The cost of the reserved services is
again almost up to the Estimates. There
is an apparent saving of £25,000 under
the head of the Judiciary and Supreme
Court, but this does not indicate an actual
reduction of that amount in the cost of
the service, since the receipts from the
sale of reserved fee stamps, which previously went direct to the Exchequer, are
now being appropriated in aid of the
Vote, and go to diminish the gross expenditure proportionately.
I repeat that the total expenditure on
the services of the Province was
£9,861,000, to which must be added the
repayment to the Treasury of sums of
£165,000, collected on its behalf, and
which appear also on the revenue side of
our Budget. Our total outgoings were,
therefore, £10,026,000.
I proceed now to set out the Revenue
returns for last year.
REVENUE 1928-29.
The total yielded by the various Taxes
and other sources of Revenue last
year amounted to £10,203,000, or
some £61,000 above the estimate of
£10,142,000.
Our Transferred Revenues again came
in remarkably well. For one or two years
now I have been able to comment on the
receipts from Death Duties. Last year
also the yield was well maintained, and
£666,000 was realised. In passing, I
might add that in addition to this sum,
British estates of persons dying domiciled
in Ulster paid to the British Exchequer a
total of almost £200,000. In order that
our own Exchequer may benefit to the
greatest possible extent, I would urge the
great importance of holders of British
War Loan and other Government securities registering their holdings in Belfast,
in every case where this is at all possible.
As shown in the Return, Transfered
Taxes produced in all £1,079,000, and including the receipts from Motor Vehicle
Duties of £429,000, the total Returns

Reserved Taxes accounted for
£6,825,000. This total does not

quite come up to expectations. These
facts, in conjuction, possibly suggest the
wider distribution of the wealth of the
community, since rises in Customs receipts show a greater purchasing power,

Before concluding my review of last
year's operations, I wish to take this
opportunity of referring to a few of the
more important features of the Parliamentary and Administrative work that
was carried out, and of their effect on our
financial position.
In the forefront, I place the arrangements with the British Government-now
The Budget-

Finance Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
happily on a permanent Statutory basisfor the future of our Unemployment Insurance Fund. This subject was dealt
with exhaustively by my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Labour, at the
time, and I will not weary the Committee
with a recapitulation of all its details. It
is right, however, to emphasise especially
the facts, firstly, that the taxpayers of
this Province are providing no less than
£300,000 this year to keep the Fund on
a parity with the British Fund, while
Great Britain, on its part, is contributing
£470,000; and, secondly, that we have
already written off £424,000 of the old
Unemployment Insurance Debt, and have
undertaken to continue to do so by
£100,000 per annum.
We have just been careful to safeguard
the interests of our industrial workers.
We have been no less concerned with the
position of our farmers, and the arrangements embodied in the Land Act recently
passed into law at Westminster will, we
have every reason to believe, be the final
instalment of the series of settlements of
the many burning questions associated
with land purchase schemes. The determination of the 27th of last month as a
common appointed day will place an
additional burden of about £42,000 on
our Exchequer, but I count the money
well spent if it means timely relief to
fifteen or twenty thousand of our smaller
farmers.
We have naturally followed with interest the introduction of a separate currency in the Free State, more especially
since, in consequence, we became directly
concerned with various questions affecting the circulation and issue of bank
notes by the different banks operating
in our area.
But as the note issues of banks in the
Free State are now regulated by its own
Currency Commission, it is evident that
the fiduciary issues fixed for the whole of
Ireland could not equitably be applied to
the restricted area of the Six Counties,
and an apportionment became necessary.
This matter, though apparently
academic in character, has an important
bearing on the ordinary trade and industry of the Province, and we are all,
therefore, under an obligation to the
Treasury for the very helpful attitude
they displayed which greatly facilitated
the settlement of the question. The new
arrangements received the force of law
by an Act of the Imperial Parliament
passed last year.
In order to encourage banking in Ireland, the Imperial Government in 1845
allowed Irish banks the privilege of a fiduciary issue of bank notes-that is to say,
the banks were permitted to issue their
own notes up to certain limits without
holding cash as cover against the issue.
There is no doubt that this policy brought
about the results it was intended to
achieve; it enabled the banks to open
branches in small towns and villages
where the volume of business alone would
would not have enabled a bank to be
carried on, and so banking facilities were
made available even in the poorest and
most scattered districts in the land.
I should, perhaps, mention to the
House that a somewhat difficult situation
arose in regard to the assessment of composition stamp duty on the expiring
issues of all-Ireland bank notes during
the transitional period between the issue
of the new Northern Ireland notes and
the withdrawal of the old note issue.
I am glad to say, however, that the
powers conferred on my Ministry by the
Finance Act of last autumn, coupled
with discussions and co-operation with the
Free State Currency Commission,
abled these difficulties to be satisfactorily
overcome.
We are, however,
however, also concerned
in another direction with the issue
of Free State currency, that is to
say, in the matter of its circulation
in our area.
It cannot be too
widely known that Free State notes
and coin are not legal tender in Ulster.
This is especially to be borne in mind by
those doing business in Border towns,
since a certain amount of confusion, and
possibly inconvenience, may arise from
ignorance of this fact.
Ulster Savings Certificates continue to
fill the place for which they were designed, namely, for the encouragement of
thrift. Sales in the last financial year
reached the total of £472,000, which is
£32,000 more than the year before; even
after taking repayments into account,
there is still a substantial increase.
34,000 of our people are availing themselves of this easy and sound method of
investment and saving. I think it has
come to stay. That it plays an important

from the fact that investments in Great

Our financial operations during the
year covered the control of the Government Loans Fund, which forms a very
useful source of capital moneys for our
Local Authorities, particularly the
smaller ones. During the past few years,
we have lent them over one and a half
million pounds for purposes which include housing, school building, construction of water works, road works, fishery
loans, and so on. Farmers have drawn
on the Fund, and in many other ways it
has contributed to the advancement of
the Province.
The Fund is financed by issues of Ulster
Loans stock. I am anxious to make these
issues of stock a popular local investment,
and I have been glad to notice that it
is gradually becoming better known
amongst small investors. It is in this
direction that the co-operation of bank
managers, stock-brokers, and others with
similar influence would be of material assistance, and I hope it may be forthcoming.
Having now completed my review of
last year, I will enter upon a consideration of the position in respect of the
financial year upon which we have already entered.
EXPENDITURE 1929-30.
I will deal firstly with expenditure,
taking the items in the order in which
they are set out in the White Paper.
The first item of Consolidated Fund
Expenditure is the interest on temporary
borrowings required to meet temporary
deficiencies in revenue during the earlier
part of the financial year, which I estimate at £81,000.
Hon. Members will appreciate that the
rise in bank rate and the consequential
increase in the cost of discounting
Treasury Bills is reflected in our expenditure under this head. Our actual requirements are difficult to forecast with
absolute definiteness, but I think provision of £81,000 should be adequate.
Payments will be made as follows:
First, to provide against the interest
which is constantly accruing on Ulster
Savings Certificates. Here, again, the
very existence of such a Fund gives investors confidence in our administration.
Next, I come to Sinking Funds, in
which I firmly believe. Not only is it
ordinary common-sense to provide against
maturing liabilities, or disappearing
assets, but the existence of sinking funds
is evidence of wise administration, and
greatly strengthens our financial standing.
On the 31st March last, £360,000
stood to the credit of the Fund. In accordance with Statute, £83,000 will be
added this year in respect of the interest
accruing during the year.
The second Sinking Fund is intended.
to secure the maintenance of the land
purchase receipts. Under the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, the yield of
the old Land Purcahse Annuities was
given to our Government as a free gift
to provide for the cost of severance, such
as the expenses connected with our Parliamentary institutions, and the develop-
Let
ment of our Services, and so on.
me here make it clear beyond doubt that
this has no connection with current land
purchase operations.
But we shall not always receive
£666,000 a year from this source, since,
as tenant purchasers complete their payments, the receipts will diminish, until
in about 63 years they will have finally
vanished. My aim in asking Parliament
in 1923 to give legislatve sanction to the
creation of this special Sinking Fund was
to provide investment income which
would ultimately take the place of this
source of revenue. It has been calculated
that the annuities are equivalent to a revenue in perpetuity of £572,000, and so
each year there is transferred to the Sinking Fund the amount by which the actual
receipts exceed this figure.
We have already accumulated £779,000
in this way, and the provision I have
made this year is £93,000.
The total to be provided under the
head of Sinking Fund is thus £176,000.

. Our responsibility for the payment of

that
this House. It is well-known
originally the contribution was fixed at

White Papers which were issued to explain the financial provisions of the Government of Ireland Act, purported to
show that Northern Ireland would, after

This promised well, but before six
months had passed, it was too clear that
these rosy anticipations would not be
realised, and following a long series of
discussions, the Colwyn Committee was
appointed to report on the matter.
The Colwyn Report has often been referred to here, and its basic principles
should be, perhaps, more clearly understood. It set up standards of revenue
and expenditure, and recommended that
in determining the contribution for future
years, regard should be had to variations
from these standards as regards both
British revenue collection and British expenditure on social services. That is to
say, the contribution reflects variations in
taxation, and changes up or down in the
expenditure on local services.
Since 1920, when the financial basis of
the Government of Ireland Act was determined, there have been many changes in
is

to
Finance Minister's Statement 490
The Budget-
12 JUNE 1929
As regards taxation, income tax has
fallen from 6s to 4s, and the rates of relief
in respect of earned income and children
have been substantially increased. It
must also be remembered that relief of
this character means a relatively much
greater loss in revenue here than in Great
Britain, since the proportion of smaller
incomes here is much higher. Corporation
Profits Tax and Excess Profits Duty have
disappeared, although a few arrears continue to be collected.
Important changes have been made in
Customs and Excise. Articles that were
on the tariff list in 1920 have disappeared;
others have been put on; and in other
cases the rates of duty have been altered.
Postage rates have come down, as have
also telephone and telegraph charges.
The Government of Ireland Act finance
was based on a reserved revenue of over
fourteen millions. Last year just over
seven and a half millions were collected,
so that circumstances altogether outside
our control have resulted in the fact that
the Estimates of 1920 exceed the actual
results of last year by no less than six
and a half millions.
On the expenditure side, the last eight
years have witnessed the introduction of
new social services, the extension of existing ones, the assumption by the State of
heavy burdens in respect of rates, and
many other forms of increased activity in
what are termed local services.
As a
federal unit of the United Kingdom, we
claimed to be allowed equal standards,
a claim that was admitted by the Colwyn
Committee.
And so
last the amount proviyear
sionally paid as contribution was just over
£1,100,000. Its final amount cannot be
ascertained until the detailed accounts for
the year have been issued. Since then,
further concessions have been made in reserved taxation, by the removal of the
tea duty, for example, and heavy additional local expenditure has been undertaken in Great Britain. We would
accordingly expect our contribution for
the current year to be in the region of
£600,000, and that is the figure which
has provisionally been agreed with the
Treasury and confirmed by the Joint Exchequer Board.
TRANSFERRED REVENUE, 1929-30.
I estimate the total of our transferred
revenue receipts at £1,445,000, against
actual receipts last year of £1,508,000.
Our estimated expenditure for the
year thus reaches the total of £10,094,000,
and I will now detail the revenues which
will be available to meet it.
Death Duties are expected to produce
£600,000. The yield of this form of
taxation is a never-ending source of surprise. Last year's returns included some
big estates, and I think it is safer to rely
on this figure, although last year we
received £666,000. Looking at the last
few years, I find that in each year a
quarter of this revenue has been derived
from one or two estates, which clearly
shows how uncertain is the yield of these
taxes.
The Stamp Duties provide a fairly
steady source of income, and I expect
them to yield £280,000 this year. While
on this subject, I would like to
take this opportunity of referring
to the Stamp Duties payable on
solicitors' licences. I propose in
the Finance Bill to include a clause to
implement the agreement arrived at between the Free State Minister of Finance
and myself, under which the privilege
accorded by the Government of Ireland
Act to solicitors in Northern and Southern
Ireland who had been admitted prior to
the year 1921, enabling them to practise
in either area without incurring double
payment of Solicitors' Licence Duty,
would be continued.
The establishment of the Irish Free
State, while not interfering with this
right of practising in either area, made it
illegal for them to practice unless their
certificates were impressed with the
double Stamp Duty. In point of fact,
until the matter was raised by the Free
State Comptroller and Auditor-General,
and by a Free State District Justice early
in the year 1928, solicitors practised in
both areas on payment of a single duty
without the legality of their certificates.
being challenged.

the assent of the Free State Minister of

Transferred Excise Duties are estimated to yield £130,000.
Lastly, I anticipate a small increase in
the yield of Motor Vehicles Duties, and I
am budgeting for £440,000. This is
balanced by payment of a like sum into
the Road Fund.
The grading of Commercial Motor
Vehicles for purposes of taxation has been
occupying my mind for some time past,
and I have appointed a Departmental
Committee to examine the question in detail, and to advise as to what changes
may be required.
But I must make my position perfectly
plain. Whatever may be done in regard
to Motor taxation, the Road Fund must
be self-supporting. In this I have the
entire support of my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Home Affairs, who is immediately responsible for the administration of that Fund. I will not be a party
to any adjustments in taxation, which
throw even a remote liability on the Exchequer so far as the upkeep and construction of roads are concerned.
I could make comparisons with Great
Britain, which would clearly prove that
our motor users are not less favourably
treated than those in Great Britain, but
such comparisons are beside the point.
The only thing that matters is that the
Road Fund must be self-supporting, and
my only concern is to secure the equitable
apportionment of this burden.
RESERVED REVENUE, 1929-30.
Estimates for the yield of reserved taxes
are provided for us by the Departments
concerned, and my comments cannot,
therefore, be of a very exhaustive nature.
Income Tax and Super Tax are put at
£2,870,000--a figure which does not differ
materially from last year's results-and
the now defunct Corporation Profits Tax
and Excess Profits Duty will produce
another £10,000.
Customs and Excise Duties on commodities retained for consumption in Northern
Ireland are estimated at £3,861,000.
This figure allows for the loss resulting
from the repeal of the duty on tea, which
is calculated to cost us £143,000. I will
not weary the Committee with a lengthy
recital of details, but I would point out
that, on the whole, the revenue under
these heads is increasing, pointing to improvement both in general conditions and
in the standard of living.
The total from reserved taxes is thus
put at £6,741,000, bringing the total estimated tax revenue up to £8,186,000.
I now come to the last head of Revenue,
namely, Non-tax Revenue, which forms a
very important part of our total receipts.
The biggest item is the Post Office,
which is expected to bring in this year
£870,000. The gradual increase in Post
Office receipts is indicative of a steady
and well-sustained improvement in general
trade conditions, and although the Post
Office is not yet on a self-supporting basis
-the Estimates show that we expect a
loss of £37,000 this year-yet I am hopeful that the day is not far distant when,
instead of showing a deficit, the Post
Office with improved facilities will actually
contribute to the general Services of the
State.
Land Purchase Annuities are estimated
to amount in all to £665,000, and, I
think, that having dealt with this subject
so extensively in the earlier part of my
statement, I need not dwell further on
the matter now.
Receipts from Church Temporary Rentcharges, etc., will produce £17,000.
Miscellaneous Receipts of £257,000 are
budgeted for in connection with mainly
interest on investments and interest payable by the Unemployment Insurance
Fund in respect of advances to it. This
is necessarily considerably below the

now in progress at Stormont. This is,

Finally, under the Unemployment Insurance Agreement, it is expected that

normal.
If the Province should be blessed with

our local autonomy. I beg to move.

small, though an efficient, Army, but we

Neither can
we compare the two small
ships of the Free State Navy
with the British Navy, or their

the Free State, in round figures,
£1,500,000 a year. That is all I want
to point out--the great services we have
at our disposal for a contribution of
£600,000 a year, compared with the
£1,500,000 which the Free State pays
for vastly inferior services.
Mr. BYRNE: I thoroughly agree with
