Sir DAWSON BATES: I feel it a
great privilege to be in the position of
moving in this House the Second Reading of the Derating Bill, because I realise
that the Bill is an epoch-making one,
which, in the days to come, will be regarded in something of the same light as
the Local Government Act of 1898,
which placed local government administration in the hands of the elected representatives of the people.
So much has been said about the Bill
in this Parliament already, so much has
been written and spoken about it outside,
and it has formed the subject of so many
conferences and discussions with local
authorities that I feel in a sense that it
is, perhaps, unnecessary for me to speak
at any great length on it, but the Bill,
as I have already stated, is such an important one, and its effects are so farreaching, that I feel I would not be doing.
justice to it or to the House were I not
to give a brief outline of the events which
have led up to its introduction and of
its object and effect.
Hon. Members who have taken the
trouble to study the history of local government administration are, no doubt,
aware that in the early days of
local government administration the
State left the local government authorities severely to themselves, and it
was only in comparatively recent
years that Parliament accepted the
principle of according State assistance.
to the local authorities in order to
relieve them, partially, of the growing
burdens which they were called upon to
assume by virtue of the improved services they were supplying to the ratepayers.
Although we have had local government for over a century, it is only a matter of 40 years ago that the first real
attempt was made to accord State assistance in relief of rates. In the year
1887 it was decided that the proceeds of
certain probate and licence duties should
be applied towards the relief of expenditure on specified local government services. After the passing of the Local
Local Government Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Government Act of 1898, a considerable
number of our public health, poor law,
asylum, and road services were subsidized
from what was known as the Local Taxation Account, which was established by
the Act, and which derived its revenue
from the proceeds of certain taxes and
duties.
Gradually, however, as time went on
Parliament began to realise that this
system of paying grants to local authorities out of what may be described as "assigned revenues' was unsatisfactory, as
it deprived Parliament of the opportunity
of controlling the financial operations of
the central local government department
in respect of these grants.
Under more recent Acts passed by the
Imperial Parliament since 1898, grants
for new services were provided each year
from voted moneys. Following this
principle, arrangements were made as
soon as possible after the establishment
of the Government of Northern Ireland
to obtain parliamentary sanction to the
alteration of the old disjointed system,
and to the substitution of a new system,
under which all the grants payable to the
local authorities would be shown in the
Estimates and voted by Parliament
annually.
One of the most important of these
grants was the grant in relief of rates
on agricultural land. This grant was
first established by the Local Government Act of 1898, and was calculated
on the basis of half poor rate and county
cess payable on agricultural land in the
standard year-that standard year was
taken as 1897-and it was realised, even
at that time, that if agricultural land
had to meet the full charge of the rates
it would involve an unduly heavy burden. It was, accordingly, a stereotyped
grant, and so it remained for nearly
thirty years.
On the establishment of the Government of Northern Ireland, it was realised
by us that with the growing burden of
local taxation a grant to the farmers,
which was fixed to meet conditions as
they existed in 1898, was inadequate
and inequitable, and, accordingly, in the
year 1924, this House was asked to double
the agricultural grant. Accordingly,
the figure of £128,644 was increased to
£257,288.
Government have now decided to accord
a still further measure of relief to agriculture, and, at the same time, to introduce a new feature into our local government system by giving a substantial
measure of rate relief to productive industry.
Having regard to the continued depression in agriculture and industry, the
This Bill gives effect to that decision,
and its main features are:--
(a) Agricultural land and farm
buildings will be relieved from all
local rates, with one or two minor exceptions, for example, rates for malicious injury decrees, drainage rates,
and certain water rates, which are
really rents.
(b) Productive industries will be
relieved of 75 per cent. of their rates.
(c) Transport undertakings (including docks and canals) will similarly be
relieved of 75 per cent. of their rates,
but on the condition that the relief is
passed on in the form of rebates to
manufacturers and farmers, in respect
of carriage of raw materials, etc.
(d) Salmon and eel fishery undertakings will benefit to the extent of 60
per cent. relief of rates on their properties.
It should not be difficult to visualise
what a distinct boon these measures will
be to industry generally. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). At present our industries and our farmers are suffering
from external competition, and, undoubtedly, the benefits of this Bill should
enable them to extend their undertakings and to improve their position in the
markets of the world.
I have, up to the present, confined my
remarks to the objects of the Bill,
namely, the relief to industry, and now
I will deal with the measures which the
Bill prescribes in connection with the recoupment to the local authorities of the
loss of revenue which will fall on them
by reason of the derating proposals. I
will take the Urban Authorities first, as
their problem is the simpler one. In the
case of the urban areas, agricultural land
forms a very small part of the hereditaments, and the derating proposals will,
therefore, apply mainly to premises used for
productive industries. The loss of rates to
the urban authorities will, accordingly,
form but a small part (approximately 12
per cent.) of the total rates to be collected by those authorities, and, accord-
13 JUNE 1929
Local Government Bill-
Second Reading.
ingly, it is our proposal to recoup in each
case to the local authorities the actual
loss of revenue sustained by them.
I now turn to the rural portions of
each of the counties, and here the problem is a much more complicated one,
by reason of the fact that in these areas
the rates on agricultural land form the
bulk (approximately 80 per cent.) of the
rates assessed by the local authorities.
Accordingly, the net result will be that,
in the future, the Ministry of Home
Affairs, acting on behalf of the Government, will become the largest ratepayer
in the counties. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
While the Ministry has been entrusted
with a certain measure of control over
the activities of the various local authorities in the counties, at a later stage, undoubtedly, it will be necessary and desirable, in view of the greater financial
responsibility which the Government is
undertaking, to accord the Ministry a
greater measure of control over the financial operations of the local government
authorities.
In the meantime, we cannot apply to
the county areas the principle which we
have agreed to apply in the case of the
urban districts-that of merely recouping
each year's loss. If we did, there would
be nothing to stop the local authorities
from spending recklessly at the expense.
of the Government, and so we have devised a scheme under which the local
authorities will be paid each year standard deficiency grants, based, generally
on what would have been required during the last three years, to meet their
losses if the farmers and the proprietors
of productive industries, etc., had been
relieved during that period of rates in
the manner which the Bill now proposes,
due allowance being made for abnormalities in expenditure.
While fixing the standard grants for the
various authorities and charges for the
next five years, we realise that in the
normal course of events during that period
there may be in some cases appropriate
and normal increases of expenditure which
may not be counterbalanced by savings
in other directions. In connection with
such increases the Government realise that
in regard to them a certain and substantial measure of relief should be available
and granted, but at the same time the
State cannot in this connection undertake
unlimited liability. The Imperial
Government has adopted in this regard a
somewhat elaborate series of formulae and
adjustments to meet growing expenditure,
but on considering the matter in the light
of the conditions which exist in Northern
Ireland, and having discussed it fully with
the representatives of the local authorities,
we have decided to adopt a more simple
and appropriate system of payment of
supplemental grants to meet growing expenditure.

of stereotyping grants for all time.
In arriving at the calculation of the
supplemental grants we have found it
necessary to make a clear distinction of a
temporary nature between the grants for
purely local government services and those
for educational services, the reason being
-as I have already pointed out-that the
latter services are still in their initial
stages and are developing with greater
rapidity than the older and wellestablished local government services. Accordingly, in the case of the ordinary local
government services we propose to work
out for each county what I may describe as
a financial pool for all the local government
authorities, the pool not to exceed in any
one year an amount equivalent to the
product of a 6d rate on the derated hereditaments in the county.
Subject to this maximum the Ministry
of Home Affairs is empowered under the
Bill to pay a supplemental grant to any
local government authority which finds
itself confronted with increased expenditure, the supplemental grants being in
the same proportion to the increase in
the net expenditure over the standard
expenditure as the standard grants bears
the standard expenditure. Hon.
Members will appreciate a simple example
of this arrangement.

will be understood that the rates had

April.
I will now deal briefly with a few minor
points of detail in the Bill. In the first
place, while the Bill makes provision for
standard and supplemental grants to
county councils and rural district councils,
for the next five years, the necessary
calculation will take time, and so we
have, at the request of the county
As soon as we had made the decision
to make the Bill apply as from the 1st
April, we found it necessary to issue instructions to the county councils not to
collect rates If we had not done so,
and had allowed even portion of the rates
to be collected we would have found it a
matter of great complication and difficulty to make the necessary refunds later.
The Bill gives covering authority for
this arrangement, and also requires the
county councils to collect the rates for
the year in one instalment, instead of in
two moieties, as at present. At the same
time, we realise that a single rate collection might operate somewhat harshly
on poorer classes of tenants, and while
provision is made for one collection in
the future, arrangements are also made
whereby the rate on smaller hereditaments, that is, £8 valuation and under,
can be collected in two moieties. Hon.
Members will see that this applies only
to the counties.
It will also be realised that the introduction of the derating principle will,
to a very considerable extent, affect the
amounts to be collected by the various
rate collectors throughout the country,
and, of course, would incidentally affect
their emoluments where these emoluments are paid by way of poundage fees.
At the same time, the collectors will still
have to visit the ratepavers generally in
their districts, and to serve demand notes
on them, even for reduced amounts, so
actually the amount of labour will be
practically the same. Accordingly,
Clause 20 of the Bill safeguards the existing rights and emoluments of the
existing collectors, subject, however, in
every case to efficient and due discharge
of their duties.
I should also draw attention to the
arrangements which are provided for in
Clause 14 of the Bill. in regard to the
time and the manner of payment of both
the standard and supplemental grants.
This is a matter which has formed the
subiect of consultation with the local
authorities, and in consequence of their
representations we have agreed to pay the
(41 Local Government Bill-

standard grant in four instalments on
fixed dates in June, September, January
and March, which will meet the full requirements and needs of the local authorities.
As regards the supplemental grants, it
will be understood that they are not of a
stereotyped character, and depend on
varying circumstances. Accordingly,
they will have to be calculated on the
basis of estimate rather than on fixed
quantity. We propose, therefore, to
adopt the same principle in regard to
them as we do in the case of the road
grants, namely, to pay 90 per cent.
during the course of the year concerned,
in four instalments, leaving the balance
of 10 per cent. over for subsequent adjustment between the Ministry and the local
authority.
I would also like to refer to Clause 7,
which provides that in the future all
charges for such purely local services as
waterworks, sewerage, etcetera, will be
borne over the rural districts concerned,
and will not be confined to townlands, to
dispensary districts, or to other local areas
of charge, as in the past. The reason for
this alteration in the law is an obvious
one. Under the old system, where no
Government grants were available, it was
difficult to persuade the council of a rural
district to accept a general financial responsibility for a service such as a waterworks or a sewerage scheme which was of
purely local benefit, and it was, accordingly, a matter of great difficulty for the
central government, that is, the Local
Government Board in Dublin, and the
Ministry of Home Affairs in Belfast, to
secure the formulation and the carrying
out of such necessary schemes owing to the
conflict between the local authority and
the people of the locality as to the areas
of charge. The rural district council
naturally wanted the local village to pay
the full cost, while the people of the
village and the neighbouring locality
were unable to undertake the financial
responsibility, and felt that the rural
district as a whole should shoulder
part of the expenses. The result was,
and is at the present time in many
country districts, that the schemes have
been abandoned simply through difficulty
in getting the rural district council to
shoulder the responsibility.
Now, however, the situation will be entirely different. As I have already
pointed out, the Government is shouldering the major portion of the financial
burden in the rural areas, and, accordingly, there is no justification whatever
for any rural district council to refuse to
bear, as a district charge, the balance of
the expense of providing a much-needed
water supply scheme, or sewerage scheme,
for a particular town or village in their
midst.
.
We realise that if this change in policy
and principle were to be applied to existing schemes, without some counterbalancing adjustment, there would be
undoubtedly some inequity and reasonable
ground for grievance on the part of the
ratepayers in those localities where such
services have not up to the present been
provided, as they would suddenly find
themselves called upon to pay their proportionate part of the district charges for
the water, sewerage and other services
have already been provided in more fortunate areas.
In order to meet such objection, the
Government will come to the rescue of
these down-trodden ratepayers, and we
are making provision in the Bill, under
which no ratepayer will be called upon
to bear any extra charge on foot of such
existing schemes. I think that it will be
agreed that this provision will dispose of
any objection to the new principle which
we are establishing in Northern Ireland.
I think that I have outlined generally
the salient points of the Bill. It will be
observed that I have, in the main, confined myself to the local government
aspect of the Bill, and have not attempted
to deal with the complications of rebates
to transport undertakings. This matter
was explained to the House at length by
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock), in November last,
when introducing the Rating and Valuation Act, 1928, and I feel sure that he will
gladly explain any points of difficulty or
doubt in this regard.
As regards the question of relief to our
salmon and eel fisheries, I should say that
these matters come within the jurisdiction
of my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Commerce (Mr. Barbour), and while I
have no doubt that this proposal will
commend itself to the House, I should
say that he, similarly, will be prepared to
explain any matters in regard to fisheries

Bankruptcy (Amendment) Bill [S.]
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time"
Mr. BARBOUR: It will be within the
knowledge of hon. Members that our
Bankruptcy Law in Ireland has grown in
the course
of years into a somewhat
shapeless fabric, in which are to be found
at several points important divergencies
from the law obtaining in England, with
whose commercial community we are so
closely linked. It was accordingly
borne in upon us, soon after I assumed
the responsibility for the direction of the
Ministry of Commerce, that a change in
the law was necessary, and, in order that
the many aspects of a difficult and complex problem might be thoroughly investigated I set up in the Autumn of 1926
a small but expert committee under the
able chairmanship of my hon. Friend, the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry
of Education, who, as the House will be
aware, has made a special study of this
subject.
Bankruptcy Bill-
Second Reading.
13 JUNE 1929
The Committee to which I have referred produced a report containing recommendations, which are the basis of
the Bill before you. The deliberations
of the Committee covered a considerable
period, and witnesses were examined
from every interest involved, whether
legal or commercial. I am satisfied that
the recommendations which the committee have made will go far towards simplifying the existing Bankruptcy Code,
and, whilst the consolidation of bankruptcy law as a whole must necessarily
take some considerable time, in view of
the ramifications of the existing law on
the subject, the Government have thought
it right to introduce this Bill immediately, in order that certain anomalies,
the most important of which I shall endeavour to explain to the House, might
be remedied forthwith, and that in
general the important step should be
taken of bringing our existing bankruptcy law into as close conformity as
local circumstances permit with the present law on the subject in England,
which, as hon. Members will be aware, has
recently undergone substantial amendment.
Before referring in any detail to the
provisions of the Bill, I should like to
make a brief reference to the legislative
position as it exists to-day. For all
practical purposes the Law of Bankruptcy in Ireland is just over 70 years
old. The law took definite shape in the
Irish Bankrupt and Insolvent Act, 1857.
This Act was amended in some respects
by the Bankruptcy (Ireland) Amendment Act, 1872, but, apart from this,
there has been no attempt to secure a
comprehensive revision in Ireland, and
so, to-day, the Act of 1857 still stands
as the corner stone of our Bankruptcy
Code.
With regard to the changes which we
propose to make, I should like to say, in
the first place, that it is not our intention
to make any radical change in the
machinery of administration. On this
point I may, perhaps, be permitted to
quote from the Report of the Committee
of Inquiry:-
In this respect we are far behind.
Great Britain. There the whole Law of
Insolvency, relating both to bankruptcy
and to private arrangement, was revised
and consolidated in 1913. Bankruptcy
and arrangement matters were given
separate Acts in 1914. Even the Bankruptcy Act of 1914, complete as it was,
was amended in certain important particulars in 1926, by an Act which owed
its inspirations largely to Chambers of
Commerce, bankers, and business men
generally, who desired to see the law still
further modernised to bring it more into
accord with post-war business conditions.
"All the
professional witnesses
familiar with local bankruptcy practice told us that it worked very well
and that the people had become accustomed to it. Under these circumstances, we do not recommend a change
in the existing system."
The Committee did, however, make
one suggestion for speeding up the procedure, which the Government has considered it very necessary to adopt. I refer to the provision contained in Sections
4 and 5 of the Bill for speeding up the
court machinery by abolishing the second
sitting before the court, both in
arrangements and compositions after
bankruptcy. The saving of time, not
less than a fortnight, and of expenses will
be found to be of the greatest advantage,
coming, as it does, in the earlier stages
of the proceedings.
The House will not, I am sure, expect
me to make a detailed reference to all the
Clauses of the Bill, some of which are of
a highly technical nature. There are
some, however, of great practical importance, which it is incumbent upon me
to explain to the House.
In the first place, a radical change has
been made with regard to the scope of
bankruptcy offences and the penalties provided. Honourable Members will notice
on reference to Clause 22 that the three
principal commercial irregularities, which
post-war conditions have considerably
aggravated, have been singled out for
the special penalty of penal servitude for
any term not exceeding five years, or to
imprisonment for a term not exceeding
two years, with or without hard labour.
These offences in relation to bankruptcy
are: Obtaining property by fraud; obtaining property under false pretence of
carrying on a business, and disposing of
property otherwise than in the normal
course of trade.
The last-mentioned offences-disposing
of goods otherwise than in the ordinary
course of business-is also further distinguished: The pledgee or receiver of the
goods with a knowledge of the circum-
Bankruptcy Bill-
€84
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
stances is deemed to be guilty of a misdemeanour. The next clause, No. 23,
also contains a very necessary reform,
making it a misdemeanour for an undischarged bankrupt to obtain credit to the
extent of £10 or upwards, without disclosing his bankruptcy.
Important evidence was tendered to
the Committee touching the losses sustained by Northern Ireland traders
through the weakness of our law in these
respects, and it has been felt that these
offences are such as should, in the interests
of the creditor, have a greater penalty
attached to them. I can assure the
House that the honest and unfortunate
debtor is in no way prejudiced by the
provisions I have mentioned. Our objective is the dishonest, evasive, or reckless debtor, and I feel sure that honourable Members will agree that against
such a one a creditor deserves all the protection he can get.
Another important provision is the
liability to keep proper books of account,
imposed by Clause 25 of the Bill.
In
English law, the failure of a bankrupt.
to keep books has always been regarded
as a serious bankruptcy offence, justifying suspension or the refusal of a discharge, but it was not until the Act of
1914, to which I have referred, that it
was made a misdemeanour, and even
then only on the trader's second bankruptcy. Now, under Section 7 of the
Bankruptcy Amendment Act of 1926,

account, as defined by the section, is

The clause to which I am now directing the particular attention of the House
virtually adopts the legislative position
as it exists in England to-day. Honourable Members will observe that a distinction is made between a first-time
bankrupt and one who has previously
failed. The former is not to be prosecuted unless his liabilities amount to
£500 or over, but in the case of a debtor
who has previously failed prosecution
may be instituted if the liabilities amount
to £100. There is no doubt that in this
matter of keeping even elementary
accounts there is a great need for improvement, especially among the small
traders in our cities and country towns,
although in recent years the operation of
We also propose to make some radical
changes in the Law of Bankruptcy as it
affects married women. These changes
are given effect to in Clauses 10 and 20
of the Bill. Some of the witnesses who
appeared before the Committee advocated
the imposition on married women of restrictions of a somewhat drastic character
in regard to trading. It has been felt,
however, that it would be inadvisable to
proceed in advance of Great Britain in
this matter. There a married woman
who carries on a trade or business is liable
to bankruptcy proceedings, irrespective of
whether her trade or business is carried
on separately from her husband or not,
and is also liable to be served with a Bankruptcy Notice on a Final Judgment or
Order as though she were personally
bound to pay the debt.
Furthermore, the husband of a bankrupt married woman is not entitled to
claim any dividend as a creditor in respect of any money, or other asset, lent
or entrusted by him to his wife for the
purposes of her trade or business, until
all claims of the other creditors of his
wife have been satisfied. Similarly, in
the bankruptcy of the husband, the
claims of the wife are postponed to those
of other creditors. In Ireland the position
of a married woman is governed by the
Married Woman's Property Act, 1882,
Section 1 (5) of which provides that
"every married woman carrying on a
trade separately from her husband shall,
in respect of her separate property, be
subject to the Bankruptcy Laws in the
same way as if she were a 'femme sole.' "
Thus as the law stands at present a
marred woman in Northern Ireland cannot be made bankrupt unless she carry on
a trade and carry it on separately from
her husband. Hon. Members will, I am
Bankruptcy Bill-
Second Reading.
13 JUNE 1929
sure, agree that for married women to continue to enjoy this privileged position coustitutes an anomaly which is completely
out of accord with post-war business conditions, and one which should be removed
without delay.
Another matter to which I desire to
make a brief reference is the scope of the
various Acts of Bankruptcy as defined in
our Bankruptcy Code. Here there has
been no great widening of the net through
the years, for there is remarkable similarity between the Acts of Bankruptcy as
enumerated for England in Section 1 of
the Act of 1914, and the list for Ireland
set forth in Section 21 of the Bankruptcy
(Ireland) Amendment Act, 1872. In this
matter we propose to go a step further
than the legislative position in England
by making [in clause 1(b)] a return of
"No Goods" by the Sheriff an Act of
Bankruptcy in Northern Ireland. Apart
from the fact that this reform was advocated by nearly all the professional and
commercial interests that gave evidence
before the Committee, it is difficult to
appreciate why a debtor who has no goods
to seize should escape this penalty which
attaches to debtors who have goods subject
to seizure. In one respect, however, we
propose to bring the law into line with
England by making [in clause 1(d)]
"Fraudulent Preference" an Act of
Bankruptcy.
Other reforms to which, perhaps, a
passing reference may be made at this
stage are:-
the sweeping away of old distinctions
between traders and non-traders
which left the latter in a very
sheltered position (Clause 1),
preventing creditors from unreasonably withholding their consent to
a Deed of Assignment outside the
Court where the debtor has secured
a proper measure of support for
his proposal (Clause 2),
giving an option to a creditor of a
deceased insolvent of proceeding in
the Bankruptcy Court instead of in
the Chancery Division (Clause 21),
imposing penalties for rash speculation or gambling by bankrupts
(Clause 24).
I have now, I think, explained the
clauses of the most importance and those
to which the commercial community will
give the greatest consideration.
ment's appreciation of the public-spirited
and disinterested manner in which professional and business men, as members
of the Bankruptcy Committee, gave their
valuable time to the consideration of this
subject. The Bill owes much to their

Mr. HEALY: I do not think that
serious objection can be taken to this
Measure on any side of the House. There
have been certain anomalies between the
law in England and the law in Ireland
for a considerable time that must have
borne harshly on creditors. For instance,
in the matter of a return of "no goods'
by the sheriff's officer-1 suppose that
sheriffs' officers are not any different from
other people and sometimes it has been
alleged that returns of this kind were
made when the facts of the situation did
not justify them, with the result, as the
Minister has pointed out, that a man who
had no goods was immune from bankruptcy, whereas a man with some goods
was liable to be made a bankrupt. I am
glad that anomaly has been wiped away
and that the failure of the sheriff's officer
to do his duty or to make a correct return
will not conduce to the benefit of a dishonest person anywhere.

There is also the question of the dis
tinction between traders and non-traders.
Hitherto, as I understand it, unless a man
was engaged in business it was difficult to
make him a bankrupt. Now, whether be
be in business or technically out of business and in private life the law is intended
to apply equally. There is one form of
fraud that is rather prevalent, probably
to a greater extent across the water than
in this country, that is what is known
as the long firm fraud, in which a man
obtains goods with the deliberate intention of disposing of them and then
clearing out.
There are three conditions under which
a person may leave himself liable to a long
term of imprisonment. The first is bv
obtaining property by fraud, the second
by obtaining property by the false pretence of carrying on a business of some
kind, and the third by disposing of property otherwise than in the ordinary way
of trade. It has sometimes happened that
people who have had no place of business
and no bona fide intention of conducting
a business have obtained credit and have
put the trustful creditors into an awkward
position. In all these matters one must
remember that if a trader be in the
Bankruptcy Bill-

[Mr. Healy]
position of finding himself unable to recover his debts in the long run the community itself must suffer. It is sometimes, for instance, held that competition
lowers prices. My view is that competition does not lower prices but has an
opposite tendency. Where there is undue
competition failure is bound to ensue and
the community in the long run suffers
when goods are sold under their value.
I am glad the tendency of the legislation
now introduced is to put an end to the
type of person who would engage in this
practice.

is well known that farmers are not in the

When he gets a decree to execute he looks

or even on promotion to another post
under the same authority. Such instances
are frequent, as many schools, with their

control of local education authorities in
accordance with the provisions of the
Education Act of 1923. It is estimated
that upwards of 1,000 public elementary

majority of whom were formerly serving

Considerable inconvenience arises also

Government Loans Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:

Mr. BARBOUR: This Bill is a short
Bill dealing with the replenishment of the
Government Loans Fund, which hon.
Members will remember was established in
order that local authorities might be
financed in the same way as similar bodies
are financed in Great Britain through the
Local Loans Fund. In our own case the
scope of the Government Loans Fund is
somewhat wider, inasmuch as the Act of
1925, which established it, provided for
advances being made to the Exchequer in
respect of housing expenditure and capital
expenditure on police barracks.
The provisions of this Bill are simple
in character. In order to explain the first
clause of the Bill, I should state that previous legislation placed two limits on our
Government Loans Fund advances, one a
time limit, beyond which advances could
not be made to local authorities, the other
a money limit. The time limit was provided for in our original Government
Loans Act of 1925, and the present limit,
which expired on the 31st March last, was
extended to that date under an amending
Government Loans Act of 1926.
As regards the money limit, this plays
a two-fold part. In the first place, it prevents issues being made to local authorities
and for the other purposes of the Government Loans Fund in an unlimited manner,
that is to say, it makes it necessary for the
£94
Government Loans Bill
Supply
13 JUNE 1929
In
Ministry of Finance to come to this House
from time to time for fresh powers.
the second place, the money limit forms
also the limit beyond which the Ministry
cannot issue Ulster Loans Stock, which is
used for feeding the Government Loans
Fund. At the present time sums amounting, approximately, to £3,500,000 have
been issued to local authorities and for the
other purposes authorised by our Government Loans Acts out of a total authorised
maximum of £4,250,000.
It may be of interest to the House to
know how we have raised this money. The
first issue of Ulster Loans Stock was made
in the year 1925 by means of a public
issue under-written on the London market.
The total of the first issue amounted to
£2,000,000. The proceeds of this issue
were exhausted in the year 1927, and in
that year a further issue of £1,100,000 was
made privately to such Irish banks and a
few insurance companies, and so forth, as
were willing to take up the stock at an
agreed price. By this means the cost of
under-writing and placing on the market
a limited amount of stock was avoided.
Early in the present year the proceeds of
the last issue were exhausted, and for a
short time the Fund was financed by temporary borrowings, but some months ago
fresh negotiations with the banks and with
other bodies, including the Belfast Corporation and the Representative Body of
the Church of Ireland, resulted in arrangements being made for a further issue of
£900,000 of stock. This stock will not, in
fact, have to be created until December
next, as it was arranged that only a part
instalment would be payable in the month
of June of this year, the remainder being
payable in December. I should like to
express my appreciation of the assistance
which has been given to the Ministry in
this matter by the banks and other
institutions.
Clause 2 empowers the Ministry of
Finance to charge and recover interest on
arrears of the principal and interest of all
loans which may be issued out of the
Government Loans Fund, and fixes the
rate of interest for this purpose at a rate
I think this
not exceeding 63 per cent.
information will suffice for the House,
and I accordingly beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Clause 1 of the Bill proposes for the
future to abolish one of the limits,
namely, the time limit, as this limit has
little or no relevance in Northern Ireland, although it exists in the British
Local Loans Acts, and we now have ample
experience of what the normal drain on
the Fund may be expected to be. On the
other hand, the money limit will remain,
but the Bill proposes to increase the
present maximum from £4,250,000 to a
total of £7,000,000. This increase will,
it is anticipated, cover the requirements
of the next two or three years.
Bill read a Second time, and committed
to a Committee of the Whole House for
to-morrow.

DIETARY SCALE IN PRISONS.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if the
prisoners confined in His Majesty's
Prisons in Northen Ireland receive butter
or margarine as part of their dietary, and,
if so, the amount of butter or margarine
allowed to each prisoner per week.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The dietaries
in H.M. Prisons in Northern Ireland,
which are similar to those in English
prisons, are divided into three main
classes, and are applicable to prisoners
as follows:-
Class 1.-Prisoners under sentence of
imprisonment for 7 days or less, and
during the first 7 days of sentences
exceeding that period, but not exceeding
4 months:
—————
There is no issue of butter or margarine.
Class 2-All ordinary prisoners other
than those in Class 1:-
-:
An issue of 3 ozs. of margarine
weekly.
Class 3.--Convicts, prisoners awaiting
trial, offenders of the first and second
divisions, debtors, and contempt of court
prisoners:-
An issue of 7 ozs. of margarine weekly.
In addition to the above classes there
is an Hospital Diet, which is issued under
the directions of the Medical Officer to
the Prison.
-:
Butter is included in this diet in such
quantities as are directed by the Medical
Officer to meet the specific requirements
of each case.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of that
answer, will the right hon. Gentleman
consider the advisability of issuing butter
to untried prisoners who have not been
convicted, and who may not be guilty of
any offence.

expenditure on Education and, while
members have occasionally criticised certain items, there has been no tendency to
suggest that there should be any attempt
to cut down the expenditure. This, I
hope, is not only because members have in
the past been satisfied that the money has
been well spent, but also because they have
constantly taken the widest view of the
matter and looked on our expenditure as
one of the most prudent investments that
the public can make.
In the second Vote-for the Educational services-there is an increase over
last year of £87,606. Many of the Subheads of this Vote are less than last year,
and the main causes of the increase will
be found in the award of annual increments to existing elementary, secondary
and technical teachers, a large increase in
the grants to secondary schools and to
local education authorities, and an increase of £23,000 in the statutory payment to the Teachers' Superannuation
Fund.
Vote 1 provides for the salaries and
expenses of the Ministry, and is £786
more than last year. The increase is entirely due to the provision for the awards
of the annual salary increments and to an
increase in the salary bonus, consequent
upon the rise in the cost-of-living index
figure from 1st March, 1929. The increase for this purpose is £902, but from
this must be deducted decreases in Subheads C, D, and F of £116, leaving a net
increase in the Vote of £786.
In Sub-head Al, Training Colleges,
there is a decrease of £560. Certain
diploma bonuses are awarded to teachers
who, having entered training colleges
prior to the 1st February, 1922, fulfil the
conditions prescribed for the award of
bonus while serving in Northern Ireland.
This system of awarding bonuses does
not apply to students who entered training since 1922, and it is, therefore, an
expiring liability, so that it has been
found possible to reduce the provisions
for these bonuses by £400. A slight decrease is anticipated in the cost of courses
of instruction in Kindergarten for junior
assistant mistresses, and a further cause
of reduction is due to the revised rates
payable in respect of the men students
in Strawberry Hill Training College:
these rates, which are identical with those
paid to that college by the English Board
of Education, have recently been reduced
from £76 13s 4d to £70 16s 3d per head.
There is a slight decrease in Sub-head
A2, and, while I do not, propose to enter
into details, I wish to call the attention
of the Committee to the token vote of
£100, which appears under this Subhead. As explained in the Estimates, it
is proposed to seek authority for the payment of £10,000 to the Belfast Education
Committee for the purpose of assisting in
the erection of a new school to replace the
Belfast Model Schools, which are only
of a temporary character. With the
same end in view, it is proposed to hand
over to the Belfast Education Committee,
as a free gift, a site in May Street, which
at present, belongs to the Government.
Legislation for this purpose will be introduced in due course, but as the grant is
not paid over until the work on the new
school is in progress, it will probably not.
be found necessary to make an actual payment in respect of it during the current
financial year. The payment of the
£10,000 and the free site are an agreed

equivalent, accepted by the Education

85.8 in Down, 84.1 in Tyrone, and

County, and in Fermanagh, decreases

Turning to Sub-head C we find an increase of £17,520, which is almost entirely
due to increased provision for increment

as the basis of entry to the training colleges recognized by the Ministry for ele-
The increase in Sub-head D1 is due to
an automatic rise in the amount required
for the award of annual increments of the
teachers' salaries, while in Sub-head D2,
provision is made for the award of an
additional technological scholarship, and,

Government of Northern Ireland that Department has limited its sphere of operations to Great Britain.
Under Sub-head F there is a very large
increase in the grants payable to local
education authorities, and it is for the
following reasons: the grant for any year
is paid in five instalments, four of which
(not to exceed in the aggregate 95 per
cent. of the grant paid for the previous
year) are paid within the year as payments on account, the final instalment not
being paid until after the audit of the
accounts in the following year.
The expenditure of the local authorities in the

large. It will be observed that the

very little short of £160,000, which is the

Considerable progress can be reported as

authorities. Several substantial grants
have been made to secondary schools,

at 31st December last was 442, and the

Having now reviewed the Estimates in
considerable detail, I should like to take
the opportunity of referring to a question
of outstanding importance to our future as
a race, namely, the making of adequate
provision for medical and dental inspection
and treatment of school children. While
in some quarters-notably the City of
Belfast-the problem is being squarely
faced, and real and most successful efforts
are being made to deal with it as a whole
and in an adequate manner, I regret to
find that there is not, as yet, in all quarters
such widespread recognition of its importance as we should be entitled to expect.
There is still far too much of the attitude
that medical (and, of course, I include
dental) inspection and treatment are
luxuries which are desirable, if funds permit-and we all know how seldom that is
the case. In this matter, if anywhere, a
wider outlook is essential; we must always
bear in mind that what we are asked to
face is whether the future of our children
and, in turn, of their children, is to be
marred by preventable illness and misery,
with its consequences of poverty and hardship, or whether it is to be healthy, strong
and vigorous.
It is for the people of Ulster, through
their representatives on local education
committees, to determine if it is worth
while shouldering some small extra burden for the purpose of securing as far
as possible that the future of a great race
shall not be spoiled by sickness and disease
which a little thought, a little foresight,
and a little money could assuredly have
prevented. We pride ourselves on
shrewdness, and, when we care to do so,
are quite able to view most problems in
our
Estimates-

Ministry of Education.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
their right proportion, and to appraise
them by a true scale of values and, for
this reason I believe, in order to ensure
that it will be honestly and adequately
dealt with, that it will only be necessary
to bring the matter prominently before the
people and to get them as conscientious
and well-meaning citizens to realise their
responsibility towards it. The importance of the aim being realised, we can
then consider how best it may be secured.
It must be clearly understood that
medical and dental inspection by themselves are of little use; they must be accompanied by treatment; and even this
is only part of the picture, for the purpose of the school medical service is not
confined to the remedying of defects, but
to their prevention-sickness must be
prevented where possible. In the words
of Sir George Newman, Chief Medical
Officer of the English Board of Education,
the aims of the school medical service may
be stated as follows:-
(1) To fit the child to receive the
education provided for it by the State.
(2) To detect any departures from
the normal physiological health and
growth, any impairments, aberrations,
defects, or disease (physical or mental),
and advise the remedy or amelioration
of them (at the school or otherwise) lest
worse befall.
(3) To seek the causes and conditions
of such defect and disease, and, as far
as may be, prevent them.
(4) To teach and practise personal
hygiene in every school, so that a habit
of hygiene may be contracted by the
children, and the way of physiological
life may be followed by each coming
generation.
Sir George adds-
The whole design is an opening of the
gates of physical opportunity. Medical inspection is merely an arrangement
to explore and unveil the condition of
each child in order that the rest of the
programme may be fulfilled with a correct regard to the facts of the case.
are not so satisfactory, and this is greatly
to be deplored, as unless cases are followed up and treated it is little use discovering the defects. Then, again,
medical inspection cannot be really effective in the lives of the children if they
spend their school days, as many of them
still do, in school buildings in which proper attention is not given to cleanliness
and fresh air. What is the use of urging
upon children the importance of personal
cleanliness if a sufficient supply of washing facilities is not available in the school;
or why should we preach the gospel of
sunshine and fresh air if the schools are
not flooded with both as often as, and
whenever, possible? I have not referred
to the need of sufficient and suitable playgrounds or to the importance of organised
games (such as are provided in secondary
schools), but these are all part of the
medical service problem and should receive increased attention.
The problem of caring for the health.
of our future citizens is, thus, no simple
one, but one which presents several sides,
each of which must receive attention.
Most of our local education authorities
have made arrangements for medical inspection, but arrangements for treatment
It is, of course, impossible at once to
do everything that should be done, but
there is a danger of hastening so slowly
that the value even of what we accomplish
is not what it might be. The rejoinder
that "times are hard" can only be met
by the importance of the problem. The
nation's children are its most precious
possession; into their hands the future of
the race and of the country must, in the
course of time, be placed, and, this being
so, I feel that we should look on all that
relates to their well-being and happiness.
in the most unselfish and far-seeing way.
Realising the magnitude as well as the
high privilege of our responsibility, I am
confident that the people will be ready
to make sacrifices, if such are necessary;
that they will make a great venture of
faith, and that they will see to it that
lack of money is the least of the obstacles
in the way of the realization of the aim
of the school medical service. As we
are always reaping our past so are we
always sowing our future; let us see to it
that it will be as bright and promising
as we can help to make it. I beg to move.
The CHAIRMAN: With reference to
these two estimates it will be observed that
the main questions of policy arise on the
second estimate, and not upon the first.
I propose, therefore, to follow the example
of a previous estimate, and leave both estimates open for discussion as far as policy
is concerned, asking the Committee to cooperate with me in keeping a clear-cut line
between policy upon the one hand, and
mere matters of detail upon the other.

Mr. POLLOCK: The matters referred
to by the Member for Mid-Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) are not exactly relevant to the
peculiar position that Magee College
occupies. Under the scheme I have outlined, we would not have had representation on the governing body if it had been
carried through. Of course, the Government is represented in the sense that it
can allocate nominees to represent it on
the governing bodies, but the objection is
that Magee College refuses to come under
our educational system. It is outside it
altogether, and it proposes to keep outside it. The fact of having representatives on their own governing body would
not affect that position in the slightest.
The governing body of Magee would not,
as I am given to understand directly from
itself, recognise any control or any authority on the part of anybody outside itself.
In other words, it would be an autonomous institution.
No one deplores the position of Trinity
more than I do. Trinity is suffering from
rather extraordinary circumstances. It
is an old foundation of 250 or 300 years,
and now finds itself in difficulties. Of
course it benefits to a very large extent
by the admission of these one hundred
students from Magee. I understand that
that is the number of students who go
from Magee to Trinity, although that is,
perhaps in excess of the number attending.
However, I hear from my hon. Friend
opposite that one hundred students are
there. The hundred students do help in
a very material degree the financial position of Trinity, and I may say that it
would be a sad disaster for Trinity, viewing it from their point of view, if they lost
the advantage accruing from the attendance of these students. I admit that,
but that is not the point.
The point is, are we going directly, or
indirectly, to subsidise an educational
institution over which we have no control,
and which is not our own property. That
is the position, unfortunately for Magee,
I had to take up, but I am sure the Committee will realise that the offer made by
the Government was very generous.
The
Government would have undertaken to
provide the necessary money to enable
their professors to live in comfort, provide
them with a pension, and place them in
the same position as if they were Professors of a University. That they refused, and insisted on maintaining their
connection with Trinity, and the Government had no other course open to it but
to refuse them a subsidy.

in rural areas. There is no doubt that

Mr. ROBB: As I would like to reply
to all the points that have been raised,
hon. Members will excuse me if I do not
deal with any one point at any great
length. I think I should deal first with
the matter on which the last speaker, the
Member for Foyle (Mr. McCarroll),
dwelt so long, namely, the grievance which
he alleges Roman Catholics suffer with
regard to building grants for their
voluntary schools. His case is based
entirely upon an allegation of a deprivation of rights they formerly enjoyed.
That allegation of former rights is unfounded. I have stated in this House before, and I repeat it now, that the
history of building grants for elementary
schools in Ireland is this. For a time
building grants were very freely given
upon a mistaken policy of the then
Resident Commissioner, who was delighted
to go every year to Parliament, and in his
Report say there had been so many schools
built in Ireland during the past year and
that, therefore, education must have been
progressing.
The result of that system was the
springing up all over Ireland of a large
number of small schools. They were not
efficient and they could not be kept up,
with the result that education was going
to the bad. It was finally borne in upon
the Treasury in England that these free
and easy grants for schools were a mistake,
and from the year 1900 that policy was
entirely reversed and grants were very
difficult to get, although it is quite true
that for a time further grants were given.
Building was entirely stopped during the
war, and when it was resumed no grant
was given except on specific proof to the
Treasury in England that the state of the
particular building was such that a new
building was required. The whole of the
arguments on behalf of Roman Catholics
for building grants for their voluntary
schools have been based upon the allegation, first of all, that the 1923 Act
abolished a right they had before.

The intention is, of course, that these
standard grants shall represent that proportion of the normal annual expenditure
of each local authority which would otherwise be met by the rates struck on pre-
The Government realise, however, that
local authorities must be put in a position
to obtain some assistance from the Government towards necessary increases in
their expenditure during each five-year
period arising out of the development of
the services under their control. The
Bill provides, therefore, for contributions.
in the form of supplemental grants
towards such increases.
I can, perhaps, best explain the way the
supplemental grant will work by an illustration. Assume a rural area's full
valuation is £60,000 and it is derated to
the extent of £50,000. The standard
grant in such a case is based on the latter
valuation, that is, 5/6ths of the total expenditure in the standard is met by the
Government, so that assuming a standard
expenditure of £24,000, a sum of £20,000
will be payable by the Government as a
Standard Grant. Now, assume the local
expenditure increases to £25,000-the
Government will contribute the same
proportion of the new expenditure, so as
to make good the loss due to derating;
that is to say five-sixths of £25,000, or
something slightly in excess of £20,800.
There must, however, obviously be some
limit to the amount of the supplemental
grant, in so far as it is not required for
educational services, otherwise there can
be no check on local expenditure, to
which the Government will be the main
contributor. This limit is achieved by

The original clause lays down specific
dates for the payment of the grant, but
a more elastic system is necessary in respect of the grants for the current year.
For instance, it will be necessary to make
payments on account of grants before the
precise figures can be ascertained, especialiy in view of the fact that for the first
six months of the year the counties have
been unable to make any collection of
rates. Further, it will probably be found
necessary to make the payments at more
frequent intervals than will be called for
when the grants are being regularly paid.
The Amendment is designed to give the
Ministry, with the approval of the
Ministry of Finance, discretion as to the
time at which the grants shall be paid
during the transitional period. This will
enable the Ministry to smooth the working of the scheme during the difficult
transitional period.

be sent down to Newry. It is a very
serious position.

perhaps, may not be aware of the various

Ministry of Home Affairs, I think it
would be appropriate that I should in connection with this Estimate, which I now
have to move, give a general survey of
all the services falling within the purview of the Ministry. As I have on
former occasions pointed out, the Ministry
of Home Affairs in reality comprises two
main Departments-the Home Office
Department, which deals with law
and order and ancillary services, and the
Local Government Department, which
supervises the activities of local government authorities generally. I propose,
therefore, in my statement, first of all,
to deal generally with the question of the
staff of the Ministry, and then to review
the activities of the two main Departments of the Ministry.
As regards the question of staff, it will
be noted that we are asking for a net
sum for the current financial year of

provided for in the Estimates last year,
the net result being an increase of £149.

the normal increase consequent on payment of increments, as it will be observed
that there has been no increase in the

no other outstanding point in this particular Estimate calling for attention.

I should, however, like to inform the
Committee that during the course of the
year the Ministry will lose the services of
two of its most valuable and efficient
officers. I refer to the Chief Crown
Solicitor, Mr. John Moorhead, and the
Chief Medical Officer, Colonel Dawson.
Mr. Moorhead has, during the past eight
years or so, given to the Ministry and the
Government, in no grudging fashion, the
full benefit of his long experience and
exceptional ability, and it would be
impossible for me to express in adequate
terms how helpful he has been to me and
to the Government, particularly during
the long and anxious time when Northern
Ireland was in a state of disorder.
Colonel Dawson has, similarly, in his
own capacity as Chief Medical Officer,
Inspector of Lunatics, and Inspector of
Prisons and Reformatory and Industrial
Schools, been of invaluable service to the
Ministry, and, indeed, to the community
as a whole. His unrivalled experience
and knowledge of matters pertaining to
the care and treatment of those affected
mentally have been most invaluable, and
through his influence with those officers
of the local authorities and public bodies
who have charge of institutions specially
provided for such infirmities, it has been
possible even in the few years that the
Government of Northern Ireland has
been in existence to effect considerable
improvements
in
the methods and
arrangements in operation for the care
and treatment of these unfortunate persons.
It is much to be regretted that owing
to the exigencies of the service it will not
be possible for me, and for the Ministry
to have at our disposal the benefit of his
advice and services during the period when
-as it is hoped-we will be carrying out
the reforms of the various local government and asylum services, but I feel sure
that with his interest in Northern Ireland
affairs he will always be ready and willing
to accord us advice, if we require it, or
assistance on any of our Committees. It
would not be out of place for me to
mention that he has, in an honorary
capacity, acted as Chairman of the Joint
Midwives and Nursing Council for
Northern Ireland, and it is, I am sure,
very largely due to his wise counsel that
the midwives and nurses of Northern
Ireland occupy such a high place in the
United Kingdom, and, indeed, perhaps,
throughout the Empire.

20 JUNE 1929
I will now turn to the activities of the
Home Office Department, which, as I have
already explained, generally deals with
all such general matters as law and order,
prisons, reformatories. and industrial
schools, Borstal institutions, police, justice, petty sessions, courts, etc. The
first and most important matter in connection with my administration-a matter which affects not only the peace but
also the prosperity of the State-is the
question of law and order, and I think
that it may be claimed that the conditions
in Northern Ireland during the last year
have been, on the whole, generally
satisfactory.
Of course, we whose business it is to
watch with meticulous care every symptom of disorder have had brought to our
notice, on several occasions during the
year, sporadic attempts which have been
made by the scattered, disloyal elements
which are still in our midst to foment disorder and to create once again those
troubles which cost us so much in lives
and money a few years ago, but I am
happy to say that owing to the powers
which Parliament has vested in us, and
owing to the activities of our police force,
we have been able to quench, at the very
outset, all such attempts. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
An index of the state of any country
will be found in the addresses which the
Judges of Assize make from time to time
to the Grand Juries. These addresses,
I think, speak more convincingly than
any remarks that I could make as to the
efficiency of our police, and the methods
for detecting and dealing with crime. For
the year ended 31st December, 1928, the
number of specially reported cases

As against this I found, on the other
hand, that during the year 1927 14 boys

was 28. This. at the outset, might be
taken to mean that crime amongst
youths had become doubled, but this is
not so. The reason for this increase is
that in the year 1927 our arrangements
for dealing with youthful criminals had
not been fully appreciated, and possibly
during that year many boys or youths
were sent to prison who might more appropriately have been dealt with in a
Borstal Institution. I am glad to say
that the Courts in Northern Ireland now
fully realise the advantage to the future
state of endeavouring to give these boys
a chance to become better citizens, and
every possible step in this direction is
being taken by us in our new Borstal
Institution at Malone.
I am also happy to say that the conduct of our prisoners at Belfast, Armagh,
and Londonderry, and of the boys at the

I will now turn to other activities of
this Department of the Ministry, and
the first service which occurs to me is
that of the administration of the Pharmacy Acts. As hon. Members are aware,
the Northern Ireland Pharmaceutical
Society was established some years ago,
and I am happy to say that since its
establishment its career has been one of
continued success. The number of
licences issued during the year 1928 was
397, as against 369 for the year 1927,
but the most important feature in connection with its position is that for the
first time in the history of pharmacy in
Northern Ireland there is now complete
statutory authority for reciprocity between the Pharmaceutical Society of
Northern Ireland and the parent body in
England. This reciprocity also involves
reciprocity and recognition as between
Northern Ireland and the British
Dominions, and I need hardly explain how
important a matter it is for the Society
and for the future generations of
chemists coming from Northern Ireland
to know that there is a career open to
them not only in Great Britain, but also
in the great Dominions across the sea.
In order to effect this scheme of reciprocity, it was necessary to accord to the
British Society special legislative powers,
and I must here, on behalf of the
Society and indeed on behalf of the
Government and Parliament of Northern Ireland, express to the Committee
and officers of the British Society, and
to the Imperial Home Secretary and his
Department, our gratification for the willing and courteous way in which they
helped to overcome all the difficulties.
I now turn to the question of the administration of the Explosives Acts, under
which the Ministry is responsible for the
arrangements made for seeing that the

For the more technical and highlyskilled branch of this work it has been

As I hope to introduce legislative proposals into this House at a very early

Several Members raised the question of

that the Government intend to continue

As regards the question of increasing the

[Mr. Black]
The police organisation in the North
of Ireland is not a county organisation
such as it is in England. It is an organisation in which we have one body of
police for the whole area which we
administer, and surely the proper and
ordinary thing is that when that body of
police is provided by the State a sufficient
number should be allotted to each district and each part of Ulster to provide
for the ordinary law and police requirements of that district. And the police,
being paid for by the State, should be
so distributed, that where there is no
excess of crime in any particular district
that district should get its police without
having to pay anything extra for them.
If the County of Down, or the County
of Antrim, or any other county, gets its
police without having to pay anything
extra, and if the City of Belfast only
requires a normal number of police,
there being no disturbances or excess of
crime or anything requiring an extra-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Ministry of Labour
[Mr. Andrews]
As regards work on relief schemes, to
which I presume the hon. Member refers,
that work is given on a strict priority
basis. One-third of the work is given to
Roman Catholics and two-thirds to Protestants in accordance with the conditions laid down by the Imperial Government when they gave us a grant of
approximately £500,000 for starting relief works in Northern Ireland. The
Advisory Committee, which was set up
at that time to assist me in the administering of that substantial sum, advised
that that proportion as between the two
sections of our community should continue to be preserved, and I have felt it
desirable to do SO for very obvious
reasons.
no
Then, again, a preference is given to
ex-Service men, and particularly to those
with families and those who have been
the longest time out of employment. Of
course, under these arrangements I admit
that single men stand a very poor chance
of getting work on relief schemes, but,
while I am sure we are all sympathetic
with the single man who wants work and
cannot get it, our sympathies are
doubt greater for those who have wives
and families to support. But I can assure hon. Members that it is the aim of
the Department to do absolutely fairly
in connection with the matter, and that
we are only too delighted to do anything
we can to give such work to those who require it most. If the hon. Member (Mr.
Byrne) would like to discuss the matter
with me at any time, and would do me
the honour of calling at the Ministry of
Labour, I will put all the cards on the
table before him, and if he can suggest
to me any fairer way in which such work
as there is should be distributed I will be
quite willing to adopt his suggestion.
I may say, however, that in Northern
Ireland at the present time we have 78
relief schemes in operation, and there
are 1,196 men employed on these schemes.
But, as hon. Members know, the work has
to be promoted, in the first instance, by
the local authorities. After it has been
promoted, or put before my Department,
by the local authority my Department is
in a position to pay a grant to the extent
of paying the wages of three out of every
four men employed on the work, leaving
the local authority to pay the fourth man
and also to pay the cost of the material.
But the initiation of the work does not
rest with my Department. All that I can
do is to encourage the local authorities,
or sometimes to press the local authorities, to put forward as much work as
possible in order that as many men as
possible may be employed in this way.
As regards the payment of unemploy
ment benefit, I would like hon. Members
to appreciate the huge sums which we are
paying every week to those for whom work
cannot be found. On an average at the
present time we are paying no less a sum
than £26,000 per week We are keeping
absolutely in step with Great Britain in
connection with the payment of unemployment benefit. It is absolutely necessary that we should continue to do so,
because of the reinsurance agreement.
I need not go into the details of that
agreement now, but the foundation upon
which it is based is, that we should keep
in parity with Great Britain, and in consideration of our so doing we get from the
British Exchequer somewhere in the
neighbourhood of half a million per
annum, and from our own Exchequer
several hundreds of thousands of pounds.
So that hon. Members will see that the
hands of my Department are tied to a
considerable extent in connection with
this matter. But I can assure the Committee that it is the desire of the Department to deal as sympathetically with.
these problems as possible, bearing in
mind that we must keep within the four
walls of the Acts of Parliament which it
is our responsibility to administer.

Mr. ANDREWS: I feel that these
Pensions Courts and the new procedure
are working wonderfully satisfactorily,
and I have really very few cases of complaints. Of course there is a difficulty, I
quite admit, in establishing age when the
birth certificate is not obtainable. But
we do not insist on a birth certificate before a pension is granted. If a birth
certificate is not obtainable we take a
baptism certificate, and if a baptism.
certificate is not obtainable in certain
circumstances affidavits that are made by
persons that are considered reliableaffidavits as to age are taken. Then.
again, if the birth certificate of one member of a family cannot be obtained and
yet the birth certificates of other members
of the family can be obtained, and if
proof can be given to show that the age
of the member of the family whose birth
certificate cannot be obtained
comes in
between two members of the family whose
birth certificates can be obtained, the
pension would probably be granted in
those instances.
I can assure you the Department is
most sympathetic, indeed, in these cases.
I am sure hon. Members on both sides of
the House will admit that some proof is
necessary of age, otherwise persons of 60
years of age would be getting the 65 pension, and persons of 66 might very readily
be getting the pension for those of 70.
The Department very often accepts proof
which would not stand in a court of law
but which is sufficient to give the Department justification for awarding pensions.
Without some justification, of course, the
Department has no power to act.
Mr. BYRNE, I just want to say that,
like the others, this is an Act which has
conferred great benefit on blind persons,
for whom we have the greatest of
sympathy. I would like to see the Act
extended and the pension paid to unemployable blind. There are a number who
are not fifty, the age at which they get
the pension, and they are not able to earn
a livelihood. I would like to see the Act
improved in such a way that the unemployable blind person would get the
pension. I hope that in the near future
that Amendment will be made. It would
confer a great benefit on these persons
deprived of one of the greatest privileges
we have, that is, deprived of sight.

EXTERN STUDENTS AT QUEEN'S
UNIVERSITY.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education whether he is prepared to make
representations to the Senate of Queen's
University to arrange that extern students,
who are obliged to work for their living,
can study for and obtain their Arts and
other degrees in the same manner as extern students of Trinity College, Dublin.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb): My reply to the
hon. Member's question is in the negative.
Under its Charter, the Queen's University
is strictly prohibited from awarding extern
degrees.
It is generally recognised that a degree.
obtained without living contact with
teachers is not satisfactory, and no university in the British Isles grants one with the
exception of Trinity College, Dublin, and
the University of London. In the case of
Trinity College, I understand that attendance at lectures is ordinarily required, but
the University authorities may exercise a
discretionary power in special cases where
attendance is difficult or impossible.
London University was established primarily for the granting of extern degrees
and is, therefore, exceptional.
I may state, however, that the authorities of Queen's University are not unmindful of the needs of those who are unable to attend the regular University
courses, and for the benefit of such persons,
have recently appointed a special lecturer
and director of extra-mural studies.
Mr. NIXON: Might I ask the Parliamentary Secretary if he has considered the
advisability of introducing legislation to
amend the charter of Queen's University
so as to enable them to grant degrees the
same as Trinity College? Of course, I am
aware from yesterday's papers that the
Government have no control over Queen's
at present.
Mr. O'NEILL: Might I ask the hon.
and learned Gentleman if he is aware of
the request for these facilities on behalf
of the teachers generally in Northern Ireland, and if he does not consider this
request fair and reasonable?
Oral Answers.

special arrangements with regard to the

STATISTICS.
DETAILED
2. Mrs. WARING asked the Minister
of Finance whether it is proposed to supplement the volumes already published
giving the results of the 1926 Census, hy
the issue of any additional and more detailed statistics
If further particulars on any definite
subject are required, they can be obtained on application to the Registrar-
General, and on repayment of the cost of
the labour involved in extracting the
information in question.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The answer to the hon. Lady's
question is, I regret to say, in the negative. I might explain that the form and
range of the published Census statistics
are designed to give as much and as detailed information as possible, having regard to the cost of the work involved.
It will be realised that the tabulating
and other machinery used in the compilation of the Census volumes could not
have been economically employed for the
extraction of details relating to each of
a large number of small areas.
Mr. O'NEILL: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman if he is aware of the cost
of the additional detailed information referred to, and if he also is aware that
in order to give the particulars of the
religious denominations in a district electoral division the cost of the whole parliamentary area would amount to something like £4. Might I further ask if he
would not consider that that information
would be both useful and necessary, and
if he will consider the possibility of giving
this information before the Census Committee is abolished?
Mr. POLLOCK: Assuming the hon.
Member's figures are correct, and I believe they are not very far from accuracy,
it would appear to me that those persons
who are interested in getting the details
of the smaller areas, such as has been indicated by the hon. Member, should not
refuse to pay such a comparatively small
sum as £4 for valuable information.
The aggregate would amount to a great
deal.
Mr. O'NEILL: Does the right hon.
Gentleman not know that this information could have been given, in the first
instance, without much additional cost?
As the right hon. Gentleman knows, it
could have been done without much
labour or expense.
