I think this is not really a serious attempt

Petroleum (Consolidation) Bill.
The following Report was made from the
Joint Committee on Consolidation Bills:
The Committee have examined the
Petroleum (Consolidation) Bill, and have
made the following Amendments:
Clause 20, page 22, lines 25 and 26,
leave out "at the Standards Departments
of the Board of Trade" and insert "as
provided by this sub-section."
Page 22, line 36, at end add: "A model
of the test apparatus described in Part I
of the Second Schedule to this Act and
(so long as the same is necessary for the
purposes of this sub-section) a model of
the test apparatus described in the First
Schedule to the Petroleum Act, 1878,
shall be deposited with the Ministry of
Commerce:
Second Schedule, page 34, leave out
lines 6 and 7.
as
Provided that, until a model,
described in either such Schedule, is so
deposited, the apparatus for testing
petroleum which has been stamped after
comparison with a model corresponding to
such description and deposited at the
Standards Department of the Board of
Trade shall be deemed to have been
verified and stamped by the Ministry of
Commerce in accordance with the provisions of the sub-section."
The Committee are satisfied that the
Bill, as amended, reproduces the existing
law without alteration, and recommend
the Bill to be proceeded with.
Ordered, That the Report do lie on the
Table.

to a Committee of the Whole House for

Mr. HENDERSON: When the debate
was adjourned yesterday I was explaining
the very complicated matter of the
penalty Clause, which will require the
careful consideration of the Minister of
Home Affairs. This is the Clause under
which anyone who puts an extension to
his house will be penalised to the
tune of £140 in Belfast, and £120
in the outlying country districts. I
understood one of the responsible
Ministers yesterday to say that the
purchaser of a house in the event of his
making an extension should be compelled
to refund to the Government and the
Corporation the £140, as it was he who
got the benefit of the subsidy.
I disagree entirely with the right hon.
Gentlemen when they make that assertion. That is not so, and I will give you
what I think is a valid reason for saying
this. To-day in all parts of Belfast there
are private speculators who in a way have
really helped the Government to do something towards solving the housing problem. But what has taken place? I
asked yesterday and none of the responsible Ministers would get up and tell me
what is the cost of constructing a subsidy
house at the present time.
The cost of the erection of a subsidy
house is from £250 to £290. The builder
gets £140 in Belfast. I do not know
exactly what the amount is in the country
districts, but I think it is £120. That
means that in Belfast the houses only
cost the contractor £100 to build owing to
the subsidy he receives from the Government and the Corporation. The Govern-

ment in this Bill have not made any attempt to see that the tenants or purchasers

week, while some of them are charging
these poor people, who are prepared to

15s a week.
These people have to pay from 12s to
15s. a week for a period of 25 years.
The
result is that a house which only cost the

Therefore, I strongly urge that when

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): My hon. Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Home Affairs, will reply to the great
variety of matters that have been introduced into the debate, but at this moment
I am concerned to touch for a few
minutes only upon one particular phase
of the subject. That is the apparent
insistence on the part of the local
authorities, by resolution, on
tension of the superficial area of subsidy houses to 950 feet, and the general
principle of the increase in the superficial
area of subsidy houses. That claim has
been voiced by some hon. Members in
this House, notably by the hon. Member
for South Tyrone (Mr. Elliott), and
others, regardless of some very important
features of the subject. I do not think
that people who talk in that way in regard
to the housing scheme realise all the
implications involved in such a large increase from 650 superficial feet to 950
superficial feet in an ordinary working
man's house, because it should be understood quite clearly that from the very
start the incidence of the scheme was that
houses should be provided for working
men who could not afford to pay a large
rent relative to their wages. That is the
essence of the whole scheme.
I agreed, after some difficult and long
discussions, and we paid a sum of £225,000
in order that the local authority here might
be indemnified for their loss in building
houses of 950 superficial feet. The scheme
was continued, however, with a subsidy of
£80, and the maximum of 950 ft. was admitted for some time until finally the Corporation-and I am now dealing with the
Belfast Corporation, because from the experience of our local Corporation you
can make your deductions came to the
Government-they came as a matter of
fact to me personally and the Minister of
Home Affairs-and represented that the
results were such that there was no possibility of solving the housing problem so
long as the maximum superficial area was
maintained at 950 feet.
Originally, and before we became an
autonomous State, an altruistic Government on the other side of the water talked
of providing homes fit for heroes to live in,
and they started out with grandiose ideas
of providing people with these houses on a
scale quite out of character with the necessities of the case as they ultimately developed. The old Local Government
Board, following that ambition, insisted
upon our Corporation building houses on
a certain scale. These houses, when they
were built, were found to be totally
unsuitable for any ordinary working
man, with the result that middleclass people, paying from £1 to 25s
a week, were introduced into these
houses that were presumably built for
working men. Of course, that brought the
whole subject into the open, with the result
that the Corporation, finding the position
they were in, came to this Government,
and under the original bargain they had
with the Imperial Government claimed
from us, when we assumed authority, the
loss sustained on those houses.
When we asked them what their solution
was they said a kitchen house of 650 superficial feet was the only method by which
the housing problem, in Belfast at any
rate, could be solved. They spoke only for
Belfast. What has been the result? We
agreed at that time-although I am bound
to say I was doubtful about finding the
necessary money-but we agreed at that
time that if the Corporation would proceed
actively with the building of houses of 650
feet superficial area we would increase the
subsidy from £80 to £100 in order to accelerate the movement that had been so
long delayed, a delay that had caused much
suffering to many working class people in
Belfast. What has been the result? My
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Home
Affairs, in his very graphic statement yesterday, showed how, immediately that
policy was adopted, the rate of building of
these smaller subsidy houses was increased
and has since gone on to such an extent
that at this moment the number of house
plans submitted from local authorities
amount to 450 monthly, or at the rate of
over 5,000 houses per year.
I calculate that if that policy be continued for another year we will practically
have reached the point when the housing.
problem for working men will be solved.
But it must be when a surplus of houses is
reached, and not when a house is provided
for every working man's family. When
such a surplus of houses is created the
ordinary and natural law of supply and
demand will force down not only the prices
but the rents of houses. What the
Government is primarily concerned about
is that the rents of houses shall be brought
down to the level the Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) has indicated. But

æsthetic character or appearance of their
In connection with this subject the word

a "slum" in the British sense of the word

The "slums" spoken of in the sense in

are herded in large numbers and in conditions which are indescribable. These

away, if you

At Westminster they have already
passed a similar Measure to this one. The
necessity for the Bill is that the Unemployment Fund in Great Britain and the
Unemployment Fund here have got into
what is tantamount to a bankrupt condition. There is no course open for us but
to ask for extended borrowing powers,
which is, of course, very objectionable,
or provide ways and means by which the
income of the Fund in future will, at any
rate, be sufficient to pay the outgoings.
The annual amount which this Bill proposes to add to our Unemployment Fund
here is £70,000. I may say that the
British Fund, on the 1st April last, was
in debt to the extent of 36 million pounds.
Our parity debt here is £784,000, and
in addition to that hon. Members are
no doubt aware that we have a suspense
debt of three million pounds. It is quite
obvious that something had to be done,
as I have said, to deal with the matter
not only here but in Great Britain.

Our debt was incurred during an abnormal

I may say at once that I always object

DISSOLUTION OF THE COUNCIL.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
what are the duties that the Donaghadee
Urban District Council have refused and
failed to perform, which were imposed on
the Council by-
(1) The Local Government Act (N.I.),
1898 to 1929;
(2) The Public Health (Ireland) Act,
1878 to 1918;
(3) Orders and Directions duly issued
or given in pursuance of the said
Act;
and whether he can state if the Order,
dated 31st July, 1929, dissolving the
Urban Council is contrary to the law.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): For some time
prior to its dissolution, the Donaghadee Urban District Council had discharged its duties in a very unsatisfactory manner, with the result that
the affairs of the town got into a
state of confusion; in fact, some time
previously the Council itself had passed
a resolution asking that it should be
dissolved.
The salaries and duties of certain
officers of the Council are, by statute, subject to the approval of the Ministry, and
cannot be varied without a like approval.
In the case of their chief technical officer,
the Council transferred an important part
of his duties without sanction to a person
who was quite unqualified. They further
reduced the salary of the officer in
question without approval. The Council
formulated no charges against the officer,
nor showed in any way that their action
was justified.
Oral Answers.

Oral Answers.
14 NOVEMBER 1929
In the circumstances, the Ministry
directed the Council to reinstate the officer
in his salary and duties, which, however,
the Council refused to do.
In view of the persistent refusal of the
Council to obey the lawful directions of
the Ministry, and the general state of
confusion into which the affairs of the
Council had fallen, the Ministry had no
ption but to dissolve it.
The Ministry has acted strictly according to law.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: As
this Bill went through Committee without
amendment, there is really nothing to
which I need refer with the exception of
one matter. The hon. Member for the
University raised a point upon the very
important proviso to Section 2, Subsection (1), sub-clause (b), and I promised
the hon. Member I would look into this
proviso to see whether it could not be
simplified. This proviso has given rise in
the corresponding Bill which was passed
by the Imperial Parliament to a considerable amount of controversy, and as a
matter of fact if hon. Members would
compare the phraseology as it is contained
in this Bill with the phraseology in the
English Act, they would find we have
made an attempt already to simplify that
phraseology.
But since the hon. Member for the University raised the point, we have considered it again, and we are prepared to
adopt the suggestion he has made that a
more simple form of phraseology would
meet the case, and that it would be quite
appropriate to leave the question in the
discretion of the court within certain
limits. I think that it is necessary that
the general rule that the applicant must
not be less than 21 years older than the
infant in respect of whom the application
is made should be retained in the Bill as
a direction to the court to pay attention
to that particular fact. But subject to
that the Government are prepared to
leave the matter in such cases in the discretion of the court. Accordingly, an
amendment will be introduced in this Bill
elsewhere to give effect to that undertaking. I beg to move.
Question put and agreed to.
Ordered, That the Clerk do carry the
Bill to the Senate and desire their
concurrence.

The Select Committee appointed by
Parliament came to the conclusion that
these words "at the Standards Department of the Board of Trade" should be
left out. The trouble arises in this way:
Under the old Petroleum Acts of 1871 and
1879 the provision was that the standards
should be kept with the Board of Trade.
Under the 1920 Act the Ministry of Commerce takes the place of the Board of
Trade, and it would be inappropriate to
have the Board of Trade in the Clause
as it stands. Therefore, the Committee
came to the conclusion that words should
be put in at the end of the Clause recognising the comparison in Northern Ireland
without any direct reference to the
Standards Department of the Board of
Trade. These words are only being struck
out so that there may be a reference in
the paragraph at the end which I propose
to move later on.

(a) an auxiliary creamery, that is
to say for the purpose of extracting
cream from the milk supplies of
several cow-keepers; or
(b) a central creamery, that is to
say, for the purpose of extracting
cream from the milk supplies of
several cow-keepers or for the assembling of cream from auxiliary
creameries, for sale as cream or for
the manufacture of butter; or
---
(c) a butter factory, that is to say,
any premises on which by way of
trade butter is blended, reworked, or
subjected to any other treatment,
but not so as to cease to be butter; or
(d) a wholesale depot for the purpose of collecting, examining or classifying butter for despatch, without
treatment, to Great Britain, the Irish
Free State or the Isle of Man;
shall be registered by the owner or
occupier thereof with the Ministry of
Agriculture (in this Act referred to as
"the Ministry") in such manner as the
Ministry may prescribe, and any person using or causing to be used for any
of the above-mentioned purposes any
premises not duly registered for those
purposes shall be guilty of an offence
under this Act:
Provided that, on application being
made by the owner or occupier of any
premises registered as a central
creamery, the Ministry may authorise,
subject to such conditions as the Ministry may prescribe, the said owner or
occupier to undertake the process of
cutting bulk creamery butter (whether
made on the premises or not) into rolls
without liability on the part of the
owner or occupier to have the premises
registered as a butter factory.
(2) The registration of any premises,
unless cancelled by the Ministry, shall
remain in force until the thirty-first
day of December of the year in respect
of which the registration takes place,
but shall be renewable annually; and
the same provisions shall apply to the
renewal of the registration of any premises as apply to the original registration thereof.
(3) A fee of one pound shall be paid
to the Ministry in respect of the registration or renewal of the registration
of any premises.
(4) The Butter Trade (Ireland) Act,
1812, and section one of the Butter and
Margarine Act, 1907, so far as it relates to butter factories, are hereby repealed.

up some kind of arbitration to decide such

Mr. DAVISON: I would like to support the views put forward by the hon.
Member for Mid Antrim (Mr. Crawford)
and the hon. and learned Member for
Derry City (Mr. Murphy) with regard to
this right of appeal. It is a point that
deserves very serious consideration. Remember we may be dealing here with the
whole livelihood of a man. We are not
merely dealing with a creamery but we are
dealing with the people who may buy this
butter and blend it or export it, and we
may leave a man's whole future and livelihood at the mercy of some official in the
Ministry who has taken a spite against
him. It is a case in which we should go
very slowly and, as far as we can, protect
the interests of the general public. There
should be some check upon any arbitrary
action on the part of the Ministry. We
have been told, and we know, that so long
as the present Minister of Agriculture
holds his job everyone will have fair treatment, but we do not know what may
happen in the future, and we ought to
legislate, of course, for the future as well
as for the present. We would like to
protect those who may need protection in
the future, and the only satisfactory protection the public can get is the protection
of the Courts of Justice set up for that
object.
I do not know where you could get a better
set of judges than the county court judges
we have in Northern Ireland. Both the
interests of the Ministry, and of the butter
trade of Northern Ireland, and those engaged in it would be perfectly safe in the
hands of the county court judges, and it
would inspire a good deal of confidence if
there were this protection for the trade by
appeal to the county court judge.
I must say I do not like these judicial
decisions by a Ministry where the financial
position and the living of the public may
be involved. That is a question that
ought ultimately to be decided by the legal
tribunals set up for the country. We
have confidence in our present Courts,
whether High Courts or County Courts.

Mr. BEATTIE: I take this opportunity to raise a question which is a very
important one to the unemployed workers
in Northern Ireland. I regret that so few
Members of both sides thought it worth
their while to remain to assist me in such
a deserving case as the one I am going to
present to this House. My party at any
rate is in full attendance here. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). I asked the
Minister of Labour to-day a question,
which was as follows:
I also asked him the reason why he had
failed to comply with the financial agreement that he came to with the British
Government by not following step by step
with Great Britain. His answer to my
question was that this Board of Assessors
was only an experiment to see how it
would work out, and that the Morris Committee in its finding had not thought it
worth while to recommend its adoption.
I said then that was not according to fact,
and I will endeavour to tell this House
that the answer is not according to facts.
The Board of Assessors is not an experiment. It has been appointed under
Statutory Regulations. It was appointed
and came into being on the 9th September,
1929. In section 21 of the Report of the
Morris Committee, which sat and took
evidence on the conditions and administration of unemployment at that period,
the opinion of the Committee is expressed
as follows:
Whether under the Unemployment
Insurance Act a Board of Assessors to
adjudicate in the "not genuinely seeking work" cases should be set up as has
been done in Great Britain from the
ninth of September.
Since the 9th September, 1929, however, by Statutory Regulations, an insurance officer at an exchange may submit to a Board of Assessors appointed
to represent employers and insured persons the question whether a claimant is
genuinely seeking work, and if the
transitional provisions (b) and (c) set
out in paragraph 12 hereof apply to the
claimant whether he satisfies those
conditions.
That is from the Morris Report, and
shows that the Board of Assessors has
been appointed under Statutory Regulations, and by no means does it show that
it is an experiment. In furtherance of
my claim I will quote the Minister of
Labour (Right hon. Margaret Bondfield)
herself. What led her to take this step
was that when the Labour Party came
into office they found that the administration under the Tories was such that
grave hardship was being inflicted upon
sufferers from unemployment. The administration had come to such a crisis that
cruelty had been applied. The investigations into the circumstances of applicants
were sometimes unbearable. The mentality of applicants at these interviews
was something bordering on chaos. and
disorder. Their answers to questions were
against their own interests.
Similar conditions prevailed in Northern Ireland. The applicant was brought
before the insurance officer and stereotyped questions were put to him in legal
phraseology. The applicant, perhaps,
simply stumbled or fell, and that stumble
N.G.S.W. Cases
Adjournment-

14 NOVEMBER 1929
or fall was put up against him when he
came before the court of referees, and on
his own evidence before the insurance
officer he was turned down. The insurance
officer submitted him to the court of referees, but he had been already condemned
and convicted, and it was only for the
purpose of having the sentence confirmed
that he was sent to the court of referees.
The Labour Party saw the damaging
effect that had on the morale of the unemployed people. They immediately
went into conference to discover if something could be brought about to relieve
that terrible state of affairs. The Minister of Labour discovered that no matter
what turn she made she was going to
violate the law. She was advised that
the only course open to her was to have
the Act amended, but that in the meantime she could under Statutory Regulations ease the situation of the unemployed.
As a result, since the 9th September
a Board of Assessors, representative of
the employers and employees, has been
in operation in each district. When insurance benefit is disallowed on the
grounds of not genuinely seeking
work the claimant can ask for the claim
to be submitted to the Board of Assessors,
and the insurance officer can ask for a
report from the representatives of the
district wherein the applicant resided.
That has been the means of relieving
thousands of cases. Under the old conditions the applicants would have been
turned down and disallowed benefit. In
Northern Ireland we are still under the
old conditions. We have not got the
right of this Court of Appeal. We
have not the right to appeal to the employers and the employees who understand the industrial conditions of the
district and who are in a position to give
advice that might likely guide the
court coming to a decision. I claim
that that is a violation of the arrangement come to with the Imperial Government in regard to Unemployment In-
Miss Bondfield is quite satisfied that it was in the public interest
that the Board of Assessors in England
was set up, and she is quite satisfied that
the public interest has been well served
by the Boards that have been appointed
in the different districts.
surance.

rates on the ground that they are not
genuinely seeking work. Belfast and
every county in the Province is being
penalised by reason of the relief that
is being given under the Poor Law system to persons who should be drawing
unemployment benefit. The Poor Law
was never intended for persons who are
genuinely seeking work and unable to

temporarily increased by a large number
of doubtful claims made when the Act

continuous rise in the monthly average
number of claims disallowed from the
four weeks ending 11th June, 1928, until
the four weeks ending 11th February,
1929. Since the latter date the number
of disallowances has steadily decreased
from month to month.

Assessors came into operation on 10th

I am one of those who think that any

should get unemployment benefit until

Exchange is a place for people who are

CASE OF PATRICK DEACON,
CRUMLIN.
1. Mr. HEALY (for Mr. Devlin) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether his
attention has been called to the arrest of
an orphan boy, Patrick Deacon, aged 14,
in Crumlin, on a charge of stealing a
bicycle lamp; whether Constable Frazer
arrested and threatened the boy on two
occasions; whether this boy bears a good
reputation in the locality; and whether
there was any justification for confining
him in the lock-up, in view of the fact
that the owner of the lamp said he never
accused the boy?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have caused inquiry
to be made into the circumstances of the
case referred to by the hon. Member, and
I am informed that the constable referred
to during the course of his investigations
into the larceny of a bicycle lamp, ascertained that the boy, Patrick Deacon, had
been observed in the vicinity of the place
where the bicycle had been left.
The constable, therefore, in the usual
course, interviewed the boy in the presence of the boy's brother, aged 22 years,
and asked the boy to accompany him to
the barrack for the purpose of being interrogated in regard to the larceny of this
bicycle lamp.
The boy consented to do so, and went
the barrack, accompanied by his
brother.

With regard to the character of the boy,

passing of the Housing Act of 1923, supplemented the Government subsidy by a

THE "GREEN-CARD" SYSTEM.
6. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether there is any other city
in the United Kingdom which has adopted
a system of placing men on relief work
similar to the "green card" system?
Mr. ANDREWS: The details of the
systems operating in other parts of the
United Kingdom vary, but I understand
that the principle of giving a preference
to men who have been longest unemployed, to ex-Servicemen before civilians
and to married men before single men
operates in Great Britain as well as in
Northern Ireland.
Mr. NIXON: There is a religious test
in Northern Ireland. Is there a religious
test in Great Britain?
Mr. ANDREWS: Religion is a test in
Northern Ireland. It is not a test in Great
Britain. I may point out the practice
of taking into account the religion of the
applicant was established on account of
the fact that the original grant from
Great Britain, under which the schemes

NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE
CLAIMS.
8. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Labour whether it is a fact that claims in
respect of National Health Insurance in
Northern Ireland are much in excess of
the actuarial estimate, and that the
societies were now paying out more than
they were receiving in contributions; and
whether, if this state of affairs continues,
some societies will not be in financial difficulties in a few years?
Mr. ANDREWS: Claims under the
National Health Insurance Acts necessarily vary greatly from time to time.
The first six months of this year showed
considerable improvement on the corresponding period of last year. I regret,
however, to say that the last four months
show an increased charge on the Funds
of Societies, and it is true to say that in
a considerable number of Societies the expenditure at present is in excess of the income, a fact which is giving me much
anxiety. As regards the question of
deficiencies, the result of the valuations
of approved Societies which is now proceeding will not be available for some
time to come.

9. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether his attention has been
called to the report that two of the largest
Oral Answers

[Mr. Healy]
British sugar refiners are contemplating

whether he can say if any representations

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The reply to each
of the first two parts of this question is
in the negative. As regards the third
part, the experiments in beet growing referred to by the hon. Member have been
discontinued.
Mr. HEALY: Arising out of that
reply, does the right hon. Gentleman not
think that beet growing would be of great
benefit to the farmers of Northern Ireland,
and if he thinks so, would he not still
experiment with regard to the possibility?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I am
afraid beet growing would not be a benefit. I would like to give the figures showing the average acreage under sugar beet
and the average yield per acre in Scotland,
England, and Wales for 1927 and 1928,
the latter being the last year for which
figures are at present available. In Scotland, in 1927, there were 10,352 acres
under sugar beet; in 1928 they came down
to 2,313, that is, they fell by 8,000 acres.
In England and Wales, in 1927, there
were 222,566 acres, and in 1928 they fell
to 175,734 acres. It will be observed that
there is a very sharp fall in the acreage.
This decline is not only due to the reduction in the prices paid to the farmers for
beet consequent on the reduced rate of
subsidy, but also to the poor average yield
in 1927. The average yield in tons per
acre for the last four years is less than
eight, a very low figure in comparison with
Continental returns.
Mr. HEALY: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that the sugar content recently
ascertained in the Free State was greater
than that both in Scotland and in England, and, in view of this fact, is it not
possible that he would find equally satisfactory results in Northern Ireland, which
has a climate which in no way materially
differs from that of the Free State?
Mr. HEALY: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that the farmers in the Free
State have benefited and are benefiting
very considerably by the sugar beet
industry?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I daresay the sugar content would be high, but
I think sugar beet is a declining industry,
and that the beet factories will only benefit the shareholders of those factories, and
not the farmers.
Colonel GORDON: Is it not a fact that
beet growing is a subsidised industry, and
if that is so why not go in for subsidising
an old-established thing like the potato
crop, instead of investing in a new experiment?
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid that does
not arise out of the answer.

with the Belfast Generating Station not
only Lisburn but also Lurgan, Portadown and other load centres. A
beginning has also been made in the
development of an electricity supply in
North Down where a high tension transmission line is nearing completion connecting Belfast with Holywood and
Bangor. Proposals are at present under
consideration for the extension of the
Bangor line and also of the Belfast-
Lisburn line.
As the hon. Member may recollect,
Parliament in the Autumn Session of last
year conferred powers on the Antrim
Electricity Supply Company to supply
electricity throughout the greater part of
County Antrim and part of County
Londonderry. That Company is now
proceeding with the first stage of its
scheme by constructing a main transmission line from Larne to Ballymena
and Randalstown. Other developments
are in contemplation, and ultimately the
proposal is that the Antrim Electricity
Company's transmission system shall be
linked up with that of the Belfast Corporation.
The hon. Member will appreciate from
the position which I have thus briefly
described that any scheme of comprehensive development in Northern Ireland in
the near future will involve the most use
being made of the efficient generating
station in Belfast. The difficulty is to
find in the country towns loads sufficient
to justify on economic grounds the considerable cost of inter-connecting transmission lines.
In regard to the final part of the hon.
Member's question, I can assure him that,
in dealing with the question of electricity
development, my Department will be glad
to consider any proposals which will lead
to the provision of cheap power for industry.

Sir DAWSON BATES: Three years
ago almost to a day, I stood at this Table
to lay before the House our proposals for
the control and regulation of motor
vehicles and traffic in Northern Ireland,
which are now embodied in the Motor
Traffic Act of 1926. Up to that time, no
serious effort had been made by any of
the Parliaments in the British Islands to
grapple in a comprehensive way with this
problem which had developed with extraordinary rapidity. The legislation then
existing with regard to mechanically propelled vehicles was entirely obsolete, having been formulated when motor traffic
was in its initial stages. It was, therefore, quite inefficient to deal with modern
conditions.
The proposals which I then put forward
constituted a comprehensive scheme for
the control of motor traffic in the Province, and bearing in mind the fact that
we had no precedents on which to found
our proposals, and that the scheme I put
forward had many features which were
novel and untried, I confess that I submitted them to the House with some little
diffidence. I am glad, therefore, to be
able to stand here to-day and to claim
that they have stood the test of experience.

The very foundation of the control of
public service vehicles under the Act of
1926 was the constitution of the licensing
authority. Prior to 1926 the licensing of
omnibuses was in the hands of each local
authority. This was a survival of the
days when omnibuses were horse-drawn
and operated only within the area controlled by the local authority, but since
traffic has become practically altogether
through traffic, such a system became obsolete, and a central authority co-ordinating the services throughout a considerable area has become essential. We
were able to persuade the House in 1926
that the system of numerous local authorities licensing vehicles without any coordination was not right, and that the
whole of Northern Ireland should be made
into a single area for licensing purposes.
The Royal Committee have now recommended a precisely similar system whereby
Great Britain will be divided into a num-

trolley systems rather than to compete

In many places the congestion on the

FLOOD DAMAGE IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
1. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister
of Finance whether he has received over
150 statements of damage, amounting to
more than £6,000 from farmers and others
in the Mourne, Owenkillew and Glenelly Valleys, who have suffered damage
from the great flood of October 6th;
whether he is aware that these men, who
are mostly small farmers, are now beginning to feel the pinch; whether he can
state what action the Government proposes to take to alleviate this distress,
and will he expedite that action.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have been asked by the
Minister of Agriculture to reply to this
question.
The reply to the first part of the question is in the affirmative. The farmers
concerned have been furnished with full
particulars, including application forms,
of the Ministry's schemes for dealing with
damage or losses due to the flooding on
the 6th October. Immediately they return the prescribed forms their applications will be dealt with.
ADVANCE OF CAPITAL TO
CREAMERIES.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have been asked by
the Minister of Agriculture to reply to
this question also.
2. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if he is
prepared to advance the necessary capital
to creameries who may be compelled to
spend large sums in order to carry out the
terms of the Marketing of Dairy Produce
Act, as has been done in New Zealand;
and, if so, whether he will amend the
Act to that effect?
The Government already possess the necessary statutory powers for the granting
of loans, and the amendment of the Bill
in this respect is not, therefore, necessary.

Do I sleep, do I dream,

Are things what they seem,
Or are visions about.

come across.

most of the opportunity, and did not con-

Friend a present of him at once, and hope

to be run on rational lines of private enterprise. It was not State aid or State regulation that brought about this transport
revolution in the country. It was due
simply and solely to private enterprise. In
a way it was indirectly due to Government
interference, because the Government interfered with regard to the railways. The
result of their interference with the railways was that nobody would travel by the
railways unless they were compelled to do
so, and trade suffered enormously because
of the very high freights. The last year
of Government control of the railways resulted in a loss to the State of something
like £60,000,000. Surely, with that
example of Government interference with
the railways before us, we should be very
careful and very chary about interfering
with this smaller but no less important
service of transport throughout the
country.
Now this House is going to allow the
Government to regulate the fares, to deal
with the routes, to say when a bus shall
or shall not start. I say the thing is hopeless, and it would be better to give it up
altogether. As with all bureaucracies an
attempt is being made to fasten a stranglehold on the country. I should have
thought that the Government, even going
so far-much further than they ought to

of whom Ulster has every right to feel

one man only, should be appointed, then

one man not responsible to Parliament

men, or women as the case might be,

The Government do not want

interference. If they had a bureau such

what was best for the country.
That
the Government do not want at all. And

That is not my experience. I understood the hon. Member for Woodvale to

motorist. I speak from a different standpoint. All these cases to which I am

The rest of this Bill arises out of, and is

that Act certain regulations and limits
have been imposed on public service

The House is now asked to give the Ministry the further powers contained in this
Bill, and all that this Bill contains is

the policy which this House affirmed
in 1926.
Prior to the Act of 1926 local bodies
were the licensing authorities for public
service vehicles. Some have power to
make conditions for granting the licences,
and thereby in effect to control the traffic,
and some have not. Some local bodies
have a motive for limiting and controlling
traffic, and some have not. The Belfast
Corporation had an obvious motive for
limiting traffic in the city, because they
were competing with it through their
tramway system, but a local body such as
an ordinary urban council, rural district
council, or county council, as a rule has
no object in either controlling or limiting
the traffic of these public service vehicles.

That is what he has done, and as I understand the criticism that is addressed to
the present Bill in this House, it is that

The first matter that has been objected

making central licensing authorities and

should have power to make conditions
for the issuing of licences, just as the
Minister of Home Affairs in Northern
Ireland has now power to make conditions.
Here are the conditions that they propose
should be imposed by those central
authorities:
(a) The traffic needs of the whole
area.
These are the matters they are to take
into consideration in granting licences.
(b) The provision of adequate and
efficient services throughout the area.
(c) The elimination of unnecessary
services.
(d) The provision, where possible, of
services on routes which in themselves
are unremunerative.
and in such manner that the legal
maximum speed limit for the vehicles
used will not be exceeded.
(e) The co-ordination of all forms of
passenger transport in the area.
Then they go on to say:
The Commissioners shall cause the
time-tables of all regular services to be
submitted to them, and shall satisfy
themselves that such time-tables are so
arranged as to provide the public with
adequate facilities at convenient hours
Then with regard to fares they say:
The Commissioners shall satisfy themselves that the fares charged or proposed
to be charged are reasonable and, if
representations have been made to them
and if they consider it necessary in the
public interest, may, after holding a
public inquiry, fix maximum and minimum fares for any service in their area.
That is to say, the routes, the number of
vehicles, and the fares are all to be fixed
by this central authority. That is precisely what is done by the Ministry of
Home Affairs in Northern Ireland under
the Motor Traffic Act of 1926, and this
Bill now before the House is only asking
for some further machinery to make more
clear what the Ministry's powers are and
what regulations are to be imposed.

In moving this Motion perhaps I might
be allowed a sentence or two to explain,
firstly, the reasons for the setting up of this
Committee, and secondly, its personnel.
When this Parliament was instituted we
had to set up some scale of fees in relation
to Private Bills. We took as a rough
and ready working model the scale in
operation in the Imperial Parliament.
Eight years have now elapsed and I think
the House will agree that the time has
come to investigate whether or not any
change, and, if so, what change, should
be made in the present scale of fees. I
want it to be clear to the House that these
are fees payable to the House and have no
relation whatever to fees charged by practitioners or any
other persons whatsoever.
The second point is as to personnel.
This is obviously a Committee on which
we should have the services of experts,
particularly as it relates to what is a
branch of legal charges. Therefore it was
that three legal Gentlemen, whose capacity
at any rate is not open to question here
or elsewhere, were recommended to serve
on this Committee. Those appear to me
to be all the reasons I need state for this
Motion.

That the tramways still form an

That the financial administration of
the Belfast City Tramways Undertaking

That the services have been on the whole

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 21st November, 1929.
The House met at Three of the clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
PERSONS RECEIVING UNEMPLOY-
MENT BENEFIT.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the number of persons signing the Unemployed.
Register in Northern Ireland who are not
receiving unemployment benefit.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): On the 21st October, 1929,
the latest date for which figures are available, 6,109 persons were signing the Unemployed Register in Northern Ireland,
and were not amongst those in receipt of
Unemployment Benefit.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like the Minister to give this House a rough estimate
of the number of persons who are unemployed and do not sign the register.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have no figures
which would justify me in speculating.
Mr. O'NEILL: Could you not say
half the population?
UNEMPLOYMENT
SCHEMES.
RELIEF
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state what
schemes he has brought forward for the
relief of the unemployed since the 11th
July, 1929, and the number of persons
taken into employment during that
period.
Mr. ANDREWS: Since the 11th July,
1929, the period in question, I have approved of 100 relief schemes, the estimated total cost of which is £369,668,
and towards this cost I have promised
grants totalling £135,853. The number
of persons taken into employment directly
on relief schemes during the period is
1,830.
BANGOR SEWERAGE SCHEME.
3. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Labour whether he is aware
that representations have been made for
the Bangor Sewerage Scheme to be taken
past Groomsport to the Briggs, and if
agreement is reached, will the Government be prepared to give financial assistance to the promoters in the work?
Mr. ANDREWS: I am aware of the
representations referred to by the hon.
and gallant Member, and I can assure him
that if any such application for financial
assistance is submitted to my Department
by the appropriate local authority, and
complies with the conditions under which
assistance may be granted, the matter
will receive my most sympathetic consideration.
Colonel GORDON: Hear, hear.
OFFICIAL AND AN ELECTION.
4. Mr. NIXON: I beg to ask the Minister of Labour whether he can state on what
authority his Department sent an official
to my private residence to question me as
to who was assisting at my election by
distributing handbills; and whether he
can state if the officials of his Department
called on the official Unionist Members,
including the Cabinet Ministers, to question them as to the names, etc., of their
bill distributors and voters?
Mr. ANDREWS: In dealing with
claims to Unemployment Benefit the Department requires to obtain information
from persons by whom there is reason to
believe claimants may have been employed
while claiming benefit. Where possible,
such inquiries are made by letter, but
personal visits by investigating officers are
occasionally necessary. The personal
inquiry referred to was, I am informed,
made in the course of such an investigation owing to the hon. Member's failure
to reply to two written communications.
Generally speaking, no difficulty whatever is experienced in securing the cooperation of employers in this respect for
the purpose of safeguarding the interests
of the Unemployment Insurance Fund,
but, where necessary, personal inquiries.
are made irrespective of the position occupied by the employer.

7. Mr. NIXON asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state if in the
instruments of transfer of schools whose
roll numbers are 8,583, 8,278 and 10,291,
the right to hold Sabbath schools on the

event of these schoolhouses being no

school purposes the premises revert to
their former owners?
SABBATH SCHOOLS IN PROVIDED
SCHOOLS.
8. Mr. NIXON asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state if in the
event of a provided school being erected
to replace a transferred school where the
right to hold a Sabbath school on its premises was conserved, the conductors of the
Sabbath school have a right to hold their
Sabbath school on the premises of the provided school?
Mr. ROBB: A right of the nature
specified in the question is not given by
the Education Acts, but could be obtained
by the transferers of a school provided
the education authority were willing to
make it one of the conditions of transfer,
and that the Ministry were prepared to
approve this course in the circumstances
of the particular case.
ABSENCE OF PRIME MINISTER.
9. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the
reasons for the absence of the Prime Minister from Northern Ireland; whether his
absence is due to official or private business?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The Prime Minister is visiting
Australia and New Zealand. His visit is
of a private and recuperative character,
rendered desirable by a period of prolonged strain and responsibility.
I may add, however, that great advantage is expected to accrue to our Province by personal touch with large
numbers of responsible people of Ulster
birth who have settled in the Dominions,
and who are anxious to develop trade with
the country of their origin. In addition,
the Prime Minister will be able to get the
views of leading men who are dealing with
problems of agriculture and commerce,
not unlike those which confront us here.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

INSTITUTION FOR IMBECILE
CHILDREN.
10. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state what progress has been made, if any, in providing
an institution for imbecile children in
Northern Ireland; whether he is aware
that owing to the inadequacy of the accommodation for every imbecile child admitted
to the Stewart Institution, eight or nine
have to be rejected; and what steps, if
any, the Government propose to take in
this matter?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance to answer this question.
The Government is fully alive to the
responsibility of making suitable provision
for the care, treatment and educationwhere practicable-of mentally defective
children.
Already steps are being taken by the
Minister of Education with a view to
making provision for this class of mentally
defective children who are capable of deriving benefit from a suitable course of
education.
Proposals are also under consideration
dealing with the care and treatment of
uneducable mentally defective children,
with a view to being included in the
general Bill dealing with mental diseases
which, it is hoped, will be brought forward
next Session.

HOUSING OF AGRICULTURAL
LABOURERS.
14. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state if
some farmers had obtained subsidies to
assist in erecting dwelling houses for
agricultural labourers, and, if so, how
many; whether the occupants of these
houses are under obligation to give their
labour to the farmers who erected them;
whether an occupant who transfers his
services to another man can be ejected;
whether the owners are under legal obligation to let them to agricultural
labourers within the meaning of the
Labourers' Acts; and whether the rents
cannot exceed a fixed standard?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that some farmers have obtained subsidies for houses erected under the Housing Acts (Northern Ireland) 1919-1928,
but as no record is kept of the occupations
of the applicants for subsidies, I am not
in a position to state the number of such
cases, nor whether the houses are for
their own occupation or for letting.
With regard to the further queries relating to the letting of such houses, subsidies are paid to farmers on exactly the
same conditions as to other persons. The
Acts impose no conditions on the builders
of subsidy houses with regard to the persons to whom they may let them.

DEATH OF CONSTABLE WALMSLEY,
GLENRAVEL STREET.
16. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will institute
a sworn public inquiry into the allegations
of neglect in connection with the death of
the late Constable Walmsley, Glenravel
Street?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have made
careful inquiries into this case, and I find
that this constable was under medical
care from the inception of his illness, and
that all the directions of the medical
officer were carried out.
Mr. NIXON: In view of the unsatisfactory nature of that answer I propose to

With these facts before me I see no

CADET SYSTEM IN R.U.C.
17. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he still retains the
cadet system of promotion in the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, and, if so, whether
he is aware that the method in Great
Britain and all the self-governing colonies
is to make all promotions from the ranks?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The system of
promotion to the position of District
Inspector is the same in the Royal Ulster
Constabulary as prevailed in the old Royal
Irish Constabulary under which half of
the vacancies for District Inspectors were
filled by cadets on the results of publie
competitive examinations, and the other
half by promotion from the ranks on the
results of examinations.
The present arrangements are working
satisfactorily, and I do not propose to
alter them.
With regard to the second part of the
question, I am not aware that it is the
universal practice to fill vacancies by promotion from the ranks, and in any event,
each Force must be governed and administered in accordance with local circumstances and requirements.
Mr. NIXON: In view of the Prime
Minister's promise to adopt the step by
step policy with Great Britain would the
Minister not consider the advisability of
carrying out these promotions in line with
Great Britain?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Prime
Minister's references were to social
services. I am not aware that the police
service is a social service.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it a fact that it is a
Socialist service?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, certainly
not.
Mr. BEATTIE: Oh, yes.

Mr. POLLOCK: In moving the Second
Reading of the Measure which if it receives Parliamentary sanction will be
known as the Drainage Act (N.I.), 1929,
I desire to occupy a few minutes of the
time of the House in a short historical
sketch of past conditions in connection
with the subject of the River Bann as the
central feature and picture. The task
which we are setting ourselves to-day is
an attack on elemental forces which have
defied the ingenuity of man since time
began. In the early dawn of the world,
when nature was upheaving continents
and tossing them in riotous glee, she was
indeed very unkind to Ulster in creating
a central basin, without making provision
for a suitable outlet for the superabundant waters with which we are on
occasion too plentifully provided. Had
that great upheaval carved a fissure from
Lough Neagh through the dip between
Carnmoney Hill and Knockagh overlooking Belfast Lough, you and I would not
now be discussing the Bann problem, and
the history itself of this little corner of
Ireland might have taken a different
course. There have been suggestions put
forward for the creation of a tunnel by
which the waters of Lough Neagh might
be relieved, but the difficulties, both engineering and financial, were so colossal
as not to come within the range of practical settlement.
cause I wish to make it clear that the
Government has recognised their full value
to the country and has determined that
the Drainage Scheme will be so handled
as to avoid any possible diminution in
this source of wealth.
The Bann has always been regarded
as one of the most important rivers of this
island. The fame of its salmon fisheries
dates from an early age, and salted salmon from the Bann and the Foyle was
exported to Spain in exchange for cargoes
of wines. The value of the fisheries is
not of modern growth; the export trade
was always there. I take this opportunity of referring to the fisheries, be-
From the military point of view, when
Ulster began gradually to fall under
English sway, the Bann developed a new
importance and this is interesting from
the point of view of a study
of ancient history. In much the
same way as the Rhine formed
the classic boundary under the Cæsars
against the incursions of the Northern barbarians, so the Bann was made
the natural line of defence by the Irish
Chieftains in Tyrone and Londonderry,
against the English incursions westward
from Carrickfergus, Larne and Glenarm.
In the days of Elizabeth thick woods
clothed the sides of the river and ran
down almost to its banks. No bridges
crossed it, but there were important
ferries at Toome and Coleraine, where
bridges stand to-day. These were the
only means of getting from the Antrim
side to the Derry side.
At this point I would like to emphasise
the fact that the floods in those days were
quite as severe as those of to-day. It is
recorded that in the year 1610, twentyfive people were drowned at Coleraine.
Half a century earlier we read of a flood
occurring in September, 1564, so serious
that the Chieftain O'Neill, falling back
across the river, had to fortify the Antrim side until he could get his army over
piecemeal in small coracles.
In the year 1573, the Earl of Essex,
who had been sent by Queen Elizabeth to
subdue Ulster, wrote to the Queen this
graphic description of the river:
The greatest cause why winter is not
apt for military service in these parts.
is the sudden rising of the rivers, especially the Bann and the Main water,
which is the cause that cattle rest between these rivers in quiet.
The military objects of the English were
mainly the destruction of cattle, in order
to starve out the enemy. This, however,
did not meet with success, as O'Neill's
followers salted large quantities of the
Bann eels and salmon for their winter
supplies. So Essex wrote further to the
Queen :-
-
Of necessity, two bridges must be
made over these rivers, whereof the one
will be at no great charge. That over

We see that in the last part of the 15th or
early part of the 16th century the value
of the salmon and eel fisheries must have
been very great. Indeed, the value of
the salmon fisheries in those days was estimated at £1,000 per annum-surely an
enormous sum at that time. This wealth
remains to some extent to-day, but another
source of wealth has gone, that is, the
woods along its banks, which were used
for centuries to manufacture the barrels
in which the salmon were packed for
export.

With regard to the navigation of the
river, it is reported that in the early days
of Irish history the hardy Norsemen rowed
their vessels up the river and built new
fleets of boats in Lough Neagh, so that
at that period at any rate there was free
admission and emission as far as navigation is concerned from the ocean
Lough Neagh. Owing to the absence of
roads and unbridged rivers, inland navigation in those early days had an importance which continued up to the early part
of the nineteenth century. With the
advance of rail transport, the value of
the river from the point of view of navigation was materially reduced, but, notwithstanding its relative unimportance, I
am happy to say that the drainage works
proposed in the Bill which I am now presenting to the House, do not contemplate the demolition or interference with
the navigation works on the Bann. Access
from Lough Neagh to the sea will be maintained, and indeed the recent growth of
motor-boat traffic for sporting and tourist
purposes in my opinion renders it unthinkable, or, at any rate, undesirable that
either of the inlets to our great Northern
lake should be allowed to fall into disuse.
I have dealt at some length on the early
history of the Bann. I do not propose to
enter into the disputed questions of the
several grants of James I. and Charles I.
to the Irish Society and to various noble
houses, whose names are to-day famous in
the annals of Ulster. The legal profession, to their great financial advantage,
no doubt, have often argued the claims to
the bed and soil of Lough Neagh and the
Bann, and to the eel fisheries and salmon
fisheries. Fresh grants and fresh leases
have been made from time to time by way
of compromise, and it is not for me to
enter into mazes where the highest judicial
authorities have lost themselves. I wish
to make it clear, therefore, that this Measure does not purport to alter the position
of the several disputing parties, who,
happily for many years past, have found
accommodation better than legal dispute.
I come now to a description of the
problem, and the action of different
Governments in respect of its treatment.
There are probably few subjects about
which so much has been said and written,
about which so many resolutions of public
bodies and others have been passed, as
this very vexed problem of Bann Drainage, with which the Bill now before the
House is primarily concerned. Nevertheless it is a subject on which there is
still much loose talk and loose writing,
and, therefore, I think it will perhaps
be convenient if I recite for the information of hon. Members, in a very brief
manner, something of the essentials of
the problem and the previous efforts which
have been made to solve it.
The catchment area of the Upper
River Bann and Lough Neagh comprises
some 1,865 square miles. For the rainfall over this vast area there is only one
outlet to the sea, the Lower Bann river.
The fall in the river from Lough Neagh
to the upper side of Portna weir is only
about four feet in 15 miles. As might
reasonably be expected, in the event of
heavy rainfall the river has not a sufficient discharge capacity to pass the run-off
from the catchment area at the same rate
at which it flows into Lough Neagh, with
the result that the level of the Lough
quickly rises and floods the adjoining
lands. As a direct consequence of the
rise in Lough Neagh the Upper Bann is
also held back, hence the serious floodings
in the Portadown district. At the same
time, the rising level of the Lough pours
an increased amount of water into the
Lower Bann river, which speedily be.
comes gorged, thus giving rise to flooding
troubles along its banks, and along the
banks of tributary rivers flowing into it.
In the year 1844, as a result of a petition addressed to the Commissioners of
Public Works in Ireland, a noted
engineer, Mr. John McMahon, surveyed
the district, and this work appears to have
occupied him for a period of twelve years.
In due course he submitted his report,
following which certain works were begun
in 1847 and completed in 1859.
The work then carried out was a combined scheme of drainage and navigation,
consisting of soft excavation and rock re-

Now I turn to the Bill itself and the
different features as they appear in the
Measure. Firstly, I touch upon Major
Shepherd's scheme, which was reported on
the 31st March, 1926, when the Government decided that it was necessary to
undertake operations. Major Shepherd's
scheme provides for, firstly, such improvement of the channel of the Lower Bann
River as to make it capable of passing
everything but the most exceptional flood
without overflowing its banks, or causing
Lough Neagh or the Upper Bann to reach
flood level; and secondly, by the insertion.
of sluices in the present fixed weirs at the
Cutts, Portna and Toome, to improve the
discharge capacity at these points and to
render it possible to lower the level of
Lough Neagh in anticipation of heavy
floods, and thus take advantage of the
large storage capacity of the Lough. That
was the report-crystallised of coursegiven to the Government in 1926, and it

I come now to Part II which treats of
another side. It is really an Amendment
of our Drainage Act of 1925, and it is designed to remove certain difficulties in the
administration of the Act of 1925 by
county councils. Experience has shown
that the somewhat elaborate procedure
laid down by that Act, whilst necessary
for those larger schemes which may have
an appreciable effect on arterial drainage,
in the case of very small schemes involves
preliminary expenses and administrative
costs out of all proportion to the cost of
the actual works. It is proposed, therefore, to simplify this procedure for schemes
costing less than £1,000, which will normally be of a purely local character. Our
proposals, which will be found in Clause
——————
(1) the county council shall be empowered to carry out the works without
the sanction of any Government Department or of the Drainage Advisory Committee, provided that a majority of the
persons whom the scheme is designed to
benefit do not object; and
(2) the rates necessary to pay for the
scheme will be assessed according to the
Poor Law Valuation of the lands affected,
thus doing away with the necessity of obtaining a valuer's estimate of the increased
annual value which will result from the
execution of the scheme.
The remaining Clauses of this part of
the Bill deal with certain Amendments of
a minor nature which I shall outline very
briefly-Clause 21 of the Bill enables the
preliminary costs of the Drainage Schemes
to be recovered by the county councils as
part of the costs of executing the Schemes.
Clause 22 deals with the question of appeals under Section 12 of the Act of 1925
Under that Act, an appeal could be made
from the county council to the Ministry of
Home Affairs in regard to the compulsory
cleaning of drains, with a further appeal
from the Ministry to the county court.
The questions involved are mainly questions of law, and it is proposed that the
jurisdiction of the Ministry of Home
Affairs shall be taken away, leaving the
appeals from the council to be made direct
to the county courts.
Under Clause 23, powers are granted to
county councils to enable them, if they so
wish, to become Trustees of Drainage
Schemes made under Section 27 of the
Northern Ireland Land Act, 1925

Drainage rating naturally divides itself
into two headings. One, the outfall
works, and the other, internal drainage
systems. For the purpose of making my
point, I want to compare an internal
drainage system with the drainage of a
house or a hospital, any large establishment which owns its own sinks, spoutings,
pipes, and so forth. Those establishments
decide how much they will spend on fitting
internal drainage systems, which
purely for their own benefit. It is obviously the same in regard to an internal
drainage system. The area of charge must
be the area of benefit. Very good. It is
obvious that the result of this internal
drainage system must go somewhere; the
drainage must get away. We know that
in cities and large towns the drainage from
private establishments goes into the main
sewer, which has its outfall works, and
from the main sewer into the sea. That
main sewer is kept up by a rate levied on
all those who use it, and nobody objects
to pay that rate.
In this case the Bann is the main sewer,
or outfall works, and it takes everybody's
drainage in a huge catchment area of
round about 2,000 square miles to the sea.
It is, therefore, I think a very fair premise
that everybody who lives in the catchment
area and whose water eventually gets to
the sea through the main drain of the
Bann should pay a very small contribution
for the improvement of their main drains
so that their neighbours' lands shall not
be flooded. I think that is how we arrived,
after a great deal of difficulty, in recommending that the catchment area should
be the area of charge.

The main reason I rise is because some
of my constituents have raised technical

The Ministry shall proceed to acquire
the land proposed in the scheme to be
acquired and for that purpose the
Land Clauses Act shall apply.
The compensation to be paid for any
land acquired compulsorily under the
scheme shall, in default of agreement,
be assessed under and in accordance
with the Acquisition of Land (Assessment of Compensation) Act, 1919.
I am informed that under the Act of
1919 no compensation is awarded for the
compulsory taking of land from the owner
and that the owner is deprived of his
right to question the award before a judge
and jury. In other words, I have been informed that the Act called the Acquisition
of Land (Assessment of Compensation)
Act, 1919, deprives the owner of land of
the opportunity of appealing against the
decision of an arbitrator to a judge and
jury, whereas the Land Clauses Act
does give him that privilege. I also understand that when the Bann Electricity
Bill was before the House of Commons it
was finally agreed with a deputation of
ratepayers from that part of the country
that compensation was to be assessed under the Lands Clauses Acts, thus giving
the parties a right of appeal to a judge
and jury. The mere existence of such a
right is a powerful check on the arbitrator.
Therefore I would appeal to the right hon.
Gentleman to change. Clause 9 so that

SCARCITY OF POTATOES IN
CANADA.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of Agriculture whether his attention
has been drawn to an article in "The
Farmers' Gazette" of 2nd instant, in
which it is stated that "there is a great
scarcity of potatoes in Canada," and
whether he will endeavour to have such
arrangements made as will enable Northern Ireland merchants to export
potatoes to Canada?
Ministry has made repeated efforts to
secure a relaxation of that embargo in
favour of Northern Ireland potatoes, but
without success, and I am satisfied that
nothing would be gained by further efforts
now to secure such relaxation.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The reply to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative. In regard to the latter part, the
Canadian authorities, by Regulations
made under their Destructive Insect and
Pest Act, have placed a complete embargo
on the importation into Canada of potatoes from any European country. My
Mr. O'NEILL: Could the Minister of
Agriculture tell us what countries potatoes
can be exported to, or if there is any
country that farmers can export
potatoes to?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: There
are several countries potatoes can be exported to, but they are not giving good
prices for them. As regards Canada, if
we could get potatoes into that country
the American authorities would stop their
export across the border.
Mr. O'NEILL: Is it a fact that no
country will take potatoes from what is
known as the scheduled or black scab
areas. Is it not a fact that France and
Belgium, to which potatoes are exported,
have absolutely refused to take potatoes
from the black scab area, and will the
right hon. Gentleman consider the question of relaxing the restrictions or taking
them off the black scab area altogether!
Mr. SPEAKER: I think that would
be a question for debate. In any case.
the Minister would probably require
notice of it.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Might I ask the
Minister of Agriculture whether he has
approached the High Commissioner for
Canada in reference to this matter?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: We have
approached the authorities in Canada
several times, but not the Canadian High
Commissioner.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether the
right hon. Gentleman is prepared to
approach the High Commissioner for
Canada to see if he will use his influence
with the Canadian Government?

When dealing with this Clause, may I

hon. Gentleman to tighten up somewhat
the offence of driving a motor vehicle by
a person who is under the influence of

is a place that is not suitable for a person
under the influence of intoxicating liquor
it is certainly behind the driving wheel

the present time for magistrates dealing
with this offence to come to a proper decision on the matter, because the medical
fraternity are so much divided themselves
on what really is a state of drunkenness.
I have heard one medical man swear that
a man was drunk, and another medical
man stating quite distinctly that, in his
opinion, the man was not drunk. I
should be delighted, therefore, if the right
hon. Gentleman would somewhat improve
this Clause, and make it quite clear that
an offence would be committed if a person
was in charge of or was driving a motorcar while he was under the influence
of liquor. I should like something to be
done along those lines, because magistrates are faced day after day with the
real hardship of deciding on the medical

charged is drunk or not drunk.

should know the wants of the people and
be able to express their needs. I think
they are more capable of controlling the
traffic than are any outside people, and
therefore I shall consider it my duty to
move Amendments in Committee to leave
the Corporation in control of city traffic.
All credit is due to the Corporation for
the great improvement that has recently
taken place in both the bus and tramway
services of the city. At the present time
the Corporation is trying to meet the requirements of the public. I am glad to
say the tramways are running at a profit
and we are also running buses to serve the
people, in some instances at a loss.
We are even going further than that.
We are running a service of trams early
in the morning which is unprofitable, but
we are doing it to meet the needs of the
public. There are certain classes of persons, such as charwomen, postmen, and so
on, who require an early service of trams,
and now that the undertaking is in a better
position and is making some money we are
spending some of it to cater for a large
number of people who were not catered for
before. Therefore I think the Minister
should agree to amend the Bill so as to
ensure that the Corporation shall continue
to exercise control over the traffic of the
streets of the city.

If a motorist becomes involved in an

the evidence is not quite good enough to

Something ought to be done, and it appears to me that this Bill provides the
right method of dealing with it.
It is no new idea. We have dozens of
Acts of Parliament enabling juries, when
a man is charged with one offence, to find
him guilty of another. We have again
and again found that difficulty has arisen
when there is only one charge before a
jury. The offence before them does not
justify conviction on that charge, and the
man gets off. Dozens of Acts of Parliament, however, give power to a jury to
find a man guilty of an alternative charge.
There is no difficulty about it. The jury
are told, "You may think this man is not
guilty of manslaughter, that his negligence is not great enough to be called
criminal negligence, which amounts to
manslaughter, but you may find him.
guilty of an offence against the Statute
which does not, in my opinion, necessitate

We do not claim, and we do not believe,
that road accidents can be entirely got rid
of by legislation or control. Something
can be done, and something has been done
in this direction. The prevention of unnecessary traffic on the roads does something to lessen the risk of accident. The
punishment of the motorist who drives
recklessly without consideration for other
road users is a step in the same direction.
The other measures which we have taken
also help, as can be seen from the accidents.
No amount of legislation, however, can
prevent the thoughtless pedestrian from
stepping suddenly from the footpath with
his back to on-coming traffic, or the child
from racing across the roadway from a
door or side street without looking whether
there is traffic coming or not. The police
cannot be everywhere, and it is impossible
to prevent motorists taking risks that they
may possibly take times out of number
with impunity but at last lead to an accident. Nor can any legislation ensure that
the motorist, no matter how skilful he may
be, will not lose his head in an emergency.
The real remedies for cases such as I have
mentioned are, first, the inculcation of a
traffic sense, both in the pedestrian and in
motorists, and in this connection I think
that the efforts of the Safety First Association are of the very greatest value, and
that the arrangements which we have
made for instruction of school children
by the traffic police in the schools are
also having a good effect.
to exercise a restraining influence on motor

In regard to the matter of the tribunal
may I read what I wanted to say as to the
importance of the tribunal, so that we may
get a clear conception of what the duties
of the tribunal will be:
The function of the tribunal will be
to fix fares. In fixing fares two elements have got to be taken into consideration, first, the cost of running a
bus on a route; and second, the average
receipts from the traffic per mile run.
To ascertain these a great deal of data
has to be collected and examined. With
regard to ascertaining running costs it
is essential that the bus operator should
disclose and submit to examination
every item which goes to make up his
running costs. Such items as wages,
petrol, and matters of that kind, are
not of a particularly private nature,
but the items which go to make up such
a very important part of running costs
as interest on capital, depreciation,
and so forth, are of a character which
no owner would be prepared to have
disclosed in public. It would entail,
for instance, the disclosure of his private arrangements with his bankers,
and it might involve even the details
of his financial position.
Such matters no owner would be prepared to allow to be investigated in
public, nor would they be prepared to
disclose them to any tribunal, any of
whose members might have any interest
in using them. In cases of this sort the
fewer people who have to have access

Mr. BARBOUR: The Resolution before the Committee deals with the provision of the necessary finance for the
Government's proposals in respect of
Bann Drainage. As was explained by
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock) in moving the
Second Reading of the Drainage Bill, the
county councils are being asked to bear
one-third of the cost of the scheme up to
a maximum contribution of £200,000.
The Exchequer will provide the remaining two-thirds of the cost in so far as such
cost is below £600,000, and, in addition,
will provide the total amount by which
the cost of the scheme is in excess of
£600,000. It is estimated that the total
cost of the scheme will be in the neighbourhood of £650,000, so that the burden to be borne by the Exchequer under
paragraphs (a) and (b) will be about
£450,000. The maximum in any one
year is likely to be £125,000. It will, of
course, be realised that in a scheme of
this nature estimating is a difficult form
of prophecy and until tenders are received the figure must be taken as very
tentative. The amount covers not only
the cost of the works themselves but of
compensation for land acquisition,
damage, and so forth, which may arise
in connection with the works.
In paragraph (c) provision is made for
charging upon Vote the expenses incurred
by the Ministry of Finance in maintaining the works when completed, including
the Lower Bann Navigation Works.
The Government already owns the
necessary dredging plant and it is anticipated, therefore, that the maintenance
charges will be comparatively light, more
especially since the gradients for the new
channel have been designed so as to avoid
so far as possible, erosion and silting.
No accurate estimate can, however, be
given until some experience has been
obtained.
The county councils will not be required to make any payment on account
of the scheme until it has been completed, and it is, therefore, necessary to
make provision for the payment of
interest up to the date of the completion
of the works on the advances which are
made from the Government Loans Fund
in respect of the contributions payable by
the councils. This provision will be found
under paragraph (d) of the Resolution
before the Committee.
The amount of interest actually payable to the Government Loans Fund will
depend entirely upon the rate of progress. As, however, it is proposed that
the contract will provide for the completion of the works within five years the

Right Hon. Sir R. Dawson Bates,

Dear Sir,
I beg to bring under you notice the
circumstances surrounding the death of
my late brother, Isaac E. Walmsley, a
constable of the R.U.C., stationed at
Glenravel Street Barrack, Belfast, the
facts of which I obtained from him
while he was a patient in Craigavon
Hospital, where he died. on 14th
October, 1928.
He reported unfit for duty owing to
a cold on the 21/9/28, on which date
Dr. Tweedie was called and gave a certificate that he was suffering from a
feverish cold, and excused him from
duty for three days. At the end of
this period he was unable to resume.
Dr. Tweedie visited him again on the
24th and gave him an extension of six
days.
On this date my brother complained
of a pain in the left side of his back,
and the doctor told him to get a plaster
put on. This happened on the 24th
September. The doctor did not say
who was to put the plaster on or appoint any fit and proper person to do
So. The barrack servant, Mrs. Morgan, who resides at 20 Norfolk Street,
got a plaster and put it on. My
brother was allowed to remain in barracks until he became very ill on the
night of the 26th September. I fail to
see why my brother was allowed to remain in barracks at all seeing there was
no sick room provided, much less a
whole week without attention, and in a
room in which twenty men were sleeping, and pass in and out at all hours.
There was no fire provided in the room,
and it must have been draughty on account of its size, and the number of
windows it contained.
The bed, I understand, is of the
biscuit type, very narrow, and unsuited
for a sick person in a state of perspiration. Again, the fact of his having to
rise to go to the lavatory must have
been a death trap in itself.
The doctor was again called about
9-30 p.m. on 26th September, and
Death of Constable Walmsley 1566

arived at 10-30 p.m., and ordered his
immediate removal to hospital as he
was suffering from pleurisy. The
ambulance was called from Craigavon
Hospital, and he was removed about 12
midnight to hospital where he lived for
seventeen days, to the 14th October,
when the cause of death was shown to
be, firstly, pleurisy and, secondly, a clot
of blood brought about by the pleurisy.
The facts of the case briefly are that
in my opinion he should have been sent

In considering the conduct of the

medical attention, whereas he was not,

was beyond doubt a stretcher case. Notwithstanding this he was taken from

I understand that the doctor made

I am, sir,

Appropriation (No. 2) (Session 2) Bill,
