Motor Vehicles and Road Traffic
[Money].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session to amend the provisions
of the Motor Vehicles (Traffic and Regulation) Act (Northern Ireland), 1926, to
make further provision for the punishment of certain offences in connection with
the driving of motor cars, to establish a
Tribunal to fix fares and rates for certain
public service vehicles, to empower the
Ministry of Home Affairs to regulate
general traffic on public highways and for
purposes connected therewith, it is expedient to charge on, and issue out of, the
Consolidated Fund of Northern Ireland,
or the growing produce thereof, and pay
to the Road Fund (Northern Ireland) in
accordance with the directions of the
Ministry of Finance, a sum equal to the
proceeds of all sums paid into the
Exchequer of Northern Ireland, and
being sums payable, in pursuance of an
Order of the said Tribunal under such
Act, by any local authority, body, or
aggrieved person as or on account of the
costs or expenses of sittings held by the
said Tribunal." (Governor's recommendation signified)-(Mr. Barbour).
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The charge on public moneys
which necessitates the passing of this Resolution is merely a formal one and arises
from the procedure already laid down by
the Roads Act, 1920, governing payments
to the Road Fund, namely, instead of
road taxation moneys going direct into the
Road Fund they are first paid into the
Exchequer and passed therefrom to the
Road Fund. This procedure gives
statutory effect to the principle embodied
in the Exchequer and Audit Act that all
revenue is to be paid to the Exchequer.
are
The Road Licence Duty is a revenue
tax the same as any other, although, in
practice, the proceeds of the tax
applied to road purposes. In the particular matter now before the Committee
certain payments in the nature of costs
will have been made by those aggrieved
bodies or persons who have applied to the
Tribunal proposed to be set up by the Bill,
but whose applications are held by the
Tribunal to have been of a vexatious and
unreasonable character. As the payments
in such circumstances are received by the
Exchequer in the first instance, this Resolution enables them to be transferred to
the Road Fund.
The amounts involved are likely to be
negligible as the salutary provision in
the Bill will act as a safeguard against
frivolous applications. I beg to move.

rank for the subsidy provided it exceeded

that is, bringing the size of the house to
700 feet, will provide a house with either
three bedrooms and two sitting-rooms or

The Government have very carefully
considered this matter, and have come to
the conclusion that to substitute a higher
class of house would simply mean that the
poorer man, the working man, would not
be provided with a suitable class of house
at all. I do not think it is necessary to

the House in introducing the Bill, but the
figures which I gave on that occasion show
that when we had the larger type of house
we only got one-quarter the number of
houses built that we got when we limited
the houses to 650 superficial feet.
I move this with a certain amount of

feet we will defeat the object with which
the Bill was introduced. I would love to
see everybody getting decent houses if

feet you will have to fight for it. You
have put up a good fight, and I hope you
will stand by your guns.
What is the future going to be for us
if we load ourselves with still further
financial burdens? I think the Government have shown extraordinary liberality in this matter. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). Perhaps I should go
further and say that they have been
more generous in their assistance in regard to housing than any other Government in the British Empire, and yet I
suppose we are the smallest or the poorest
Government that exists within the
Empire. But we had the problem to
face, and the Committee will admit that
we have faced it, and I cannot get over the
fact that if I add up the houses built by
all these urban authorities, to which I
have referred, and for which I have
given the figures, probably there are not
more than 200 houses, if there are that
number, which have been built over the
whole of Northern Ireland outside Belfast.

policy is only pursued and given a chance
to come to fruition and completion you
will get over the whole of the difficulties
in regard to housing. A person who has
a 750 feet house to-day can afford to pay
for it. That is the presumption. But
we must remember that the Government's
financial responsibility does not concern

houses, that they have already paid away

I would, therefore, appeal to my hon.
and gallant Friend (Major Shillington)
and indeed to all Members. This is not
a party question. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). It has nothing to do with

here as representatives of the peoplethe whole people-of Ulster, and the
burden that the people of Ulster are
called upon to bear, both as taxpayers
and as ratepayers. I would ask them to
remember that there must be a limit to
the responsibilities which the Government undertake. I appeal to every hon.
Member of the Committee to have regard not only to the financial side of the
problem but also to the great complexity
of the question and the necessity for pursuing a policy which in the past has been
a success, and which, if pursued for the
future, I am satisfied we can make a
success, and thus overcome the whole
problem in the best interests of the
Province.

28 NOVEMBER 1929
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 28th November, 1929.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
SHORT SHIPMENT OF SHEEP.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he is aware
that on 11th and 12th November, 1929,
sheep and lambs consigned from Belfast
to Heysham were short shipped, resulting
in loss of markets and trade; and whether
he will state what action he has taken
in the matter?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I have been
asked to take this question.
I am aware that on the dates specified
sheep and lambs intended for shipment
from Belfast to Heysham were left behind owing to want of shipping accommodation. With a view to surmounting
this recurring difficulty of the shipment.
of such animals from Belfast on Monday
and Tuesday nights, frequent meetings
of representatives of the Shipping Companies, the North of Ireland Cattle
Traders' Association, the Ulster Farmers'
Union, and the Ministry, have been held
within the last twelve months. I regret
that so far, these conferences have failed
to solve the problem, which is not by
any means a simple one. I hope, however, that the negotiations will be continued, and so far as I am concerned, I
shall do anything within my power to
help towards a solution.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Owing to
the importance of this subject, and the
nature of the Minister's reply, I give
notice that I will raise the matter on
the Adjournment.
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid the hon.
Member cannot raise that subject on this
Question.
Mr. COLLINS: Arising out of this
Question, may I ask if the Government
will take any notice of the overcrowding
of passengers on the Cross-Channel
steamers?
THE TELEPHONE SERVICE.
2. Mr. McALEER asked the Minister
of Commerce whether County Agricultural
Committees and other public bodies in
Northern Ireland had adopted resolutions
in favour of the extension of the telephone service all over Northern Ireland
to give farmers an opportunity of being
kept in close touch with the markets; and
whether the Government will make representation to the Imperial Government for
a greater extension of the telephone
service in Northern Ireland?
The
area
MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): My attention has been
called to resolutions to the effect indicated
in the question recently passed by the
Londonderry and Tyrone Agricultural
Committees, and by the Tyrone County
Council. While I am fully alive to the
importance of securing the widest possible
extension of the telephone service throughout Northern Ireland, I would point out
that the terms upon which the Postmaster-
General is prepared to provide telephone
facilities in any particular district in our
are precisely the same as those
obtaining in any corresponding district in
England, Scotland or Wales. In these
circumstances I do not feel that I should
be justified in making representations in
the sense suggested in the latter part of
the question. As showing the development of the telephone service that has recently taken place in our rural areas I
might mention that since April last 103

at rural Post Offices, and rural Railway
Stations situate within two miles of an
existing Telephone Exchange, and that
the question of installing Call Offices at

SCHOOL-LEAVING AGE.
3. Mr. COLLINS (for Mr. Beattie):
asked the Minister of Finance whether he
can state if the policy declared by responsible Members of the Government on
making the school-leaving age 15 years is
the policy of the Cabinet, and, if not,
whether he can state the policy of the
Cabinet, and whether they are prepared
to follow step by step with Great Britain
in this matter?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am not aware of any definite
announcement of future policy having
been made on behalf of the Government
in regard to the question of raising the
age of compulsory attendance at public
elementary schools.
The hon. Member will appreciate the
manifold complexities which surround a
question of such far-reaching importance,
and while I am not in a position to give
any indication of the policy which will
ultimately be decided upon, I would
assure him that the problem with all its
implications will be considered most carefully.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES.
4. Mr. McALEER asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if representations by resolutions, or otherwise, have
reached the Government as to the desire
that occupiers of labourers' cottages should
get an opportunity of buying out their
houses and plots on the same, or even more
favourable, terms than the tenant farmers
who purchased their holdings under the
Land Purchase Acts; whether the rates
will be abolished, or largely reduced, on
these cottage plots; and whether legislation embodying the above proposals will
be introduced by the Government?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
Resolutions have been received by the
Government from a few rural district
councils and other bodies in favour of
legislation permitting the occupiers of
labourers' cottages to purchase the cottages
in which they reside.
I do not, however, consider that such
a scheme is practicable or desirable, and
would refer the hon. Member to the debate
on the subject which took place on the
Committee stage of the Labourers' Bill
on the 30th October, 1923, and to replies
to questions in this House on the same
subject on the 25th October, 1927, and
18th October, 1928.
The land attached to these cottages will
be derated under the Local Government
(Rating and Finance) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1929.
It is not proposed to introduce legislation on the lines suggested in the ques
tion.
Mr. McALEER: Would it not be
possible to secure this million of money
that was earmarked for, and unclaimed in
connection with, the Labourers Act of
1883, and have it extended to Northern
Ireland, so that more labourers' cottages
could be erected, and the plots bought out
if the tenants desired to do so?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I really do not
know what my hon. Friend refers to. I
did not think there was so much money
in connection with the subject as a million.
All I can tell the hon. Member is that
the Government are doing everything
possible to provide labourers' cottages.
The Government provide something like
36 per cent. of the cost, which I am sure
the hon. Member will agree is most
generous.
Mr. O'NEILL: Will you inquire about
this million?

OMAGH UNION FEVER HOSPITAL.

of Home Affairs whether he au state
if the night nurse in the Omagh Union

Hospital, stating that she had been moved

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I beg to
move, in Clause 20, page 19, line 31, to
leave out "one thousand" ("one thousand
pounds'), and to insert instead thereof
"two thousand five hundred."
I rise not as a drainage expert, for my
knowledge of drainage is very limited, but
because I am informed by those who will
have to administer Part 2 of this Bill that
£1,000 is much too small a sum, and that
unless it is increased, it will make the
rest of this Bill of very little use. With
such a limited amount, the county councils could undertake only very minor
schemes; indeed, it is doubtful if this Part
2 as it stands will enable the county
councils to undertake any schemes at all.
I put this up for the consideration of the
Minister. He knows what the county
councils will have to do under this Clause,
and if he cannot see his way to give the
whole sum I shall be very glad if he would
divide with me.
I
Captain CHICHESTER-CLARK:
want to support the Amendment moved by
my hon. and gallant Friend, the Member
for East Down. As one of the originators
of the Report on which this Bill was based,
I have watched with considerable interest
how it has been going through, how it has
been standing the test of critical examination. So far it has gone so well that
I feel the Advisory Committee might almost say they made a mistake when they
took the figure of £1,000 as being a suitable figure for a minor scheme. This is
rather an important point that affects all
the Six Counties and not only the dwellers
in the catchment area, and I think there
is no doubt that £1,000 is much too low.
It really means that you can only deal
with schemes costing about £500, because
no county surveyor will take the risk of
estimating very accurately what a scheme
will cost. If he is limited to £1,000, it
is obvious that he will only deal with a
scheme estimated to cost about £500.
I go one step further. The real failure
-if we can use the word failure-of the
1925 Act was due to the complicated procedure which practically prevented all the
county councils from using that scheme 'n
the way they would have liked to use it.
If the Committee will bear with me I will
give an example of what generally happens when a drainage scheme is put up.
A certain section of people say they want
to adopt a scheme, and they say to the
county council, "kindly supply us with
the county surveyor." The county council turn on those people with great fury,
and they say, "Let you have the county
surveyor! Gracious, he has all the roads
of the county to look after !
Of course,
you cannot have the surveyor. You must
get an engineer of your own to work the
scheme." They form a small committee,
and get an engineer, which is a matter
of some difficulty, because there are very
few skilled hydraulic engineers in the Six
Counties capable of dealing with these
schemes.

After a year's work, taking measurements and levels, he produces a scheme,
and the committee lay it before the county
surveyor. The county surveyor says,
"This scheme is no use; take it away, and
do it in a different way.' The private
hydraulic engineer takes the scheme away,
and prepares another scheme in accordance
with the wishes of the county surveyor.
That is passed, and in due course it is put
before the Drainage Advisory Committee.
It is examined by the senior inspector of
the Office of Works. He turns it down.
He says, "I do not like this scheme; it is
all wrong; you must go and do it another
way."
The scheme goes back to the unfortunate hydraulic engineer engaged by
the committee, and he starts again,
another year having been wasted.
At the present moment I am trying to
get through a drainage scheme of a kind
which the Drainage Act of 1925 was
actually brought in to cover. After four
years' struggling, we have just been turned
down by Major Shepherd. I got him
down. He was very sympathetic, and I
used every sort of bribery to get him to
pass the scheme-luncheons and plenty of
drinks but he was adamant. He said the
scheme would not do; it would have to be
done another way. After four years'
work, we are back where we started.
That is all because the Bill was much too
complicated for the county councils to
work it. Here we have a Clause which
will help the county councils to get on
with the work without this long procedure.
I submit that we should go one further,
and make this figure £3,000, which means
that the county surveyor will be able to
estimate for a scheme which he thinks is
going to cost £1,500.

Mr. POLLOCK : The Amendment
which is on the paper in my name involves the dropping of the present
Clause 22 of the Bill in the form in which
it appears in the Bill as introduced and
the substitution of an entirely new Clause
which appears to be of a formidable
character, but in reality simplifies matters. The Clause in the Bill involves
legislation by reference and it is proposed
to replace it by a self-contained clause or
rather series of clauses, the purport of
which I will now explain.
Section 12 of the Act of 1925 enabled
the county council to serve notice on any
person who is liable, by prescription or
otherwise, to keep clean any watercourse
or drain, requiring him to scour out the
watercourse or drain, and in the event of
his non-compliance with the notice the
county council could enter on his lands and
do the work, subsequently recovering from
the person liable. Any person aggrieved
could appeal to the Ministry of Home
Affairs.
A recent case in the County Court which
went on appeal to the High Court, and
on which judgment was only given last
week establishes two weaknesses in Section 12 of the 1925 Act, which had not
emerged at the time the present Bill was
given its First Reading-these are, firstly,
that the onus of proving liability to scour
a drain rests on the county council;
secondly, that if a council in compulsorily
scouring a drain itself widens it, in order
to give a better flow-through, the cost of
widening remains an expense of the council and the occupier can only be charged
with the actual cost of cleaning. It is
obvious, therefore, that the 1925 Act is
defective in these two particulars and the
original provision if left is likely to become a dead letter.
The first of the present Amendments,
therefore, that in sub-clause 1 of the new
Clause, is designed to give the county
council power to take the appropriate
action with regard to any person who appears to be liable, thus throwing on that
person the onus of proving that he is not
liable. The second of the Amendments
will be found in sub-clause 2, which provides for any necessary widening of the
drain and the deposit of spoil on the land.

A further Amendment is involved in the
new Clause 12, namely, it takes away the
right of appeal to the Ministry of Home.
Affairs.

Mr. POLLOCK : The questions involved have been found to be mainly questions of law, and it is considered that the
appeal ought, therefore, to be to a court of
law in every case, namely, the County
Court. The 1925 Act in fact provides in
Section 26 for an appeal to the County
Court either as an alternative to appeal to
the Ministry or from a decision of the
Ministry. The Ministry's intervention is
in fact unnecessary.
The Amendment of Section 26 proposed
in the new clauses is consequential on the
proposal to abolish Home Affairs jurisdiction, and the final Amendment is designed to prevent the new provisions having retrospective effect in the case of judgments already given or proceedings already begun. I beg to move.

result I appeared for the plaintiff in it

and steps were taken by the county council

notice had been served and the work had
been done it appeared that the plaintiff,
who was my client, was not liable by prescription or otherwise for the cleaning of
this drain. The result was he succeeded.
As I understand by the Clause the right
hon. Gentleman now submits the onus will
be thrown upon the person who is served
with notice. I do not think it is unfair
that the onus should be thrown on him.
He has the full right of appeal. He can
go to the county court judge if aggrieved
by that notice. It is a cheap and adequate
remedy. If the Clause remained as it was
in the Act of 1925 the county councils
whenever they took any steps in connection with such matters would always be
faced with the difficulty in the case referred to.

Colonel GORDON: I rise on the Adjournment to bring up the question of the
shipment of lambs from the Port of
Belfast. This question is. a most important one, affecting as it does the whole
shipping industry of Northern Ireland.
It was only the other day that the Minister
of Agriculture told this House that the
sheep population of Northern Ireland last
year was 642,000.
There may be some in this House who
do not know how this trade is carried on,
and I, therefore, propose to explain it
shortly. Every Monday in the two large
stockyards in the City of Belfast and
throughout the week in the country an
average of some 2,360 sheep or lambs are
sold for shipment to the English market.
This number is the average from April to
December, and then it slackens a bit in
the early part of the year. The principal
centres these sheep go to are Manchester,
Liverpool, Blackpool, and, in fact, all the
industrial centres and holiday resorts in
the North, and West, and Midlands.
These lambs are bought in the sale yards
here and throughout the country by agents
of the master butchers and large meat
firms on the other side of the water.
These are figures which I have taken
from the Ulster Year Book. The estimated number of sheep sold off farms in
Northern Ireland last year was 205,000
and their value was £595,000, while the

Mr. BLACK: This 1s the Clause

into the matter. I have since discussed

been inserted in the last two lines on the
Order Paper. The reason for my suggesting this Clause is this. Under the
provisions of the Housing Acts, considerable numbers of houses have
been built by local authorities, particularly in Belfast, and with
gard to those houses the local
authorities-the Belfast Corporation at
any rate are pursuing a policy of selling
the houses to the occupiers on very favourable terms Those terms incorporate the
giving to the occupier-that is the purchasing tenant-the benefit of the £100
free loan. They also include provisions
by which the price is payable by instalments, and that the £100 free loan is
repayable by instalments spread over
a twenty-five years' period. In circumstances such as that, it is necessary that
there should be some provision as to the
conditions under which houses can be
held, the privileges that the occupier has
in regard to the house, the privileges that
the local authority has if the house is not
used properly, or if the occupier falls behind in paying the instalments and so forth.
In regard to this matter, there is a code
in the Small Dwellings Acquisition Act
which applies to houses in respect of
which the local authorities have made an
advance under that Act. It would
seem that the
the
provisions of

regulating the terms on which these houses
should be held. Accordingly, in the
Clause I submit I have incorporated the
provisions of the Small Dwellings Acquisition Act, which appear to be relevant
and important. I submit this Clause to
the House so as to enable proper conditions to be arranged between the local
authorities and tenant purchasers, dealing with the various matters which must
arise in regard to that relationship.

SURPLUS POTATOES.
Mr. MINFORD: I should like to inform the House that we have to-day in
the hands of Ulster farmers 1 million
tons of potatoes. According to the figures
of the Ministry of Agriculture it takes
£4,000,000 to produce that quantity.
We have grown in Northern Ireland
151,802 acres of potatoes, and that multiplied by eight brings in the quantity I
have mentioned. Our export trade to
other countries has been somewhere about
a quarter of a million tons per annum.
Last year our export trade dropped to
156,689 tons, and this year, up to the
moment, it is only somewhere in the
neighbourhood of 3,000 tons, which leaves
a large quantity to be shipped within four
months. Hon. Members know that
£4,000,000 to farmers in these depressing
times is something one must not lose sight
of. Farmers are prepared to take
£2,000,000 for the crop; that is to say
they lose £2,000,000 in order to get
£2,000,000. The Minister of Agriculture
has done good work in telling the farmers
to grow big crops, but if bigger crops are
grown they fail to get a market for them.
My question earlier in the day was as to
the establishment of a factory, or factories, where potatoes could be utilised
in the manufacture of Farino. I would
like to point out to the Minister that when
we began the housing scheme it was
suggested that the building of a lot of
houses would mean a solution of the housing problem. I suggest that the Minister
of Agriculture and the Minister of
Commerce should take some steps to
enable us to get a market for our potatoes.
About 1,000 tons of Farino and Dextine
were imported into Belfast last year. This
product costs, roughly, £10 to £15 a ton.
It takes about 5,000 tons of potatoes to
make that quantity of Farino. It may be
pointed out that this is not an economic
question, but it is a strange thing that
they have a Farino factory in the Free
State, and this will be sending flour into
the shops of the Belfast merchants. If
the Free State is able to do that with their
potatoes, we should, I think, be in a position to utilise the vast amount of surplus
potatoes we have to-day.
Adjournment-
Surplus Potatoes
3 DECEMBER 1929
We have a tremendous outlet for Farino
flour round Manchester, where it is at
present imported from Amsterdam and
Brussels. I consider that the Minister of
Agriculture and Minister of Commerce
should get into touch with the Ministers
of Agriculture in Amsterdam and Brussels and find out all information about this
industry. We are on good terms with
our European neighbours. I also consider it is the duty of this Government to
endeavour to relieve the farmers of this
glut of potatoes. It is true that the farmers have been derated, have had land
purchase conferred on them, and have got
considerable reductions in rent by way of
the annuities, and although I am not
blaming the Government, these are only
drops in the bucket compared with the
loss incurred by the enormous quantity of
potatoes going to loss. Even if 10,000
tons could be utilised in the manufacture
of Farino it would relieve the pressure to
some extent.
Last year we had all round our shores
thousands upon thousands of tons of potatoes thrown into the sea. Surely that was
a pity when we are importing so much
maize meal. We should do something with
the potatoes. I got into touch with the
Ministries and threw out a feasible suggestion, but I have been told it is an uneconomic proposition, as to turn potatoes
into Farino to-day is not practicable owing
to foreign competition. Surely the people
in Amsterdam and Brussels do not get
potatoes for nothing. To-day the prices
of potatoes in Northern Ireland are something appalling. I believe you can buy
them for 25s a ton in the Ards Peninsula.
We have in Belfast a factory for the
manufacture of desiccated soup, and we
hear Members in this House talking about
encouraging Ulster industries. Here is a
soup which is not known in Belfast, but is
known in every house in London. I think
it is up to the Ministry to take some steps
to push this industry. Surely there is no
use in pushing Ulster industries if we are
going to allow £4,000,000 worth of potatoes to develop into manure. It amounts
to that. Here we have debated the
question of voting £600,000 for the Bann
drainage. I am not against it, but I think
steps should be taken to see that the land
worth being put under cultivation should
be cultivated.
It may be true that the farmers themselves should get into touch with one
another and establish a factory, but in my
opinion the Government should call all
interests together. They should get the
potato merchants, the farmers, the linen
trade, and everyone who is concerned together. Perhaps also the owner of
this desiccated soup factory would
be glad to enter into consultation with the
Ministry. I think it is surely worth while
doing something to prevent this important
industry of agriculture-which embraces
50 per cent. of the population-from
getting into such a terrible state. Indeed,
I would like to know from the Minister
of Finance what proportion of the annuities are paid in November. I cannot see
how the farmers in Ulster can go on when
they grow a potato crop worth £4,000,000
and £2,000,000 is going to be lost. How
long will agriculture carry on under those
conditions? Last year we had the same
thing. What is the result going to be next
year?
It may be there will be a glut of potatoes, and I think it a step in the right
direction to ask the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Commerce to call
a conference of all the people concerned in
order to find out what should be done. I
understand there was a factory at Portaferry some years ago. I did not go into
details of what it did accomplish, or
whether there was a loss or a profit, but
we have at the moment a factory in Belfast
which is working night and day making
this desiccated soup. The Ministers might
get into touch with the owners of that
firm. Then there was a firm in Comber
some years ago, controlled, I think, by
some people in London. I can give the
right hon. Gentlemen their addresses if
they want them.
When all is said and done it amounts to
this. The Government should make in
this House a final declaration as to whether
or not it is going to be of any assistance
in the marketing of potatoes or if it is
going to give any assistance for the establishment of a factory in order to help
private enterprise. The farmers all over
the Six Counties are asking what is going
to be done with the potato crop. I do not
think we need look to England at the
moment for a large trade, because they are
in as bad a state as we are. When a
factory in Athlone can be erected and the
products of that factory be put into the
hands of the Belfast merchants the
Ministry of Agriculture and the Ministry
of Commerce should surely get into touch
and see what can be done in the way of a
factory or factories here.

Surplus Potatoes

Ulster. Why should you have to-day the

They will be turned out of employment.
They, fortunately or unfortunately, cannot get unemployment benefit. What is

I hope the Ministers will take some steps
to explore new avenues. In regard to

the Ulster farmers.

Here we are with our ports open to the

The question suggested a means of getting rid of the surplus potatoes by the
manufacture of starch. Well, now, that
is entering into a very difficult field, and

owing to the nature of its origin, starch
is the most abundant substance present in

amongst the different countries producing it.
And so the potato is only one
source of very many from which starch
can be derived.

That they had considered Burns's

through the Bill and made amendments

Rankin's Divorce Bill.
The following Report was made from

That they had considered Rankin's
Divorce Bill, and that the averments in

through the Bill and made amendments
thereto.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Drainage Bill.
As amended considered.
CLAUSE 20 (Procedure in connection
with county councils' drainage schemes).
(1) Section one of the Drainage Act
(Northern Ireland), 1925 (in this Part
of this Act referred to as "the Act of
1925'') shall have effect as if the following sub-section were substituted for
sub-section (3) thereof:—
(3) Where the county surveyor, or
other duly authorised officer of the
county council, certifies that the probable cost of the scheme for undertaking
drainage works will amount to a sum
less than one thousand pounds, and the
scheme will not involve the compulsory
acquisition of land, the scheme may be
carried out by the county council upon
being confirmed by them. A scheme to
which this sub-section applies is in this
Act referred to as a "minor scheme,"
and a minor scheme shall specify such
matters and contain such provisions as
are authorised by, or may be prescribed
under, this Act.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In regard to the amendments
to this Measure that have been suggested
and I think agreed to generally, the first
is to be found on page 19, and it is intended to leave out the word "one"
("one thousand pounds") and insert
"two." It will be recalled that during
the discussion in the Committee stage
some doubts were entertained by those representing the county authorities that
£1,000 for a minor scheme was too low.
I was myself doubtful about it, because
I had not any expert knowledge, and
suggested it should lie over to the Report
stage. It has been considered, and
having received advice from those who
claim to know, and also those representing the county authorities, it has been
suggested that £2,000 might be inserted
in the Measure instead of £1,000. I
think it is generally conceded that this is
agreeable to the authorities.
I beg to
move.
Amendment agreed to.

Motor Vehicles and Road Traffic Bill.
Considered in Committee
28th November).
(Progress

CLAUSE 1 (Amendments as to penalties for speed offences).
(1) Where a person is convicted of a
speed offence under the Motor Vehicles
(Traffic and Regulation) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1926 (in this Act referred to
as "the principal Act"), no previous
convictions of that person for a speed
offence shall be taken into account for
the purpose of determining the penalty
for the first-mentioned offence, or in
connection with the suspension of the
licence of that person for the first-mentioned offence, if a period of twelve
months or more has elapsed since his
last such previous conviction; and paragraph (i) of the proviso to sub-section.
(1) of section four, and sub-section (2)
of section six, of the principal Act shall
be subject to the provisions of this section.
(2) The right of a person, under subsection (3) of section four of the principal Act, to obtain a new licence free
from endorsement shall, in a case where
the endorsements on the endorsed
licence relate to speed offences only,
arise when no conviction for a speed
offence has been endorsed thereon during a continuous period of twelve
months.
(3) In this section the expression
"speed offence" means an offence under
sub-section (2) of section six of the principal Act consisting of the driving of a
motor car at a speed exceeding a speed
limit referred to in that sub-section.

Professor R. J. JOHNSTONE:
hope the Committee will not be too much
swayed by what the hon. and learned
Member for Derry City (Mr. Murphy)
has said. I should like to look at this
matter not from the lawyer's point of
view, but from the point of view of a

The hon. and learned Member for Derry
City has explained to us all the legal
processes through which an action of this
kind must pass before it can come to the
High Court. I should like to take the
Committee back to a different matter
altogether, that is to the circumstances
under which the death of a person occurs

the common danger of the public. That
is the offence for which in the 1926 Act
-the principal Act-we have laid down
a specific penalty. We have laid down.
a specific penalty for reckless and wanton
driving.
I beg to submit to the Committee that
the fact that a man is killed does not
specifically alter the offence that has been
committed. He might not have been
killed; he might only have been brought
down to the verge of the grave, and in
that case there would be no action for
manslaughter at all. The fact that a
fellow citizen has been injured or killed
does not specifically alter the offence under
the Motor Car Act. The offence under
the Motor Car Act is the offence of driving
recklessly or wantonly to the danger of
the public, and I submit that the mere
fact that a man has been injured, or that
someone has been killed is more or less in
the nature of an accident. To my mind
it does not enhance the gravity of the
offence, because a man who would drive
recklessly and wantonly is always taking
the risk of injuring or killing someone, or
of doing damage to property, and if he
succeeds in avoiding that, in spite of the
fact that he is driving recklessly or
wantonly, he has only to thank the
Providence that is watching over us all,
and it does not in the slightest degree
lessen the legal liability which he ought
to incur.
That is one reason why I think it is a
great mistake to have two separate and
distinct penalties for that offence. We
have one penalty laid down in the Motor
Car Act of 1926, and you are now laying
down a different and very much stricter

and more severe penalty. The fact that

occur. I think they certainly want to see

The judge will have discretion, and will

all, but simply fine him. We are only
providing here that he should have discretion in the very worst cases to sentence the prisoner to two years' imprisonment.
The first point made was that the
offence was made no worse by its result,
that is, that the prisoner should not be
punished for the result of his negligence,
that it is unreasonable to punish a man
more because he unfortunately kills a
man than in a case where death does
not result. That may be so. But
Members of the Committee must recollect
that in practically all criminal cases the
result is taken into account.
If an
attack is made by one man on another
and that simply results in injury he is
only liable to be prosecuted for assault,
common assault, or one of the more
serious forms of assault. But if this
attack results in death he is liable to
prosecution for murder or manslaughter
according to the circumstances. There
is a case where the punishment would be
comparatively small in the case of assault.
If the assault causes death he may be
liable to penal servitude for life or even
the extreme penalty of death.
We are now legislating for a case
where death has resulted and

"(3) Sub-section (1) of section two of
the principal Act shall have effect as if
the words 'drunk while in charge on any

car' were omitted, and the following

as to be incapable of having proper
control of such machine'."
The Committee will be glad to know that
I have very little to add to what I said on
this subject in the course of the debate on
the Second Reading. As we know the law
as it stands is that a man found drunk in
charge of a motor car on the public highway is guilty of an offence. This Amendment is simply to find a satisfactory equivalent for the word "drunk." There is
general agreement everywhere that the law
as it stands is not ideal. The Royal Commission, which is dealing with the matter
at present, has reported in favour of a
change. The Automobile Association is
also in favour of a change, and I notice
that the Imperial Government in their
Bill, which was published on Saturday
last, have introduced a Clause very like
that which I suggest. I notice even that
such a staid and circumspect organ of
public opinion as the "Belfast Telegraph"
favours the changing of the law in this
respect.
Perhaps you would allow me just to quote
a sentence from the evidence given a few
days ago before the Royal Commission by
Sir Robert Wallace, Chairman of the
County of London Quarter Sessions and
Licensing Committee. He said:
"It is ridiculous to maintain the law
as it stands. I have suggested to the
authorities that the word 'drunk' should
be dropped altogether. Instead, the
charge should be one of taking intoxicants so as to render anyone unable to
take charge of a motor car. The word
'drunk' has such a different meaning
when applied to almost everybody.
Then we come to this remarkable statement:
"Some men after taking drink can talk
quite reasonably, yet when the time.
comes for them to drive a car they are
incapable of doing it. It is ridiculous.
to use the word 'drunk.' I suggest a
great modification in the law as it
stands."
I may say that I inserted this Amendment
in the place I did as an amateur, and I
may also say that I was very gratified at
the way in which the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Hanna) received this suggestion.
I set down this Amendment just to jog his
memory on the subject on the advice of an
old parliamentarian. I hope the Government will accept the Amendment and
insert it in its proper place.

enough. Therefore, after the word

For a long time I have been very much

owing to the conviviality and hospitality
of their friends, have had rather too much

later found by the police, promptly arrested, and taken off to the barracks. I
do think that is not exactly in accordance
with justice or with the intention which
lies at the back of making drunkenness in
charge of a motor car a penal offence.
The idea of making drunkenness in charge
of a motor car a penal offence is to protect the public. What better thing
could a man who is too drunk to drive
his car do than to pull his car
in to the side of the road, and,
in colloquial language, to sleep it off?
I think the police, instead of arresting a
man like that should encourage him.

I am moving this new Clause in the
interests of two classes of people. The

class, for whose benefit I am moving it,
are those people in Northern Ireland who
are not motor drivers. I listened to the
Second Reading debate here with a great
deal of interest. One fact emerged very
clearly from that debate, and that was
that there are a number of people in
Road Traffic Bill-

Northern Ireland, as I suppose there are
everywhere else, who have a certain
amount of prejudice against motor
drivers, and a number of other people who
have a prejudice in their favour. If that
be the case in such a very impartial and
judicial assembly as this it must also be
the case in connection with the various
J.P.'s who sit on the different benches.
If one reads the reports of the various
prosecutions brought under the Motor
Acts and listens to the stories one hears,
one must come to the conclusion that there

that there are other benches of magistrates who seem to find it equally difficult
to believe any evidence, no matter how
strong it may be, that tends to convict
a motor driver of an alleged offence.
When I say this I do not wish to impeach
the whole body of the magistracy.
know that a great number-I may say
the majority of the gentlemen who are
entitled to write "J.P." after their

I am afraid it will be the case as long as

themselves. I think the time has come
when we ought to define our position with
regard to magistrates. It is about time.
we boldly faced the question of whether
or not we are going to trust our magistrates. We have been taking one
jurisdiction after another from them.
There is also the point that our modern
system of legislation has given the magistrate such wide jurisdiction that it is impossible that it would be properly
exercised by the ordinary lay magistrate
or the business man who only comes to
court at stated intervals. Besides, it is a
very unfortunate position in which to put
a man. Take, for instance, the merchant
who is a magistrate in a country town.
He has to come to court and decide questions in which the interests of his
customers are involved and in which it is
a very difficult matter for him to exercise
his jurisdiction impartially. I say you
should decide now-if we cannot do it on
this Bill we can do it on some otherwhether we should not leave the jurisdiction in all these cases to resident
magistrates sitting alone. We have done
that in a great many instances. I think
the magistrates themselves would be delighted to be freed from the responsibility
of deciding cases against motorists and
other people of that kind.
There may be some Members of the
Committee who may think that it is not
necessary that a Resident Magistrate
sitting alone should be any more impartial
than a bench of magistrates, but I think
there is something to be said in favour of
one single man sitting alone. He stands
or falls by his decisions, and if he is
actuated by prejudice he is very soon.
pulled up. On the other hand, when you
have a bench of magistrates sitting together it is quite possible that individual
magistrates, who are swayed by prejudice
one way or the other, may give their vote
knowing perfectly well that they escape
in the majority or the minority as the
case may be. I need hardly remind the
Committee that the power of deciding
cases under the Licensing Act was given
to resident magistrates sitting alone. I
would ask the Committee to accept the
principle of this Clause and to decide that
prosecutions for motoring offences should
be heard and decided by resident magistrates sitting alone.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This Money Resolution which
I am about to submit to the Committee
is the natural corollary of the Widows',
Orphans and Old Age Contributory Pensions Bill, which received a Second
Reading in this House a few days ago.
The Money Resolution relates to the
additional charge which will be thrown
upon the public funds by reason of the
provisions of that Measure. First, I
should say that a White Paper was prepared some time ago, and I think it has
been in the hands of Members for some
If it is convenient or in their
days.
hands it would greatly simplify the explanation which I propose to offer in connection with the Money Resolution.
The first part of the Resolution authorises the payment to the Ministry of
Finance Pensions Account of the additional State contributions required in the
years up to March 31, 1946, to enable
that account to meet its liabilities in that
period. The Bill makes no increase in
the amount of the contributions payable
by insured persons or their employers, so
that the cost of the new pensions brought
into existence by this Bill will have to be
found entirely out of public funds. This
additional charge is represented by the
figure of £1,050,000, shown on page 6
of the White Paper, as being the estimated additional cost in the period up to
31st March, 1936, and the sum of
£1,150,000, which is estimated to be the
total additional charge in the subsequent
ten years' period ending on the 31st
March, 1946. These Estimates are based
on the best data available, but the subject
is naturally a very complex one. These
are only estimates made by the actuaries
to the best of their ability.
In addition to these amounts, however,
a further sum of about £500,000 has to
be provided in the period ending on the
31st March, 1936, to meet the deficiency
in the Ministry of Finance Pensions
Account, which would otherwise have
arisen had the annual State contribution
to the account been limited to the sum of
£140,000 per annum provided for by the
original Act. As has been explained in
the White Paper, the income from contributions has not come up to the figure
estimated when the finance of the 1925
Act was being considered, so that the
annual State payment of £140,000 provided for by that Act has fallen short of
the amount required by a sum estimated
at approximately half-a-million pounds in
the period up to 31st March, 1936.

expected that it will be very considerable.

or attempting to drive a motor car.

Objection has been made that we have
put in the words "in charge of." Those
were the words in the 1926 Act, and the
definition offered by the hon. Member
for the University (Professor Corkey)
omitted those words. We were anxious that
they should come in for this reason. You
remember that during the discussion on
this matter it was suggested that it was
evidence to some extent at least of an
element of wisdom on the part of a man
who was drunk in a car if he drove that
car to the side of the road and slept off
the effects of his drunkenness. In that
case, if at the moment the policeman
came he was sitting there not driving,
and not attempting to drive, he would not
have been committing an offence if the
law had been made as the Clause was
originally drafted. But if you put in
those words "or in charge of" then certainly he is committing an offence, and I
think it must be clear to all hon. Members of the Committee that a
man in
charge of a motor car in a public place
ought to be sober-at least he ought to
be sober enough to drive and to control
his car without causing danger to those
who have as good a right to use the roads
as he has himself. It is for that reason
that these words have been introduced
into this Clause, to make for clarity. I
really cannot understand any great difficulty in understanding when a man is so
intoxicated as to be incapable of driving
a car.
So far as the point raised by my hon.
Friend (Mr. Grant) behind me is concerned, that is a pure question of law
which he has put up to us, and this is

and learned Friends or myself should be
provoked to make answer on a question
of law. I have not the slightest doubt
that if the hon. Member were to give

and in another place we would do our

Major BLAKISTON-HOUSTON: I
would like to ask the Minister of Home
Affairs if he could stiffen the back of
either the rural district councils or the
county councils, or whatever authorities
there are who build subsidy houses.
When a man builds a house on his own
he has a perfect right to build it where
he likes and how he likes, but once he
gets a grant from either the State or any
other authority it should be built on
ground that is absolutely dry and not on
swampy ground. I know a great number
of subsidy houses that have been built on
ground that is only dry in the driest
summer and that is wet in the winter
time. We should not encourage these, as
we may call them, rheumatism halls. I
would like very much to ask the Minister
of Home Affairs if he could stiffen their
backs by an Order so as to prevent these
wet and unhealthy houses being erected.
It should be done in the beginning before
the plans come in. A man should not be
allowed to build before the site is passed.

Oral Answers to Questions.
DAMAGE BY FLOODING.
1. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
number of applications for assistance
received from farmers and others in consequence of the flooding on 6th October
last?
The MINISTER of AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The number of
applications received to date for assistance
under the emergency schemes for the
making good of losses due to flooding on
the 6th of October last is thirty-four.
Nine of these applications are for grants
to assist in the repair of river embankments, fences, drains, etc., and twentyfive of the applications are for loans to
cover losses of crops and live stock.
Mr. MILLER: Can the right hon.
Gentleman say how many of these applications are from the Mourne Valley and
how many from the whole of County
Tyrone?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: Eleven
applications had been received from the
Mourne Valley area, of which seven applications are for loans to cover losses of
crops and live stock and four are for
grants to assist in the repair of embankments, fences, etc. In all fifteen applica-
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
10 DECEMBER 1929
tions have been received from County
Tyrone, of which ten are for loans and
five for grants.
Mr. MILLER: Could the Minister
give the House an opportunity of discussing this scheme and finding out why
advantage has not been taken of it?
NORTHERN IRELAND EGGS IN
COLD STORAGE.
2. Mr. MARK asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether it is a fact that eggs
from Northern Ireland, when put into
cold storage in Great Britain, are stamped
when taken out "Chilled or Cold Stored,'
whereas Polish, Dutch, Belgium or any
foreign eggs can be put into cold storage
in the month of April, taken out in
December, and only require to bear a
stamp indicating the country of origin
without any reference to the fact that
they have been in cold storage; whether
the facts are as stated, and, if so, will the
Minister take the necessary steps to ensure
that the home producer is no longer prejudiced in this respect?
""
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: The
facts relating to the marketing of cold.
stored eggs are as stated. I am, however, not prepared to take any steps in
the matter as the question raised was very
thoroughly investigated in
in connection
with the Imperial Agricultural Produce.
(Grading and Marking) Act, 1928, and
the Marketing of Eggs Act, 1928. By
far the greatest proportion, probably
nine-tenths, of imported eggs which are
sold in the United Kingdom after being
cold stored are not cold stored in the
United Kingdom at all. The marking of
such a proportion as are cold stored in the
United Kingdom would, accordingly,
serve no useful purpose and, in fact, it
would merely result in diverting the trade
in cold storing of imported eggs to
countries other than the United Kingdom.
FLOODGATES ON THE RIVER
QUOILE.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The suggested scheme for improving the drainage of the River Quoile
put forward on behalf of the Down
County Council is now under examination
by my Ministry's Engineers in consultation with the County Surveyor. Owing
to pressure of cther work, more particularly, the preparation of the plans and
specifications for the Bann Drainage
Scheme, it was not found possible to concentrate on the Quoile Scheme until
recent date. The hon. and gallant Member may rest assured that the examination
will now proceed without a break, but it
is, of course, quite impossible to say at
the present time whether the scheme is a
sound one and, consequently, to indicate
when work would be begun.

The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND
MEANS: Perhaps a word from me would
dispel all fears and anxieties as well as
relieve all existing doubts respecting this
matter. By general Resolution at the
setting up of this Parliament we adopted
the practice in operation in the Imperial
Parliament. That meant that when any
hon. Member called the attention of Mr.
Speaker or the Chairman of Committees
to the fact that ten Members are not present the division bells are rung for two
minutes. Mr. Speaker or the Chairman
of Committees then proceeds to count the
House, and if it be found then or earlier
that ten or more Members are present,
the business proceeds. That has been the
practice, and the addition of these words
will in no degree alter or
vary the
practice. All it will do will be, as is done
in the Imperial Parliament, so to clarify
the Standing Order as to conform strictly
in accordance with the practice. That is
the whole of the Gunpowder Plot.

strictly in accordance with the Resolution.
passed by this House.

Mr. ANDREWS: As hon. Members
know the health and pensions
tributions form one joint contribution,
usually in the form of weekly stamps. I
understand that in Great Britain` some
of the larger firms are using automatic
machines for this purpose. Some of our

This motion is simply to authorise the
Committee to widen the scope of the Bill.
I beg to move.
con-
Mr. BEATTIE: I understand that this
Motion is to bring into operation the
system in England, and widen the class
of stamps that may be put on the cards.
If that is not the meaning of the Resolution then we will have to make further
investigation. I do not think we can
reasonably object to this, except there
Pensions Bill—

might be a greater opening for bogus
stamps to be put on. That is the only
danger I see at the moment. We have
a uniform stamp and no automatic

in one uniform way. Do I understand

Mr. ANDREWS: This is only to extend

Mr. BEATTIE: I think before we allow

then I claim we

Mr. ANDREWS: If the hon. Member
prefers to have the discussion now I do
not object. In England I understand
there is a practice which has been adopted
by some of the largest firms. Instead of
going through the somewhat tortuous proceeding of putting on stamps they use an
automatic machine for the purpose. And
all the Clause, which will be moved later,
provides is where this involves any additional cost upon the Department, the
Department, with the approval of the
Minister of Finance, can demand from the
employer adopting that course any additional expense which the Department may
be called upon to bear.
As far as the insured person is concerned
it really makes no difference whatever,
because there is no more likelihood of
irregularities, I am advised, taking place
under this automatic system of stamping
than under the old. I am sure the hon.
Member has no desire to inconvenience employers unnecessarily. If, where thousands of workers' cards have got to be
stamped, a better and a cheaper method
can be adopted by the employer I am sure
it will meet with the approval of the

think such an arrangement would not

Mr. ANDREWS: I am very pleased to
have another opportunity of explaining to
the hon. Member just how the position
stands. In the first place, he is aware of
the fact that there is no pension scheme
in the Free State, and that therefore you
cannot interchange stamps. The hon.
Member has said quite clearly and
definitely that he does not desire there
should be pensions in the Free State; that
the people in the Free State are quite
satisfied to have the social services that
exist in the Free State. He is a better
judge of whether that is so or not than
I am, but it occurs to me that it is not
very natural that they should be satisfied
with conditions so inferior to the conditions that exist in Northern Ireland.
Mr. HEALY: They do not admit they
are inferior.
Mr. ANDREWS: In my opinion the
two years' residence qualification is the
best test possible, because if a North of
Ireland person lives in Northern Ireland
for two years, under these conditions he
is not disqualified if he goes to the Free
State and becomes a voluntary contributor
there just in the same way as if he goes to
any other dominion. There is no discrimination as far as that is concerned,
but this is where the discrimination comes
in. We have a proposition to deal with
here which they have not got in Great
Britain, because it is not possible for a
Free State person to live in the Free State
and at the same time work in Great
Britain, but it is possible to live in one of
the border towns in the Free State and
work in one of our towns in Northern Ireland. It is to prevent such a person becoming entitled to benefit that this two
years' qualification is applied.
After this explanation I think the hon.
Member will see that this is a very easy
test to comply with. No Northern Ireland person can be deprived of the
benefits of this Bill by virtue of this
Clause provided that when in the Free
State he becomes a voluntary contributor
and in that way pays something to the
fund from which, later on, he hopes and
expects to get very considerable advantages. It would not be reasonable to allow
a North of Ireland person to go to the
Free State and pay nothing all the time
he was there, for two or three years, or
perhaps longer, and that when he died
his widow should get exactly the same
advantage as if he had lived in Northern
Ireland and contributed to the fund all
the time. It is extremely reasonable that
we should say, "you are quite entitled to
go to the Free State if you desire to, but
during the time you are in the Free State
you must contribute to the fund from
which later on you expect to benefit.” I
do not think the hon. Member can think
otherwise than that that is a very reasonable condition.
Mr. HEALY: The difficulty that
Members on the Government back benches
cannot appreciate is this; that a man
from Northern Ireland who goes to the
Free State has to pay his contributions in
the Free State, and simultaneously he
has to pay his contributions to the
Northern Ireland Fund.
Mr. ANDREWS: No. They have no
pension fund in the Free State to contribute to. Therefore, they are not asked
to pay twice for the same benefits.
You
cannot have reciprocity with persons who
have nothing to give. Reciprocity means
that each gives something to the other to
receive benefits from each other.

When we come to the question of compulsory insurance, the initial difficulty
is this. First of all every insurance
policy is drafted with the object of giving
protection to the insured, and secondly,
of limiting the liability of the insurance
company. Our object in compulsory insurance is the protection of the public,
Road Traffic Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Report.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
and not the protection of either the owner
or the insurance company. That is
exactly where the whole difficulty arises.
It must be clear to everyone that the
views of the insurance company and the
insured person on the one hand, and
those of the Ministry, as representing the
general public on the other hand, are as
wide apart as the poles.
We also found that if the public are to
have adequate protection it is necessary
in all cases that the insurance policies
should be materially modified with a substantial increase of risk on the part of the
insurance company. Therefore, as I
have already said, one of our difficulties
was to obtain the necessary modifications
in the form of the insurance policies.
May I take one case as an example.
Buses are insured on a basis of so much
per seat, but every insurance policy contains a Clause which provides that, in the
event of the bus being overcrowded, the
liability of the insurance company is
limited to a proportionate number of the
total number carried. The balance of the
risk is to be provided for by the owner.
Take, for example, a 32-seater bus which
is insured, It is overcrowded and carrying 44 passengers when the accident takes
place. The insurance company is only
liable for 32/44ths of the damage, and
there is, therefore, no guarantee whatever that the owner is in a position to bear
the balance of the costs, namely 12/44ths.
Here, again, as a result of negotiations
with the insurance companies, we got an
agreement from the companies that they
would bear the total cost in the first instance and trust to getting the money back
from the insured owner.
There is another difficulty. Hon. Members are aware that the basis on which
an insurance policy is founded is the
original proposal form, and it is the
settled law that if, innocently or otherwise, there is a material mis-statement
the policy is void from the very commencement. If, for example, an applicant,
bona fide, makes a mis-statement as to
the number of accidents in which he has
been involved, that policy would be void.
I would like to ask the House, and my
hon. and gallant Friend who has moved
this amendment, how is an eventuality
like this to be guarded against. It is
not practical politics to examine and
verify proposals for insurance, and I confess at the moment I see no solution.

LOCAL AND DIVORCE BILLS.
SCALES OF FEES.
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND
MEANS (Mr. Moles): When the Motion
that stands in my name was before the
House yesterday, I pointed out that it
represented the unanimous recommendations of a Select Committee which had
been set up to find out what changes ought
to be made in the scale of fees in relation
to Private Bills. You, Sir, pointed out
that it was the usual practice when the
House had delegated this authority to such
a Select Committee to rely on that Committee as having explored the whole question, and in the interests of the House
had brought forward these recommendations. I ventured to support the
recommendations in a speech which I
thought was marked by such clarity, such
a wealth of information and such eloquence as is rarely heard that it would
have carried conviction. I need hardly
say I was deeply disappointed to be told
that it left the position as clear as mud. I
will now attempt the responsible task of
elucidating the matter.
This scale of fees represents the scale
approximately that was in operation in relation to some Bills when promoted before
the Imperial Parliament. A very large
saving was effected by reason of the fact
that, instead of having to transport a great
body of witnesses and officials to Westminster and keeping them there sometimes
for weeks and even months on end, here
the moment we took a Bill in the Committee stage that Bill was pursued day
1955 Local and Divorce Bills-
Fees
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Moles]
after day until its completion in say three
or four days, sometimes only one day.
There was a large saving. We propose to
effect in the interests of those who desire
to promote Bills a still further and greater
saving. Experience shows us that we can
push these Bills through upon a lesser
scale of fees than at the moment obtains.
It is to be observed that the fees lodged
are the fees payable to this House and not
otherwise. It is not the policy to make
profit out of the promotion of Private
Bills. It is the policy to see that such
cost as is incidental in the working of this
House shall be discharged by the persons
promoting them. This reduction represents what we think is as far as we can
safely go in the matter of the reduction
of fees. It will almost exactly equal
the sum which would be necessary to expend in the discharge of the various functions in private Committees of the House.
That, I hope, has succeeded in throwing
light on places not sufficiently illuminated.
I turn to one other matter calling for
explanation, that is the scale of fees in
relation to Divorce Bills. I was asked
yesterday whether I would state what
would be the amount of reduction. The
old scale of fees represented about £45 or
over, for the promotion of a Divorce Bill.
The new scale of fees which we think we
may safely introduce will bring the cost
down to about £13. The Committee do
not see their way to recommend more than
that at the moment, and I am sure the
House will be content to be guided by the
Committee of experts who have thoroughly
examined the whole question.

The House will appreciate the fact that

matter carefully came to the conclusion
that the fees which were adopted
originally in connection with proceedings.
in Committee were somewhat too high,
that is to say, instead of £10 which has
to be paid now every day by the promoters of a Private Bill if they appeared
by counsel, that sum should be reduced
and that the reduction should be to a
figure which now appears in the existing
Standing Orders when the promoters of
a Bill appear by agent.
I may be under a misapprehension, but
it did occur to me that the hon. Member
for Pottinger did not entirely appreciate
the difference that exists. May I enlighten him if possible? Most Private
Bills, as I am sure most Members of this
House quite realise, are of such a
relatively complicated character that the
promoters do in fact appear by counsel,
but some are of a simpler nature, and
instead of retaining counsel the promoters
appear by agent, that means by their
solicitor, while in some cases- -I do not
know that it has even happened-it is
possible for a promoter instead of appearing by his counsel or by his solicitor to
appear in person. The House will notice
that in that case the fee payable by such
a promoter for every day the Committee
shall sit is nil.
The Select Committee having considered the matter very carefully, and
having had before them the fees chargeable in England, and comparing those
fees with the fees charged under the existing Standing Orders came to the conclusion that a reduction of that sum of £10

the sum of £5 should appear and should

before the Committee, and should be paid
by the promoter It is a fee, as the hon.
Member for Pottinger understands, paid
to this House, and the reduction proposed by the Committee is a reduction of
50 per cent.

Oral Answers to Questions.
DRAINAGE
OF RIVER BLACK-
WATER.
1.
Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Finance whether the Government would
be prepared to give financial assistance to
the County Councils of Tyrone and
Armagh, in order to assist them to formulate a joint county scheme to remove obstructions in the River Blackwater, and
also repair the damaged river banks, and
thereby reduce very considerably the flooding in the whole Clogher Valley area.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The Government has not so far
adopted the principle of grants in aid of
drainage schemes undertaken by county
councils. In some cases where unemployed
labour may have been specially recruited
for the works grants on the usual basis have
been made available from the Employment
Services Vote. In view of the heavy cost
to the Exchequer of derating agricultural
land from all rates save drainage and
malicious injuries, I cannot hold out anv
hope that the Government will find itself
in a position to depart from its present
practice.
BATTLEHILL, DERRYHALE, AND
RICHHILL P.E. SCHOOLS.
2. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Finance whether it is a fact
that in July last his Ministry proposed
to transfer certain endowments in connection with three Public Elementary Schools
in County Armagh, namely, Battlehill,
Derryhale and Richhill, to the Armagh
County Council or the Education Authority for the county, and whether he can
state why this arrangement has not been
carried out.
Mr. POLLOCK : The answer to the
first part of the hon. and gallant Member's
question is in the affirmative.
As regards the second part of the question, I should explain that Richhill School
is a newly-built provided school, while
Battlehill and Derryhale Schools are old
school buildings. The endowments belonging to the two last-named schools pass
to the Education Authority with the premises themselves, in pursuance of statutory
arrangements made under the Education
Act (Northern Ireland), 1923, but so far
my Ministry has been unable to act, as it
is still awaiting a reply from the Education Authority in regard to the formality
of transferring the securities.
The third endowment was attached to
the old Richhill School, which has not
been transferred, though it has ceased to

DEATH OF MARGARET MCGLADE,

3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister

any inquiries have been made into the
death of Margaret McGlade, whose dead
body was found in a room in a house in
Boyne Square, Belfast; and whether he is
likely to make an announcement on the

of knowing how death was caused.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The case referred to
has been the subject of an inquest held on
October 18th, at which a verdict was found

therefore, in a position to furnish any
further particulars at the moment.

A young widow of 28 years was left in
1927 with two small children-one seven
and the other four years old. Her husband
was an insured worker from 1912 to 1924.
He paid his contributions during that
period. In 1924 slackness came about in
his employment. He was a shipyard
worker. Before he would loaf or hang
round the bureau he set himself the task
of building subsidy houses. He would
have built a house for any individual who
could put down the capital. He did that
for two and a half years, and at the end
of that time his health broke down, and he
died in 1927, only three years from 1924.
He left a widow and two children. To-day
the Minister says, "I cannot interfere in
the matter as the Ministry has decided that
the average of three years has not been
conformed with." The rules and regulations here relating to the average basis do
not meet the claim, but I am satisfied that
if we had Mr. Greenwood here as Minister
the widow would be granted her pension.

When the day comes when we on this
side of the House shall take over the
government of the country, I assure you
that we shall introduce still further improvements. It has been the policy of
the Nationalist party since its foundation
to be in favour of pensions, and it is a
satisfaction to us to know that as the
years go by more people are benefiting by
pensions. I think it is the duty of every
Government, no matter who they are, to
look after those in want.
There will be many widows and orphans
not included in this Bill. They will not
benefit to the extent I would like to see.
However, I suppose the day for making
improvements is past, and we can only
assure whoever is in power, as I said I do
not care who they are, that when they
come along with further Amendments
they will have our whole-hearted support.

like to pay a tribute to the present umpire, as he has been very satisfactory in

something about the court of referees, because it deals with administration. I
would like the court of referees to take a
leaf out of the umpire's book. If they
would do that it would be to the advantage
of a lot of poor people. I notice in Sub-

will be as good as the umpire we have.
I believe I am entitled to criticise administration here, and I have one case in
my mind at the present time that is not
to the credit of the Ministry. It is the
case of a man named Adair, who lives in
Ashmore Street. My dates will be approximate, because I have not the particulars with me, but they will be very
nearly accurate. This man became unemployed, roughly, about the end of April
last, and the Ministry could not make
up their mind whether he was entitled to
a contributory pension or not, because
there was a question of his age. Finally,
and recently, they decided that he was entitled to a contributory pension, and the
pension was given only from, say, October.
That may not be the correct date, but I
do know that for three, or four, or five
months he got neither benefit nor pension.
Surely he was entitled to one or the other.
I had some correspondence with the Minister about this case, which is a case of
great hardship. Generally speaking, there
is a lot of hardship in regard to administration.
I see here in Clause 6 something about
repayment in case of fraud. I came
across the case of a man who improperly
took from £18 to £20 from the Ministry
of Labour. He was prosecuted and fined,
roughly, from £18 to £20. That was all
right. The next time he came in for
benefit the Ministry started deducting so
that he would be punished twice for the
same offence. He was fined a sum equivalent to the amount he defrauded the
Ministry of, which was quite right, and
now they are going to fine him again for
the same thing. That is contrary to all
principles of British justice that I am
acquainted with. It was always a principle of British justice not to punish a
man twice for the same offence.
Now, I dare say I can say something
about courts of referees. Courts of referees are paid by the session. They get,
I think, two guineas a session, consequently, the more courts they have the
more money the Chairman gets. I am not
saying they do it, but by rejecting claims.
there is the temptation that the case may
come on again, and if it is rejected again
it comes on once more, and the more
claims they reject the more claims they
have to hear and the more sessions they
get. That is a wrong principle.
I am
not saying they do it. I am not saying
that it affects their judgment, but I am
saying the temptation is there. If
they reject a great many claims these
people are likely to appeal and come back,
and there will be another session and
another two guineas.

Where at the date of the commencement of this Act any infant is in the

or two spouses jointly as his, her or their

consent should be required and that an

is to give the court complete discretion in
the case of de facto adoptions.

Oral Answer to Question.
FLOODING IN DONEGALL AVENUE
AREA, BELFAST.
Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
certain houses forming a new colony in
the Donegall Avenue area, Belfast, on
which a Government subsidy is being paid,
are erected on ground that was formerly
a series of cesspools; whether flooding took
place there two years ago; and whether
on Saturday, the 7th instant, the houses
were flooded to the extent of two feet;
whether he can state who approved of the
sites, and, in view of the recent report of
the Tuberculosis Medical Officer for Belfast, whether he will exercise a stricter
supervision in this matter in future.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In reply to the first
part of the question, I have caused inquiries to be made, and am informed that
no cesspools have ever existed in this area.
The flooding was due to the overflow
of the Blackstaff River, which rose to the
height of 3 feet above the crown of the
bridge. The street is only in course of
construction at present, and the necessary
gullies to carry off surface water have not
yet been provided.
With regard to the second part of the
question, it is not the case that houses
were flooded to the depth of two feet.
The water did not reach floor level, but in
some cases water was driven by the wind
under the doors. Only six houses were
affected.
I understand that the Corporation has
under consideration a scheme for preventing flooding by the Blackstaff.
In all cases the Ministry of Home
Affairs before passing a house for subsidy
satisfies itself that the site is suitable and
insists on proper precautions being taken
for drainage.
I need hardly point out that the recent
floods were abnormal.
Mr. HEALY: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that the flooding was of a
depth of two feet and extended over an
area of an English mile from these houses
to a place called Stockman's Lane, that
it was in width half a mile, and that
photographs which I can give to the right
hon. Gentleman show the actual flooding?
Is the right hon. Gentleman also aware
that Dr. Thomson, Medical Officer of
Health, and Dr. Trimble, Tuberculosis
Medical Officer, have constantly been laying emphasis on the importance of healthy
housing conditions being provided by the
Corporation, and that the Corporation are
apparently ignoring that advice?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
can hardly deny that he is making something in the nature of a speech.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
stated that the houses were not flooded
to the depth indicated.
Mr. HEALY: Let the right hon.
Gentleman look at these photographs and
repeat his answer if he dare.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think those
bear out my contention.
Mr. HEALY: What?
Mr. SPEAKER: This photographic
discussion may take place in the Lobby
after the House has risen.
Mr. HEALY: I beg to give notice that
I will raise this matter on the Adjournment.
