Mr. HEALY: I have just been calling
attention to the flooding at the Donegall
Avenue area, and I am rather surprised
at the reply of the Minister of Home
Affairs. It shows, I think, apparently,
that unless you have proof in this House
very often the statements furnished to
Ministers are going to override the facts
that are very often supplied to
Members. The right hon. Gentleman
admits that this flooding is caused by the
overflowing of the Blackstaff. I would
Adjournment-
Flooding
19 DECEMBER 1929
like to ask the right hon. Gentleman
whether in view of the facts he does not
think the scheme suggested by the Corporation ought not to be put into force.
at once? I would like to refer to the
photographs I have handed in. To the
right of picture No. 1 is the Linfield Football Club. The houses marked X in No.
2 picture are the Corporation houses which
were similarly flooded, after being erected
only about two years ago. Seen to the
left of No. 3 picture is the builder's paraphernalia which is used in the erection of
incomplete rows of houses A and B. The
notice board seen is a bit satirical. Standing in the middle of the flood it announces
further ground for letting for building
purposes. There could not be a greater
censure both of the Corporation and the
Government than that notice board should
stand in the middle of a flood announcing
that the ground on which it stands is for
letting purposes.
What is the good of the Tuberculosis
Officer making recommendations to the
Government and the Corporation, and
what is the good of the Medical Officer of
Health making certain suggestions if both
the Corporation and the Government are
going to ignore them? Anybody knows,
apart altogether from what the Medical
Officer may say in this matter, that it is
very unhealthy to build houses in swamps,
and that there should exist in the City of
Belfast an area of this kind subject to
periodic flooding is the best condemnation
of the whole Corporation scheme, and also
of the subsidies granted by the Government. Some of these houses are erected
by the Corporation, and some of them are
being erected by private builders, but
whether they be one or other, they are
receiving the subsidy, and the Government,
therefore, have equal responsibility for
them. My information is that this is
filled ground, that before the houses were
erected on this plot, perhaps two or three
years ago, there were a number of cesspools there, and that it is absolutely and
entirely unsuited for the erection of artisans' dwellings or any sort of houses.
there must be some explanation for choosing a locality of this kind on which to
build subsidy houses.
In the circumstances I think that the
Government have a very grave responsibility and that they ought not to waste the
public money in this way. There are
plenty of healthy sites in the vicinity of
Belfast, without selecting swamps of this
character. I make no allegation as to any
ulterior motives, either on the part of the
Corporation or private individuals, but
As to the cost of this flooding I could
quote from the "Belfast Evening Telegraph" of Friday, the 13th inst., a speech
delivered by, I suppose, a supporter of
the Government, Mr. Donald Cheyne, in
which he estimates the cost as anything between £150,000 and £200,000. This is an
exceedingly serious matter, and one that
will not be completely met by the very
unsatisfactory reply the Minister of Home.
Affairs has given this afternoon.

When there is flooding in Tyrone and
the other counties the Minister of Agriculture comes here and grants
pensation according to the amount of the
destruction, but when a question relating
to the city is raised we are told by a
representative from a city constituency
that this is all piffle and rot. I want the
hon. and gallant Member to understand
that when a condition of affairs such as
that stated by the hon. Member (Mr.
Healy) exists in a working-class district I
am going to see that it gets the same respect in this House as the other question
in the outlying districts got. That is why
I got up in amazement and disgust at the
remarks that fell from the lips of the hon.
and gallant Member (Major Houston).
I say it is most ridiculous for the Corporation to allow these houses to be built,
and it is far more ridiculous for the
Minister of Home Affairs to attempt to
allow that land to be let for houses for
the working-class people. Let me tell you
this. In the Minister's own domain,
which I had the honour to represent in the
past and will represent again in the
future, flooding takes place about every
three months in winter to a depth of three
feet, and no voice was ever raised in this
House to compensate those poor people for
the damage caused by the flooding which is
all due to the apathy of the Belfast Corporation.
This is too serious a question for political capital to be made out of it. As
the hon. Member (Mr. Healy) says, these
houses were flooded, and the photographs
have proved it. No Corporation or Government can deny the photographs.
Therefore, I say it is time the Home
Office took action. That action should be
taken immediately, not only in regard to
this place in Donegall Avenue but also in
regard to the dumps now being let for
building purposes by the landed gentry
both in Ballymacarrett and in the Donegall Road area.
I know places that are flooded every
month in the winter, and they are erecting working class houses there. That is
alongside the Connswater, a beautiful
outlook. Kernaghan's old cornfield, on
the Dixon estate, a marshy field that could
not be let for grazing, is now let out for
building more death traps for the workingclass people. The houses are to be let at
12s 6d a week. That is the sort of stuff
the Minister of Labour is prepared to say
is good enough for building homes on for
working-class people.

Tuesday, 26th February, 1929.
The Fifth Session of the Second Parliament of Northern Ireland, appointed to
meet on the 26th February, 1929, in the
Nineteenth year of the Reign of King
George V, was opened by Commission,
the Commissioners being their Excellencies the Lord Chief Justice (The Right
Honourable William Moore), the Right
Honourable Lord Justice Andrews, and
Colonel the Right Honourable R. D.
Perceval-Maxwell, D.S.O., D.L.
The House met at Ten minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(The Right Honourable Hugh O'Neill,
D.L., M.P.) in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black
Rod (Major T. Dalby Hackett, D.S.O.),
was announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman Usher said:-
I am commanded by the Senate to
inform this Honourable House that
the Speech of his Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland at the opening of
this Session of Parliament will be communicated in the Senate forthwith.
Further, I am commanded to desire
this Honourable House to attend in
the Senate to hear the said Speech.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three
of the Clock, and then resumed.

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such perscns as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such Bribery or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
that
Resolved: That if it shall appear
any person hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime or
misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Oredered: That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant at
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND
RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings,
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
that he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no person but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges be appointed.

King's Speech
King's Speech

HOUSE OF COMMONS
KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report to
the House that the House has this day
attended in the Senate, where a speech to
both Houses of Parliament was delivered
by the Lord Chief Justice, acting as Commissioner for His Grace the Governor, on
behalf of His Majesty the King; of which
I have for greater accuracy obtained a
copy. The Speech is as follows:-
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
It is with profound relief and a deep
feeling of thankfulness to Divine Providence that I am able to record a steady
improvement in the health of His
Majesty the King. In no part of His
Majesty's Empire has there been
evinced greater anxiety throughout His
protracted illness or more heartfelt
gratification at the progress being made
towards recovery than by His loyal
subjects in Northern Ireland.
I observe with satisfaction that the
improvement in the shipbuilding industry continues, and that although
the linen trade has not recovered from
a protracted period of depression its
condition during the past few months
has been somewhat better.
I am pleased to learn that my
Government has entered into an agreement with the British Government for
placing upon a permanent basis the
arrangement made in 1926 assimilating
the burdens on the Exchequers of the
United Kingdom and of Northern Ireland in respect of Unemployment
Insurance. This agreement will require ratification by both Parliaments
and the necessary measure will be
introduced in due course.
I shall observe with interest the
results of the change in the law relating
to Health Insurance which came into
operation at the beginning of this year
extending the free period of insurance
of persons after they cease to be insurably employed, and enabling those who
are insured and are over 60 years of
age to qualify more easily for Contributory Old Age Pensions. Other provisions permit insured persons who
cannot, by reason of poor health, gain
admission to an Approved Society to
participate more fully in the benefits
provided by the Health Insurance
Scheme.
The continued development of the
education system of Northern Ireland
is very gratifying and the striking increase in the numbers of the pupils
attending secondary schools in particular, bears witness to marked progress
in the extent to which the facilities provided by the Education Act are taken
advantage of by the public.
It is satisfactory to note that the
steady upward movement in the
numbers of live stock which has taken
place since 1925 was substantially accelerated in 1928; that there was also
a considerable increase in the export of
cattle, sheep and poultry in that
period; and that the area under tillage
was over 11,000 acres above the corresponding figure for 1927.
Proposals will be laid before you for
the abolition of Proportional Representation in its application to elections
to the House of Commons of Northern
Ireland, and for the adoption of the
principle of single-member constituencies.
Proposals will also be laid before you
for relieving productive industry of a
substantial proportion of the rates
which it at present has to bear in connection with the cost of Local Government services and for exempting agricultural land and farm buildings
entirely from this burden.
Bills dealing with the following

Registration of Nursing and

The storage and transport of

The amendment of the law relating

of inspection under Part I of the

Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public Services
will be laid before you in due course.
You will be asked to make provision

of which industry and agriculture will
be exempt.
The publicity campaign organised by
the Linen Industry and assisted by substantial grants from public funds has
been extended to cover the Home and
Dominion markets in addition to those
of the United States to which it was
confined in its initial stages. While it
is yet too early to gauge the results
which may attend the extension of the
campaign to the Home and Dominion

Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
My Government will continue to give
sympathetic and unremitting attention
to all practicable measures for assisting
agriculture and industry; stimulating
trade and promoting employment.
In addition to the action which has
already been taken to achieve these
ends I trust that the proposals indicated
for relieving agriculture and productive
industry from the burden of rates and
the provision of a Juvenile Training
Centre will be of great benefit to the
whole community.
And I pray that the blessing of

Debate on the Address.
Major SHILLINGTON (in morning
dress): I beg to move:
"That an humble address be presented to His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland, as followeth--
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland, in Parliament assembled,
beg leave to offer our humble thanks
to Your Grace for the Speech which
Your Grace has addressed to both
Houses of Parliament."
In moving this Address I am sure I am
voicing the feelings of all Members of this
House in saying that we share the profound sense of relief and thankfulness at
the steady if slow improvement in the
health of His Gracious Majesty. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The wonderful
fortitude, patience and courage shown by
His Majesty during his long and trying
illness has awakened feelings of the deepest sympathy and the most intense interest throughout the whole of the British Empire, and, indeed, throughout the
whole world, but in no part of the world
have these feelings been evinced in a
greater degree than in the loyal province
of Northern Ireland.
It would not be wrong for me to say
that our people have watched with
anxiety the progress of His Majesty's illness and have at all times in their innermost hearts felt the deepest sympathy
with Her Gracious Majesty the Queen,
His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales
and other members of the Royal Family.
I am sure I am also voicing the feelings.
of every Member of this House when I say
how much we regret the unavoidable abscence to-day of His Grace our well-beloved Governor, and our sincere hope is
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Shillington]
that he may soon be fully restored to
health and strength again. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
This is the second time on which the
honour of moving the Address has been
conferred on me by the Government, and
I would desire to say how much I appreciate the compliment that has been again
paid to me, and to the Constituency which
I represent.
I feel sure that every Member of this
House and every other person who has
any interest in Northern Ireland shares
the feelings of satisfaction at the steady
improvement in our ship-building industry, largely brought about by the measures adopted by the Government under
the Loans Guarantee Act. The Government's policy in this respect has proved
of incalculable benefit to Northern Ireland. We look forward with hope and
courage to the day when our great Northern Ireland industry, that is, the linen
trade, will have been restored to its former position in the industry of the world.
It is very gratifying to learn that a
satisfactory arrangement of a permanent
character has been entered into between
the Government of Northern Ireland and
the Imperial Government in connection
with the Unemployment Insurance.
I am afraid that in some quarters the
advantages we have already derived from
this source have not been fully realised or
have been deliberately belittled, but, by
virtue of the position of Chairman of the
Belfast Employment Committee which.
I held for several years, I have had special
opportunity of appreciating the true
position, and I am frankly of opinion.
that the original agreement and this present one should be numbered as outstanding achievements of our Government.
While, perhaps, it might be out of
place for me to dilate at any length on
the proposed legislation in connection
with Elections to the Parliament of Northern Ireland, I cannot help expressing in the strongest possible terms the
feeling of satisfaction which I have and
which I know is shared by the majority
of people in Northern Ireland at the prospect of the abandonment of the system
of Proportional Representation and the reintroduction of the old system of singlemember Constituencies.

Mr. BEATTIE: What about the University?
Major SHILLINGTON: Speaking as
one of four members who have since the
establishment of the Parliament of Northern Ireland represented the County of
Armagh, I can, unhesitatingly, state that
the existing system has occasioned
numerous disadvantages, not only for me
a Member of Parliament, but more
important still, for the electors and the
people of the County as a whole.
as
To each elector in the County I was just
one of four representatives, and no elector
could claim me as his individual Member
of Parliament. On the other hand I, like
the three other Members representing the
County, had to assume a Parliamentary
responsibility for a much larger area and
much larger population than perhaps I
was capable of doing. The present system precludes any possibility of that
necessary personal touch and close relationship which should exist between the
Parliamentary elector and his Parliamentary representative.
While this new legislation which is to
be introduced is of vital importance from
a Parliamentary point of view, pride of
place must, I think, be given by me as
representing an agricultural County to
proposals which are outlined in the
King's Speech in connection with the derating of agriculture and industry.
If some years ago the farmers and the
leaders of industry of Northern Ireland
had been informed that a time would
come
when they would be relieved
of such a very substantial burden they
would hardly have believed it, but in
these days developments take place
quickly and in every year that passes we
find the Government introducing new proposals which are gladly accepted by Parliament in that they confer on the people
as a whole greater and greater benefits.
It would be idle for me to recapitulate
the various benefits which have accrued
to the people of Northern Ireland during
recent years. It will, perhaps, be sufficient to mention a few. In the first place
we have had the enormous development
in building, particularly of small houses.
for the working classes, which development is entirely due to the generous
financial assistance granted by Parliament at the instigation of the Government.
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
26 FEBRUARY 1929
We also see a rapid development in the
improvement of our road systems, due to
the co-operation between the road
authorities and the Government. We
have also had beneficial legislation in recent years in regard to Widows', Orphans', and Old Age Contributory Pensions, while, finally, our agricultural
industry has been helped in a remarkable
manner owing to the care and attention
devoted to this important service by the
Government.
While referring to these great benefits,
I think I am not wrong in suggesting that
the new benefit which is promised to us
in the King's Speech will stand out preeminently and will redound in a marked
degree to the prosperity of the whole community. The farmers of Northern Ireland will be relieved entirely of the rates
on their lands and farm buildings, while
productive industry will also derive a substantial and important benefit from the
new proposals.
Mr. BEATTIE: Where is the money
to come from?
Major SHILLINGTON: Turning to
some of the other matters referred to in
the King's Speech, I am glad to find that
steps are to be taken to place our Nursing Homes and Maternity Homes on a
regulated basis similar to what has been
done in Great Britain in recent years.
As a member of the Roads Advisory
Committee I await with interest the legislation that is to be introduced for extending the Motor Traffic Act of 1926.
This
is with the object, I understand, of ensuring a better system of control of public
service vehicle traffic in Northern
Ireland.
The rapid increase in motor omnibus
traffic has been a matter of concern to all
road and traffic authorities for some
years, having regard to the heavy expenditure involved on these authorities in keeping the roads up to a proper standard of
repair. While I generally approve of
this increased traffic, I cannot help
feeling that the time has come when care
should be taken that the traffic should
be limited, in some degree at any rate, to
the requirements of the travelling public,
and that wasteful competition should as
far as possible be avoided, not only in the
interests of the roads but also in the interests of public safety.
I am aware that some fears have been
felt and, indeed, expressed lest the
Government's proposals in this respect
would have a hampering effect on industry
or on proper development, but I feel sure
that the Government of Northern Ireland
are fully alive to these fears and that any
principles introduced in the Bill will not
tend towards an absolute limitation, but
will be directed towards development
under suitable control.
I have but one other matter to refer to.
I am glad to see a reference to town planning in the King's Speech. This matter.
was mentioned in several debates in this
House during the last Session. The Government has deserved well of the whole
community by its efforts to encourage the
building of small houses and so reduce
the considerable housing shortage which
existed after the War.
There is always a danger, however, in
such cases of building being carried on
without vision or foresight, and I feel
sure that the time has now come when
local authorities should be accorded ample
town-planning powers within their respective areas. I, accordingly, welcome
this proposal. I beg to move.
Mr. GRANT: It is a high honour to be
asked to second this Motion, but I do not
take the compliment to myself. I regard
it more as a compliment to the working
classes whom I represent in this House,
and I am sure that is how it will be regarded outside.
The hon. and gallant Member for
Armagh (Major Shillington) has covered
everything in the King's Speech so fully
and so ably that there is little left for me
to deal with, but at the risk of repetition
I must say something.
It is with deep gratification we learn.
that His Majesty the King is on the way
to recovery. He has had a prolonged and
trying illness, and in no place in the British Empire has there been more anxiety
than among his loyal and devoted subjects in Northern Ireland. In every
respect King George has been an ideal
ruler. He has entered into the very lives
of the people; he has rejoiced with them
in their joys and sympathised with them
in their sorrows. He truly possesses that
one touch of nature which makes the
whole world kin. We are delighted that
His Majesty has been spared to us, and
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
we join in the hope that he may live long,
to reign over a happy and contented
people. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Taking the subjects in the order in
which they are referred to in the King's
Speech, I am sure hon. Members, irrespective of party, are glad to know that the
shipbuilding trade has greatly improved.
Messrs. Harland & Wolff are now busy,
and Messrs. Workman & Clark under their
new management are fairly active. For
that happy state of affairs the Government are to be thanked, because it is
largely due to their action, in guaranteeing big loans, that so many orders have
come to Belfast.
I believe that since 1922 orders for the
construction of some fifty ships have been
received and as a consequence thousands
of men on both sides of the Lagan have
been engaged. Not only shipbuilding
but other industries have benefited by
these guaranteed loans which, up to the
present, amount to about £10,000,000.
That is a real earnest of the Government's
desire to help, with more to follow.
Unfortunately, the linen trade is not in
as prosperous a condition as we would like,
but that is not the fault of the Government. Some thousands of pounds have
been spent in advertising Ulster linen
goods, not only in the United States, but
in the home and Dominion markets, and
it is expected that this expenditure will
bring a satisfactory return. We would
all like to see our mills and factories again
going full steam ahead, and I do not think
anyone should complain if the Government votes a further sum towards the publicity campaign. Judicious advertising
should produce more orders.
In a speech in May last the Minister of
Labour (Mr. Andrews) said:-
•
"We have encouraged industry in
every way possible. We have guaranteed loans to shipowners in order to
bring work into our shipbuilding yards.
We have assisted our linen
industry in every way in which we have
been asked to assist that great industry,
and we have supported new industries wherever they have been started
and where we have been approached in
connection with the matter."
We want encouragement of a practical
kind and we say to the Government, "Go
on with your good work."
As a Member representing a workingclass constituency I am particularly
pleased with the reference in the Gracious
Speech to what has come to be known as
the re-insurance agreement for Unemployment Insurance. I am not sure that
even now this beneficent arrangement
has been fully appreciated in Northern
Ireland. It is, to my mind, among the
most important achievements of the Minister of Labour.
I would ask hon. Members to cast their
minds back to the position of the Unemployment Fund in 1926. Bankruptcy
seemed to be imminent and there appeared to be no alternative but to reduce
benefits and to increase contributions.
Thanks to the re-insurance agreement
these desperate measures were not required, and our Fund is now kept in the
same financial condition as the Imperial
Fund, by means of special contributions
by the Exchequers of Great Britain and
Northern Ireland. It is gratifying to
learn that the arrangement has passed
what may be regarded as the experimental
stage and that it will now be placed upon
a permanent footing.
Hon. Members have doubtless read the
terms of the agreement which were published last week in the form of a White
Paper. Full particulars are there given
as to the liquidation of the deficit on our
Fund amounting to about £3,500,000.
From every point of view this re-insurance
agreement has been of tremendous advantage to our working people. Our
social standards have been maintained on
an equal footing with those in Great Britain. We have had similar legislation
and equal administration. Had we not
kept step with Great Britain the agreement could not have been possible.
What we want above everything else is
work for the people, and I would here
like to pay a tribute to the zealous efforts
of the Minister of Labour. Through the
encouragement given by his Department,
schemes of utility have been undertaken
by public and other bodies with a view
to creating employment. Since 1922 no
fewer than 1,005 such schemes, at an estimated cost of over £5,800,000 have been
sanctioned. Just think for a moment
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
26 FEBRUARY 1929
what that meant to those out of work!
Well might I say that the Government's
policy is one of deeds not words. Some
970 firms are now on the King's National
Roll and give employment to approximately 5,000 disabled ex-Servicemen.
I am sure it is gratifying to hon.
Members that industrial peace has prevailed. In that respect we enjoy a reputation second to none. That is mainly
due to a desire on behalf of both employers and labour to accommodate
each other, to negotiate with each other,
and to help each other to the greatest
extent. Long may the spirit of give-andtake and of mutual dependence exist.
Reference is next made in the King's
Speech to the changes made last year in
the law relating to health insurance.
When the Bill was before the House in
May last the Parliamentary Secretary of
the Ministry of Labour (Mr. Gordon)
dealt fully with the question, and I should
like to tell him and the Government that
the extended or additional benefits are
greatly appreciated. I understand that
about 332,000 persons are now covered
by the Health Insurance Acts, and that
since 1922 the sum of £3,500,000 has been
spent in benefits. It is our duty to protect the aged and genuinely unemployed
and to increase the benefits of those
physically unfit, and I am pleased that
the Government have done so much in
that direction.
I might here say that Widows',
Orphans' and Old Age Pensions have
proved a great boon and blessing, the
total number of people now in receipt of
pensions being about 78,000. Over
250,000 persons are covered by the Unemployment Insurance Acts, and since 1922
the benefits have reached a sum of
£12,000,000. It is well sometimes to remember these figures. Pensions are being
paid to 5,400 widows, with allowances for
over 10,000 dependent children and to
over 800 orphans. Contributory pensions
free from restrictions as to means are
being paid to 9,700 men and women between the ages of 65 and 70, and to 9,500
over 70 years of age, while blind and noncontributory pensions are being paid to
42,700 persons. The weekly expenditure
in benefits and pensions comes roughly to
£80,000.
The Unemployment Act passed last year
removes a number of grievances and gives
benefit as a right, wipes out all past
arrears, abolishes the family income test,
and provides for financial assistance towards the training of unemployed juveniles. Yet we are told by some people
that the Government are doing nothing
for the people.
With reference to our educational
system, it is on a much sounder basis.
Close on £1,900,000 is annually spent by
the Government upon education. That is
no small sum. We want our people properly educated, especially the working
classes. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Since the establishment of the Government
nearly half a million pounds has been
spent, or is being spent, on school buildings. Scholarships are available for the
assistance of promising boys and girls
who desire to attend secondary schools or
universities, but who without this aid
would be debarred from doing so.
Medical inspection of school children is
in operation in the great majority of districts. Afflicted children are being cared
for and statutory provision made for the
feeding of necessitous children.
The Belfast Education Committee in
the last financial year provided 325,326
free meals surely a splendid lead to
other municipalities. Not only has
progress been made in primary or elementary education but also in secondary education, and the Queen's University is
being generously supported by the Government. Again I say these are facts worth
remembering.
I do not claim to be conversant with
agriculture. But, like everybody else, 1
know that the farmers have been very hard
hit, and they are entitled to our sympathy
and support. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). The Government have not been
neglectful of their interests, and by grants
in relief of rates and in other ways have
come to their aid. Everything possible
has been done to improve the breed of
livestock and to increase the cultivation
of crops. Research and educational work
has been closely attended to, and the
agriculturists with their sounder knowledge are able to overcome many of the
difficulties with which they are confronted.
When I tell you that the estimated value
of the output of livestock and livestock
products from Northern Ireland comes to
close on £12,000,000 per annum, while
the total for farm crops, including fruit
and vegetables, is something
like

Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
£3,500,000 a year, you will realize how
important this great industry is to our
Province. The lady voters may be interested to learn that the total value of
the eggs exported last year amounted to
close on £2,000,000.
Coming to the legislation foreshadowed,
I see that proposals are to be laid
before the House for the abolition of Proportional Representation. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). That is a good job,
and the vast majority of the population
will rejoice. Only the cranks will be
sorry. The P.R. system of voting is complicated, cumbersome, and expensive, and
as it involves unwieldly constituencies,
the electors could not maintain that close
relationship with their representatives
which is so desirable. With singlemember divisions, the people will be
better able to express their wishes.
particularly glad for the sake of the ladies
who are now being placed on the register
for the first time, that they will have the
direct vote. I should not care to see them
hoodwinked, the way some of the electors
have been by P.R.
I am
Then we are to have a derating scheme
which perhaps transcends all others in importance. We all feel that those engaged
in industry and farming operations should
not be placed in any less favourable position than those in Great Britain. Relief
from rates is to be given to agricultural
land and buildings, to productive industry, and in respect of freight transport,
and this relief should in turn lead to lessened costs of production, cheaper
commodities, higher wages and more employment.
Most of the details of this scheme are
known to hon. Members, and I hope the
Minister of Finance is correct when he
said that he believes the scheme will have
a greater bearing upon the prosperity of
the Province than anything which has
ever before been done by the Government.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Anything
that will revive our industries and bring
back prosperity should be hailed with delight. It is estimated that under the
scheme Ulster agriculturists, taking land
and buildings together, will benefit to the
extent of £512,000 per annum, while the
total relief to productive industry will be
about £120,000 a year. Local rating
authorities need not be alarmed at this relief, as a Bill is to be introduced to recoup
them in respect of rates of which agriculture and industry will be exempt.
Notice is given in the King's Speech of
the introduction of some nine Bills dealing with a variety of matters. An effort
is to be made to prevent the employment
of school children in connection with betting operations. Betting is a great eviljust as great as the drink curse and we
must try to keep our children from being
contaminated. Once the betting spirit is
imbibed it is hard to eradicate, and hon.
Members know the terrible consequences
that sometimes ensue from gambling.
The amendment of the law in connection with the control of licensing of public service vehicles will doubtless arouse
discussion, and until the Government produce their Bill I shall say nothing except
that while owners should be fairly and
justly treated, stringent control is necessary in the interests of the travelling public.
Hon. Members should welcome the
announcement that an adequate sum is to
be placed on the Estimates to establish
and maintain a training centre for the
benefit of young persons out of work. As
hon. Members know, a Juvenile Advisory
Committee for Belfast was set up last year
by the Minister of Labour, under the
chairmanship of Mr. R. V. Williams, to
study the problem of how best to maintain and improve the employability of
boys and girls registering at the Employment Exchange during spells of unemployment. This Committee made two definite
recommendations: First, the removal of
the Belfast Juvenile Employment Exchange to a separate building, apart from
the adult Exchange; second, the formation of a juvenile centre for unemployed
boys and girls to be administered in connection with the Juvenile Employment
Exchange and in the same building.
I take it that the Government intend
to carry out some such scheme. The
numbers of boys and girls attending the
Belfast Employment Exchange warrant
the setting up of a separate Exchange. If
classes are formed it should be possible to
occupy these young people in a useful and
attractive way, and thus counteract the
ill-effects consequent upon enforced
periods of unemployment. They would
be taught to maintain their self-respect
and improve their value to the community.
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
26 FEBRUARY 1929
Altogether, I think the programme outlined by the Government is a practical
one. It is not a vote-catching programme. It is one for the benefit of
Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). The Prime Minister and
members of the Cabinet are, therefore,
entitled to the trust and goodwill of the
whole community, not only for what they
have accomplished but for what they intend to do. They stand for loyalty to the
King and Constitution, for the maintenance of the British Empire, for the
fostering of patriotic and industrial enterprise, and for the uplifting of the
people. They have done everything in
their power to foster the cause of peace
and industry, realising that only through
the harmonious co-operation of all engaged in industry can we hope to regain
our former high level of prosperity. I
beg to second. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: I think
the customary congratulations can neither
be withheld nor denied to the two hon.
Members who have proposed and seconded
this Resolution. That part of their remarks in which they expressed satisfaction
at the improvement in the health of his
Majesty the King will, I am sure, be received with approval by all sides of the
House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
The two hon. Members who have proposed
and seconded this Resolution have, if I
may say so, added to their reputations
as orators in this House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Considering that
they have not had a good case to make
I think it required a good bit of skill on
the part of both hon. Members to defend
the action of the Government during its
lifetime, particularly in this final court
before they come up for judgment before
the people. I am afraid, notwithstanding
the case they have made, the Government
need not expect a very favourable judgment when that date comes along.
With regard to the Speech itself, there
are some things in it that are really bewildering to people who understand the
condition of affairs existing over the
Six Counties. One would think from the
speeches made that things were quite rosy
in all our industries, when as a matter
of fact such is not the case. The principal industry, farming, was never in a
worse plight than at the present time.
There does not seem to be any remedy
forthcoming as far as this House is concerned. I suppose we will be told that the
Derating Bill will be the cure for all the
ills of the farming community or farming
industry. I question very much whether
the shifting of the rates from one industry
to another will be an improvement at all.
I think it was the Minister of Finance in
this House some time ago-I do not remember exactly the date-gave us particulars as to the size and valuations of
the different farms in Northern Ireland.
He pointed out that there were 120,000
agricultural holdings in Northern Ireland,
and of these some 80,000 were holdings of
a valuation of £15 or less.
If we took the average valuation of
these holdings as £10 and if the rates on
such holdings amounted to £5 in the year,
I venture to say that only a small proportion of the farmers would get a rebate of
£5 a year. Assuming that all the farmers
got a rebate of £5 in the rates it would
not be at all equivalent, in my judgment,
to an increase in the price of farm
produce. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
At the present time farmers are having
great difficulty in actually getting rid of
potatoes in some instances at 25s per ton.
Anyone can see that that is not an economic price for farm produce of this sort.
If they were able to get what might be
considered an economic price, even twice
25s per ton, it would be much better than
being relieved of all the rates they pay
on their holdings. Therefore, I say that
this new Derating Bill will not be the
great relief to the farming community
it is supposed to be. It would be
much better for the farming community
and the farming industry-the principal industry in Northern Ireland-if the
Government were to do something to get
an
economic price for the farmers'
produce.
It has been mentioned that arable land
has been increased during the past year,
that something like 10,000 acres or 11,000
acres were ploughed more than in the preceding year in which, I understand, the
smallest acreage was ploughed for probably fifty years. But this increase of
10,000 acres is due to the farmers sowing
flax seed, as 10,000 acres of flax were
sown. And what is the result? The
price of flax has fallen some 30s per cwt.
I am not sure whether that figure is right,
but it has fallen from 120s per cwt. to 90s
per cwt. according to a report issued by
the Ministry of Agriculture recently.
Without following the figures issued by

The PRIME MINISTER: The reason

to make the government of Northern Ireland impossible. I am satisfied that there is
undoubtedly a strong movement to place the
Ulster people under an all-Ireland Parliament, and what I wish to say is that, first,
I am very grateful to the House of Commons for renewing the Act of Parliament
that enables us to deal with any untoward
circumstances that may occur, and,
secondly, for their allowing us to have
upon our Estimates a sufficient sum of
money to keep our Special Constabulary in

over again will be the policy of this Government so long as I have the honour to
lead it. Having secured law and order,
the second duty of our Government is to
maintain law and order, and I wish to
make it perfectly clear, beyond any misunderstanding, that our intentions of
doing that are as strong to-day as they
were in the years 1921 and 1922. That is
the preface to my remarks.
The second administration, as everybody is aware, was occupied by the Government and by this House in setting our
house in order. We had to accustom the
Ulster people to their new type of constitution; we had to perfect the parliamentary institution, and to establish all the
Departments for carrying on the various
activities of the Government. We had a
more or less peaceful time, and considerable development took place. As my two
hon. Friends behind me have said, we
were busy helping where we could helpto build houses, to help local authorities to
develop the great main roads throughout
the length and breadth of our country,
to assist in every way that lay in our
power to promote industry, and to help
those who were least able to help themselves.
Now, towards the close of this second
administration, as will be observed by
the Gracious Speech from the Throne, it
is our intention to make way for a new
system of election to this House of Commons, and to replace Proportional Representation by single-member constituencies.
That, I think, will give general satisfaction throughout the country. I am not
going to argue the question in any way
to-day, because when the Bill comes before
the House, as it will shortly, it will be
open to hon. Members opposite once more
to express their opinions upon that subject. although if I remember aright, it
was very exhaustively debated here last.
Session. However, my own feelings
about it can be summed up in a very few
words. It will be difficult for anyone,
when we are returned by single-member
constituencies, to humbug the electors.
The electors will be able to choose whether
they will have one Member or another,
and they will see the results of their own
action. What I have been so afraid of
under the system of Proportional Representation was that certain Members might
be returned to this House who, in a crisis
upon the one point of vital importance to
the Ulster people, might not stand by
whichever side it was intended they should
stand when they were elected to this
House.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
I have already indicated outside the
House that if the Chambers of Commerce
and Chambers of Trade will back us up
by passing resolutions in favour of the
safeguarding of the linen industry, I will
ask this House to pass a resolution to a
similar effect, in order that we may
bring the very utmost of our pressure to
bear upon the British Government to
allow us to have our case taken at an
early date under the new proposals that
they have already indicated to the
country. We have always done what we
can in this connection, but unfortunately
up to the present the trade have been
unsuccessful in securing the safeguarding
of our premier industry. I believe the
second attempt will be successful if we all
pull together, if Ulster as a whole and
this House are prepared to back up the
Government in the attempt that we will
make in this direction.
I come next to the question that perhaps has been before the public more than
any other during the past few weeks-l
refer to unemployment. In order to
correct a very wide misunderstanding on
this subject, I would like to ask the House
to bear with me for a few moments whilst
I deal with the actual facts so far as the
Government are concerned. First of all,
we have approached the British Government and successfully approached it-in
order to make quite sure that the satisfactory arrangement entered into with
regard to unemployment insurance shall
be made perpetual instead of merely for
a short period of five years. I may say
that this is one of the most anxious questions in connection with the finances of
the Government that we have had to consider for several years past. Nothing has
given us more anxiety than the question.
of what would happen if we were left to
look after the unemployed ourselves. I
would like to thank the British Government, at this Box to-day, for the statesmanlike way in which they have met us.
It is rather interesting to know that.
whilst we are discussing the matter in
this slight manner, they are actually asking the Imperial House of Commons, at
this very moment, to pass the Financial
Resolution to enable the agreement to be
carried out from their point of view.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I really
fail to find words in which to express the
catastrophe that might happen to us if
we had not been met by the Chancellor of
the Exchequer in the way he has done.
The whole fabric for which my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Pollock) is responsible would
be brought to such a condition that I
doubt very much whether in the long run
Ulster could overcome the difficulty in
which she would find herself.
But, whilst I say that, I hope that no
one will misunderstand that in the first
place this agreement was an error for
which we can take

easily understood, but it must not be

parallel lines with Great Britain we do

One of the things that moved me-it
was by pure accident that I got into this
conspiracy with the other hon. Members
--was that I happened to come away from
a place where a little child was lying dead
in West Belfast. A neighbour had come
to borrow money to bury that child, and
when inquiries were made it was found
that the father had been out of employment and knocked off the bureau for four
or five weeks. There were four children
in the room with no blankets to cover
them. Friends of mine got blankets and
went to the house and buried the child.
But most marvellous of all was that an
hour afterwards the person to whom the
pound was lent came back, gave it back,
and said they had found out since that
the child was insured for five pounds, and
the parents did not want to take the
money. "But, for God's sake,'
" he said,
"do not take the pound back, because
they have no fires or anything else in the
house." That was the case to which I
was just listening before I entered into
this conspiracy.
Again, I met a doctor who told me he
was just coming from a case where a
woman had asked him for a tonic for her
baby. As the doctor put it to me, they
all ask for tonics, when what the babies
really want is milk, and they cannot get
it. He said, "I gave them money for
milk. The next day I was sent for and

to be entirely derated, with three exceptions. I am quite in agreement with

am not like the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Gyle) who has been interjecting remarks and trying to interrupt.
I believe in laying on pure water, and I
believe that if there is a supply of water
laid on farms the farmers should pay for
pure water. I much prefer that a farmer
should pay for water than for the other
stuff the hon. Member represents.
I would like to have the assurance of

farm buildings, and that by derating he
means that all separate charges of every
other description for local management
of local affairs will be included in his derating scheme. I take it that that is so,
but I would like to have the assurance

that no other rates will be chargeable

I was rather surprised to hear the hon.
Member for Down (Mr. O'Neill) belittle this proposed Measure. Is he

relieve the farmer of his burden of rates?

of about £120,000, making a grand total

seen
any announcement made by the

say anything disparaging about
Government of Northern Ireland which
has allowed the Corporation to be in
existence so long.
Mr. KYLE: They are your friends.

hon. Member (Mr. T. Henderson) was
fair to the Government. He tried to get a
tremendous lot of praise that is due to the
Government transferred to the shoulders
of the Corporation when he said how much
the Corporation had done to relieve unemployment. I would like to have reminded the hon. Member, if he were here,
that had it not been for the generosity of
the Government in providing funds the
Belfast Corporation would have been able
to do very little to reduce unemployment
in their area. And so I want to say on
behalf of the unemployed people of
Northern Ireland who have since got employment through the generosity of the
Government that if the hon. Member who
spoke yesterday does not appreciate what
has been done by the Government they at
least do. I recognise the good work done
by the Minister of Labour. No man
could have done more to relieve unemployment than the Minister of Labour has
done, because he has not held his hand
but distributed money unsparingly and unstintingly to any worthy object in Northern Ireland when a scheme was put forward by any local authority. We congratulate the Minister of Labour and those
associated with him on what has already
been done, and I can only hope that the
fresh legislation which has been passed
will enable him to do still more to remove
from our midst the grim spectre of unemployment, and I can assure him that in
any scheme he puts forward for that purpose he will have the wholehearted support of those who sit on the Government
back benches.
The hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin), whom we are always glad
to see and to hear, in spite of his professions of modesty, spoke in very violent
and denunciatory terms of the Government. The fact that the Prime Minister
stated that the Government had restored

maintaining law and order, seemed particularly nauseous to the hon. Member.
I can assure the Prime Minister and the
Government that nothing will give the
Loyalists of the Border counties more
satisfaction than such a statement, and

resident inside this area.
We want peace
and security to continue, and this can
only be done while the law remains a
terror to all evil doers and a praise to

going to ask this House, if the Chambers
of Commerce over the Six Counties would

think the Prime Minister's observations

just like to ask the Prime Minister a few

Minister has in view when he says he

dressed flax. In the year 1927 there
was imported into the port of Belfast
23,397 tons of dressed flax, of an estimated value of £1,945,531. That is

really the finished article of the farmer,

The next thing I want to say is this:
If they are in earnest about safeguarding

market, I would like to ask them how

also, is included in that scheme. I find
that linen and cotton yarns are included.
and that linen and cotton cloths are included. How are the Government going
to reconcile their policy of safeguarding
Ulster linen with their action in giving a
bounty to the foreigner in the de-rating
scheme for the stuff he sends in here?

before it can be adopted.
I am

course, apprehend that what you have

There is another point I want to raise.

There is another point that I want to

with regard to the Unemployment Fund.
He said practically that if this rearrangement had not been made, Ulster could

Where are we with regard to these financial matters? I cannot tell. If it is
Ulster's monev. Ulster should be able to
use her own monev
Now, come again to the question of derating. I congratulate the Government
with regard to their attitude on de-rating
for at the eleventh hour falling into line
with the Imperial Parliament. That is
a policy I have advocated since I came
into this House. I want to point out
this, that in the year 1926, I think it was,
or 1927, when our Minister of Finance

Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. G. Henderson]
was robbing the rates in Northern Ireland
by putting his hand into the grant in aid
of rates on agricultural land and taking
out £32,000-when I got up in this House
and said I thought that until our farmers
had been put in the same position as the
farmers in England with regard to the
relief in rates we should not pay any Imperial contribution; that is, before we
pay any Imperial contribution we should
at least see that our farmers get the same
relief in rates on agricultural land as the
farmers in England get, the Minister of
Finance told me I was talking great bosh
--talking nonsense. He said these things
were fixed on a population basis.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
He
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON:
said that they could not touch this fund
for it. Now, when we asked him in this
House last year where he was going to
get the money to carry out this derating
scheme, which is a far bigger thing-
Mr. POLLOCK: You object to it, of
course?
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: No. I
do not think the Minister of Finance can
read that into what I am saying. I do
not object at all. But I want to get back
at the Minister of Finance for some things
he said with regard to my ideas of finance
in the past. Now, when we asked him
last Session where he was going to get the
money to carry out this de-rating scheme
he did not deign to give us an answer.
We did not get the answer to that in this
House. But when he went to the more
august assembly downstairs in the Senate,
and the Senate asked him where he was
going to get this money-it is going to
cost a lot of money-the Minister of
Finance said we are going to get this
money in the final adjustment of our
accounts in England-the very thing the
Prime Minister said yesterday. If the
Minister of Finance is right now he must
have been wrong in 1926, and I must
have been right when I said that before
the Minister of Finance should consent
to pay over any Imperial contribution
our farmers should be placed in as favourable position as the English farmer.
For
two years the Minister of Finance I say,
if he is right now, has robbed our rates
to the extent of £64,000 and more, because even before he took the money from
the grant in aid of rates on agricultural
land we were only receiving 52 per cent.
of relief while the English farmer was
receiving 75 per cent.
I congratulate the Government on the
reversal of that policy, and the adoption
of the policy I advocated that the farmer
should be put in the same position.
Although late in the day I am glad the
Government have been converted in their
policy. All the same it is very hard to
understand our financial relations with
the Imperial Parliament.
There is another thing. The Prime
Minister criticised rather severely the
Member for Down (Mr. P. O'Neill) when
he said that this de-rating scheme was to
some extent shifting the burden from one
leg to another. If I can see it I just
want to read what a very ardent supporter
of the Prime Minister said with regard
to this from the district of Ballymoney.
Indeed I have heard this lady's name
mentioned as a possible Government
candidate at the next election. I do not
know how true that may be. She said
this: "Mrs. Montgomery-The Derating Bill was not the lifting but the
shifting of the burden, and the people
Iwill have to find the debt somehow.
Derating would not save money to the
country, as there were no economies being
introduced with it, and the same amount
of money would have to be found.'
Now, I am entirely in favour of the derating scheme because I believe if it is a
shifting of the burden it is a shifting
from one leg that is very severely penalized to another that is more able to bear
it. At the same time it is very difficult
for an industry like the agricultural industry which we were told in this House
yesterday produced about 18 or 19
million pounds worth of wealth in this
community-it is very difficult, in fact
impossible, for an industry that produces
that amount of wealth to escape the
incidence of taxation, because indirect
taxation in the long run generally has a
way of finding its way back either to the
producer or consumer.
There is one other matter I want to
mention in the King's Speech. I think it is
a question that is exercising the best minds
in this community not a little recently.
It is a question that should be particularly
interesting to all people at the present
time in the face of the general elections.

It is the question of personation at elections. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I
do feel that the time is come when something drastic should be done to combat
this growing evil. It has grown to such
proportions at the present time I do feel
it is assailing the very foundations of our
representative institutions. Now, what
is the position of the Government with regard to this? The Prime Minister said
two years ago that it was a growing evil,
and that it was a grave scandal.
the quotation here, but I do not think I
can see to read it. But I think that is
not representing him unfairly. He said
a growing evil and a grave scandal.
I have
Since that time has that evil abated?
I think instead of abating it is still growing. And the worst feature of the
situation to my mind is this, that in the
olden days personation was largely confined to what I may call the work of the
corner boy. Nobody with any respectability about him would be identified with
it, and it was only done in isolated cases.
Now respectability seems no bar, and the
thing is done wholesale. Therefore, I feel
if our representative institutions are not
to be menaced this evil will have to be
dealt with. What is the position of the
Government? The position of the Government as expressed by the Prime Minister is this: that the present law and the
present arrangements are sufficient to
combat this evil. Nobody thinks that
but the Government themselves. Nobody
else thinks the present state of the law
is sufficient to curb this growing evil.
It has been suggested that this matter
should be put in the hands of the police.
Why should it not? In every other
department the detection of crime is in
the hands of the police. There is another
suggestion which would not be half as degrading as what is going on at the present
time. The suggestion is that each voter
as he records his vote should have an indelible stamp put on his hand. That is
a drastic step, but I feel that until this
matter is stamped out it is not much too
drastic. What are the Government going
to do about it? Are they going to take
any action?
With regard to the abolition of Proportional Representation-I do not want
to keep the House-I just want to say
this: Proportional Representation would
be an ideal system for electing members,
and it has this virtue that it is peculiarly
adapted to this Province in that Proportional Representation, more than any
other system of election, secures for a substantial minority representation in Parliament and in other institutions outside
Parliament, in
in accordance with their
numbers. I have said before that the
very composition of this present House
of Commons is the finest example of the
fruits of Proportional Representation,
because if you take the composition of
this House you will find that the
different sections to-day are represented
with wonderful accuracy. The number
of first preference votes cast corresponds to
the number of representatives secured
for each party. Why are the Government going to abolish Proportional Representation? It is only another link in
the chain of their self-preservation. It
is the one thing that this Government
seems always out to do-to preserve their
own lives. That is the main object for
which they live. This will curb and
crush any expression of independent
political thought out of this House and
out of this Parliament.
There are one or two other minor matters I should like to mention in connection with this King's Speech. I find
there is no mention made in the King's
Speech of the Adoption of Children Act.
This Act has been in operation in
England for two years. I understand it
is working fairly well. There was a Bill
introduced, I think, by the Government
leader in the Senate last year, but it was
dropped. I want to know what the
attitude of the Government is with regard to that Act. I understand from
people interested in the welfare of women
and children that this Act was promised
by the Minister of Home Affairs two
years ago along with another Act, that
is the Registration of Nursing and
Maternity Homes Act. Now I am glad
to see that the Government have included
that second Act in the King's Speech
this year.
I hope it is not included and
predestined to be dropped like the
Adoption of Children Act last year.
There is another question which is
agitating people who take an interest in
the social conditions of women and
children. That is the question of maternity mortality. It is rather significant
that in the last 50 years there has been
C

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. G. Henderson]
practically no change in the proportion of
deaths in these cases. There has been a
great decrease in practically every other
case in the proportion of deaths. I
think is a question that deserves the attention of this House because there is no
greater calamity than when the mother
is taken away at that critical time of
life. It is a calamity to the family and
the child if the child is still spared. I
understand in London in 1927 there was
a conference and an expert committee
was set up to inquire into every case of
maternity mortality in England. I
wonder if this is not a question that
might interest this community quite as
much as the question of the Border. If
we could for once just have the activities
of this Parliament centred for a time on
our own problems in Northern Ireland
and leave other people alone for a wee
bit-centre on our own Province and on
the question of public health.
There is another question to which I
want to refer. I am very disappointed
that no mention is made in the King's
Speech on legislation on behalf of leaseholders and town tenants. This matter
was referred to a committee, and during
the last Session I put some questions with
regard to when the report of that Committee would be available. I was always
told it would be available in a very short
time, but so far that report has not come
to hand. This is a very urgent question
in many places in the Six Counties. The
need for this legislation to protect lease
holders, holders of short-term building
leases, and town tenants is pressing. Do
the Government intend in this Session of
Parliament to legislate on this question?
If they do not intend to legislate I know
there will be very deep disappointment in
many places where this is a burning and
urgent question because leases are dropping out. The people are being deprived
of premises they have built themselves,
and the landlord has taken over at the
end of the lease, in some cases without
any compensation.
I see there is also a reference in the
King's Speech to an improvement of the
bankruptcy laws. I do not know whether
that will help a bankrupt Government or
not. If it would, the sooner they get this
legislation put on the Statute Book the
better, because to my mind they seem
bankrupt in ideas and bankrupt in policy.
The only thing the Prime Minister has to
say when he comes to this House is:
"Put me in power for another four or
five years; I have something up my sleeve
which is going to act like magic. You
are all going to be prosperous."
Mr. MCALLISTER: It is a humiliating
thing at this time of the day that public
representatives elected by the minority in
the Six Counties, unless they are sycophants, should be compelled day by day
to raise the issue of their rights and privileges in this House. Two things in connection with the King's Speech will endure. One is the abolition of Proportional Representation, and the other is
the intolerable and disgraceful record of
the Prime Minister's speech in this House
yesterday.
When I heard the Prime Minister
yesterday the first thought that occurred
to me was this: one thing must be done,
and that is an appeal must be made to the
honest, respectable, decent, Protestant
businessmen and professional men and the
Protestant working men to read that
speech, to dissect it, to ponder over it,
and then to go back and re-readalthough it is not pleasant reading-the
episodes following up the notorious visit
and speech of his at the Queen's Island.
What were the facts? The Catholic
working people were driven from the
Queen's Island, and the Prime Minister
of Northern Ireland, holding the most
reponsible position in Northern Ireland,
went down to Queen's Island and said,
"I approve of what you did."
What was
the result? There are 20,000,000 Irish
people in America. Those 20,000,000
Irish people were the most active and
effective agents for the Northern Ireland
linen trade in America. They were
voluntary workers. When that speech
was made every loom in Northern Ireland
was humming, but to-day there is silence
in the looms of Northern Ireland. I say
here with deliberation-and there is no
one more anxious for the advancement
and prosperity and progress of Ulster
than I am that the speech of the Prime
Minister yesterday when it is published
in the papers-because it must be published-will damn and ruin for years and
years to come any prospect of the regeneration of the linen industry which was
our pride and joy in Northern Ireland.
We all believe that speech by the Prime
Minister was so defenceless and so hopeless that the Unionist Press of Northern
Debate on Address

27 FEBRUARY 1929
Ireland refused to publish it. It would
not bear the light of day.
One would think with the agricultural
industry at the lowest level that has ever
been recorded in Northern Ireland, with
the linen trade struggling for its very
existence, with hundreds of men and
women ready, anxious, and willing to
work walking idly through the streets of
Belfast and the provincial towns, with
poverty, destitution, and starvation
stalking through the land, with the little
children of Northern Ireland-the future
men and women of the race-growing up
in hunger, unfed, and badly clad, growing up without any opportunity of a trade
or education or of working their way in
life one would think that with that
state of affairs any Government with the
most elementary sense of duty would have
avoided all contentious matters, would
have concentrated all their time and
talents, such as they have, and energies,
and would have invited co-operation with
men and women of every sect and creed
to regenerate these industries.
Instead of that, in total disregard of
their sense of duty and in opposition to
their duty as public trustees for equal
administration for all classes and creeds,
they introduce the most contentious legislation it is possible for a Government to
introduce, and for the most selfish purpose possible. Proportional Representation was expressly put into the Act of
1920 by the English Government to protect the interests of the minority in
Northern Ireland. No doubt, at the end
of three years the Government here were
permitted to change the system of
franchise, but the English Government
thought that three years would enable the
Government here to progress, and prosper,
and advance. Instead of that, their
mental outlook, their mental stagnation,
their narrow-mindedness, and their shortness of vision are worse to-day than when
the English Government considered it was
necessary to provide special protection for
the minority in Northern Ireland.
The thought has occurred to me that
England professed to go to war for the
sanctity of a scrap of paper. We will
want to know from the English Government if she went to war for a scrap of
paper that did not directly concern herfor the preservation of the neutrality of
Belgium-is she going to stand by and
permit a subordinate Parliament, whose
legislation she must ratify, to tear to
tatters not only a scrap of paper but the
Act of her own Imperial Parliament? We
have had handed to us to-day a memorandum showing the proposed future constituencies in Northern Ireland. We have
only had an opportunity of looking at it
in a most casual way, but, so far as we can
see, in the eyes of all honest, decent men
it stands condemned. In after
page page
and line after line hypocrisy brands the
action of the Northern Government.
No Government have had the opportunity this Government have had. When
they came into power after last election,
that was in 1924, we came into this
House as the representatives of the
minority of the people in Northern
Ireland, ready, and anxious, and passionately willing to assist in promoting a
better outlook, in advancing industry,
and in co-operating with them in every
possible way for the betterment of the
people of the Six Counties. Every opportunity has been taken to turn us
against them. Now the climax has been
reached. This new Franchise Bill has
been prepared by the Unionist clubsthat is a notorious fact-sitting in secret.
They mapped out this part and that part
so as to get a Unionist majority for the
Government at the next election. If
they come back at the next election they
will create a precedent, for no Government in any country in the history of the
world has ever been returned to power
with a record of inefficiency such as this
Government has had during the past
eight years. When they came into power
agriculture in Northern Ireland was as
progressive as in any country in the world
and to-day agriculture here is on the
verge of bankruptcy.
With regard to the de-rating scheme,
the childish argument was put forward
by the Prime Minister, the hon. Member
for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Elliott)
and others, that because we criticised it
and said it did not go far enough we were
hostile to it. As a matter of fact we on
these benches, on every occasion, have
advocated the abolition of rating in connection with farms. Only this time last
vear I had a Motion in my own name suggesting that the Government should take
over the roads of Northern Ireland in
order to relieve the farmers from the
burden of the upkeep of the roads for
mtotor transport.

It is a significant thing in connection
with these election laws that the only

take steps to prevent personation.
know myself in County Antrim where

On a later occasion I will have an opportunity, with others, of developing arguments with regard to the De-rating Bill
and agriculture generally. At this stage.

Mr. COLLINS: My professional duties
bring me into touch with many people, and
in all my long experience I have never
been brought more into touch with
poverty and with starvation that I have
within the past few years. The state of
trade is desperate. We who live near
the Border can see the effects of the political efforts of the Gentlemen who now
form the Government of Northern Ireland. In a moment of lunacy they let go
three million customers. The Six Counties form part of the geographical Ireland.
It was the industrial area that supplied
the goods in the first place for all Ireland,
and after that provided them for export.
Here, through politics, they have allowed
three million customers to get away, and,
of course, our factories are closed and we
are without work.
There is no use in preaching to this
Government about what they should know.
I have told them about the mills of
Newry being closed up and the machinery
sold. Six hundred workers were thrown
out in one mill, and 300 in another. Not
a thing has been done to help to find work
for these people who are living in a hopeless condition. When I came to this
House to hear the Speech from the Throne
I thought some effort would have been
made to put before us something reasonable to try to absorb some of the unemployed.
I want candidly to confess in this
House that the speech of the Prime
Minister at Derry made a great impression upon me, and I thought that at last
he had wakened up to the realities of
the situation. But when I came to the
House yesterday what was the remedy I
found?
It was to start the old ghost
again by reading the speech of a professional English politician. The reason he
gave for reading it was that it had appeared in the London "Times." I had
not read the article, nor would I read it.
I know what these gentlemen are. So
long as they are dealing with Ireland
when they have us split, as they have the
Indians split, they are happy.
The Prime Minister in this House said
that Mr. Winston Churchill had pointed
out that two divisions of the Irish Republican Army were actually in existence in
Northern Ireland after the Northern
Parliament had been set up. What
short memories the Prime Minister must
think people have. I went to some
trouble this morning after hearing that
speech. I went to a newspaper office. I
want to call the attention of this House
to the fact that this Parliament was
opened in June, 1921. Listen to what
happened at British headquarters on the
9th July, 1921.
At the British military headquarters
in Parkgate Street, Dublin, a truce
was entered into between General
Macready, Colonel J. Brind, and Mr.
A. W. Cope, Assistant Under-Secretary, acting for the British Army, and
Commandant R. C. Barton, I.D., and
Commandant E. J. Duggan, I.D.,
acting for the Army of the Republic.
On behalf of the British Army it is
agreed as follows:-
(1) No incoming troops, R.I.C., and
auxiliary police, and munitions;
and no movements for military
purposes of troops and munitions
except maintenance drafts.
(2) No provocative display of forces,
armed or unarmed.
(3) It is understood that all provisions
of this truce apply to the martial
law area equally with the rest of
Ireland.

(e) To discontinue and prevent any
action likely to cause disturbance
of the peace which might necessitate military interference.
Is it to be believed that the British Government specially provided for two
divisions of the Republican Army to exist
in the Six Counties under this truce?
We are not going to be led away as simply
as the Prime Minister thinks.
(4) No pursuit of Irish officers or men
or war material or military stores.
(5) No secret agents noting descriptions or movements, and no interference with the movements of
Irish persons, military or civil;
and no attempts to discover the
haunts or habits of Irish officers
and men.
Note. This supposes the abandonment of Curfew restrictions.
(6) No pursuit or observance of lines
of communication or connection.
On behalf of the Irish Army it is
agreed that:-
(a) Attacks on Crown forces and
civilians to cease.
(b) No provocative displays of forces,
armed or unarmed.
(c) No interference with Government
or private property.
(d) To discontinue and prevent any
action likely to cause disturbance
of the peace which might necessitate military interference.
This is from British headquarters:
Mr. De Valera having decided to
accept the Prime Minister's invitation
to confer with him in London, is issuing
instructions to his supporters:
(a) To cease all attacks on Crown
forces and civilians.
(b) Prohibit use of arms.
(c) To cease military manœuvres of all
kinds.
(d) To abstain from interference with
public or private property.
In order to co-operate in providing
an atmosphere in which peaceful dismay be possible the Government
has directed thatcussion
(a) All raids and searches by military
and police shall cease.
(b) Military activity shall be restricted
to the support of police in their
normal civic duties.
(c) Curfew restrictions shall be removed.
(d) The dispatch of reinforcements
from England shall be suspended.
(e) The police functions in Dublin to
be carried out by the D.M.P.
In order to give the necessary time
for these instructions to reach all concerned the date from which they shall
come into force has been fixed at 12
noon on Monday, July, 11th, 1921.
Yesterday we were told how shocked the
Prime Minister was at the statement that
after this Parliament was established the
3rd and 4th Divisions of the Republican
Army existed in the Six Counties, although General Macready gave them safe
conduct and undertook not to molest or
interfere with them. Mr. de Valera gave
his instructions to his followers. You all
remember them. The Government ought
to remember them. There was not a
breach of that truce up to the signing of
the Treaty. Everyone knows that perfect
order was kept in this country.
Having settled that question raised by
the Prime Minister, I will now deal with
His Majesty's Speech. There is one thing
I notice there is little talk about, and it
is the most useful thing as far as I can
see that the Government could have put
into the Speech-that is the amendment of
of the Bankruptcy laws. I can assure the
House that if things go on as they are
now permitted to go there will be no
need for amendment of the Bankruptcy
laws.

suppose I can quote them too. I want to

I
The Conservative Government has
been driven to fake finance. We see
this in the unemployment insurance.
expenditure. Instead of frankly
acknowledging that the £350,000 weekly
we are spending now on unemployment
beyond the receipts under the Unemployment Act is actual money spent and
never recoverable, it is funded and

Both these cost this country a great deal

There is the Fund which we are told by an
Englishman is faked finance. We are
spending £350,000 weekly, and it will
