Fund with it. I hope you will get twice
as much out of them. That is my wish.
There is a reference in the King's
Speech to the Education Act. And I
want to say that the Government might
have spared our side of the House the
insult that we are getting in the reference
to that Act in the Speech from the Throne.
Everyone knows our position. The rates.
to which we are contributing are going to
the building of those new schools you see
photographed in the "Belfast Telegraph"
ou many occasions, and yet when we want
to build or repair our schools we have to
do SO out of our own pockets.
The reason for that is that under no
circumstances will a Catholic Irishman
give up religious teaching in his school.
The Government know that but still they
penalise us and take money from us in
this way.
Then they insult us in this
Speech from the Throne by telling us how
gratifying is the way the Act is working.
The Members of the Government, and
particularly the Minister of Labour, all
know the history of Ireland. They know

called an ignorant man, because he would
not give up his religion.

matches valued £37,000,

THE WHAN CASE.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Attorney-
General whether it is a fact that the evidence which Head-Constable Slacke gave
before Mr. O'Donoghue in February,
1928, related to a conversation which the
head-constable had with Mrs. John Walker
while Mrs. Whan was confined in the
Armagh Jail awaiting her trial; whether
he can tell the House what means Mrs.
Whan's legal advisers had of knowing
what passed at that conversation in the
Detective Office, so that they could call
Head-Constable Slacke as a witness for
Mrs. Whan at her trial in January, 1923;
whether this was part of the evidence
which District-Inspector Allen said in his
report should have been produced by the
Crown at the trial of Mrs. Whan, and
whether it is not a recognised principle in
the administration of the criminal law that
the Crown should produce at the trial evidence in their possession in favour of as
well as against a prisoner.
(Mr.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL
Babington): The suggestion contained in
this question is that certain evidence was
suppressed by the Crown which would
have established or helped to establish the
innocence of Mrs. Whan. This suggestion is quite unfounded.
The conversation referred to related to
a ring brought to Head-Constable Slacke
by Mrs. Whan's son, and Mrs. Walker
was not asked any questions with reference
to it at the trial although her advisers
must have known all about it.
When the case was before the R.M.,
Head-Constable Slacke gave evidence as to
inquiries made by him from Mrs. Walker
as to the ring.
The R.M. attached no importance to the
incident, and I agree with him. No evidence was suppressed, and, for reasons already given by me, District-Inspector
Allen's report cannot be either disclosed or
discussed.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask the
Attorney-General whether he is aware
that this conversation which took place in
the Detective Office and which is embodied
in District-Inspector Allen's report, was
proof-positive to any court or to any judge.
and jury of the innocence of Mrs. Whan,
and whether in view of that fact the Crown
is justified in refusing to give information
in favour of the prisoner when they gave
information against her. I would ask
the Attorney-General to reconsider his
reply and give us the exact reason why.
Failing that, I will have to put a Motion
on the Paper and bring the matter before the House again.

VACANCIES IN CIVIL SERVICE.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Finance whether there are any positions,
and if so, what the positions are, in the
Civil Service of Northern Ireland which,
when a vacancy occurs, will not be filled
by the Civil Service Commissioners as a
result of open competition, if after full
consideration of the claims of all eligible
officers in the Service it is found there is
no officer with the necessary qualifications.
Mr. POLLOCK: The only permanent
positions in the Civil Service of Northern
Ireland which, in the circumstances mentioned by the hon. Member, would not
be filled by the Civil Service Commissioners by way of open competition, are
a limited number of professional and
special posts in the Ministry of Home
Affairs and in the offices of the Houses of
Parliament to which appointments are
made by the Minister of Home Affairs and
the Speakers of the Houses, respectively.
In these cases the functions of the Civil
Service Commission are limited to inquiring into and certifying as to the qualifications of the candidates chosen for
appointment. The positions referred to
in the Ministry of Home Affairs are set
forth in Regulations made by the Ministry
of Finance and published in the "Belfast
Gazette" dated 4th June, 1926, and 28th
September, 1928, respectively.

GRANTS FOR SECOND-CLASS
ROADS.
Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is the intention of the Government to follow the lead
given by the Imperial Government and
increase to 50 per cent. the grants given
for maintenance of second-class roads.
Sir DAWSON BATES: For five years
past the grants from the Northern Ireland Road Fund to road authorities have
been on a considerably higher basis than
the grants payable to corresponding road
authorities in Great Britain, the object
of the Government of Northern Ireland
being to encourage the reconstruction and
the improvement of our road systems.
By adopting this principle the Road
Fund Reserve has been completely exhausted and as the commitments of the
Fund are at present if anything in excess
of the income it would not be possible
under present circumstances to increase
the percentage grants to Class II roads.
However, the position will be carefully
watched from time to time.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is the Road Fund not
exhausted owing to the contribution given.
to Derry Bridge?
Mr. GRANT: Or to Newry?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No.
BELFAST AND COUNTY DOWN
RAILWAY BUSES.
6.
Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state his
reasons for granting to the Belfast and
County Down Railway a licence to run
omnibuses between the City of Belfast
and Holywood; and whether he is not
aware that there is an adequate service
being maintained on this route by two
small omnibus owners.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Belfast
and County Down Railway had started a
road service on the Belfast-Holywood road
after the 27th August, 1928, but before
the restrictions came into force.
There were six operators working on this
road. Two have ceased working, and one
has reduced his service to very small
dimensions. In these circumstances, I
consider that there is sufficient traffic to
warrant the issue of two route cards to the
railway company, and that this addition.
was required to deal adequately with the
volume of traffic. I do not propose to
increase the number of permits on this
road further in the present circumstances.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask

of the declaration he made in this House
and whether he remembers the promise he
made to the small bus owners, and
whether he is aware that the Belfast and
County Down Railway had no interest in
this road prior to the 27th August, 1928;
whether he is aware that by an accident
two buses of one of the owners were burned
and before he had time or had been requested to make up additional two buses
the Minister of Home Affairs granted the
Belfast and County Down Railway a road
licence in violation of the promises given
to the small bus owners and to Members
of this House.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: Will
the right hon. Gentleman tell us whether
it is owing to Government persecution of
these small bus owners that they had to
go off the roads?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon.
Friend has already heard from his Colleague (Mr. Beattie) that it was owing
to the fact that the buses were burned.
Mr. BEATTIE: But opportunity was
taken of that fact to give the County
Down Railway a privilege.

CIVIL SERVANTS AND POLITICS.
8. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime
Minister whether he is aware that a
circular has recently been issued by the
Government to all civil servants, restricting them from taking part in politics,
and what action he proposes to take to curb
the political activities of the Secretary to
the Cabinet, who is a civil servant paid by
the public irrespective of party, and to
curb the activities of servants of the
Government who are civil servants who are
also taking part in municipal as well as
national politics.
Mr. POLLOCK: I will reply to this
question. A circular was issued by the
Ministry of Finance in June, 1926, in
which it was laid down that no member
of the Civil Service might undertake work
identified in any way with the activities
of a political party, group or organisation. So far as I am aware this rule has
been generally adhered to throughout the
Service, and has been meticulously observed by the Secretary to the Cabinet.
Mr. KYLE: In the public Press of
Belfast it was stated that Mr. C. H.
Blackmore, who is Secretary of the
Cabinet, attended a Unionist meeting in
the Plaza in Belfast, and it was also
stated in the public Press of Belfast that
Mr. Burn, an employee of the Government, took the chair, and spoke at a
Unionist meeting in Cromac ward at the
recent municipal elections? Is the right
hon. Gentleman's head in the sand that
he does not know of these things?

NUMBERS OF APPLICANTS DIS-
ALLOWED BENEFIT.
9. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state how many
persons have been disallowed unemployment benefit from the 1st January, 1928,
until the 31st January 1929, (1) for not
genuinely seeking work, and (2) because
first statutory conditions have not been
fulfilled, and the total number of persons from all causes; and whether he can
state the total number disallowed who
have since found employment.
Mr. ANDREWS: The present first
statutory condition did not come into
force until 19th April, 1928; and the
figures which I shall now give will relate
to the period between that date and 14th
January, 1929.
During that period 14,493 claims were
disallowed on the ground that the
claimants had not proved to the satisfaction of the Insurance Authorities
that they were making genuine efforts to
get work, and 10,209 were disallowed on
the ground that the first statutory condition, or the transitional conditions
which may be substituted for it, were not
satisfied. The total claims disallowed
finally for all causes numbered 25,954.
In many cases a disallowance was imposed
on more than one claim made by the same
person; so the number of individuals
affected is considerably less than the
figures indicate.
I am unable to state the number of disallowed claimants who have since found
work; but as disallowance on the ground
that an applicant is not genuinely seeking work operates for six weeks only, it
may be assumed that the majority of the
persons disallowed on that ground either
found work during the currency of the
disallowance or were again granted benefit at the end of the six weeks period.

We know it from personal contact, and
if the Government have not been moved
by the articles in the Press and by the
stories printed there regarding the appalling poverty that exists not only in the
slums but in the artisans' dwellings in the
city they should now take some action.
I think I am safe in saying that these conditions of poverty are worse to-day
than they have been for a considerable number of years, and, at the
same time, we are experiencing
much colder spell of weather than we
had for the past thirty or forty years.
What intense suffering this cold in addition to the poverty will bring to those who
are short of food, short of clothes, and
short of fuel, words—at least my wordsare incapable of expressing.
a
Those of you who have imagination,
even the feeblest imagination, might insist along with us that the Government
should take notice of this important question and do more than they have been
doing to make less this intense suffering.
In my judgment it is not only a question
of the suffering that exists now, terrible
as that is, but it is bound to mean that
the whole physique of our people will
suffer, because if the children and the
adults are being starved to-day it seems
to me that the next generation is going
to be much more stunted than the present
And we know what has been stated
about the present generation by the recruiting authorities. We find them statone.
Debate on Address

28 FEBRUARY 1929
ing that about 50 out of every 100 who
apply for admission to the British Army
are rejected as not being physically fit to
be members of that army.
That is the present generation, but how
much worse is the next generation going
to be if something is not done immediately
to arrest the evil that is going on at the
present time? What sort of mothers and
fathers are the children going to be when
they are at present being starved and
stunted and denied any chance of growing
to healthy womanhood and manhood? No
wonder our maternal mortality is so high,
as the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. G.
Henderson) pointed out yesterday. No
wonder it can be stated with truth that
it is four times as dangerous to be a mother
in Ireland as it is to work in the mines
in Great Britain. In other words, the
bearing of children is a much more
dangerous occupation than mining. If
that can be burnt into the minds or the
imagination of the Government surely it
will make them realise the state of affairs
that exists at the present time.
Is it any wonder then that our death
rate in Belfast is so high? The death rate
in Belfast, spread over a much larger area
than in a similar town of the same population in Great Britain, is between two
and three per thousand higher. Our sickness rate, as can be demonstrated by our
National Health Insurance returns, is
higher in Northern Ireland than in any
portion of Britain or the Free State. This
is all a consequence of the neglect of the
important matter of looking after the
health and well-being of the people by
providing sources of employment. These
the Government have hitherto neglected
to supply. In my opinion these rates are
bound to go up.
The maternal death
rate, the ordinary death rate, and the
sickness rate are bound to go up in the
future. If it is your pockets you who
represent the wealthy classes in this House
are afraid of, remember that it is you,
or your sons, or your daughters who are
going to pay a hundredfold for the present
neglect.
Do not forget the saying that the sins.
of the fathers are visited upon the children.
I say, and say deliberately, that the
wealthy classes who are represented in the
Government to-day and who are deliberately and of malice aforethought not providing for the people of this generation
will have to pay, and pay through the
nose, and they will deserve it when it
comes. The Government may say that
there are bodies to deal with this problem, and that where the bodies who are
supposed to deal with this problem do
not cover the ground the Distress Committee which I have mentioned will step
in. I have said that the Distress Committee is good in so far as it shows that
men of goodwill in the City of Belfast are
not content with the apathy of the
Government and with the neglect of the
bodies who are set up to look after extreme poverty and distress. Good as it
is, it will take time before it gets into
operation, but the starvation that is going
on now requires immediate attention.

Belfast, it is true, as the hon. Gentleman

in the Six Counties--
Mr. HEALY: Hear, hear.
Mr. KYLE- that emergency provisions should be made at the present time

The Government provide unemployment
insurance and pay a certain proportion of

There have been some complimentary

ticular grounds. Therefore, I accuse the

The
par-
The schemes of work that have been
provided by local authorities have done
a certain amount to relieve unemployment, but at a time like this these schemes
are needed on a very much wider scale,
and it is the Government's duty not only
to assist the local authorities but to undertake schemes of work themselves. What
is happening in Belfast, and what has
happened elsewhere, is that Belfast is
being compelled to do work now which is
burdening the ratepayers of the City of
Belfast to a very great extent indeed. If

part of the country. In my judgment we
should not only assist the local authorities
but the Government themselves should
undertake schemes of work.
I would like to ask again what about
the recommendations of the Development
Commission that sat for almost three years
in Northern Ireland. What about the
many excellent reports that were issued by
that Commission on the development of
our resources in Northern Ireland? Has
anything been done to carry any of these
recommendations into effect? I submit
that very little has been done and that the
Commission itself was established by the
Prime Minister of Northern Ireland with
the deliberate object of side-tracking the
whole question of the development of our
resources in Northern Ireland.
Something has been said about the advertising grant to the linen industry. I
want to submit that a grant for advertising is not enough. The hon. Member
for Antrim (Mr. George Henderson), who
sits behind me, has mentioned the possibilities of the encouragement of the
growth of flax, and has quoted from Mr.
Larmour, who was present in Belfast the
other day and who spoke on that particular problem. It seems to me that the
development of the growth of flax would
imply, and does imply, the stabilisation.
of prices and, perhaps, the organisation.
of the flax growing industry in the same
way as has been done on the Continent.
The Latvian Government a year ago
organised a body of workpeople who went
round the farms in Latvia, pulled the flax,
retted it, marketed it for the farmers,
gave the farmers a fixed price, and a
bonus on top of the fixed price owing to
the prices which the Latvian Government
were able to get for the flax which the
farmers produced in that province. If it
is possible for this to be done in other
countries why on earth cannot it be done
in Northern Ireland? Northern Ireland
has been called the home of the linen trade.
I saw recently in the paper that the
Chinese are going to use linen again, that
they are tired of using silk. That is one
of the very favourable reports of the exhibition of goods that is taking place now
in Birmingham and London. If there is

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Kyle]
going to be a development-which we hope
to see in the linen trade, then surely it

Edward Archdale) and the Government
of Northern Ireland not to be so thick in
the heads and so stick-in-the-mud as they

they should go ahead and do something to
organise the growth and development of
the flax industry. It would help our farmers and it would help our trade. Eighty
per cent of the flax formerly used in Northern Ireland came from the Baltic Provinces or from Russia. That supply has
been largely cut off, so it is up to us in
Northern Ireland, where we can grow
flax, to make good the deficiencies that
exist to-day.
In regard to the linen trade, hon. Gentlemen opposite should know that the method
by which the Swiss Government put us
out of the embroidery trade in Switzerland was by giving a subvention to those
people who worked at that particular class
of business. They gave a subvention to
the embroiderers in Switzerland and cut
down very considerably our embroidery
trade in Northern Ireland. We all
know that even since the war subventions have been granted to trade
in Germany. We all know the statements that have been made by people
in Britain about the alleged attempts of
Germany to evade payment of reparations,
and we all know the complaints that have
been made in regard to the methods by
which Germany stimulated her own trade.
If these methods have been successful on
the Continent and apparently they have
been-then I want to submit to this
House that there is no reason under the
sun why something along the same lines
should not be done in Northern Ireland.
Mention has already been made of it, so
I need not stress the point about the development of the artificial silk industry.
I saw in the commercial edition of the
"Manchester Guardian" a prospectus issued by a new company formed for the
development of artificial cotton. This
cotton, I understand, can be grown anywhere owing to the many crossings that
have taken place from the original cotton
seed. I understand that this cotton,
which is called artificial cotton, can be
produced in large quantities in almost any
climate. Therefore, I want to know from
the Government have they done anything
to investigate the possibilities of the development of this particular trade in
Northern Ireland. I do not pretend to be
an authority, but I think we are entitled
to ask are the Government aware of what
has been done in this matter and what
are they doing in Northern Ireland on
this important subject.
I have already mentioned that I think
the Minister of Education should send a
circular to all schools in the Six Counties.
He might go further and call a conference
of the education committees of Northern
Ireland and use all the pressure of the

got in the 1923 Act to give emergency

children. In Belfast a considerable number of meals are being provided, but even
more could be done at the present time
in the way of emergency feeding, and I
suggest that the Minister of Home Affairs
might do the same in regard to milk for
mothers. There were 64 mothers in Belfast who got free milk last year. Out of
a population of 415,000, that was the
provision of milk for expectant mothers
in Belfast. Surely it is the Government's
job to see what can be done and to do
these things.
The Government are always saying to
the Opposition that we have no constructive proposals to put forward. Apparently
the Government do not listen to constructive proposals when they are made, for
constructive proposals have been made
again and again from this side of the
House, and very little, if any, attention
has been paid to them. Take, for example, the speech of the hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. George Henderson) last
evening. No reply has been forthcoming
from the Government, and a more damning indictment of the Government's policy
has never yet been made in this House
than the speech I have referred to. Many
useful suggestions and constructive proposals have been put to the Government
from time to time, and very little, if anything, has been done by the Government
to carry out those proposals. In other
words, the Government want the emoluments of office without the job of thinking
and planning and working for the good of
the Province. They want the Back
Benchers and the Members on this side of
the House to make constructive proposals.
What is their job but to make constructive proposals? What is their job

are properly attended to, particularly at

of Northern Ireland. You can sit two

I would like to ask the Members of this
House of what importance are the bankruptcy laws or the licensing of motor
vehicles? How many of our people do
they affect as compared with those who
are in poverty and misery, and compared
with the large numbers who are in need
of food and clothing and shelter in the
Six Counties? This ought not to be a
party question; it is a human question.
It is a question that should affect us all
the same way, and it should be our duty
as men, never to speak of Christians, to
see that our brethren and our sisters are
fed and clothed and housed. Surely after
2,000 years of Christianity, it is not too
much to expect that a Government might
pay attention to these important matters.
Therefore I say, and I think I am justified in saying, that this ought not to be
a party question; it is a human question.
And yet the people all over this country,
all over Britain, are more and more driven
to realize that there is only one party in
the State that is interested in this matter
in the right way, and that is the Labour
party.

We are earnestly praying that something

Counties. The Government go rambling

never find.

such as we,
Who search for a hidden city that we
shall never see."

son of the King of England, and would
go into the distressed areas, not in Durham and Northumberland, but in Belfast
city, in Keady town in Armagh, in one

I should have been glad if I could have
discussed this question without approaching it from a single controversial aspect.
From the beginning I have expressed my
anxiety regarding it. I feel that there
are only two questions that count-at
least I think so. The Government do not
think so. There are two questions only
that count in the life of Northern Ireland to-day, and these questions are
unemployment and poverty. These are
the only two questions. You may harangue the multitude, but the multitude
is a rare capricious element in the life of
the community. You may utter the old.
war cries and shibboleths and try to drag
the people back again to 1886; you may
raise bogies, but they will not frighten
even children. You may do all that, but
believe me the mentality of the people has
reached that stage just now when they are
looking at things from a different angle.
Speaking, not only as a representative,
but as an old politician, I say that the
people would be as worthy of contempt as
they are treated if they failed to realise
that there should be only one form of
politics now, and that is the well-being
and comfort of the community.
I say, therefore, that the only two
questions the only two problems-that
ought to be most in the minds of the
people are the problems of unemployment
and poverty. I distinguish between
these two things as I have distinguished
between them in previous contributions
to the debate. You can deal with the
question of unemployment by paying the
unemployment grant. Nobody believes
in that process of solving this question.
It was a necessity that arose out of a
grave and unprecedented national situation affecting not only Northern Ireland
but affecting every part of these islands.

election, but believe me, if they go on as
they are at the present time, giving the
people passions instead of bread, politics
instead of solutions of the industrial and
economic problem, and catchwords when
they are starving-if they continue that
policy they may win at one election but
in four more years they will be the most
discredited political party that
existed in any community.

For my part, I would infinitely prefer
that there should be brought prosperity
to the Province, comfort to the people,
heat to the fireplaces, and food to the
tables of the struggling masses of the
people than that any party should secure
a political advantage through the present
situation. I have said that we call as
witnesses in this House to our assistance

Then we have the report of the Committee which recently went into this
matter. They have had a thousand cases

Why should it be left to private
munificence and to the humanitarian
spirit of individual citizens to deal with
these matters? Surely the primary
responsibility of the State ought to be to
give the people the only form of existence which can justify them, that is food,
and clothes, and fire. The right hon.
Gentleman, the Minister of Finance, can
say it is not their business to do these
things. He may say that, and he may
justify it from a certain point of view.
I quite agree that this is not directly the
function of the State, but there is a
higher conception of civic duty, and that
is the Christian conception, when cases
are as appalling as those in the records I
have read, and I gave some even worse
cases in the speech I delivered on Tuesday.
Supposing private citizens took the
same view of their duty as Governments
do, supposing philanthropic men and women say to themselves, "This is not our
business at all, it is the business of the
Government, or it is nobody's business,"
what would be the result? But there is
the starvation. I was told of a little child
that died the other day in a house in
which there was no money to bury it, and
on the floor there were four other children
lying on a bed of old blankets. There is
another case of a poor woman being sent
to the lunatic asylum, not because she was
mad but because she had four children
and no food or fire. The doctor sent her
Debate on Address

to Purdysburn Asylum and she only

I say then that no matter what the
theoretical idea may be as to the Government's duty in any great crisis of this sort
there is the grim reality of the situation

The hon. Member went on to say that
it was impossible to satisfy the Courts of
Referees that a claim was a just and
proper one. In Belfast alone we have
20,000 persons receiving benefit each
week, and only 310 claims are turned
down each week. In Northern Ireland
at the end of January we had 41,000
persons receiving benefit, and only 615
claims were turned down weekly.
Although these claims are turned down
one week they are very frequently granted
within a short time, because I would like
it to be understood that even if a man is
turned down for not genuinely seeking
work he is not turned down, as some
people think, for all time, but he is only
turned down for six weeks and at the end
of that time his claim may be admitted.
Surely that is not unreasonable or unfair.
If I may say so I think it is very improper
for hon. Members to be continually
criticising these Courts of Referees.
They should remember what their constitution is. No claim can be decided by
other than a fully constituted Court if the
claimant so wishes, because the claimant
can object to his claim being considered
if there is not a complete Court.
The Court consists of a workers' representative, who is not likely to be prejudiced against the worker, an employers'
representative who would have no interest
in unreasonably objecting to a worker's
claim, and there is a legal gentleman who
is there because he is neutral. Therefore,
I maintain that these claims are considered as Parliament provides they should
be. Of course. it is inevitable that when
a claim is turned down the claimant
thinks he has a grievance, but it is not
the fault of the Court that he is turned
down. It is because his claim does not
come within the four walls of the Act of
Parliament which we have passed in keeping with the British Act of Parliament,
of which it is a duplicate.
It was suggested in the debate on Tuesday that the Acts are not administered as
sympathetically as they are in Great

wrong to suggest to our people that they
are not getting the justice which the
Government desires they should get
and which their fellow countrymen get
across the water. And, therefore, I really

70 per cent. of the cases with which I

Debate on Address
Debate on Address
28 FEBRUARY 1929
CONDITION OF AGRICULTURE.
Mr. LEEKE: I beg to move as an
Amendment to the Address, at the end
to add the words:
"but humbly regret that no mention
is made in the Gracious Speech from the
Throne of any legislation to relieve the
existing distress in agriculture."
I think it will not be denied by any Member that the most important factor in the
industrial life of Northern Ireland is agriculture. With agriculture is linked up
the success of the townships and all industrial areas. Consequently, I would
have thought that more serious attention
would have been given in the King's
Speech to the question of agriculture. The
Prime Minister accused the hon. Member for Down (Mr. P. O'Neill) of dealing
in an airy fashion with the Derating
Bill. I think the Prime Minister himself
dealt in an airy manner with the question
of agriculture. He has promised a
Drainage Bill without giving any details
regarding it. I agree with the Derating
Bill, I say that frankly here and now.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). It is a
step in the right direction, and it will be
a great boom to the Ulster farmers. At
the same time I do not agree that the
agriculturist is relieved of all rates. I remember being one of a deputation that
waited upon the Prime Minister recently,
and he told us that there would still be
certain rates on farmers. There will be
the Drainage rate.
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, if there is one.
Mr. LEEKE: There is likely to be one
in the area I represent-Derry. There
will also be the education rate. There
will also be the rates on the dwellinghouses. These will be small, but at the
same time you could have a high rate on
a small valuation, so that the farmer will
still have some burden to bear in that way.
As to the derating of transport freight, I
would like to draw the attention of the
Minister of Finance to this fact.
You
must remember that the produce raised
by the farmers is not all carried by the
railways. I can take you to several parts
of the country where the produce is totally
and solely carried by motor transport.
Take, for instance, Greenloughs in Derry.
There is no railway there. Motor lorries
collect feeding stuffs and manures at the
merchants' stores here and run them
direct to Greenloughs. They load up with
potatoes coming back. Will those farmers be allowed advantage of the derating scheme if the stuff goes by motor instead of by rail?
Mr. POLLOCK: No.
Mr. LEEKE: There is one handicap.
You must send the stuff by rail otherwise
you do not get any advantage of the derating scheme. You are simply subsidising the railway company. It is a protection for them against motor transport.
I hope that when the Bill comes before the
House the Minister will see that that part
is amended.
Mr. POLLOCK:
They pay no rates.
Mr. BEATTIE: They pay taxes.
Mr. LEEKE: Yes, they pay taxes. It
will be agreed unquestionably that potatoes are the most important crop of Ulster
farmers. If they have a good crop and
get a good price they can struggle through
despite a lower price for other commodities
they raise, but this year the prices are abnormally low. They are being produced
at a loss. While I do not hold the Government altogether responsible for the
depressed condition of the market I do
think the Department of Agriculture
might have given a little more attention
to the question of finding foreign markets
for the Ulster potato crop. There is, as
he knows, at the present time an outlet
for Ulster potatoes in two foreign markets.
If the Department gave more encouragement, got lower rates, and sent out a
representative to these market centres to
encourage the sale of Ulster potatoes, even
if it cost £1,000 in expenses, I think it
would be a great asset and would assist
materially the Ulster farmer in his attempt
to get rid of his crop. Unless some such
outlet is found this year I am afraid a
big percentage of the potatoes will be left
in the hands of the farmers who will not
get any return for their labour and industry last year in producing them. I
think everybody is agreed that in the
whole history of farming in this
country farmers never had a worse
time than to-day. There have been times
when there have been bad prices, and that
will always occur, but if it occurred in the
past it must be remembered that the
farmers had not the present high expenses,
wages and prices to pay for labour, rates,
manures, feeding stuffs and everything
else. That is one of the greatest handicaps facing the farmers.

for their generosity.
The hon. Meinber for Down said the
small farmer would get no benefit, and
that it would be much better to guarantee him a bigger price for his potatoes.
A farmer with a valuation of £15 would
have about £3 on his house and £12 on
his land. If he paid 10s in the £ each
year in rates, the amount mentioned by
the Member for Down, he would pay
£7 10s. When this De-rating Bill comes
into force he will only have to pay £1,
and he can put £6 10s in his pocket.
A man with a farm of that size could not
sell more than about five tons of potatoes.
The Member for Down suggested that this
farmer should be given an extra pound for
his potatoes, but he is in a much better
position through the application of the
de-rating scheme than he would be if the
Government guaranteed him an extra 25s
a ton for his potatoes. There is also this
important factor, which has not been
mentioned by any hon. Member, and that
is that the potatoes the farmer sells go
on the market at a cheap price to help
the poor people of the city.
On behalf of the farmers I sincerely
thank the Government for this De-rating
Bill. One or two little things might be
included in it to help the farmers a little
more. My colleague for Antrim on the
other side of the House suggested-and I
agree with him-that dressed flax might

be included in the Bill, and I hope the

I believe that before some of the Members of the Opposition came into this

I do
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON:
not intend to keep the House very many

think it will be admitted by every section
of the House that the economic stability
and prosperity of this country depend to
a greater extent on the agricultural industry them on any other factor. Therefore,
I think it demands and requires the first

community. Now, I do not think the

best thought to it. I think a great many

the Government is probably typified by

when most Members have gone home.
Very few of them are in the House to

Now, I do blame the Government

Export Association here which said that

of eggs was going through this House I
did
press on the Government and the

Now, I find that this is in the new grading

that we are all agreed about, and that is

I do not think the Government are entirely to blame for that.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: We
have been passing through very severe

yellow meal. I remember in my own

a ton. That was a very low cut. To-day
I think the price would range somewhere

Mr. ELLIOTT: You are quite right.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: There

Then there is another point. During
the passage of the Potato Inpsection Bill
through the House last year I asked the
Minister of Agriculture to postpone the
operation of that Act for at least a year
because I had an assurance from men who
were in the trade and knew the trade
from bottom to top that if these regulations were put into force this season it
would mean extra expense of handling of
at least 7s 6d a ton. At the present price
of potatoes that would be a tremendous
handicap on the trade. If that estimate
was right I think the Minister of Agriculture would have been very well advised
not to have started this experiment this
year when potatoes were at such a low
price and so very hard to market.
I have always held that the prosperity
of the agriculture of this country was
largely bound up with the dairying industry, and I feel that the Ministry of
Agriculture has not done all that it
might. Indeed it has done very little in
my opinion to re-establish the dairying
industry and to give it a chance to get
back to the position it once occupied in
this country. I do not blame the present
Ministry of Agriculture for the misdeeds
of the old Board, but there is no mistake
about it that the idea that prevailed for
a very long time in the Ministry of Agriculture in regard to livestock was that
nothing but beef mattered. That was a
great factor in helping-I was going to
say ruin, but helping to retard the dairying industry, because it reduced the
average production of milk in our cattle.
I know the Department at the present
time is doing something through milkrecording societies to try to raise the
average production of cows per head. I
think our dairying industry needs reorganisation from top to bottom. I think
the prosperity of agriculture in this
Province is largely bound up with the
production of milk and milk products.
There is another question and that is
the growing of flax. I feel the Government have hardly realised the importance
not only to the agricultural but to our
linen industry of encouraging the increase
in the growth of our flax crop. I do feel
that our business experts ought to get
together. The question is one bristling
with difficulties, but if they got together
they could surely hammer out some
scheme that would induce the farmers to
increase the production of flax. I do not
like the paying of subsidies, but there is
one thing I dislike worse and that is paying money away for which there is no
return-paying money away in unemployment doles-and if we could in any way
stabilise the price of flax to the farmer
and guarantee a price for, say, five years,
it would aid employment, not only in the
agricultural industry, but help to create
employment in the linen industry as well.
I was informed by a man in the linen
industry lately that if we could stabilise
the price of raw material for three or four
years it would be a great assistance to
the linen industry and would enable it
to give more employment and absorb a
great many workers into the industry.
There is another way in which the
Government might help the agricultural
industry and that is in the production of

owing to the wet seasons. We have any
amount of limestone in Northern Ireland,
and if some of the money given in unemployment benefit could have been
employed in producing lime and sold to

another point the Government have control over that might help to tide the
farming community over the present
financial stringency, that is, by extending
the years for the re-payment of land purchase annuities. I understand the Government of Northern Ireland have full
control because they collect them and pay
them into the Exchequer of Northern
Ireland.
Mr. POLLOCK : No.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I
understand they have control of these

the years of repayment and reduced the
annuities at the present time. I am glad

for years--at least to some extent they

You see, a general election is coming and

scheme of loans to farmers for manures
and drainage purposes. I hope they will

Mr. HARBISON: I only intervene

have heard my colleague in the represention of Tyrone and Fermanagh speak,
and I have heard my Friend on my left
Iso speak. I did not hear all the debate,

Tyrone and Fermanagh says.
I think it
was because he did not compliment him on

it pleases him I will congratulate him on
it, but more than that I will congratulate
the British Government, because the one
was the corollary of the other.
I live in the heart of an agricultural
country, and I have heard a great deal
about bad prices and the hard times the
farmers have, as indeed they have. Nobody knows that better than the men at
present engaged in my profession. I
know their difficulties, and I know they
are making a terrible struggle to keep their
end up.
But I have a solution of the
problem. It may be looked upon as
Utopian, but it has been tried in other
countries and it has proved a success. We
have here the Farmers' Union and other
farmers' associations, but there does not
seem to be any cohesion amongst these
farmers. They are combinations, but
there is no universal combination. There
is no doubt any child can see it-that
the farmer is being robbed.
I met an Englishman a couple of
months ago. He was an agent for some
English company, I do not know the company, but he resided in County Monaghan. He seemed to have all his business
here in Belfast. On one morning as he was
leaving Monaghan to come to Belfast his
wife asked him, on his way through the
local town to buy her 2 lbs. of bacon for
the house. He did so, and paid 'tenpence
retail price. On another occasion, subsequently, he got the same commission
from his wife, and he forgot in passing
through the local town to execute the
commission. He came on to Belfast, but
he was bound to bring that 2 lbs. of bacon
home to his wife. I should have said in
the first instance that she wanted Sinclair's cured bacon. He bought 2 lbs. of
bacon in Belfast, and how much did he
pay for it? He paid 1s 4d per lb. for the
bacon that he paid tenpence for in
Monaghan. That shows that the farmer
is being exploited by the middleman and
ultimately by the retailer, who is selling
his produce at 300 or 400 per cent. profit.
In my opinion there is only one cure for
that. It has been adopted in one part of
the British Dominions-in British
Columbia, and there there has been a
Coercion Act passed compelling the farmer to combine and pool his stuff. The
Government of the country takes charge of
the stuff, and as soon as the farmer has it
harvested the Government pays him 75
per cent. of the value of that produce.
They hold it until the market is favourable to sell. By doing that the farmers
there have made over 100 per cent. more
than before that procedure existed. Unless the farmers of Ireland combine farming, in my opinion, here is not going to be
a profitable interest to the farmer.
This is the first opportunity I have had
in this House of enunciating that proposi
tion, and I would ask the Minister of
Agriculture to think it over, and, if necessary, communicate with British Columbia
and find out what they have done there,
and what the result has been to the
farmer. I am sure, as happened in
British Columbia, that there will be resistence here to it in the first instance.
Well, even if we have to coerce a man for
his own benefit I would say coerce him to
save the country and the farming interests.
That is my contribution to the debate.
I sympathise with the farmer in his present difficulty. The farming industry at
present is in a deplorable state. As I
say, in our profession, perhaps we know
more of the private affairs of farmers
than most men, and I know he is a rare
farmer to-day who can meet his liabilities

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £2,165 be granted to His Majesty
for the Service of the year ending the
31st March, 1929, to defray the Salaries
and Expenses of the Ministry of Finance
(15 and 16 Geo. V., c. 3, s. 4 (N.I.) ),
including the administration of Revenue
Services, Valuation, Registration, Loan
Services, Public Works, Charity Funds,
Stationery Office, Teachers' Pensions,
Civil Service Commission, Ulster Savings
Certificates, Loans Guarantee Act (N.I.),
1922; Land Law Acts, Collection of Land
Purchase Annuities and Tithe Rent
Charges, Intoxicating Liquor Acts (N.I.),
1923 and 1925; the Census of Northern
Ireland, 1926, and Sundry Agency Services (10 and 11 Geo. V., c. 67, s. 63)."
Mr. BARBOUR: The first two subheads under which this supplementary
provision is required relate to certain
works services necessitated by an additional
technical staff, which has had to be recruited to deal with the preparation of
drawings necessary to enable tenders to
be called for the work in connection with
the Bann drainage scheme, and in connection with the investigation of certain
harbour schemes. This expenditure, obviously, could not be foreseen at the time
that the original estimates for the year
were being prepared.
The item of £1,390 in connection with
the teachers' superannuation fund is the
amount claimed by the Imperial Government Actuary's Department for the work
of that Department during the last
eighteen months on the investigation into
the actuarial position of the fund. The
Teachers' Superannuation Act (Northern
Ireland), 1926, provided for the holding
of an investigation once every five years,
or at lesser intervals, commencing from
the date of that Act. It was decided
that in order to have information on the
position of the fund at an early date,
having regard to various new factors
which had arisen, namely, the increase of
salaries, the admission of new classes of
teacher to superannuation, etc., an investigation should be held before the first
five-year period had elapsed, and the
Imperial Government Actuary was asked
to carry out the work on behalf of the
Ministry of Finance.
I should like here to express publicly
the Government's appreciation of the care
and trouble taken by the Government
Actuary and his Department in the carrying out of this investigation. I may say
that the statistics and general data on
which the investigation was based were
compiled by the three Departments, viz.,
my own Ministry and the Ministries of
Education and Agriculture. As a matter
of interest, I may mention that amongst
other things the work involved the employment of a number of ex-Servicemen
for some months in the filling in of between 8,000 and 9,000 cards, giving
various statistical information about all
the teachers in the schools, as well as
about pensioners in receipt of teachers'
pensions from the superannuation fund.
The expenditure in carrying out that
part of the work has already been borne
by other sub-heads of the Ministry of
Finance and Educational votes.
The last sub-head-Expenses of Local
Committees makes provision for an additional sum of £725 for the payment of
compassionate gratuities to ex-clerks of
old-age pension committees. The original
estimate for the year was a token provision of £500, as it was not then possible to
estimate either the number of the applicants or the amounts which would be
awarded. Up to the present time
approximately nineteen persons have
received compensation, the awards ranging between £30 and £200, according to
the varying degrees of hardship arising
from the cessation of income received as
clerks of these committees. I beg to
move.

the sum of £100. I do so because
I think these Supplementary Estimates
are very often
often the breeding ground
new jobs. The first item of

the architectural and engineering services.

deal first with the questions asked by the

We have encountered considerable difficulties in doing the preliminary work in

hon. Member (Mr. P. ONeill) the reason
why we did this work was that we are
bound by our own Act, the Teachers'
Superannuation Act of 1926, which provides that an actuarial investigation
should be made, and since we have provided that the investigation should be
made we thought we could not turn to

Actuary's Department. We feel that

be made is in connection with the technical staff of the Ministry of Finance, and

CLASS II. No. 3.
PUBLIC WORKS AND BUILDINGS.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £18,285 be granted to His Majesty to
defray the amount required in the year
ending 31st March, 1929, in respect of
Public Works and Services."
Mr. BARBOUR: The estimates
already approved by the House for the
current financial year have, in the main,
proved sufficient to meet all foreseen
demands, and the supplementary sum now
required is necessitated by new and unforeseen items of expenditure. The
nature of these items is indicated briefly
under the various headings, but, for the
information of hon. Members, I will now
proceed to amplify these.
The major portion of the sum now
required is in respect of "Section II"
services; that is to say, Northern Ireland
Works Services, the cost of which cannot
be charged against any particular Northern Ireland Public Department. They
comprise the purchase of a dredger and
auxiliary craft, and the acquisition of
additional land at Stormont Estate.
Prior to the establishment of the Northern Ireland Government, dredging craft
had been maintained in Ireland for work
at the various harbours around the coast,
including the five Royal Harbours. The
Government has, for some time, been convinced of the necessity of providing some
form of dredging craft for Northern
Ireland, and arrangements have been now
made for the purchase of suitable craft at
a sum of £15,285. The craft for which
provision is now sought consists of
dredger, rock-driller, motor-launch,
tug and two hopper barges, and is of the
type and dimensions suitable both for
small harbour and inland water dredging
operations.
a
In arriving at this decision the Government was largely influenced by the
evidence contained in the Report of the
Departmental Advisory Committee on the
Development of Fishery Harbours. Consideration was first of all given to the
alternative method of hiring plant to meet
the necessities of the case, but in view of
the results of the engineering survey
showing that there is every probability of
reasonably continuous employment for a
Government-owned plant at
harbours
throughout the summer season and on
sheltered waterways during the winter, it
was decided that the interests of the
local authorities owning fishery harbours and of the Government itself as
regards Royal Harbours would be better
served by acquiring plant for these purposes. Had it only been a question of
dredging Government-owned harbours at
Ardglass and Donaghadee, the Ministry
would probably have repeated the arrangement made some time ago, under which a
dredger was hired from the Dublin Office
of Works. I should here like to express
our obligations to the Dublin Department
for its readiness and courtesy in meeting
our request for hiring their dredger in the
past.
The Government has intimated to the
Councils who own some of the smaller
harbours in Northern Ireland its readiness
to undertake dredging work and to meet
approximately one-half of the cost
involved, this decision being based on the
necessity of affording our fishermen as
safe anchorage, etc., as is physically
possible.
The second item on which hon. Members may require some information is in

token Vote. The Imperial Government.
entered into an arrangement with the
Canadian Government to supply harvesters in order to deal with the Canadian
harvest, and a certain number of vacancies were granted to us to fill, provided

Our
quota was 100, and we advertised the
vacancies and about 1,400 of our people
volunteered for the work. These were
examined by the Canadian authorities and
100 were selected. Of the 100, ninetyeight went to Canada, and the other two,
through some misunderstanding as to the
sailing of the steamer, were unfortunately
left behind. About 28 of these harvesters
have remained in Canada, and I am informed they are satisfied with the conditions there. The balance have returned
home, and I am glad to say that from

their treatment while out there.
I beg
to move.
Mr. KYLE: I want, if I can, to get
some information from the right hon.
Gentleman about these harvesters who left
Northern Ireland and went to Canada to
reap the Canadian harvest. I want to
know if he can give us any particulars as
to the conditions under which these men
were employed, and whether the conditions were anything approaching the conditions which we read of in the newspapers, and which were discussed in the
Imperial House of Commons. It did
seem to me that the conditions that were
imposed on these men who went to
Canada were extremely onerous, and were
conditions under which no man should be
asked to work at all.
No provision was made, either by this
Government or by the Imperial Government, to ensure that there would be at
least sleeping accommodation for the men
when they went to Canada. The men,
as I understand, were brought to Canada;
they were dumped down there, and were
practically left to fend for themselves.
There was no condition laid down that
the farmer employing the men should pay
them any particular rate of wages, with
the result that the Canadian people themselves entered protests against those men
being brought from our shores and
dumped down in Canada without any
provision having been made for them.
I want to protest on the ground that
this is the first occasion on which this
matter has ever been mentioned in this
House. The right hon. Gentleman made
some arrangement with the British Government. The facts of that arrangement
were never made known to the public of
Northern Ireland or to this House in any
way. Now we are asked to pass this
Vote. It is a token Vote, I grant you,
but nevertheless it establishes this principle, that we send out men at the
request of the Canadian Government.
The Canadian Government, I understand,
does not make any arrangements in regard to the conditions under which the
men shall work. Therefore, I want to
protest strongly against the action of the
Ministry in this matter.

Oral Answers to Questions.
A MONEYLENDERS BILL.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state if the
Government intends to introduce the
Moneylenders Bill, which was recently
passed in the British House of Commons,
into Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The attitude of the
Government remains as outlined in my two
previous replies to questions from the hon.
Member on this subject, namely, conditions in Northern Ireland are not quite
similar to those obtaining in the larger
industrial centres in Great Britain, and so
far the need for legislation here on the
lines of the Moneylenders Act of 1927 has
not been proved. I am, however, keeping
in touch with developments, and if the
hon. Member has in his possession any information which would go to show the desirability of the application in Northern
Ireland of the provisions of the 1927 enactment to which I have referred I shall
be happy to consider this.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to know
whether the Minister could answer this
question. Is there any truth in the statement that the moneylenders who failed to
receive registration in Great Britain are
coming into Northern Ireland to carry on
a branch of moneylending to which we in
this country have not been accustomed,
and if so is he not prepared to have similar
legislation in Northern Ireland to protect
the class of people who have to go to
moneylenders from the unscrupulous conduct of these undesirable people?
Mr. BARBOUR: I have looked over
the recent registrations of moneylenders in
Northern Ireland and I think I can assure
the hon. Member that there is no increase
such as would indicate any influx of
moneylenders.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is not my point.
It is whether he is aware that this class of
moneylender does not seek registration,
and whether this class of moneylender now
being ousted from Scotland and England
is taking up residence in Northern Ireland
and carrying on operations.
Mr. DEVLIN: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman what exactly are the
reasons which have inspired him in declining to introduce similar legislation to
what has been passed in England? What
are the reasons? Considering that this
Bill was steered through its stormy passage by Lord Carson that ought to encourage the right hon. Gentleman to
reproduce it here.
Mr. BARBOUR: If there is any
moneylender carrying on a moneylending
business in Northern Ireland without
being properly registered I would be very
glad if the hon. Member would furnish me
with information, on receipt of which I
shall be glad to go into the matter further.
In reply to the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin), I stated in my
original reply that the conditions in regard
to moneylending are very different in
Northern Ireland. It has not developed
to anything like the scale on which it
exists in Great Britain. I think I might
mention to illustrate the point that, if
you take for instance a city like Liverpool,
there are in Liverpool no fewer than 1,400
moneylenders, and of them I believe about
80 per cent. are women. In the whole of
the Northern Ireland area there are, I
think, about 140 moneylenders, and not
more than one-third of them conducting
business on a large or even moderate scale.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is not the principle the
same wherever the evil exists? It is not

a question of corresponding numbers in
Liverpool and Belfast. This is an evil

Mr. BARBOUR: I hope our Northern Province may remain free from many
of the evils that exist in England and
Scotland. The time may arrive, which

there may be a corresponding necessity to
Ideal with the evil here. If any abuse of

Mr. HEALY: Does the right hon.
Gentleman not think that some of the
British philanthropists might come across
to relieve the Government from its embarrassments?

BELFAST ART GALLERY AND
MUSEUM.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the amount
of money received by the Northern Government in lieu of the grants from the
British Exchequer to the National Services of Ireland; whether any such
moneys were earmarked or have been
used for such services as the establishment
of a National Gallery and Museum in
Northern Ireland; and whether, in view
of the fact that Belfast has the nucleus
of such a museum, he is prepared to allocate some moneys to the Belfast Art Gallery and Museum.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked
by the right hon. Gentleman to reply to
this question. Apparently the hon. Member is referring to the grant of £400,000
paid to Northern Ireland by the Imperial
Government in the year 1924 on the recommendation of the Colwyn Committee.
as a liquidation of the liability of the Imperial Government under the Government
of Ireland Act to provide in Northern
Ireland the equivalent of certain buildings (not being headquarters offices)
situated in Dublin and the South of Ireland, of which there was no counterpart
in the North.
The allocation of this sum was settled
by Act of this Parliament, namely, the
Exchequer and Financial Provisions Act.
(Northern Ireland), 1924. That allocation does not include any item in respect
of a State Gallery of Art or Museum, because it was not anticipated that, after
the essential needs of the Northern Ireland Services were met, any sum would
remain over for purposes such as that indicated by the hon. Member, however desirable they may be. I do not anticipate
that the Estimate formed in 1924 of
essential expenditure, which I may say is
still proceeding, is likely to prove other
than correct.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman pay attention to the last portion of the question-whether the Government is prepared to allocate some money
to the Belfast Art Gallery and Museum to
carry on the work it has to carry on in
Northern Ireland like the National
Gallery in Dublin? Perhaps the right
hon. Gentleman does not appreciate the
point of the question. In his reply he

CRICHTON LOAN SOCIETY, LTD.
4. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Finance whether he has seen the report of
the Crichton Loan Society, Ltd., for
1928; whether it contained provisions for
further increase of the salaries of the two
part-time officials; and can he state how
many increases those officials have received

Mr. BARBOUR: The question put by
the hon. Member would appear to have
been based upon a misapprehension,
namely, that the Ministry of Finance is in
any way responsible for the general supervision of the Crichton Loan Society, Ltd.
This society, being a company limited by
guarantee and registered under the Companies Acts for the purposes laid down in
its Memorandum and Articles of Association, is not subject to supervision on the
part of a Government Department, save
as regards the distribution of any surplus
profits to any charitable object, or, in the
event of a winding-up or dissolution
of the company, to the administration of
any available property among any such
charitable objects.
Mr. HEALY: Does the right hon.
Gentleman tell me that the society is not
liable to any Department of the Government in the matter of audit, in the matter
of the disposal of its funds, and in the
matter of its depositors?
Is the right
hon. Gentleman aware that in 1926 the
surplus of £6 was eaten up by an increase
in salaries to the two officials who work
only about two hours per week, and that
a similar condition of things existed in the
report for 1928? Is he prepared in view
of the fact that the Government has some
responsibility for a company registered in
Belfast to go on sanctioning this condition
of things?
Mr. BARBOUR: No sanction on our
part is necessary.
Mr. HEALY: Will the right hon.
Gentleman tell me what Department of
the Government this society is amenable
or responsible to? If it is not responsible
to the Department of Finance it must be
responsible to something.
Mr. BARBOUR: It is recognised
under the Companies Act.

DISPOSAL OF SEIZED FIREARMS.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
procedure laid down for the disposal of all
firearms which are seized or surrendered to
the police.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Each case must be
decided on its merits, having regard to its
attendant circumstances, but the general
procedure may be set out as follows:-
(1) Firearms seized by, or surrendered
to the Constabulary are taken on Constabulary charge.
(2) Where the circumstances of the
case admit the firearms may be returned to the owners if these are persons
to whom the necessary certificates or
permits can be issued or may be handed
over with the authority of the owners
to persons to whom such certificates can
be issued.
(3) If the arms are worthless destruction may be authorized, subject in the
case of surrendered arms to the consent
of the owners.
(4) Unless disposed of as above, the
retained on Constabulary
arms

SEIZURE OF GUN AT DERRY.
6. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state if
the gun which was seized by the police in
the gaol murder in Derry, in 1921, was
ever forwarded to the Depot at Sprucefield or destroyed by order of the Inspector-General, and, if not, in whose
possession it now is.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The gun to
which the hon. Member refers is possibly
one which was found by the police in an
abandoned motor-car in the vicinity of the
gaol on the morning of the Derry Gaol
murder.
The gun in question, which was in a
very dilapidated condition and would have
been dangerous to use, was broken up in
the usual course.
POSSESSION OF A GUN.
7. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether any inquiries were
made by the police as to how Mr. T. J.
Listin, of Londonderry, came into possession of a gun for which he had got
a permit from the police in 1926.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The gentleman
in question come to reside in Londonderry
from Buncrana in 1925 and applied for a
firearms certificate for a gun which he had
in his possession prior to his arrival in
Northern Ireland.
After full inquiry, the police authority
was satisfied that this gentleman was a
person entitled to be granted a firearms
certificate, and the question as to how he
came into possession of the gun prior to his
arrival in Northern Ireland did not arise.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman satisfied that this is not the
gun that was found outside Derry gaol
on the morning after the murder?
Sir DAWSON BATES: If my hon.
Friend would indicate to me why he has
formed that opinion I shall be delighted
to inquire into it.
Mr. BEATTIE: It is not my own
opinion. It is information that was sent
to me by Derry residents, and I was asked
to put these questions. I am asking
whether the right hon. Gentleman is satisfied that this is not the gun that was
found outside Derry gaol?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am perfectly
satisfied. If my hon. Friend refers to
the answer to the previous question he will
find that the gun was destroyed.
I may
tell him that all the information he gets
is not necessarily accurate.
Mr. GRANT: Hear, hear.
LAND PURCHASE CONFERENCE

8. Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON asked
the Prime Minister whether he will state

The PRIME MINISTER: I was, myself, responsible for the issue of the invitations to the Conference to which the
hon. Member alludes. The Land Purchase Committee of the Ulster Farmers'
Union was invited to meet representatives
of the landlords, because it represented by
far the greatest number of the unbought
tenants. I am unable to state if any

of land which had actually been excluded.
but several were owners of holdings where
exclusion had been claimed. I have no
information which would enable me to
answer the last part of the question.
I can assure the hon. Member that
practically every class of case arising
under the Act was represented.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON:
right hon. Gentleman aware that
means that hundreds of farmers-

this
Yes,

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I would

The PRIME MINISTER: If the hon.
Member is in any way dissatisfied with

that he has just as much right and privilege as I have to call a conference of landlords and unbought tenants, and endeavour
to reach a better agreement. There is
really no more to be said over it, becausé
I was only acting as a mediator and in no

landlords and tenants, who were fully
represented and had counsel present, came
to the present arrangement. Each side
thought it was best to clear up the outstanding difficulties of the Land Purchase
Act. A member of the Imperial Government was present at all the conferences
in order to be quite sure that there was
no pressure brought to bear on either side
in regard to the matter. I prefaced my
remarks when presiding over the party by

to an agreement. We reached agreement,

Mr. BARBOUR: I had started
Friday last to explain to the Committee
that this Financial Resolution is required
to give the necessary financial authority
for the introduction of a Bill to confirm
the Agreement which was reached between
the Imperial Treasury and the Ministry
of Finance on the 14th December last.
This Agreement is supplemental to the
main Unemployment Insurance Agreement of 1926, the purpose of which was
to assimilate the burdens falling upon the
respective Exchequers of Great Britain
and Northern Ireland in connection with
Unemployment Insurance, by providing
that the Unemployment Funds of the two
countries should, from the 30th September,
1925, be kept in a state of parity on the
basis of insured populations. Under this
scheme additional Exchequer grants are
made to the poorer Fund, a substantial
part of the extra burden being spread over
the taxpayers of both Great Britain and
Northern Ireland.
This earlier Agreement was, of course,
necessitated by the fact that the burden
of unemployment in Northern Ireland had
proved to be proportionately much heavier.
than the burden of unemployment in
Great Britain. In the circumstances, the
British Government recognised the fact
that continued maintenance of rates of
contributions and benefits in Northern
Ireland on the same level as Great Britain
-a policy which has been followed by the
Government of Northern Ireland from the
beginning could only be secured by the
imposition on the Exchequer of Northern
Ireland of burdens disproportionate to the
financial resources placed at its disposal
under the Government of Ireland Act, and
the original Agreement was, therefore,
signed under the certain knowledge that
for some time the British Exchequer must
undertake liabilities in the form of direct
Exchequer payments in relief of the
Northern Ireland Exchequer. It may be
of interest to hon. Members to know the
total annual payments thus made to the
Northern Ireland Exchequer under that
Agreement. They are:-
Financial Year.
1925 (6 months)


...
1928 (estimated)
£706,069
879,591
289,750
550,000
I regret to say that present indications
do not tend towards any change in the
relative figures of unemployment in the
two areas, and accordingly it may be anticipated that any proposal to continue the
provisions of the Agreement of 1926 beyond 30th March, 1930, on which date
the Scheme will terminate unless extended
by further legislation, will mean the continuation of substantial payments from
the British Exchequer to the Northern
Ireland Exchequer.
The supplemental Agreement which has
now been reached with the British Government is in effect an undertaking by that
Government to continue this form of assistance as long as the state of unemployment
in Northern Ireland requires it. I need
not emphasise the importance to our
Province of this decision. In return for
this concession, this Government has, on
its part, undertaken to write off over a
period of years the part of the deficit on
the Northern Ireland Unemployment
Fund as at 30th September, 1925, in so far
as it exceeded a due proportion of the
British deficit at that date, the excess
361 Unemployment Insurance-

4 MARCH, 1929
Committee.
being £3,424,434-a debt to the Northern
Ireland Exchequer which, under the
earlier Agreement, was placed in a
Suspense Account. The interest payable
on this Suspense deficit continued to be
charged on the Northern Ireland Unemployment Fund, with the result that it
nas been automatically included in the
amount of the Equalisation Payment towards which substantial contributions
have been made by the British Exchequer.
The Agreement of 1926 did not contain
any provision for the liquidation of this
debt, but the present Agreement provides
for the taking of definite steps to extinguish it over a period of 30 years.
Accordingly, this Resolution and the
Bill which will follow it propose to write
off on 31st of this month a sum of
£424,434. The balance of £3,000,000 is
to be reduced at the rate of £100,000
annually until the whole of the excess
debt has been extinguished.
I am sure that hon. Members will welcome an Agreement which places on a
more permanent basis the present close
relationship with Great Britain in matters.
of unemployment insurance.
Turning now to the wording of the
Resolution itself, the first part confirms
the new Agreement and authorises the payment which would require to be made from
the Northern Ireland Exchequer to the
Great Britain Exchequer in the event of
a reversal of present unemployment conditions as between the two areas.
Part 2 continues the charge on the
Northern Ireland Vote for financial years
beyond the present limit of March, 1930,
in respect of the gross amount of the
equalisation payment. Hon. Members
will be aware that the contribution from
the richer country is brought to account
not as an appropriation-in-aid of the Vote
but by direct transfer to the Exchequer of
the poorer country.
Part 3 deals with the writing off of the
liabilities of the Fund which were placed
in suspense in September, 1925. I beg to
move.

myself I object to this attempt which is
very frequently made in this House to
separate town and country. You cannot
do it. The country benefits from the
prosperity of the town, and the city and
town benefits from the prosperity of the
country, and they are so wrapped together
in connection with all these matters that
you cannot separate them. Take the Derating Bill. There the benefit is very
largely being derived by the farming community, and yet the Exchequer is paying
it all. If, on the other hand, the city
and town workers are getting somewhat
of an advantage by this Agreement surely
it is only right and fair, and is it not
proof positive that you cannot separate
the two interests, because they are really
one.
I am glad that hon. Members on both
sides of the House welcome this Agreement. It may not be all that we would all
wish for, but it is the best that could be
done, and, therefore, I feel the Government did the right thing in making the

the workers here as was given to the
workers in Great Britain. As he raised

saying just this, that that is not so, and I

CLASS VI. No. 2.
AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £1,800 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1929, to defray the expenses of
the Ministry of Agriculture in respect of
Agricultural Education and Research,
Improvement of Live Stock, Agricultural
Development, Agricultural Statistics,
Afforestation, and Diseases of Animals,
including sundry Grants in Aid and certain capital expenditure under 15 and 16
Geo. V., c. 17, s. 13 (1) (N.I.), and 16
Geo. V., c. 4 (N.I.)."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): Under the heading "Agricultural Education" there are
two items-Ulster Dairy School, Cookstown, £500; Greenmount Agricultural
College, Antrim. £2,207. The first
item is for the purchase of 15 additional
acres of land at Cookstown. This additional land lies practically in the middle
of the Cookstown farm. The number of
students coming to this school is increasing, and we found there was not enough
land available when watering cattle in
connection with the
dairy farm.
We got an opportunity of buying this
Supply-
Supplementary Estimates
4 MARCH, 1929
extra land which fitted in with our own.
Before that we had to rent land every
year for watering cattle. We had to
provide more cows so that the dairymaids could be taught their work, and
there was not enough land available.
The expenditure of £2,207 in connection with Greenmount College is for the
purchase of 56 acres of land. When we
took over Greenmount it was only suitable for 25 pupils. We had to enlarge
the place and have now 50 pupils. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). This land which
we have now got we were in the habit of
renting every year. We found a chance
of buying it and purchased it for the
sum mentioned.
As to the replacement of livestock,
this refers to the additional discount contribution payable by the Government to
the banks on loans issued by them. These
loans were originally for one year, but
on account of the depressed state in which
farmers found themselves the loans were
extended for three years. Consequently,
a much larger sum has to be paid to the
banks. The farmers were only charged
2 per cent., and the Government paid
3 per cent. This £1,475 which is asked
for is the three per cent. discount the
Government have paid to the banks on
account of loans to farmers.
As to afforestation, for which £2,900 is
asked, during the past year we have
secured 2,500 acres, and we are purchasing
5,000 more. This money is to go towards the purchase and help on the work.
We planted 800 acres this last year, and
we purpose planting 1,000 more in the
next two or three years.
Since the Ministry began functioning they have planted
four and a half million trees. It will be
agreed that we have done a little bit towards increasing the area planted with
trees.
The next item deals with the Empire
marketing schemes. We are trying to find
some way of helping to market Northern
Ireland produce. We are trying in fact
to find some way by which farmers can
dispose of their produce more satisfactorily
than they are able to do at present. We
are, therefore, providing for a marketing
investigator and produce inspector. The
cost, which will include these officials'
travelling expenses, will be paid for by the
Empire Marketing Board. Another item
is "Economics of small farms in Northern
Ireland." We consider we can show how
small farms can be managed economically.
We pointed out to the Empire Marketing
Board that there were more small farms
in Northern Ireland than in any other
part of Great Britain, and they consented
to pay half the cost of the experiment, our
Government paying the other half. The
amount asked to pay for a costings officer,
clerical assistance and travelling expenses
is £200.

Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE:
Northern Ireland.
