The PRIME MINISTER: I can only
say this: I did all that lay in my power in
the matter. I thought when the agreement was reached and when I saw the Bill
in print that a great service had been performed for the unbought tenants of
Ulster. I think they would have been
foolish in the extreme to have scrapped the
Bill. When one reads it from start to
finish, one cannot but recognise that it
confers very great benefits indeed, benefits that would make me very sorry to see
any party of men banding together in
order to have the Bill dropped by the
British Government. I hope nothing of
the kind will be done. All through the
correspondence that has taken place I
have not seen one single case where any
tenant received as much as twenty-five
years' purchase on the valuation for his
holding; not one single case have I seen,
nor have I had one case brought to my
notice of twenty-five years' purchase being
paid for a holding of the kind. And it is
twenty-five years' purchase on the valuation of the farm and buildings, if there
happen to be any buildings inside the area
which has been pre-empted. The hon.
Member spoke as if this were applicable
to all agricultural land that is as yet
unbought. This is merely applicable to
such parts of agricultural holdings as are
held by the Land Commission to have
potential building value at the present
time, and, accordingly, there will be a
far smaller number than the hon. Member seems to suggest.
However, I have only done my best in
the matter. I was asked by the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. George Henderson) to do it, and I have done it. I
called the meetings. The landlords and
tenants came to an agreement. That
agreement was embodied in the Bill, and
I say that taking it all over, from the
first line to the last, it is a good Bill for
the unbought tenants in Ulster. I wish
better terms could have been secured.
Naturally everybody would like to get
more than this Agreement led to, but I
must say that I thought it was a very fair
agreement. I thought the landlords.
acted very fairly towards the tenants, and
I thought both sides showed remarkable
anxiety to come to a mutual understanding, rather than have any grievance outstanding when the Bill was passed. It is
easy enough for people to say that 15s a
week is not enough for a man and his
wife and it ought to be 20s. It is easy
enough to get someone to come along and
say it ought to be 21s or 25s, and it is
easy to say that twenty-five years' purchase is not sufficient and it ought to be
thirty or forty years. Of course, it is
simple enough to say all that, but the
point is, can you get agreement on it,
and if you cannot, are you prepared to sacrifice the whole Bill? I say,
with all the knowledge I possess, that the
unbought tenants of Ulster would be
foolish in the extreme if they were to
throw away a Bill which, in my opinion,
confers upon them great, and not only
great, but enormous advantages.

the Prime Minister and the Government
had had to get every member of the farming community to agree to this Bill, the

heen perpetuated for all time.
I really do not think that the hon.

by trying to inflame feeling over this

Now, what is the truth with reference

dominion over his property. Nothing
could be further from the truth. We
always must start with this: That in all

in it was that he was the owner of the
agricultural interest. You have only to
look through our Land Acts to see that
all other interests from the time the Land
Acts started were reserved to the landlord.
and one of the matters reserved to the
landlord was this matter of enhanced value
owing to the land having become valuable

Act of 1925 the landlord could have
walked in upon his tenant's holdingunder the Act of 1881-and could have
said: "This holding has a building value.
I am prepared to produce a building
scheme, and you must thereupon hand the
land back to me," and compensation was
given for that.
That compensation given by the Act of
1881 was lower than the compensation
provided under this Bill that is now before the Imperial House-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-infinitely lower.
Therefore, when the Act of 1925 came
along-and I would ask the House to bear
in mind that it was a compulsory Act-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)-the landlord had the right to get his ground for
building under certain circumstances, and
the tenant had the right to get it for
agricultural purposes. When this compulsory Act comes in how are those two
rights to be resolved? The only way in
which they can be resolved is that the
right of the tenant is to remain if there
is no potential building value connected.
with the holding, and the landlord is to
have the right on certain terms to get it
back if it has a potential building value.

the Act of 1903 was a purchase Act.

Oral Answer to Question.
DISTURBANCE IN MEADOW
STREET.
Mr. DEVLIN (for Mr. Kyle) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
is aware that at the recent election held
in Dock Ward a mob gathered in Meadow
Street, broke a window, and kicked the
door of a well-known supporter of the
Labour candidate; whether the police
were informed of certain ringleaders in the
crowd, and what action, if any, has been
taken in this matter to ensure that there
will be fair play at election times in
Belfast.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): On the date of the
recent election at Dock Ward, a constable
on duty in Meadow Street was informed
by the occupier of a house in that street
that a pane of glass 16 inches by 12
inches had been broken by a crowd of
people passing some time previously, but
as the complainant had been in her
kitchen when the damage was committed
she could not tell by whom this had been
done. No complaint was made that the
door had been kicked.
Every effort has been made to obtain
definite evidence as to the persons who
committed this damage, but so far without success.
I am satisfied that all necessary precautions were taken to ensure fair play to
all parties at the election, and such will
continue to be taken in future.
Mr. KYLE: Is it not a fact that the
lady whose house was attacked by this
mob laid an information with the police
and gave the name of one of the persons
who were in the crowd? That has already
been admitted by the sergeant of police,
and surely the Home Secretary should
know?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I can only say
that if evidence had been forthcoming
which would have enabled the police to
bring a prosecution they certainly would
have done so.

Representation. I am going to be very

I am right in saying, however, that the
has been for a long time a general desire
throughout the whole of Ulster to get rid
of that horrible system of P.R. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear, and "No, no").
There has been a general desire, although
of course from time to time it suits to
argue the other way. The reason why
P.R. was first included in the Act of 1920
was at the earnest request of the then
British Government, who, it must be borne
in mind, were setting up a Parliamentary
institution not alone for the Ulster area
but also for the Southern
area. A
balance was arranged between the two
Parliaments and the British Government
with regard to finance and a great many
other affairs, but although Great Britain
refused to entertain for a moment the
idea of imposing P.R. upon its own area
it did for its own reasons believe that it
would be satisfactory to have P.R. in the
South of Ireland and also in the North of
Ireland. The reason for doing that was
a matter that was quite obscure to me at
the time, but strong pressure was brought
to bear upon all the Ulster Members of
the Imperial Parliament to help the
British Government in the great difficulty
in which they were. They said "We want
this done and we ask you to allow it to
be included in the Act of 1920." We all
objected most strongly, and I think that
all the debates if they are turned up in
Hansard will show that no Irishman from
either North or South ever gave a vote in
favour of P.R. But still knowing
the difficulties that the British Government were in at the time, knowing
that Ulster had never failed to
help where it could fairly do so in an
emergency which so greatly affected the
Mother Country, we agreed that
would have this system tested for a period
of three years after which we were to
be free as an institution of our own to
reverse the principle and go back to the
o'd-fashioned British and better system of
single-member constituencies.

[The Prime Minister]
Then Mr. Arthur Henderson, who was
Home Secretary in May, 1924, when the
Labour Government was in power in Great
Britain, refused to adopt a Bill that was
brought in by a private Member or to give
it facilities. He refused either to back it
up or to give it facilities. It was defeated
by 238 votes to 144. That was when the
Labour Government was in power.
Mr. John Humphreys, the secretary of
the Proportional Representation Society,
in October, 1926, said:
It is a matter of profound regret that
in its closing session the Labour Party
Conference, with little discussion, passed
a resolution condemning the proposals
of the P.R. Society.
Sir Reginald Wake, the principal agent
said:
Proportional Representation was an
attempt to load the dice against Labour.
I think, therefore, we may take it that
there is a general opinion, not only
throughout Great Britain and Ireland,
not only in the Tory ranks but in the
Liberal ranks and in the Labour ranks
that P.R. is not a good system for our
requirements here. Not only is it so in
Great Britain and the Empire, but
great many countries abroad have found
it is an impossible system and are doing
away with it.

-because
The PRIME MINISTERit suits the University that that should
not be done. I asked that the matter

there is an entire difference between P.R.
for a University and P.R. for large constituencies such as now exist and will exist
under this Bill in Northern Ireland.
The University voting is done, as everyone knows, by circular, and there is not
the overcrowding of the booths, there is
not the rush of thousands of people to
vote, there is not a long panel of names.
More time can be given. It is easier
amongst the few candidates that are put
up for a University to make a selection
than it is in a large area, where there may
be 20 or 25 names submitted to the electorate. At all events, in this we have
followed the precedent in Great Britain,

P.R. generally throughout the areas, they
have, for convenience sake, adopted it in
the universities, and I do not think it
makes a great deal of difference, but as an
expression of opinion that it should be retained has reached me from the University I think they are quite entitled to do
So. That covers Clause 1 of the Bill, and

Clause 5 deals with the readjustment of
the sum that candidates are permitted to
spend upon elections. It will be observed
that, owing to the size of the constituency
having been cut down from a whole county
with four, five, six or seven members.
naturally the expenses will be slightly
heavier upon the candidate for one of the
smaller constituencies than it would upon
a team of eight all pooling their expenses
in the larger constituencies. Therefore,
and I think this will be felt a convenience
by everybody, I have included the word
"fivepence" instead of the word "twopence" which hitherto, as everybody.
knows, has been the sum allowed.
Mr. COLLINS: That will make the
elections more costly.
The PRIME MINISTER: If it is a
little bit more costly, at all events I feel
very strongly that there should be no
spending of money behind backs at election times. I think it is better to be on
the safe side, and to give a sum which
enables a candidate to fight his election
fairly without any of those stories that
one used to hear of in the old days leaking out afterwards that an election cost.
far more than the amount authorised by
Act of Parliament. I am strongly of
opinion that it is far better to give what
is a reasonable sum for Members to spend
-and that refers to all seats in the House
-rather than to have anything of the
kind referred to occurring. However, if
hon. Members think fivepence is too much.
it is open to discussion. I have taken
very great pains with my calculations, and
I think that for both town and country it
works out at a comparatively reasonable
sum.

think it requires any particular exposition
from me, especially as some of it is more
or less obscure so far as I am concerned.
I am not learned in the law, but I under-
-tand it is to fulfil the other Clauses of

That is the Bill, and by that Bill I
stand, believing, as I said in my opening
remarks, that when the election is overand that is the only time we will be able
to decide whether my words are correct or
not-it will be found to be a fair Bill

beg to move. (Hon. Members: Hear,

am aware that it is the first time a Motion

I am attempting to take an unbiassed
view of the whole situation, and I do say
that the judgment of the Deputy-Speaker
was badly at fault in ordering the hon.
Member (Mr. Healy) to resume his seat,
and then, without provocation, asking the
hon. Gentleman to withdraw from the
House. Had that incident not occurred
the things that followed would not have
occurred, and therefore any intelligent
person is driven willy-nilly to the conclusion that the whole responsibility lies unioubtedly on the Deputy-Speaker. How,
therefore, under these circumstances the
Prime Minister and his colleagues have
the hardihood to attribute the subsequent scenes or enactments to unseemly
behaviour on the part of hon. Gentlemen
on this side is a thing no intelligent person could comprehend.
You have got to look for the cause of
the whole thing, and the cause was the
regrettable error of judgment on the part
of the Deputy-Speaker, because if anyone
deserved a rebuke it was the hon. Member
for North Belfast (Mr. Grant), and I suppose the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Labour (Mr. Gordon), who invariably backs up any interjections of
that hon. Member.
Had the Deputy-
Speaker been discharging his duty impartially, the party rebuked would have
been the hon. Member for North Belfast
Mr. Grant), and the person to have been
expelled would have been the Prime
Minister. Had I been in control of the
situation, the first person I would have
suspended would have been the Prime
Minister, and the second one would have
been the hon. Member for North Belfast.
So long as you have a gentleman whose
bias prevents him from taking an impartial view of the whole situation, so long
will you have the scenes that occurred on
this particular occasion.
Therefore, I say, first, that the
responsibility was on
on the Government
benches and, secondly, there was a regrettable error of judgment on the part of the

judgment was actuated, as suggested by
the hon. Member (Mr. Healy), by partisanship. I put that Hansard into the

escape one or other of two conclusions,
either that the Deputy-Speaker was partial or incapable, or that he was to blame.

ACQUISITION OF LAND AT
STORMONT.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the exact
acreage of land recently purchased at
Stormont for £6,000 and what is the exact
frontage measurements looking to the
main Dundonald Road.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The plot of land to which the
hon. Member refers comprises 21 acres
0 roods 16 perches, with a frontage to the
main Dundonald Road of 534 feet 4
inches.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask the
Minister of Finance whether he considers
it advisable to spend such an enormous
amount of money at this period on land
that is going to be of absolutely no value
to this State. I would like if he would
answer that.
Mr. POLLOCK: The hon. Member
asks my opinion. I I am not a land
valuer, but my ordinary intelligence
Oral Answers
Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
would suggest that it is a good speculation
if speculation were involved in it. But it
was not bought for the purpose of speculation. It was bought because the amenities
of Parliament House would have been
seriously interfered with if that land had
not been acquired. Therefore, I think
the Government were quite justified in
acquiring the property.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister aware
that, as I am given to understand, this
land was on the market at £500 and that
the reason of that was that the land was
so low-lying that sewers could not be put
in so as to make it fit for building ground?
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not know
whether the hon. Member is accurate or
not in the sum of £500 he has mentioned
as the value of the land, but I would remind him that it is only a very small
portion of this land that can be regarded
as low or flat. The main portion is on
rising ground and I have no doubt at all
that, if it were a question of speculation,
in a very short time, with all the lands
being rapidly acquired round that property at Stormont, this land would be
much more valuable than it is to-day.
WHAN CASE-CREGAGH POLICE
TRANSFERS.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of policemen, including the sergeant, transferred from Cregagh barracks,
Co. Down, to other places between May,
1923, and August, 1924; whether it is a
fact that before District-Inspector Allen
was able to discover the conspiracy of the
alleged outrages at John and Agnes
Walker's house, at the Braniel, Co. Down,
the entire personnel of the Cregagh barracks had to be changed; and whether in
fairness to the police stationed at Cregagh
from October, 1921, until January, 1923,
as well as to Head-Constable Slacke,
Belfast, he does not think the time has
arrived to appoint an impartial tribunal
of Members of this House to investigate
the whole circumstances under which Mrs.
Ellen Whan was wrongfully imprisoned.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): One sergeant and
three constables of the Royal Ulster Constabulary were transferred from Cregagh
barracks, Co. Down, to other stations between May, 1923, and August, 1924.
These transfers were made in the ordinary course, and there is no foundation
whatever for the suggestion, which I
strongly deprecate, that these members of
the Force were transferred for reasons in
connection with the case of Mrs. Whan.
The latter part of the question does not,
therefore, arise.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Would
the right hon. Gentleman say the total
personnel in the barracks at that stage?
Sir DAWSON BATES: If my hon.
Friend will give me notice I will answer
that.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman whether he
thinks that justice is being done to this
House and to the public in general by the
case, to which this question refers, being
concealed in the Home Office, and whether
he is now prepared to bring pressure on
the Government to
expose publicly
District-Inspector Allen's report?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would refer
my hon. Friend to the answer given by
the right hon. and learned Attorney-
General (Mr. Babington).
Mr. BEATTIE: Seeing the answer is
unsatisfactory, I will be compelled to raise
this whole matter on the Adjournment.
SILENT VALLEY WATER SCHEME.
3. Mr. W. McMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether it is a
fact that the cost of the Silent Valley
Water Scheme is being paid for by the
ratepayers of Belfast; whether he can
state the total number of workmen employed on the scheme; the number who
are residents of Belfast, the number of
non-residents, and the wages and hours of
employment of those employed.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The expenses
incidental to the Silent Valley Water
Scheme are borne out of the funds of the
Belfast and District Water Commissioners,
which in their turn are derived from the
rates and water charges levied under
statute by the Commissioners, not only on
the City of Belfast but on the other

districts in the Counties of Antrim and
Down which are provided with water by

POST OFFICE TELEPHONE
DEPARTMENT.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that a number
of men engaged in the overhead and underground department of the Post Office
Telephone Department are being paid off,
and men are being brought over from
England who are displacing local labour;
and whether he is prepared to make representations to the proper authorities to end
this practice and give employment to our
workers in Belfast.
:
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) I am informed that at the
beginning of the winter the Post Office
Engineering Department advanced their
programme of telephone development work
in Northern Ireland in order to give as
much employment as possible during the
winter months.
Large sections of this work, together
with the laying of the Ballyhornan cable,
have been completed so far as unskilled
and semi-skilled men are concerned, and
some men have consequently been paid off.
As a result of the acceleration of the
normal development work, however, the
amount of skilled work remaining to be
done is greater than the local permanent
staff could cope with and 20 permanent
skilled men have been temporarily obtained on loan from telephone districts in
Great Britain. I am informed that this
work could not be undertaken by any but
telephone department permanent staff,
and there is, therefore, no question of displacement of local labour.
PREVENTION OF PERSONATION
AT ELECTIONS.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Prime
Minister whether he is prepared to introduce a Bill at an early date to amend the
law of elections in Northern Ireland, with
a view to abolishing personation, as demanded by all fair-minded citizens.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked to reply. The Government have
had this matter under consideration for
some time past, having regard to the representations made to them from time to time
by various public bodies. The principal
difficulty in dealing with the admitted evil
of personation appears to me to be not any
inadequacy of the law or failure to ad-

Committee to inquire into and report on
the whole matter. This I propose to do,
and it will be open to any person with any
practical suggestion to make to come forward and given evidence.

Mr. DEVLIN: Very well, it will

from very important personages in the

Mr. Ramsay MacDonald and Mr. Kevin

MacDonald and Mr. Kevin O'Higgins in

who are very strongly in favour of the application of P.R. to our electoral system.
The first person whom I would quote is

I
thought the noble Lord would have quoted
Lord Birkenhead as an old friend and
colleague in the days of the Ulster revolution, but he seems to have forgotten that
Lord Birkenhead exists or that he has an
opinion in regard to a vital matter of this
sort. In order to remind him I shall
quote his opinion. He says:
We are convinced that only by the
principles of proportional representation
can we secure elections which are completely honest, only by the application.
of these principles can we restore
equality and stability to our representative institutions.
That is the opinion of Lord Birkenhead.
I will take the opinion of another British
statesman who is now, I think, the
Colonial Minister in the Baldwin Government--the Right Hon. L. S. Amery, M.P.
Mr. Amery used to be one of the chief
standard bearers of the right hon. Gentleman. I remember when I was in the Imperial Parliament he was the most violent
-he has somewhat moderated his tone
since or I would say the most vicious of
all the spokesmen of the Prime Minister
and his friends. Surely Mr. Amery's
opinion and Lord Birkenhead's opinion
would have been valuable opinions to give
to the Ulster Parliament in order to justify the attitude the right hon. Gentleman has taken in the change he is making
in our electoral system and machinery.
What does Mr. Amery say? He says:
The existing system is no longer
working even tolerably well, but is tending to lead in an ever-increasing degree
to results which threaten unsatisfactory
and even perilous consequences to the
national life and to our whole free constitutional system. I believe the need
for readjustment in our political
machinery is urgent and now overdue.
and it is for that reason that I cordially and wholeheartedly support proportional representation.
Those are very strong views and one
would naturally think that the gentlemen whom I have quoted, who gave
strength and power to the present Northern Government, who by their political
attitude practically placed them where
they are one would naturally think that

would be considered. One would naturally

My complaint is this, that while this is

of the population in Southern Ireland, we
who are 33 per cent. of the population
in Northern Ireland are treated as if we

those Benches. When the Senate of
Southern Ireland was set up, I believe
that nearly half of the appointments were
by nomination. The Government nominated the Senate, and what did the Government of Southern Ireland proceed to
do? They proceeded to select men belonging to the old Unionist party whom
they regarded as men of character and of
position-landlords, lords who were not
landlords, leading merchants and others--
and they put them into the Senate to the
extent, I think, of one-half of the number
nominated. They were put there to represent the 7 per cent., or perhaps it was
14 per cent. then, of the population of
Southern Ireland.
Take our Senate here. We have not a
single Catholic in the Senate-not one.
Of the Catholic 33 per cent. of the population, there is not one of us fit to sit in
the Senate. I said yesterday, and I repeat now, that in point of intellectual
capacity, of professional skill, and of efficiency in various walks of life, we stand
on an equality with Unionists. We are

Has P.R. protected minorities in this
community? Has it given minorities fair
representation in this House in accordance with their voting power? I say it
has. It was inserted in the 1920 Act by
the Imperial Parliament as a protection
for minorities, and in its actual working
out it has proved that the Imperial Parliament was right when it inserted this
provision in the Act, and that it has
carried out the intention of the Imperial
Parliament. What really is the reason,
as far as one can gather from the speeches
of Members of the Government and hon.
Members opposite, for the abolition of
Proportional Representation? I think the
real reason is that the Prime Minister is
determined to stamp out from this House
any expression of independent political
thought, and he is endeavouring to stereotype the political activities and the political thought of this Province along very
well-defined lines that would divide the
people into two political camps, and that
division would be largely along sectarian
lines. 1 feel that that is the very worst
development that could happen to this
Province, and that development would
place the noble Lord and his party in
permanent power in Ulster, and would
stereotype the political thought of Ulster
for at least a generation to come.
That is the intention of the Government, because their main activities and
their whole political history bears out
that their chief purpose is to preserve
their own lives. This is just another link
in the chain of life-preservation the
Government have indulged in throughout
their political life.
The Government themselves form a
minority in this country, and they are a
very sensitive minority. If there is any
party in the United Kingdom or anywhere
in the world which should have regard for
the feelings of minorities it should be the
party of the Prime Minister. It may be
that the Government will snatch a temporary political advantage from the abolition of Proportional Representation, but
what really is the fundamental foundation of our representative institutions?
Is it not that these representative institutions of ours should reflect as far as possible the views of substantial minorities
in the various areas. While P.R. may not
be an ideal system so far as securing that
is concerned, it certainly is far away in
advance of the old method of single-member constituencies and the single vote.

Under Proportional Representation

It is nearly impossible to follow this

"I, Bernard Hughes, was born in Lisbellaw, and resided there for 35 years
and carried on a tailoring business until

broken. I thought it best to go to my

go to the County Monaghan, and on

I wrote to the D.I. of the "B" Specials,

ignored my letter. The key of the

Union Jack on the house, and next day
gave it to a family from the Free State.

Bernard Hughes."

Oral Answers to Questions.
SEAFORDE GUN PROSECUTION.
1. Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether Mr.
John Magreevey, Moneylane, and Mr.
James Watson, Knocksticken, were fined
20s at Seaforde Petty Sessions, on 30th
December, 1927, notwithstanding the fact
that both had authority to carry shot guns,
which were taken from them by members
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary; whether
such conviction was reversed by the acting
County Court Judge; and whether £5
damages was awarded by the Lord Chief
Justice to these two men in an action for
trover and conversion; whether any disciplinary action has been taken against any
members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and, if so, whether he can state
who were the members of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary concerned.
The ATTORNEY - GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to answer this question.
John Magreevey and James Watson were
prosecuted at Seaforde Petty Sessions on
the 27th January, 1928, for an offence
against the Poaching Prevention Act,
1862. They were convicted and fined as
stated, and the Court ordered that the
guns which they were carrying should be
forfeited. The fact that these men had
authority to carry guns was not material
to the case, and the statute under which
the police acted required that the guns
should be seized.
An appeal was lodged against this
decision, and at Downpatrick Quarter
Sessions on the 20th April, 1928, the
decision of justices was reversed, but the
county court judge remarked that had he
been in the place of the police, he would
in all probability have acted as they did,
and that the constables had reasonable
grounds for suspicion that the appellants
were coming off lands where they had
been unlawfully in pursuit of game.
On the 21st April, a civil action, taken
by Magreevey and Watson against the
constables, was dismissed.
An appeal to Assizes against this dismiss
was upheld by the Lord Chief Justice, who
awarded each appellant £5 damages.
As the constables had reasonable
grounds for suspecting that the offence had
been committed, the fact that the prosecution proved abortive did not justify
disclipinary action being taken against the
constables concerned. It would be quite
improper in the circumstances to make any
reference to the names of the constables
concerned.
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: Could the
right hon. Gentleman tell the House who
paid the £5 damages awarded by the
Lord Chief Justice?
ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
I
The
could not. I presume that the constables
who were decreed were the persons who
paid it. If the hon. Member thinks this
is material and requires any further
answer, if he will give me notice I will
have it inquired into.

like to know in case the constables have

£5.

Mr. BEATTIE: In resuming this
debate on P.R. I think the time of the
House will be well spent in considering
the case put forward by the Prime
Minister in the House this week and also
the case placed before the House in 1927.
I would like before proceeding to ask
where the demand for the abolition of
P.R. came from? What organization or
organizations made a demand to the
Government for the abolition of P.R.?
I have been a constant reader of the Press,
and I have never yet found any such
demand coming from any democratic
body. Therefore, I say that the Government in the absence of that demand had
no right to pursue a different course from
public opinion.
We have been referred to the 1920 Act
which sets out that after a period of three
years the Northern Government have the
right to change the system of P.R., but
there are two words following which
should be considered. I am not a lawyer,
and therefore cannot follow the exact
meaning of the words. Any layman,
however, would interpret those words as
meaning that if a change in the system.
took place the minority have the right to
say it is in violation of the 1920 Act. I
leave that point to my hon. Friends who
are legal men. We are also told that this
change of system is likely to assist the
poor man, that it will take away the
power of the caucuses, and that it is going
to give more independence. Let us see
how the change will affect the working
candidate. As my colleague (Mr. Wm.
McMullen) said yesterday-I am not
ashamed to say it when I headed the

We got the £150, we contested the election, we won that election by an overwhelming majority, and the working-class
representative was able to take his seat
against the wealthy man who spent
thousands in that election under P.R.

straight vote. Let the Chief Whip and
myself fight on a straight vote in East
Belfast.

at an election, and that the voters should
be able to vote one way or the other.

in a triangular contest?
These are some of the advantages of

I have referred, under P.R. the person
elected must get a clear majority of the
votes. Under the old system a candidate
may be elected a Member of this House
who has not a bare majority of the votes.
Under P.R. decently substantial minorities get representation in the House, but

County Tyrone. The next experience we
had of gerrymandering, as some of my

when Proportional Representation was

instead of being grouped in numbers of
five or three, or in other odd numbers
where the majority would tell, the county
was divided into five areas each returning
four members. For the purpose of P.R.
four is the worst possible number to represent any constituency and defeats the
object of the Act. In a four-member area
40 per cent. of the population gets exactly
the same representation as 60 per cent.
The Nationalists in Tyrone had at that
time between 50 and 60 per cent. of the
population, and the areas were divided
into four-member areas so that that preponderance of population would not tell.
and thus the Unionists could secure at
least the same number of members on the
county council as the Nationalists could
secure, but in spite of that the Nationalists secured a majority on the council.
When the first elections were held under
Proportional Representation there were
six rural districts in the county and the
Nationalists secured a majority in Omagh
Rural, Strabane Rural, Cookstown Rural,
and Dungannon Rural-four out of the
six rural districts returned Nationalist
members. Then in 1922 we had the
gerrymander of the Local Government
areas, and in Omagh Rural District, where
two-thirds of the population is Nationalist and where two-thirds of the members
elected under P.R. were Nationalist, it
was so arranged that to-day we cannot
secure a majority there. Under P.R. we
secured 26 out of 39 seats-exactly twothirds but after the gerrymander we
could only secure 18 out of 39 seats-less
than one-half-which shows you how complete and thorough the gerrymander was.
Now we come to this final scheme of
gerrymander. When this Parliament was
set up first if there had been fair distribution of the electoral areas the Nationalists, according to the population, should
have 17 seats in this House instead of 12,
and now even that number of 12 is going
to be reduced, and, as far as we can judge,
the outside number we can elect will now
be ten. I submit that this Bill has been
introduced not for the purpose of simplifying the system of election, and not for
rendering the duties of the electors any
more easy to be discharged, but to perpetuate the power of the ascendancy party
in this House.
a
I have frequently heard right hon.
Members and hon. Members opposite refer
in their speeches to the "nation" to the
"country" or to the "province." I would
like to point out that the Six County area
is not a nation, it is not
country, it is not even a province.
It is the rump of a province, and this is
a modern Rump Parliament. This area
was carved out by England in 1920 to suit
her own purposes.
In America the
United States Government have set up
reservations for Red Indians. England
in 1920 set up a reservation here for her
white parasites, and the object of introducing this Measure is not, as I say, to
simplify the method of election or to
abolish Proportional Representation but
to perpetuate the power of these parasites,
to keep the ascendancy party here in
office for all time.
If I would be in order, I would like in

of the party we are asked to keep here in

ployment insurance agreement. What I
want to draw the attention of the House
to is that the percentage of insured persons recorded as unemployed in Northern
Ireland in 1925 was no less than 24.2almost a quarter of the insured persons
unemployed after five years of the rule of
this Government.

county.

I

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: This
debate has wandered over
a very wide
area and over a very large number of
topics, but I will do the best I can to confine myself within very narrow limits. I
come back to the point at which the last
hon. Member who spoke left off, namely,
the proposition as to whether Proportional Representation should be abolished
or not. After all, that is the main object of this Bill, notwithstanding the fact
that the abolition of P.R. brings as its
necessary corrollary a redistribution of
seats. Although many of the hon. Members who have spoken from the Opposition
benches have suggested that the latter
object was the primary one in the mind
of the Government, I can assure the
House there is a desire to get rid of this
system of P.R. which was imposed upon
this country without its consent.
The system, as has been stated several
times in the course of the debate, is a
cumbersome one, and, as the last speaker
said, it was costly. We all know that.
It is also complicated and in practice it
is not fair. Possibly it is not unfair to
a party, because a party may secure or
may not secure adequate representation
under it. If it does secure adequate representation then it is not unfair. But
I suggest it is unfair to the electorate
because you very often find that in large
constituencies the persons who are elected
do not really represent the people except
perhaps upon one very narrow point.
the risk of provoking comments from hon.
Members opposite may I again quote Mr.
Ramsay MacDonald upon this very point.
I do not quote this because of the position the right hon. Gentleman occupies,
but because of what I consider to be the
good sense that is contained in his statement. Speaking in the British House of
Commons on this question of Proportional
Representation, he said:-
At
The essential characteristic of representation is that the majority which
rules the House and which is responsible for its business is a majority which
has been elected to carry out a programme in accordance with the wishes
of the country, whereas under this
system of individual representation vou
get a man elected by the minority in a
huge constituency upon one point and
he comes here in the interests of that
one point and does not represent his
constituency at all.
I say that that is good sense. Take,
for example, County Down where you
have eight or nine Members. The electors cannot possibly be acquainted with
the qualifications of all those Members.
If they are acquainted with the qualifications of one or two it is as much as
one could expect. The hon. Member for
Down (Mr. P. O'Neill) said that notwithstanding the difficulties of the new
system of election, at the election under
P.R. in 1921 there was only one per
cent. of spoiled votes. Well, I do not
attribute that to the intelligence of the
voters. I think it is a great tribute to
the party machine under which they
voted, and I have not the slightest doubt
that most of the people went into the
polling booth with a list of the people
they were to vote for in their pocket
and with very little knowledge of the
personal qualifications of more than one
or two of them.
When we turn to other countries we
find that P.R. has not met with acceptance in the Dominions. It was turned
down in the Australian Commonwealth
and in South Africa. We have already
been told about New South Wales, and
we find that the two great English-speaking countries, England and the United
States, have not adopted it. Therefore
I say it is an experiment that has been
tried on us and the sooner we get rid of
it the better. I believe that when this
Bill becomes law, so far as the electors
are concerned, P.R. will depart unwent,
unhonoured, and unsung. By the abolition of P.R. there is one small advantage to be gained that is personal to this
House. I have often myself found a
difficulty in endeavouring to refer to a
Member of the Opposition according to
Rules of Debate, and I noticed only yesterday, or the day before, that the hon.
Member for West Belfast was driven to
refer to hon. Members by name. Where

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: I am
not going to argue these questions in detail
at this stage of the Bill. Some of the hon.
Members who sit behind me and some hon.
Members opposite have been arguing with
regard to some of these constituencies.
All I will say is that taking the Schedules
and looking at them as a whole I think it
will be apparent that they are on a greater
equality than the old constituencies, and
certainly on a greater equality than the
constituencies across the water.
Two right hon. Gentlemen opposite
criticized the way in which Derry City is
dealt with. That, of course, will have to
be dealt with in detail upon its merits
when it comes up in Committee. Sufficient
for me at this stage to state that so far as
the general arrangement and plan were
concerned, the city itself was, having regard to population, too small conveniently
to make it into two constituencies and it
was too big to leave it a single-member
constituency. Therefore, certain areas,
all of which are either now in the liberties
of the city, or were at one time in the
liberties of the city, are brought in to give
the city sufficient population to enable it
to be properly given to two Members.
Mr. HARBISON: Explain why part of
the city was thrown out of the city if it
was too small.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: That,
as I said before, is an argument that can
be addressed later on when this Bill goes
into Committee. It is not for me to indicate at present the reason for treating
Derry City in the way in which it is
treated in this Bill. I do not think there
is very much more that I need say now.
This Bill has been very fully discussed.
In the first place, it abolishes Proportional
Representation. Then we have the
Schedules, to which so much objection has
been taken, but I think that when the
matter has been argued out in Committee
hon. Members opposite will see that the
fears which apparently have now fallen
upon them will not be justified. They
will find, I think, that they get adequate
representation under the Bill, and, of
course, there are always, perhaps, opportunities of their representation increasing.
It is impossible to say what may happen.
May I say that having been convinced that
it was necessary and proper in the interests of the community that this form of
Proportional Representation should be
done away with, it would have been
cowardly upon the part of the Government
to evade that issue simply because it was
bound to be stated when they came to
redistribute the seats that they redistributed them in their own interest. Accordingly, I beg to support the Bill which
is now before the House.

Oral Answers to Questions.
PRICE OF COAL.
1. Mr. P. O'NEILL (for Mr. Collins)
asked the Minister of Commerce whether
he can state why his Department has not
taken steps to protect the public from the
heavy losses they have sustained owing
to the excessive charges made for coal in
Northern Ireland; whether he is aware
that the cost per ton for best English
and Welsh coal, f.o.b., in September,
1928, was 15s 4d, and in January, 1929,
15s 6d, and, as the freight on coal between British and Irish ports averages
about 4s per ton, can he justify the retail
prices charged in Northern Ireland for
this essential commodity.
The MINISTER OF
COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): As a result of inquiries
which I have made, I am informed that
the price of best Lancashire and Staffordshire house coal in September, 1928, was
28s 6d per ton, f.o.b., and in January,
1929, 29s 6d per ton, f.o.b. I am further informed that the great bulk of the
domestic coal consumed in Northern Ireland is drawn from those districts.
Welsh coal does not appear to be imported into Northern Ireland for household purposes. Net freights in September, 1928, averaged 3s per ton, and in
January, 1929, 4s per ton.
From the figures which I have quoted
it would, therefore, appear that the hon.
Member's question has been based upon
a misapprehension of the facts.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Colonel Woods]
and, if so, how many girls are so employed,

of the work (1) by the present staff of girl

Mr. POLLOCK: The Government's
de-rating scheme has, this year, necessitated a great deal of additional work in
the Valuation Branch. Three copies of
the Valuation Lists, which contain upwards of 300,000 entries, are required to
be made before next June. If the work
were performed by hand, each copy would.
have to be written separately, whereas,
by the use of a typewriter and carbon
paper three copies of each list can be
produced simultaneously. It is the policy
of the Government in cases such as this
to follow the practice adopted by every
sound business firm by employing typists
for such work, since it can obviously be
performed more economically and expeditiously in this way The legibility of the
finished product is also an important
factor.
Eighteen typists are at present employed on this work, which will cost
approximately £600, and occupy them for
about four months. It is estimated that
30 men would take about five months to
do the work at a cost of roughly £2,000.
I am satisfied that, even allowing for the
unemployment benefit factor mentioned
by the hon. and gallant Member, the
method adopted for carrying out the work
referred to will prove economical. I feel,
however, that it would be against the
interests of the ex-Servicemen to pursue
the matter further, as the additional cost
which the Government is bearing through
its preferential employment of ex-Servicemen is very heavy.

APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL
OFFICER BY BANBRIDGE
URBAN COUNCIL.
10. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether his attention
has been drawn to the recent action of the
Banbridge Urban Council in deciding to
delete from an advertisment relating to
the appointment of a Medical Officer the
words: "Other things being equal, preference will be given to an ex-Service
candidate;" whether the appointment in
question is subject to confirmation by the
Minister of Home Affairs, and, if so,
whether he proposes to satisfy himself that
-other things being equal-a preference
is in fact given to an ex-Service doctor
before confirming the appointment.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am aware that the
Banbridge Board of Guardians at a recent
meeting decided not to make any reference
in their advertisment for a dispensary
doctor to the fact that preference would
be given to an ex-Service candidate.
While the Guardians adopted this particular course, it is not to be assumed that
when they come to make their selection
they will not, in effect, give careful and
sympathetic consideration to the claims
of any ex-Service candidates.
The Ministry of Home Affairs has on
repeated occasions encouraged local authorities, when making an appointment, to
give preference to ex-Service candidates,
but the Ministry has no authority to refuse to sanction an appointment merely
on the grounds that the person appointed
is not an ex-Service candidate.

Fox was reported as not being genuinely

LISNASKEA BOARD OF
GUARDIANS.
14. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether his attention has
been drawn to a letter, dated 17th November, 1928, from his Department, addressed
to the Lisnaskea Board of Guardians, relative to the setting up of a range, bath
and four grates in the Workhouse premises, for which his officials considered
£10 sufficient; whether his Department
approved in the letter of the 19th January
last of £32 10s Od for the same work, with
merely the addition of a press of common
wood valued at £5; and whether, in view
of the recent prosecution and fine of the
contractor, Mr. Bloomfield, can he give
the name of the engineer who has certified
for the items in the various contracts.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The facts of
the case referred to in the hon. Member's
question are as follow:-
On receipt by the Ministry of the
minutes of proceedings of the meeting of
the Lisnaskea Board of Guardians, held
on the 20th October last, it was found that
the Guardians had accepted a tender at a
sum of £32 10s Od for the setting in of
the range, bath and four grates in the
workhouse premises.
The Ministry's technical experts were
of opinion that this tender was excessive,
and that the work referred to in the
minutes might reasonably have been
carried out for, approximately, £10, and
the Ministry wrote, accordingly, to the
Guardians on the 17th November.
It appeared, however, subsequently,
that in addition to the items referred to
above, the work also included the following items:
Setting in of a new copper cylinder;
plastering of the jambs and breast of the
fireplace for the range; setting in seven
Hue fires, and rebuilding of the fireplaces,
the repairing of the hearths where the
grates and fires were set and the fitting
of a linen press.
According to the estimate of the Ministry's Technical Advisers, the latter
article is valued for over £11 and not £5
as suggested in the question. Accordingly, the Ministry informed the
Guardians on the 19th January last that
in view of the further explanation
afforded by the Guardians, the Ministry
had no further observations to make in
connection with the tender which was
accepted.
The works were certified by the Engineer to the Board of Guardians Mr.
Kelly.
Mr. HEALY: Has the right hon.
Gentleman satisfied himself that the
articles enumerated in the reply have
really been supplied to the Board of
Guardians? Is he also aware that the
Chairman of the Board of Guardians is
also the contractor referred to, and also a
prominent supporter of his?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that the contractor who carried out that
work illegally was accordingly prosecuted,
but that does not enter into this
question.
Mr. COOPER: May I ask if there are

to put an end to this illegal contracting?
Mr. HEALY: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that all the influence possible

prevent these proceedings, notwithstanding they have been taken?
Mr. WM. McMULLEN: Is this gentleman still acting in the capacity of Chairman of the Board of Guardians?

15. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister

reason for arresting Mr. Eamonn Donnelly, M.P., whilst coming to address his
constituents in Armagh on Sunday last.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Mr. Donnelly
was arrested at Armagh on the 3rd March,
1929, for a breach of an Order made on
the 16th October, 1924, under the Civil
Authorities (Special Powers) Act, 1922,
which had been served upon him on the
28th September, 1925, and under which
he was prohibited from entering the
County of Armagh.
Mr. HEALY: In view of the fact that

Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon.
Friend really loses sight of the whole point.
The point is that an order was served
upon this individual preventing him coming into Armagh. He chose to break the
law and must take the consequences.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Mr. HEALY: Does the right hon.

Mr. DEVLIN: Is the right hon.

RENTS OF LABOURERS' COTTAGES
IN BALLYMENA DISTRICT.
16. Mr. G. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether it is a
fact that his Department sanctioned an
increase of 25 per cent. on the rents of
labourers' cottages in the Ballymena
Rural District; whether a further increase
of 3d per week is now being charged where
there is a change of tenant, and whether
his Department has sanctioned this further
increase.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The facts of
this case are generally as stated in the
question.
The Rural District Council originally
proposed to raise the rents of the cottages
by 50 per cent., which would have involved
increases varying from 2s 2d to 3s 3d a
month, or 6d and 9d a week respectively.
After having carefully inquired into
the whole circumstances the Ministry intimated to the Council that they were unable
to sanction a general increase of such an
extent as that proposed by the Rural
District Council, but finally authorised an
increase of 25 per cent. all round on the
rents of the labourers' cottages which
meant additions to the rents ranging from
1s 1d a month to 1s 7d a month or 3d and
4d a week respectively.
The Ministry also authorised a further
increase of 3d a week in the case of new
tenancies.

GIRLS EMPLOYED IN MINISTRY

19. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): No duties in
the Belfast Employment Exchange performed by ex-Service men prior to the
date of transfer of services are now
carried out by women. On the contrary,
the concentration of the work of the Exchange in one building at Corporation
Street made possible the substitution of

AUGHNACLOY TAILORS' UNEM-
PLOYMENT BENEFIT.
21. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister

tailors, named Taylor, Hagan, Taylor
and Cahill, of Aughnacloy, have been
refused unemployment benefit on the
ground that they refused to work as farm
labourers when asked to do so by the
referee.
Mr. GORDON: The claims of these
tailors who had been working short-time
for some months were considered, on
appeal, by a fully constituted Court of
Referees which, after carefully considering their representations, came to the
unanimous conclusion that the statutory
conditions for the receipt of benefit were
not all satisfied.

disallowed because of their refusal to
accept farm work.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Insurance (Agreement)
Bill.
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair).
Ordered: That the Preamble be postponed.
Mr. BEATTIE: What was that?
That the Preamble of the Bill be postponed?
The CHAIRMAN: The procedure is
that where there is a Preamble to a Bill
it stands postponed until the Bill and

there should be substantial changes in

CLAUSE 1 (Confirmation of supplemental agreement).
Motion made and Question proposed
that the Clause stand part of the Bill.
Mr. POLLOCK: This short Clause of
two lines is really the essence of the whole
Measure. All the other Clauses are
merely subsidiary or explanatory. This
Clause in effect ensures the continuity—
the unlimited continuity, if I may say so,
of the Agreement entered into in the
year
1926 with the Imperial Government in
respect of the unemployment insurance
scheme. The Agreement was based on the
fact of our insured population being entirely too small to support an effective
insurance scheme, If we compare our
area with corresponding districts in
Britain we find that unemployment is
greater in quite a number of areas in
Great Britain than ours. For example,
in the Clyde district it is 21 per cent.
against our 17, and the Welsh is 22
against our 17.
The original Agreement covered a period
of five years, and as we learned from
our experience in the past we thought it
highly improbable, indeed, that the conditions would so adjust themselves that
we would be able to reach something like
parity, that is to say, that our own unemployment should reach something like
normal conditions on a basis comparable
to that of Great Britain. Under these
circumstances, therefore, we considered it
politic and indeed almost obligatory upon
us as a Government to approach the
British Government with a view to endeavouring to discover the possibility of
making the Agreement permanent.
703 Unemployment Insurance Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee
[Mr. Pollock]
you will see from the Bill now submitted
to the House, we have succeeded in that
application. We are now here presenting
the Bill for the approval of our Parliament.
The Clause is, as I say, perfectly simple.
It confirms the continuity of the original
compact entered into in the year 1926
which was confirmed by a Measure in this
Parliament, and I think, if and when it
is passed, the Bill will ensure that our
workers shall not suffer anything by comparison with those workers of Great
Britain under the unemployment scheme
there. I beg to move.

I want to try to disabuse his mind of it.

I

The reason why I suggest a Committee

opinion. The evil of personation is an
evil which started a very long time ago,

enlargement of the franchise has added
another large mass of voters to the electorate so that at the present time you
have practically adult suffrage over the

electors is so great that it is impossible for
anyone, or even for a very considerable
number of personation agents to have the

walk into a booth and personate somebody
else.

in place of the present measures for the

summary method should
method should be adopted.
Personally I should say I am very much in
agreement with that suggestion myself.
I think at the present time the machinery
for the punishment of personation is, if
anything, much too cumbrous and also
that the penalty is much too high. After
all, at the present time a man who personates merely goes to ask for a vote which
does not belong to him. That is all it is
necessary to prove, and the person is
liable on conviction to two years with hard
labour. If he has taken the declaration
as well as ask for the vote he is liable also

the punishment at the present time is very
severe. I think to a certain extent a very
severe punishment more or less defeats
the object for which it was established,
because juries-and these men come before juries are apt to take a lenient view
of what some people in Belfast look on as
a sporting adventure, and they are inclined to throw out the Bill because they
feel that it is very hard that a respectable
citizen should be penalised with two years
hard labour.
Therefore, I would prefer an easier
punishment, and I would prefer also a
much more summary jurisdiction
established so that a man who personates
should be hauled up at once, and get

was fresh. I do not feel that even if a
summary form of justice were established
we are going to get rid of the evil of personation. For one thing the feeling of

feeling in a community that it is not

representatives do not approve of the

You have only to go to any of the elections that are taking place in the city and
you will see what is occurring. You see
these people standing convenient to the
polling stations. You see them going into
the stations in rags, and they come out
dressed like ladies. They go in like ladies
and they come out in rags.
That is taking
place all day. My father, who I regret to
say is dead, was going to be arrested at
the Baptist Church on polling day in
connection with the election for a member
for the Imperial Parliament. He was
very strong and bitter against a minister
of the Gospel who was actually slapping
people on the back and telling them:
"Go in, you are doing great work today." That shows you to what extent
this outrage is being perpetrated in the
city. It is getting worse every year, and
no effort is made by right hon. Gentlemen to stop it.
What happened at a recent election?
One magistrate actually admitted to me
that had it not been for him a high person
would not have been returned. One of
the agents of the successful candidate sent
out a note at 11-30 o'clock in the day.
He gave it to a boy at the door. The
mother of this boy was working for the
official Unionist, and another son was
working for the Independent, because he
was more enlightened. The boy was told
to take the note over to the tally rooms,
and he brought it to our tally rooms.
We took the note up to the tally rooms in
Cambrai Street, and the hand-writing was

and others. What was in that note? It
told the people in the tally rooms to send
in as many votes between Nos. 1 and 702
as they possibly could. That is the pitch
this thing has got to. The Government
know that they could stop this evil immediately if they wanted to do so. I sup
pose the Attorney-General will say that

Under the Representation of the People
Act of 1850 agents may be appointed by
all the political parties. That was done
for the very good reason that it was
impossible for the police, or for the officers.
who are appointed to act in the booths at
an election, to know all the people who
present themselves to vote. These officers
come not necessarily from the particular
constituency or area in which every booth
is situated, and the policeman who may be
on duty may have come from the other
end of the Province a day or so before he
is posted to that particular duty. Therefore, as it is impossible for a public servant to be acquainted with the individual
appearance of the various persons who
present themselves to vote, the legislature
so far back as 1850 gave to the political
parties the right to have personating
agents, and, as the booth is a place which
under the Ballot Act is held to be secret,
these personating agents have to take an
oath of secrecy before their returning
officer before they enter upon their duties.
That is the reason why these prosecutions are not, in the first place, undertaken by the police, and I might say,
incidentally, so far as ordinary prosecutions are concerned, that they are not
undertaken in this sense by the police
either. The police prosecute upon an
information that is sworn by an individual, supposing he has come forward and
gives evidence of the commission of some
offence he has witnessed and to which he
Personation at Elections
Personation at Elections
12 MARCH 1929
is able to testify. In some cases, of
course, it is perfectly true that the police
do prosecute, because occasionally the
police themselves witness offences being
committed. In such cases the policeman
himself makes an information, but in the
vast majority of cases the information is
made not by the police themselves but by
some individual member of the public.
In these particular cases it is obvious that
the information must always be made by
the personating agent, who is in the booth
under his oath of secrecy, because the
police cannot under our law be admitted
to the booth, and if they were they would
not be of any service there because they
are not acquainted with the various persons who come in to vote.
A remark was made the other day in
this House-I think by some Member on
the other side that this evil of personation had got very much worse since we
have had Proportional Representation. I
think that is true for this reason: When
a person presents himself for election for
a limited constituency it is possible for
him to have a sufficient number of personating agents in the various booths. It
is quite impossible for an individual who
is not backed by a large party organisation to have personating agents in every
booth, say, in County Down, which is an
eight-Member constituency-quite impossible and I think the House will probably agree that a great deal of the increase in personation is due to the fact
that it has been impossible for the parties
to oversee the various booths in these
enormous constituencies. I hope that, if
the House ultimately passes the Bill which
is now before the House, and it ultimately
becomes law, it will go some way at any
rate towards solving this difficulty.
Having given the parties to an election
power to appoint agents, the Act of 1850
then goes on to say that if at any time a
person tenders his vote, or after he has
voted. the agent who is in the booth,
under oath of secrecy, declares to the returning officer, who is the authority, that
he believes and undertakes to prove the
charge of personation against that individual. the returning officer must then
give that person into custody. That is
the way in which these personation charges
come before the courts. The agent challenges the man in the booth.
He says:
"That is not the man he represents himself to be. I undertake to prove that,"
and the returning officer is bound then to
call in a constable and give the man into
custody. But if there is no one there for
the purpose of challenging an individual.
vote then the individual voter gets away
scot free, because it is quite impossible
and would be quite improper to put the
onus of challenging a voter upon the
persiding officer.
After all I have heard of cases, and I
daresay hon. Members opposite have also
heard of cases, when presiding officers have
had persons coming before them and tendering votes when they themselves actually knew that the person tendering the
votes were not the persons they represented themselves to be. But those cases
are comparatively few, and the effect of
giving the presiding officer, who is bound
to be an impartial person, and whose only
duty is mechanical, namely, to record the
vote, and if the man is challenged to see
that the oath is read to the man, and that
he takes it before he gets his ballot paper
-it would be impossible and unfair to
put upon him the onus, which now falls
upon the personating agent, of challenging any individual who might come forward to vote. The number that would be
challenged and that would be brought to
book in that way would be relatively
small, and it would have no real effect
upon the general body of personation.
In 1872 the law was tightened up to
some extent, and it was made an offence,
not only for a man to tender a vote, but
for him to go into the polling booth and apply for a ballot paper in the name of some
person other than himself. The offence
is complete when the man walks into the
booth and asks for a ballot paper in the
wrong name. And even then, if the
agent knows that he is the wrong man he
can challenge him at once and he can give
him in charge at once for an offence under
the Corrupt Practices Act. And he is
then liable to imprisonment, upon being
convicted, up to a maximum of two years
with hard labour.
Now, it is suggested by the hon. Member who moved this Amendment that that
is too severe, and that is one of the matters that will have to be considered by
this Committee when they come to consider this question as a whole, namely,
whether it would be possible to put down
this evil of personation by trying persons
for it summarily, and by a very much less
penalty than there is at present. That

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 13th March, 1929.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
BILL.
Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of
Labour whether, in view of the fact that
the Imperial Government has decided to
introduce an Unemployment Insurance
Bill to extend the transitional period for
another year, he proposes to introduce a
similar Measure for Northern Ireland.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): My right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Labour, has asked
me to say that the answer is in the affirmative.
Mr. GRANT: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask if the hon. Gentleman
can give us any indication as to when this
Bill is likely to be introduced?
Mr. GORDON: I would like notice of
that question.
Vote on Account-Procedure.
Mr. SPEAKER: Before I leave the
Chair, I should like to mention the Vote
on Account, which is the first Order today. Hon. Members will understand
that the Motion for the Vote on Account
is always considered an opportune time
for raising any questions on the administrative policy of the Government which
they desire to criticise-education or anything of that sort. I do not know
whether they have given notice that they
intend to raise any of these matters, but
that is the usual procedure. Of course,
we have nothing whatever to do with the
actual figures, because the Estimates are
not yet before the House.

Now we come to unemployment.
policy of the Government here is clear,

Ulster Architects' meeting? He said

in this city. One would have thought

to the other is a mass of granite and produces the best stone in the world.
All we have to do is to take him to the

new Northern Bank there. Sometimes
we are told by the Minister of Finance

say that this Government is not as rich as
the Northern Bank with all its overdrafts

Office is another example; the Newry

ever erected by the Protestants in Ireland

stopped a considerable amount of it by

Now I come to the question of education. We feel very keenly on this matter.

We
must talk clearly about it. I have said

laws. By giving up this question of religion they could have had everything in
this world. You know the history of
their clergy, how they were forbidden to

left ignorant, insulted by the English and
called the ignorant Irish because they
would not give up this right. Is it fair
of you, because you are a minority in
this country of ours-

Mr. BEATTIE: I want to raise a very
important point here, and I think it will
fall upon you, Mr. Speaker, to carry this
duty out. It is a matter to which I certainly invite your strict attention because
I am not quite sure what the procedure is.
At the Belfast Board of Guardians yesterday a discussion took place which, to my
mind, constitutes a contempt of the Parliamentary rights conferred upon the
Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson-
Bates) and upon the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. William McMullen)
who sits behind me. The contempt is
such that it devolves upon me as an hon.
Member of this House to do what I can
to guard the privileges and liberties of
hon. Members, no matter upon which side
of the House they sit. In reading that
discussion my mind went back to the procedure in the British House of Commons
when members of an outside board had
ridiculed and criticized Members of Parliament, and Mr. Speaker at the first opportunity summoned those members to the
Bar of the House to answer for their
conduct.
The Minister of Home Affairs has the
right to the protection of this House and
to get any information necessary when
questions are put to him. I understand
that in this instance he pursued that
course and that his name along with the
name of my hon. Friend (Mr. William
McMullen) was attached to the document
requesting information. What I understand to be unparliamentary language was
used and their names were drawn into
contempt in a manner against which this
House should protest. I want to ask is
it not a duty that now devolves upon you
to call upon those who were guilty of this
conduct to appear at the Bar of this House
within a given period so that you may
give them to understand that the liberties
and rights of Members of this House are
such that no member of any outside board
can criticize them in the manner in which
it was done by gentlemen named Mr. John
Wilson and Mr. McKegney, of the Belfast
Board of Guardians. I think it is a
shame and a disgrace that any Minister
or any Member of this House should be
retarded and handicapped in the execution
of his duties in accordance with the powers
conferred upon him by this House as a
whole. I want that expressed from the
Chair, and I want your opinion as to
whether it is your duty to call upon these
men to answer for their conduct.
Mr. SPEAKER: I certainly should be
the last to say that it is not within the
right of anybody to criticize Members of
Parliament. I am afraid Members of
Parliament by reason of their very position are subject almost to more criticism
than any other body of people-and quite
rightly. It is part of our constitution.
We are here to be criticized.

Mr. BEATTIE: That is not the point.
My point is that the Minister of Home
Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates) wrote to the
Board of Guardians, which is subject to
his control, for certain information in
answer to a question put by my hon.
Friend (Mr. William McMullen). Both
these Gentlemen have Parliamentary
rights, but because of their acting on those
Parliamentary rights they have been subjected to ridicule and abuse by a public
board and publicity has been given to the
matter throughout Northern Ireland. In
my opinion it is a violation of the privileges of Parliament and they are bound
to have the protection of the House.
Mr. SPEAKER: Before I can come to
any decision I must see the words complained of. The only thing it might be
would be a breach of privilege. In that
case the proper course is to move a Resolution declaring it to be a breach of
privilege. If the House agrees that it is
then the matter is referred to a Committee
of Privileges.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am aware of that.
Mr. SPEAKER: The usual course is
that the Committee of Privileges, unless
it is a matter of very extreme importance,
generally let it lapse. Summoning
people to the Bar of the House of Commons is very unusual. Although technically it can be done, the common sense of
Parliament generally decides that it is
undesirable. In this particular case I
think the hon. Member must be careful,
if he is going to suggest that other
boards should not criticize this House,
that this House does not criticize other
elected bodies. It must be either one
way or the other.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am not going to restrict the criticism of any board if it is
fair. But if the Home Secretary writes
to a board for information to be given to
this House, and an hon. Member has
asked the Minister for that information
I think it is the duty of that board to
give that information without criticism.
That is their duty to this House. They
have challenged the right of Parliament
to ask questions such as the question put
on the Order Paper by my hon. Friend.
From that point of view it is a question
of privilege I am raising.
Mr. SPEAKER: I think the best plan
would be for the hon. Member to raise

But, as I say, that is a very extreme
