14 MARCH 1929
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 14th March, 1929.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
RECOVERY OF RENT ANNUITIES.
1. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Finance if he can state the total number
of civil bills issued in County Fermanagh
for rent annuities due within the past six
months; whether the rents were accepted
last March without legal costs, and what
was the reason for the change this year.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The total number of civil bills
issued in County Fermanagh for arrears
of Land Purchase Annuities in the past
six months, that is to say, for the Quarter
Sessions which are about to be held, is
873.
With regard to the remainder of the
question, it is not correct to say that
arrears were accepted last March without
legal costs. The practice is that as soon
as the civil bills are issued, payments of
arrears are not accepted without costs
being also paid, but tenants in many cases
wait until the bills are about to be issued
and then make their payments at the very
last moment. This, for instance, happened last year. This year, however, a
large number of the defaulters failed to
realise that Easter, and consequently
Quarter Sessions, would come earlier than
usual, and these last-minute payments
were not made; they must, in consequence,
pay in addition to the outstanding annuities the costs incurred in connection with
the issue of the civil bills.
The altered situation in which the defaulters find themselves this year is, therefore, due to Easter being a movable feast,
an occurrence for which, I believe, the
early Christian Church is responsible, and
certainly not my Ministry.
Mr. HEALY: Does the right hon.
Gentleman think that it is helpful to enter
a plea of this kind-a semi-theological
plea about the incidence of Easter; and
would it not be far more practical if the
right hon. Gentleman would carry out the
arrangement that he had in force last year,
enabling the people to pay the annuities
a week or two later? The right hon.
Gentleman's Department is not exactly
like the laws of the Medes and Persians,
unchanging and unchangeable.
EX-SERVICE MAN'S LICENCE IN
COMBER.
2. Mr. LEEKE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
James Griffith, a time-expired Serviceman, disposed of part of his pension to
enable him to purchase licensed premises
in Comber; whether this man was compelled, through an error on the part of
the police, to relinquish the wholesale end
of his business; whether, after he had disposed at a sacrifice of his stock and
machinery, the police again called and
informed him that he could resume business; and whether, in view of this error
on the part of the police, the Govern:nent
will award compensation to the trader.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am familiar with
the facts of this case, but I cannot agree
with the complexion put upon them by
the hon. Member. Mr. Griffith in February, 1925, held a wholesale and retail
licence in respect of his premises at
Comber. The police, acting upon a strict
interpretation of Section 6 of the Intoxicating Liquor Act (Northern Ireland),
1923, informed Mr. Griffith that in
carrying on a wholesale and retail liquor
business in the same premises he was committing an offence against the Section referred to, which prohibited the carrying
on of a mixed business unless structural
separation between the two businesses was
affected, and as a result Mr. Griffith decided to surrender his wholesale licence.
The intimation conveyed to Mr.
Griffith, which was based upon the advice
of the Law Officers, could not, of course,
be regarded as a binding ruling as the
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
point was one which could be decided by
a court of law alone, and it was open to
Mr. Griffith to test the matter, if he so
desired, in court.
The question of law involved was at the
same time doubtful, and when the matter
was further considered later in the year,
the Law Officers advised that in the ab
sence of any judicial ruling to the contrary, a less rigid interpretation of the
Section referred to might safely be
adopted, and that such cases might be
regarded as not constituting an infringement of the Section. Mr. Griffith was
informed accordingly.
As I have already pointed out, it was
open to Mr. Griffith to challenge the original view as conveyed to him by the
police, and to have the matter definitely
established by a decision of a court.
The Government cannot accept any responsibility in the matter.
I may add that provision was made in
Section 1 of the recent Intoxicating
Liquor Act to put the matter in question
beyond dispute.
Mr. LEEKE: As the Minister of
Home Affairs has practically admitted
that it was an error on the part of the
Government's servants that wrecked this
man's business, surely in all fairness he
will see his way to give him some compensation? Would the Minister also
apply for the records in the barrack books
in this matter which are kept in the barracks, and recorded at the time the incident occurred?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot admit that the Home Office or the Government are responsible in this matter. They
had taken the advice of the law officers.
Of course I may remind the hon. Member that the law officers only give their
interpretation of the law as a matter of
courtesy. The only tribunals that can
give a final decision as to the correct view
of the law are the courts which are open
to this gentleman in the ordinary way.
Mr. HEALY: Can the right hon.
Gentleman say whether his Department
is prepared to rectify the error of the law
officers in the way the Prime Minister
rectified the error in Land Purchase.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not admit
that the law officers are in error in the
slightest degree.
Mr. GYLE: Might I ask the right hon.
Gentleman how it came that the strict
interpretation of the law as given to this
gentleman by the Home Office was found
out to be wrong, and under these circumstances would he not reconsider the case?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid
my hon. Friend is under a misunderstanding in regard to the obligations of the
Home Office. The Home Office are only
able to give the benefit of their views
the views of the legal officer who interpreted the case for them. At the same
time they are only members of the profession, and the only tribunals that can
give a final decision in regard to any
matter are the courts, and this gentleman
had a right to go to the courts to test the
matter.
Mr. HEALY: Cannot the right hon.
Gentleman appoint law officers who are
competent advisers?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do resent the
suggestion that the law officers are not
competent.
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not think it was
made very seriously.

LAND PURCHASE IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
Mr. KYLE: I want to ask the Prime
Minister a question of which I have given
him private notice. It is: To ask the
Prime Minister whether he can state the
result of his visit to London in connection
with the unbought tenants of Northern
Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER (who was received with cheers): I am pleased to be
able to inform the House that as a consequence of meetings which I was able to
arrange on Monday last with representatives of the landlords and with the Land
Purchase Committee of the Ulster Farmers' Union, followed by a visit to London, the House of Lords amended the
Northern Ireland Land Bill, 1929, on
Third Reading, shortly to the effect that
25 years purchase on the rateable value
of the holding has been increased to 30
years in the case of land claimed within
10 years, and 30 years has been increased
to 35 years in the case of land claimed
after the expiration of 10 years from the
date of the passing of the Act; and where,
before the passing of the Act, any buildings have been erected upon the holding
or the part thereof comprised in the
notice, the tenant or the landlord may at
any time before the expiration of the
notice apply to the civil bill court to determine the amount of compensation to
be paid in respect of such buildings, and
the civil bill court shall determine
the amount of compensation by reference
to the increase in the value of the holding fairly attributable to the buildings;
and in that case the amount of compensation shall be calculated according to the
provisions of the last preceding paragraph
in respect of the holding (or the part
thereof comprised in the notice) apart from
such buildings, with the addition thereto
of the amount determined by the civil bill
Breach of Privilege

[The Prime Minister]
court as compensation in respect of such
buildings.
Any person aggrieved by any decision
of the civil bill court under this Section
may appeal to the Court of Appeal in
Northern Ireland, and the decision of
that court shall be final.
I wish to avail myself of this opportunity of paying a tribute to Lord Desborough, Lord Carson, Lord Buckmaster,
Mr. D. D. Reid and the Home Office
for their kindness and helpfulness in embodying these further agreed terms in the
Bill.

Question of Breach of Privilege.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member for

not know whether he proposes to raise it
now.
Mr. BEATTIE: I have considered the
position that you put up to me last night
as to a violation of the privileges and
liberties of Members of this House. There
was especially a violation of those privileges in regard to two hon. Members.
That being so, I think the statement contained in the "Belfast News-Letter" yesterday morning should be submitted to the
Committee of Privileges and leave the
question to them to decide whether it is
necessary or not that the matter should
be carried forward to this House. In
justice to the two hon. Members we should
refer this matter to the Committee of
Privileges, and I beg to move accordingly.
Mr. SPEAKER: That is one way of
dealing with the matter, but I think the
hon. Member ought to give the House the
quotation. I asked him last night if he
could let us have the words complained of.
It is essential to give what the breach of
privilege is.
Mr. BEATTIE: I complained of the
interference of the Guardians in regard to
information sought from this House. The
other complaint was as to the interference
of the Guardians with Members on this
side of the House who, because they asked

breach of the privileges of Members of this
House.
Mr. SPEAKER: That may be, but I
did ask the hon. Member yesterday evening if when he raised the point to-day he
would read to the House the words complained of. I do not know if anybody has
got the words complained of.
Mr. BEATTIE: I understand that
gave me liberty to raise the question on a
Motion and present the Committee of
Privileges with the statement contained
in the newspaper.
I also understood that
the Home Office would be asked to give a
detailed report of the meeting as it was
submitted to that Department. I think
that was the procedure you advised me to
pursue, and that is why I am pursuing it.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Perhaps I
might be allowed to put the House in
possession of the real facts of the case.
My hon. Friend (Mr. W. McMullen) put
a question to me to ascertain certain information. To enable me to get that information I had of necessity to apply to

supplied to me. I quite admit that according to the newspaper reports one
does not attach too much importance to
what appears in the Press-(hon. Members: Oh!)-there was a certain amount
of criticism. I can readily understand
that certain members of the Belfast Board
of Guardians said this added to their
labour. At all events I received the in-

seen
Mr. SPEAKER: I have often
these things raised in another place, and
the invariable custom is for the Member

from any other source. As a matter of

I did ask the hon. Member (Mr. Beattie)
to read them out. I take it that the

Mr. J. Wilson said he desired to protest against any Members of Parliament
being allowed to ask questions regarding relief, with the result that the Ministry had to obtain from the Board detailed information on individual cases.
He questioned the right of the Ministry
to expect such information, and declared that the Board of Guardians was

Are these the words?

attack against my hon. Friend (Mr. Wm.
McMullen) in another newspaper, not the
"Belfast News-Letter." From inside information I have received that is not a

it
Mr. SPEAKER: I am inclined to think
if this is a breach of privilege you can
deal with it by Motion in the House.
We can leave it at that if it is thought
to be a breach of privilege. As a matter
of fact as regards this particular question.
which was asked by the hon. Member
(Mr. W. McMullen) I was doubtful myself about it and I held up the question
for a day, because I was not sure whether
was within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Home Affairs to ask about the
individual relief paid to individual per-
I thought that might be a matter
entirely for the Guardians, but on making inquiries I ascertained that owing to

last Session, the Ministry has certain
jurisdiction-more jurisdiction than it
sons.
would have apart from that Act, and
apart from the fact that Belfast has been
declared a place of exceptional distress.
Therefore, I came to the conclusion that
the question was allowable, and I allowed it to be asked. The only point
I can see that might possibly be a technical breach of privilege was where this
gentleman stated he protests against any
Members of Parliament being allowed to
ask questions regarding relief. That, of
course, is a technical reflection on me for

up the precedents and I think if the hon.
Member really wishes to press it to the
extent of a Motion he can do so. Possibly it is a technical breach of privilege,
and if the hon. Member really does wish
to press it-it is not often wise to press
these too much—I suggest that the House
pass a formal Motion and leave it at that.

tion originating in what is called the

formal stage. It is never discussed in

The PRIME MINISTER: In rising
to move the Motion which stands in my
name, I should point out that it will be
in the common knowledge of the House
that so far we have been able to get
through our proceedings without adopting
the system of putting down what is commonly known as a guillotine Motion, but
the Government felt that in regard to a
Measure such as this large and comprehensive Bill, to which a Second Reading
has been given, it would be very difficult
for Members on all sides of the House
unless at the very beginning they knew
exactly day by day what our proceedings
would be and when they might make
arrangements to rise. Complaints have
been made from time to time by the
Opposition that they had difficulty in
finding out what the programme for the
forthcoming week or month was, and I
think, therefore, they will welcome a timetable of this kind, which will lay down
exactly when we begin certain parts of the
Bill, and when the House can be expected
to rise. In introducing a measure of this
kind it may interest the House to know
that the guillotine had its origin in the
first instance in the Liberal party on the
other side of the Channel. It was they
who first brought forward the guillotine
for first-class Measures.

It was instituted for the purpose of getting rid of kings and tyrants, and it is a

Gentleman will learn later on, because I

This is the last tyrannical action of an

They have been for eight years now in
power, and the result of their work
during that period has been almost industrial ruin and commercial bankruptcy,
a dissatisfied populace, and a widespread
resentment against the existence of the
Government of Northern Ireland. That
constitutes their position to-day in the
public life of Northern Ireland. Now he
tells us and I agree with him—that this

it is the finest accomplishment of the
Government. They propose now, tottering

the minority of the essential right which
was conceded to them by the English

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
Amendment that is before the House
relates to the time that is being allotted
to the Committee stage, and it is objected that five allotted days are not
sufficient for the discussion of the Bill.
I submit that five allotted days are
sufficient for the discussion of this Bill.
Let me for a moment refer the House
to the Table that is appended to the
Motion. The first allotted day is devoted
to Instructions and Clause 1 of the Bill,
and if the House will turn to the Instructions and Clause 1 of the Bill it will be
seen at once that Clause 1 deals with
the alteration of the method of voting at
contested Parliamentary elections, that it
does away with the system of P.R., and
substitutes for it the system of singlemember constituencies. That matter has
been already debated on the Second Reading of this Bill, and, notwithstanding
that, for the discussion of this matter of
principle which is involved in the very
forefront of the Bill, and which is embodied in Clause 1, there is allowed a
further six hours. For all the discussion
of the Committee stage of this Bill there
are 39 sitting hours of the House allotted.
Then we come to the second allotted
day, which has been criticised by some
hon. Members on the other side of the
House, Clauses 2 to 8, new Clauses, and
Articles 1, 2 and 3 in Part I of the First
Schedule, are allotted two hours. Might
I point out to the House that once the
question of principle in Clause I has been
decided, as it has been already decided
upon the Second Reading of this Bill, all
these other matters are ancillary to that
decision?
Clause 2 deals with the distribution of
seats. It merely says that the areas
mentioned in the Schedule shall be the
areas to return the Members to the new
Parliament. The arrangement of the
polling districts is provided for by Clause
3. Then the returning officer and the
place of election are provided for in
Clause 4. The alteration of the scale of
election expenses is provided for in Clause
5, and minor amendments of election laws,
which are purely ancillary, are provided
for in Clause 6. Then we come to Clause
7 dealing with the commencement of the
Act and first elections. All these matters are purely formal, except in so far as
they may be revised in matters of small
detail, and are dependent upon the main
principle, which is contained in Clause
1 of the Bill.
I submit that under those circumstances
the time that the Government have
allowed for the discussion of Clause 1,
and of Clauses 2 to the end of the Bill, together with the three Articles in the
First Schedule, is amply sufficient. It has
been suggested that the matters contained
in the First Schedule would necessitate a considerable amount of discussion.
That first Schedule only deals with formal
matters; there is no matter of principle
involved. It simply says that the names,
contents and boundaries of the Parliamentary borough and county divisions shall
be those specified in Parts 1 and II of this
Schedule. There is no question of principle involved in that, and when you come
to the Schedule setting out the various
Parliamentary boroughs and Parliamentary counties then matters arise upon the
areas of those particular divisions.
The result is this, that for the discussion of the question of principle, and for
the discussion of the various areas which
are included, there are in all 39 hours
allowed in this House. It has been stated
by the hon. Member for North Belfast
who moved this Amendment (Mr. Kyle),
that it was unprecedented and unconstitutional to provide that at the conclusion
of the Committee stage of the Bill the
Chairman should report the Bill to the
House without Question put, as set out
in the third paragraph at the top of
page 3 on the Order Paper. This method
of dealing with the conclusion of the Committee stage is not without precedent or
unprecedented, because in the last Local
Government Bill in the Imperial House
of Commons, when a Motion allocating
time for the discussion of that Measure
was passed, a similar Clause was put into
the Instructions, namely, that at the conclusion of the Committee stage the Chairman should report the Bill to the House
without Question put.
So far as constitutional practice and
precedent are concerned, this is a matter
which has often been dealt with in a precisely similar way.
The hon. Member
who seconded this Amendment said that
argument was to be stifled. I should have

Oral Answers.
19 MARCH 1929
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 19th March, 1929.
The House met at Three of the clock.
The Clerk at the Table informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
Speaker from this day's Sitting.
Whereupon Mr. Moles, the Chairman
of Ways and Means, proceeded to the
Table, and, after Prayers, took the Chair
as Deputy Speaker, pursuant to Standing
Order.
LOCAL BILLS.
Belfast Water Bill.
Resolved: "That the Chairman of Ways
and Means and Mr. M'Bride be appointed
by this House to join with the Members
of the Senate appointed by that House to
constitute the Joint Unopposed Committee on the Belfast Water Bill."-(The
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Education-Mr. Robb).
Newry Urban District Council and Newry
Port and Harbour Trust Bill.
Resolved: "That Mr. Grant, Mr Crawford, and Mr. Healy be appointed by this
House to constitute the Joint Opposed
Committee on the Newry Urban Disrict
Council and Newry Port and Harbour
Trust Bill."-(The Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education).
Oral Answers to Questions.
LABOUR EXCHANGES AS HIRING
1.
FAIRS.
Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr.
(for Mr. W.
McMullen) asked the Minister of
Labour whether, in view of the existence
of Labour Exchanges in all important
parts of Northern Ireland, he will consider the advisability of utilising this
machinery to supersede the hiring fairs
which are held periodically in many parts
of the Province.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The Employment Exchanges
of the Ministry of Labour are available
for farmers and farm servants as for all
other classes of the community, and
einployment is found each year through
their agency for considerable numbers of
agricultural and other workers.
It is the Government's policy to develop
rather than restrict in any way other
opportunities for obtaining employment
which are available.
Mr. KYLE: The right hon. Gentleman knows of this iniquitous principle of
hiring men like cattle, and what the hon.
Member for West Belfast is asking him to
do is to extend this availability of Labour
Exchanges so that farmers might employ
labourers through the Labour Exchanges
rather than by this brutal policy.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have already stated
that the Labour Exchanges are available
for farmers and farm workers and are
being availed of by both.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Would he give
an undertaking to use the machinery of the
Ministry of Labour in order to displace
the hiring fairs?
Mr. ANDREWS: We are using the
machinery of the Ministry of Labour to
obtain work for farm labourers. It
would require coercive legislation to do
away with hiring fairs, and the Government are not in a position to undertake
that at the present time.
VALUE OF LAND AT STORMONT.
2. Mr. W. McMULLEN asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state if
it is a fact that the land in the vicinity of
Stormont has increased in value since the
acquisition of the site for the Parliament
buildings; whether this is due to the expenditure of public money, and, if so,
what steps the Government propose to
take to secure for the public the increased
value which is being created by community effort.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): There is reason to believe that
land in the vicinity of Stormont has
increased in value during the past few
years, but I am not in a position to determine whether such increase is due to the
normal growth of the city, or to the
expenditure involved in the erection of
the Parliament Buildings. It is not the
intention of the Government to take the
action indicated in the last part of the
question.

Mr. BEATTIE: I am very glad I was
in the House, because this might have
been passed through too swiftly. This
Bill gives an opportunity to Members on
this side and also on the other side to
bring forward various questions that
arise on the different Estimates. I think
there is not a thing on the Estimates that
cannot be touched. There is one very
important thing I would like to refer to
right away, and it deals with a question.
of policy affecting the prestige of the
Public Accounts Committee, which was
appointed by this House, and also the
prestige of the Minister of Finance. I
think that a Committee appointed by this.
House should be given some consideration by the Cabinet. The Cabinet has
overruled the Public Accounts Committee, and also the opinion expressed by
the Minister of Finance in regard to the
locomotion allowances for county and
district-inspectors of the R.U.C.
For the guidance of the House I will
read a quotation from the Report dealing with the Appropriation and Consolidated Fund Services Accounts for
1927-28, and hon. Members will perhaps
be able to follow what the action of the
Cabinet really means. It is under
Class III-Vote 2-Royal Ulster Constabulary, and it says:-

their 1927 Report (dealing with the

of the Public Accounts Committee.
sum of £160 was to disappear, but where

quarters allowance. We find that the

When the question is asked why the £80

head-
"Headquarters allowances." The same

I want to ask the Cabinet why they set
up a Committee to inquire into and investigate the position of affairs as it exists.
in the R.U.C., and especially as regards
their grade of officers? We are asked to
make recommendations, and yet when we
find there was a possibility of the expenditure being reduced to meet the needs and
requirements of the taxpayers' purse the
Cabinet step in and say, "No, if you
abolish the locomotion allowance of £160
you will have to include it under another
heading, and perhaps when the public see

this description-deceiving the Public
Accounts Committee, deceiving this
House, legalising daylight robbery, and
themselves taking part in the robbery.
This action of the Cabinet calls for the
condemnation of this House, and I want
an answer from the Cabinet as to why
they tried to get this £160 a year put
under the heading of headquarters allowances.

Mr. BEATTIE: Well, he should be
here. I believe the Minister of Finance
is right, and I believe that the opinion of
the Public Accounts Committee is right.
We have seen officers who had cars lying
up for two years with never a wheel
turned, and yet they were getting £160
a year for having those cars. I will give
you an illustration. A sum of £30 was
paid for a certain car so that the officer
if he were challenged and asked where was
his car, he could say that it was in the
garage. That officer received £165 for
that car, and while he had it it was sitting
in the Musgrave Street yard at the expense of the taxpayers.
There is another thing I want to call
attention to. I think that drastic steps
have got to be taken regarding the cost of
the present Government. I am not going
to pursue the policy of hunting one man.
I am going to take them collectively and
deal with them collectively. I say that
the expenditure under the heading of
Cabinet Offices, Hospitality and Parliament Buildings has got to come down by
50 per cent. immediately. We have such
exhibitions of squandermania since I
came into this House that I am not surprised at anything the Government may
do. In the upkeep of the present Cabinet
and the various Ministers, as well as their
respective staffs, we have a very heavy cost.
I claim that there is not sufficient work
for them to do. If they were engaged in
any other industry they would be put on
short time, and their wages would be
reduced accordingly.
We have the most costly head in the
world when we consider the acreage and
He is
population of the Six Counties.
more costly indeed than the King of England. People might think that we are
rich in abundance, but if they looked at
the number of unemployed and at the
state industry is in they would come to
the conclusion that if there is any money
in Northern Ireland it is not with those
on the small side of the House, but with
the people who have large purses, and
very little of it is extended to the unemployed and distressed people at the
moment. Unemployment seems to be
coming down rapidly. It has now got to
17 per cent. But that is one of the tricks
of the trade, I presume, on the part of
the Minister of Labour-to bring down
the figures of unemployment to such a
position that an atmosphere will be
brought about indicating that all is well
in this land of ours. I would like to
think everything was well. I would like
every man, woman and child to be secured
in the Six Counties. I would like to
think there were no hungry men, women
and children. But that is not the position. The position is that there are
thousands of unemployed walking the
streets who have been denied the right of
unemployment benefit.
There are thousands of widows and
orphans who have been denied the right
to widows' and orphans' pensions, and
there are old people who have been denied
the right to old-age pensions. I think
that when those thousands of people are
upon the verge of starvation in our midst
all is not right with this land of ours.
I am going to make a suggestion to the
Government, and I hope it will bear
fruit. The Prime Minister says that a
reduction in Cabinet Offices would only
amount to about 3d per head of the people
in regard to taxation. Assuming we
took that from those who have more than
they require and gave it to those who are
in need we could bring in somewhere
about £30,000 a year more to assist the
destitute poor who are now crying out for
help from the different boards throughout Northern Ireland. That would be
one good way of spending this money, and
it would be a way that I would not object
to.

it is dealt with according to Act of Parliament; and if you write to him about an

Where is the human touch? Gone.

There is another point I wish to refer

Act. I do not wish to develop that to

been done. I do not wish to repeat it
here, but I do not think it would be unfair that all tenants and all landlords
undealt with after the 28th May next

they are entitled to with a remission of

Mr. HEALY: I have been speaking
to this House before regarding the Colwyn
Committee. I think the basis of the
Colwyn Committee has been one of the
most misunderstood matters in this House.
The original idea was that the Northern
Parliament should contribute to the
Imperial Exchequer a sum of £8,000,000.
The Colwyn Committee adopted a policy
of whittling that down, and it has gone on
from year to year from that date.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Mr. HEALY: To-day the position is
this, that so far from paying the Imperial
Exchequer anything in the way of a contribution this Parliament is actually receiving money from Great Britain.
Mr. POLLOCK: Are you not glad?
Mr. HEALY: Yes, I am perfectly
satisfied on that head, but what I do not
like about it is that hon. Gentlemen should
call on the "Daily Mail" and other Imperial
organs and tell them we are paying a
magnificent contribution when, the fact
remains, we pay nothing. I like to be
honest about the matter. I like honest
dealing in this matter whether it be from
the Government or Imperial side. On
these Estimates year after year, whatever
they may be, we always see supplementary Estimates, so that in reality the
figures as given here are not real at all.
Under the 1920 Act certain guarantees
were given to the minority in the North-
East, and just as the Imperial contribution has been whittled down and a coach

guarantees been cast to the wind, and
onwards you have walked deliberately
through the provisions of the 1920 Act,
whether it applies to the financial side or
whether it applies to those minorities over

Recently the Minister of Finance, with

bankrupt to the extent of £3,000,000.

the attention of the House to one of my

I now want to take the opportunity of

served almost five years overseas-I do not

their iniquitous test scheme last year,

Appropriation Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
outside Parliament-that I have no objection whatever to decent, and even
generous, salaries being paid to men in
positions of public trust. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I do not believe in
cheap labour, whether it be at the top of
the social ladder or at the bottom. I
believe that if men render public service
they should be well paid for it, because
the only guarantee for efficient and pure
public service is to make public servants
feel that they are amply requited for the
labours they perform and the services they
give.
But what I am opposed to is the outrageous extravagance of this Government
upon services that are not essential.
When you go to the English Parliament
to make an appeal for economy you do
not ask that so-and-so's salary should be
reduced by £50 or £100 a year.
You do
not make your case for economy by asking
for a reduction of £50 or £100 a year in
salaries. What you do is to deal with the
great national costing services, the Army,
the Navy, the Air Service, and all the
big and costly services that constitute the
real cost and are the real burden which the
taxpayers have to bear. We have no Army,
we have no Navy, and we have no Air
Service. We have none of these services,
and, therefore, our extravagance does not
lie in that direction. But we have other
services in which our extravagance is more
grotesque and indefensible.
I will not deal with the police as a
whole, though I believe that the cost of
the police force, amounting to nearly
£1,000,000 could be considerably reduced.
That police force was constituted at a
time when there were discord and trouble
existing in Northern Ireland, when it was
essential, perhaps when you had fervid
orations from the Prime Minister and Under-Secretaries rousing passion and bitterness amongst the people, forming
religious rancours and hatreds, and building upon these passions the positions they
created for themselves-no doubt then you
required a very large number of police.
But in these times of peace and goodwill,
which exist universally, and which all men
desire should exist, outside the Government ranks, there is no need to maintain
so large a police force as we have in Northern Ireland. We spend nearly
£1,000,000 upon police to keep law and
to preserve order in an area almost as
small as Glasgow and with a population
almost equal to that of Glasgow.
But I do not regard that in itself as the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I propose to
deal with the points raised by various
Members relating to my Department.
With regard to the question raised by my
hon. Friend the Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford), who sits behind me, in reference to probationers, I quite agree with
him when he states the enormous advantage it is to have probationers. For some
time past I am glad to say in Belfast the
magistrates have taken full advantage of
the Probation of Offenders Act, but in
the country the situation is more difficult,
because the magistrates there are rather
antagonistic to adopting the Act when
they might very reasonably have done so.
The result is that there are comparatively
few cases, and, consequently, there was
a difficulty in appointing a probation
officer, because in a scattered district
where perhaps for miles there might only
be half-a-dozen cases it was not worth
while for anyone to take on the task at
the pay then prevailing. With a view of
trying to improve matters we raised the
pay something like 40 per cent. both on
probation officers in Belfast and in the
country. And only in last January-
January, 1928-my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance permitted me to increase the pay by another 25 per cent.
In addition to that, I circularized the
magistrates on several occasions pointing
out the enormous advantage to the boy
who gets into trouble if the magistrates
would take advantage of this Act and
appoint probation officers. I am glad to
think there has been a steady improvement, although I will admit that in
several districts they have not yet taken
advantage of the Act. So far as the
Government are concerned we are doing
all we can to get magistrates to take advantage of the Act and appoint probation
officers. The appointment lies entirely in
the hands of the magistrates.

there is a great deal of misunderstanding.
When our new force was formed officers

what they enjoyed in Dublin, and if my

District-inspectors receive a consolidated
allowance of £200. They were not expected to keep a car, and the Government
had, in addition to that where there was
occasion to use cars, to provide one for
the purpose. Down here it is perfectly
true that when we formed the force we
divided that allowance up into two sums
-£100 in the case of a county-inspector
as headquarters allowance, and £160 for
a car, making a total of £260. That was
the sum fixed in the first instance. And,
of course, it was understood that a countyinspector at that time would not have
occasion to use a car to the same extent
as a county-inspector did in the country.
It was regarded as one of his emoluments.
However, on further consideration, at a
later period, the headquarters allowance
was reduced to £80 in the case of a countyinspector, and the car to £160, making a
total of £240 as against the old allowance
of £250. As regards district-inspectors,
they enjoyed a total allowance of £160 as
against the old allowance they enjoyed in
the old days, if they were stationed at
headquarters, of £200. In the one case
there was a saving of £40 in the districtinspector and a saving of £10 in the case
of the county-inspector. In addition to
that, if the necessity should arise for a
car, they must provide one at their own
expense.

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I will

industry dying here? It is because of
the neglect of the Minister of Finance

situation that requires drastic remedies.
The Prime Minister and other Ministers
are well aware that while mills and factories here are on short time a considerable amount of linen is being brought in
here from foreign countries, and it is sold
in Northern Ireland. I do not know
whether the Minister of Commerce knows
the people responsible for this crime. It
is a crime to sell an article as genuine

question.

if the noble Lord took a motor drive over
the hills of Northern Ireland he would see
the poverty that exists in the country.
What I have seen during the past year

Prime Minister solves this question before

the most important question, and up to

could be sold for something like £250, but,
as a matter of fact, I know they are
getting as much as £450 for a house and
if in addition they are getting the Government grant of £100, then I say the

is where the additional trouble comes in.
These houses were intended for workingclass people, but in many instances they
are not getting them. They are sold by
the builders to people who are in a position to build for themselves. After a
builder has completed a house, and got
the subsidy of £100 and the relief from
rates, he sells it to people who are able
to build a house, and who are not workingclass people at all.
I think that some new conditions ought
to be made applicable to builders of
houses of this description. I admit the
necessity for houses, and I think it is a

but I do not agree that a ring of builders

the conditions under which grants are
given for the building of houses.

cord anywhere of his birth or baptism.
By reason of that fact, and notwithstanding these two declarations by two most
respectable men, this old man's claim
was turned down. I think there is something wrong with that system.
The other case was that of a man who
had met with misfortune. He had always
been insured, and had had some periods

benefit again he was turned down. I

that when the matter was brought to their

This all shows to me clearly that there is
something wrong with some of the Departments of the administration. I do
not at all accuse the Ministry of being

It is in the mode of administering this
pension scheme that there is something
wrong. Another question arises in regard
to these new houses that are being built.
I am glad to see in the town where I come
from there is a tremendous lot of new
houses being built, and all, I am glad to
say, are being occupied. But if the
builders get the subsidy for these houses,
which are being built for little more than
the actual amount of the subsidy, or,
perhaps, £50 to £70 over and above the
subsidy, and these men have the houses
let at say 7s or 8s a week, then on the
capital expenditure plus wages, whatever
that would amount to, they have a rent
of about £20 a year out of each of these
houses. I think that is not an economic
proposition, and it is not fair to these
people who are forced into these houses,
and whose wages are not sufficient to
pay the rent.
I was glad to get from the Minister of
Finance an undertaking, or rather a statement, that he had actually called upon
some men-I do not know who they are
-to act on a committee on that question

an extraordinary thing when you look at

are going up. There is nothing for distress. I have been doing my best to try
to do something for the distressed people

Mr. ANDREWS: Almost every hon.
Member opposite who has spoken has referred to work which my Department is
charged with the responsibility of doing in
the public interest. I make no complaint of the way in which hon. Members
have expressed their views, with one exception, to which I will not refer. But the
speech which really impressed me most
was, if I may say so, the one delivered
by the Socialist Member for North Belfast,
because he did not stoop to personal abuse.
He simply asked a few important questions, which he had a perfect right to ask,
and to which I desire to give quite a frank
reply.
The first matter he raised was the administration of unemployment insurance.
Now, he knows, as I know, that it is a very
difficult fund to administer. Certain tests
have to be satisfied before an unemployed
person is entitled to get benefit, and one
of those tests is what is known as the test
to ensure that the claimant is really looking for work. As a matter of fact, I
think that hon. Members opposite will
admit that a test of this kind is necessary,
otherwise those who are not looking for
work would get benefit just in the same
way as those who are looking for work
do, which would be obviously unfair and
most demoralising. Now the G.S.W. test
is the one which was first made a statutory
condition for benefit of both kinds by the
Socialist Government when in office, and
I quite admit that a test of the kind
should be applied. But the feeling is
abroad that that test is applied by my Department, and many people hold the view
that it is applied by myself. Of course,
it is not.
The test is applied by courts set up for
the purpose, and the constitution or personnel of these courts is frequently criticised. Well, I think a fairer court could
not be conceived than a court presided over
by a neutral gentleman with local knowledge and of high reputation, and a
workers' representative and an employers'
representative. It is true that sometimes
the workers' representative may not be
there, and at other times, and very frequently, the employers' representative is
not there. But a claimant has the right
to refuse to have his case heard unless
there is a full court. And, in addition,
every opportunity is given to claimants to
have their case presented in the fairest
possible way. As the hon. Member for
North Belfast knows, if a claimant wishes
to be represented by some friend or by the
trades union leader he has a right to be
represented in that way. Now, I cannot
conceive a fairer method.
But there is a general feeling abroad
that because a claimant is turned down
under this G.S.W. test he is turned down
for all time; I would like to correct that
wrong impression. The claimant's claim
is disallowed for six weeks, and at the end
of that time the claimant can have his
or her case reconsidered. Although on
the previous occasion when the case was
considered it was turned down, it does not
at all follow that it will be turned down a
second time.
Mr. BEATTIE: It has been done.
Appropriation Bill-
Second Reading.

Mr. ANDREWS: The claimant has got
a warning, and a necessary warning, and
the claimant during the six weeks has an
opportunity of making special efforts to
obtain work. If the claimant does that
there is little fear of the claim being turned
down on the second occasion.
But again, in certain cases the claimant
has the right to have the case, which has
been turned down by the Court of Referees, considered by an umpire-an absolutely impartial man, independent of me
and my Department altogether. When
hon. Members criticise, as they do, and
condemn the system which the Socialist
party, when in power, approved of, I
think they ought to say what system or
method they suggest would be fairer to
put in its place. I am sure if a fairer
scheme could be devised, it would not only
be adopted by this Government, but by
the Imperial Government as well, because
neither Government has any desire to
turn down claims which ought to be admitted. All that we desire to do is to
sift out those claims which are entitled to
be considered favourably from those claims
that are not.
The old-age pensions administration
has also been criticised. Of course, a
certain number of claims have to be
turned down. People often make claims
that could not possibly be agreed to.
They say: "We have a sporting chance,
and we will try it." Many of the claims
made are absurd, and cannot be agreed
to. Here, again, I am not the man who
tries the case. I am not the man who
grants the pension. Pensions Courts have
been established to go into the claims, and
there is an appeal to the umpire. Further still, as the hon. Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr. Harbison) has
stated, even though a claim may be turned
down by the Pensions Court, and also
turned down by the umpire, if fresh evidence can be submitted to my Department
or to me, we will ask the Courts to
reconsider the claim, so that the claimant
may get every chance. The hon. Member suggested, because sometimes the
Ministry referred back the claim in this
way, that there was something wrong
with the administration. I would argue
on the other side that, because we do it,
it shows an absolute desire on our part
to be absolutely just and fair, and it also
proves that the claimants do get justice.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) asked if the savings in administration in connection with these Pensions
Courts were what were anticipated. The
Minister of Finance said he hoped that the
saving would amount to £10,000 per

at least that sum will be saved by the new
form of administration. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). I want also to say that I
feel deeply indebted to the ladies and
gentlemen, who are serving on these Pensions Courts, for the public services which
they are rendering. In almost every instance those who acted on the former
Pensions Committees are helping to administer the new system which, on the
whole, I think, has given as general satisfaction as any system of that kind could
possibly give.

There is only one other matter to which

keep saying that this unemployment problem could and should be solved. I quite
agree it is very desirable that it should be
solved, if it could be solved, but it is not
in the power of this or any other Government to solve it. The point is this——————
Mr. COLLINS: Have you read Lloyd
George's proposals?
Mr. ANDREWS: I have studied them
very closely, and they really amount
to relief schemes of a necessarily
temporary character being more widely
embarked upon. Those are the proposals,
and if he ever attempts, or gets an opportunity to attempt, to put those proposals
into force he will find the difficulties he is
up against. Is he going to supersede the
local authorities-wipe them out-and
start to make trunk roads here, there, and
everywhere? However, I must not enlarge upon that now, but I am prepared to
deal later on with those proposals if it is
necessary to do so.
What I would just like to say is this:
Let us be practical; let us look at the
thing from a reasonable standpoint.
Northern Ireland, apart from agriculture,
has two great industries, the linen trade
and shipbuilding. We can do, and have
done, a great deal to induce shipowners to
place orders with our local yards, and
6,000 or 7,000 people are working on those
ships to-day who would not be working but
for the Government's efforts in this direction. But the practical difficulty is that
it is very hard to get shipowners to order
ships if ships are not required, and,
again, it is very difficult to get Americans,
or people in other lands, to order linen if
they do not want to do so. All we can
do is to encourage them to do so; all we
can do is to help to bring our wares before
those people.
It is true to say-I am sorry to have to
say it-that the problem cannot be solved
except by industry itself becoming more
prosperous and our customers requiring
that which industry produces. In conclusion, I would say that no Government
has ever done more than this Government
to help our working people during this
long-drawn-out period of industrial depression, and if this was the last speech I
were to make at this Box I would say that
I defy any man to show that anything has
been left undone which it was possible for
my colleagues or myself to do.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Exchequer and Financial Provisions Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): In moving the Money Resolution, which
was the forerunner of
this Bill, I drew the attention of the
Committee to the fact that the Bill
naturally resolved itself into two heads.
The first part of the Bill deals with the
allocation of a sum of £120,000 out of
last year's surplus of £248,000 to a Rating Relief Suspense Account, and of a
further sum of £300,000 to be paid to the
same account out of the income of the
financial year, which will close on the
31st instant. It is desirable that in this
matter we should follow the lead of the
Imperial Government in their Finance
Act of last year and set aside a certain
sum to be available towards meeting in
the early stages part of the expenditure
which will arise under the derating proposals.
The second Clause of the Bill makes
provision for giving guarantees to Joint
Stock Banks in respect of short-term loans
to farmers to enable them to purchase
seeds and artificial fertilisers. The maximum sum to be guaranteed is £250,000,
and no guarantees will be issued in respect
of applications received after 31st December next. It is anticipated that most of
the applications will be received in the
course of the next two months, but as fertilisers are often put on grass lands in the
late Autumn, the Government has thought
it desirable to leave the date for receiving
applications open until 31st December,
next. As stated in moving the Money
Resolution, it is very difficult to estimate
how far these facilities will be availed of,
but the figure may be regarded as an outside one.
Some Members may ask why it has been
thought necessary to introduce such a form
of guarantee at the present time. The
reason is that owing to the poor prices
which farmers have obtained during recent months for their produce, more particularly for cattle and potatoes, a considerable number of them find it difficult
to obtain continued facilities from the "
banks without a Government guarantee at
the back of the loan owing to their inability to pay off outstanding promissory
notes. The guarantee is, therefore, intended to tide over a mere temporary
phase.
The arrangements proposed to be made
with the banks are that each individual
loan will require to be approved by the
Ministry of Agriculture on behalf of the
Ministry of Finance. The loan will be
made in the form of a promissory note
secured by two securities, and the banks
have agreed to issue the loans against the
promissory notes at a rate of interest of
5 per cent. Owing to the recent rise in
the bank rate, farmers without this
guarantee would in most cases, I understand, have to pay a rate of interest of
7 per cent., and for this reason, if for no
other, I anticipate that a substantial demand will be made for these facilities.
It will be necessary for the Ministry of
Agriculture to employ a certain amount
of temporary staff in connection with the
approval of the loans, but the charge for
this will be borne on the Ministry's Administrative Vote. I anticipate that the
House will approve in general of these
proposals, but, if necessary, on the Committee stage they can be considered in
fuller detail when either the Minister of
Agriculture or myself will be prepared
to reply to any questions. I beg to move.

take it that this Bill is really a protective
measure to protect the farming community and others from the exploitations
of the banks. The bank rate has gone up.
Poor farmers who have been in need in
the past have applied to the bank for
assistance, but that assistance was only
given on certain conditions. As high as

loans which the farmers required for
carrying on their industry. I believe the

when we as a Parliament should consider
the advisability of establishing a State
bank.
Mr. SPEAKER: I am sure the hon.
Member will realise that that opens a far
bigger question than is covered by this

give these guarantees on the existing basis.
Mr. BEATTIE: It is an illustration
I am about to give. That is the reason
why I think that Parliament should consider the advisability of establishing a

like to see an extension of this Bill to
other industries. Under our present
system industry to-day is being strangled
by what I would call an octopus. This

strangling and dragging it down to bankruptcy.
One of my objections to the Bill is that

industries as well as agriculture require

I am sure everybody on this side would

Let us judge the situation. What do
you get for your money lying in the bank?
Two and a half per cent. I think onehalf per cent. per £100 is quite sufficient
for the management of the bank. We
could then have money out of our own
bank for building houses, for industry,

see progressing. We cannot get what we

worth £200,000,000, and £200,000,000
representing these goods and finished
products was withdrawn from circulation.
There was not sufficient currency, therefore, to purchase the goods already on the
market. That is hard for any class of the
community; it is hard for the agricultural
class most of all. In 1918 a farmer who
owed a bank £40 could have paid that
loan by selling two cows. To-day if a man
wanted to pay a bank a loan of £40 he
has to sell four cows. Now cows are just
as valuable to-day from the human standpoint as then. It is only the deflation
policy of the banks that put farmers and
manufacturers and the whole of our agricultural industry into that extraordinary
plight. I would, therefore, like to have
seen the Government adopt the suggestion

that he requires, and where the managers

Mr. BARBOUR: The law relating to
Industrial and Provident Societies was
consolidated and amended by the Industrial and Provident Societies Act, 1893.
Section 22 of that Act provided that the
rules of a registered society should bind
it and all its members, and all persons
claiming through them, just as if each
member had subscribed his name and
affixed his seal, and there was a covenant
on the part of each member, his heirs,
executors, administrators and assigns to
conform thereto. This Clause has been
found in practice to have the unexpected
results of obliging members of a society
to take up and pay for further shares in
a society from time to time if the rules
of the society contain or are amended so
as to embody a rule to that effect. Such
a construction has, in fact, been placed
upon the Section by the Courts in the
recent case of the Agricultural Wholesale
Society v. Biddulph and District Agricultural Society, which was ultimately
carried to the House of Lords.
It will be appreciated that there are
cogent reasons why members of industrial
and provident societies should not be
placed under compulsion to take up additional shares or to accept unforeseen
liabilities upon existing shares. Το
remedy the defect in existing law which
the recent litigation has brought to light
the Imperial Parliament placed on the
Statute Book last year the Industrial and
Provident Societies (Amendment) Act,
1928, which enacts that notwithstanding
anything in Section 22 of the Industrial
and Provident Societies Act, 1893, a
member of a society registered under that
Act shall not, without his consent in
writing having been first obtained, be
bound by any amendment of rules registered after he became a member, and after
the passing of the Act, if and so far as
such amendment requires him to take or
subscribe for more shares than the number held by him at the date of registration
of the amendment, or to pay upon the
shares so held any sum exceeding the
amount unpaid upon them at that date,
or in any other way increases the liability
of the member to contribute to the share
or loan capital of the society.
As hon. Members are aware, the cooperative movement is strongly established
in Northern Ireland, and the Government
seeks by this Bill to extend to the members of societies in Northern Ireland the
same measure of protection as was conferred in Great Britain last year by the
Imperial Measure. I beg to move.

is to be the 30th May. I think it is in
accordance with Constitutional procedure
and fair play that the Imperial Government have communicated to the public
when the general election is likely to be.
I would like to know from the Prime
Minister what the position is here in Northern Ireland. When does he propose to
dissolve this Parliament and to hold the
general election? Every Unionist organisation in Belfast and Northern Ireland is
in possession of all the facts. They know
the situation, and it is not fair that information should be given to distinctive
political parties without the general body
of the public being informed. This is
not a matter that concerns party alone;
it concerns the whole community, because
the whole community, I take it, are very
concerned about the future of Northern
Ireland. As a matter of fact all the
candidates of the Prime Minister's party
have now been practically selected.
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not think it
would be constitutionally proper to make
any announcement in Parliament about
this. As far as I know, the question of
dissolving Parliament is entirely a matter
for the Governor, acting on the advice
given by the Prime Minister. I do not
think this is a matter on which any announcement ever has been, or could properly be, made in Parliament.
Mr. DEVLIN. I would like to know
from the Prime Minister whether he can
inform us what advice he is about to give
the Governor as to the time when the
general election is likely to take placewhether we will have an election in Northern Ireland first, and the Imperial
elections afterwards, or whether both
elections will be on the same day? There
seems to be a great deal of mystery about
this, and I am sure the noble Lord will
be very glad to inform us as to what the
intentions of the Government are.
Mr. BEATTIE: The Prime Minister
refuses to answer the request put forward.
I would also like to put a further question
to the Prime Minister, and I think I am
within my Parliamentary right in doing
this. At what date and for what time is
this House rising for the Easter holidays,
and when is the House to re-assemble
again I think I am justified in raising
this question at this particular moment,
because the Prime Minister in the British
House of Commons has stated that that
House will adjourn for the usual time at
Easter, and will not re-assemble until the
16th April. There is a rumour that the
Government in their haste to get the
elections before the Imperial elections are
going to sit during Easter week. Members on this side have engagements to fulfil during that week, and consideration
should be given to them. I would like a
definite statement made by the Prime
Minister as to whether this House is going
to enjoy the usual Easter holiday.
If we
are to have the Derating Bill and the
Budget before the election I am right in
assuming that our election will not take
place until after the Imperial elections.
As the Government are not likely to go to
the hustings until July I suggest that the
guillotine Motion be withdrawn and that
the Redistribution of Seats Bill and the
Derating Bill get the full consideration
of the House.
It is pro-

WAGES OF FORESTRY EM-
PLOYEES AT HILLSBOROUGH.
1.
Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether it is a fact that the
men engaged in planting trees at Hillsborough are only being paid 24s per
week; whether he is prepared to recommend an increase of wages to these men,
and whether it is a fact that these men
are forbidden to join a trade union
to enable them to get more reasonable
wages.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): It is not a fact
that the labourers employed by the
Ministry at Hillsborough are being paid
only 24s a week. The wage paid at
present at this forestry centre to ordinary
labourers is 27s a week. I see no reason
to recommend that this wage be increased.
There is no foundation for the suggestion
that these workers are forbidden to join
trades' unions.

Gentleman say if, in his opinion, 27s a
week is enough to enable a man to keep
his wife and family in Co. Down?

wages which we pay at all our forestry
centres are on a higher scale than the
wages in the localities concerned.

Gentleman say whether these men would
not be better on the dole?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE:
are better working.

COMMITTEE ON PERSONATION.
2. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state what will be the
composition of the proposed Committee
on Personation at Elections; whether he
will arrange that all political parties.
have representation on the Committee;
and whether, seeing that the Belfast
Chamber of Trade have taken a special
interest in the question, he will ask that
body to nominate a member.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I propose in this
connection to appoint a small impartial
Committee of legal experts.
I am in communication with certain
gentlemen on the subject, but have not
yet completed my inquiries nor received
the necessary consents from those whom I
have provisionally invited to act.
The subject matter is not one of party
politics, but, of course, all interests and
organizations will have ample opportunity
of putting forward their respective views
before the Committee.

right hon. Gentleman say, pending the

Constabulary, and so prevent this crime.
occurring during the coming elections?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, I think in
the course of his speech my right hon.
Friend the Attorney-General said he was
satisfied it would be better not to allow
the police to interfere in this matter.

Sir DAWSON BATES: From what I
know
of the gentlemen who have

voluntarily.

have the result of their deliberations incorporated in the Bill which we are to
discuss to-day?

Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move, "That
it be an instruction to the Committee that
they have power to amend the Bill so as
to include provisions regulating the deposits paid by candidates, the use of
vehicles, and the situation of polling
places at Parliamentary elections."
I think those are three very important
matters that the Committee on a Bill of
this kind should have full power to go
into. As the Government did not find it
necessary to include three of the most important items as far as elections are concerned, I have put down this Motion asking the House to send forward an instruction to the Committee. The deposit
fee for candidates, as we are all aware, is
£150. That £150 is equal to a contest in
four seats, and from now onward the deposit fee should only be equal to onefourth of £150. I am going a
little higher than one-fourth, because
I see the dangers that lie in bringing
the deposit fee too low, and I
am going to ask the Prime Minister and
the House to agree with me that £50 is
a fairly reasonable amount to fix as a deposit. The sum of £50 for each of the
four constituencies would total £200 as
against the £150 necessary previously.
Therefore, I think that is a reasonable
request.
I will try to substantiate my contention by giving another illustration. This
is a rich man's Bill, and is the rich man's
idea of trying to oust the poorer parties, ¡
such as the party to which I have the
honour to belong, which have to depend
for their income on the working-class
people, but the contributions of these
people are very small owing to the small
Parker, Mrs. Dehra
Pollock, Rt. Hon. Hugh Ma Do vell
Robb, John Hanna
Shillington, Major David Graham

wages they are in receipt of. My party
stand in an altogether different position
from the party the right hon. Gentlemen
opposite belong to or the Lloyd Georgian
party. We have nothing to sell, and we
do not believe in selling anything for the
purpose of gathering in party funds. The
Unionist party have piled up millions of
pounds in their party exchequer, and the
reason for that is that they occupied the
seats of the mighty in the Imperial House of
Commons, and on every New Year's Day
they were able, for substantial contributions, to name some baronets, earls.
dukes, or something like that. The sale
of titles built up their funds, and, therefore, they have at hand large sums of
money to meet the needs and requirements of an election such as will be held
in Northern Ireland on or about the 10th
day of May, 1929.
We in the Labour party might realise
£600 under the old system, and that £600
represented sixteen seats contested. That
gave every man and woman who had the
vote an opportunity of going to the poll
and declaring what he or she stood for.
Under the new system to contest those
seats and give the electors an opportunity
of going to the poll to support the policy
we think would serve them best would
take £2,400. That is a financial transaction which I am sure the Government
took into consideration. They knew perfectly well there was only one way of retarding the progress of Labour, and that
was by strangling it financially, by putting
the noose round its neck and drawing it
tight. If you allow the deposit for the
four divisions in Belfast to be £600 we
are prepared to give every elector an
opportunity of coming forward at the next
election and using the franchise in the
manner he thinks best, but under the new
conditions £2,400 will have to be set aside
as deposit fees. That is financially impossible.

I believe the country districts are, comparatively speaking, worse off than the
City of Belfast, and that the financial
difficulties in the various counties will be
considerably greater under this new redistribution than under the old system.
Take the case of County Down, that is
represented by the Prime Minister and
Mr. Eamon de Valera-
Mr. HEALY: A good combination.
Mr. BEATTIE: A good combination.
In County Down eight candidates are in
the field, and eight times £150 is £1,200.
I do not think that is reasonable. I think
this is proving the first opinions I gave
about the Bill, namely, that it is a rich
man's Bill, and that it is a question of
gold versus service. The Government
want to make the people accept the gold
standard as against service by a candidate
who gives his time and attention to the
requirements of the people. Some very
cute politicians tried to make capital out
of the last speech I made on the gold basis
when I said that £7,000 or £8,000 was
spent in my division, but notwithstanding
that I topped the poll by a thousand. I
know that at the next election gold will
again come forward, but I am pleased to
say that all the gold and wealth that is at
the disposal of the Tory party--I am only
taking this as an isolated case is not
able to buy the votes of the people who
sent me here. The people are as staunch
to-day as ever they were. They never
will be bought by money. I want to
make it clear and distinct that the people
of East Belfast never were bought and
never will be bought by the gold or wealth
that is thrown about at election times.
I want to say that if this House does
not send forward to the Committee this
recommendation for the reduction of the
deposit fee to £50 I am going to take it
that the Craigavon Government, and the
noble Lord's party are really desirous
that rich men, and rich men only, should
represent the industrial classes in Belfast.
I want to tell the Prime Minister that if
the industrial classes in Belfast had dispensed with the rich men fifty years ago
the conditions under which they are living
to-day would be much better. Thev would
have a higher standard, they would be
more happy and contented, and our industries would be more prosperous than
they are at the moment.
The next thing I want to point out is
that it is clearly illegal for public service
vehicles of any kind to take part in an
election. Why that has been allowed to
go on in the North of Ireland for so many
years I cannot understand. If a candidate raises an objection to a public service vehicle being on the street with canvassers and with "Vote for So-and-so" on
the front and back, no notice is taken. I
am given to understand that is quite
sufficient to unseat any candidate who
uses that method of bringing his voters to
the poll. Therefore, I want the Committee to take into consideration the present law, which is now dead, because it
is never put into operation, and to see,
if that law is dead, that it is revived and
placed in the present Bill to protect poorer
candidates from the abuse of public service vehicles being hired and used against
them on the days of elections.
I understand that one candidate in
England recently purchased forty new
cars for his election day. The reason he
did that was that he knew he was not
allowed to accept either a private hackney car or a public service car, that the
use of any car that is licensed is illegal
at an election. He bought the forty cars
so that they could operate for him on the
day of the election. I understand he
only bought them for the day and re-sold
them the next day, but that proves conclusively that in England, Scotland, or
in Wales it is an unknown thing to have
licensed vehicles used during elections.
The representative of Lord Scone shakes
his head. I would not be surprised at
anything Lord Scone used yesterday
trying to bring voters to the booths.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

Mr. BEATTIE: The person for whom
you were speaking across in Scotland

and I do not speak as an individual in

The three requests I have made are

Mr. KYLE: I want to second the
Motion proposed by the hon. Member for

the deposit fee is £100. If £100 is

As the law stands at present, £150 is

found in the city of Belfast, for instance,
where a deposit of £25 is necessary in

any of those which are being carved out

candidatures.
The main reason why this £150 deposit
was put in in the first instance was to prevent freak candidatures in order that the
State and the public should not be put
to the inconvenience of having elections
for people who possibly thought that they
were important, but with whose idea of
their own importance the public did not
agree. We have eliminated freak
candidatures, so far as the municipality
is concerned, by a deposit fee of £25.
How much less likely is it that we would
have freak candidatures for Parliament ?
The deposit fee of £50 would prevent the
adoption or nomination of freak candidates for the city of Belfast, or for any
of the county constituencies. Therefore,
I put it to the Government that it is
desirable that they should reduce the
amount of money that it is necessary for
candidates to deposit.

It is obvious that, if you take the Conservative
party in Belfast-and in
Northern Ireland, I suppose, speaking
generally-if we are to judge the future
by the past then the Conservative party
and the richer parties, whose friends have

that the poorer candidates have not the
same opportunities of bringing their

a form of bribery. I think that is not
too strong a word to use. It is a form
of corruption and of bribery that the
Unionist party use in order to snare the
people on election day. They send round
a beautiful limousine to some of the
slum districts of Belfast to bring people
to the poll. Of course, that is all the
people ever see of those cars except when
they are splashed by them in town on a

I think it would be desirable in this
democratic age-or in this alleged democratic age-that the State itself should

or women who are interested in an election should be able and willing to go to

no favour.
The unfortunate part about the thing

all the working-class man
wants as the rich man's party. It

or other
parties for their particular causes, then

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: I rise
to ask the House to reject this instruction. The first point that was made was
with reference to the deposit of £150
which, by our law as it stands at present,
has to be paid by every candidate who
seeks election. That £150 deposit was
originally prescribed by the Representation of the People Act of 1918, which
applied equally to England, Scotland and
Ireland, and when the Government of
Ireland Act of 1920 was passed the same
rule was applied to the elections for our
Parliament. No doubt by the Government of Ireland Act Proportional Representation was substituted for direct
representation, and the result of that was
that there were four or more candidates
up for each constituency, and the constituencies were very much larger.
But I really cannot understand the
argument that because the constituencies
are being altered from Proportional
Representation constituencies to singlemember constituencies therefore this
deposit should be reduced. The hon.
Member who moved the instruction said
that £150 was paid by a candidate in a
contest where there were four candidates
under Proportional Representation, and,
therefore, under the direct system it
should be reduced to £50. The truth is
this: that it makes no difference so far as
the deposit is concerned whether the election is conducted under Proportional
Representation or under the direct vote,
because under the Proportional Representation system there were four Members
and four or more candidates, and each
candidate had to pay £150, and the fact
of the change makes no difference at all.
Each can-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
didate still has to pay £150 although he
does not have to canvass or submit himself
to the large Proportional Representation
electorate. Under the new system you
still have the same number of candidates
for the same area elected, presumably by
the same number of voters. Therefore, I
say the argument that has been addressed
to the House on this branch of this instruction is really no argument at all, because no change has been made by the Bill
at present before the House.
Might I remind the House that this is
a deposit only; it is not a payment out
and out. It was considered in 1918 when
the Representation of the People Act was
passed by the whole United Kingdom of
Great Britain and Ireland that this sum
of £150 should be paid as a deposit as a

known.

That
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
is always a question of proof. The actual
use of the vehicle is prohibited by law,
and the person who is guilty of the offence
of employing or hiring this vehicle is liable
on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding £100. It is well known in other
parts of the Province, though possibly it
may not be well known in Belfast, and
there can be no doubt whatever that that
Section of the Act of 1883 applies to motor
cars, because the Locomotives and Highways Act of 1896 defined a light locomotive, which includes a motor car, as
being deemed to be a carriage within the
meaning of any Act of Parliament. Therefore a motor car is within the prohibitory
provisions of the Act of 1883, and it is a
breach of that Act for any person to use
a public service vehicle. He is liable to
a fine of £100 for so using it, and the
candidate is liable to be unseated if it can
be brought home to the candidate.
There is only one exception, and that is
contained in the Act itself. Nothing in
the Act is to prevent a carriage or animal
being let for hire, employed or used by
an elector or several electors at their joint
cost for the purpose of being conveyed to
and from the poll. That is to say, if two
or more electors wish to go to the poll and
to hire an ordinary taxi cab for their own
purposes, that is not an illegal practice
within the meaning of the Section, but
the general use of public service vehicles
at elections-it may as well be stated—is
absolutely illegal.

an election should be done away with.
Motor cars should only be allowed to be
used for invalids and those unable to
walk. If that were done you would not
only get fairer elections but better representation in Parliament.
There is one thing I would like to point

would be delighted to see the defender of

If there is one man who has been an asset

deposit of £150. It is monstrous to ask
candidates to put down a deposit of £150.
and I support the Motion before the

The question of the nomination deposit

right hon. and learned Gentleman most
unconvincing. The retention of the £150
deposit fee is a distinct handicap to a

party that would attempt to contest all

their disposal. How can any party such

deposits amounting to £2,400? The

and large funds at their disposal are almost bound to have a walk-over in a number of the constituencies in Belfast.
That is not a good thing from the point
