Mr. DEVLIN: I beg to move to leave
out Clause 1. I would gladly give way
to the Prime Minister if he were
willing to state the concessions which he
is prepared to make to those of us who
represent the minority in Northern Ireland, or failing that if he is prepared to
give justification for the introduction of
this Measure. There have been only
three speakers from the Government side
on this Bill. The first was the Prime
Minister, the second was the hon. and
learned Member for the University (Mr.
Robb), and the third was the Attorney-
General. I take it, therefore, the best
brains of the Government have been requisitioned in this debate to make the
best case they can in bringing in the
proposals now before the House. I confess
that in my memory of this Parliament,
and of greater Parliaments than this, I
have never witnessed such a complete
Parliamentary impoverishment as that
which has just been manifested by those
who have come here to submit this Bill to
the House and to defend it.
In the first place I would ask even now
to have an answer to this question: I
want to know what is the reason why the
Government introduced this Bill. It is
not customary for Governments to bring
about vast changes either in the life of the
community or in regard to their constitutional liberties unless there is some clamant
demand upon the part of the people. I
have not yet at any stage of these proceedings, or even in discussions outside the
House, known of any intelligent demand
from any quarter for the abolition of Proportional Representation, and I can only
come to the conclusion, therefore, that
this is not a skilful, because it is too
obvious, but a deliberate, conspiracy to
rob, first of all, the minority we represent
of those rights and privileges, limited
though they were, granted to us by the
Imperial Government when the Act of
1920 was passed. I would like, before I
proceed, to say that you may pass this Bill
through this House, you may carry it by
a majority, which you are entitled to do
and will do, but we do not intend to leave
it where it is.
Mr. MCALLISTER: Hear, hear.
Mr. DEVLIN: We will proceed to take
steps to find out whether the English
Government who forced this Act of 1920
down the throats of the Irish people,
North and South, against their wills,
because it is a strange thing that the Act
of 1920, which now stands upon the
Statute Book, had not the sanction of a
single Parliamentary representative either
from Northern Ireland or from Southern
Ireland. Yet in that Act they inserted
a Clause of course, it was ridiculous so
far as the minority was concerned, but,
notwithstanding that, they inserted it, and
in inserting it they stated that it was inserted as a safeguard-that the method of
election was to be by Proportional Representation, and Sir Laming Worthington
Evans stated that it was as a guarantee,
as a safeguard that it was inserted in the
Measure.
Now, I stated the last day, and I repeat
it here, that this is the first instance in
which the safeguards of the rights of
minorities have ever been taken away by
the majority in any land without the consent of the minority. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). In the Indian Constitution,
as I pointed out on the previous occasion,
no majority can take away minority rights
without the consent of the minority. The
Prime Minister can consult his legal advisers and find out whether I am justified
or not in making that statement. I
understand I have asked Mr. Speaker,
and he has so informed me that this
Measure has been submitted to the British
Government and that they have sanctioned
it.
Therefore, the British Government
are responsible for this transaction. The
men who made this bargain with the
minority are responsible for this transaction of the Northern Government.
I do not know what our rights are when
these matters will be contested either before the Privy Council or some other
Imperial tribunal. I do not know what
the legal interpretation of that Clause will
be, but if this is carried, if we are robbed
of this simple right-not much of a privilege, as I have said, but still a safeguardif we are robbed of it, and if we are denied
justice before the Judicial Committee of
the Privy Council then we will deem it
our duty to appeal to a higher tribunal.
and we will appeal to the League of
Nations. The right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Pollock) smiles. Very well. They laugh
best who laugh last, and we will see. I

I
pass now to the proposal in this

the burning character of those grievances,

twelve. We all know the reason why.

riot at the coming election" and, therefore, there will only be two parties-the

Mr. HEALY: When the Act of 1920
was passed through the Imperial Parliament the Prime Minister knows perfectly
well that the big question was the question of minorities. People had very
serious misgivings then as to what was
going to take place with regard to the
8 per cent. of Unionists who were left
under the Southern Government, and
more serious misgivings still with regard
to the 33 1-3 per cent. which were to be
left under the Northern Government.
The Imperial Government, I take it,
were anxious that the minority both in
Northern and Southern Ireland should
be able to return Members to both
Parliaments in proportion to their num
bers. That provision was not so essential in the case of the South as it was
in the case of the North, because there is
not any county in Southern Ireland where
the Unionists have a majority, but there
are several counties in the North where
Nationalists have a majority, and, therefore, it was felt that if these Parliaments
were to co-operate successfully, and were
really to register the voice of the whole
people, the minority in the South and
the minority in the North equally ought
to be adequately represented in both
places.

I have a map here, which I exhibited
before in this House. It shows you how

when the Union areas were originally
formed they were formed on the basis of

workhouse was built in the centre of a
particular area. If you take those three
Unions, the areas of Irvinestown, Enniskillen, and Lisnaskea, you can form three
compact constituencies with actually
equal numbers of people, and that will
give adequate representation to all parties.
Evidently that would not suit the Prime
Minister and his friends, the gerrymanderers, and so we proceed to form a constituency that runs from the County Monaghan, right along the Monaghan border,
the Cavan border, and the Leitrim border,
until it arrives at the Donegall border.
Did anybody ever know of such a formation on a map as that of South Fermanagh.
South Fermanagh, curiously enough, is
North Fermanagh. On this
the
map
South is the North. You have changed

would have had Enniskillen, the chief

in South Fermanagh, or the Lisnaskea
area, Lisnaskea, the market town, would

and from the point of view of convenience
the areas we suggest would be the most

It is difficult to find words to describe
one's feelings in a matter of this kind.
What can a representative say to people
in County Fermanagh who tell you that
there is no good trying to play with these
people. "They will not play fair," they
say; they have no sense of justice, and
all your talk and all your efforts would
be merely as the wind passing over."
What reply can a man make to that?
None. You must confess that it is a
hopeless task for any minority to secure
justice in this House. The cry of Cromwell was "To hell or Connaught." You
have a new cry, and it is, "Crucify the
Nationalists," and, for that matter,
"Crucify all the Opposition." You have
driven them from their employment in
the Queen's Island, you have driven them
from the county councils and from the
district councils and boards of guardians,
and now you want to drive them out of
this House, or reduce their numbers to
such an extent that they will be so inadequately represented here that they
will not come at all.
I feel, as the Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) feels, that it is all so futile
attempting to reason with the Government. They are not open to reason, they
are not open to do the right thing, and
the just thing. In the Imperial Parliament one can at least be certain of this;
that one can secure a reasonable hearing,
and if they are not prepared to go the
whole way to meet you, at all events they
are prepared to go some way.
But in my
short experience in this House I have
never seen an Amendment from this side
of the House accepted by the Government.
Surely we stand for something. According to the Government we stand for
nothing because you give no consideration
whatever to any view we put forward or
to any interest we represent.
Therefore, I say that if justice cannot
be secured here-and it appears now that
justice cannot be secured-we are being
reluctantly driven to another Court.
We may be a small minority, but the
League of Nations has already made provision for people circumstanced somewhat
as we are circumstanced, and at all events
we will drag the veil of hypocrisy from
England's face. She cannot go on posing
as the champion of persecuted minorities
on the Continent and allow the minority
here not only to be persecuted but to be
miserably sacrificed to every expediency
and every passion. I have, therefore,
great pleasure in seconding the Amendment.

to co-operate with one another in the

—in fact, I am sure of it was only
camouflage and window-dressing for the

for the purpose of the people of America.
The Government of a country are in
the position of trustees. They are
trustees of the rights not only of their
own followers but of the people. I submit that the first thing that should animate a trustee would be to discharge the
trust with honour. I think there never
was any Government acted so politically
dishonourably as the Government of
Northern Ireland are doing at the present time. I have been moving about
amongst the people since the Bill was introduced, and I have not met a single
person who has not radically condemned
the injustice this Bill is perpetrating. I
have met those who differ from me in
religion, and in other walks of life, pursuing other avocations, honourable men;
poor men, merchants, and professional
men of every description. All these
people are walking about in shame and
horror at the wrong that is being perpetrated upon the 38,000 people of
Antrim. It was stated the other day in
this House that instead of what any
other Government in the world would do
-set up a proper impartial tribunal
having the confidence of the people to
map out the constituencies-what took
place? I stood for Antrim at the last

poll to Mr. Speaker and the Minister of
Commerce, notwithstanding that there
were miles and miles where there was not
a single Nationalist voter, and a Unionist
sub-agent in Antrim stated shamefacedly
that the whole register was personated.
Notwithstanding that fact I was returned
third on the poll above the two Parliamentary Secretaries.
What actually took place was this: I
was voted in not for any merit of my
own, but for what I stood for the voice
of the people. Mr. McDowell-I am not
going to say anything against him-Mr.
Megaw and Senator Leslie, who, I understand, is asking for a seat in Antrim, sat
down at the table in the Unionist office
to wipe out the Nationalist representative
of Antrim when the people had voted him
in. I suggest to the House that that state
of affairs could not exist in any place outside Northern Ireland. When a Bill with
far-reaching consequences like this is introduced into Parliament there is usually
some evidence of a demand having been
made for it. I am at a loss to know of
a single public body in Northern Ireland
that voiced an opinion in favour of a
change in legislation. Not only that,
but there has not been a single logical
argument or a single reason given by the
Government in defence of this diabolical
outrage which they are perpetrating on
one-third
of the people of Northern
Ireland.
The only answer given is that Proportional Representation is costly and cumbersome. There is no complaint from the

less costly and less cumbersome to hold 52

five under the 1920 Act. I always notice
that when the Government are in an indefensible position on every occasion the

entirely contrary to the provisions of the

Now, I submit to the House that when

protection to minorities. Because Section

What did it matter the size of the population? It was not the size; it was the
nature of the representation of the

I go further. It is the contention of

be something similar in population to the

in Fermanagh and Tyrone you have varied

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Friday, 22nd March, 1929.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Paper Presented.
Ministry of Commerce:
Return of Assurance Companies for the
year 1928. (By Act).
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
House of Commons (Method of Voting
and Redistribution of Seats) Bill.
SECOND ALLOTTED DAY.
Considered in Committee (Progress 21st
March).
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
CLAUSE 2 (Redistribution of Seats).
(1) Each of the areas mentioned in
the first column of Part I of the First
Schedule to this Act shall be a parliamentary borough returning the number
of members of the House of Commons
specified opposite to the name of that
borough in the said Part, and shall be
divided into the divisions specified therein, and each such division shall return
one member.
(2) Each of the areas mentioned in
the first column of Part II of the First
Schedule to this Act shall be a parliamentary county returning the number
of members of the House of Commons
specified opposite to the name of that
county in the said Part, and shall be
divided into the divisions specified therein, and each such division shall return
one member.

Mr. KYLE: I want to speak against the
Motion that the Clause stand part. I
think this Clause in itself is one of the
worst Clauses that could possibly be conceived in a Redistribution Bill. It has
always been the practice when a Redistribution Bill was introduced that nothing
was left to the imagination or even the deliberation of the Minister. The Representation of the People Act, 1918, set out
specifically all the rights and powers of
electors and of the Government. When a
redistribution took place there was to be
nothing left to the Minister to determine
in the vague form that you will find is
contained in paragraph 4 (2) of this
Clause. You will see it in the fourth line:
shall be framed and expressed in such
manner and form as may be necessary.
I want to say that that is as vague as
vagueness could possibly be. The Government should not ask the Committee to
agree to such vague phraseology as I have
read out. What may be necessary in the
opinion of the Prime Minister or Attorney-
General may not be necessary in the view
of nine-tenths or 99/100ths of the electors.
I submit that this Clause is very badly
drafted indeed in that connection. Imagine legislation by reference on a question
for the redistribution of seats. This
Clause refers you to the Act of 1920, and
also Section 6 of the Representation of the
People (Northern Ireland) Act, 1928. I
do not think there has been in any former
Redistribution Bill such a thing as legislation by reference. It could be set out
specifically and clearly in this Bill what
the Government's intention was and what
the law was to be afterwards, even if
they had to go to the trouble of citing
or re-enacting, as it were, the Government
of Ireland Act, 1920, which, by the way,
they have no power to re-enact. This
legislation by reference on a question of
redistribution is a policy that was never
carried out by the Government of Great
Britain at any time, not even in 1867 or
1884. It was never done.

Voting and Redistribution Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee
[The Attorney-General]
there is no substance in this Amendment.
It is one which is necessary owing to the
faulty description which appeared in the
Schedule as it was originally drafted. If
Members of the Committee will compare
the words which are proposed to be substituted on pages 9 and 10 with the words
which are referred to in the Amendment,
they will find that the areas are absolutely
identical, and that the words are practically identical both in the Schedule as
it originally stood and in the Amendment.
But the Committee will realize
that in the description of some of these
boundaries it is sometimes difficult to set
them out in words with complete accuracy, and after the Bill had been drafted,
in order to ensure that there should be
no error or misconception, the areas and
boundaries were checked over again, and
it was found that after taking a larger
scale map and going through this particular Schedule one of the streets,
namely, Rosebery Road, which forms
part of the boundary of the Ballynafeigh
division, had a different orientation on
the small map from that shown on the
larger and more up-to-date map when
compared on the spot. The consequence
is that in order to put the matter right it
becomes necessary to alter in the
Schedule a few of the bearings of the
compass, not the names of the streets or
the areas themselves, and it is merely
for the purpose of having the description
absolutely accurate. For example, if you
take the Amendment and the original
Schedule, you will find that southeasterly becomes east and north-westerly
becomes north, and in two places it has
been found necessary to alter east into
south. It arose originally through a mistake in the assumption as to the points of
the compass on the Rosebery Road. These
changes do not in any way affect the
constitution of the Ballynafeigh division
as it originally appeared in the Bill and
in the Schedule, nor do they alter it in
any of the maps which have been already
prepared. They merely make it clear
that the portions of that division which
are included in the maps will correspond
with the description in the Schedule.
does not alter the numbers of voters.
is merely for the purpose of description.

Mr. MCALLISTER: I offer my most
deliberate hostility to this Schedule of the
Bill as an attempt to gerrymander the
minority in Belfast out of their proper representation. They can only hope and
believe that when this matter is finally
settled, the attempt will not have succeeded. I think it is common ground that
according to the test of population the
Catholics of Belfast should be entitled to
four Members. By this Bill the most
they can receive is two. Taking the Central and Falls divisions, you have laid it
down as a principle of equality, justice
and fair-play, that under the Northern
Government it requires 33,000 Catholics
to elect one Member of Parliament, whilst
18,000 Unionists can elect one Member.
This is an attempt to supplement the
gerrymandering scheme of the Imperial
Government that was carried through
some time ago at the behest and by the
direction of the present Members of the
Government of Northern Ireland. Bv
that scheme in order to deprive the
Nationalists of Belfast of the services of
my hon. Friend, the Member for West
Belfast who sits beside me (Mr. Devlin),
the constituencies for the Imperial Parliament were reconstituted according to the
following figures: The population of East
Belfast is 93.622; the population of North
Belfast consists of 100,917; and the popu
lation of South Belfast consists of 91,018,
but in order to gerrymander the minority
in Belfast out of even one seat in the Imperial Parliament the Imperial Government at the behest and by the direction of
the right hon. and hon. Gentlemen who
now form the Government of Ireland
turned a number of Unionist electors from
other areas into the old West Belfast constituency until as at present constituted
it toals 129,594.
Notwithstanding all the
attempts
by this dishonest means to silence
the hon. Member for West Belfast
in the Imperial Parliament, and to deprive the Nationalist people of his services,
the pleasing fact remains-and the
Government know it-that in spite of
their gerrymandering schemes at an election in West Belfast to-morrow he would
swamp any Unionist candidate who had
the courage to oppose him. We can only
hope that, notwithstanding this attempt
to gerrymander, history will repeat itself,
and that in a very short time a similar
state of affairs will prevail in every
division for the Parliament of Northern
Ireland.
I am convinced as I stand here that if
not at this election at any rate before four
years are over the Northern Government
will be swamped in Northern Ireland in
the way the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr Thomas Henderson) can now
swamp them for a seat in the Imperial
Parliament. I say with deliberation, if
this system of government goes on, unless
the electors of Northern Ireland, Catholic
and Protestant alike, smash the Northern
Government, the Northern Government
will smash them. That is my deliberate
judgment.
I submit, again, that this Schedule is
ultra vires, and I do so for this reason.
T say that the whole context of the Act of
1920 goes to show that the principal thing
to which it directed attention was the protection of minorities in Northern Ireland.
Committee

Voting and Redistribution Bill-
22 MARCH 1929
It was discussed in the Imperial Parliament around that question. It was discussed and passed at a time when passions
were roused and intense feeling prevailed,
and in order as they thought effectively to
protect the minority in Northern Ireland
the Imperial Parliament inserted Clause
5 in the 1920 Act, which amongst other
things provided that no legislation was to
be passed that would cause disadvantage
to any section of the people of Northern
Ireland by reason of their religion.
In conjunction with Section 5 you must
read Section 14, which provides that in
any scheme of redistribution due regard
must be had to the population. I say
that those two Sections must be read together, and that all this talk that each
constituency must be made up of similar
numbers is rank humbug. I say that
that undoubtedly means not that you
ought to have due regard to the numbers
of the population, but due regard to the
different sections of the population. Read
in conjunction with Clause 5, it means
that you are not to map out the constituencies to deprive the minority of Northern Ireland of its proper representation
of seventeen Members, and to cut it down
to eight or nine. I suggest, therefore,
that this Bill as it stands is ultra vires.
Apart from the fact that it is ultra vires.
I do suggest that it would not stand the
test of examination for five minutes by
any impartial tribunal, legal or diplomatic.
I am not in a position to discuss the
whole Schedule with regard to Belfast--
I am not familiar with it but I do say
that a scheme which requires 33,000

The House met at Three of the Clock.
The Clerk at the Table informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
Speaker from this day's Sitting.
Whereupon Mr. Moles, the Chairman
of Ways and Means, proceeded to the
Table, and, after Prayers, took the Chair
as Deputy-Speaker, pursuant to the

Oral Answers to Questions.
OLD-AGE PENSIONS TO RETIRED
P.E. TEACHERS.
1. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN (for
Mr. Beattie) asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the number
of retired public elementary teachers receiving old-age pensions; the amount
which they receive; and what the cost
would be if the amount of the old-age
pensions to which these teachers are entitled was added to ex-public elementary
teachers' pensions whose incomes qualify
them for old-age pensions.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I beg to refer the hon. Member
to the reply given to a similar question
by the hon. and gallant Member for West
Belfast (Colonel Woods) on the 29th
March, 1928, to the effect that information as to the number of retired public
elementary school teachers in receipt of
old-age pensions could not be made available without a large amount of labour,
the cost of which could not be justified by
the results to be achieved.
I may add that without the data implied in the first two portions of the
question, it would be impossible to give
the figures sought in the concluding
sentence.
TEACHERS' PENSION
SCHEME, 1914.
2. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN (for
Mr. Beattie) asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the number
of retired public elementary teachers who
were on the active list at the date of the
passing of the Teachers' Pension Scheme
of 1914, and who declined to join that
scheme; and what the difference is between the pensions which they are each
actually drawing now and the pensions
which they would each be drawing had
they joined the said scheme.
Mr. POLLOCK: I assume that the
hon. Member is referring to those all-
Ireland public elementary teachers on the
retired list in the year 1922, for the payment of whose pensions my Ministry, on
the division of the pension roll, undertook
the liability from that year, together with
such additional pensioners as have come
on the pension roll since the year 1922.
I regret, however, that the labour involved in ascertaining the numbers of
such pensioners who had declined to
accept the Teachers' Pension Scheme of
1914 would be incommensurate with the
results likely to be achieved, and I find
myself, therefore, unable to supply the
information. The figures sought in the
latter part of the question could not in
fact be ascertained without involving the
Teachers' Pension Office in Dublin in
compiling a very lengthy and exhaustive
return which it would be quite unreasonable for us to expect.

ERECTION OF LABOURERS'
COTTAGES.
4. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN (for
Mr. Beattie) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he can state the number
of improvement schemes approved under
the Labourers Act, 1923; the number of
labourers' cottages erected under that
Act; the number of improvement schemes
approved under the Labourers' Cottages
(Loans) Act, 1927; the number of
labourers' cottages erected under that
Act; and whether it is proposed to amend
the last-mentioned Act so that rural agricultural labourers residing in unsanitary
houses or unprovided with houses may be
provided with suitable dwellings.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Twenty-two schemes
were approved under the Labourers Act
(Northern Ireland), 1923, and 1,233 cottages have been erected. A further 524
cottages have been authorised under the
provisions of the Act.
No schemes have yet been approved
under the Labourers' Cottages (Loans)
Act, 1927, but one scheme has been submitted, and I understand that several
local authorities have schemes in contemplation.
The Act provides generous assistance to
Rural District Councils erecting labourers'
cottages, as under its provisions the Exchequr bears 40 per cent. of the cost, of
the charges. The Government do not
propose any amendment of the Act.

UNIVERSITY PARLIA-
MENTARY VOTERS.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether he could state the number of
parliamentary voters entitled to vote for
the return of four Members for Queen's
University.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked to reply to this question.
According to information received by
me from the Registration Officer, the
number of electors on the register of
parliamentary electors of the Queen's
University, which came into operation on
the 1st October, 1928, is 3,330. The
number is made up of 3,026 men, and 304
women.
It is expected that there will be an increase of approximately 200 electors on
the Register which will come into operation on the 1st May next. The estimated
total number of electors on that Register
will, therefore, be 3,530.

FIRST SCHEDULE, Part I (Parliamentary Boroughs).
Question proposed: "That so much of
Part I of the First Schedule as relates to
the Parliamentary Borough of Londonderry stand part of the Schedule."
Mr. HARBISON: I would like to say
a few words about the Parliamentary
Borough of Londonderry. As I understand it, the city area has sufficient population to have two Members, and in order
to deprive the majority in the city of their
just representation in this Parliament outside districts have been taken into the area
of the city. That is not as it should be.
We in other parts of the Six Counties
where we have a large percentage of the
voters will have no representation whatever, and in Derry City, where we have
the right to the representation of the city,
we are robbed of half our claim. By all
the rules of fair play we would be entitled
to the city Members, but on one side of
the city a large proportion of our population is cast out of the city into the rural
area and on the other side a large part of
the rural area is brought into the city,
thereby creating an abnormal and, I say,
false constituency.
We have, for instance-I believe it is
coming on to-day in connection with the
County of Antrim-a very large population deprived of their representation in
County Antrim. In Derry we are entitled to the whole representation of the
city, but by the bringing in of outside
areas we are deprived of a Member there.
I think that is a state of affairs that requires some explanation from the Prime
Minister. All we ask for in Derry and
in every other constituency in the Six
Counties is to have our just representation.
In Derry city we have been deprived of
it. This Motion refers entirely to the
City of Derry, and I only want to confine
myself for the moment to the City of
Derry. We, the Nationalists of the North,
represent a very large section of the community-over one-third, and we are not
getting one-fourth, or in or about onefourth of the representation. That inequality might have been remedied had
fair play and justice been given to our
people. I beg, therefore, to oppose this
Motion.
a
Mr. HEALY: I, too, have to join my
colleague in protesting against what has
been adopted in the City of Derry.
Derry City has been historically
kind of political battleground for many
years. There is, I understand, on the
Parliamentary Register a Nationalist
majority of 2,000. One would think in
these circumstances that the city itself
apart from the surburbs ought to have
been formed into a constituency, because
when you amalgamate a purely rural area
with a city area there is not a great deal
of community of interest between one and
the other. This city affords another example of the deplorable results that have
accrued from the gerrymandering of constituencies. Although the Nationalist
people there, as I say, have a majority on
the local government register of about
1,600 to-day if every vote were cast for
every Nationalist candidate the minority
could elect two-thirds and the majority
could only elect one-third. Now, I think
that is the best commentary upon what
has occurred in Derry under your gerrymandering of local government
stituencies, and probably will occur, or
what is intended to occur, with regard to
your re-arrangement of Parliamentary
areas.
con-
It is a curious circumstance that in
making an arrangement of this kind so
vital to every interest of the people no
judicial inquiry should have been held to
ascertain whether the people would
approve of a scheme of this kind. Indeed, I think the Government understood
perfectly well that if a scheme of this sort
were submitted to any judicial tribunal
no commissioner, however complacent a
place-man may be, could be relied upon
to produce a scheme of this kind. So
they decided to have no judicial inquiry.
They were afraid that the titled gentleman who was sent down to Fermanagh
and Tyrone would not, if the figures and
facts were presented to him, have the
complacency or hardihood to produce a
scheme of this kind. We see, therefore,

The PRIME MINISTER: The arguments that have been put forward to-day
are not very convincing. To begin with,
as we stand at present under P.R. the
historic City of Londonderry is incorporated along with the county, and all
that we are doing here is to perpetuate in
a minor degree the association of some of
the rural areas along with the Maiden
City. I think everybody is agreed
that with a population of
45,000 it would have been too large,
in comparison with all the other seats
that are mentioned in the Schedule
to this Bill, for one Member to sit for the
City of Derry. On the other hand if you
divide the 45,000 into two it only gives
22,500, which is much smaller than the
population basis of either Antrim
Armagh on the same page. By the scheme
that has been adopted the City of Londonderry division would have a population of
27,404 and the Foyle division a population
of 26,411. If one would cast one's eye
down the page it will be observed that this
harmonises almost exactly with the small
variations that take place through the
whole of the County of Antrim and the
Parliamentary County of Armagh.

The PRIME MINISTER: Now, I
come to the second part of the criticism.
The two hon. Members who have just

close examination that this will be found
to be so. As we sit in this House to-day
there are three hon. Members and an hon.
lady Member sitting on this side against

City and County of Derry. When the
result of the next election takes place I
would be very surprised if exactly
the same proportion is not found in
this House. I do not think from
any point of view that the slightest
objection can be taken to the skilful
manner in which Derry has been
allocated two seats. There is another
point I would like to mention and it is
this. As the City of Derry expands there
is no doubt it will encroach both North
and South and East and West upon that
rural area that has been in the meantime
included for the purpose of the division,
so really a strong argument can be advanced for the way in which the city has
been divided to-day, but no argument I
have heard would persuade me that it
would be better to deal with the matter
in a different way. I think it will be
found as a result of the election that the
representation will be exactly the same as
it is under P.R.

discussing and raising this question of
doing justice to the minority in County

dealt with as North Antrim, but in
order that the matter might be properly
tabled and in proper legal form, I have
dealt with the whole County of Antrim.
Outside the proposed constituency of
North Antrim, with which I propose to
deal, it is a matter of indifference to me
how the other areas may be mapped out,
but the fair sense and judgment of the
Committee should accept the Amendment
with regard to North Antrim. Any
criticism with regard to the constituencies
other than North Antrim would be entirely irrelevant and immaterial, so far
as the purpose of the Amendment is concerned, because they can be mapped out
by the Government in any way they wish
without detrimentally affecting the interests of the Catholics and Nationalists of
the Six Counties.
If I were asked to present this Amendment and endeavour, on my part, to
preserve the franchise for 38,619 Catholics

heavy burden upon my shoulders if I
were asked to present that case to an impartial Committee, but that burden is
lightened and eased by the fact that I
know that, no matter what facts or figures
I may produce, and, no matter what any
Member who may represent County
Antrim could do or say so far as the
Catholic population of Antrim is concerned, it would fall on deaf ears.

ances to which the minority have been

this robbery of the

I have met men in all walks of life, and
every man in County Antrim, every decent Protestant, be he as humble as he
may, be he a professional man or a business man, is ashamed and staggered at the
audacity of the crime you are perpetrating
in regard to the franchise in County
Antrim.
very
There are 191,643 of a population in
County Antrim-and might I say in passing that the hon. Member for Fermanagh
and Tyrone (Mr. Cooper) was
anxious to know how we on this side of
the Committee got the exact figures.
It is a very simple matter. Anyone who
has followed the memorandum that has
been issued in connection with this Bill
and compared the figures will see that
this Bill is founded on the Census of 1911.
That is beyond all question, and that is
where we got our information. As I
stated, there are 191,643 of a population
in County Antrim. Of that 38,619 are
Catholics. We form over 20 per cent. of
the population. We are entitled to a
Member and a half out of the seven seats
into which County Antrim has been
divided. Under Proportional Representation we secured one Member, and we
have claimed no more. But this Bill
beyond all question deprives the Nationalists and Catholics of Antrim of their
most elementary rights of citizenship in
respect of the franchise and Parliamentary representation.
I respect the methods of the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. Grant) who
sits on the benches behind the Government. He gets up and states "Whether
you are entitled to this or not, we will not
give it to you." That, at all events, has
the credit of being honest. But I have
no respect for and I loathe the man who
will get up in this Committee and try to
throw dust in the eyes of the people by
saying "Oh, yes. The Catholics of Antrim are entitled to a representative and
I would love to give them one, but it
cannot be done.' I cannot tolerate that.
As I say, I respect the methods of the
hon. Member for North Belfast who
truthfully speaks out his mind.
Mr. GRANT: Might I ask the hon.
Member when I made the statement to
which he refers? I am not disputing it,
but I would just like to know when I
made that statement.
Mr. MCALLISTER: I was not speaking of the hon. Member's conduct in
regard to this matter alone, but in regard
to his general conduct in this House. He
is never evasive. He is direct, and states
his mind openly, and I have more respect
for that line of conduct than for the man
who has not the courage to do it. I will
show you, in the first instance, how the
constituencies can be marked out to do
justice to the Catholics of County Antrim.
I have gone into this matter very carefully,
and I find there is a constituency in North
Antrim running from Ballintoy down to
Glenarm, compact, self-contained, and
from the picturesque point of view one of
the most regular-looking constituencies
that can be mapped out, with a population
of practically 21,000, which will give
Catholics a majority. We are told in this
House that you cannot differentiate in
population between different constituencies. But how are you going to argue that
you cannot differentiate between a population of 20,000 and 27,000 in the County
Antrim when you differentiate by varying
the population in Belfast 18,000 or 20,000
in a Unionist constituency to 33,000 or
34,000 in a Nationalist constituency? It
cannot be said for the purpose of argument
that Belfast requires special treatment in
this respect. The constituency of Fermanagh is one constituency at the present time
under this Act of the British Government
and you have divided Fermanagh and
Tyrone into eight constituencies-three
with approximately 19,000 and five with.
a population varying from 25,000 to
27.000.
No man can logically or honestly stand
at that Table and argue that whilst to
suit your purpose in Belfast you can make
a variation of 18,000 to 33,000 and in
Fermanagh and Tyrone of 19,000 to
27,000, you cannot for the purpose of
dealing out justice, equity and fair play to
the Catholic people of Antrim vary that
seat from 20,000 to 27,000. I think our
argument is unassailable and unchallengeable. I do not intend to deal with the
constitutional question at length, but may
I say in passing that on that aspect of
Clause 14 the reference to the redistribution of constituencies having regard to the
population, no matter how that Clause is
construed we are, as the lawyers say,
standing on velvet, because even accord.
ing to the numbers of the population this
Bill would not stand five minutes before

Mr. McALLISTER: You have not

It can be tested by the Privy Council,

ask you to do anything unprecedented.
We are told to go step by step with Great
Britain in this House, and I merely ask
you to follow their precedent and create
a constituency similar to some in Scotland and to add to the constituency in
North Antrim, that I have referred to,
three electoral divisions, or four, if you
will, around Toome, and by doing so you
will create a constituency of 26,000 or
27,000 giving a majority to Catholics and
representation in this House. In making this demand-I do not come here to
plead for anything I would refer to the
speech of the Prime Minister, I think it
was on Friday last. When he was justifying this Bill he said that the disparity
in the population in Great Britain was
much greater than in this Bill.
There is another aspect that I am interested to see, and that is how it will
work out in the lobbies when this Amendment is put. Prior to the last election
every Unionist candidate for Antrim
stated in the most definite and emphatic
form that the Catholics of Antrim were
entitled to one representative out of
seven. They stated that at every public.
meeting, and in order to prove their sincerity instead of putting up seven Members they said they would only put up six.
I want to know how these Unionist Members are to go back to their constituents
and explain their breach of an emphatic,
deliberate and unambiguous pledge which
they gave to the electors of Antrim before
seeking election. They received a mandate from their own electors to preserve
intact as a matter of justice and fair play
one seat for the Catholic population of
Antrim. After pledging themselves in
that way are they going to break their
pledge, and instead of being voted out are
the Catholics going to be mapped out by
the candidates and others who were defeated at the last election?
This Bill would not stand before an impartial tribunal ten minutes. What tribunal would stand for the method by
which it is being brought in? As the
hon. Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone
said, instead of a disinterested tribunal
being set up where all parties in Northern
Ireland could give their evidence and
state the facts and have proper constituencies fair and just to everyone mapped
out—instead of that what took place with
regard to Antrim? I was elected third on
the poll to Mr. Speaker and the right
hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Commerce, notwithstanding that mile after
mile of Unionist territory in Antrim was
personated 100 per cent., on the admission of the Unionist sub-agent. Notwithstanding that I was elected third on the
poll. Two
Parliamentary Secretaries
were
substantially behind me. Mr.
Megaw was beaten at the election. Mr.
Megaw and others, after being voted out
of Antrim, sat down at a table in the
Unionist room and mapped me out where
the electors had voted me in. Would
that sort of conduct stand the test for five
minutes before any tribunal? I make
that statement and I defy contradiction.
Mr. Megaw, assisted by Senator Leslie
and others, in the privacy of the Unionist
council chamber, mapped me out where
the electors of Antrim had voted me in.
Mr. DEVLIN: The modern form of
democracy.
Mr. MCALLISTER: I ask the Government of Northern Ireland, before the enlightened public opinion of this 20th
century in a supposedly civilised country,
if they can go before the people and
vindicate an action of that description.

The Prime Minister has stated that he
has spent sleepless nights in working it
out.
Mr. DEVLIN: It is no wonder he did
not sleep.
Mr. MCALLISTER: Mr. Megaw saved
him the trouble of sleepless nights. I
say in solemn earnest if his conscience--
Mr. HEALY: He will have difficulty
finding it.
Mr. MCALLISTER- -if his conscience revives he will, before all this is
over, pass sleepless nights when his conscience moves him, at the atrocity, at the
diabolical outrage and bigoted, narrowminded action of which he has been guilty
during the past two weeks. When his
conscience awakens, this fortnight will
haunt him and cause him many sleepless
nights. By a strange irony of fate, I, a
Catholic representative, one of the seven
representatives of Antrim, am fighting
with my back to the wall defending the
honour, and justice and integrity of the
decent Protestant people of Antrim, for
that is my duty in presenting this Amendment. As I said, the Catholics and
Nationalists of Antrim may be deprived
of the franchise. They may be denied representation, but there is one thing they
cannot be deprived of and that is their
honour. They bear no dishonour with
regard to this Bill. I do say you have
reflected dishonour and discredit and
you have trailed in the dust the name for
decency and fair play of the Protestants
of Antrim.
I came into this House with the highest
ideals to co-operate with every decent,
honest man who was prepared to serve no
party but was prepared to stem the tide
of industrial depression. But since I came
in we have had no opportunity of concentrating upon those vital things to save this
country from starvation and to stop the
ruins of Northern Ireland falling down
upon their heads. We have been compelled by the programme placed before us
to waste our time passing discreditable
Acts of Parliament, fomenting strife and
discord instead of union and brotherly
love that should prevail. I have no doubt
in my mind that as sure as I stand at
this chair before four years are over this
Bill will not save you. No Bill will save
you. Nothing will save you from the vote
of censure and honest indignation of the
Protestant electorate of Northern Ireland.

Mr. COLLINS: It is my duty to
second this Amendment proposed by my
hon. Friend the Member for Antrim.
doing so I want to tell you that County
Antrim has historical associations, and a
very warm place in the hearts of all Irishmen, even of those who do not belong to it.
But the unfortunate County Antrim seems
to have an unfortunate reputation in
history for dirty transactions which is
following it to this day. It is unnecessary
for me to remind you of the fearful transaction that happened in Antrim when they
hanged William Orr. You remember the
transaction in that jury room when they
sat up all night to bring in that unjust
verdict against that man and deprived him
of his life.
Mr. GRANT: What about Castledawson?
Mr. COLLINS: Go and read history,
and do not interrupt. Now history is repeating itself, and we have this Government performing another filthy and dirty
transaction in depriving all the Nationalist
people of Antrim of the representation to
which they are entitled. What are the
facts? They can not be got away from.
The total population of Antrim is 191,643
of all persuasions. Those people are entitled to seven representatives in this
House, and if one divides seven into that
191,643 one will find that 27,379 people
are entitled to one representative. But
what has the Government done? It has
mapped out and
and gerrymandered this
county in such a way that 38,619 Nationalists are left without representation. That
was a skilful thing to do, but it is a thing
the Government cannot justify.
Prime Minister said that it was his wish
that all parties in this House should have
about the same representation after this
dirty work is done. Here is one county
in which he is depriving the Nationalists
of representation, and there is no other

That is, 20,026 persons of other denominations can elect one representative

our people.

South Armagh before P.R. was introduced, and they have crushed out of the
new division of South Armagh the following district electoral divisions. The district electoral division of Mullaghglass,
which contains a large Unionist majority,
and which always belonged to South
Armagh; the district electoral divisions of
Tullyhappy, Mountnorris, Drumbanagher,
and Poyntzpass, in all of which there are

down the Nationalists portion of the Primatial city, so that they will have a
Unionist supporter of the Government to
represent Mid Armagh, and there will be
only one Nationalist representative in the

for this. No reason whatever can be
given for it, because if there were any
attempt at fair play the two Nationalist
representatives for Armagh would have
remained. It could have been done by

in these Unionist district electoral areas
that I have told you about, and putting
out the urban district of Keady and those
other Nationalist areas which are some
twenty miles away from Newry.

even to gerrymander the figures of the
population. They made the population
for North Armagh 26,000, the Central
Division of Armagh, 27.000 odd, and

crushed in no less than 28,880 people. It

principle of the 1920 Act which states:
Provided that in any new distribution
the number of the members shall not be
altered, and due regard shall be had to

these grounds I think the Amendment I

The argument of the Prime Minister

by the Opposition.

steamroller?

here and simply be a registering machine,
a rubber stamp for the work done by the
Unionist clubs in the country, and approved in the Government offices, then I
say Parliamentary representation in
Northern Ireland is a hollow sham, and
this Parliament is a mere luxury, performing no useful function. It would be well
that the people of Northern Ireland should
address their attention to the proceedings
before the Committee during this week,
particularly if the Government refuse this
Amendment and in view of their refusal
of the last Amendment. In the eyes of
the people of Northern Ireland there can
be no justification, no defence offered for
refusing the suggestion of my hon. Friend,
the Member for Down, that this transfer
should be made from one Nationalist constituency to another.
If the Prime Minister refuses this
Amendment I would ask him to tell us
really what our function is here. As an
Opposition we have been making constructive suggestions which, had they been
accepted, would have promoted a better
feeling of harmony, would have been to
the interest of Northern Ireland as a
whole, and would have consolidated the
position of this Parliament by giving us
something of real substance. If this
Parliament is being made a farce at the
present time it is by the action of the
Government in refusing to accept the
Amendment just voted on, and if they
further insult the Committee by refusing
to accept this Amendment, then I say the
Government of Northern Ireland are
hopeless.

Reading when he said if there was any

We were discussing during the earlier
part of this afternoon the question of the
gerrymandering of the Mourne Mountains
and now we come to the gerrymandering
of Lough Erne. A special Resolution
was introduced into this House some time
ago dealing with personation, and a promise was given that that evil would be
dealt with quickly. Now I think that,
great as the evil of personation may be,
it pales into insignificance in comparison
with the evil of gerrymandering.
people who take part in personation
are usually folk who are prompted by the
bravado of the thing on the one hand or
by the desire to earn a few shillings on
the other hand, but the people who take
part in gerrymandering are of a different
type. They are the people who sit on
those benches and their supporters outside. They are the Prime Minister and
his colleagues in the Cabinet, and if it is
disgraceful, and I hold it is, for a woman
of the working class to go into a booth
and personate her neighbours then it is
a great deal more disgraceful for the
Prime Minister to father this scheme of
gerrymandering.
Mr. GORDON: Do your people not believe in gerrymandering?
Mr. HEALY: We have never gerrymandered anybody. (Hon. Members:
Oh! Oh!) You have heard a good many
statements with regard to the position in
County Antrim where 38,000 electors are
left without representation, but I think
County Fermanagh presents an even
worse problem than that. The Attorney-
General explained yesterday why a seat
could not be found for the 38,000
Nationalists in County Antrim. He
pointed out that the minority being so
scattered, the formation of an area to
contain a Nationalist majority would be
what he describes as impossible, and the
Prime Minister pointed out later on with
regard to the question of the distribution
of the population a difficulty on somewhat
similar lines.
If the Attorney-General will look at the
three constituencies he has formed in
County Fermanagh I think he will either
be ashamed of the plea he made yesterday
or else it is impossible to arouse shame
on those benches, and if the Prime Minister will look at this question of the distribution of population he will find that
while he could not give 38,000 people in
County Antrim one representative he
could give 12,000 in County Fermanagh
one. The 38,000 in Antrim were his opponents and the 12,000 in Fermanagh are
his friends. That is the only difference.
There is no use in this smug hypocrisy,
in standing up and making statements
on those benches if the Members who sit
there know they are not the truth. The
hon. Member (Mr. Cooper) was controverting here the other evening some
figures I had given with regard to the

offered to hand me during the debate a
map showing that it covered only a distance of 35 miles. I have here a map
prepared by the Northern Government,
and also a ruler.

inches, with 4 miles to the inch, which
makes 68 miles. If the hon. Member
wants the details I can give them.
Mr. COOPER: Show me them and
I will believe you.
Mr. HEALY: I will give him the

that when these facts are given he will

The status of the Dominions, both

stated before, we were faced with the possibility on the one hand of still treating
the two separate counties of Tyrone and
Fermanagh as one Parliamentary unit and

Ulster like to be counties. I think I have

in being able to say I represent County
Down. Although my brother has represented County Antrim for many years in

he has preferred to represent County
Antrim. And I think it is a little bit

Therefore, when the chance came of dividing it back and saying to a Fermanagh

Mr. LEEKE: We have heard a lot
to-day regarding Fermanagh and Tyrone
and the divisions formed there by the

It undoubtedly retains the old names of
the Foyle and the Bann, but the geographical line is something new and
picturesque, and is irrespective of any
political or electoral boundary. It runs
away to the mountains of Fermanagh,
and it seems to me that it will always be
impossible to obtain anything like a true
reflex of public opinion owing to the difficulty of getting people to the poll.
Then we come to the next two constituencies, which look very small. They
look lob-sided; in fact, I hardly know
Derry County from this map. Londonderry is the main room, the kitchen, and
the next two constituencies are the bedrooms. They are very small and all
corners, and I do not think that if the
people of County Derry, even the supporters of the Government, saw this map
of these constituencies they would be
satisfied with them. I hope that for
their own sakes the two Unionist representatives of County Derry had nothing.

emphatic protest against Part III of this
Schedule standing part. Yesterday I
asked a question in this House as to the

Home Affairs, that 3,530 graduates were
entitled to vote in Northern Ireland for
four Members for Queen's University. In
other words, it means that 900 University
graduates are equal to 34,000 electors in
the Protestant area of Woodvale, Belfast.
Nine hundred University graduates are
equal to 33,000 of the population in Central division of Belfast. Nine hundred
graduates are equal to 29,000 of the population in Falls, and 900 graduates are equal
to a population of 31,000 in St. Anne's.
Now, I would like to hear the representative of the University getting up in this
House and saying that 900 University

even 10,000 ordinary electors-that it is
equitable that 900 graduates should have

I am speaking now apart
from politics altogether. This hon. and
learned Gentleman occupied a peculiarly

But
tary of the Minister of Education.
there is a caucus in the University, which
should be free from caucuses, and which

They did not like some of the opinions
that he held in regard to the administration of the Education Act, and they proceeded by the methods of the caucus, unworthy of ward politics, to put him out of
that position. I believe in fair play even
to opponents, and this has not really
established my confidence in universities,
even though this House would be richer
for the entrance into it of octogenarians,
who if they never offered any words of

say that that in itself is one of the reasons
why we should not have university representation.
In the second place, the University and
its representatives ought to be an example
in one thing which is needed, and that is
in the manifestation of a spirit of intellectual independence. You go to any
university in Europe, and you will find
that the great protagonists of causes are
university professors. I do not say that
they are very good guides-I believe that
Bolshevism was created by professors of
universities but in an atmosphere like
that of Northern Ireland, where if there
is anything needed it is a demonstration
of independent thought, we never get it
from the University that claims to have
four representatives here.
They attach themselves to a political
party, and they are not faithful to the
political party to which they attach themselves, for if they were they would not
have turned down Mr. Robb-the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education-the way they did the other
day. They are not faithful even to their
own party, and what claim can they have
to a specially delegated right to 3,000 odd
graduates to return four Members to this
House? Why, in the constituency of
West Belfast, which I speak for at the
moment, 62,000 of us can only return two
Members, while 3,300 graduates can return four Members.
In addition to that, as my hon. Friend
has pointed out, those people have votes as
citizens if they live in Northern Ireland.
I would not give a vote to any man unless
he was a citizen. Those men, if they are
not citizens, have not to obey our laws;
they have not to be subjected to our administration, they have not to conform
to any of our conventions, they can only
view us from afar, and because they view
us from afar they have the right to have
four Members as against the two Members
given to 62,000 people who have to live
under your laws, are affected by your
legislation, are subjected to your administration, and who have to suffer whatever
grievances there are to be suffered under
your régime. The thing is not arguable.
In the old days the universities got
representation not because they were homes
of culture, though they were, and produced some of the mightiest intellects the
world has ever known, but because the
universities were peopled by rich men,
and it is that tradition of giving special
representation to the wealthier classes
that has been running through all the intervening period, and they have preserved
that right ever since. Apart altogether

from the feeling of resentment against

I would be glad in our modern system if

giving us the advantage of their wide experience, their genius or their knowledge
in any branch of intellectual or commercial activity, I would be in favour of coopting them in Parliament. But this

Mr. DEVLIN- -and I am

Wednesday, 27th March, 1929.
The House met at Three of the Clock.
The Clerk at the Table informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
Speaker from this day's Sitting.
Whereupon Mr. Moles, the Chairman
of Ways and Means, proceeded to the
Table, and, after Prayers, took the Chair
as Deputy-Speaker, pursuant to the
Standing Order.

Oral Answers to Questions.
QUEEN'S UNIVERSITY
PARLIA-
MENTARY ELECTORS.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state how
many of the electors entitled to vote as
graduates of Queen's University are resident in Northern Ireland, and how
many of those entitled to vote do not live
under the jurisdiction of the Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am informed by
the Registration Officer for the Queen's
University that the information asked
for by the hon. Member is not available,
as the Register of Electors for the University is at present being reprinted. I
shall, however, be happy to supply the
hon. Member with the information desired as soon as the Register is returned
from the printer.
RECRUITMENT OF POLICE-
WOMEN.
2. Mr HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
arrangements made for the recruitment of
policewomen, their initial salaries, age
limit, and duties, together with the number required.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There are at
present two policewomen attached to the
Royal Ulster Constabulary in Belfast city
for special duties. These policewomen
were taken over by the R.Ü.C. on the
disbandment of the R.I.C. At the time
of the transfer they were employed on a
temporary basis only, but in pursuance of
the recommendation of the Departmental
Committee of Inquiry on Police Reorganisation in Northern Ireland of 1922 they
were placed on a regular scale of pay commencing at 42s a week and rising by
annual increments of 2s to 60s a week.
They also receive an allowance for the
provision of uniform.
The special duties on which these two
policewomen are engaged include the taking of statements from women and
children, acting as escorts to female
prisoners, assisting in looking after
juveniles on probation, attendance on
women jurors and generally such other
duties as can be more appropriately
carried out by women.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask the Home
Secretary whether he had any of these
policewomen engaged in the investigation
of the Whan casę?
That
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER:
really does not arise out of this question.
It would be better to put down a distinct
question on that point.
Mr. BEATTIE: Of course, it does not
arise directly, but it does indirectly. If
the Minister of Home Affairs was left to
his own discretion I am sure he would
answer the question.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: The object
of a supplementary question is to supplement the related matter in the original
question. There is no relevance in this
case, and it would be better to put down
a distinct question.
HOME FOR MENTALLY DEFECTIVE
CHILDREN.
3. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON (for
Mr. Thomas Henderson) asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state if
the Government have secured a site for the
erection of a home for mentally defective
children, and whether he can state when it
is the intention of the Government to start
building operations.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
27 MARCH 1929
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb): I have been asked
to reply to this question.
The question of the acquisition of a site
for the purpose stated is not at present
under consideration as the Government is
in negotiation with a view to ascertaining
if suitable arrangements can be made with
the trustees of a local institution for the
conduct of a home for educable mentally
deficient children.
PERSONATION-COMMITTEE OF
INQUIRY.
4. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
now state the composition of the Committee of Inquiry into the question of personation at elections.
The following question stood on the
Paper in the name of Mr. JOHNSTONE:
5. To ask the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can give the House any further
information in regard to the Committee to
be set up to inquire into the most suitable
method to prevent personation at elections
in Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I propose to
answer this question as well as the following question on the Order Paper together.
As I have already stated in this House,
the Committee is a small one composed of
experts, and the following have been appointed as the members:-
Mr. R. H. Carson, Crown Solicitor,
Omagh.
Sir F. Henry Miller, Town Clerk and
Town Solicitor, Londonderry.
Mr. P. J. O'Donoghue, Barrister-at-
Law and Resident Magistrate.
Mr. Samuel Porter, Barrister-at-Law.
Mr. James Quail, Solicitor and Under-
Sheriff, City of Belfast.
Mr. P. J. O'Donoghue has been appointed as Chairman of the Committee.
The Terms of Reference of the Committee are as follow:-
:-
"To inquire into the law relating to
personation at Parliamentary and Local
Government elections and to make
recommendations how these laws might
suitably be amended so as to secure the
prevention of this evil.”
Colonel WOODS: If the Committee
recommended that compulsory voting
would be a good solution of the difficulty,
would this be considered by the
Government?
Mr.
DEPUTY-SPEAKER:
That
would be anticipating the findings of the
Committee, which 18 not within the
province of the House at the moment.
RICHHILL TRAINING SCHEME.
6. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON (for
Mr. Thomas Henderson) asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state what steps
his Department take to ensure that when
men are sent to Canada under the Richhill
Training Scheme, farmers pay the wages
proposed under the contract when the men
enter their employment; and whether he
can state if any Government representatives visit the farms to see that these men
are properly housed and fed.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The Canadian Government Department
of Immigration and Colonization arranges
for the placing in employment of men
arriving in Canada from the Richhill
Centre and other corresponding centres in
Great Britain and also for the subsequent
supervision of these men by inspectors,
who periodically visit the farms where the
men are employed to ascertain if they are
properly treated by the farmers. In the
case of a trainee being dissatisfied with his
condition he is transferred to another farm
if he so desires. I have made exhaustive
inquiries myself on the spot and am satisfied that proper supervision is exercised
by the Canadian Government officials.

watering cattle; and what steps he proposes to take to expedite the building of
a school in this area, and so put a stop
to the pollution of this stream, which is
endangering the health of the children in
the neighbourhood.

with regard to the Education Act; and

Mr. ROBB: I have seen the series of

The Government would welcome an expression of the views of all persons interested in suggestions for Amendments of
the Education Act, including the
managers referred to.
Mr. HEALY: Does this not suggest a

House and outside it must form his own

Mr. HEALY: I have no doubt the

9. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked
the Prime Minister whether he can state
the reason for the continued delay in publishing the Report of the Leaseholders'
and Town Tenants' Committee, and
whether he can state if the necessary legislation will be introduced before the dissolution of this Parliament.

asked to answer this question.

NEW SCHOOL IN MAY STREET,
BELFAST.
10. Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Finance whether he

The MINISTER of Finance (Mr.
Pollock): The owner of the derelict buildings on the May Street site was Mr.
William Charles Pollock, of Ballymoney,
while the ground landlord was Mrs.
Florence Joy.
As explained to this House at the date
of purchase, the future use to which the
ground would be put was left over for later

the Belfast Education Authority.
The amount paid to the vendor was

sum in respect of compensation for losses
previously incurred, the amount of which
cannot be definitely determined, as the
final price was left as a composite figure.
Since the original purchase, the ground
rent has been acquired by the Ministry at
the price of £1,225.

NORTH ANTRIM REGIONAL EDU-
CATION COMMITTEE.
Mr. BEATTIE: The following question
was on the Order Paper on Monday, 25th
inst., and was postponed until to-day:
Oral Answers.
Easter Adjournment.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
To ask the Parliamentary Secretary of
the Ministry of Education whether the
three urban district councils in the area
of operation of North Antrim Regional
Education Committee, after the urban
district council elections, superseded their
representatives on the said Committee and
appointed other representatives; whether
the new representatives of two of these
councils (Portrush and Ballycastle) were
summoned by the Secretary of the
Regional Committee to attend its meetings; whether the new representatives of
the remaining council (Ballycastle) were
not summoned to the Committee by the
Secretary; whether the Secretary summoned the former representatives whom
the urban district council had dismissed;
and whether the Secretary of a Regional
Education Committee has the right to
veto appointments to these Committees
and to summon former members to attend,
whose constituent councils have terminated their appointments.
Mr. ROBB: At a meeting of the North
Antrim Regional Education Committee,
held on 14th February last, letters from
the Antrim County Council were read
giving the names of two gentlemen who
had been appointed as their representatives upon the Regional Committee by
the Urban District Councils of Ballycastle and Portrush in place of former
representatives who were no longer members of those Urban Councils. The
Minutes record that at the meeting of the
Regional Education Committee, held on
14th March, a letter was received from
the Ballymoney Urban District Council
forwarding the names of two gentlemen
and stating that they had been appointed
by the Urban District Council as its representatives. This letter was forwarded
by the Regional Committee to the Secretary of the Antrim County Council.
As the two gentlemen who represented
Ballymoney Urban District Council immediately prior to the elections of last
January are still members of that
Council they are not, subject to fulfilment of the other conditions of the
scheme, obliged by the scheme under
which Regional Education Committees in
County Antrim are appointed, to vacate
their appointments upon the North Antrim Regional Education Committee until
June, 1930.
It would thus appear that the action
of the Secretary of the North Antrim
Regional Education Committee in continuing to summon the representatives of
Ballymoney Urban District Council was
quite correct.

Mr. DEVLIN: I rise for the purpose
of moving this Amendment in order to
give the Members of the House a considerable time to give thought to the various
proposals that were adumbrated in the
speech from the Throne, and which it was
impossible for the House to give adequate
consideration to in view of the way our
time has been occupied in dealing with
the gerrymandering Bill. I understand
that the Budget is to be introduced into
the British Parliament on the 17th
April, and we cannot consider our Budget
until the Budget of the Imperial Chancellor of the Exchequer has been presented. Therefore, it is very important
that we should have time to consider the
Budget proposals of the Imperial Chancellor of the Exchequer before we come to
the consideration of our own, which will
be based on that financial statement. In
addition to that there is a Derating Bill,
which has been one of the chief ornaments
in the political windows of both the reactionary parties in this country and
England. Up to the present the English
House of Commons has had an opportunity
of discussing the derating proposals of
their Government. We have never had a
single moment of Parliamentary time devoted to our derating proposals.
Mr. POLLOCK:
Oh, yes.
Mr. DEVLIN: The Minister of
Finance no doubt made an elaborate and
comprehensive statement at a Unionist
meeting somewhere or other-
Mr. POLLOCK : In the House.
Mr. DEVLIN-before Parliament
met. I thought at the time if they were
to introduce a new principle in legislative
finance in Northern Ireland naturally the
proper place for the statement to be made
would not be at a small political meeting
in a small room in a back street in Cromac
ward, but here in the Northern Parliament. I may be, perhaps, making too
large a demand on the ordinary Parliamentary conventions, but in the simplicity
of my Parliamentary heart I imagined
that if there was one place above all
others where a great new idea-and I bethat if there was one place above all
visionary politicians either on this side or
in England have fashioned during the
last seven or eight years I imagined
that a new idea of that sort would have
been brought before this House, and that
the proposals would have been explained
in all detail, but that was not done.
There is a series of Bills mentioned in
the King's Speech that we have not had
printed yet, and about which we know
nothing. There are also the Estimatesthe most important part of our Parliamentary deliberations, because we have
this Session before the general election,
in order to enlighten the electorate on the
future of their responsibility, to pursue
a policy in regard to these Estimates of
meticulous dissection and analysis. In
view of these facts, I think it is most

at least to Members to turn over in their

presented for our consideration. I, there
fore, beg to move the Amendment.

I proposed this Amendment before, but
owing to the absence of my colleague in

not at all certain what the ultimate effect

divisions in North Belfast to some slight
extent. If the Polling District B is withdrawn from Oldpark and put into
Shankill division, and Polling District D
is taken out of Shankill and put into Oldpark it will still maintain that principle
which the Prime Minister enunciated
when introducing this Bill, that it would
only be in polling districts that any

This Amendment does not ask you to
cut across any particular polling district,

district from one division to another. As

Reading speech in response to an interjection of my own, that he was prepared to

Let me just refer to one other matter.
I will not go back to Sir Laming Worthington Evans's pledge. I intended to deal

I would not have fought against this

feeling that I have done if it merely

think there is a more fatal objection to
it, and that is, that this Measure was
fashioned and intended to stifle, to destroy, and to drive out of this House all
independent thought. We are not fools
in this House. One is not necessarily a
fool because he is elected to the Ulster
Parliament. We followed the peregrinations of Ministers opposite, we
watched their itineraries from one place

House.
No party politician, I admit, likes
Independents, they are always, of course,
objectionable to the machine. But the
one thing that would have justified this
Parliament was not to make it a machine
Parliament. You should have made it a
place in which various shades of opinion.
gathered for the purpose of contributing
whatever they could contribute to the
general welfare and prosperity and advancement of the section of the Province
in which we live. The fatal mistake made
by this Parliament from the very first
was to fashion it upon the lines of the
Imperial Parliament. It should have
been what it is: a rather unintelligent
county council. We should have come
here to sit round a table, or perhaps it
would be more acceptable if I said to sit
as a board of directors. We should have
sat round a table. We should have had
no party whips. We should have had
none of the picturesque machinery. We
should have remembered we were dealing
only with an area covering a few counties, with a population not greater than
the population of Glasgow.
We should have remembered that we
have got away-though they try to bring
us back to it from the old passions and
hatreds, and feuds, and religious dissensions that blighted and cursed and
poisoned our public life for nearly a century. We had got away from those
things, and our business was to sit down
at a table, without party whips, and to
let every man contribute whatever gift
he had to the common reservoir of general
wisdom in the interests of the community
as a whole. If one man knew something
about the land question, let him give his
views. If another man knew something
about the liquor question, let him give
his views. If some one knew something
about local option, let him give his views
-and they should support me, because
in a few days they will be no longer articulate. If another knew something about
the law, let him give his views.
another knew something about commerce
and industry, let him give his views. We
should have gathered here in a small
assembly and applied ourselves to the one
task, and the only task which in my judgment counts for anything in the affairs of
Northern Ireland, namely, that of reducing unemployment, of reconstructing our
industrial system, of grappling with
those economic questions that are pressing closely upon our people, of taking
advantage of the money we have to clear
away slums, of trying to destroy hunger
and thirst and povery. These are not
things that are to be done by full dress
debates, by one man standing up on the
other side of the House and making a
speech.

That is from the "Irish Independent,"
and a peculiar thing about the election is
that under P.R., which is supposed to give
fair play to minorities, and which is supposed to give every minority an opportunity to assert itself, there was not a
single Protestant elected to the Cork City
Council.
Analysing the figures of the election
under P.R., I find that while the Independents, with an aggregate vote of 4,063,
were able to return seven members, the
Labour men, with a vote of 2,329, were
only able to return two members. In
other words, it took 1,164 Labour votes
to secure a representative, while 580 votes
were able to return an Independent.
Evidently the Independents do not count
for much even in the city of Cork; they
are a rather cheap commodity. For this
and other reasons I heartily support the

have been imposed upon the people of

not doing an injustice to anyone in removing it from the Statute Book, having a
