FLOODING IN DOWNPATRICK
DISTRICT.
3. Mr. P. O'NEILL asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether anything has yet
been done regarding the periodical flooding in the Urban District of Downpatrick,
and, if not, what is the cause of the delay.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates). No scheme for the
drainage of Downpatrick has been submitted to my Department by the Down
County Council, which, under the Drainage Act (Northern Ireland), 1925, must,
in the first instance, submit a scheme for
carrying out any drainage works which
may be necessary in County Down.
As pointed out by me in this House on
the 28th March, 1928, the County Council, however, has given the matter careful
and constant attention during the past
few years, and has shown itself to be fully
alive to the serious nature of its responsibilities in this regard.
From the correspondence which has
passed between the County Council and
my Department, it appears that the
County Council is unable to reach an
agreement with the Downpatrick Urban
District Council as to the extent of the
area which would be benefited by and
should, therefore, bear the cost of a scheme
such as is being proposed, and the former
body appears to be unwilling to submit a
scheme for confirmation until these matters have been settled and
a joint
recommendation as to the area of charge
can be put forward with it. The question
in dispute is one of very considerable
difficulty, involving as it does not merely
the manner of raising a large sum of
money from the ratepayers, but also
certain questions of a highly technical
nature, e.g., the proportions in which the
Urban District and the adjacent rural
areas would respectively be benefited by a
drainage scheme, and also the extent to
which the provision of an effective sewerage
system for the Urban District is depend.
ent upon the carrying out of such a
scheme.
The Ministry of Home Affairs, though
it has no statutory functions in the matter until a scheme has been formulated
and presented for confirmation, has expressed its willingness to assist the County
Council, in so far as its statutory powers
admit, in agreeing to the adoption of a
procedure which would enable an area of
charge for the preliminary expenses in
connection with the preparation and confirmation of a scheme agreeable to all
persons concerned, to be fixed provisionally
before any such expenditure would be
incurred.
Mr. P. O'NEILL: Might I ask the
right hon. Gentleman if neither of these
two authorities proposed a scheme what
is to happen in this place that is so constantly flooded for so many years?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer is
perfectly obvious. If the representatives
of the ratepayers do not give satisfaction
to the ratepayers the ratepayers have the
matter in their own hands.
Mr. DEVLIN: If the ratepayers cannot flood them are they to flood the ratepayers? (Laughter).
WORKING OF RENT RESTRIC-
TIONS ACT.
4. Mr. HEALY (for Mr. Beattie)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether it is a fact that in cases of houses
under £8 valuation becoming vacant,
landlords are compelling the incoming
tenants to enter into a hire purchase
agreement for a period of years, and
charging an excessive rent for them;
whether this is a violation of the Rent
Restriction Act; and what action he proposes to take in the matter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have not received any complaints that landlords are
refusing to relet houses of £8 valuation
and under which become vacant.
It is not illegal nor contrary to the provisions of the Rent Restrictions Acts for
an owner to sell a house of which he has
obtained possession, and to accept payment of the price by instalments.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Insurance (Transitional
Provisions Amendment) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The PARLIAMENTRY SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR
(Mr. Gordon): In moving the Second
Reading of this Bill I would invite the
co-operation of every Section of the
House having the interest of the unemployed at heart to assist in passing this
Measure into law. We all recognise that
the question of unemployment, affecting
as it does so many of our working people,
is a big and difficult problem, a solution
of which can only be found in obtaining
a market for the goods which we manufacture. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
But we are not without hope-neither are
we gloomy or morbid. We believe that
our industries will recover their former
prosperity. They are gradually improving and we are anxious that that improvement should continue.
It will be within the recollection of the
House that the Unemployment Insurance
Act of 1928 reconstructed, to a very great
extent, the conditions governing unemployment insurance, and, amongst other
things, provided that a statutory condition for the receipt of unemployment
benefit would be that the insured
claimant must have 30 contributions
standing to his credit. It further provided that his claim to benefit would be
examined periodically, in order to find
whether he still conformed to the "30
contributions condition" laid down in the
Act. I have no doubt that hon. Memhers are aware that this change in the
statutory conditions was made on the
recommendation of the Blanesborough
Committee-which, as you all know, was
composed of different parties in the Imperial House of Commons, as well as
others outside the House.
This Committee, however, recognised
the unreasonableness of enforcing this
first statutory condition, whilst the trade
conditions of the country were abnormal
and unemployment remained at a high
peak, and consequently a further recommendation was made. This was that a
period should elapse before the new conditions of the Act became operative, and
during such a period modified conditions
should operate to enable the unemployed
applicant to draw benefit, even although
he failed to show the necessary 30 contributions over the past two years. This
meant that transitional conditions for a
limited period were introduced into the
1928 Act, and we propose in this Bill to
prolong these transitional conditions in
the interest of the unemployed, and make
it easier for unemployed persons to obtain
benefit.
In order to refresh the minds of hon.
Members, I will briefly state what these
transitional conditions are under which
the applicant for benefit is tested. He
must prove that he had eight contributions
paid during the last two years, or 30
contributions at any time. He must, of
course, show that he was normally employed in an insurable occupation, and
that he had a reasonable amount of insurable employment during the last two
years.
These conditions are applicable
to all claimants over 18 years of age, and
I think hon. Members will agree that
they are neither harsh nor unreasonable,
and will not, I hope, press unduly upon
any applicant who is insured. They are
limited in their operation and come to an
end on April 19th.
At the present moment a number of
persons drawing benefit will cease to be
entitled under the 1928 Act if it remains
unamended. Many are in an unfortunate position of being unable to find
employment, and the Government has a
real and deep concern for these people.
This Bill is a proof of our desire to tide
them over a period of depression, and is
an indication of our sympathy with them.
as they struggle through a difficult and
harassing time bravely facing an abnormal
situation. I hope that this Bill will
meet with the unanimous support of all
hon. Members in the House. It is the
desire of the Government to move along
lines similar to those in the Imperial.
House.
The recent Insurance Agreement makes
it possible to conform to British
1583 Unemployment Insurance Bill--

Mr. Gordon]
this beneficent Measure.
standards and pay benefits on the same
basis as are being paid in Great Britain.
Those who have made a study of employment and unemployment will recognise
the difficulty of definitely stating what
the position might be in six or twelve
months time. We are extending the
transitional period for twelve months,
and hope by then that the depressing
conditions will have disappeared, and
that men and women will again become
absorbed in the industries of the country.
But whilst unemployed we want them to
feel a sense of greater financial security.
The uncertainty which they would have
faced if the conditions were to remain unaltered will now be removed by this Measure. The unemployed person can now make
renewed efforts to obtain work stimulated
by the knowledge that his rights to
benefit are made easier through the Bill
which I now invite the House to give a
Second Reading.
I should say to the Members present
that we are anxious that this Bill should
be brought into law at the earliest opportunity, and I would invite the support
and co-operation of those who are
interested in the conditions of affairs as
they exist at the present time with regard
to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
We are desirous that the transitional conditions shall be extended for a further
period of twelve months. I invite hon.
Members to assist the Government in
passing this Measure so that it will bring
much-needed help to those members of
the community who are suffering from
unemployment, and whose benefit is likely
to be cut off at an early date. I have
much pleasure in moving the Second
Reading of this Bill. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
Mr. Wm. McMULLEN: I am sure
the House is delighted to have had the

effort from the hon. Gentleman who has
just resumed his seat. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). During the time the hon.
Gentleman was speaking I imagined he
was in the hustings at the forthcoming
general election, and I rather thought that
his was a good general election speech,
because after all there was a tremendous
amount of camouflage in the hon.
Gentleman's speech. Anyone listening
to the hon. Gentleman would assume for
a moment that the Government were
entirely responsible for the introduction of
Nothing could
be further from the truth. This Government is slavishly following the step
decided upon by the British Parliament.
I do not want to withhold any meed of

I think I prophesied, when

The Blanesborough Committee that the

in Great Britain, unfortunately, has

If the Government wanted to do something of importance, from the point of

to the British Parliament that legislation
that is suitable for Great Britain is not

because it is possible for people to get
employment more readily in Great
Britain, owing to the many and varied
industries that exist in that country,

that point of view I am certainly pleased

regard to cotton.
Surely the Northern Government, if
they look at this matter in a sensible way,
will see that the remedy for it is not
merely extending the period for a further
twelve months but getting at the very
roots of the trouble. The Minister of
Agriculture, if he were here, would
realize that butter and bacon are practically in the same parlous plight as linen.

Nursing Homes Bill
The imports of butter and bacon into
Northern Ireland have actually increased
during the last two years.
If that be so
surely the Northern Government ought to
visualize some policy of reversing that condition of things.
I notice from a speech of the Leader of
the Government party in England that
they are going to tackle the question of
Protection in the new Parliament. The
Northern Parliament have no power whatever to safeguard themselves if the
English electorate want another period of
Free Trade. If that is so, the Northern
Government must be satisfied to see the
quays of Belfast filled with foreign linen,
foreign cotton, foreign bacon, foreign
eggs, and other commodities.
Do they
not realize the hapless condition in
which they stand due entirely to the
limitations imposed by the 1920 Act?
The hon. Member (Mr. Grant) who
spoke last controverted the statement of
my hon. Friend (Mr. William McMullen)
on this side of the House, and said the
English Labour party were not prepared
to give more favourable terms to the unemployed in Northern Ireland than in
Great Britain, but I think the fact that
the percentage of unemployment has been
higher in Northern Ireland for a long

Fund shows they have at all events been
giving you preferential treatment in that

point seriously contend that the workers.
in Northern Ireland should suffer.
The unemployed in the City of Belfast
and in the City of Derry may benefit by

to the colonies shows that they cannot
secure constant employment-
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid my

Midwives and Nursing Homes Bill (S.)
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think very
few words are necessary for me to introduce this Bill. The urgency of it has
been impressed upon me from time to time
by both the medical and nursing professions. The Bill is divided into two
parts and generally follows the English
Act. The first part deals with some
Amendments which are necessary in connection with the Midwives Act of 1918.
The other part of the Bill deals entirely
with the registration and supervision of
nursing homes, including maternity homes.
With regard to Clause I of the Bill,
this proposes to amend Section 1, subsection 2 of the Midwives (Ireland) Act,
1918, which provides that no woman, unless certified under that Act, should use
the name "midwife." It also provides
that that woman should not attend for
gain any woman in childbirth unless
under the direction of a medical practitioner.
The object of this Section, as hon.
Members will appreciate, was to ensure
that a woman in childbirth should only
be attended by individuals who were
properly qualified. Up to the passing of
that Act, unskilled attention in midwifery cases had been one of the most
serious causes of maternal mortality, and
the result of the passing of this Act has
had a most beneficial result. Unfortunately, however, it has been found that
Nursing Homes Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
there are one or two defects in that Act
which leave considerable loopholes for
the unskilled practitioner. It is a curious
thing that while the Act prevents an untrained woman attending a midwifery
case, it does not prohibit an unskilled
man attending in such a case.
Then there is a further defect. It has
been found that it is frequently difficult
to prove the unskilled practitioner has
attended a midwifery case for the purpose
of gain, and, therefore, we propose in this
Bill to provide that no person, either male
or female, who is not properly qualified
shall attend a woman in childbirth except
under the personal direction and supervision of a qualified medical practitioner.
I might point out here that the medical
practitioner will have to remain in constant attendance where the midwife is not
qualified. I should also point out that
we make provision for the case of assistance given in the case of sudden or
urgent necessity, and we also except from
the provision of the Clause persons who
are undergoing training.
There is just one other Clause-Clause
11-which deals with a defect which has
arisen from time to time under the 1918
Act. The Act of 1918 provides for the
calling in of medical assistance in the case
of emergency, and makes the local
authority, that is the County Council or
the County Borough Council as the case
may be, responsible for the payment of
the doctor's fees, unless the patient is entitled to medical relief under the Poor
Relief Act, when in that case, the Board
of Guardians would be liable.
The wording of the Section of the 1918
Act has caused some difficulty in deciding what case should be paid for by the
Council, and what case should be paid for
by the Guardians, and it is desirable to
have some test which could be easily
applied to determine the liability, and
accordingly we propose that the County
Council, or the County Borough Council,
as the case may be, will be liable, unless
the patient has obtained a ticket for
medical attention under Section 9 of the
Poor Relief Act, 1815.
Turning to the second part of the Bill
which deals with the registration and
supervision of nursing homes, up to the
present time these homes have not been
required to be registered, or to be subject
to any supervision, and while it is perfectly true that in the majority of cases
these homes do maintain a high standard
both as to the premises and as to the staffing arrangements, it is very desirable that
there should be a general standard of
efficiency.
The principle of the Bill is that no one
in the future will be allowed to carry on
a nursing home without having first
obtained from the local authority a
licence for the purpose. The authority
for the purpose will be the County Council
or the County Borough Council, as the
case may be.
The local authority may refuse a licence
on certain specific grounds, which are set
out in the Sixth Clause of the Bill. Perhaps I might summarise the position as
follows:-
The authority may refuse a licence on
the ground of :-
. -
(1) The unsuitability of the applicant, or of some person employed by
him in the home;
(2) The unsuitability of the premises
and the equipment; and
(3) The unsuitability of the staff.
For example, they may refuse it if the
applicant or any person employed by him
or her at the home is not a fit person,
whether by reason of age or otherwise, to
carry on, or be employed in, a nursing
home of the description as is applied for.
In the second place, they may refuse
an application on the grounds that for
reasons connected with the constitution,
construction, accommodation or equipment, the house or premises used in connection therewith are not fit to be used for
a nursing home of the kind; or again the
application may be refused on the ground
that a nursing home was about to be used
for purposes which were improper or undesirable.
The remaining reasons for which a
licence may be refused are those connected with the qualifications of the
staff, and in this connection I would draw
the attention of the House to the distinction between the provisions as regards
homes which are in existence at the date
of the passing of the Act and those which
came into existence afterwards. There is
a large number of houses where the person
in charge is not a qualified nurse, though
she has, at her disposal, a staff which is
properly qualified, and there can be no
doubt that it would create hardships to
apply the provisions which we propose to
apply to the new homes.
Taking, first, the case of the nursing
homes other than maternity homes, the
Nursing Homes Bill-
Second Reading.
9 APRIL 1929
Bill provides that where a nursing home
was not in existence at the date of the
passing of this Act, the application may
be refused on the ground that the home
is not in charge of an individual who is
either a duly qualified medical practitioner, or a qualified nurse resident in
the home, or that there is not a proper
proportion of qualified nurses among the
persons employed in the nursing of the
patients in the home.
As regards the case of a home which
was in existence at the date of the Act,
the requirement is that the nursing of the
patients in the home shall in the future
be under the superintendence of a qualified nurse who is resident in the home,
even though the person who is in general
charge of the home may not be SO
qualified.
As regards the case of a maternity home
which is not in existence at the date of
the Act, the application may be refused
on the ground that the person having the
superintendence of the nursing of the
patients in the home is not either a qualified nurse, or a certified midwife, or that
the person employed in attendance on
the patients in the home is not either a
duly qualified medical practitioner, a
certified midwife, or a pupil midwife.
As regards the case of a maternity home.
which is in existence at the date of the
Act, the application may be refused on
the ground that any person employed in
attending on another patient is not either
a duly qualified medical practitioner, a
certified midwife or a pupil midwife, even
though the person in charge of the home
may not be properly qualified.
While we draw this distinction between the homes in existence at the passing of the Act and new homes, we do not
consider that this distinction should be
permanent. While we think it reasonable that unqualified persons in charge at
present should not be disturbed, provided
that proper nursing, as I have indicated
above, is provided for, at the same time
we feel that when the unqualified person
in charge ceases to hold office that his or
her place should be filled by others holding proper nursing qualifications. Therefore the Bill provides that when an unqualified person ceases to hold office in an
existing home, that home shall become
subject to the rules laid down for a home
not in existence at the commencement of
the Act.
Hon. Members will appreciate that
considerable power is placed in the hands
of the local authorities, and, therefore,
we consider that it is right that the applicant for registration should have some
form of appeal from the decision of the
authority in case of their refusal. It is
desirable that an appeal of this kind
should be heard at the earliest possible
moment, and the Government have decided that the best tribunal for hearing
these appeals should be a Court of Summary Jurisdiction composed of one
more resident magistrates.
or
The only other clause to which I think
there is any necessity to refer is that
which provides for inspection.
Clause 10 authorises inspection of
nursing homes by an officer duly authorised by the local authority, or an officer
duly authorised by the Ministry of Home
Affairs. While it is necessary to have
this inspection, we make it perfectly clear
in that Clause that the power of inspection does not include the power to inspect
the medical records of the various cases
in the house, and I think that hon.
Members will agree that such a power will
clearly be open to strong objection.
Those are the main points in the Bill,
which I commend to the House. I beg
to move.
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: This Bill,
like the previous one passed a few moments
ago, is one to which I do not think
many hon. Members can take exception.
But I should have thought that the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates), in

might have given the House some information as to where the demand came from
for this particular Measure. To the first
part of the Bill relating to midwives I do
not think anyone can take exception. It

profession should be attended to in the
way this Bill lays down, but it is a different
matter with regard to the nursing homes.
I must confess that I have never heard

have been run. I do not know whether

they are, or have been, then in fairness

medical profession. He has not told us
that, but he has told us that in future
these nursing homes are to be inspected
and registered, and that the registration
authority is to be the county council of a
county or the borough council of a city.

can quite understand serious resentment

Mr. JOHNSTONE: I should like on
behalf of the medical profession to welcome this Bill. First of all, I welcome
the provisions in regard to midwives,
which mark a very important advance.
The Midwives Act, which was passed in
1918, I think, inaugurated a new era in
regard to the care of women in childbirth
because it laid down the general principle
that only trained women should act as
midwives. Of course, there had to be a
period of transition between the old state
of affairs and the new state of affairs,
partly owing to the fact that there were
not sufficient fully trained midwives to
look after the women who were in childbirth, and because a certain number of
women who by experience and by acting
under the direction of medical men had
acquired a very considerable amount of
skill would have been thrown out of
occupation altogether if they had been
prohibited immediately from acting.
This Bill marks the end of the transition
period, and I hope that from the time this
Bill passes this Parliament and receives
the Royal Assent it will not be possible for
untrained women to look after women in
childbirth, a condition in which a woman
must always undergo a certain amount of
danger. I welcome that part of the Bill,
and I think it perfectly right that, whatever measures may be adopted in order to
render childbirth more safe for mothers,
they should not be embodied in this Bill
which deals with one specific point. We
do not want an Omnibus Bill in regard to
this matter. I do not think that legislation by itself is ever likely to lower the
rate of maternal mortality. Pure legislation can do very little in that direction.
What legislation can do is to insist that
only fully trained midwives take charge at
the time of this serious event in a mother's
life. That is what this Bill endeavours to
do. To my mind, that is very nearly as
much as legislation by itself can do.
Regarding the question as to whether
there are sufficient doctors and midwives
provided by the dispensary service, that
is a matter of administration, and it is a
matter of administration that falls on the
authorities who look after the dispensary
medical services at the present time. I do
not think myself there is any such shortage
as the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
William McMullen) has suggested. I
have not the recent statistics, but I know
that a very few years ago there was a
question at the Board of Guardians of dispensing with the services of a certain
number of these ladies because they had
nothing to do. Whether they are now
overpressed with work I do not know, but
I am quite certain that the Dispensaries.
Committee of the Board of Guardians will
appoint extra midwives if they are necessary in order to deal with the work that
comes before them.
As regards the second part of the Bill,
which deals with nursing homes, I think
the hon. Member for Down (Mr. Patrick
O'Neill) has expressed doubts and fears
which really have no existence in fact.
As a matter of fact, this part of the Bill
is aimed not at the well-conducted nursing
homes to which he has referred, and which
I myself know, but against those nursing
homes which are more or less, if I may
say so, a disgrace to the name of nursing
homes. I know that there are such
nursing homes. I am personally acquainted with some of those, and I can
assure this House that when the very fact

Petroleum (Amendment) Bill [S.].
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): This Bill is introduced for the purpose of amending and
bringing up to date the enactments dealing with the storage, transport, testing
and general use of petroleum and similar
liquid fuels. In its main provisions it
follows closely on the lines of legislation
recently passed in Great Britain, which
does not apply to Northern Ireland. The
last enactment touching on this subject
and now in force in Northern Ireland is
over 30 years old, being contained in the
Locomotives on Highways Act, 1896, but
the main portion of the legislation now in
force is some 60 years old being the Petroleum Act of 1871. In those days the use
of the lighter and more volatile forms of
petroleum derivatives, such as petrol, was
practically nil, and the enormously extended use now made of such liquids, and
the many dangers attendant thereon call
for wider and more effective methods of
supervision and control. The present
Bill, although it contains a large number
of Clauses, does not, with a few exceptions, seek to introduce any new principles
as regards the subject, but merely amends
existing legislation so as to bring it into.
line with modern requirements.
I may mention, for the information of
hon. Members, that after this Bill becomes law it is intended to introduce a
Consolidation Bill which will combine in
one enactment all the legislation dealing
with petroleum.
For the information of hon. Members, I
will now indicate shortly the object of
each clause of the Bill.
Clause 1 merely amends the definition
of the term "harbour" and "harbour
authority" as laid down in Section 2 of
the Petroleum Act, 1871, and defines the
term "dock." It is entirely explanatory
and the alterations are not of serious importance.
Clause 2 repeals Section 3 of the Petroleum Act of 1871 and substitutes a fresh
definition of petroleum and of the lighter
and more volatile derivatives of petroleum,
such as petrol, which is now for the first
time given the statutory designation of
petroleum spirit. The test of whether a
liquid is petroleum or petroleum spirit is
the temperature at which such liquid
gives off an inflammable vapour. This
temperature is now fixed at 73 degrees.
Clause 3 deals with the verification of
the apparatus for testing for petroleum
spirit as mentioned in the previous clause.
Clause 4 refers to the First Schedule to
this Act, in which is described in somewhat
complicated detail the apparatus which is
to be used for carrying out the tests referred to in the last two clauses, and the
method of using it. The description is
highly technical, but I can assure hon.
Members it has been prepared with great
Petroleum Bill-
Second Reading
9 APRIL 1929
care by our technical advisers, and it
would not take me more than a quarter of
a minute to tell hon. Members of this
House all I know about it. (Laughter).
Clause 5 extends the powers of an officer
of a local authority under Section 11 of the
Petroleum Act of 1871, so as to enable him
to exercise supervision, not only over persons who deal in petroleum (which includes
petroleum spirit) but also over any person
who keeps petroleum spirit for the purpose
of any trade or industry carried on by
him. In view of the dangerous nature of
petroleum spirit. I think that these wider
powers are called for, and I may say that
they have been in force in Great Britain
for some time.
Clause 6 deals with the by-laws which
are to be framed under Section 4 of the
Petroleum Act by Harbour Authorities,
and lays down that such by-laws shall include provision for the loading of ships
with petroleum spirit.
Clause 7 amends the penalties to which
persons who are guilty of a breach of
Sections 6 or 7 of the Petroleum Act, 1871,
as regards the keeping, sending, or selling
of a petroleum spirit are liable. Under
that Act the forfeiture of all petroleum
kept or sent in contravention was compulsory, and in addition a penalty of £5 for
breach of Section 6, or £20 for a breach of
Section 7, was laid down. We think it
best in the present clause that the forfeiture of the petroleum spirit in respect
of which the offence was committed should
not be compulsory but should be left to
the discretion of the Court.
Clause 8 lays down penalties for a breach
of any conditions under which a licence for
the storage of petroleum is issued, and requires a copy of such conditions to be
posted up by the occupier of the premises.
Clause 9 amends the scale of fees
which are chargeable for licences to store
petroleum. Under former legislation a
flat rate of 5s was chargeable no matter
what quantity was authorised by the
licence. The fees now payable, which are
laid down in the Second Schedule to the
Bill, vary from 5s in the case of a quantity not exceeding 100 gallons, to £5 for
quantities exceeding 50,000 gallons. This
alteration will not affect the small user,
and it is, I think, more equitable that a
graduated scale should apply to the larger
users.
Clause 10 applies certain provisions of
the Explosives Act of 1875 (which are set
out in the Third Schedule to the Bill) to
petroleum spirit, the most important of
these being the power which is conferred
upon the Minister of Home Affairs to
make regulations regarding its conveyance
by road and to regulate the description and
construction of carriages used for such conveyance. The clause also empowers that
Minister to direct an inquiry to be made
as to the cause of any accident which is
due to the conveyance or storage of such
spirit, and defines the powers exercisable
by the persons holding such an inquiry,
as regards calling witnesses, administering
oaths, and other matters which are necessary for the purposes of the inquiry.
Clause 11 provides for the exercise by
the Minister of Home Affairs of the
powers formerly exercised by a Secretary
of State under Section 5 of the Locomotives on Highways Act, 1896, as regards making regulations as to the keeping and use of petroleum or any other
inflammable liquid for the purposes of
light locomotives.
Clause 12 empowers the Minister of
Home Affairs, if he is satisfied that any
petroleum spirit is dangerous or likely to
be injurious to health, either to prohibit
its sale and use altogether or to prescribe
certain conditions and precautions which
are to be observed.
Clause 13 lays down that all regulations
made by the Minister of Home Affairs
under the Act shall be laid before each
House of Parliament, and that if an Address be presented to the Governor of Northern Ireland by either House within the
statutory period, the regulations shall be
annulled.
Clause 14 empowers the Council of any
county, county borough, borough or urban
district to make by-laws either prohibiting
the establishment of petroleum-filling
stations or regulating their appearance.
This is an entirely new principle as regards legislation for petroleum, and is
designed to prevent the disfigurement of
scenery or places of historic interest by
unsuitable and unsightly erections. The
clause provides that any occupier of a
petroleum-filling station already in
existence may be called upon to remove
it within six months after receiving a
notice to that effect, but entitles such
owner to recover from the Council any
expenses reasonably incurred in carrying
out the removal, and also compensation
for any loss sustained by him. In the
event of a dispute the matter will be decided by the County Court Judge.

Clause 15 confers upon canal
panies the power to make by-laws for the
loading, conveyance and landing of petroleum spirit in and upon the canal, and
provides that such by-laws shall not be
effective until they have been confirmed by
the Ministry of Commerce. Under former legislation canal companies did not
possess this power, which seems to be very
necessary
in the interests of the public
safety.
Clause 16 provides that the Governor
of Northern Ireland may, by Order in
Council, apply the provisions of the
Petroleum Acts to any substance which
may be specified in the Order.
Clause 17 is merely an adaptation of
the Petroleum Acts of 1871 and 1879, so
as to make them applicable to Northern.
Ireland, but paragraph (c) of this clause
lays down a fresh definition of "local
authority" for the purpose of granting
licences to store petroleum spirit.
The remaining clauses are purely definitive and are not of very much importance except from the legal point of view.
I beg to move.

Mr. DEVLIN: I do not think that

to explore the whole situation from a new
angle. They ought to consider again the

The first thing they ought to do is to give
a grant out of the public revenue for the

to take cases like the houses at Whiterock
and see that there is a reduction in the

This matter has been fully discussed before, and my suggestion is simply to set up
a Committee or Commission to go into the
whole question. All their schemes have
been in operation. They have been tested
for their value. Great good no doubt has
been done, but there are countless people
at present living in slums and they are a
class of people whom everybody seems to
forget. Another thing I would suggest.
There is a great feeling amongst all the
working classes against removing from
houses where they live at present-mostly
houses near the works where they are employed. It would be an ideal system if
you could build suburban houses for the
working classes, if you could take them
away from the places where they work
into the country. If you could build
cheap houses and have cheap transit it
would be far better for their health and
happiness, but, knowing human nature as
we know human nature, there is not only
a tendency but almost a prejudice amongst
the large masses of the working people
against being compelled to live at a long
distance from the places where they are
employed. What I would suggest in that
case is that the Government ought to use
portion of the public revenue to reconstruct and recondition these houses and to
make them healthy and clean.
In doing that you would not only be
serving that particular end, but you would
be giving employment to a much larger
number of unemployed, such as plasterers
and painters and other people engaged in
the work of constructing, developing, and
improving these houses. These are the
suggestion I have to make. I do not, as
I say, want to make political capital out
of the matter, but I do think that now
at the end of eight years it is time the
Government reconsidered the whole problem from every point of view to see
whether something could not be done to
meet the conditions that exist.

I have already dealt with the one point

My experience of houses in the slums is
that you really cannot recondition them.
They have to be rebuilt.
But what is the alternative if the suggestions of my hon. Friend are carried
out? Are we going to continue, as we
have been for a long time past, to see
working people having to live in one or
two rooms and pay rents of 20s and 25s
a week. That is the alternative. My
hon. Friend (Mr. Devlin), with great respect to him, has not put forward a single
practical suggestion. He told us about
this Committee that sat in London. The
only result, as far as Northern Ireland
was concerned, that flowed from that

1,600 houses. I claim on behalf of this
Government, and as a result of our legislation, that in the short period from 1923
to the present time we have produced
over 15,000 houses.

It is nothing short of scandalous that
tenants should be expected to pay rents
which they are utterly unable to pay at
the present time. Take the rents which
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.

If the Government are not prepared to

valuation?

The whole question of rents, in other

Reference has been made to the hurried
and unstudied character of the proposals
of the Government from time to time in
regard to this vital question of housing.
I am sure every Member of the House
will agree with the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) in this connection,
that on housing depends a great deal of

Decent houses to live in means a
tremendous lot in the building up of the
character and morale of the people of
the Province. As everybody agrees on
that question, it seems to me that a definite policy should be adopted by the
Government in regard to house building.
The right hon. Gentleman stated that
there had been a failure in State- or municipally-built houses. We have been decidedly unfortunate in Belfast city, I
agree. But that is because Belfast
municipality has been governed by Tory
administrators--I do not think anybody
can deny this-who have been more concerned about the selling of land to the
Corporation, and more concerned about
their own private interests, than they
have been about the public good. Therefore, as I say, we have been decidedly
unfortunate. Let me take you to Birmingham, where there is a Tory municipality also. Let me take you to Manchester, where Labour is not in a majority.
Let me take you to other centres in England-to Sheffield, to the slum district of
Bermondsey, even to a city like Leeds.
There are no fewer that 27 municipalities
in Great Britain in which Labour is in
the majority, and they have direct labour
housing schemes. In all those schemes a
saving of from £50 to £100 has been
effected by direct labour on the prices of
contractors.
Yet the right hon. Gentleman has the
audacity, the blazing cheek, to get up in
this House and state that this scheme of
direct municipal responsibility has failed,
so far as the building of houses is concerned. I never heard a more glaring
example of the inepitude of the Minister
of Home Affairs, or a more blatant justification of what was said about him the
other day in the Press as to his worth to
the community. Does he treat us all as
a lot of children, as people who are prepared to say "Amen' or "Hear, hear"
to everything he says? It is not only a
disgrace to the House itself, but to the
party of which he is a Member.

One is accustomed to speeches from

in which they say they do not need to
put forward a programme. "You know
my convictions for the last thirty years.
I have always stood for union with the

However, I am glad to say that a change of
opinion is being brought about in Northern Ireland, and I only hope that,
either inside or outside this House, we
may be able to compel the Government to
deal with affairs as they find them, irrespective of histrionics, whether on election
platforms or not.
The housing schemes, so far as Northern
Ireland are concerned, have gone a little
way towards reducing the shortage. We
want to see those schemes going further.
As a matter of fact, I think our suggestion that the subsidy should be given
in respect of houses with an extra 100
superficial feet met with the approval of
every Member of the House. Members
on the opposite side said that they
agreed with the idea of granting the £100
subsidy to houses of more than 650 superficial feet. I think I am right in saying
that Members agreed, although they were
not prepared at that time to alter the
Bill before the House, which granted the
£100 subsidy to houses of 650 superficial
feet. Most people agree that it is necessary to have the subsidy for a larger type
of house than that.
Even the cheapest of these houses,
those let at 8s 6d a week, can only be
tenanted by men who are in receipt of
about £2 12s a week-that is the ordinary
tradesman in Belfast. Those houses are
not suitable, as I suggest, for the shipyard labourer or the textile labourer.
They are suitable for only the upper strata
of the working classes, not for the people
who in the halcyon days before the war
got houses for 3s a week. As the right
hon. Gentleman stated, those were the
days when there were 10,000 surplus
houses in Belfast. Now there are not
houses available for the people. What is
the Government prepared to do to help
those people?
I agree with the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) that we should get
the best houses possible for the working
people, and that employers of labour,
Government Departments, and municipal
authorities should pay wages that would
enable people to live in decent houses.
But that has not come about. The
inexorable laws of supply and demand in
industry, particularly in the export trade,
have compelled the workers in the linen
trade, for example, to accept wages of
from 21s to 25s for women, and from 30s
to 50s for men, with the result that they
are unable to pay even that 8s 6d a week
for the cheapest type of subsidy house.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Kyle]
What are we going to do? We are
going to insist on making the Government
of the day realise their responsibility to
those people to the extent, if you like, of
subsidising the people who, own their
houses, so that the people may live in
more decency and comfort than they do
at the present time. Those are the points
that I think should be stressed, particularly in regard to the payment of rents
by the people who are residing in those
new houses let at from 8s 6d to 23s a
week. The Government are going to be
compelled to step in. What happens is
this. A young man and a young woman
take one of those new houses at 8s 6d a
week. In the course of a few years the
children start to come, with the result
that the parents are unable to pay the
rent of the house, and they have to live
in abject poverty, Those houses themselves, will, I am afraid, become slums in
10 to 20 years from now.
I know that this question raises the
whole economic system under which we
live, but I cannot see any hope of the
Government tackling that matter. They
will, however, have to face this question
of the housing of the people. Is there
anything unreasonable or undesirable in
asking that a Committee of public spirited
people should be set up in Northern Ireland to report on the operation of the
Housing Acts, and to inquire into the
facts which need not be taken in the
frothy words of Members of Parliament
or even aspiring Members of Parliament.
The question could be examined in cold
blood, and the Committee could bring in
a Report for the Government of the day
suggesting what action should be taken to
relieve these people of this tremendous
burden.
If that Committee is set up and reports,
as I expect it will report, that further
housing schemes are necessary, I hope that
the Government, through the municipalities and local authorities will see that a
sufficient number of houses are built to
overcome the shortage in Northern Ireland, and that those houses will be let,
not at economic rents, but at rents that
the people can pay. If that will entail,
as it will entail, a further inquiry into
what should be the standard wage and the
living conditions for men, women and
children, then so much the better for the
future of the State of Northern Ireland.
I support the Motion moved by the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin).

Mr. Speaker's Retirement.
Mr. SPEAKER (The Right Hon. Hugh
O'Neill), announcing his intention of retiring from the Chair, all the Members
being uncovered, said: Before we start
our proceedings to-day I have a communication to make to the House. I desire
to intimate formally what is already
known informally to hon. Members,
namely, that I have decided with very
great regret not to offer myself for reelection to the office of Speaker of this
House when the time comes to choose a
Speaker at the commencement of the next
Parliament. In fact I shall then no
longer be a Member of the House. As I
understand the Prime Minister intends to
put down a Motion on the matter for discussion to-morrow I shall reserve what I
have to say further until then.
The PRIME MINISTER: Mr.
Speaker, Sir, the statement which you
have just made to the House is one that
will be received by every Member of the
House with profound regret. I am quite
certain it will be the desire of the House
to take the earliest opportunity to-morrow
to give full and formal expression to their
feelings. With that object in view I ask
your leave to read to the House the Motion
which I propose to put on the Order
Paper to-night. It is as follows:
"(1) That the thanks of this House
be given to Mr. Speaker for his distinguished services in the Chair for the
past eight years; that he be assured
that this House fully appreciates the
zeal, ability and impartiality with
which he has discharged the duties of
his high office, and the judgment and
firmness with which he has maintained
its privileges and dignity; that it tenders its hearty congratulations to him.
upon being the first Speaker of the
House of Commons of Northern Ireland
and expresses its thanks for his
courtesy to individual Members in
assisting them to the better understanding of the procedure of the House,
which kindly action has contributed to
the respect and esteem in which he is
held by the whole assembly.
"(2) That an humble address be presented to his Grace the Governor praying his Grace to approach his Majesty
to ascertain his pleasure regarding the
conferment of some signal mark of his
Royal Favour upon the Right Honourable Hugh O'Neill, Speaker of the
House, for his eminent services during
the important period in which he has
with such distinguished ability and
dignity presided in the Chair of this
House."
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

As I pointed out yesterday, this matter

Possibly the general election had a great

no Government, either Tory, Liberal or

first statutory condition making thirty
stamps obligatory under the circumstances,

fact that if that was enforced thousands of
people who could qualify for benefit would
as a result automatically become disqualified.
My quarrel with this thing is that it
is not dealt with here as sympathetically
as it is in England. There is wonderful
unanimity amongst those who have experience of the Courts of Referees that
this thing is not being sympathetically administered. I come in contact with a
large number of applicants, and incidentally I come in contact with a large
number of representatives of all shades
of political thought. The Tory representatives, few as they are, who attend those
Courts of Referees, are as strong, or even
stronger, in their condemnation of the
conduct of the Courts of Referees as the
Labour representatives are.
The only
people who attempt to deny that the Act
is not sympathetically administered are the
Minister of Labour and the Parliamentary
Secretary. I have scarcely missed 21 days
at the Courts of Referees since this Act
was introduced in 1928, and I know what
I am speaking about. During that time
I have represented some hundreds of
applicants, and I do not know of more
than half a dozen cases that have been
allowed where the applicant had only eight
stamps.
I only wish this Clause was put into
operation. I do not know whether our

of 1928 to continue after the 19th of this
month and thus deprive many of our

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: This is

me. It is very hard to know what

make regulations-very drastic powersand then again in Clause 15 the Ministry

Department. There seems to be a

power under the Bill. I object to it on

I consider unwise, namely in the direction.
of the delegation of the powers of Parliament. Take, for instance, Clause 16,
which says
"The Governor of Northern Ireland
may by Order in Council apply to any
substance any of the provisions of the
Petroleum Acts, 1871 and 1879, or this
Act, specified in the Order, with such
modifications, if any, as may seem to
the said Governor to be desirable having regard to the nature of the substance to which the Order relates."
I have never in any Bill read a more
ridiculous proposal than that the Governor

of Northern Ireland, who, I presume,
would be advised by the heads of Departments as to what action he would take in
this matter, should have power to apply
the provisions of this Bill to any substance. It seems to me that this is giving
power to the Governor of the day to make
the provisions of this Bill, which applies
to petroleum, apply to any substance
found in Northern Ireland. I would like
if the Minister would give the House some
justification for these very wide powers
the Government are seeking in regard to
the making of regulations, and also in
regard to this Clause 16. These are the
few points that struck me as I glanced
through the Bill. It seems to me to be a
confused bit of legislation, and the
authority for the making and approving
of by-laws seems to be divided. The
Government would be well advised at the
present time to accept the Amendment
which has been put before the House.

EX-SERVICE TEMPORARY CIVIL

4. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister

Servants who have been appointed to permanent posts under the scheme for filling
one hundred appointments with these
men; the number of men recomended but
rejected upon medical or other grounds;
and whether the one hundred appointments will be definitely made at an early
date.
Mr. POLLOCK: Eighty-four ex-
Service temporary clerks have been
appointed to permanent posts in the
Civil Service under the scheme referred
to by the hon. and gallant Member.
These include two who replaced
a similar number of candidates
recommended for appointments who were
rejected on grounds of character. One
candidate has failed to produce satisfactory evidence as to Army service, and

officer, or the carrying out of dental or
minor surgical treatment which he reported to be necessary. All appointments
will have retrospective effect from the 1st
February last.

Sir DAWSON BATES: James Strannix
was convicted by a Jury and sentenced at
the Winter Assizes in December last to
three years' penal servitude and 15 strokes
of the cat. The corporal punishment was
remitted on health considerations, and in
the exercise of the prerogative of mercy the
prisoner was released on the 21st March
last.
It would be contrary to public usage
and policy to disclose the grounds upon
which the clemency of the Crown is extended in any particular case, but I should
point out that the exercise of the
prerogative of mercy by His Grace the
Governor does not necessarily indicate the
innocence of the party concerned, and
there can be no question of compensation
in this case.
As the postal service is a reserved
service, I have no information as to the
action which the Post Office authorities
may take in regard to this man's reinstatement.

Retirement of Mr. Speaker.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move,
"(1) That the thanks of this House be
given to Mr. Speaker for his distinguished
services in the Chair for the past eight
years; that he be assured that this House
fully appreciates the zeal, ability and impartiality with which he has discharged
the duties of his high office, and the judgment and firmness with which he has
maintained its privileges and dignity;
that it tenders its hearty congratulations
to him upon being the first Speaker of
the House of Commons of Northern Ireland, and expresses its thanks for his
courtesy to individual Members in assisting them to the better understanding of
the procedure of the House, which kindly
action has contributed to the respect and
esteem in which he is held by the whole
assembly."
In the year 1921 and again in 1925 you,
Sir, were unanimously chosen by this
House to act as Speaker, and I am confident in saying that were it possible for
you to continue to be a Member of the
Parliament of Northern Ireland you
would have occupied that seat just so long
as you desired to do so. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). In the first Resolution that
stands in my name I have endeavoured to
convey in as short a compass as possible
what I believe will be the universal feeling
throughout all quarters of the House regarding yourself. We have been extremely fortunate in having a member of
one of the oldest Ulster families to preside
over our deliberations, and no one will
deny that in fairness, in dignity, in kindliness, and in courtesy to all sides of the
House you could not possibly have done
better during the years you have occupied
the Chair. (Hon. Members:
Hear,
hear).
We feel most grateful. It is, of course,
very much easier to maintain traditions
that have been handed down than it is to
establish a precedent for generations that
are to come. Your duty was a most difficult one. This is a young Parliament, a
comparatively small House, and the bulk
of the Members were quite unaccustomed
to the traditions of any parliamentary
proceedings, and, therefore, in your hands
more than in those of anyone else lay the
responsibility, not only of guiding us
throughout our debates but also of setting
a tone to the House and of giving that
atmosphere which I sincerely trust, as it
has been set upon so high and lofty a
level, will mark our deliberations for
years and years to come. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
You came here with a splendid parliamentary record, and we are deeply indebted to the fact that you must have
spent a period of your time in the Imperial
House in studying the intricacies of the
procedure of the House of Commons, and
to that diligence and perseverance on your
part you owe a great deal of the success
of your tenure of the Chair. I have from
time to time duties to perform of a joyful
nature and a sad nature, and
this is
one of the latter. It
is indeed with deep regret that
we all part from you here to-day. I think
it is no breach of confidence on my part
to say that your life-long friends endeavoured to secure that you should remain on here and preside over our proceedings, but you found it impossible for
reasons which we need not, and cannot,
go into to accede to our request. But I
do wish to assure you that although you
leave this Assembly the memory of the
dignity and the competence with which
you carried out the duties of the first
Speaker of the Parliament of Northern
Ireland will never be forgotten by the
youngest Member in this House.
In moving this Resolution we bid you
farewell, and I would like to say that

that

This is not what I call a young Parliament, but it is a new Parliament. It is

warm and affectionate regard.

exception from every Member, let him sit

Mr. SPEAKER (who was received with
general cheers): I have almost thought
during the last quarter hour that I was
back again in the days of the first Parliament of Northern Ireland, when it was
said as a criticism that it was nothing
but a mutual admiration society. I have
rather felt to-day that we had gone back
to that state of affairs. But seriously, it
is naturally with feelings of emotion that I
rise to reply to the very kind and flattering remarks that have been made from
all quarters of the House this afternoon.
The step which I contemplate is based
upon reasons partly public and partly
private which I need not enlarge upon in
detail on this occasion. It will suffice if
I
say that my decision to retire has not
been reached without profound regret and
genuine sorrow. It is the end of a
chapter of one's life, and as such I
naturally feel it very keenly.
The hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Kyle) has referred to the qualities
which are supposed to be necessary for a
successful occupant of the Chair. I think
he pretty well hit the mark when he described those qualities. At any rate I
have certainly endeavoured while I have
occupied the Chair here to set before me
as my standard of conduct, above all else,
a determination to try to give fair play,
as he said, to everybody. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). That sort of quality is
really far more important, in my view, in
the occupant of the Chair than any mere
technical knowledge of procedure. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). The nearer the
Speaker can get to that main principle the
more successful undoubtedly will he be.
I remember being rather appalled at the
prospect when it was suggested to me that
I might have to be responsible for creating the forms of procedure and conduct
of a new Parliament-not, like most, new
Parliaments, in a new country, but a new
Parliament in a portion of a very old
country. And there was the further
complication that it was a Parliament
which at that time nobody wanted. In
the result, however, the task proved
easier than I expected. That has been
due to the support I have received from
the House as a whole. It is essential
that a Speaker should receive such support. Otherwise he is bound to fail.
The confidence of
one party is not
sufficient. It must be the confidence of
all, and it is on that which he must rely
in the last resort. I know I can claim
that I have had that confidence. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). The Government, from the Prime Minister down,
1719 Retirement of Mr. Speaker HOUSE OF COMMONS
Adjournment of the House 1720
[Mr. Speaker]
have never failed in according it to me
in unstinted measure, and I thank them
for it and for their unfailing courtesy and
consideration. To the Opposition I must
also express my thanks. Many of them
came into the House under protest, and
with the further disadvantage of being
without the steadying influence which
a past tradition of power and office alone
can give. They have, nevertheless,
played their part with success and ability
often in face of great difficulties.
Nothing has impressed me more than the
way in which hon. Members on all sides
of the House have adopted the Parliamentary form and manner of speech and
deportment. I can say without fear of
contradiction that our proceedings here
will stand comparison with those of any
other Parliamentary institution in the
world-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
and, after all, this side of Parliamentary
life is important; at least I hold it to
be so. We live in a time when throughout
the civilised world democratic institutions
are in a sense upon their trial. As a result of the war, we have seen first, thrones
and then parliaments tumbling down in
all directions; and it has been evident
that a parliament will exist only so long
as it commands the respect of the mass
of the people whom it represents. Otherwise it will fail. We have got examples
of the failure of democratic institutions
in countries like Russia, Italy, Spain, and
Jugoslavia, in Europe. That is why I emphasize the importance of maintaining a
high standard of conduct and of proceedings in our Parliamentary institutions,
and I believe Members on all sides of this
House fully appreciate that what I say is
true. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
After the very kind words that have
been spoken, I can truly say that I shall
carry away with me when I go nothing
but the very happiest recollections of the
kindness, consideration, and may I say,
affection, which I have received from every
Member of the House, be he Union -
ist, Nationalist, Socialist or Independent.
I give up my office with a genuine sense
of gratitude and thanks to all the
Members of this House, whom I know I
can call with truth, and without affectation, my honourable friends. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
My last word can only be an earnest
hope and prayer that the standard of
procedure and conduct which, thanks to
the co-operation of all, has existed in
these first two Parliaments over which 1
have had the honour to preside, will
never be allowed to lapse.
The Prime Minister in his concluding
words said he hoped I would be in the
Chair on Tuesday next. I certainly shall
be, for while I announced officially my
resignation to-day, I do not think it will
technically come into force until after this
Parliament is dissolved. (General Cheers).

Mr. HANNA: I can give the hon.

borough and urban councils that have the

situation of pumps and filling stations.
As there are so many of these councils

well, with a view to having more uniformity in the by-laws, that the by-laws

Ministry of Home Affairs. In this matter
there is no drastic power being vested in
the Ministry. I can assure the Committee that the people interested-the traders
themselves are very much in favour of
this Bill. The bigger traders have asked
that the Bill be got through the House
as soon as possible. The Committee will
see we are acting in sympathy with the
people who are most concerned. The
whole object in regard to this matter is to
secure the safety of the general public,
and in particular the safety of the people
who have to live in the vicinity of these
inflammable things. The duties of the
Home Secretary in relation to these bylaws will be carried out in no selfish
manner.

public attention in Northern Ireland, or
in any other country in the world.

limits that have been laid down. I shall

allow him to go.
Mr. DEVLIN: Though disagreeing
entirely, not with your ruling but with
the spirit behind it, which is a matter of
most tremendous importance, I hold that
where the liberty of the subject is involved to the extent to which the liberty
of this young man was involved, it is a
very serious thing that Parliament should
be denied an opportunity of discussing it
and having it dealt with. I will recollect
your ruling, Sir, and keep within its
limits as far as I can. In this case of
James Strannix I asked a question today. I asked whether in view of the
flogging portion of the sentence not having been put into operation, and in view
of his being released that was due to the
fact that he was innocent. If he was
guilty of the charge on which he was convicted then it was eminently the duty of
the Government to see that the sentence
was carried out. That is a principle so
universally admitted and accepted that
we need not argue it.
If James Strannix were released and the
most brutal part of his sentence not put
into operation then he must have been
innocent. If he is innocent, what a grave
wrong has been done to this boy. One of
the things that almost harrows my feelings
is the fact that this boy, for a crime he
never committed, was ordered to be
flogged. I have all my life been opposed
to flogging. I remember when I voted
against flogging in the British Parliament.
I had been invited by Mr. Winston
Churchill to a conference with the Prime
Minister and, I think, Lord Londonderry,
and he tried to use all his influence to get
me to withdraw my opposition on the
grounds of the heinous nature of the
crimes for which flogging was inflicted. I
refused, because I do not think that
brutality is to be countered by brutality,
and I hold that the introduction of a
system of flogging into any country is a
bad policy. I protested, and I say I was
justified in voting against that infamous
proposal to mete out the punishment of
flogging. But here is an innocent boy,
and I protest he is innocent until you prove
him guilty.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): He was proved guilty by the
verdict of the jury.

As the hon. Member for West Belfast
has stated, the boy is either guilty or he
is innocent. There is only the one thing
or the other. I believe I have not the
exact knowledge-the boy to be innocent,
judging from the statements I have heard
from my Friends on this side of the
House. Even the right hon. Gentleman
has been so far convinced that he has
pleaded with the Crown to get this boy
out of prison. That being so, is the Government prepared to set up an impartial
tribunal, any tribunal, to inquire into the
whole case, or is it to go out that they do
not care whether a person suffers for something that he has not done? Do the
public of Northern Ireland not matter to
the Government because they have got
the "Belfast Telegraph," "The Northern
Whig," or the "News-Letter," or the
papers they have throughout the Province
to distort the facts and to suppress the
truth in the interests of the Government?
In other words, is innocence not worth
while because they have a strong Unionist
Government that is prepared to try to
defend the indefensible, to maintain injustice, and to continue this infamy.
I think anybody will agree that it is
infamous, if it can be proved that this
boy is innocent, as we believe it can be
proved, that he should be put to the indignity of suffering a sentence of three
years and fifteen strokes of the "cat."
I think it is perfectly monstrous that
Members of the Government should treat
this as a laughing matter, and should try
to misrepresent the facts. I do not care
whether he is a Sinn Feiner or not. I
do not know the boy, and I do not care
what he is, but I do say if a wrong has
been done it should be righted. I
believe that a wrong has been done. and
so does the right hon. Gentleman or he
would not have recommended that the boy
should be let out.
That being the case, what are you going
to do? Here is a lad who has worked for
a certain length of time. He was arrested,
and was put in prison for a certain time.
He comes out, and he cannot get his job
back. You Gentlemen know nothing
about it. The Back Benchers may know
something about what it means to lose
one's employment at a time like this. To
lose his employment in such a way means
that he cannot get a job at all with this
thing hanging over his head. You are
going to ruin that boy, and perhaps all
connected with him, simply to save your
own faces, and to save the Unionist administration in Northern Ireland. That
is a monstrous state of affairs. Surely we
have not sunk to such depths that we are
prepared to sit dumb, and to allow the
continuance of this injustice, if it is an
injustice.
You can remedy this state of affairs.
The boy ought to be compensated if he
has been wrongfully imprisoned. I submit that the hon. Member for West Belfast has made out a perfect case for the
compensation of the boy, but failing that,
for the setting up of a tribunal to inquire
into all the facts of the case. I can say
this for myself-I cannot speak for the
hon. Gentleman--that if the tribunal you
set up proves he is guiltv I will eat all
the words I have said so far as the
Unionist administration in this case is
concerned.

The
ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
The
matter has gone so far that I think in
justice to the Administration I might be
entitled to state this fact, that whether
that point was taken in Court or not, the
conviction of this boy Strannix by the
jury was on the evidence of two eye-witnesses who were present when the raid
took place, and both of whom positively
identified him as being the boy who was
there. It was upon that the jury convicted. Now, what happens when a person is convicted by a jury? He receives
his sentence, and under our law as it
stands at present there is no appeal from
that, because we are the only portion of
the United Kingdom that has not got a
Court of Criminal Appeal, where cases of
this sort could be reviewed.
Mr. DEVLIN: You will have to get it.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: Therefore, the verdict of the jury in criminal
cases is absolutely irrevocable, and there
is no machinery known to our law by
which a mistake that is made can be remedied. The only way in which the matter can be dealt with after a verdict is on
the prerogative of mercy by my right
hon. Friend Sir Dawson Bates, who can
inquire into the circumstances and can recommend the Governor to remit the sentence, or if he is satisfied upon the evidence
produced to him that it is clear beyond all
doubt that the verdict of the jury was
wrong, then he can go a step further and
advise His Grace the Governor to give the
person who has been convicted a free
pardon.
That is the distinction between
the case we are dealing with in the House
at the present moment and one of the
cases that were referred to this afternoon,
namely, the case of Oscar Slater.
Oscar Slater was convicted by a jury in
Scotland at a time when there was no
Adjournment-
Case of James Strannix
11 APRIL 1929
Court of Criminal Appeal, and fifteen
years afterwards, after numerous representations to the Home Office in London
has been made, a Court of Criminal Appeal was set up for Scotland, and the first
case that was brought before it was the
case of Oscar Slater. The learned judges
who heard that case in the Court of
Criminal Appeal had the record of the
case before them and they came to the
conclusion that whether he was innocent
or whether he was guilty he had been
wrongfully convicted upon the course of
the trial, and consequently their judgment in the case set aside the original
conviction of the jury, and from that day
Oscar Slater was a free man, just as much
as if he had received a pardon from His
Majesty under the prerogative of mercy.
He was given compensation because he
was then cleared of the charge; and so a
man may be given compensation in a case
where a free pardon is granted because he
has been wrongly convicted. I am sure
the Member for West Belfast will remember the case of Adolf Beck, who was
convicted of stealing a watch upon evidence of identity which some two or three
months afterwards, he being still in gaol,
turned out to be wrong because the real
thief who had stolen the watch was discovered.
Mr. DEVLIN: And confessed.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: And
confessed. There was no doubt about
that case and he got a free pardon and
also, I understand, compensation from
the Government. But in cases of the
kind now before the House, where there
is not sufficient evidence for my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Home
Affairs, to advise the Governor that a
free pardon should be granted, then the
prerogative of mercy is put in force, and
the sentence, or portion of the sentence, is
remitted. There has never been a case
of that kind in respect of which compensation has been granted, and I defy hon.
Members opposite to produce one single
precedent where compensation has been
granted in a case of that sort.
After all,
if one comes to think of it, it must necessarily be so.
Take the case of the Court of Criminal
Appeal in England to-day. A man is
tried by a jury. He is kept in gaol for
two or three months before his trial. He
is convicted and kept in gaol another two
or three months before his case comes before the Court of Criminal Appeal.
He
is put to the expense of his defence and
he has to bear all the mental torture and
anguish of his trial, and if the verdict is
ultimately set aside he gets no compensation. That occurs every day in our
own community. There are frequent cases
in which the Minister of Home Affairs
exercises the prerogative of mercy after
portion of a sentence has been served although in none of those cases has compensation ever been granted. I must
say that unless hon. Members opposite
can produce absolutely clear and cogent
evidence which will show that the verdict
of the jury in this case was obtained upon
evidence which was false, there is no way
in which the Minister of Home Affairs can
advise his Grace the Governor to grant a
free pardon. Personally, I would be delighted if they could produce such evidence, but in the absence of that evidence
the verdict of the jury stands.
I think hon. Members opposite are confused between a case where a sentence is
remitted without a free pardon and a case
where it is proved beyond a shadow of
doubt that a verdict was wrongly obtained
and that therefore there must be a free
pardon. It is obvious then that an injustice has been done. I wish to repudiate the suggestion that there was any
evidence withheld from the jury in this
case. All the evidence that could be laid
before the jury was laid before them, the
boy Strannix was defended by most able
and competent counsel, and the jury
found him guilty. I do not wish to cri
ticise, because it is not my affair, the
correctness or otherwise of my right hon.
Friend's decision to exercise the prerogative of mercy, but I do say that having
exercised it does not show that the conviction was wrongfully obtained, and unless some clear evidence to that effect is
produced by hon. Members opposite--
which I am sure my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Home Affairs, will be only
too glad to consider-then I say the matter must stand where it is.
It is not competent for this Parliament
to vote this boy compensation. So far as
his position in the Post Office is concerned
I am sure that all the evidence and all
the reports that can in any way influence
the officials of the Post Office will be laid
before them in order that they may independently make up their minds as to
whether, notwithstanding the verdict of
the jury, there is such a doubt about it

The only thing I would say in conclusion
on this matter is this. I think that this
case shows once again that as a protection,
not only to those who are responsible for
prosecutions and for the administration of
justice, but also as a protection to my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Home
Affairs, who advises the Governor with
respect to the exercise of the preroga ive
of mercy, the sooner a Court of Criminal
Appeal is set up in this Province the
better for the administration of justice

that administration is not only fair and
pure, but that it is absolutely above suspicion. But I may point out, with reference to the setting up of a Court of
Criminal Appeal in Northern Ireland,
that that deals with the Judiciary, which
is a reserved service. It is a matter for
the Imperial Parliament and not for this
Parliament, but I understand that my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Home
Affairs, has been in consultation with the
Imperial authorities for the last eighteen
months with a view to this very muchneeded reform being brought about at the
earliest possible moment.

man and have him restored to the Post
Office if he is innocent as he would appear undoubtedly to be. I will go further. In answering the question the hon.
Member for West Belfast put upon the
Paper as to why this man was not restored to the Post Office it was rightly
stated that the Post Office is a reserved
service. But I assume, and it has been
Adjournment-
Case of James Strannix
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McAllister].
stated in this House very frequently, and
it has not been contradicted, that the
Government are agents that someone in
this House, the Minister of Commerce, I
think, acts as agent for the Post Office. I
presume that some communication has
taken place with the English Government
with regard to this particular case.
lf
it has not it is open to him now to do
it, and I would suggest to the Minister
of Commerce if he is satisfied-from
what I have heard I am satisfied at all
events that a grave injustice has been
done to this man, he should, in his
capacity as agent to the English Government, take up this question of his
restitution to his position in the Post
Office and so secure to this man the means
of earning his living.
Colonel WOODS: I would like to make
a suggestion to the Government in this
particular case in view of the fact that
there is no Criminal Court of Appeal in
Northern Ireland. It is that the Government itself should hold a further investigation into this case, and if they are
satisfied that the boy is innocent let them
say so in this House or in a more public
place. If the man is guilty he should be
punished by the withdrawal of his remission of term of imprisonment. If he
is a guilty man I think he is taking a
terrible risk in having this debate instituted. If he is innocent he is justified in
doing it. I suggest to the Government
that there should be a further investigation into this matter. I hope they
will act in a straightforward manner as
they are entitled to do in this case. I
would like an undertaking from the Government that they will do this.
Question, "That this House do now adjourn," put, and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at Six
o'clock until Tuesday, 16th
April, at a quarter before
Twelve o'clock, pursuant to
the Resolution of the House
of this day.
