Oral Answers to Questions.
NETTING OF SALMON IN NON-
TIDAL WATERS.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked
the Minister of Commerce whether he is
aware that the owner of a several fishery
in the River Bush takes and kills salmon
by netting at a place called the Bushfoot;
whether such methods are illegal on a
river that is not tidal; whether it is a
fact that at Workman's Mill Weir, at
Bushmills, where a King's Gap should be
open to allow salmon up the river from
Saturday night to Monday morning, the
gap is never opened, and at Currie's Mill
Weir the King's Gap is netted with
netting wire, the water stopped, and the
fish left in such shallow water that they
can be lifted out with a hand net; whether
these methods of taking fish are illegal,
and, if so, what steps he proposes to take
to have the law enforced.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The answer to the hon. Member's inquiry
as to the legality of netting salmon in
non-tidal waters is that the use of nets
is permissible where the user is the owner
of a several fishery in such waters, but not
otherwise. With regard to the remainder
of the question, it has been ascertained by
inspection that the weirs referred to are
not fishing weirs, but are weirs designed
to provide water supply to mill machinery.
In such weirs the Fisheries Acts do not
require a King's Gap to be provided as
such a Gap would obviously destroy the
efficacy of the weir. At Workman's Mill,
which is not at present in use, the sluice
in the weir is permanently closed, but a
free passage for ascending and descending
fish is available through the head-race
the sluice in which is kept open throughout the whole of the year. At Currie's
Mill there is no trace of wire netting as
suggested in the question, nor has any
evidence of illegal fishing of the type mentioned been found. The head-race at this
mill is, however, utilised at times by the
owner of the Fishery in the Bush for the
purpose of impounding breeding fish for
stripping in connection with artificial propagation operations at the Bushmills
Hatchery, and it is possible that the use
of the head-race in this manner may have
formed the basis of the hon. Member's
inquiry.
DRAINAGE OF LOUGH ERNE.
2. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Healy)
asked the Minister of Finance whether
he can state when the joint report of the
engineering experts of his Department
and the Free State on the drainage of
Lough Erne will be published.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The report referred to is a report by the Technical Officers of my
Ministry, who, in accordance with the
agreed arrangements, are in consultation
with the Chief Engineer of the Irish Free
State Office of Public Works in regard to
the general lines which the drainage
scheme to be put forward will take.
I anticipate that the report will be in
my hands in about two months' time.
and before publication it will be necessary
for its implications to be carefully considered by my Ministry in consultation
with the Commissioners of Works in
Dublin.
COURT OF CRIMINAL APPEAL FOR
NORTHERN IRELAND
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether, in view of the
danger of a miscarriage of justice, as suggested by recent cases in the Courts in
Northern Ireland, he is prepared to recommend the establishment of a Court of
Criminal Appeal in Northern Ireland.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I have been
asked to answer this question.
The question of the establishment of a
Court of Criminal Appeal in Northern
Ireland has been the subject of consideration by me for some time past, and of
correspondence with the Imperial Government.
Written Answers
King's Speech
16 APRIL 1929
The hon. Member is no doubt aware
that the establishment of such a Court
can only be effected as the result of legislation in the Imperial Parliament, and
from the assurances already received by
me, I am not without hope that my representations will be acceded to.
Written Answers to Questions.
PROPOSED TOWNS PLANNING
SCHEME.
Mr. T. HENDERSON asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can tell
the House if a conference has taken place
between his Department and the Local
Authorities of Northern Ireland in relation to a Towns Planning Scheme, and,
if so, whether he can state the result of
that conference.
The MINISTER OF HOME AF-
FAIRS: The Ministry has been in communication with the Association of Municipalities on this matter, and various suggestions that have been put forward are
under consideration.
SANITARY CONVENIENCES IN
BELFAST.
Mr. T. HENDERSON asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he is aware
that hundreds of houses in Belfast have
still the old system of dry closets; and
whether he can state whether it is the intention of his Department to instruct the
Local Authority to make the owners of
these houses install a proper sanitary system.
The MINISTER OF HOME AF-
FAIRS: There are 282 houses out of a
total of 82,000 in the County Borough of
Belfast which have dry closets.
Almost all these houses are situate in
the semi-rural areas where no sewers are
available, and where it would not be
practicable to install water-closets.
I am assured that the Public Health
Department of the Corporation are watching this matter closely, and I do not see
any reason for interference on the part
of the Ministry.
UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT-
SANDWICH BOARD MEN.
Mr. T. HENDERSON asked the Minister of Labour whether he can state if it
is the intention of the Government to introduce legislation to prevent the exploitation of men who are compelled to seek
employment as sandwich board men as a
means of getting a living.
If I
The MINISTER OF LABOUR:
am furnished with particulars of the allegation I will be glad to look into the
matter.

postponed
PROROGATION.
Message from the Senate.
A Message was delivered by the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod as follows:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the Clerk's
place at the Table): I have to acquaint
the House that the House has this day
attended in the Senate, where His Grace
the Governor, on behalf of His Majesty
the King, delivered his Speech to both
Houses of Parliament as follows:
KING'S SPEECH.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I thank you for passing the legislative Measures which have been placed
on the Statute Book, and which were
foreshadowed in my Speech at the
opening of Parliament on 26th February
last. I note, however, it has been
found impracticable to deal with certain other matters therein referred to,
but these will be submitted for consideration in the new Session
Proclamation
End of Session
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Members of the House of Commons.
I thank you for the provision of supplies for the public services.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
In bidding you farewell, I pray that
the blessing of Almighty God may rest
upon your labours
After which the Proclamation proroguing Parliament was read as follows:
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR
OF NORTHERN IRELAND.

For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said
Act, that the Governor of Northern Ireland shall in His Majesty's name sumdissolve
prorogue and
Parliament of Northern Ireland:
mon,
the
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT ED-
WARD, Duke of Abercorn, Knight of the
Most Noble Order of the Garter, Knight
of the Most Illustrious Order of Saint
Patrick, Governor of Northern Ireland,
by this Proclamation do publish and declare His Majesty's Pleasure that the said
Parliament be, as from the reading of
this Proclamation in the Parliament of
Northern Ireland, prorogued to Thursday
the sixteenth day of May, one thousand
nine hundred and twenty-nine, to be
then holden.
Given at the Council Chamber, Belfast,
this twelfth day of April, One Thousand
Nine Hundred and Twenty-nine.
(Signed by his own hand),
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
